Innovation Ranking Criteria

Papers are ranked from most to least innovative by a composite score from 0 to 100. Each paper is scored on six dimensions: (1) novelty, (2) scientific rigor, (3) non-obviousness, (4) completeness, (5) resilience, and (6) practical impact. The composite is a weighted average of the six scores under one of three weight profiles (empirical, theoretical, or systems), chosen per paper. Each paper includes a justification explaining its placement.

≥90 Groundbreaking
≥75 Highly Innovative
≥60 Innovative
≥40 Moderately Innovative
≥20 Incremental
<20 Routine

#1 — Highly Innovative (82)

StrideWorld: Benchmarking Scene Rigidity and Action Consistency in Interactive Video World Model (12 ▲ )

Chuang Wang, Rui Nie, Jie Song, Junyuan Gao, Jiahe Song, Haitao Zhou, Boyu Zhu, Xing Li, Jiang Wu, Conghui He, Qian Yu, Weijia Li · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 19 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces StrideWorld, a benchmark that evaluates interactive video world models for scene rigidity against ground-truth start-view geometry and for action consistency against each model's own calibrated action strides, over 54,600 videos from 15 open models. - Why it's important: Existing world-model benchmarks fit their references (3D reconstructions, scale-aligned trajectories) to the very video under test, so gradual scene deformation and mid-route pace changes pass undetected — the paper shows a VGGT-based reprojection error separates only 3 of 15 deforming models while its offset separates all 15. - How it does it: The core trick is disjoint, pre-fixed references: 3D anchors lifted from ground-truth start-view depth are split into pose-fitting and held-out test sets (rigidity), and each action's per-step motion (stride) is calibrated on the model's first 4 steps in se(2) and then used to predict all later steps and composed-route endpoints (pace and composition), so no scale or reconstruction is ever fitted to the video being judged. - The good: Validation is unusually thorough — camera recovery on rendered videos with known motion is accurate to a median 1.5% translation / 0.3% rotation under degradations, controlled deformations of known amplitude are tracked linearly by the rigidity metric, and blinded human raters (n=10, Fleiss' κ 0.87) agree with the scores at AUC 0.88 (control), 0.83 (swap pairs), and 39/39 untied rigidity choices. - The missing: The protocol requires start-view surfaces to remain visible, restricting evaluation to short routes (8–14 steps) with modest motion and excluding long-horizon exploration, dynamic scenes, and full 6-DoF trajectories; closed-source leaders like Genie 3 get only a direction check via a web interface rather than the full stride-based protocol. - Read it or not: Anyone building, selecting, or benchmarking interactive video world models should read it — it both exposes a concrete failure mode (route composition) that current metrics miss and provides a reusable protocol — while readers outside world-model evaluation can skip it.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. This benchmark paper is the strongest in the cluster: Rigor (90) is exceptional for a benchmark — controlled perturbation injections, known-motion accuracy floors, 2,000-resample bootstrap intervals, a pre-registered human study (κ 0.87, AUC 0.88), exhaustive sensitivity sweeps, and a released code/data/leaderboard artifact. Novelty (80) rests on a genuine evaluation principle (fixed-before-motion references via disjoint anchor holdout and self-calibrated strides) rather than machinery, with the actionable finding that route composition, not pace or direction, is the dominant failure mode. Non-Obviousness (78) — showing that scale-fitted trajectory error and VGGT reprojection absorb exactly the failures StrideWorld detects. Completeness (80) and Resilience (80) benefit from direct, non-minimizing limitation disclosure; Practical Impact (78) reflects the reusable protocol. Weighted composite: 0.20*80 + 0.25*90 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*80 + 0.10*78 = 82.

Problem & Motivation: Interactive video world models (Genie 3, Matrix-Game, HY-World families, etc.) generate scenes that respond to user commands; for the output to function as a world rather than plausible frames, the scene must keep its 3D structure as the camera moves, and each command must have a stable, predictable effect. Existing evaluation falls into two traps: geometric benchmarks (WBench, WorldScore, WorldExam, MEt3R-style) reconstruct a reference from the generated frames themselves, and 3D foundation models can fit coherent geometry to inconsistent images, so gradual deformation is absorbed into the reference; control benchmarks align recovered trajectories to commanded ones with a free scale estimated from the trajectory under test, so a model whose step length drifts midway still matches the commanded path. Loop-closure tests avoid rescaling but assume opposite commands cancel — an assumption the paper empirically refutes (App. H.3). No prior benchmark tests geometry and action control against references fixed independently of the video under test. Key Idea: Judge every motion against a reference fixed before the motion happens: (1) rigidity is measured by whether held-out 3D anchors, placed at ground-truth depth of the start view and disjoint from the anchors used to fit each frame's camera, stay on their predicted viewing rays; (2) action consistency is measured in each model's own unit of motion — the stride, the camera motion of one command averaged over the first four steps — so the stride predicts every later step (pace) and chains into route endpoints (composition), removing the need for a shared motion unit across heterogeneous interfaces (keys, camera poses, text). Methodology: Three tests. (1) Rigidity: SIFT/Shi–Tomasi anchor pixels on the start view are lifted to 3D via ground-truth depth and intrinsics, split alternately into pose set P and held-out set Q; CoTracker3 tracks anchors into each generated frame; the camera is fit to P via EPnP+RANSAC with Levenberg–Marquardt refinement, and the Rigidity offset is the mean angular residual of Q's rays (median over route frames at 2°–8° image motion), compared against a rigid re-rendering of the true scene along the same recovered camera path. (2) Pace: per-action strides U_a are Lie-algebra means of the first four per-step SE(2) poses; the pace ratio compares observed displacement at step 16 to prediction; the Pace score maps endpoint relative error to 100/(1+r). (3) Composition: 1,120 routes per model in four designed pair families (cancel, three swap variants) whose two routes should end identically; each route is compared to its chained-stride prediction (position/heading errors in units of the model's own median strides), swap-pair routes are compared to each other, stalls are steps moving <10% of stride, and the Composition score averages s(r) over routes and pairs with incomplete routes scoring zero. Critical design decisions: disjoint pose/test anchors (well-justified — prevents deformation absorption); per-model/per-view/per-seed stride calibration (justified by the demonstrated 139× spread in per-step motion across models); rigid counterparts rendered per-model at matched codec/path (justified — establishes a per-model noise floor). The benchmark spans 140 start views (104 UE5 with dense depth, 36 ETH3D with laser-scan depth), 6 actions, 3 seeds for single actions, 15 models, 54,600 videos total. Key Results: All but one of 14 ranked models exceed their rigid counterpart's rigidity offset by 1.6×–7.3× with 95% bootstrap intervals entirely above 1.0; only Lyra 2.0 (which conditions on an explicit 3D cache) collapses toward 1.0 when anchor depths are freed, indicating fixed depth error rather than deformation. Twelve of 14 models hold a steady pace (median ratio in 0.8–1.25); DreamX-World (2.11) and AlayaWorld (4.17, unranked) accelerate. Composition is where models fail: only HY-World 2.0 (Near 84.3%) and Lyra 2.0 (75.9%) — both scaling commands by estimated scene depth — bring most routes within one stride; most others do so for under a quarter (EVOKE 3.1%, H3-World 0.2%). Stalls affect >36% of routes in four models (HY-World 1.5 54%, Matrix-Game 3.5 47%). End errors are systematic: median route end error is 1.8–3.7× the across-seed spread of route ends. Scale-fitted trajectory error flags only 43% of held videos whose pace grows 1.5×, versus 94% for the Pace test at matched 5% false-alarm rate; direction accuracy correlates 0.02 with Composition score. Fine-tuning LoRA adapters on 112 rendered Blender clips reduces stalled routes from 72.0% to 11.2% (HY-World 1.5) and 57.9% to 23.1% (SANA-WM), more than doubles both Composition scores, and preserves MUSIQ quality. Baselines compared include WorldScore-style fitted trajectory errors, direction checks, VGGT reprojection, and Sim(3)-aligned ATE — all shown insensitive to the failures StrideWorld detects. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the fixed-before-motion reference principle — disjoint ground-truth-depth anchor holdout for rigidity, and self-calibrated per-model strides as the unit for pace and open-route composition with designed route pairs — plus the benchmark-scale finding that route composition, not pace or direction, is the dominant failure mode and that depth-scaled command interfaces compose best. The underlying machinery (point tracking, PnP, Lie-group averaging, LoRA fine-tuning) is a competent combination of standard techniques in a new evaluation setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Exceptional for a benchmark paper. Ablations cover stride estimators (K4/M4/M2–5), calibration lengths (2/4/6/8 steps), stall thresholds, anchor sets (P/P1/P2/Q), response thresholds, command magnitudes (0.5×/1×/2× for three models), and matched-camera-motion route subsets — with rank correlations ≥0.95–0.98 throughout. Uncertainty is quantified via 2,000-resample scene-bootstrap 95% intervals; three-seed regeneration isolates systematic from stochastic error. Measurement validity is established on known camera motion (median 1.48% translation error) and controlled injections of deformation, pace change, carry-over, and stalls, where stride-based metrics respond and existing metrics do not. Human agreement: 10 blinded raters, pre-registered analysis, Fleiss' κ 0.87/0.83/0.86, AUC 0.88 vs. 0.53–0.71 for competing scores. Code, data, and a leaderboard are released at https://github.com/chuangwang123/strideworld. Concerns: camera recovery is only demonstrated where start-view surfaces stay visible (the authors tune command magnitudes to enforce this for some models, e.g., halving SolarWM's default translation); the fine-tuning study uses only two non-distilled models; several evaluated models are concurrent preprints, so results on them are provisional. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark plus measurement study, with a small fine-tuning experiment). - Practical: Runs on standard hardware — generation uses each model's released inference configuration and evaluation is CPU/GPU tracking plus geometric fitting; no exotic compute is required to use the benchmark. - Efficient: 3,640 videos per model is substantial but bounded; stride calibration adds 24 single-action videos per view before scoring routes, and the protocol cannot be applied to models that move start-view content out of frame quickly (e.g., unmodified default turn commands were rescaled for four models). - Effective: The evidence shows the metrics detect exactly the failures they target on controlled injections and correlate with human judgment, so it measures scene rigidity and action consistency as defined; whether these proxy long-horizon world-model usability is not tested by design. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 8–14-step routes and ≤16-step holds; the authors themselves state extending to dynamic scenes, 6-DoF, and long-horizon exploration is future work, so behavior at 10× the horizon is unmeasured and likely requires a different mechanism than start-view anchor visibility. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: code, data (30 scenes, 140 views with depth), adapters for 15 models, and a public leaderboard. Strengths: - The disjoint-anchor rigidity test is a clean methodological contribution: it sidesteps the reference-fitting failure of reconstruction-based metrics with a directly verifiable demonstration (VGGT reprojection separates only 3/15 models; texture drift and blur raise it as much as deformation). - The stride formalism solves a real measurement problem — heterogeneous interfaces with a 139× spread in per-step motion — without imposing a shared unit, and the designed route pairs (cancel/swap) turn composition into a falsifiable, model-relative prediction rather than an absolute trajectory match. - The empirical findings are actionable: rigidity and composition rankings are uncorrelated (ρ ≈ −0.01), depth-scaled command interfaces dominate composition, and 112 fine-tuning clips fix most stalls — a complete measure-then-fix arc. - Validation discipline is well above norm: known-motion accuracy floors, controlled perturbation response curves, sensitivity sweeps, scene-bootstrap intervals, and a pre-registered human study with κ and AUC comparisons against alternative scores. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper states the benchmark's scope directly (App. M, App. A): sequences are short (8–14 step routes, ≤16-step holds) so that start-view surfaces remain trackable, excluding long-horizon exploration, revisits, and loop closures; only static scenes are covered (dynamic scenes and full 6-DoF trajectories are named as next steps); AlayaWorld's stride is unmeasurable and it is left unranked; Genie 3 and GameCraft receive only directional tests due to interface constraints; the fine-tuning study is limited to two non-distilled models and rendered training data (though it transfers to real ETH3D views). The authors confront these honestly rather than minimize them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The rigidity metric depends on CoTracker3's tracks; tracking failure on heavily deformed or low-resolution output could bias offsets, and while degradation tests cover blur/compression/flicker, no test establishes tracker behavior on the most deformed generated content itself. - Several models require author-chosen command magnitudes (e.g., SolarWM at half its default translation, AlayaWorld scaled up), which is a defensible but non-blind intervention that could interact with model performance in unquantified ways beyond the 0.5×/1×/2× check on three models. - The fine-tuning result uses only 112 clips and two models, with no test of whether gains transfer to other architectures or to training at scale; the perturbed-step-length control is a good start but the claim that rendered clips suffice rests on one architecture family. - Evaluation is dominated by synthetic UE5 scenes (104 of 140 views); the 36 ETH3D views use sparse laser-scan depth, so anchor density and rigidity measurement may differ systematically across domains (domain-split results are reported, but depth-source confounds are not fully disentangled). - Route endpoints are evaluated against stride predictions in SE(2) (planar), so vertical motion and pitch effects on composition are outside the headline metrics; models with significant roll or elevation errors in composition are not penalized by the main score. Bottom Line: This is the most methodologically careful benchmark for interactive video world models published to date and the first to catch deformation and composition failures that reconstruction- and scale-fitting metrics absorb, so any practitioner training, selecting, or deploying these models should adopt it — the only reason to look elsewhere is if you specifically need long-horizon, dynamic-scene, or 6-DoF evaluation, which StrideWorld deliberately excludes.

#2 — Highly Innovative (80)

Harness Matters: Measuring and Dissecting Security Resilience in Web Agents

X Wu, J Chen, JY Dong, G Hong, X Pan, J Dai, M Liu… · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WebTrapFarm, an evaluation framework of 505 attack tasks with paired usability-calibration tasks that measures how web-agent execution harnesses (not just backend LLMs) shape security, and localizes where defensive behavior emerges across a four-stage agent workflow. - Why it's important: Deployed web agents execute real transactions on untrusted webpages, and prior security evaluations conflate successful defense with simple task incapability, systematically overestimating robustness and misattributing failures to the model rather than the system design. - How it does it: The core move is pairing every attack task with a usability task that preserves the interaction but removes the adversarial trigger — an attack failure counts as defense only if the agent can complete the same interaction benignly — plus harness-agnostic JavaScript instrumentation of task webpages for outcome measurement. - The good: A mixed-effects logistic regression over 6 harnesses × 7 backend models shows harness, model, and their interaction all significantly affect security outcomes (all p < 10⁻⁴⁵), robust to sensitivity analyses — direct statistical evidence that the harness is a first-class security factor. - The missing: Several harness-component conclusions (textual vs. multimodal perception, single- vs. multi-role planning, rule- vs. LLM-based grounding) rest on observational cross-harness differences rather than controlled ablations, and the paper's own appended meta-review flags this confound. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate web agents or agent-security benchmarks; skip it if you only care about prompt-injection attacks on chat models, since the framework's value is its measurement methodology, not new attacks.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. This is the most rigorous measurement treatment of agent security in the cluster: the paired-usability calibration that separates defense success from capability failure is a genuine methodological contribution (Novelty 80 — new benchmark plus new formulation), and the GLMM attribution (harness, model, interaction all p < 10⁻⁴⁵) plus the naive-attack result give high Non-Obviousness (80). Rigor (85) is anchored by LLM-judge validation at 99.55% agreement, κ = 0.96 annotator validation, three full-benchmark repetitions, and sensitivity analyses surviving adversarial relabeling; deductions for observational-only support on half the harness-component taxonomy and ablations restricted to one backend and 100-task samples. Completeness (80) and Resilience (78) benefit from a limitations section that confronts the meta-review's own criticisms rather than suppressing them. Impact (70) reflects a reusable framework and benchmark artifact, tempered by a possibly corrupted repo reference. Weighted composite: 0.20*80 + 0.25*85 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*78 + 0.10*70 = 80.

Problem & Motivation: Web agents (LLM/LMM-driven browser-automation systems) are exposed to three attack surfaces: malicious user prompts, webpage prompt injection, and deceptive interface design. Prior benchmarks (BrowserART, SafeArena, WASP, EIA, AgentBait) each cover a fragment of this space, are coupled to specific agent harnesses, and — most critically — label any attack failure as a security success, even when the agent simply lacked the capability to complete the interaction. Practitioners deploying agents therefore cannot tell whether their system is secure or merely incompetent, and cannot attribute observed vulnerability to the backend model versus the surrounding harness (goal interpretation, webpage perception, planning, action grounding). Key Idea: Treat the harness as a measurable security boundary by (i) abstracting all web agents into a four-stage workflow (goal interpretation → webpage perception → reasoning/planning → action execution) with categorical component choices per stage, (ii) calibrating every attack with a paired usability task so defense success and capability failure are statistically separable, and (iii) localizing defense in execution traces via safe/unsafe state-transition analysis, yielding a Conditional DSR per workflow stage. The usability calibration is the load-bearing trick: it changes the denominator of security metrics to exclude capability failures. Methodology: The framework has three phases. (1) Dataset construction: 505 attack tasks organized along attack goal × method × content — 160 Malicious User Prompts (adapted from BrowserART), 158 Malicious Prompt Injections (adapted from EIA; injection sites include visible/invisible form text, ARIA attributes, URLs, long context), and 187 Deceptive Website Design tasks (adapted from AgentBait; pop-ups, ads, leading/trailing form fields, default selections) — each with a paired usability task that strips the adversarial trigger. Only attack methods validated in ≥2 independent prior works are included; a "naive" content type with no explicit attack text serves as a harness-intrinsic-vulnerability baseline. (2) Execution monitoring: JavaScript instrumentation of task webpages records clicks, form submissions, downloads, and permission grants, sent to a backend server — deliberately bypassing agent-side logs so closed-source commercial agents can be evaluated identically. (3) Scoring: rule-based outcome checks for structured interactions; GPT-4o LLM-as-judge for open-ended Malicious User Prompt outputs (validated at 99.55% agreement with human consensus on a 672/6,720 sample; inter-annotator agreement 99.26%). Outcome labeling classifies each attack task as Attack Success, Defense Success, or Capability Failure, yielding ASR, DSR, and TCR metrics with capability failures excluded from ASR/DSR denominators. Defense localization annotates each stage per interaction round as safe/unsafe (GPT-4o annotation validated at κ = 0.96, 98.67% match), then applies surface-specific rules: first safe state for user-side attacks, last unsafe-to-safe transition for web-side attacks. Statistical attribution uses a GLMM with harness, model, their interaction, and attack category as fixed effects and task as random intercept. Critical design decisions: the paired-usability calibration (well-justified and validated via sensitivity analyses on extreme relabelings); webpage-side rather than agent-side monitoring (well-justified for cross-harness fairness, but loses reasoning-trace visibility for open-source agents — they recover it via optional logging); and temperature-0 decoding with three full benchmark repetitions (measured std 1.73 pp) rather than per-task seeds (moderate justification; no per-task confidence intervals). Key Results: Across 6 open-source harnesses (SeeAct, Browser Use text/vision, Agent-E, Skyvern 1.0/2.0) × 7 backends (GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, Claude-Opus-4.5, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Qwen3-VL-30B/235B), the overall ASR is 32.55%, ranging from 20.24% (Agent-E) to 42.31% (SeeAct). The two commercial systems fare better but remain vulnerable: Gemini Computer Use 15.14% and Claude Computer Use 16.85% overall ASR, with 25.51% and 22.12% respectively under deceptive web design. Harness effect under a fixed backend is large: with GPT-4o, Agent-E reaches 83.79% DSR versus Skyvern 2.0's 42.89% — a 40.90-point gap. The GLMM finds harness (χ² = 331.17), model (χ² = 437.63), and interaction (χ² = 299.81) all significant at p < 10⁻⁴⁵. Two findings are counter-intuitive: (1) naive attacks with no explicit adversarial content achieve ASRs comparable to or exceeding explicit attacks (e.g., SeeAct 50.00% naive vs. 49.37% non-naive under MPI), indicating harness-intrinsic vulnerability; (2) capability and security decouple — Skyvern 2.0 has the highest TCR (85.25%) but near-lowest DSR (58.01%), while Agent-E has the highest DSR (79.76%) with TCR of only 61.33%. Ablations (100 tasks each, GPT-4o fixed) quantify four mechanisms: degrading Agent-E's intent-interpretation prompt cuts Stage I Conditional DSR by 21.76 points; removing risk-awareness cues from reasoning prompts costs 30.43 points (Browser Use Vision) and 23.09 points (Agent-E) at Stage III; relaxing Agent-E's perception filtering costs 6.24 points at Stage II; removing/adding goal-anchoring in planning swings Skyvern 1.0 (−16.68) and Agent-E (+24.24) at Stage III. Rule-based action grounding shows 0.00% Conditional DSR at Stage IV in all configurations. Model safety does not transfer across surfaces: Claude-Opus-4.5 resists malicious user prompts (3.25% ASR) but hits 36.03% under prompt injection, and its 77.10% average DSR drops to 75.19% inside Agent-E — below GPT-4o's 83.79% in the same harness. Baselines are current (2025–2026 frontier models and popular open-source harnesses); the scale is a controlled benchmark of 505 tasks, not live web deployment. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a NEW FORMULATION component (usability-calibrated ASR/DSR/TCR metrics and stage-localized Conditional DSR). The genuinely novel contributions are the paired-usability calibration that separates defense from incapability, the harness-independent webpage-side monitoring protocol, and the first quantitative (GLMM) attribution of web-agent security to harness versus model. The individual attack techniques are all drawn from validated prior work by design; the four-stage harness taxonomy is a competent synthesis of 40 papers and 68 GitHub projects rather than a new architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist but only for four mechanisms (intent interpretation, risk-aware reasoning cues, perception filtering, goal anchoring); component-category conclusions (encoder type, planner structure, grounding type) are observational correlations across harnesses, not ablations — the paper's appended S&P meta-review explicitly notes this. Reliability is well-supported: three full-benchmark repetitions (std 1.73 pp), human validation of both the LLM judge (99.55% on 672 outputs) and the stage-state annotator (κ = 0.96 on 300 instances), plus sensitivity analyses modeling capability-dependent missingness and extreme relabelings (all effects remain p < 10⁻³⁹). No per-task error bars or significance tests on individual harness comparisons are reported. Code is referenced at a GitHub repository (github.com/Agrfeblve/WebTrapFarm), though the URL as printed appears possibly corrupted; dataset construction reuses webpages from prior public datasets (BrowserART, EIA, AgentBait). Methodological concerns: the authors' own prior work (AgentBait, reference 11) is one of the three adapted sources; ablations use only 100 sampled tasks per surface with a single backend (GPT-4o); the ablation that swaps Agent-E's interpreter prompt for Skyvern 2.0's confounds prompt detail with other implementation differences. Commercial-system results are measured, not vendor-reported, which strengthens credibility. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement framework and benchmark evaluated experimentally; the framework itself is a reusable tool). - Practical: Yes — runs on standard LLM APIs and open-source browser-automation harnesses; webpage instrumentation is lightweight JavaScript requiring no special infrastructure. - Efficient: Evaluation cost is dominated by agent LLM inference across 505 attack tasks plus paired usability tasks (roughly 2× task executions); the monitoring layer itself adds negligible overhead, and ablations were deliberately limited to 100 tasks each to control cost. - Effective: The evidence shows the framework correctly measures the stated construct — defense versus capability failure — with the GLMM and ablation results confirming that harness design, not just the model, drives security outcomes; however, it measures security on simulated websites, a proxy for real deployment. - Scalable: Not tested beyond the current 505 tasks and 8 agent systems; extensibility to new attacks is claimed via the paired-task template but demonstrated only through adaptation of three existing datasets. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (the WebTrapFarm framework and benchmark, with a public repository reference) plus a reusable measurement methodology (paired usability calibration, stage-localized Conditional DSR, GLMM attribution design). Strengths: - The usability-calibration design is a genuine methodological contribution: it fixes a real, quantifiable bias in prior web-agent security evaluation (counting incapability as defense) and the paper backs it with sensitivity analyses showing conclusions survive adversarial relabeling. - The GLMM attribution (harness, model, interaction all p < 10⁻⁴⁵; 40.90-point DSR gap under a fixed GPT-4o backend) converts an intuition — "the harness matters" — into quantitative evidence with properly modeled repeated measures. - The naive-attack result (unsafe execution without any adversarial content, sometimes exceeding explicit-attack ASR) is a non-obvious empirical finding with direct deployment implications: harness execution logic can be the vulnerability itself. - The stage-localization analysis with conditional metrics, validated annotators (κ = 0.96), and targeted ablations yields actionable, mechanism-level guidance (intent interpretation, perception filtering, goal anchoring) rather than just leaderboard numbers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three limitations directly: coverage restricted to three attack categories (excluding e.g. malicious tools, though the framework is claimed extensible); evaluation in controlled web environments rather than real-world dynamic sites; and execution randomness, mitigated by dataset size, fixed parameters, and repeated runs. They confront these honestly and do not minimize; the appended S&P meta-review additionally records the benchmark-staleness concern (static attacks age) and the observational basis of some component conclusions, which the authors include rather than suppress — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The ablation set covers only four of the eight harness components in the paper's own taxonomy; encoder type, planner structure, and grounding type — half the design space — are supported only by cross-harness correlation, which is confounded by every other difference between harnesses. - All ablations use a single backend (GPT-4o) and 100-task samples; the mechanism conclusions are not verified to hold under stronger or more safety-aligned models (e.g., Claude-Opus-4.5), where the paper itself shows different security profiles. - The "naive attack" baseline has no corresponding usability-task analysis reported, so the boundary between harness-intrinsic vulnerability and capability pressure on naive tasks is asserted from log inspection rather than measured with the paper's own calibration machinery. - Only two commercial agents are evaluated, with default (non-swappable) models, limiting the generalization of the commercial-vs-open-source security gap. - Defense localization patterns are extracted from 100 manually inspected defense-success logs per agent and annotated by GPT-4o; prompt-induced annotation bias toward the taxonomy's own pattern definitions cannot be ruled out, and the last-unsafe-to-safe-transition heuristic for web-side attacks is justified by argument rather than validated against ground truth on multi-round traces. - No live-web or adversarially adaptive evaluation: an attacker who knows the harness (e.g., targets Agent-E's perception filter specifically) is not studied. Bottom Line: For anyone building, deploying, or benchmarking web agents, this is worth reading — the usability-calibration methodology and the harness-vs-model attribution are the most rigorous treatment of agent security measurement to date, and its prescriptions (filter perception, anchor planning to user intent, don't rely on prompt-level safety) are immediately actionable; researchers seeking new attacks or adaptive adversaries will find nothing beyond a well-constructed measurement instrument.

V-JEPA-LM: Video-Language Models That Read Dynamics Beyond Static, Text-Aligned Representations (22 ▲ )

Keuntae Kim, Dongjun Kim, Yong Suk Choi · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 16 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds V-JEPA-LM, a family of 1B–8B video LLMs on a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder that are trained with counterfactual supervision — pixel-transformed video pairs whose answers are set by the transformation — and shows the 4B model scores 72.14 on a 12-score average over eleven video benchmarks versus 61.08 for the best open 4B model, using 4.53M samples in a single stage. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or train video LLMs or study representation geometry — the analysis of where dynamics lives in frozen encoders and the cheap counterfactual data recipe are directly reusable; skip it if you need long-video or knowledge-heavy QA results, which the paper explicitly does not target.

Problem & Motivation: Video LLM practitioners face a paradox: encoders that learn physics from video alone (V-JEPA family) are turned into VLMs with the standard image-text recipe of alignment, pre-training and instruction tuning on captions and QA pairs. Because each caption or question names only a few attributes and most items are answerable from one frame, the language model learns to retrieve named attributes rather than read the clip's dynamics — Meta's own controlled comparison shows the improved V-JEPA 2.1 encoder lowers TemporalBench and TOMATO scores under the same recipe. Only the encoders of these models are released, so how a language model can actually read what a predictive encoder knows is an open problem. The gap this paper closes: prior temporal training signals (arrow-of-time, temporal preferences, perturbed-clip negatives) use one or a few transformations and are not chosen based on measured encoder structure, and none demonstrate that supervision — not encoder scale — is the bottleneck. Key Idea: The single insight: for predictive spatiotemporal encoders like V-JEPA, the effect of a dynamics transformation (reversal, re-timing) on token content is a change component d that is shared in direction across videos (cross-video consistency κ 20–100× higher than in frame-wise text-aligned encoders like SigLIP), so a language model can learn to read it from a handful of counterfactual pairs; and a pair loss on a clip and its transformed copy — where the answer differs by construction — has a gradient whose content term cancels at equal margins (Proposition 3), so the readout is driven to depend on the change alone. The supervision design is therefore derived from a measured property of the frozen encoder rather than guessed. Methodology: Three phases. (1) Encoder analysis: for transformations T with answer map πT and token permutation ΠT, decompose aligned tokens into content c = ½(z(v)+z(Tv)) and change d = ½(z(v)−z(Tv)); measure relative change size (rd), cross-video consistency (κ), content overlap (ρ), 8-pair prototype accuracy, and linear probes on 1,200 SSv2 clips for SigLIP so400m, ViCLIP, VideoMAE, and V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L/ViT-g. Propositions 1–5 (with proofs) predict which transformations yield a shared, content-free component per encoder family. (2) Data generation: a generator renders fourteen constructions in six families (sign flip, order, position, magnitude, count, stop/cut) from 33 public sources (509k rows, 6.11% of the mixture) at training time, balancing answer letters, option-length rank, and text-prior, with no new annotation or LLM in the loop; a label audit checks apparent motion against speed labels on 300 rows per source (100% agreement on faster/slower rows). (3) Training: frozen V-JEPA encoder (32 frames) → spectral bridge (fixed PCA rotation/rescaling then trainable MLP) to 1,024 tokens per clip → full fine-tuning of Qwen3 or Llama (1B–8B) in a single stage on 4.53M rows from 175 sources, 499 H100-hours for the 4B model. Critical design decisions: frozen encoder with a compact bridge (justified by inference-cost analysis and matched comparisons), answer-balanced constructions over explicit pairs (ablated: pairing mainly improves cross-pair consistency, 96.7 vs 84.4), and choice of transformations guided by measured κ (validated: speed and sign-flip gains track κ; order gains are equal across encoders as predicted). Key Results: On a 12-score average over eleven benchmarks (MVBench, PerceptionTest, TVBench, TempCompass, TOMATO, MotionBench, NExT-QA, MVP, TemporalBench, SSv2, Vinoground text/video), all evaluated by the authors under one protocol (32 frames, option-letter scoring): V-JEPA-LM-4B scores 72.14 vs 61.08 (Molmo2-4B), 2B scores 66.02 vs 52.45 (Qwen3-VL-2B), 8B-Q 70.11 vs 64.79 (PLM-8B); the Llama variants lead similarly. Largest margins are on dynamics: TOMATO 53.5 vs 36.5 (4B class), Vinoground video 66.8 vs 33.8. Against Meta's unreleased V-JEPA video LLMs (numbers quoted from their papers), the 8B models lead by 6.7 and 4.9 points on six shared benchmarks with roughly 1/20 the training data. The controlled 2×2 study: counterfactual rows add +4.5 (V-JEPA) and +3.3/+3.6 (SigLIP) average points at matched budget and +38.1 on speed ability for V-JEPA at the final step, while an arrow-of-time-only arm (95.9% on its own target) changes nothing (−0.4) and annotation-based temporal QA gives +1.6 — isolating the counterfactual construction as the active ingredient. Six held-out sets (unseen speed ratios 1.6/2.5/4.0, unseen corpora, unseen combinations, unseen simulator) score 94.5–96.3 vs 43.5–55.5 for open models; successive playback (a construction never trained) scores 92.5–99.2 vs 19.4–51.9. Open-model baselines are current (Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, PLM, Molmo2, VideoLLaMA3, Apollo, all 2025–2026), evaluated by the authors rather than copied, with 40 of 51 self-reported scores reproduced within 3 points (median difference 1.3). Notably weak for the method: NExT-QA and PerceptionTest still favor data-heavier open models, and general knowledge is unchanged by counterfactual data. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (counterfactual supervision chosen by measured encoder structure, applied to a frozen predictive encoder) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (dynamics is present in frozen V-JEPA features but unread by caption/QA-trained VLMs; the encoder decides what can be read, the supervision what is read) + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (released 1B–8B model family and extensible data generator). The pixel-transformation pretext idea itself is old (arrow-of-time, speed prediction, order shuffling in self-supervised video learning), and answer-balanced temporal instructions exist (TIME); the genuinely new parts are grounding the transformation choice in a measured shared-change subspace (κ, ρ), the pair-loss content-cancellation argument with proofs, the fourteen-family generator requiring no annotation, and the controlled encoder × supervision attribution. This is a substantial but incremental-over-pretext-work synthesis executed at an unusually rigorous standard. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: 2×2 encoder × supervision with matched mixture and schedule, arrow-of-time and temporal-QA controls at matched weight, a 4B no-CF control, explicit-pairs vs unpaired ablation, subspace-removal interventions with energy-matched random and content-PC controls, and a single-frame control showing held-out sets are not solvable from layout (scores drop to ~37.6 vs chance 33.3). Uncertainty: 95% paired bootstrap intervals on ability gains and ±0.7 on 12-score averages; probes use 5-fold grouped CV with 4 seeds (s.d. ≤1.8). However, each headline model is trained exactly once — no seed variance on the main results. A train–evaluation audit matched video identifiers across all 175 training sources and 35,488 evaluation items, finding 0.41% overlap with ≤0.42-point effect when removed — a level of audit few video LLM papers report. Weights, inference code and model cards are released (GitHub: kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM; Hugging Face collection); training code, the data generator and manifests are only promised to "follow." Concerns: Meta V-JEPA video LLM comparisons quote self-reported numbers from papers under different settings (models unreleased); the 12-score benchmark suite itself was assembled by the authors; the SSv2 benchmark draws on the same clip distribution as several counterfactual sources (mitigated by the reported without-SSv2/Vinoground result, 70.1 vs 66.0); held-out sets reuse the training generator's question wordings and option pools. This is a preprint (arXiv 2611.17831, Nov 2026), not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a strong SYSTEMS artifact — six released models). Practical: Runs on H100s at inference (first token 70–182 ms per clip); the frozen-encoder design means no encoder training. Efficient: 1,024 visual tokens per clip regardless of resolution gives 2–18× fewer language-model prefill FLOPs than open models with 8,192 tokens; training cost 229–648 H100-hours per model, 2–38× less data than open competitors — but V-JEPA's joint spatiotemporal attention costs 13.9–37.8 TFLOPs per clip and is slower than frame-wise encoders at 480p for small models. Effective: Strong causal evidence it solves the targeted dynamics problem (held-out constructions, interventions), but it does not solve knowledge-heavy QA (NExT-QA, PerceptionTest remain below PLM/Molmo2) or single-image/text tasks, which the authors concede. Scalable: Only tested to 8B and 4.5M samples; the authors explicitly state scaling to general-purpose VLM scale is outside the study's resources, so 10–100× behavior is claimed-by-indication (counterfactual data is cheap to generate), not measured. Delivers a concrete software artifact (six trained model checkpoints, inference code) plus a reusable measurement-and-analysis technique (κ/ρ encoder profiling) that outlives the specific models. Strengths: - The claim–evidence chain is unusually tight: the paper measures where dynamics lives (κ, ρ across four encoders), predicts from that measurement which constructions should help which encoder, and then confirms the prediction in a matched 2×2 experiment — theory (Propositions 1–5 with honest scope statements, e.g., speed is not covered by Proposition 2 and rests on measured κ alone) and experiment reinforce each other. - The causal subspace-removal intervention (speed directions → 98.9→65.7 on unseen speed vs 97.2 for energy-matched random; content benchmarks barely move) moves the paper beyond correlational probing. - The counterfactual generator is a real practical contribution: any public video collection becomes labeled temporal training data from a short script, with no manual annotation and no LLM, plus automatic balancing of answer letters, option length, and text-only priors — attacking the shortcut-learning problem at the data-construction level. - Evaluation hygiene exceeds field norms: one protocol for all models, item-level train–eval video audit (0.41% overlap, bounded effect), reproduced-vs-reported check across 51 scores, and matched-sample-count comparisons. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: 32-frame short-clip scope only, with hour-long video (needing memory and long-context data) deferred as future work; no image QA or text recognition because V-JEPA never aligned to text, which is why open models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks (NExT-QA, PerceptionTest); training limited to one run per model at ≤650 H100-hours, with general-purpose VLM scale (hundreds of millions of samples) explicitly outside the study's purpose and resources. These are confronted directly in a dedicated scope section rather than minimized — a credibility positive. They also candidly report where the theory does not apply (speed in Proposition 2, position-dependent readouts, the SigLIP normalized-embedding case falling back to measurement). Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limits: (1) no proprietary baselines (Gemini, GPT-class models) — the claim "leads every size class" holds only within the open-weights pool the authors evaluated; (2) single training runs mean the 4.5-point counterfactual effect, while consistent across checkpoints and sizes, carries no seed-level uncertainty on the headline averages; (3) the counterfactual questions are template-generated with balanced priors, so the models may inherit a distribution of question styles narrower than natural video QA — the TOMATO/TempCompass gains partially answer this, but free-form generation quality (as opposed to option-letter scoring) is never evaluated, and no open-ended captioning or description metric appears anywhere; (4) SSv2's 92.2 (vs 57–68 for open models) sits adjacent to a heavily-mined training source, and although the without-SSv2 result is reported, a per-benchmark contamination-adjacent sensitivity analysis beyond the three flagged sets is absent; (5) the physical-plausibility construction (66k rows, the largest single source) comes from a simulator, and transfer from synthetic impossible-event supervision to real-world physics reasoning is not separately tested; (6) the bridge's fixed PCA whitening is computed from training-mix statistics — a minor but unexamined train-time dependency. None of these undermine the core result, but the "best video LLM" framing should be read as "best measured open model under this protocol on this suite." Bottom Line: For anyone training video LLMs or studying what world-model encoders actually represent, this is worth reading in full — the encoder measurement methodology and the annotation-free counterfactual generator are immediately reusable, and the controlled attribution of gains to supervision versus encoder is more convincing than most temporal-fine-tuning papers in this line, even accounting for the preprint status, self-assembled benchmark suite, and open-weights-only comparisons.

#4 — Highly Innovative (80)

When Copying Is Hard to Beat: A Negative Result in Clinical Assessment Forecasting

M Fracarolli, S Riezler · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper reports a negative result showing that supervised GRU encoders, baseline-gated predictors, and pretrained time-series forecasters (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, MIRA) fail to consistently beat persistence-based copying when forecasting next-day values of 45 recorded ICU assessment items across 29,715 day-pairs from 2,789 encounters. - Why it's important: Clinical forecasting evaluations routinely ignore that the strongest baseline is part of the data-generating process itself — the tablet interface pre-fills yesterday's answers — so reported ML gains may reflect nothing more than documentation persistence that simple copying already captures for free. - How it does it: The authors evaluate a logit-space gated model whose baseline path (persistence or a one-line organ-acuity rule) is a parameter-free special case, and exhaustively vary three evaluation choices — physiology input cutoff, observation mask (filled vs. explicitly entered cells), and decoding rule — under patient-disjoint splits with paired patient-clustered bootstrap intervals. - The good: The best gated model's headline macro-F1 gain of +0.0019 [+0.0006, +0.0031] over the clinical rule vanishes under either an honest input cutoff (+0.0001 [−0.0006, +0.0008]) or an explicit-cell mask (0.0000), while its accuracy loss of −0.0022 is stable across all five settings — a meticulously documented demonstration that the conclusion is an artifact of evaluation conventions. - The missing: The study is single-center, uses only GRU-scale models (no modern sequence architectures on the physiology stream), and the data cannot separate documentation persistence from genuine clinical stability — so the negative result may not transfer to other instruments, institutions, or model classes. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on clinical time-series prediction or benchmark evaluation, because it is a model case study in how input cutoffs, observation masks, and decoding rules manufacture or destroy apparent progress; skip it if you need a positive forecasting method — it deliberately delivers none.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (80) are driven by the genuinely surprising framing that persistence is part of the data-generating process (the tablet pre-fills prior answers) and the quantified demonstration that scoring conventions alone induce a 0.41 macro-F1 swing — a finding that reshapes how clinical assessment forecasting must be evaluated. Completeness (85) is a standout: limitations are confronted directly and at length, with sensitivity analyses on the load-bearing label correction. Resilience (78) is strong because claims are carefully bounded (no unpredictability or equivalence claims), though the GRU-only hypothesis class and single-center scope limit generalization; Practical Impact (68) reflects a released evaluation harness likely to change practitioner behavior despite no dataset release. Problem & Motivation: The problem is next-day forecasting of 45 recorded clinical assessment items (diagnostic judgments, infection localizations, organ dysfunction fields) on a surgical ICU, where the target labels come from a structured questionnaire completed daily by attending physicians. The domain gap the paper closes is methodological: prior work (including the authors' own earlier version, which it corrects) evaluated forecasters against weak baselines on an encounter-based split that leaked 24 patients across folds, with a physiology window that overlapped the interval the target form assessed, and with 68.5% of scored cells materialized from conditional parent answers rather than clinician entries. Anyone building predictive models on recorded clinical assessments has this problem: labels whose stability partly reflects how they are collected (the tablet displays the physician's prior entries) are trivially forecast by copying, and evaluations that inherit preprocessing defaults can credit models for reproducing the recording process rather than anticipating clinical change. Key Idea: The core insight is that persistence is not merely a statistical baseline but a component of the recording process, so any honest evaluation must make the baseline a selectable special case of the model (via a parameter-free gated logit path), vary the task definition along the three axes that determine it (input cutoff, observation mask, decoding rule), and attribute conclusions only to contrasts that survive these variations. A secondary insight is the accuracy decomposition (Eq. 2: Acc − Acc_pers = r·Acc∆ − (1−r)·FCR), which makes explicit that with 3.81% cell-change prevalence, gains on changed cells must outweigh false changes on the 96% stable ones — quantifying why beating copying is structurally hard. Methodology: The pipeline: (1) cohort construction from 585,791 item entries / 3,736 ICU encounters / 39,148 questionnaire days, retaining 29,715 consecutive day-pairs requiring ≥4 completed items on both days; (2) patient-disjoint splitting (18,688/4,708/6,319 day-pairs; 1,724/431/539 patients; zero overlap), correcting the earlier encounter-based split; (3) baseline fitting — persistence (copy day D), a one-line organ-acuity rule (new→acute), and a per-item first-order transition matrix shown by enumeration to contain exactly the rule's eight redirections; (4) supervised GRU encoders over 24h of 107 hourly clinical variables with concatenation fusion and item-wise cross-entropy heads, including a gated variant mixing model logits z_j(x) with baseline logits b_j(y_D) via a learned per-item gate γ_j(x) ∈ [0,1] (Eq. 1); (5) zero-shot and fine-tuned evaluation of Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, and an open MIRA checkpoint under the same harness; (6) single-pass test evaluation with five seeds (means 42/123/456/789/1337), 2,000-resample paired patient-clustered bootstrap, and a categorical read-out control mapping forecast quantiles to classes via per-item multinomial regression. Critical design decisions: (a) the gate's baseline path carries no parameters, so γ≡0 reproduces the baseline exactly — well justified, making the baseline an inductive bias rather than an external competitor; (b) an authorized label correction (27 new→new organ-acuity cells rewritten to acute) is load-bearing for the rule's zero false-change rate, and the authors honestly report the full sensitivity with all rows retrained on raw labels; (c) hyperparameter selection inherits configurations from an earlier exploratory search on a leaked split — acknowledged as not preregistered, a moderate weakness. Key Results: Persistence attains 0.9619 accuracy / 0.8705 item-macro-F1 on 281,952 test cells (3.81% changing); the rule reaches 0.9632/0.8711 and the transition matrix 0.9634/0.8681 (matrix-vs-rule difference not established). The macro-F1-selected gate over the rule achieves 0.8730 macro-F1 (+0.0019 [+0.0006, +0.0031]) but loses accuracy (−0.0022 [−0.0026, −0.0019]) with FCR rising from 0.0000 to 0.0027. Under the matched cutoff the macro-F1 gain is +0.0001 [−0.0006, +0.0008]; under the explicit mask (31.5% of cells retained, change rate 5.96%) it is 0.0000; under both combined it is −0.54×10⁻⁴ — significantly negative. The gate's destination-accuracy gain on changed cells (+0.0094 to +0.0004 across settings, all intervals excluding zero) and its accuracy loss are the only stable effects. Ungated GRUs break 35–37 cells per 1,000 to correct 5–8; change-weighted objectives fare similarly. All pretrained forecasters fall below persistence zero-shot (Chronos-Bolt small: 0.9599/0.8542; MIRA: 0.9500/0.8231); fine-tuned Chronos-Bolt small differs from copying on 2 of 281,952 cells, and fine-tuned MIRA improves to 0.9607/0.8585 but still falls short. The categorical read-out moves changed-cell accuracy eightfold (1.18%→9.51%) on frozen forecasts, yet a state-only control scores higher overall (0.9634/0.8681) and numerically reproduces the transition matrix. A chronological COVID-era holdout (heavily case-mix-shifted) preserves the pattern: gate +0.0020 macro-F1, −0.0030 accuracy vs. the rule. Baselines are appropriately current for the question posed (persistence, rule, transition matrix); the pretrained models are 2024–2025 checkpoints. Scale is single-center, standard — not a stress test. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (persistence dominance over learned and pretrained forecasters on recorded clinical assessments, with a controlled decomposition of which evaluation choices manufacture apparent gains) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL in a minor sense (a released evaluation harness with run manifests). The gated architecture is a standard logit-mixing combination of known ideas; the genuinely novel content is the audit itself — the enumeration proof that a data-driven transition table recovers the clinicians' rule exactly, the mask-comparability demonstration (a 0.41 macro-F1 spread induced by scoring convention alone on identical predictions), and the forecast-vs-state read-out control bounding what pretrained-forecaster adaptations can claim. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are extensive and central to the argument: cutoff (Table 8), label version (Table 7, all rows retrained), mask (Table 2), per-item decomposition (Table 9 showing the +0.0019 gain concentrates as +0.0027 from eight organ-acuity items and −0.0008 from the other 37), seed means vs. ensembles (Table 6), and chronological transfer (Table 13). Uncertainty is handled carefully: five-seed means, 2,000 paired patient-clustered bootstrap resamples, differences called "established" only when intervals exclude zero. The paper self-audits its own earlier version, correcting an irreproducible encounter count (3,020→2,789), replacing a leaky split, and fixing a bootstrap-unit error (day-pairs→patients). Code and evaluation artifacts are released at https://github.com/StatNLP/FMTS_2026_When-Copying-Is-Hard-to-Beat; data cannot be released (identifying routine-care records), and per-cell predictions are withheld because they would re-identify patients. Concerns: the hyperparameter search ran on a leaked split and was not repeated (mitigated by validation-based reselection, but not preregistered); pretrained-forecaster rows are single runs, not seed means; the authors developed and evaluated the label correction on the same data the rule is scored on, though the 27-cell correction is shown to be sensitivity-bounded and, if anything, hurts persistence. This is a preprint/workshop paper (NeurIPS 2026 workshop on Foundation Models for Temporal Systems), not a peer-reviewed venue result. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (retrospective models and evaluation harness; no deployment). - Practical: Yes — GRU encoders and small pretrained checkpoints run on commodity hardware; no compute figures are given, but nothing suggests exotic requirements. - Efficient: Not directly quantified; the negative result implies the cheapest "model" (copying, zero compute) is the right default, which is itself an efficiency claim. - Effective: The evidence shows the evaluated models do not solve the stated forecasting problem better than copying; the paper is explicit that this establishes neither unpredictability nor equivalence. - Scalable: Not tested beyond one center's ~39k questionnaire days; the authors claim no scalability, and the single-instrument, single-center scope limits any extrapolation. The work delivers a software artifact (analysis/training/evaluation code with run manifests and aggregate metrics); no trained model weights or dataset are released. Strengths: - Unusually honest negative-result methodology: the paper audits and corrects its own earlier version (leaked split, non-reproducible counts, wrong bootstrap unit), which is rare and raises confidence in the final numbers. - The observation-mask analysis is a genuine methodological contribution: showing that derived-cell exclusion changes persistence accuracy from 96.19% to 94.04%, discards 51% of transitions, and induces a 0.41 macro-F1 swing from scoring convention alone makes the "state your mask" point quantitatively rather than rhetorically. - The control structure around the pretrained-forecaster comparison is well designed: the enumerated equivalence of the thresholded transition table to the clinicians' rule, the state-only read-out control that numerically reproduces the transition matrix, and the decoding-on-frozen-forecasts design cleanly attribute effects to the right causes. - The accuracy decomposition (Eq. 2) and the per-1,000-cells departure counts (Figure 3) make the cost structure of departing from persistence legible — ungated models break 35–37 cells per 1,000 to fix 5–8. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (a credibility positive). They state: single-center data; inability to separate documentation persistence from clinical stability; no entry/signing timestamps so prediction-time availability is unmeasurable; the load-bearing label correction whose zero-FCR consequence is arithmetic rather than empirical; one target not comparable across questionnaire versions; 539 test patients with only 150 positive new-acuity cells; the non-preregistered selection protocol informed by a leaked-split search; explicit disclaimers that they establish neither unpredictability nor equivalence, and that the chronological row measures case-mix robustness rather than elapsed-time robustness. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The learned predictor class is limited to shallow GRUs with concatenation fusion — no attention-based or contemporary clinical-sequence architectures are tried, so the negative result covers only a modest hypothesis class, and the authors do not flag this scope limit explicitly. (2) The gate's macro-F1-selected configuration was chosen among candidates (a–c) whose differences were found on a leaked split; a fresh search on the clean split might find a gate that beats the rule more robustly, or might not — this is acknowledged but its asymmetry (search favors the authors' model, which still lost) is worth noting as cutting both ways. (3) The paper reports no calibration analysis or decision-theoretic evaluation of the accuracy-vs-changed-accuracy trade-off — it correctly refuses alert-budget claims, but a clinician reader gets no guidance on which side of the trade-off matters for which use case beyond generic statements. (4) The explicit-mask macro-F1 rows rest on thin class support (30 of 45 items reduced to a single class), which the authors disclose but which makes the "no advantage under explicit mask" macro-F1 claim weakly informative in isolation — the accuracy rows carry it. Beyond these, the paper is solid; the main gaps are scope-of-generalization rather than internal validity. Bottom Line: A practitioner building predictive models on recorded clinical assessments should absolutely read this — it is the clearest available demonstration that persistence baselines, observation masks, and input cutoffs decide such evaluations, and it will likely save more projects than any positive-result paper in the same space.

AlphaProof Code : Verifying Signal's Security at the Machine- Code Level

S Chaudhuri, A Ferraiuolo, A Kovsharov, T Chajed… · deepmind.google · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AlphaProof Code, a human-guided multi-agent framework for AI-driven formal specification and proof, and uses it to produce the first machine-checked proofs of protocol-level security properties (forward secrecy, post-compromise security, authentication, handshake secrecy) for the unmodified, stock-compiler-compiled AArch64 machine code of libsignal, Signal's reference implementation. - Why it's important: Formal verification has historically cost person-decades (seL4 took ~20 person-years) and was applied only to code written for verifiability; this work shows AI agents can collapse that labor cost enough to verify a pre-existing, widely deployed cryptographic library protecting billions of users, removing the Rust compiler and source semantics from the trusted computing base. - How it does it: Human-supervised agents write trusted Lean specifications, the unmodified Rust is compiled with stock rustc and loaded into Lean under a formal AArch64/Linux semantics, and teams of 40–80 autonomous prover agents produce proofs accepted only after Lean kernel checking plus a comparator check against a held-out copy of the approved specification, with a critic-gated amendment process preventing specification weakening. - The good: The verification is end-to-end and adversarially stress-tested: ~6.5 million lines of kernel-checked Lean over ~18,000 lines of trusted specification, two historically real libsignal bugs re-injected and machine-provably shown to violate the symbolic security theorem, and explicit discovery of ~15 gaps/errors in the published computational analysis of the Double Ratchet and errors in printed ProVerif queries of prior Signal analyses. - The missing: The campaign covers only one-to-one sessions of libsignal-cli (key generation unverified, one-time Kyber prekeys unmodeled, group messaging and trust-on-first-use out of scope), the computational bound becomes vacuous at moderate scale (~25,000 messages per session or 2^20 sessions of 2^10 messages), and there is no evaluation of the agent framework itself against baselines, ablations, or alternative verification strategies. - Read it or not: Essential reading for formal-methods, security-protocol, and AI-for-math/proof researchers — it is the strongest published demonstration that agentic AI changes the economics of machine-code verification — while practitioners seeking a general-purpose verification tool should note the framework is not yet released as usable software beyond the open-sourced Lean artifact.

Problem & Motivation: Formal verification promises proofs that rule out entire classes of bugs, but prior successes either verified code written specifically for verification (seL4, CompCert, miTLS, LibSignal★) or verified abstract protocol models disconnected from deployed implementations. For a production library like libsignal — the reference implementation of Signal, deployed in WhatsApp, Messenger, and Google Messages — no prior work proves protocol-level security properties (forward secrecy, post-compromise security, authentication) of the actual code; existing analyses target models, verification-friendly reimplementations, or narrower properties like panic-freedom. The gap: connecting research-literature security specifications (symbolic Dolev–Yao models and computational game-based proofs) to the unmodified binary as compiled by an optimizing compiler, which historically required years of expert labor. Key Idea: Once a trusted Lean specification is fixed, multi-million-line machine-code proofs can be produced autonomously by agent teams whose correctness is guaranteed by Lean's kernel and a comparator-checked held-out specification — so the binding constraint shifts from proof labor to specification engineering. The connecting trick for the target itself is refinement-up-to-collisions: a concretization homomorphism maps Dolev–Yao terms to bytes (never bytes back to terms), so every collision-free hardware trace of the binary is explained by a symbolic model trace, and separately, an embedded reduction language with an explicit cost semantics makes computational security bounds non-vacuous (reductions must be efficient by construction, not by informal assertion). Methodology: Four pipeline stages. (1) Specification writing: a spec-writer agent drafts Lean theorems/definitions from literature models (Bhargavan et al.'s PQXDH analysis, Cheval et al.'s Double Ratchet analysis, composed and extended to the deployed protocol including SPQR), reviewer agents critique drafts, and humans approve a pinned baseline; strength is tested via vacuity checks, mutation testing (e.g., removing ciphertext MAC verification must falsify the theorem), and historical-bug refutation. (2) Machine-code semantics: a 7,532-line Lean semantics of user-mode AArch64 Linux covering 467 instructions and 31 system calls, defining ElfRunsTo over ELF binaries; trusted definitions are validated in lockstep against Unicorn/QEMU and the Sail Armv9.4-A model. (3) Proof synthesis: an orchestrator, team leads, workers, architect, and integrator (40–80 agents, single machine, 24–72 hours per campaign) prove the specification; agents cannot edit the specification, only propose amendments to a critic that never sees proof attempts, under necessity/no-weakening/smallness conditions. (4) Gatekeeping: a comparator tool confirms proofs match a held-out specification copy, use only standard axioms, and pass Lean's kernel; sorry and native_decide are rejected. The security results come in two independent proofs: a symbolic proof (DyLean model, ten theorems, refinement–preservation over a trusted event layer and concretization function γ) and a computational proof (a composed PQXDH + Triple Ratchet game following Fiedler–Günther and ACD19, hybrid composition over sessions, coupling to the binary via a separation-logic refinement proved by symbolic execution, with concrete advantage bounds including a 2^-64 MAC-forgery term and joint Gap-DH/XEdDSA assumptions for the single-key handshake). Critical design decisions: proofs stated over whole process runs (CLI, musl allocator, protobuf, state machines) rather than Rust functions; 39 hooked routines (crypto primitives, five libc routines, output functions) replaced by trusted contracts; a proof that no run exhausts the modeled 1 GiB heap, so bounds carry no out-of-memory exception. Key Results: The artifact comprises ~7 million lines of Lean: ~6.5 million proof lines (5.3M shared binary proofs, ~860K computational, ~350K symbolic, 140K bug refutations, 70K allocator verification) against ~140,000 AArch64 instructions (~560 KB) of verified libsignal v0.105.4 + spqr v1.6.0 code compiled by rustc 1.98.1; the trusted base is ~18,000 lines of specification plus ~8,000 lines of AArch64 semantics and extracted symbol names. Symbolic: ten theorems on every collision-free execution — forward secrecy, post-compromise security, initiator/responder secrecy, authentication, and five PQXDH corollaries including KCI resistance and harvest-now-decrypt-later resistance against a quantum attacker. Computational: Theorem 2 gives a concrete advantage bound for confidentiality/authenticity of the composed protocol, summing cost-bounded reduction advantages against Gap-DH, XEdDSA unforgeability, Kyber1024 collision resistance, and HKDF/HMAC PRF security, plus statistical terms (δ_kem ≤ 2^-174 per Kyber spec). Sanity checks: scripted scenarios ran identically on the real binary and the Lean semantics (15.6M instructions across 10 invocations); both re-injected historical bugs yield machine-checked disproofs of the symbolic theorem (¬Sec(Asm_bug)) requiring no assumptions beyond Lean's standard axioms. The campaign took five people four weeks, with zero human-written proof code. No peer review yet — this is a corporate preprint-style report, though the underlying proofs are independently checkable artifacts. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the AlphaProof Code framework: gated multi-agent proof synthesis with amendment control) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (protocol-level security of unmodified deployed cryptographic code at machine level is achievable at ~4-week human cost) — the first such proofs by the authors' and this reviewer's assessment of the related-work survey. The individual ingredients are largely standard and competent assembled: refinement up to collisions follows Arquint et al.'s concretization, the symbolic model and theorems replicate the symbolic state of the art (the authors say so explicitly), the ACD19/Fiedler–Günther games are adopted from the literature, and the AArch64 semantics builds on Arm's ASL. What is genuinely new is the AI-driven proof labor model, the adversarially hardened specification pipeline (mutation testing of specifications, critic-gated amendments, comparator gatekeeping), and the costed reduction language making computational bounds formally meaningful. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for the verification artifact, weak for the AI framework itself. Strengths: every proof is kernel-checked; specifications are stress-tested by vacuity detection, mutation testing, and historical-bug refutation; the semantics is differentially tested against two independent oracles (Unicorn, Sail); the TCB is explicitly enumerated and deliberately excludes the Rust compiler and source. The Lean development is open-sourced (https://google-deepmind.github.io/code-verification), enabling independent re-checking. Concerns: this is a vendor self-report from Google DeepMind on both the AI system and its headline application, and the framework itself receives no controlled evaluation — no ablation of agent-team design, no comparison of agent-produced proofs against human or single-agent baselines, no compute/cost accounting beyond "one machine, 24–72 hours per campaign," and no error bars on any agent-level claim (e.g., that reviewer agents "were effective" is anecdotal). The specification remains a human-audited trusted artifact whose soundness is argued, not proven; the amendment process is human-judgment-dependent. A report of this significance would ideally include an independent replication of at least one campaign. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built verification framework evaluated by a deployment campaign; the deliverable includes machine-checked proofs plus open-source Lean code). - Practical: The proof campaigns ran on single workstations with commercial LLMs (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Opus 5.5), so the approach is reproducible by well-resourced teams, though the framework's skills and orchestration tooling are described but not shipped as a usable product. - Efficient: Human cost collapsed from ~20 person-years (seL4) to 5 people × 4 weeks, but compute cost is non-trivial — clean proof builds took hours, small changes forced large proof repairs early on, and authors note substantial optimization headroom; no FLOP/token/cost figures are given. - Effective: The evidence is genuine end-to-end security theorems about the real compiled binary with demonstrated bug-catching power (re-injected historical bugs provably falsify the specification), though the guarantees stop at the hooked crypto primitives' contracts and a narrower scenario than the full protocol (no group messaging, no TOFU, fixed roles, bounded inputs). - Scalable: Unproven beyond this single case study; the authors claim the workflow extends to group messaging, sealed sender, and per-release re-verification, and that bound-tightening is "a natural task for AI," but none of this is tested. The work delivers a concrete artifact — an open-source Lean development with specifications, semantics, and proofs — plus a reusable methodology; it stops short of a reusable tool release of AlphaProof Code itself. Strengths: - A genuine first: protocol-level security properties (FS, PCS, authentication, handshake secrecy including post-quantum harvest-now-decrypt-later in the symbolic model) proved for unmodified production cryptographic code at the machine-code level, removing the compiler from the TCB — a milestone the field has pursued for two decades. - Exceptional adversarial hardening of the specification pipeline: mutation testing of specifications, machine-checked vacuity/non-vacuity witnesses, a critic that adjudicates amendments without seeing proof attempts, and comparator-checked held-out specifications — directly addressing known LLM failure modes like specification weakening (citing the swarm-cheating incident of [78]). - Honest accounting of prior work's errors: the campaign surfaced ~15 gaps in the published ACD19 Double Ratchet analysis and concrete errors in printed ProVerif queries of Cheval et al. and Bhargavan et al. — evidence the specifications are non-trivially strong and that the paper's self-assessment is calibrated, not promotional. - The bug-refutation methodology (proving ¬Sec(Asm_bug) for two real historical libsignal bugs, with Lean stepping the actual injected binary through witness traces) is the most convincing demonstration that the specification catches real vulnerabilities rather than weak abstractions. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Extensive and candid — a credibility positive. The authors state: key generation is unverified; one-time Kyber prekeys and group messaging are out of scope; the symbolic result assumes fresh coins, idealized hooked primitives, an authentic PKI (TOFU path unexercised), and bounds collision probability nowhere; the replay-based forward-secrecy loss of Cheval et al. is not ruled out; SPQR's post-quantum healing is not proved (ratchet theorems let the attacker choose SPQR keys); the computational theorem covers no quantum adversary, restricts the adversary (no adversarial first messages to promoted sessions, corruption refused at certain points), assumes one session per promotion and fixed message lengths, and becomes vacuous at ~25,000 messages per session or 2^20 sessions × 2^10 messages; results apply to libsignal-cli, not Signal's own apps; some environment assumptions are argued informally; and the TCB still requires reading ~18,000 lines of specification plus trust in Lean's kernel. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No evaluation of the AI framework as an AI contribution: no baseline (single agent, no reviewer pool, no amendment process), no ablation of team structure (orchestrator/leads/workers), no success-rate or cost-per-lemma metrics, and no evidence on which of the framework's mechanisms actually mattered — the reader must take the workflow design on faith. - Human effort is under-reported relative to the headline claim: five people × four weeks is the campaign, but designing and iterating the agent skills "took a lot of human time" early on and the specification engineering (the paper's own core lesson) consumed "the majority of our effort" — the total person-cost and its breakdown are not quantified, weakening the cost-comparison against seL4's twenty person-years. - Single case study, deeply resourced team, and close collaboration with Signal's own developers (acknowledged) on a codebase with existing high-quality formal models to start from; transferability to systems lacking literature-grade specifications — the common case — is untested. - The AArch64 semantics' soundness against real hardware is unprovable and only tested; lockstep testing against QEMU/Sail covers exercised behaviors, and the paper acknowledges this trust placement, but the residual hardware-trust gap deserves more emphasis than "keep the trusted definitions small." - The trusted contracts for the low-level crypto routines are idealizations justified by the assumption that real primitives meet them; connecting them to verified implementations (HACL★, libcrux) is deferred to future work, so the chain from Silicon to theorem still has idealization links. - No discussion of compute cost or energy footprint of 40–80-agent campaigns, relevant to any honest deployability assessment. Bottom Line: This is a landmark paper that any formal-methods, security, or AI-for-verification researcher must read — the first machine-checked protocol-security proofs for unmodified deployed code at machine level, with unusually honest limitation reporting — but its AI-framework claims rest on a single, resourced, self-reported case study, so practitioners should treat the cost-collapse claim as promising and partially evidenced rather than established.
