Beyond transformers: Sums, maxima and the price of order

NDB Bruce · socs.uoguelph.ca · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper derives seven architecture-agnostic conditions (tether, routing budget, null, address/cargo separation, gain control, arrow, writer) that any content-routing sequence machine must satisfy, prices six of them with propositions proved within declared model classes, and builds a max-statistic attention head from the theory whose abstention and retrieval weights survive 8× length extrapolation in 125M language models with YaRN. - Why it's important: Anyone designing post-transformer architectures (linear attention, SSMs, MoE, walkers, memories) currently lacks a common account of what must be bought and in which currency (logit range, samples, state, address bits, positional range); this paper supplies lower bounds and failure laws intended to hold across all such machines. - How it does it: The core move is separating two routing limits — an "evidence wall" set by the keys (Gaussian-channel capacity; no read can beat the argmax under a joint-likelihood condition) and a "gain wall" set by the read — then showing that decisions summing over all N items (softmax normalizers, competitive nulls) need a ln N schedule while decisions reading a maximum need none up to the evidence wall. - The good: Preregistered constructed-key experiments match the closed-form laws closely — softmax onsets follow τc − ln m(τ) in all 57 registered mean-field comparisons (max deviation 0.40 nats), evidence onsets match F(c)^(N−1) with largest |z| 2.80 against a 4.06 threshold, and select-walker gains of 1.066–1.070 nats per nat of ln M confirm the exchange rate — with several registered prediction failures honestly reported rather than buried. - The missing: The flagship trained result measures attention weights, not behavior (no head reached the registered retrieval-identification threshold), the trained tests are tiny (594k- and 141k-parameter models, 3–10 seeds), and the entire empirical program rests on synthetic keys and the author's own companion papers rather than independent baselines. - Read it or not: Read it if you design or theorize about attention alternatives and want the sharpest available formal framing of what every token-mixing machine must pay; skip it if you want practical architectural recipes — the paper explicitly prices no machine on a common budget and reports no capability gains.

Problem & Motivation: The transformer's success factors (content-based routing, value maps, residual path, repetition) are usually read as a specific design, but they describe a design space. The paper addresses researchers proposing transformer alternatives who lack a principled account of which properties are essential, what each costs, and in what resource each architecture pays. It closes the gap left by prior work (including the author's own "protection lattice," Bruce 2026d) that described protections only for softmax transformers; here the protections are restated as conditions on any machine where content decides who talks to whom, something else decides what is said, and the step repeats. Key Idea: The single organizing insight is the law of sums versus maxima: any decision whose null or normalizer sums over all N items pays a ln N schedule against exchangeable backgrounds, while any decision reading a per-item maximum pays no schedule and stops only at an evidence wall owned by the keys — and beneath both, naming one of N items costs ~ln N nats regardless of the currency (logit range, samples, state, positional range) in which a machine pays. This immediately yields a design: a head whose route and null both read maxima should abstain and retrieve at every length without a schedule. Methodology: The paper interleaves theory, preregistered synthetic experiments, and small trained tests. (1) Seven conditions are each stated as a test with a removal signature and a set of currencies, priced by propositions proved in Appendix A within declared machine classes: the evidence result (Prop 1, an argmax/MAP optimality argument), gain exchange (Prop 2, order statistics, binomial majority, and a soft-tree result showing partition-function-weighted trees equal the flat softmax), abstention (Prop 3, competitive vs. absolute vs. sampled nulls), tethering (Prop 4, a restart-resolvent fixed-point analysis connected to Friedkin–Johnsen social influence), a gain certificate (Prop 5, contraction/Lipschitz sufficiency for a tethered attention map), address/cargo contamination (Theorem 6, exact argmax cost under class-shared cargo), and the price of order (Prop 11, Turán-graph bounds with an optimal staircase, a quadratic penalty for ALiBi-style linear bias, and a mean-field margin result). (2) Registered tests on constructed keys (isotropic spherical keys; product keys with D = 128, two 64-d halves) measure evidence walls, gain walls, abstention onsets, memory recall rates (linear attention ≈ 1/π nats per number, delta rule 0.272–0.275), and positional-code range (unary grows ~n², rotary within 3.1× of the ln(n−1) floor). (3) A max-statistic head (top-k softmax route plus a logistic gate σ(a[maxⱼ sⱼ − θ]) on the largest score) is trained in 125M models; seven machine families (softmax, walker, block-router "tree," LSH address book, relaxation network, Sinkhorn, sigmoid binding, linear/bounded state) are trained end-to-end as token mixers in ~141k-parameter CIFAR-10 and ~594k-parameter WikiText-2 models. Critical design decisions: preregistration with frozen thresholds (well justified — it forces reporting of failed predictions like the averaging-walker convergence and log-N-training structural claims); proving only within declared classes (honest but limits transfer to trained models); and deliberately tiny trained scale (acknowledged as exploratory). Key Results: All quantitative wall measurements are on synthetic constructions; trained results are on toy-scale models plus one 125M test. Evidence capacity: measured onsets matched the exact law in all 20 settings of cosine c and dimension D (400 trials each; largest |z| 2.80), and the D-slope matched Gaussian-channel capacity C(c) (e.g., 0.499 vs 0.511 at c = 0.8), not the small-signal c²/2 approximation. Gain: softmax onset followed τc − ln m(τ) in 57/57 registered comparisons; select walkers gained 1.066–1.070 nats of ln N per nat of ln M; averaging walkers bought nothing (the registered prediction that they match softmax failed); a hard tree showed no gain wall to 2³⁰ slots. Abstention: fixed softmax sinks lost abstention within 0.43 nats of the predicted onset; absolute (maximum-based) tests held to the evidence wall. Order: the staircase attains the K/(K+1) bound; linear bias leaves 2.16–2.29× more unordered pairs; optimized rotary codes reach only 72–89% of the staircase bound. Small trained tests: all machines train (image accuracy 0.549–0.609 vs 0.602 softmax; LM 2.14–2.28 bits/byte vs 2.24); length transfer Δ₅₁₂ was +0.0102 for softmax, +0.0198 for the walker, −0.0327 for the bounded state; a trained log-N scale failed to remove the length penalty (registered structural prediction refuted; softmax Δ₅₁₂ rose 0.0029, 95% CI 0.0020–0.0039). The max-statistic head in 125M models was the only rule whose null and match weights both stayed within half a nat of log-odds to 8× training length with YaRN (−0.27/−0.17 seed means, jointly in 2 of 3 seeds); natively it failed as the background maximum grew with uninterpolated positions. The readout battery on small models was inconclusive by its registered rule: zero heads qualified as retrieval heads, and trained heads sit far outside the sufficient gain-certificate region (κ̂ medians 13.3–35.2 against the bound of 1). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a NEW METHOD component (the max-statistic head) and elements of a position/survey (the 43-family catalog). The genuinely novel core is the two-budget (evidence/gain) decomposition, the sum-vs-max law for null schedules, the proved price of soft order (staircase optimality, mean-field margin result), and the family of ln N lower bounds framed as currency exchange. The max-statistic head is a straightforward composition of a top-k softmax and a logistic threshold gate — its interest is entirely derivational from the theory. The catalog is a competent synthesis; the tether analysis recasts known restart/resolve operators (personalized PageRank, Friedkin–Johnsen) in new service. Rigor & Reproducibility: Unusually rigorous in one respect: tests are preregistered with frozen thresholds, and multiple registered predictions are reported as failed (averaging-walker convergence, the fuzzy-addressing slope check at 2 of 4 flip rates, the log-N-training structural claim, seven fine-grid verdict reversals on recomputation). Ablations over gain τ, sample budget M, cosine c, dimension D, and tether α are systematic. However: no confidence intervals were retained for seed-level spread in most constructed tests ("no seed intervals were retained" recurs); the gain certificate is empirically conservative by 9.6–400×, and the paper cannot locate the true multistability onset; the trained evidence involves 3–10 seeds of sub-million-parameter models; the 125M test has 3 seeds and passes its registered prediction on means in only 2 of 3 seeds. The theoretical framework is developed, tested, and evaluated largely within the author's own artifact ecosystem — the propositions, companion monograph (Bruce 2026a), prior softmax law (2026c), and protection lattice (2026d) are all self-cited Zenodo releases, and the 125M harness is the author's prior work. Code/records appear to be released ("the package," Zenodo DOIs 10.5281/zenodo.23541723, -1963, -2051), though no repository URL for the current paper's code is explicitly given beyond these. No external, independent baseline is compared anywhere; capability is never measured. Deployability: Profile: primarily THEORETICAL (propositions and bounds are the contribution), with supporting EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS validation (preregistered tests, a trained head). Sound: Proofs are complete within explicitly declared classes, with counterexamples (a three-item non-factorizable case; a soft-tree counterexample) marking exactly where premises break. General: Conditions are restrictive — independent or exchangeable backgrounds with monotone likelihood ratio, mean-field concentration, orthonormal inputs, fixed visible sets — and the paper concedes real clustered keys can violate the key premise. Tight: The evidence wall is essentially tight (matches Gaussian-channel capacity to within a few percent); the gain certificate is loose by 1–2 orders of magnitude and admittedly only sufficient. Implementable: Yes — the max-statistic head and staircase recency rule are concrete, and the head was trained; the theory also suggests nine concrete next experiments. Deliverables: a code/test package and companion texts on Zenodo, plus a specifiable architectural head; no competitive trained model or library for practitioners. Strengths: - The sum-vs-max law and the evidence/gain budget split give a genuinely reusable lens: they correctly predict, with closed forms, where softmax, walkers, trees, and nulls fail across five different ledgers, including the counter-intuitive result that averaging samples buys nothing while selection buys a nat per nat. - Preregistration with reported prediction failures is rare in ML theory-adjacent work and materially raises trust in the numbers that are reported (e.g., the 1.066–1.070 select slopes and 57/57 mean-field onset matches). - The price-of-order result is a real theorem with a matching construction: the Turán/staircase bound K/(K+1), the quantified ~2× penalty of ALiBi-style linear bias, and the mean-field margin statement that no soft positional term reaches 0.9 latest-write success while all positions stay retrievable. - Intellectual honesty throughout: the paper repeatedly downgrades its own claims ("these are attention weights, not behaviour," "inconclusive" registered verdicts, refuted structural predictions), which is the opposite of vendor-style overclaiming. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that constructed tests use synthetic keys while real keys are clustered (violating the evidence proposition's joint-likelihood condition); that propositions hold only within declared classes and trained models may sit outside them; that trained tests are small (under 600k parameters, short contexts, 3 seeds at 125M); that the gain certificate is sufficient only and empirically very conservative; that the max-statistic head result concerns attention weights, not behavior, and gives no guarantee beyond 8× with YaRN; that physical/biological catalog entries are untested readings; and that the paper prices no machine on a common budget and does not predict capability. The authors confront limitations directly and repeatedly — this is a credibility strength. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The flagship deliverable (max-statistic head) is never shown to help a task: no perplexity, accuracy, or retrieval-behavior outcome is reported, only attention-weight probes — the chain from the law of sums to practical benefit is asserted, not measured. - The entire empirical validation loop is endogamous: propositions, test harnesses, prior results, and evaluation thresholds all originate with the author; no independent replication or external baseline (e.g., comparison to existing scalable-softmax, sink-token, or recurrent-memory methods on shared benchmarks) exists. - Key theory–practice links are untested: whether trained retrieval heads fail at their evidence wall is left "inconclusive" by the battery's own rule, so the central diagnostic claim (failure location distinguishes representation vs. routing bottlenecks) is demonstrated only on synthetic keys. - The small trained tests lack compute matching (acknowledged), and their length-transfer differences (Δ₅₁₂ spread of ~0.05 bits/byte) are far too small to establish practical relevance at real context lengths. - The 125M result passes its registered prediction on seed means in 2 of 3 seeds and depends entirely on YaRN — i.e., the "no schedule" head still requires an external positional fix, which softens the headline claim that maxima need no schedule. - Some registered checks failed quietly in ways a less careful paper would omit (fuzzy-addressing slopes 14.4% and 10.4% above capacity at two flip rates; seven reversed verdicts on the fine grid), which, while honestly reported, indicate the theory's finite-sample accuracy is imperfect. Bottom Line: A theory-first paper that any researcher building attention alternatives should read for its proved sum/max price laws and preregistered wall measurements, but practitioners seeking a deployable transformer replacement or validated capability gains will find none here — the trained evidence is toy-scale, self-referential, and behavioral validation is explicitly left to future work.

Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization (17 ▲ )

Bowen Liu, Yuhan Li, Nuo Chen, Weile Luo, Miao Peng, Qintong Zhang, Qifan Zhang, Jia Li, Ziqi Gao, Lydell Huang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 17 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 workload-defined CPU optimization tasks from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions, plus an evaluation of 16 coding agents and a trajectory-level analysis of how those agents optimize. - Why it's important: Existing optimization benchmarks (SWE-Perf, GSO, SWE-fficiency, KernelBench) anchor tasks to known human commits or isolated functions, so they cannot measure whether an agent can discover where and how to intervene in a complete application when no reference patch exists. - How it does it: Each task fixes the computation, outputs, timing boundaries, and permitted edit scope while leaving the optimization strategy open; agents iterate against a public test, and a separate private verifier scores the final submission on held-out inputs, with reward defined as the fraction of baseline runtime saved (r = C·max(0, 1 − T/B)). - The good: The measurement discipline is unusually thorough — verifier validation controls (all 8 invalid shortcuts rejected), unchanged-source calibration (0.923×–1.017×), re-judging and run-to-run variance quantification, and scoring-sensitivity analyses — plus controlled replays showing identical source ranges from 0.29× to 2.12× on build/runtime settings alone. - The missing: The v1.1 ranking rests on one run per agent, the analysis sample (480 runs, 5 agents) covers only mid/low-tier agents from v1.0 and not the leading Claude agents, and model is confounded with harness (13 of 16 agents run in Claude Code). - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or evaluating coding agents for performance engineering — it defines the workload-defined task formulation and sets a high bar for benchmark verification rigor — but model developers seeking leaderboard signal alone can read Table 1 and skip the appendices.
Why this rank
Scored using SYSTEMS profile. This is the most rigorous benchmark paper in the cluster, and Rigor (85) earns it: verifier validation controls with invalid-shortcut rejection, unchanged-source calibration on every task, explicit separation of re-judging noise from agent search variance, frozen pre-committed baselines, and quantified bootstrap intervals — with only the preprint status and promised-not-released code holding it below 90. Novelty (80) reflects the workload-defined (rather than commit-derived) task formulation, a genuine conceptual contribution, and Non-Obviousness (80) is driven by the transferable interaction findings (identical source spanning 0.29×–2.12× on settings alone; a 1.01× change becoming 6.4× conditioned on another). Completeness (80) is strong given direct confrontation of CPU-only scope, harness confounds, and reward saturation; Resilience (70) loses points because the abstract still reads as model-capability comparisons despite 13/16 agents sharing a harness. Practical Impact (75) reflects a well-designed, cheap-to-run benchmark artifact, capped by unavailability at review time. Weighted composite: 0.15*80 + 0.15*85 + 0.10*80 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*70 + 0.30*75 = 77.75 → 78.

Problem & Motivation: Application-level performance optimization is an iterative engineering process spanning algorithms, implementation, compiler/build configuration, dependencies, and hardware parallelism, where success is defined end-to-end: a valid patch may leave total runtime unchanged, and gains from one change can depend on others. Prior benchmarks anchor evaluation around known optimization artifacts — commit-derived tasks (GSO, SWE-Perf, SWE-fficiency), isolated functions (KernelBench, AlgoTune), or expert references — which conflates "reproduce a known patch" with "discover an optimization." The unaddressed question is whether an agent can optimize a complete application when the required behavior and workload are specified but no known optimization patch determines where to intervene. The intended audience is agent builders and HPC practitioners assessing whether coding agents can automate real performance engineering. Key Idea: The core move is defining optimization tasks by workload contract rather than by reference patch: each task fixes the computation that must be preserved (outputs, numerical tolerances, stateful checks like checkpoint recovery), the timed workflow, and the permitted edit space (source, compiler options, dependencies, runtime configuration), then scores only the end-to-end runtime of the final submission on private inputs via a verifier the agent never sees. This makes correctness enforcement the load-bearing component — shortcuts that skip required computation fail checks rather than earn speedups — and makes local improvements count only proportionally to their share of the timed workflow. Methodology: The benchmark construction pipeline adapts 32 tasks from six supercomputing competitions (ASC, SC SCC, PAC, ISC SCC, IndySCC, IPCC) into containerized single-node workloads (4–8 CPU cores, 4–32 GiB, 8-hour agent budget, timed verification), standardized build/execution entry points, and per-task contracts specifying editable paths, timed stages, and output checks. 29 tasks build on competition applications (GROMACS, SU2, NEMO, OpenMC, HPCG-derived, etc.); 3 are task-authored workflows (Paged LM generation, Tucker reconstruction, Graph sparsification). Evaluation uses reward r_t = C_t·max(0, 1 − T_t/B_t), aggregated as Score@1 (mean over equally weighted tasks), A_τ (fraction correct with ≥τ-fold speedup, τ ∈ {1.25, 2, 5, 10}), and geometric-mean speedup. The process analysis labels 480 v1.0 runs (5 agents × 3 runs × 32 tasks) using GPT-5.6 Luna for technique classification (audited against source), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for full-trajectory action annotation (96% decision-label accuracy on an 80-call audit), and a stratified reviewed random sample (following prediction-powered-inference practice) to estimate dependency prevalence. Critical design decisions: (1) private verification on held-out, often larger or freshly randomized inputs — justified to prevent overfitting to public tests; (2) timing boundaries excluding build/setup — well-justified with the configuration-only baseline showing build tuning alone rarely exceeds 1.25× (only GROMACS at 2.23×); (3) workload downscaling from multi-node competition scale to single-node — acknowledged as a scope restriction, mitigated by private inputs often being larger than public ones. Key Results: On v1.1, 16 agents (model + harness pairs) score between 25.5% (Hy3) and 67.4% (Claude Sonnet 5.5) on Score@1; Claude Opus 5.5 scores 59.4% (65.6% excluding 3 runs stopped by provider safety classifiers). Correctness is nearly saturated: 472 of 512 outcomes pass, and every agent is correct on 26–32 of 32 tasks, so speedup magnitude separates agents — the two Claude agents reach ≥2× on 22–23 tasks, the other fourteen on 8–17, with 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25×. Bootstrap intervals separate Claude Sonnet 5.5 from all non-Claude agents by ≥13.4 points but cannot order neighbors below the top two. Task-level results: on HPCG-derived, most agents exceed 28× (one GPT-6 Astra replay hit 26.3×, beating an independently written direct solver by 1.19–1.25×); on seven tasks (Fluidity, ICON, miniVite, NEMO, Quantum ESPRESSO, QuEST, VPIC) no v1.0 agent reached 1.25×. The process analysis finds computation/reuse changes in 225 of 476 labeled runs versus compiler/build tuning in only 40, yet controlled replays show build/runtime settings alone move one unchanged GROMACS source from 0.289× to 2.123×, and one QiboTN change (deferred library loading) is worth 1.01× alone but 6.3–6.4× when another change (broad simulator dispatch) is present. An estimated 52% (95% CI 41–63%) of analyzed runs contain a dependency affecting an optimization's speed or correctness. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the workload-defined (rather than commit-derived) task formulation with private verification of complete applications, and the controlled-replay evidence that optimization gains interact across code/build/runtime layers in ways agents must navigate. The scoring machinery (correctness-gated runtime savings, public-test/private-verifier split) is a competent combination of existing ideas from SWE-bench-style verification, KernelBench's joint correctness-and-speed criterion, and ALE-Bench/RE-Bench's iterative-improvement format, applied to a new setting; the trajectory annotation pipeline is careful but methodologically standard LLM-assisted labeling with audits. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is among the more rigorous benchmark papers I have reviewed. Ablation-style evidence is present in unusual depth: verifier validation controls (14 planned controls on 2 tasks — every valid variant passes, all 8 invalid variants fail the check they violate, including 4 attention variants that pass component checks but fail application checks); unchanged-source timing calibration (0.923×–1.017×, median 0.999×); re-judging variance of fixed submissions (SD ~1.5 Score@1 points) versus independent-run variance (SD 2.5–4.4 points), with an honest statement that single runs do not order agents a few points apart; sensitivity analyses over scoring rules, savings gates, references, and workload aggregation; and a fixed configuration-only baseline recipe frozen before any run. Uncertainty is quantified via task-bootstrap intervals throughout, though pointwise, not adjusted for multiple comparisons. LLM annotators are audited (96% decision-label accuracy; relationship records deliberately demoted to evidence-locators due to lower reliability). The authors pre-commit that v1.0/v1.1 results are never combined and report incomplete data honestly (Gemini-3.8-Flash v1.1 runs unfinished; Claude Opus safety-stopped runs counted as failures, with cross-benchmark comparison of handling policies). Versioned task packages, public tests, and verifiers are promised for release with the published version; code is not yet available at review time, and the paper is a preprint. Methodological concerns: the trajectory analysis (Section 5) runs on v1.0 with five mid/low-tier agents and explicitly does not explain the v1.1 ranking; 2 of 32 tasks are task-authored rather than competition-derived (though Kendall's τ_b ≥ 0.95 without them); and the HPCG-derived task admits a direct-solver shortcut the authors flag. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a benchmark artifact with an evaluation protocol), with a strong EMPIRICAL evaluation component. - Practical: Yes — every task runs on a single node with 4–8 CPU cores and 4–32 GiB, no GPU or cluster required, in Docker containers. - Efficient: Moderate — 8 agent-hours per task per run (512 scored v1.1 runs plus 480 v1.0 analysis runs), verifier times from 30 minutes to ~14 hours (QiboTN); far cheaper than multi-node HPC but substantial in aggregate. - Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark measures what it claims — correct-and-faster programs on held-out inputs — though speedups are relative to task-provided baselines of varying tuning rather than expert or optimal references. - Scalable: Untested beyond single-node CPU; the authors state results at other scales, hardware, and production environments require separate evaluation, and multi-node/GPU tasks are out of scope. The deliverable is the benchmark itself: versioned task packages, public tests, verifiers, and all 512+ runs with trajectories (promised for release; not yet public). No library or trained model is released. Strengths: - The workload-defined task formulation is a real conceptual contribution: it tests optimization discovery rather than patch reproduction, and the correctness contract design (stateful checks like checkpoint recovery, workflow-timed stages) is what makes local-kernel-gaming ineffective — demonstrated by controls where component-check-passing variants fail application checks. - Measurement rigor that exceeds field norms: frozen configuration baseline, unchanged-source calibration on every task, explicit separation of re-judging noise from agent search variance, and published run-accounting for all 768 v1.0 panel runs including 215 API-failure replacements. - The interaction findings are the paper's most transferable insight: identical source spanning 0.289×–2.123× across build/runtime settings, and the QiboTN factorial showing a 1.01× change becoming 6.4× conditioned on another change — direct quantitative evidence that benchmark designs scoring isolated edits understate real optimization difficulty. - Honest treatment of failures and ambiguity: safety-classifier-stopped runs counted as zeros with a 65.6% counterfactual reported, incomplete Gemini runs disclosed, and explicit statements that trajectory findings are illustrative observations over the analyzed runs, not prevalence claims beyond them. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly (a credibility positive). They state: (1) coverage is CPU-only at specified scales, with speedups relative to baselines of varying tuning, and the HPCG-derived task admits a direct-solver structure; (2) scores conflate model capability with harness behavior, inference compute, and execution conditions — 13 of 16 agents run in Claude Code, and only two agents have repeated runs; (3) v1.0 and v1.1 are reported separately and never combined, with the trajectory analysis on v1.0 only; (4) trajectory analysis covers five agents, LLM-assisted labels are audited but not perfect, version histories cover only 31 runs, and most candidates have a single timing observation. These are stated plainly rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The "how agents optimize" analysis excludes the leading agents entirely — all five analyzed models score ≤30% on v1.0 — so claims about agent optimization behavior are untested on the agents that actually solve the benchmark; the behavior of Claude Sonnet/Opus, which reach 2× on 22+ tasks, may differ qualitatively (e.g., in build tuning or profiling use). - The harness confound is more severe than acknowledged for headline conclusions: with only 3 of 16 agents in Codex and the rest in Claude Code, the paper cannot support any claim about relative model capability, only about model+harness combinations — yet the abstract and discussion read as agent-level comparisons. - The reward function saturates (2× earns 0.5, 10× earns 0.9), compressing exactly the large speedups that distinguish top agents; A_τ mitigates this, but the primary metric structurally understates the largest differentiator (authors note this only in an appendix). - The benchmark had not been publicly released at paper time despite being a benchmark paper; reproducibility claims rest on promised release of versioned packages. - Correctness was nondeterministic for some submissions (10 changed between re-judgments due to tolerance-proximity and fresh private inputs), meaning the correctness gate itself injects variance into scores — quantified but not resolved (e.g., via repeated correctness trials in the score). - Only 3 of 32 tasks are task-authored, but 3 candidate tasks were dropped pre-evaluation for verifier failures; the paper reports this selection rule transparently, though the full task-construction funnel (how many candidates considered) is not documented. Bottom Line: Any group building, selecting, or benchmarking coding agents for performance engineering should read this paper — it is the most rigorous application-level optimization benchmark available and its interaction findings alone justify the read — but practitioners should treat the model rankings as single-run, harness-confounded signals rather than capability verdicts.

What a CAGE 4 Score Measures: An Audit of a Learned Cyber -Defense Benchmark, Its Reference Defenders, and the Tables Built on Them

J Rice, JH Park, A Kwasinski · arxiv.org · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper audits the CAGE Challenge 4 benchmark for learned multi-agent cyber defense, reproducing its two reference defenders in a pinned container and showing with a custom step-level recording instrument that its scores are inflated by a silent action-drop mechanism, an unseeded policy sampler, an undisclosed Restore penalty, and non-comparable recovery-precision criteria. - Why it's important: CAGE 4 scores are how the learned-cyber-defense field decides which defender is better, so any defect in what those scores measure propagates into every published comparison built on them — and the paper shows five published comparison tables (2024–2026) are not demonstrably comparable. - How it does it: The core move is an instrument that records, at every simulator step, what was asserted versus what executed versus the true network state, enabling a variance decomposition, a charge accounting, paired-seed retraining with/without the busy-flag check, and a disclosure audit of published tables. - The good: Both published defender numbers fall inside tight reproduction intervals (KEEP −191.34 [−202.61, −180.07] vs published −193.68; H-MARL −131.34 [−140.61, −122.08] vs −129.53), so the audit's findings cannot be dismissed as a failed reproduction, and the headline mechanism (dropped directives charged as Restores) is isolated to the point on H-MARL (cost 145.98 = charge 145.98 exactly, executed actions identical step-for-step). - The missing: The retraining conclusion rests on only 3–4 paired training seeds with a wide across-seed spread (126.7 points), the training-effect mechanism (credit assignment vs. check) is read from code but not measured, and no agent built on the challenge's documented vector observation is actually run. - Read it or not: Anyone publishing, reviewing, or building on CAGE/CybORG results must read this — it changes how every existing and future table on this benchmark should be interpreted; for RL-benchmark-audit outsiders it is also a model of the genre, but skippable if you work on neither security simulators nor benchmark methodology.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile (with a systems component in the released instrument). This is a model of the benchmark-audit genre: Rigor (75) is high for the field — paired seeds, bootstrap intervals, pre-registered continuation seeds, explicit multiple-comparison accounting, deterministic cross-machine reproduction — docked for the preprint status and the underpowered 3–4-seed retraining conclusion. Novelty (80) is anchored by the first audit of a sequential-decision security benchmark and the previously unreported silent-drop mechanism; Non-Obviousness (85) reflects that the finding (dropped directives charged as Restores, 88.9% of variance from the sampling draw) was invisible to every published table and reverses the authors' own prior conclusions. Completeness (75) and Resilience (80) benefit from unusually direct limitation disclosure and tightly bounded claims backed by tight reproduction intervals; Impact (75) is driven by the released step-record instrument, pinned containers, patches, and disclosure checklist that CAGE users must act on. Problem & Motivation: Autonomous cyber defense via reinforcement learning is evaluated almost entirely in simulators, and CAGE Challenge 4 (built on CybORG) is the shared ground on which learned multi-agent defenders are compared — its leaderboard scores are read as properties of the defenders. Yet the RL literature's own history (Henderson et al. on seeds and implementations; Agarwal et al. on point estimates) and the security-ML literature's catalog of evaluation pitfalls suggest such scores turn on undisclosed details. Prior to this paper, no audit existed of how results on a sequential-decision security benchmark are computed and reported; neighboring audits (Emerson et al. on CybORG/CAGE 2) did not cover the multi-agent, action-duration setting of CAGE 4. Practitioners who retrain KEEP or H-MARL, or who supervise learned defenders with injected interventions (human-in-the-loop work), inherit defects they cannot see. Key Idea: The key insight is that CybORG's controller silently discards any action asserted while an agent's previous action is running (no error, no queue), charges one point for a discarded Restore as for an executed one, and the busy flag needed to comply is absent from the challenge's documented observation — so a CAGE 4 score is partly a measurement of how a harness or wrapper handles a hidden state, not purely of the policy. Once this is seen, everything follows: ablate the busy check, split every score difference into the Restore charge and the "rest," decompose variance into sampling vs. scenario, and re-read published conclusions (directability, burst-vs-spread, decoy value, recovery precision) to see which survive held delivery. Methodology: The paper builds a pinned reproduction environment (per-defender Docker images, undeclared dependency pins identified, checkpoint digests), then a step-record instrument capturing per-step executed actions, asserted interventions, rewards, and (on some arms) raw observations and true state — the benchmark's own evaluator writes none of these. Layers: (1) Reproduce both released checkpoints on 100 paired environment seeds with multiple sampling seeds, reporting t-intervals over draws. (2) Tiered defect catalog (Tier A: silent drop + Restore charge + hidden busy flag; Tier B: unseeded policy sampling, parallel-eval seed reuse, trainer defects — unseeded workers, one scenario draw replayed every update, learner reads 5 of 25 episodes; Tier C: no per-step reward/true state in the record, broken get_reward_breakdown). (3) Measure the drop via a supervisory rule (O1, Restore on compromised hosts) delivered fired vs held, on 100 paired episodes, with 95% bootstrap intervals and sign tests, under the stock adversary and a hand-specified impact-focused adversary (Wrecker, a modified transition table yielding ~6× the stock loss). (4) Variance decomposition (one-way random effects, episode as factor, sampling seeds as replicates). (5) Retrain KEEP from scratch with/without the busy check on 4 paired seeds, crossing the check at scoring, continuing the check-on arm to 2,000 updates on 3 pre-registered seeds with fixed-layout and read-all controls. (6) Score recovery precision against two criteria (ground truth vs. latched evidence). (7) Audit five published tables against four disclosure axes. The overall framework is paired-episode evaluation with interval-based reporting (Agarwal et al.-style), applied to a simulator audit. Critical design decisions — paired seeds, held-delivery as control, pre-registered continuation seeds (fixed Oct 19, 2026 before three of four 400-update scores were read) — are justified explicitly and mostly well; the charge/rest split is careful about its own undercounting errors, which is unusually honest. Key Results: Reproduction: KEEP −191.34 (SE 3.54, published −193.68); H-MARL Expert −131.34 (published −129.53, independent −132.63); both intervals ~20 points wide, four times the leaderboard's 1st–2nd place gap (4.65). Drop cost: switching KEEP's busy check off costs 99.58 points/episode at the published setting (charge 103.45; rest −3.87, indistinguishable from zero), 81.79–155.05 across nine adversaries; H-MARL's mask off costs exactly 145.98 (the charge to the point; executed actions identical on 100/100 episodes). Supervisory harness (Wrecker): held delivery worth 172.7 points on KEEP and 316.3 on H-MARL (intervals [133.8, 212.2] and [241.5, 393.9]; sign test p < 0.001); at stock, 25.3 and 27.6. Variance: 88.9% of KEEP's per-episode outcome variance at stock (interval 71.6–99.8%) is the policy's sampling draw; one-seed 100-episode mean SE ≈ 6.3 points at stock, 32.4 under Wrecker; two identical policies differ by up to 14.9 points; the same checkpoint scores −552.22 greedy vs −187.32 sampled (2.95×). Accounting: the Restore charge is 41.4% of KEEP's loss at the published setting, and 40.3 of the 50.89 points separating the two defenders. Training: without the check, KEEP leads at 100 updates in 4/4 seeds (by 454.4–1,654.0 points) and trails from 200 updates on in 4/4 (by 62.6–460.0); continued to 2,000 updates on 3 seeds, four-draw means are −316.72, −218.71, −189.97 against the released −191.34 — one inside the released interval, two short by 125.4 and 27.4 points, with a 126.7-point across-seed spread. Precision: KEEP's Restores score 45.6% under ground truth and 71.6% under the evidence criterion; a rule arm at 65.2% recovers more than KEEP yet trails it by 332.97 points when fired, almost all Restore charge. Disclosure audit: none of five published tables (leaderboard, Trident, ACDZero, HC-MARL, Shaikh et al.) states all four of artifact identity, seed/dispersion, criterion/scenario, and adversary. Baselines are the field's own reference defenders and the audit checks published numbers against them fairly; scale is standard benchmark scale (100-episode episodes × 500 steps), not stress-scale, but appropriate to the question. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the silent-drop mechanism, its charge, and the sampling-variance dominance are previously unreported properties of a widely used benchmark) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the step-record instrument, pinned reproduction, one-command defect checks, patches) and a methodological contribution (a five-item disclosure checklist that is the sequential-decision counterpart of Henderson/Agarwal/Arp-style checklists). The statistical techniques (paired bootstrap, variance decomposition, sign tests) are standard; the novelty is in what they are applied to and the forensic code-reading that makes the defects measurable. The paper's own claim — the first audit of how results on a sequential-decision security benchmark are reported — is credible. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is high for the genre. Ablations are present and load-bearing: the check-off ablation at evaluation (Table 6, ten adversaries), the paired retraining with/without the check (Table 7), the fixed-layout (S) and read-all (R) controls (Table 8). Bootstrap intervals and win counts accompany paired differences; sign tests where p-values are printed; the paper explicitly flags which of its ~30 paired differences would survive family-wise correction and which would not. Determinism is established before any number is reported (a seeded two-episode run reproduces to the digit across two machines). One-command reproductions of each defect ship in a released artifact, along with checkpoint digests, code revisions, and patches to both defenders' code. Concerns: (a) this is a preprint (arXiv:2611.14068), not peer-reviewed; (b) several conclusions rest on 3–4 training seeds (exact sign test p = 0.125 for the 4/4 reversal; permutation p = 0.004 for between-seed spread, which the authors note would not survive a 30-test correction); (c) the audit evaluates the benchmark it built its instrument on, but this is inherent to the question and the reproduction intervals guard against a failed-reproduction confound; (d) the charge accounting carries known undercounting errors the authors bound but do not eliminate; (e) the authors disclose their own prior measurement error (true-state capture point) — a credibility positive. No external replication exists yet. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component in the released instrument). - Practical: Yes — everything runs on CPU-only pinned Docker images (they pin the CPU torch wheel index), and the artifacts are the two defenders' public checkpoints. - Efficient: The audit itself is cheap (100-episode evaluations, 2,000-update PPO runs); the instrument adds recording overhead but the read-all control consumes 5× episodes per update at 5× batch size, so total compute is modest by RL standards. - Effective: The evidence convincingly shows the benchmark's scores measure what the authors claim (wrapper busy-handling, sampling draw, Restore charge) — the mechanism is demonstrated on real released policies and traced in controller code, not merely a proxy; what it does not show is a fix adopted by the benchmark. - Scalable: Not tested beyond the shipped scenario scale (5 blue agents, one enterprise topology, 500-step episodes); the authors claim nothing about other simulators, and the drop's behavior on red-side LLM agents or Cyberwheel is explicitly left open. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: the step-record instrument, pinned containers, patches to both defenders' evaluation/training code, per-arm traces, and a checklist — not just a paper. Strengths: - The forensic chain from controller code (`actions_in_progress` check with no else branch) to measured cost (99.58 / 145.98 points, the H-MARL figure equal to the charge to the point with executed actions identical step-for-step) is airtight and cannot be explained away as an evaluation artifact. - The instrument separates asserted from executed actions — the quantity no published table could report with the shipped evaluator — and this single capability reverses three concrete published-style conclusions (directability, burst-vs-spread, decoy value) the authors had themselves drawn, which is the most persuasive possible demonstration of the stakes. - Statistical hygiene exceeds field norms: paired episodes, bootstrap intervals, win counts, sign tests, pre-registered continuation seeds, explicit identification of which p-values survive multiple-comparison correction, and a null band from identical-policy redraws. - The variance finding (88.9% of outcome variance is the sampling draw; SE ≈ 6.3 on a one-seed 100-episode mean vs. a 4.65-point leaderboard gap) is a direct, quantified indictment of the leaderboard's resolution. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (a strong credibility signal): results are confined to CAGE 4 and two defenders; the drop's cost on supervised arms is measured on injected interventions, not on policies that lack a busy check; no agent is run on the challenge's documented vector observation; the training effect is early-in-training only (paired through 400 updates) and the continuation covers the check-on arm alone; the mechanism of the training effect is read from code, not measured (the credit-assignment-vs-check arm is named as future work); the two defenders' sampling shares are not measured on the same footing (different generator reseeding); the parallel-path defect is reported, not repaired; evidence-criterion shares rest on one reading of a latch implemented differently per team; supervision results concern a scripted rule, not a human. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The retraining result — arguably the paper's most consequential training-side claim — is underpowered: 4 paired seeds give sign-test p = 0.125, and the continuation covers only 3 seeds at a single budget with two of three arms still moving at the endpoint; the authors acknowledge this but the framing ("the released score is reachable... on at least one seed") still risks over-reading a noisier picture. - The paper does not contact or test whether the maintainers would accept the proposed InvalidAction fix, so the benchmark-remediation path is unverified; the maintainers' stated reason for leaving code unchanged (comparability across submissions) is not engaged. - The Wrecker adversary is hand-specified by the authors; no sensitivity analysis of its transition-table choices (beyond the Q04–Q48 ladder for one parameter) is given, so "held delivery is worth 172.7–316.3" is a claim about one chosen adversary shape. - Five published tables are audited, but the authors' own related-work identifies 2025 papers (Castro et al., Jiang et al.) excluded for technical reasons; the audit's coverage of "every table from 2026" may not exhaust the field. - The keep-vs-H-MARL 46.40-point check-value comparison (vs. their 50.89-point score gap) is suggestive but the two check figures come from different architectures and the attribution of the leaderboard gap to busy-handling remains an accounting observation, not a causal claim. - No external party has yet re-run the artifact, so the one-command reproducibility claims are self-reported (though unusually well structured for verification). Bottom Line: This is the rare benchmark audit that every CAGE/CybORG user must act on — its findings invalidate naive cross-table comparisons on the field's primary defender benchmark and hand maintainers a specific four-item fix list — and even readers outside cyber defense will find it a rigorous template for auditing sequential-decision benchmarks generally.

DafnyCert: Certifying Specification Strength in Dafny

Á Silva, I Amaral, R Martins, A Mendes · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DafnyCert, a tool that produces independently checkable certificates of whether a Dafny specification is strong (admits exactly one output per admissible input) or weak (admits multiple), and releases the first benchmark of 3,910 Dafny methods where every specification is backed by such a certificate. - Why it's important: Verified code is only as trustworthy as its specification, and the paper shows 16.3% of strength labels in existing LLM-focused benchmarks (Dafny-Synthesis, VeriEquivBench) — whether human- or LLM-assigned — are wrong, undermining how specification-generation tools are evaluated. - How it does it: Strength is proven by verifying a two-call equivalence harness against which Dafny must show both calls return identical results; weakness is shown by mutating the implementation (MutDafny + 9 new operators), retaining mutants that still verify, and finding a witness input via Hypothesis-based property testing where the mutant and original diverge. - The good: 91.3% (3,570/3,910) of methods are certified fully automatically, the resulting labels reach MCC 0.9004 against the completed ground truth versus 0.6569 for VEB-Check and 0.4881 for ProofPulse, and every certificate can be re-checked by anyone with just `dafny verify`, `dafny run`, and a validator — trusting neither the tool nor its authors. - The missing: The dataset is filtered to exclude 2,880 of the original methods (including 2,612 that Dafny cannot verify), so all results are on verified, self-contained benchmark methods rather than industrial code, and no error bars or multi-run statistics are reported despite a random, budget-limited weakness search. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate Dafny/Verus-style specification generation or verification benchmarks — the certified dataset directly invalidates a large fraction of prior labels — and skim it if you work on mutation testing or proof-strength measurement more broadly.

Problem & Motivation: Formal verification with Dafny proves an implementation satisfies its specification, but not that the specification captures intent. An overly permissive postcondition (e.g., only `result >= 0` for a ladder-rung problem) admits multiple, divergent implementations, all of which verify — the IronFleet and CompCert specification bugs are cited as real instances. The problem has sharpened with LLM-generated specifications: benchmarks like Dafny-Synthesis and VeriEquivBench label specifications strong or weak to serve as evaluation ground truth, but those labels come from human annotators or LLMs and carry no checkable evidence. Prior tools either prove strength but cannot establish weakness (VEB-Check) or produce only heuristic scores (mutation rates, proof coverage, LLM judges). Key Idea: Turn specification-strength assessment into independently verifiable artifacts. The core insight for strength is that because Dafny reasons about a callee only through its contract, a harness that calls the method twice on the same admissible input and asserts equal outputs can verify if and only if the specification pins down a unique output — the method body is opaque, so the proof obligation reduces to: any two outputs admitted by the contract must coincide. The core insight for weakness is that a verified mutant plus one runtime witness input where the mutant and original diverge is a self-contained, re-executable proof of permissiveness. Both certificate types are templates with bounded, marked fill-in regions so a validator can detect tampering or unsound constructs (`assume`, `{:axiom}`, `{:verify false}`). Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Certify Strong: generate a harness H(S) that duplicates the input (with independent storage for mutable values), calls M twice, and requires equal results and post-states; optional ghost proof augmentations Π (lemmas, assertions, loop annotations — no `assume`) may be added. Vacuity is probed by appending `assert false` to the harness. Formal definitions: S is strong iff X_P ≠ ∅ and |A_S(x)| = 1 for all x in X_P. (2) Certify Weak: compile M to Python, sample ~200 precondition-satisfying inputs with a Hypothesis frontend that both maps Dafny types to strategies and parses common precondition patterns from the resolved AST (bounds, sortedness, uniqueness, memberships — recognizing 88.3% of 10,242 precondition elements) to construct inputs rather than filter them; concurrently, MutDafny generates mutants that are verified against the unchanged contract; alive mutants are run on the sampled inputs and any output divergence becomes a candidate certificate checked by `dafny verify`/`dafny run`. Nine new mutation operators (collection content/order, arithmetic, whole-method stub) were designed by inspecting Dafny-Synthesis weaknesses. (3) Validator: checks structure, byte-identical template grounding, absence of unsound constructs, same-input equivalence, verification success, non-vacuity, and runtime divergence; certificate producers are untrusted. Operator selection is formulated as a minimum-cost partial set cover (minimize mutants generated subject to a coverage floor p over a 491-method Selection Set). Critical design decisions: two real calls instead of VEB-Check's havoc-based encoding (justified by concrete failures where havocing loses allocation/frame information); constructive precondition-guided input generation (justified: median accepted-draw fraction 100.0% vs 11.8% unguided); reduced operator set (justified: 2.2× speedup and, due to time budgets, paradoxically more witnesses found). Key Results: On 3,910 methods (3,692 VeriEquivBench, 218 Dafny-Synthesis; 587 ultimately strong, 3,323 weak), DafnyCert automatically certifies 3,570 (91.3%): 515/587 strong (87.7%) and 3,055/3,323 weak (91.9%). Against the completed ground truth, DafnyCert reaches MCC 0.9004 (0.9226 on the 3,570 fully-classified subset) versus 0.6569/0.8837 for VEB-Check and 0.4881/0.5228 for ProofPulse. Cost: 58.0 summed CPU hours (median 2.6 s per strong certification, 35.0 s per weak) versus 2.1 h and 4.2 h for the baselines. Certified labels disagree with benchmark labels for 638/3,910 methods (16.3%): among single-method VeriEquivBench files, 252 of 359 specifications labeled strong (70.2%) are certified weak, and in human-labeled Dafny-Synthesis, 19 of 20 disagreements are strong-labeled-but-certified-weak. A manual review of 10 sampled weak→strong disagreements found the benchmark's weak label wrong in all 10. The selected 12-operator set generates 22.7% of the mutants of the full catalogue, retains 100.0% of witnesses on the Selection Set, and certifies 91.6% of weak specifications on the unseen Transfer Set; precondition guidance raises methods with at least one admissible input from 87.8% to 96.4%. The remaining 340 methods were certified via a Claude Code agent (Claude Sonnet 5) at $90.09 total ($0.27/method), all passing the same validator. Scale is standard-benchmark, not stress-scale; baselines are the current relevant tools in this niche. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (checkable weakness certificates via verified-mutant-plus-witness, and a validator-checked certificate template making both labels trust-minimized) and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (first specification-strength dataset where every label is backed by a re-checkable certificate). The strength harness is a direct improvement of VEB-Check's existing equivalence check (different encoding, broader construct support), and MutDafny, Hypothesis, and minimum-cost set cover are existing tools/techniques; the genuine novelty lies in the certificate formulation, the validator's trust decomposition, and the two-directional certification — not in any single component. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: operator-reduction is evaluated on Selection vs. Transfer Sets with an unsupervised-by-construction split, precondition guidance is isolated (E8), and a failure analysis categorizes all 340 uncertified methods (107 no admissible inputs, 145 no divergence, 72 strong-spec harness failures needing inductive lemmas). The LLM-completed ground truth is validated by the same mechanism, decoupling label correctness from label producer. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, and the weakness search is explicitly nondeterministic (random sampling + 300 s budget; 97 methods time out), so reruns may differ — the authors say so but do not quantify variance. The mutation-score fallback is correctly shown to be nearly useless at threshold τ=1 (MCC 0.0968 on uncertified methods). Code, Docker image, prompts, and certificates are archived on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/23326759). Methodological concerns: (a) the dataset excludes 2,880 methods, 2,612 of them because Dafny cannot verify them — all headline numbers are conditional on already-verified code; (b) strong-certification results are evaluated against ground truth partially completed using DafnyCert's own techniques plus LLM effort, so ground-truth errors in the 340 completed cases could bias the comparison, though the validator check mitigates this; (c) the added operators were designed on Dafny-Synthesis, which the authors flag when reporting that dataset's 98.0% transfer figure. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built tool with a large-scale evaluation). Practical: Yes — runs on a 16-core workstation with 30 GiB RAM, Dafny 4.11.1/Z3 4.12.1, packaged as a Docker image. Efficient: Weakness certification dominates cost at a median 35 s per weak method (58 CPU hours total), 25–27× more than the heuristic baselines, but this buys certificates rather than guesses; the cheap strong path is 2.6 s median. Effective: Yes for the tested population — 91.3% automatic certification and MCC 0.9004 against the completed labels, and the certificates directly demonstrate the property (unique behavior / divergent pair) rather than a proxy. Scalable: Methods are independent and embarrassingly parallel (~4.8 h wall-clock on 12 cores); the paper does not test industrial-scale code with large heap footprints or module structure, and explicitly expects that to be harder. The work delivers a software artifact (tool, validator, certificate dataset, replication package), not just a paper. Strengths: - The trust decomposition is the paper's best idea: certificates are templates whose fill-in regions the validator grounds byte-identically and screens for unsound constructs, so a bug in any producer (tool, human, or LLM agent) can cause a missed certificate but never a false one. This cleanly lets an LLM agent complete the ground truth without contaminating it. - Weakness certificates are executable counterexamples — a verified alternative implementation plus a witness input — which is strictly stronger evidence than any heuristic mutation score or LLM judgment, and the empirical payoff is concrete: 70.2% of strong-labeled single-method VeriEquivBench specifications and 19 human-labeled strong Dafny-Synthesis specifications are proven weak. - The harness encoding fix (two real calls instead of havocing) is a small but well-motivated contribution, with a concrete failure case showing why VEB-Check's encoding loses allocation and frame information. - Honest and detailed accounting of failures: the 340-method residue is decomposed per failure mode (Table 7), the mutation-score fallback's near-zero MCC at the deployed threshold is reported rather than hidden, and the tuned-threshold alternative is explicitly rejected as Goodharting. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: methods must be deterministic (randomized algorithms out of scope); strong certificates assume satisfiable preconditions and the vacuity check cannot rule out all vacuous cases due to solver incompleteness; weak certificates rely on the soundness of Dafny's compiler and its runtime precondition checks; the dataset is benchmark code, not industrial Dafny; self-referential reference types and some precondition patterns (existentials, recursive predicates) are unsupported; the weakness search is randomized and budget-limited so reruns vary slightly. These are confronted directly in §5.5 and §6, which is a credibility positive. They also correctly distinguish their intrinsic labels from the benchmarks' extrinsic intent labels. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The certified dataset is drawn from a filtered population: 2,612 of the excluded methods are excluded precisely because Dafny cannot verify them. Strength/weakness rates and certification rates may shift substantially on unverified or partially verified code, which is where LLM-generated specifications most often live — no discussion of this selection effect's impact on the headline 91.3%. - The intrinsic/extrinsic distinction is acknowledged but then partially blurred in the headline framing: a specification can be certified strong yet still be wrong relative to intent (the single Dafny-Synthesis weak→strong case proves this happens). Practitioners importing the certified dataset as ground truth for spec-generation evaluation should note it certifies uniqueness, not correctness. - Ground-truth completion for 336/340 residual methods is done by a single LLM agent with the authors' own prompt and few-shot examples; while validator-checked, systematic blind spots shared by the agent and the validator (e.g., subtly wrong proof augmentations that still verify) are not probed — no independent second rater on the completed strong certificates is reported (the manual review E10 covers only 10 VeriEquivBench weak→strong cases). - No variance quantification: given random sampling and a 300 s budget, the automatic certification rate and witness yield have unknown run-to-run spread; a handful of reruns with confidence intervals would materially strengthen the 91.9%-weak / 87.7%-strong figures. - The cost comparison against VEB-Check and ProofPulse is inherently asymmetric — those tools answer a weaker question faster — and the paper's MCC comparison is fair but the 58-hour budget is not contextualized against what an equivalently thorough baseline effort would cost. Bottom Line: For anyone building, benchmarking, or trusting LLM-generated Dafny specifications, this paper is essential reading — it both invalidates a large fraction of existing benchmark labels with checkable evidence and ships the certified replacement dataset — while readers outside the verification-aware-languages niche will find the certificate/validator design instructive but the results domain-specific.

Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II: Unlocking the Memory Potential of Pre-trained File Operations for Long - Horizon Tasks via On-Policy Distillation

L Luo, K Mao, X Yang, R Li, L Chen, K Wong, Y Guo… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CAMP-II, an on-policy distillation recipe that teaches a small agent policy to use ordinary Bash file operations as episodic memory, trained jointly across five new long-horizon environments (CAMG-II), and shows it obtains 2.97x the gain of the strongest memory-OPD baseline (64.6% vs 51.8% average success on CAMG-II for 4B students). - Why it's important: Long-horizon agents lose task-critical information when their context is replaced, and prior memory-distillation methods fail because neither the teacher nor the student has a prior over bespoke memory tools or compaction protocols, making supervision uninformative and training unstable. - How it does it: The core move is choosing the memory interface to be plain file operations that both the frozen teacher (Qwen3.8-27B) and student (Qwen3.5-4B/9B) already have a pre-training prior for, so the student emits memory actions often enough to be supervised and the teacher can rank memory content it actually understands; the OPD loss is clipped reverse-KL on student-sampled tokens with importance-ratio correction for asynchronous rollouts. - The good: The causal evidence chain is unusually complete for this area: interface ablations (swapping files for tools or compaction costs 16-17 points), a gradient-masking ablation (47.3 vs 64.6, vs 63.3 for a budget-matched random mask), paired memory-content interventions at context boundaries (intact 1.00 / shuffled 0.67 / removed 0.45 purchase score), five-seed replication (64.9 ± 0.5), and transfer to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2. - The missing: There is no supervised-fine-tuning-on-teacher-trajectories baseline, so the specific benefit of on-policy distillation through the file interface (versus cheaper offline imitation of the same teacher through the same interface) is not isolated; code is promised only at camera-ready, and the memory baselines are all recently proposed, author-reimplemented systems rather than established methods. - Read it or not: Read it if you are training small agentic models with distillation or designing memory interfaces — the two-sided "interface prior" argument and its measurement toolkit are directly actionable; skip it if you only care about frontier-scale agents, since the largest student tested is 9B.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks accumulate interaction history that exceeds the active context, so they must decide what to persist and what to read back, and when. Recent work makes memory control part of the policy via on-policy distillation (OPD), but the memory interfaces used — dedicated memory tools and context-compaction protocols — lie outside both models' pre-training. This fails on two sides: the teacher cannot score content on an interface it has never used (uninformative or negative advantages), and the student rarely samples meaningful memory actions for the teacher to score, destabilizing training. The paper asks whether a teacher can teach memory through operations both models already have a prior for. Key Idea: Treat the memory interface as the remaining free design variable in memory-oriented OPD, and select it so that both the student-side coverage requirement and the teacher-side supervision-quality requirement are satisfied by a shared pre-training prior — ordinary Bash/file operations on an episode-persistent workspace, with a bounded CONTINUATION.md written at each context replacement. Appendix B formalizes this with a two-factor cost law, N ∝ 1/(Q₀·u₀), where Q₀ is the student's initial probability of emitting the action and u₀ the initial teacher-student log-odds gap: an interface with high Q₀ and low u₀ is exponentially cheaper to teach. Methodology: CAMG-II comprises five environments (Shop: six-session WebShop purchase chains; Coding: 11,218 executable SWE-smith tasks from 93 repositories; AutoResearch: 931 OpenMLE task packages; General: MiMo enterprise tasks with rubric judging; Visual: MiMo website briefs with screenshot-based rubric grading). Each pairs a native task interface with a single Bash action and a private workspace persisting across forced context replacements; the policy must write a valid nonempty continuation file (≤8,192 bytes) before the wrapper clears the context, and only the file path survives. CAMP-II trains Qwen3.5-4B/9B students with fully asynchronous OPD from a frozen Qwen3.8-27B teacher: rollout workers generate with published weights, the frozen teacher scores every sampled token (including memory-write tokens), and the learner applies a clipped, importance-ratio-corrected reverse-KL surrogate (PPO-style clip ε=0.2, dual-clip 3) with no task rewards, no critic, 100 learner rounds × 64 episodes = 6,400 episodes per run. Critical design decisions: (i) file interface instead of dedicated tools/compaction — justified by surprisal measurements (teacher NLL on file content is lowest of the three interfaces) and by the teacher's preference accuracy for task-matched writes (76.5% on file vs 70.0% compaction, 63.8% tools, over 400 paired decisions); (ii) pure distillation without task reward — justified by comparison against task-reward CAMP-I; (iii) bounded continuation file plus free-form notes — plausible but the byte limit's value is not separately ablated. Key Results: On the CAMG-II test set (128 tasks per domain, 640 total), CAMP-II-4B reaches 64.6% average success vs 54.2% for task-reward CAMP-I, 51.8% for MemOPD w/SFT (which scores 0.0 without its SFT cold start), 48.9% Hy-Memory, 49.8% HELM single-model (36.6% as published), and 48.2% CompactOPD; the frozen 4B student is 45.3% and the frozen 27B teacher 76.0%. CAMP-II-9B reaches 66.5%, closing 63% of the student-teacher gap. Five training seeds give 64.9 ± 0.5. Training cost is ~250 GPU-hours on 8 GPUs for the 4B run. Transfer: CAMP-II-4B gains +6.9 points on both Terminal-Bench 2.1 (30.0 vs 23.1) and SWE-Bench Pro V2 (18.1 vs 11.2); CAMP-II-9B reaches 38.0 and 30.1, beating the larger Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (33.8/27.4). Notable mechanistic findings: memory actions are 21.6% of student actions on the file interface vs 7.8% (tools) and 5.9% (compaction); mean negative advantage roughly doubles from file to compaction; masked-gradient-on-memory-tokens ablation drops the average to 47.3 while a token-count-matched random mask retains 63.3. Shop saturates at 100% for both CAMP variants and the teacher, so that domain discriminates nothing. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (interface selection as the active design variable in memory OPD, with a supporting cost-law analysis) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (CAMG-II extends the authors' prior CAMG with two new domains and a standardized file-memory interface). The distillation objective itself is standard clipped reverse-KL OPD; the contribution is the argument and evidence that the memory interface must lie in the shared teacher-student prior, plus the environment suite — a genuine insight, well-instrumented, though adjacent to the authors' own CAMP-I, which already used file memory with task-reward RL. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: interface substitution, gradient masking (with a token-budget-matched control), memory-content interventions (intact/shuffled/removed), removal of the forced-write requirement (62.6 evaluated, 64.0 retrained), and five training seeds with reported standard deviation. Pre-training probes (surprisal, RSA of teacher-student similarity structure with jackknife intervals, gradient-norm and participation-ratio analyses, teacher preference with exact binomial intervals and Fisher tests) are unusually careful. Concerns: (i) code is only promised at camera-ready — no public release yet, though a project website exists; (ii) all baselines are author re-implementations of 2026 preprints or OpenReview manuscripts, some not peer-reviewed, and the 0.0% MemOPD result depends on omitting its published cold start; (iii) the method is developed and evaluated on the authors' own benchmark (Goodhart risk), partially mitigated by external transfer; (iv) transfer evaluations appear to be single runs without error bars; (v) the teacher and students are all Qwen-family models, so the "shared prior" claim is confounded with shared tokenizer/pre-training lineage and is not tested across model families. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained policies evaluated on benchmarks) with a SYSTEMS component (environment suite). - Practical: Yes — Qwen3.5-4B/9B students, a frozen 27B teacher, and Bash sandboxes run on commercial hardware; the 4B recipe took ~250 GPU-hours on 8 GPUs. - Efficient: Training is cheaper than task-reward RL alternatives at equal scale (no critic, no reward-driven exploration waste); at inference the student is 4B-9B, beating a 35B-A3B model on transfer benchmarks. - Effective: Evidence covers the stated problem on CAMG-II and transfers positively to two external suites, though SWE-Bench Pro V2 success remains low in absolute terms (18.1% for 4B). - Scalable: Untested above 9B students and a single 27B teacher — the authors state this explicitly; the asynchronous OPD infrastructure suggests scaling headroom but no 10-100x experiment is reported. The work delivers trained policies (CAMP-II-4B/9B) and an environment suite; code release is pending camera-ready. Strengths: - The two-sided "interface prior" framing is a real, transferable design insight: it converts an opaque training-instability problem (negative advantage on unfamiliar interfaces) into a measurable property of interface choice, supported by surprisal, coverage, preference-accuracy, and gradient-norm measurements. - The causal chain from mechanism to outcome is closed unusually well: the memory-content intervention (shuffled/removed memory at the boundary) and the gradient-masking-vs-random-mask contrast show the gain lives in supervised memory content, not in extra supervision budget or generic file access. - The Appendix B cost model (N ∝ 1/(Q₀u₀)) gives the empirical interface comparisons a quantitative rationale, with numerical checks of the asymptotics — rare in this subfield. - Honest baseline treatment in one direction: reporting MemOPD both with and without its SFT cold start, and HELM both as published and single-model, exposes failure modes rather than hiding them. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Limitations section states that students are capped at Qwen3.5-9B, a single frozen teacher is used, and whether gains persist at larger scale or under multi-teacher OPD is untested. The authors also confront, rather than minimize, several weaknesses in the body: MemOPD's zero-score regime, HELM's separation cost, Shop saturation, and the fact that Visual is a rubric score rather than binary success. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No SFT-on-teacher-trajectories baseline through the same file interface: without it, the paper cannot separate the value of on-policy distillation from simply imitating the teacher's file-memory behavior offline, which would be far cheaper. - The shared-prior claim is only tested within the Qwen model family (Qwen3.5 students, Qwen3.8 teacher); cross-family teacher-student pairs would test whether the effect is about the interface or about shared lineage. - The memory baselines (MemOPD, ACM, HELM, Hy-Memory) are contemporaneous preprints/OpenReview manuscripts without established reputations; the strongest OPD baseline being a method the authors must resurrect with an SFT cold start weakens the "2.97x" headline. - Transfer results are single runs without variance estimates, and Terminal-Bench/SWE-Bench evaluations exclude network-dependent tasks — a subset choice that is stated but whose sensitivity is unquantified. - Behavioral side effects of distillation (diversity loss, thinking collapse, context-restoration fragility) that the extended related work itself surveys are explicitly left out of the evaluation, so "distilled into a deployable 4B policy" is certified only by success rates. - The cost law of Appendix B is derived for a two-token reduction and acknowledged not to extend verbatim to full teacher support; it is used qualitatively to motivate design, which is fine, but the paper's framing occasionally leans on it as if it were a predictive law. Bottom Line: A practitioner training small agentic models should read this: the interface-prior argument, its measurement toolkit, and the CAMG-II environments are immediately usable, and the paper is more causally careful than its neighbors — but the missing SFT baseline and the single-family, single-teacher scope mean the headline gains should be treated as strong evidence for the interface choice, not yet for on-policy distillation as the necessary vehicle.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Game2Player, an agentic pipeline that converts 568 in-the-wild web games into state-verified task environments (3,436 tasks), uses a Builder agent plus two automated players to validate and repair them, and distills 15.7K collected trajectories (307 hours) into VLM game agents via progress-weighted SFT. - Why it's important: Training visual game agents is bottlenecked by expensive human gameplay recording and action-free online videos; skippable for those seeking a new training algorithm, as progress-weighted SFT is a modest variant of step-level filtering.
