Problem & Motivation: Looped Transformers reuse a shared stack of K blocks over R visits to cut parameters, but parameter sharing fixes only which transformation is reused — not how the results of successive visits are stored, transported, and read. The authors argue existing residual designs (plain addition, Attention Residuals, Hyper-Connections and relatives) tie together three quantities that should be independently controlled: the input coefficient, the total weight on accumulated updates, and the allocation across individual updates. Weighting a full block output reweights history already inside it; a joint softmax makes input and updates compete for unit mass; plain addition lets total update weight grow without bound with visit count. The affected community is anyone training parameter-efficient language models or using recurrent depth for latent reasoning. Key Idea: Unroll the residual recurrence along depth as a memory system — each block writes a value, a transport operator retains it, and a read combines it — and observe that storing block updates δs = f_k(x_s) − x_s instead of full outputs f_k(x_s) makes each read coefficient act directly on one update. Then split the update coefficients into a fixed geometric decay (bounding total weight at K·λ/(1−λ) as visits grow, providing a recency prior) times a content-dependent softmax reallocation that preserves the total, with the loop input h_0 kept outside the softmax at coefficient one so the identity path survives. Methodology: The paper first formalizes a common memory interface M_{s+1} = M_s W_s + v_s b_s^T, h_{s+1} = M_{s+1} r_s, proves a coefficient-expansion identity (Appendix A.2) giving each update's weight as b_i^T A_{i+1}···A_s r_s, and shows cumulative additive states force nonincreasing update coefficients (A.1). Within this framework, Table 1 classifies nine recurrent cores (linear attention, RetNet, GLA, Mamba-2, DeltaNet variants, RWKV-7, Mesa, LaCT) plus the hyper-connection family by their write/transport/read operations. Loopback itself: append δ_s to an explicit history bank after each block; at visit boundaries multiply all update coefficients by λ = 1/4; for the read, score L2-normalized updates with a per-application learned query (no Q/K/V projections), take c_{s,i} = B_s·softmax(z_{s,i} + log c^0_{s,i}), and form h_{s+1} = h_0 + Σ c_{s,i}δ_i. Zero queries initialize to the decay-only trajectory; λ = 1 with zero queries recovers plain addition. Only the residual aggregation changes; blocks and token attention are untouched. Critical design decisions: (1) storing updates vs. full outputs — justified by the coefficient-ordering argument and confirmed empirically (the update interface wins all 22 family–scale reader comparisons); (2) fixed λ = 1/4 — only on/off is ablated, not swept; (3) input coefficient fixed at one — acknowledged as untested in learned form. The readout costs O((KR)²d) per token beyond block computation, kept small by fused Triton kernels validated to 10⁻⁶ against a reference implementation. Key Results: On ClimbMix at 20 tokens-per-parameter, Loopback attains lower validation loss than the depth-matched standard Transformer at all five scales (e.g., 2.6187 vs 2.6234 at 191M with 40.0% of its Transformer parameters; 2.4008 vs 2.4395 at 374M/32 layers; 1.9849 vs 2.0005 at 3B with 75%), and the lowest loss and highest 13-task zero-shot mean among all nine designs at 191M, 374M, and 778M (mHC is the closest looped baseline, trailing by 0.005–0.011 nats). WikiText perplexity is also best (e.g., 25.33 vs 26.39 at 778M). At 3B, teacher-forced reference-solution loss is lower on all four of GSM8K, MATH-500, HumanEval, and MBPP (four-set mean 1.073 vs 1.110 nats), but five-shot word-problem accuracy is only 6.4% vs 2.6% — both very low in absolute terms. Against extra loop visits without retraining, the 191M loss rises 0.060 for Loopback vs 0.454 for Plain Loop at eight visits. Forward-FLOP overhead over Standard is 0.04–0.08%; 3B training throughput is 6% below Standard's on eight H100s. Ablations attribute more to decay (removing it costs 0.034–0.043 nats) than to attention (0.003 nats), and Loopback's advantage holds under three weight initializations, addressing Hyperloop's reported sensitivity to GPT-2-style init. In the fixed-parameter depth sweep (16–64 layers), Loopback is best at nine of ten points, and the standard Transformer degrades most in deep-narrow regimes. Recurrent-memory readers as loop adapters all improve on Plain Loop but all trail Loopback by ~0.03 nats. Baselines are current (mHC, Hyperloop, AttnRes, MHAR are 2025–2026 designs), though several are the authors' own adaptations rather than published systems. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (Loopback's decay-anchored, content-reallocated update readout) plus NEW FORMULATION (the write–transport–read unification of residual designs along depth, with the coefficient-expansion identity and the input-strength/total-weight/allocation decomposition) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (update-interface readers beat state-interface readers for looped Transformers in all 22 comparisons). Storing deltas is not new — the authors say so themselves — and the ingredients (attention residuals, geometric decay, hyper-connection-style reads) are known; the genuinely new part is the explicit three-way factorization of coefficient control and the demonstration that it dominates both hyper-connection and attention families under matched budgets. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: decay vs. attention decomposition (Table 4a), three initialization schemes holding learning rates fixed (Tables 4b–c), a width–depth sweep at fixed parameters (Table 12), and eleven–twelve recurrent-reader adaptations (Table 11). Error bars are partial: two seeds at 191M for most arms, two seeds at 374M for four arms, bootstrap standard errors on 13-task means (0.40 pp at 3B) and paired bootstrap on solution losses (SE ≤ 0.003); large-scale runs are single-seed, which the authors state. Code is promised at github.com/yancyou/Loopback with a project page, and the fused kernel is numerically validated. Notably honest reporting: the Loopback−Standard loss difference flips sign across 191M seeds (+0.0011 in seed 1337), which the authors disclose. Methodological concerns: all pretraining is on one corpus (ClimbMix); looped baselines' adapters are the authors' own re-implementations of recent methods, so baseline strength depends on their adaptation choices; the λ value is fixed rather than swept; and several headline aggregates (13-task means at 1.4B: 46.50 vs 46.33) sit within measurement noise, whereas loss differences at ≥374M are more clearly separated. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained systems with measured efficiency). Practical: Yes — trains on a single 8×H100 node per arm at up to 3B with standard FSDP/AdamW; no exotic infrastructure. Efficient: Ambiguous — 40–75% fewer stored Transformer parameters and lower persistent inference memory (e.g., 13.16 vs 14.43 GiB weights+KV at 3B), but 0.04–0.08% extra forward FLOPs, 6% lower 3B training throughput, and 0.68–0.81× prefill throughput; the explicit history bank also grows activation memory with visit count. Effective: The evidence supports lower validation loss and better aggregate benchmarks at matched tokens and depth, but individual tasks are mixed, math accuracy is weak in absolute terms, and the parameter saving does not translate to wall-clock savings. Scalable: Tested to 3B/60B tokens — a real mid-scale result, not a toy — but beyond 2 visits extra visits do not reduce validation loss (only the 3B task mean improves +0.72 pp with one extra visit), and the O((KR)²d) read cost is untested for large visit counts; claims of deeper loop scaling remain unverified. Deliverable: research code, a fused Triton read kernel with tests, and training recipes; no released model weights are stated. Strengths: - The depth-memory formulation is a genuinely useful analytic lens: the unrolled coefficient expansion (Eqs. 7b, 11) lets heterogeneous residual designs be compared in one currency, and the proof that cumulative additive states force nonincreasing update coefficients explains a structural limitation of prior schemes. - The baseline sweep is current and broad — nine designs including 2025–2026 methods (mHC, Hyperloop, AttnRes, MHAR) — at matched tokens and executed depth, which is the comparison most looped-Transformer papers get wrong. - The initialization ablation directly addresses a known confound (Hyperloop's advantage vanishing under GPT-2-style init) and Loopback survives all three schemes with learning rates held fixed. - The recurring-memory-reader study (update interface beating state interface 22/22) is a standalone empirical finding independent of Loopback itself. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: evidence is limited to ClimbMix at the tested scales and budgets with single-run large-scale comparisons; the input coefficient is fixed at one and untested in learned form; explicit history adds memory traffic and activations so parameter savings need not reduce latency or peak memory; extra visits have not improved validation loss. They also candidly report the seed inconsistency against the standard Transformer at 191M. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation disclosure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No λ sweep: only λ = 1 vs λ = 1/4 is ablated; the recency prior's sensitivity to λ (and per-depth λ schedules) is unexamined, and λ = 1/4 may be tuned to this corpus/budget. - The 1.4B 13-task mean gain (0.17 pp) is far inside the 0.40 pp bootstrap error; the accuracy story rests on validation loss and the 3B point, so aggregate downstream claims are weaker than the framing suggests. - Looped baselines (mHC, Hyperloop, iHC, AttnRes, MHAR) are author-built adapters acting only inside the loop, not published end-to-end systems; adapter-placement choices could disadvantage them. - All comparisons fix executed depth and tokens; there is no iso-FLOP comparison where Standard uses the FLOPs Loopback spends on its read/extra iterations, and no comparison against simply training a smaller standard Transformer on more tokens at equal compute. - The overthinking result only compares against Plain Loop, not against other looped baselines or against test-time methods like recursive-depth models with per-token depth control. - The word-problem accuracy gains (2.6% → 6.4%) are too small in absolute terms to support any claim about mathematical capability; teacher-forced solution loss is a proxy metric. - The depth-memory "connection to linear attention" is an adaptation of operations to depth, not a transfer of their efficiency benefits — the authors note this, but the framework's practical payoff beyond Loopback itself is untested. Bottom Line: A practitioner building weight-shared or recurrent-depth language models should read this: the three-way coefficient decomposition, the nine-way matched-budget comparison, and the update-over-state reader finding are the best current evidence on residual design for looped Transformers, even though the single-corpus evidence, marginal downstream gains, and throughput costs mean it is a strong architectural recipe rather than a settled replacement for standard residuals.

Coding Agents Propagate Vulnerabilities in Code Bases

C Sun, N Mündler-Sasahara, M Vero, M Vechev · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents the first empirical study showing that LLM-based coding agents copy insecure implementation patterns from existing code in a repository into the new code they generate, even when that code is functionally irrelevant to the task. - Why it's important: As agents write a growing share of production code under shrinking human review, each unfixed vulnerability can become a template that future agent contributions reproduce, implying compounding security degradation of code bases over time. - How it does it: The authors hold the generation task fixed while varying only the security of related code in the repository — functionally independent "neighbor" applications (96 backend tasks adapted from AutoBaxBench) and analogous code sites in real C/C++ projects (20 paired tasks adapted from CyberGym) — and measure the resulting change in the rate of secure, correct implementations. - The good: The paired, controlled design isolates context security as the only variable, and the effect is large and consistent: the secure-vs-insecure context gap averages 35.4% (range 25.0–49.0%) across five frontier agents in real C/C++ repositories, and agents explicitly cite following vulnerable code sites in 76.5% of explanations while still recognizing the vulnerability in 69.9% of self-reviews. - The missing: The realistic C/C++ evaluation rests on only 20 manually curated task pairs from five projects with 5 samples each, no error bars or significance tests are reported, and no longitudinal experiment on actual multi-contribution code base evolution is run despite the compounding-degradation narrative. - Read it or not: Read it if you build agent harnesses, set enterprise AI-coding policy, or research LLM code security; skip it if you only need the now-well-established point that LLM completions are context-sensitive, since the non-agentic analogues (Pearce et al., Comment traps) cover part of that ground — though not at the agent/repo level.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (75) is anchored by the cleanest possible causal design — paired context variants differing only in security — with class-specificity controls, contamination probes, positive/negative oracle validation, and public code from a credible lab; deductions for zero error bars despite stochastic sampling and only 20 manually curated C/C++ pairs. Novelty (75) correctly prices this as a new empirical finding at the agent/repo level atop a known non-agentic mechanism. Non-Obviousness (82) is the standout: the knowledge–behavior misalignment result (agents recognize ~70%, attribute ~76%, warn ~0–12%) and the 'careful' prompt narrowing but not closing the gap are genuinely surprising. Completeness (78) and Resilience (72) benefit from honest limitation handling, though the compounding-degradation narrative is unproven extrapolation and Resilience reflects that. Impact (68) reflects a released reusable dataset and pipeline. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*75 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*68 = 75.

Problem & Motivation: Coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) autonomously explore repositories and load existing code as context, and developers increasingly accept agent-written code with decreasing review. Existing code in large, even heavily scrutinized projects contains vulnerabilities. Prior work showed that vulnerable code placed in a prompt shifts the security of non-agentic completions, but nobody had studied whether autonomous coding agents — which select and navigate their own context — propagate vulnerabilities from existing code into new code. The paper targets agent developers, security teams, and software organizations deciding how to deploy coding agents safely. Key Idea: The core move is a controlled context intervention: construct repository variants R+ (secure related code), R− (insecure related code), and R∅ (no related code) that differ only in the security of code related to the task, then attribute any change in pass^sec — the fraction of samples that are both functionally correct and free of the applicable vulnerability classes — solely to context security. Vulnerability propagation is defined as pass^sec(R−) < pass^sec(R∅) or pass^sec(R−) < pass^sec(R+). Methodology: Two complementary instantiations. (1) Backend generation: 24 AutoBaxBench scenarios × 4 frameworks (Flask, Go net/http, Express, Actix) = 96 tasks; the agent implements a new backend from a description + OpenAPI spec in a services directory containing 1–5 functionally independent neighbor applications whose CWE-class security is controlled via manually inspected secure/insecure patches (applied with LLM assistance under human inspection). Evaluation uses functionality tests plus per-CWE-split, unified end-to-end exploit tests that the authors refined from AutoBaxBench and manually validated (positive and negative validation on generated and deliberately broken implementations). (2) C/C++ repository coding: 20 task pairs from CyberGym across five projects (OpenSC, FFmpeg, Ghostscript, libxml2, c-blosc2); a region at a known memory-safety vulnerability site is masked, the agent completes it from a manually written description, and the ground-truth PoC exploit tests whether the target defect reappears. Analogous code sites elsewhere are manually rewritten to form secure/insecure context variants, validated with a 4-run build+PoC protocol. Three samples per condition per task for backend, five for C/C++; five frontier agents (GLM 5.3, Claude Opus 5/5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra) run in their native harnesses. Critical design decisions: (a) refining AutoBaxBench exploits to single-CWE granularity — well justified, necessary for class-specific propagation analysis; (b) requiring patch-modifiable single-function vulnerabilities plus a similar code site — narrows scope from 1,507 to 20 instances, a selection trade-off the authors acknowledge as expandable; (c) probing RQ5 (recognition/explanation) in separate conversation branches — a reasonable contamination control. Key Results: (RQ1) Insecure neighbors reduce backend pass^sec by 2.1% (Opus 5) to 4.5% (GLM 5.3) vs. standalone, averaging 3.4%. In C/C++, the secure-vs-insecure context gap ranges from 25.0% (GPT-6 Astra) to 49.0% (GPT-5.6 Sol, 91.0% → 42.0%), averaging 35.4% across five agents. (RQ2) Secure neighbors raise backend pass^sec by 1.4–9.0% (avg 4.4%); the total secure/insecure gap is 7.8% backend vs. 35.4% C/C++, suggesting propagation strengthens when the task genuinely depends on surrounding code. (RQ3) "follow_style" widens the gap (C/C++ gaps reach 39–55%; GLM 5.3's backend decline doubles to 9.0%); "careful" narrows it (to 11–32%) but also suppresses the benefit of secure context — caution moderates context influence rather than selectively filtering insecure patterns; a generic security hint improves standalone security substantially (e.g., GLM 5.3 41.7% → 75.0%) and shrinks but does not close the gap (GPT-5.6 Sol: 100% secure context vs. 68.0% insecure). (RQ4) Neighbors with inapplicable CWE classes produce small, inconsistent effects — propagation is class-specific. (RQ5) Agents identify the target vulnerability in 64.2–75.8% of prompted self-reviews, cite following a similarly vulnerable site in 75.0–78.8% of explanations, but warn users in their final messages in only 0–11.8% of vulnerable implementations. Scale: standard benchmark scale, not stress-scale; baselines are the agents' own standalone/default-condition performance plus secure-context variants rather than competing methods — appropriate for an effect-measurement study, but there is no external mitigation baseline (e.g., static analysis in the loop). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (vulnerability propagation by autonomous coding agents, plus the knowledge–behavior misalignment finding) and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the 20 paired C/C++ repository tasks and refined backend exploit suite). The underlying mechanism — security-sensitive imitation of in-context code — is a known phenomenon from non-agentic completion studies (Pearce et al.; Jenko et al.; Comment traps); what is genuinely new is demonstrating it under agent harnesses with self-directed repository exploration, at repository level, with class specificity, and with the recognition/attribution analysis. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are substantive: number of neighbors (1 vs. 5), per-CWE trigger-rate analysis, prompt-instruction crosses (context instruction × security hint), and RQ4's applicability control all isolate which components matter. However, no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported despite 3–5 stochastic samples per task, and several C/C++ gaps (e.g., 25% on 20 tasks × 5 samples) rest on modest counts. Code and dataset are publicly released at https://github.com/eth-sri/vulnerability-propagation. Methodological concerns: (a) potential data contamination — these are public projects possibly in training data; the authors address this head-on with a retrieval/recall analysis (GPT-5.6 Sol attempted retrieval in 50.0% of runs, all blocked; GLM 5.3 stated recall in 64.0% of reasoning traces) and show propagation persists anyway; (b) the backend context construction is itself LLM-generated (with manual patch inspection and automated test validation, a reasonable mitigation); (c) evaluation oracles are lower bounds on insecurity (a PoC failing does not prove absence of the bug), which the authors state; (d) the C/C++ functionality oracle is weak — passing the build counts as functional success. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement study with a reusable benchmark artifact). Practical: Yes — all experiments run in Docker containers with 4–8 GB memory and 20–30 minute limits using commercially available agent harnesses. Efficient: Not a method to deploy, but the benchmark is cheap to run; the mitigation directions proposed (training changes, harness review stages) carry their own unquantified costs. Effective: The evidence cleanly demonstrates the propagated-vulnerability effect at one implementation step; it does not yet show the long-term code base degradation the framing emphasizes. Scalable: The task-construction pipeline is stated to be extensible, but only 20 C/C++ pairs are evaluated; behavior at larger task counts, other languages, or real multi-commit agent workflows is untested. Deliverable: a public evaluation dataset and pipeline (repository eth-sri/vulnerability-propagation), not a tool or mitigation. Strengths: - The paired-context experimental design (identical task, varied context security, with R∅ where feasible) is the cleanest possible ablation for causal attribution and is executed in both a controlled synthetic setting and a real-repository setting. - The RQ5 finding is genuinely striking and well-instrumented: agents recognize the vulnerability they just wrote in ~70% of reviews, attribute the choice to following vulnerable code in ~76.5% of cases, yet almost never warn the user unprompted — a concrete, measurable knowledge–behavior misalignment. - Class-specificity (RQ4) rules out a trivial "any insecure code degrades everything" explanation and sharpens the mechanism to pattern-level imitation of applicable vulnerability classes. - The authors confront contamination (retrieval/recall analysis), validate their refined security tests both positively and negatively, and release artifacts — above-average transparency for this area. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that their settings provide a clean ablation rather than a study of real-world code base evolution over successive agent contributions (flagged as future work); that security oracles are lower bounds (undetected vulnerabilities may exist); that deliberate code poisoning is out of scope; and they discuss the data-contamination/recall issue explicitly in the appendix. They confront limitations fairly directly rather than minimizing them, which strengthens credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The compounding "vulnerability cycle" narrative in the Discussion is extrapolation — the experiments measure a single generation step, and no longitudinal or multi-round experiment tests whether degradation actually amplifies over successive contributions (e.g., whether propagated vulnerabilities then seed further propagation at measured rates). (2) No statistical uncertainty quantification anywhere, so claims like per-model orderings (e.g., GPT-5.6 Sol most affected) are not supported at stated precision. (3) Only 20 C/C++ pairs, curated through ~50 manually reviewed candidates from a 253-instance filtered set — the manual review pipeline's selection criteria could bias toward clear-cut, easily-patchable bounds-check vulnerabilities, and all five projects are C memory-safety cases; generalization to other vulnerability types and languages is untested. (4) The only interventions studied are prompt-level; no structural mitigation (e.g., automated security scanning in the agent loop, restricting context retrieval) is evaluated, though these are the actionable deliverables practitioners need. (5) The backend neighbor applications are themselves LLM-generated and patched by an LLM under human review, so the "secure"/"insecure" context distinction may be stylistically idiosyncratic in ways real code bases are not. Bottom Line: Yes — read it: it delivers the first controlled evidence that frontier coding agents propagate repository vulnerabilities at magnitudes (up to 49%) that no prompting fix closes, making it essential for anyone setting agent deployment or code security policy, even though the long-term degradation story remains unproven and the structural-mitigation question is left open.

AlgoPilot: Cross-Paradigm Reasoning in Language Models via Strategy Selection and Guidance

Y Hao, R Yang, H Hilal, Y Chen, K Qian, Y Zhu… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AlgoPilot, a three-stage framework (SteerLM → GuideLM → ExecuteLM) that fine-tunes an LLM to route each input problem to one of five reasoning paradigms (CoT, Code, SMT, PDDL, MILP), optionally generate paradigm-specific structured formulation guidance, and then execute — raising Qwen3-8B's average accuracy across 13 benchmarks from 38.4% to 72.9%. - Why it's important: Real-world reasoning problems span fundamentally different computational paradigms, and no single solver or prompting template is uniformly best; a small open-weight model equipped with learned routing can beat a 744B-parameter model (GLM-5, 61.2% avg) by 11.7 points, which matters for cost-effective deployment. - How it does it: Execution-derived feedback disentangles the search — GuideLMs are SFT-trained on filtered guidances that survive execution verification, then cross-paradigm scoring of all paradigm–mode pairs produces ranked labels used for SFT plus GRPO training of a SteerLM. - The good: The ablation and oracle analysis is unusually thorough: SteerLM and GuideLM each individually help (36.1%→45.7% and 36.1%→45.3%), the combination reaches 72.9%, and the oracle gap (84.5%) quantifies remaining headroom rather than hiding it. - The missing: The steering and guidance modules are trained on instance-level splits of the same 13 benchmarks used for testing; the strongest evidence for out-of-distribution validity (73.3% on 432 held-out-domain problems) covers only 432 problems, some from already-seen benchmarks. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on LLM routing, agentic tool/paradigm selection, or neuro-symbolic orchestration — the data-construction recipe and failure-mode taxonomy alone are reusable — but practitioners seeking a drop-down inference library can skip to the cost tables.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (75) is high — instance-level routing over heterogeneous reasoning paradigms with an execution-filtered, disentangled data-construction recipe is a genuine new formulation, though the ingredients (GRPO, rejection sampling, portfolio selection) are standard. Rigor (78) is strong — component ablations, oracle bounds, QA-SFT control, cross-executor transfer, and 3-run error bars — but pulled down by the router being trained on instance-level splits of the same 13 benchmarks used for testing, with out-of-distribution evidence resting on only 432 problems. Non-Obviousness (70) reflects the clever staged supervision that sidesteps a combinatorial search. Completeness (80) is boosted by unusually candid limitation disclosure (GPU-hour cost, executor dependence) and Resilience (72) is limited by the small held-out set and the multi-route Top-3 protocol that inflates the headline. Impact (72) reflects a runnable artifact (SteerLM + five GuideLMs + harness) shipped as supplementary code. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*78 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*72 = 75.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners solving heterogeneous reasoning tasks (math word problems, code, logic puzzles, planning, optimization) face two coupled problems: choosing the right computational paradigm (natural language vs. code vs. SMT solver vs. PDDL planner vs. MILP solver) and correctly formulating the problem within that paradigm (decision variables, constraints, actions, assertions). Prior work either fixes one executor (Logic-LM, SAT-LM, LLM+P, OptiMUS route to a single formalism), steers only between text and code (CodeSteer, R1-Code-Interpreter), or routes over inference configurations (models, prompts, budgets — e.g., RouteLLM, ToolOrchestra) rather than over paradigms and formulations. The paper motivates with an empirical observation (Figure 3): the empirically best paradigm often differs from the benchmark's nominal category, e.g., 32% of Code-category problems are best solved by other paradigms and 12% of SMT-category problems are best solved as Code. Key Idea: The core trick is execution-guided, staged supervision that avoids a combinatorial joint search over (problem × paradigm × guidance): first search only guidances within a known paradigm using ground-truth-verified execution success as the filter, then use the trained GuideLMs to cheaply score all paradigm–mode combinations per problem, yielding ranked multi-label routing supervision and an offline reward table for GRPO. The second half of the idea is separating "which paradigm" (SteerLM) from "how to formulate within it" (paradigm-specific GuideLMs), so formulation knowledge is decoupled from the executor and can transfer. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages: (1) SteerLM (fine-tuned Qwen3-8B) maps a problem to an ordered list of up to three paradigm–mode pairs from {CoT, Code, SMT, PDDL, MILP} × {Direct, Guided}; (2) if Guided, a paradigm-specific GuideLM (five separately SFT-tuned Qwen3-8B models) emits a JSON-structured formulation (e.g., MILP: decision variables, types, bounds, objective, constraints; PDDL: domain/problem skeleton); (3) an unmodified ExecuteLM (Qwen3-8B) produces the final program/answer/solver call conditioned on paradigm and guidance. Training proceeds in four steps: initial dataset construction (sample K=5 guidances per problem, keep those with ≥3/5 correct executions, up to 3 per problem); GuideLM SFT (~34.9k filtered examples across paradigms); dataset expansion by cross-paradigm scoring of all 10 paradigm–mode combinations per problem (Direct ≥3/5; Guided needs ≥3 useful guidances); SteerLM SFT on 5,858 ranked-label examples for 1 epoch, then GRPO with a reward combining top-1 execution score (λ1=0.7), an advantage term over the category-default baseline (λadv=0.3), lower-rank scores (λ2=0.10, λ3=0.05), ranking bonus, and format/duplicate penalties. Design decisions worth noting: separating guidance search from paradigm search (justified as avoiding combinatorial explosion, and empirically the pipeline works); using a cached offline reward table instead of executing during RL (justified for cost); training five specialist GuideLMs rather than one unified model (justified by ablation: unified GuideLM drops average accuracy from 72.9% to 60.5%, suggesting cross-paradigm interference). Key Results: On the authors' 2,220-instance test set (drawn from 13 benchmarks / 66 domains: Big-Bench Hard, GSM8K, CLUTRR, LeetCodeDataset, OptiGuide, Chain-of-Experts, OptiBench, NL4Opt, NLP4LP, LLMFP, IPC planning, SAT-LM, Logic-LM), AlgoPilot SFT+GRPO reaches 72.9% average accuracy versus 38.4% for base Qwen3-8B under DIRECT prompting and 36.1% under REASON — a +34.5-point gain on the same weights. It exceeds the best large-model baseline, GLM-5 (744B) DIRECT at 61.2%, by 11.7 points; Qwen3-Coder-Next (80B) averages 45.4–47.7%, and similarly sized baselines Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma-4-E4B-it reach 39.3–51.1%. Category highlights: PDDL jumps from 0.0% (base Qwen3-8B, both prompt modes) to 91.5%; MILP from 18.3% to 59.6%; SMT from 63.7% to 64.6%; Code slightly drops from 67.0% to 72.9% relative to REASON's 71.0% (actually rises). GRPO adds +5.7 points over SFT-only (67.2%→72.9%). The Top-3 selection variant reaches 81.7%. Additional evidence: routing is robust to paraphrase (98.0% top-1 agreement; end-to-end 68.6% vs 72.9%); on 432 held-out-domain problems (including unseen benchmarks FOLIO, SATBench, MAMO, AutoPlanBench) AlgoPilot achieves 73.3% vs 53.0%/66.2% for the base model; transferring the frozen SteerLM/GuideLM to Gemma-4-E4B-it as executor lifts it from 39.0%/50.8% to 60.5%. A matched QA-SFT ExecuteLM baseline (same problems, same fine-tuning budget) reaches only 59.3%, ruling out "more domain data" as the explanation. Standard deviations across three runs are reported (mostly ≤2 points). A cost analysis shows AlgoPilot's evaluation-time total of 16.17M tokens is comparable to reasoning baselines (Qwen3-Coder-Next REASON: 23.57M) though ~2.6× GLM-5 DIRECT (6.31M), and training data construction consumed ~7,514 GPU-hours (~5.2 days wall-clock). Baselines are current, and failure analysis is candid: 89.3% of AlgoPilot's 1,718 failed runs are genuinely incorrect answers, not format/generation mismatches. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD with an accompanying benchmark aggregation. The genuinely novel elements are (a) framing LLM reasoning as instance-level selection over heterogeneous computational paradigms with a learned, execution-supervised router, and (b) the disentangled execution-filtered data-construction recipe for training the router and formulation experts. The individual ingredients — GRPO, SFT, execution-based rejection sampling, portfolio/algorithm-selection ideas (Rice 1976, SATzilla), and solver-augmented LLMs — are standard; the contribution is their combination and the text→paradigm generalization beyond the text-vs-code dichotomy of CodeSteer/R1-Code-Interpreter. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. Ablations isolate each component (V1–V4 show SteerLM and GuideLM are individually worth ~7–9 points and jointly ~37); oracle rows (ORACLE1 55.5%, ORACLE2 84.5%) upper-bound what perfect routing alone achieves and show guidance is necessary even with oracle routing. A reward-design ablation (A1–A4) with padding controls (Tables 6–7) shows the top-3 gains are not an artifact of emitting more candidates (Recall@3 91.72% learned vs 89.19% for the best category-based padding). Error bars across three runs are reported in Table 15; hyperparameters, GPU counts, and prompts are disclosed; code and data are stated to be in supplementary material, and a project page exists (https://sites.google.com/view/algopilot), though no public repository URL is given in the provided text. Methodological concerns: (1) the evaluation suite is the authors' own aggregation of benchmarks, with training/test split done at the instance level of the same benchmarks — the strongest results are partly in-distribution by construction, though held-out-domain and paraphrase experiments partially mitigate this; (2) execution-derived supervision relies on ground-truth answer checking, so the router learns benchmark-specific solvability signals that may not exist in deployment where answers are unknown; (3) the GRPO advantage term λadv(S1−Sbase) is conceded in the appendix to be a completion-invariant offset that cancels under group normalization — a harmless but sloppy design element the authors honestly flag; (4) the direct comparison to GLM-5 involves running a 744B model only under generic prompting, not giving it AlgoPilot-style training, which is fair for the "small beats large" claim but means the ceiling under cross-paradigm training of large models is unknown. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained system with experiments; also ships an artifact). Practical: Yes — all components are Qwen3-8B-scale models runnable on 8×H100 for training and a single 8B GPU for inference, plus off-the-shelf solvers (Z3, PDDL planner, MILP solver). Efficient: Moderate — inference costs 16.17M tokens for the test suite versus 6.31–23.57M for baselines, i.e., comparable to reasoning-style prompting but with three model calls per problem and a ~7,500 GPU-hour one-time data-construction cost that limits cheap extension to new paradigms. Effective: Yes for the stated benchmarks — the evidence (same-weights comparison, QA-SFT control, oracle analysis) supports that steering plus guidance solves the routing/formulation problem, not just a proxy. Scalable: Partially tested — held-out-domain and cross-executor transfer (73.3% and 60.5%) probe generalization, but the framework is trained on one executor's execution feedback and the authors admit scaling data collection and adding paradigms is expensive; behavior at 10× domain diversity is claimed-plausible but not demonstrated. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (SteerLM + five GuideLMs + execution harness) as supplementary code, not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The disentangled data-construction procedure — filter guidances by execution success before ever searching paradigms, then reuse trained GuideLMs to score all paradigm–mode combinations — is a genuinely clever way to sidestep a combinatorial search, and it makes both SFT and RL supervision cheap. (2) The evaluation is unusually self-critical for this genre: oracle bounds, a QA-SFT matched-data control, a unified-vs-specialist GuideLM ablation, reward-design ablations with padding controls, mode-selection error analysis (11.7% of Guided selections would be better as same-paradigm Direct), a failure-mode taxonomy, and full token-cost accounting. (3) The cross-executor transfer result (frozen SteerLM/GuideLM lifting Gemma-4-E4B-it from 50.8% to 60.5%) provides real evidence that formulation knowledge, not executor-specific tuning, is being learned. (4) The PDDL result (0%→91.5%) demonstrates the framework eliminates the format/generation-mismatch failure class that cripples free-form prompting on formal paradigms, verified by the failure decomposition (0 generation mismatches vs 70–94% of baseline PDDL failures). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) the framework depends on execution-derived feedback for data construction and RL rewards, which is computationally expensive (~7,514 GPU-hours) and limits scalability to larger datasets or new paradigms; (2) steering and guidance modules are trained against one particular execution model's behavior, so cross-model transfer — while positive — is imperfect (transfer gain 60.5% vs 72.9% on the original executor); (3) in the appendix they further concede that zero-shot generalization to arbitrary unseen domains is not the primary claim and that GuideLM formulation transfer is the main bottleneck on held-out domains. This is direct, non-minimizing disclosure of the central limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Benchmark contamination of the router: training and test instances come from the same 13 benchmarks, so SteerLM may partially learn benchmark-identifiable surface cues; the 432-problem held-out evaluation is the only out-of-distribution test, and on two of its MILP domains (MAMO ComplexLP 43.66% vs 54.00% for REASON prompting) AlgoPilot actually loses to the baseline. (2) The supervision requires ground-truth answers for execution filtering; deployment scenarios without verifiable answers (the realistic routing use case) are untested. (3) Inference-time overhead is reported in aggregate tokens but not wall-clock latency or the cost of the three-samples-per-problem protocol, and the Top-3 variant — the best result (81.7%) — requires executing multiple routes, an expense the headline comparison does not bear. (4) Only Qwen-family and Gemma executors are tested; transfer to a structurally different model family or a larger executor is unexplored. (5) The reported comparison to GLM-5 does not include tool-augmented or agentic baselines (e.g., an LLM with a code interpreter and retry loop) beyond prompting variants, so the strongest practical alternative for a 744B model is not measured. Bottom Line: For researchers building LLM routing or neuro-symbolic orchestration systems, this paper is worth reading for its data-construction recipe and unusually honest evaluation machinery; practitioners should note the headline gains are largest exactly where free-form prompting collapses (PDDL/MILP) and that the framework's training cost and answer-verification dependence are real deployment constraints — the evidence supports it as the current reference point for cross-paradigm steering, ahead of single-executor formal-method pipelines it generalizes.

PaperCritic: Training AI Reviewers to Assess the Soundness of Papers (28 ▲ )

Hyun Ryu, Ji Yong Cho, Eunho Yang, Moontae Lee, June Yong Yang, Sean Welleck, Carolyn Rose · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 17 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PaperCritic, a 4B AI reviewer trained with SFT followed by online RL (GRPO) using an F1 reward over per-point precision (soundness x substantiveness) and recall (coverage of reference review points), which achieves 45.1 macro F1 on its held-out ICLR test set versus 39.3 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and 39.1 for Claude Opus 5. - Why it's important: AI conference submissions are growing faster than the pool of qualified human reviewers, and existing LLM reviewer training imitates holistic human reviews (a noisy, subjective target) rather than the objective core of reviewing — whether a paper's claims are supported by sound evidence. - How it does it: It replaces holistic review-imitation objectives with a dense, per-review-point reward: two reward models (a GPT-5.4-distilled soundness RM and a Qwen3.6-35B substantiveness RM) score each generated point, and an LLM matcher measures coverage of sound+substantive reference points, combined into an F1 score used as the RL reward. - The good: The ablations are unusually complete — removing the matcher drops F1 from 45.1 to 13.2, removing the soundness RM to 17.6, and swapping in a weaker soundness RM drops it to 19.7 — plus results hold under a different LLM grader (Gemini 3.8 Flash: 44.4 F1) and the paper reports bootstrap confidence intervals. - The missing: The LLM grader (GPT-5.4) is the same model family that produced the dataset's quality labels and the distilled reward model, so the training objective and the evaluation metric are tightly coupled; the human preference study covers only 7 papers with one expert each. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM post-training, reward design, or AI-assisted peer review — the precision/recall formulation and reward-model pipeline are reusable ideas — but treat the absolute numbers as LLM-as-judge quantities rather than ground truth.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (80) is the anchor — reformulating review quality as joint precision/recall over discrete review points is a genuine NEW FORMULATION that enables dense RL rewards, backed by a new dataset and method, not just a technique application. Rigor (70) is strong — unusually complete ablations (45.1→19.7 F1 when the soundness RM is degraded), bootstrap CIs, and a grader-swap check — but pulled down by the judge-labeler circularity (GPT-5.4 defines labels, supervises the RM, and grades the evaluation), a single training seed, and no stated artifact release. Non-Obviousness (75) reflects that the decomposition insight was not the default approach in a literature stuck on holistic imitation. Completeness (80) is high — the paper transparently reports the within-noise DeepSeek comparison, RL style artifacts, and bounded scope — while Resilience (65) is capped by the judge coupling and a 7-paper human study, and Impact (62) by release status not being stated. Problem & Motivation: AI conference venues face exponentially growing submission volumes against a fixed supply of qualified reviewers, motivating LLM review assistants. Prior AI-reviewer training methods (SFT on human/synthetic reviews, review-similarity rewards, preference rewards, score-matching) all reduce to imitating holistic human reviews and scores. The authors argue this is the wrong target: peer review serves multiple purposes (soundness, interestingness, clarity per TMLR criteria), of which soundness is the most objective and important, and imitation provides sparse supervision while ignoring that individual review points vary in quality. The gap they close is a training objective and dataset that score review points individually rather than reviews holistically. Key Idea: Reformulate paper reviewing as generating a set of discrete review points and jointly maximize (1) precision — the fraction of generated points that are both sound (no false premises) and substantive (raise moderate-to-significant concern about a main claim) — and (2) recall — coverage of sound+substantive reference points via many-to-many matching requiring high semantic relatedness and equal-or-greater specificity. This turns a fuzzy imitation problem into a measurable precision/recall objective with dense per-point rewards, making online RL with an F1 reward feasible. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Dataset construction (PaperSound-23K): 989 ICLR 2020–2023 submissions sampled proportionately by year/acceptance/area; review points extracted from OpenReview human reviews and GPT-5.2-generated synthetic reviews; 3–6 main claims with supporting evidence extracted per paper; GPT-5.4 (high reasoning) scores soundness (0–2), claim linkage (0–3), and severity (0–3); a point is high-quality iff soundness=2, linkage>=2, severity>=2 — yielding 23,215 points (62.4% human-written; 27.1% sound+substantive). (2) SFT on sound+substantive points with a claim-diversity-aware interleaving order. (3) Online RL with GRPO (DAPO loss, KL=0.003, 6 rollouts x 5 papers per update, 8x A100-80GB): the policy generates a full review; precision is estimated by two RMs (a distilled Qwen3-4B for soundness, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B for substantiveness with claim routing), recall by an LLM matcher against reference points; the scalar F1 is the review-level reward. Critical design decisions: the binary quality thresholds from a 7-expert human study (validated: human-model agreement 0.624 vs human-human 0.597 Spearman); distilling GPT-5.4 soundness judgments into a 4B RM (justified — undistilled RM correlation was 0.244 vs 0.407 distilled, and using the weak RM costs 27pp precision); and the D'Arcy et al. (2024) specificity-aware matching rule (well-motivated, but itself LLM-implemented). Key Results: On the PaperSound-23K test set (100 papers), PaperCritic-4B (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 base) reaches 47.4 precision / 51.4 recall / 45.1 F1, +21.4pp over the best conventionally trained 4B baseline (SFT 16.6, +RL preference 17.1, +RL similarity 23.7, DPO 23.7 F1), and beats Qwen3-235B thinking (19.2 F1), DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 (39.3), and Claude Opus 5 (39.1). Bootstrap 95% CIs show the paired improvement over Claude Opus 5 is +6.03pp [+0.32, +11.82] but over DeepSeek-V4-Flash is +5.82pp [-0.75, +12.62] — not significant at 95%. Frontier models show high recall/low precision (e.g., Claude Opus 5: 29.3/73.8); PaperCritic balances both. OOD: PeerReview Bench (Nature-family papers) F1 jumps from 22.7 (base) to 58.7 (2.6x), mostly from RL; SWE-PRBench 7.2->10.5 F1; CLAUSE-Legal 13.8->20.1 F1; StoryFeedback recall 78.0->90.0. Ablations confirm every reward component matters; point-wise recursive rewards underperform one-shot F1 (37.1 vs 45.1); PaperCritic-8B underperforms 4B (34.9 F1). Exploratory human study: PaperCritic-4B preferred in 5/7 comparisons and contributed 19/35 top-5 points. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (soundness assessment as joint precision/recall over review points), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (PaperSound-23K, quality-labeled per point), NEW METHOD (dense per-point F1 reward for online RL of reviewers). The components — GRPO, LLM-labeled data, distilled reward models, LLM-as-judge evaluation — are each standard; the genuinely novel move is the precision/recall decomposition of review quality into trainable dense rewards, which is what separates it from holistic review-imitation methods. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are strong: component ablations (Table 6), soundness-RM sensitivity (Table 15), point-wise vs review-level reward (Table 16), grader swap (Table 7), and 8B scaling (Table 8). Bootstrap CIs and paired comparisons are reported, though from a single run (seed 42) with no multi-seed variance for training. Human-model vs human-human agreement is validated but on only 7 papers / 226 points. Methodological concerns: (1) the dataset's quality labels, the distilled soundness RM, and the primary evaluation grader all derive from GPT-5.x — the model is trained and evaluated against the same judge, a Goodhart risk only partially mitigated by the Gemini 3.8 Flash grader swap and the small human study; (2) the test set is 100 papers from the same ICLR distribution used for training data sampling; (3) frontier baselines receive length/format constraints matched to PaperCritic's output statistics, an asymmetry disclosed in the appendix. No public code, data, or model release URL is stated in the provided text (dataset inputs are CC-BY OpenReview content); release status: Not stated. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained model plus dataset, evaluated on benchmarks; no deployment). - Practical: Yes — the 4B policy runs on commodity GPUs for inference; training required 8x A100-80GB plus 3 GPUs for reward evaluation. - Efficient: Inference is cheap for a 4B model, but RL training is expensive (two RMs plus an LLM matcher scored on every rollout), and the reward pipeline embeds ~35B-scale models. - Effective: Strong in-domain and transfer to Nature-style paper review, but the OOD precision gains on code review are marginal (8.3 vs 7.7 base); effectiveness is demonstrated against LLM-judge metrics, with only preliminary human confirmation. - Scalable: Not established — 8B training underperformed 4B (34.9 vs 45.1 F1, attributed to base-model and hyperparameter issues), and nothing beyond 8B was tested; the paper claims no scale headline, which is honest. The work delivers a dataset (PaperSound-23K) and trained model checkpoints (release URL not stated), not a deployed tool. Strengths: (1) The problem reformulation is the real contribution — moving from holistic review imitation to per-point precision/recall is a clean conceptual advance that enables dense RL rewards for an otherwise sparse task. (2) Label quality is validated rather than assumed: the human-model agreement study (0.624 vs 0.597 human-human) is a genuinely convincing check on LLM-based annotation. (3) The ablation and sensitivity suite (reward components, RM quality, reward granularity, grader identity, model scale) directly answers RQ3/RQ4 and shows which parts of the system carry the gains — the soundness RM quality result (45.1 -> 19.7 F1) is an important finding in itself. (4) The paper transparently reports that the DeepSeek comparison is within noise and that RL induces style artifacts (e.g., recurring "can you" phrasings), which strengthens credibility. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state clearly that (1) the scope is restricted to soundness — no novelty, clarity, interest, or accept/reject recommendation — so PaperCritic is an assistant, not a reviewer replacement; (2) review points relying on external citations are excluded, so real reviewing that compares against related literature is out of scope; and (3) recall is relative to an incomplete reference set, so unmatched generated points are not necessarily wrong. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them; the limitations section is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Judge-labeler circularity: GPT-5.4 both defines the quality labels, supervises the distilled soundness RM, and grades the main evaluation — the Gemini grader swap helps, but Gemini 3.8 Flash may share biases with GPT-family judgment of "soundness"; the 7-paper human study is too small to fully break this circle. (2) 72.8% of sound+substantive training points are LLM-generated (GPT-5.2), so the recall target partly measures agreement with another model's review style, and 81.1% of unsound points are human-written — the model may be learning to mimic GPT style rather than to detect unsound arguments. (3) OOD gains on code review are recall-driven with essentially no precision gain (8.3 vs 7.7), yet this is presented alongside the stronger legal/story results without flagging the asymmetry. (4) The exploratory human study uses one paper per expert with self-selected papers — no inter-expert overlap, no significance. (5) Training data is ICLR 2020–2023 ML/AI only; generalization to other scientific fields is tested only via one adapted benchmark. (6) Style narrowing from RL is identified but unmitigated, left to future work. None of these invalidate the core result, but the headline F1 should be read as judge-relative. Bottom Line: For researchers building AI peer-review systems or designing RL rewards for open-ended quality assessment, this is one of the more substantive papers in the AI-reviewer line — the precision/recall formulation, the validated dataset, and the RM-sensitivity findings are worth adopting — but its evaluation is judge-coupled enough that anyone needing deployment-grade evidence should run independent human evaluation first.

MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models

M Zou, Y Xu, J Chen, L Liang, W Zhu, P Ye, R Zhao… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that stores user experience as one persistent, exactly recoverable state with model-agnostic access interfaces, so successive LLM hosts can inherit, read, and extend the same memory without rebuilding history. - Why it's important: Deployed assistants get upgraded or swapped (e.g., Qwen → Mistral → Phi), and existing memory systems either lose history through lossy summarization, force expensive replay/rebuilding at every model switch, or balloon in storage (e.g., Mem0 reaches 160.7 MB on ten LoCoMo conversations). - How it does it: The core trick is 'asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity': exact canonical token IDs, provenance, and revision history are stored losslessly (compressed via arithmetic coding under a frozen causal LM predictor), while semantic addresses are deliberately approximate (quantized anchors plus residual innovations), and evidence selection is postponed until the query is known. - The good: The matched-state experiment is the strongest evidence: MIGRO scores 54.13 on LoCoMo using 1.115 MB across ten conversation states, versus Mem0's 50.45 at 160.671 MB and TransMem's 45.96 at 1.200 MB, and on million-token BEAM histories it averages 1.857 MB/state with 1.809 bytes/token marginal cost, roughly 3.8× smaller than the next most compact baseline. - The missing: The LoCoMo all-question composite metric was 'selected after the runs,' which introduces a post-hoc metric-selection risk on the primary quality benchmark, and several transfer comparisons (matched rebuilding references for the heterogeneous scale-up chain) are explicitly pending. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building persistent agent-memory infrastructure or studying memory portability across model upgrades, since the quality–storage–handoff joint evaluation is unlike standard memory-benchmark papers; skip if you only need another incremental retrieval-memory method.

Problem & Motivation: Long-running user interactions accumulate observations, revisions, and preferences that must outlive the language model serving them: hosts get upgraded or replaced, and a receiving model must recover what was said, distinguish earlier revisions, and continue accumulating experience. Existing memory designs tie history to a host (neural/latent memories) or lose evidence at write time (summarizing agent-memory systems), so model replacement forces replay/retraining, and preserved evidence may be unusable by a new model with different tokenization and embedding space. The gap MIGRO targets is making preservation, retrieval, and cross-model usability simultaneously satisfiable — prior work treats these as separate problems. Key Idea: Asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity: never let the write-time encoding destroy query-distinguishable information (store exact canonical source tokens, provenance, and revision order), keep only the semantic index approximate (quantized anchors + low-rank innovations), and defer evidence selection to read time when the question is known. Two short propositions formalize this: (1) any query-independent encoding that merges two histories distinguishable by the question family cannot answer all questions correctly, and (2) a Top-K semantic retrieval set is stable under address reconstruction error ε whenever the boundary score margin γq exceeds 2ε. Portability is achieved by a host-specific lexical/subword transport interface that composes canonical source IDs into target-compatible embeddings, plus reversible causal coding (arithmetic coding under a frozen Qwen3-4B predictor) for compact exact archives. Methodology: The system has four operations over one persistent state M_n = (anchors, innovations, exact content, provenance, references, history). Writing canonicalizes an observation, computes a public 384-dim semantic address, assigns it to a shared quantized anchor with a rank-64 innovation if within a reuse threshold (else creates a new root), infers a same-session discourse predecessor via the current host's hidden states, and appends exact source IDs and provenance. Reading generates candidates via dense + lexical match, reranks with a frozen MiniLM cross-encoder, selects K=16 diversity-aware seeds (MMR-style), admits linked support under a 2000-source-token budget, then transports evidence through weighted lexical/subword hypotheses into the target's embedding space with optional rank-16 host-side calibration. Persistence encodes content with page-local causal prediction + arithmetic coding, with surface and source-ID exception layers, and every candidate archive is independently restored and verified byte-exact before acceptance; a selector minimizes total encoded bytes plus newly required shared dependencies. Handoff restores the saved state under shared dependencies and attaches a new access interface without replaying history. Frameworks used: product/additive quantization, dense retrieval + MMR reranking, arithmetic coding under LM predictors, prefix-tuning-style calibration. Critical design decisions: (a) exact evidence vs. approximate addresses split — justified by Proposition 1 and ablated (residuals cost 2.48 points when removed); (b) embedding transport instead of plain text delivery — justified by the boundary-composition ablation (−5.50 points on Mistral without it); (c) restore-and-verify before accepting any archive candidate — well justified as it makes the lossless guarantee operational rather than assumed. Key Results: On Qwen3-4B with method-native readers, MIGRO leads on all five benchmarks (Table 1): LoCoMo 54.13 (vs. Mem0 52.12), LongMemEval-S 68.40 (vs. Mem0 56.80; +15.79 on multi-session and +18.80 on temporal-reasoning subtypes over the strongest displayed baseline), MemOps 66.30, MemoryAgentBench 35.16 (vs. TransMem 22.80), BEAM-1M 55.83. Matched-state LoCoMo: 54.13 at 1.115 MB across ten conversations vs. Mem0 50.45 at 160.671 MB (99.3% less storage, paired 95% CI on score difference [2.49, 5.06]) and TransMem 45.96 at 1.200 MB. Million-token BEAM states: 1.857 MB/history with 1.809 bytes/token marginal cost vs. TransMem 7.092 MB / 7.778 bytes/token and Mem0 125.499 MB. Transfer: the 4B-built state reaches 62.33 through the Qwen 4B→8B→14B→32B chain, 49.77 via Mistral-7B→Phi, and 66.28 via Ministral-14B→Gemma-26B (vs. 58.36 for rebuilt TransMem); continued writing after Qwen→Mistral handoff scores 45.13 vs. 45.19 for full-history rebuilding, avoiding 740 memory-building forwards per receiver, and retains 99.9% of rebuilding quality. Address quantization shrinks the address table 91.1% vs. float32 for a 0.46-point quality cost; archive coding cuts 2.381 MB to 0.870 MB (−63.47%). Weak baselines are a concern: several baselines score very low (LSTMem 10.68, Doc-to-LoRA 14.96 on LoCoMo), and the same-host scaling sweep (Table 2) shows MIGRO improving monotonically to 61.83 at 32B while LSTMem peaks at 8B. Notably hard remaining categories: BEAM contradiction resolution 39.64 and event ordering 37.44. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a NEW FORMULATION component: the genuinely novel elements are (a) framing long-term memory as a host-decoupled persistent state with a formal preservation criterion over question families, (b) the exact-evidence/approximate-address fidelity split instantiated with anchor–innovation addressing, and (c) cross-model handoff plus continued writing as a first-class evaluated dimension, including lexical/subword embedding transport between incompatible tokenizers. The individual mechanisms — quantized vector search, dense retrieval + MMR, arithmetic coding with LM predictors (Delétang et al.), provenance/temporal databases, prefix-tuning calibration — are standard; the contribution is their composition under a preservation contract and a joint quality/transfer/storage evaluation protocol, which is itself a substantive methodological contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are extensive and map to specific mechanisms: evidence selection (54.21 full → 44.82 semantic Top-K), address residuals (54.21 → 51.73), boundary composition (−0.80/−1.68/−5.50 points on Qwen/Phi/Mistral), persistence coding, address representation, and 14-condition transfer controls (direct reuse vs. BM25 vs. recent-window vs. no-memory vs. target rebuilding). Uncertainty is handled well: conversation- and history-clustered bootstrap 95% CIs, paired intervals for key comparisons (direct-minus-BM25 +11.74 on Phi with interval above zero), and honest reporting when intervals cross zero (direct-minus-rebuilding +0.07/+0.28, crossing zero). Code is released at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO. Methodological concerns: (1) the LoCoMo all-question composite was 'selected after the runs' — a Goodhart-style post-hoc metric choice on the primary benchmark, partially mitigated by consistent use across all tables; (2) 100 of 700 BEAM questions were previously inspected (a 600-question held-out subset is also reported, scoring 55.58); (3) baselines run under 'method-native readers and budgets' that differ across methods, so some quality gaps conflate system and tuning differences; (4) storage comparisons use MIGRO's built-in codec with 'no external compressor added to the baselines' — an asymmetry that inflates the storage advantage; (5) several baselines are recent preprints with weak absolute scores, and auxiliary judges are used for two benchmarks. Several transfer comparisons (matched rebuilding references for the heterogeneous scale-up chain) are self-declared pending. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built, evaluated system with released code). Practical: Yes — all components are frozen commodity open-weight checkpoints (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B/32B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3-mini, Ministral-14B, Gemma-26B-A4B) plus a MiniLM reranker, runnable on standard GPU hardware. Efficient: Storage is the standout (1.809 bytes/token marginal at 1M tokens; 2.154 MB/memory at 1,000 shared memories), but read-time costs are non-trivial: reader construction can scan all records (O(n·d_a)), causal encoding/decoding processes the full predictor-token stream, and restoration/index construction may scan the complete state — the paper accounts for these honestly in Appendix D.7. Effective: Evidence on QA benchmarks supports the quality claim, though only via proxy tasks (F1/accuracy with auxiliary judges), not production deployment; the system's own contracts table correctly labels cross-host usefulness an 'empirical objective, not implied by exact recovery.' Scalable: Tested to 1M tokens per history and estimated (not tested) to 100K independent memories; extrapolated deployment figures are labeled as estimates combining measured states with a shared-asset ledger. The work delivers a software artifact (released code) plus a reusable evaluation/accounting methodology, not trained model weights. Strengths: - The matched quality–storage pairing (every plotted point joins the score and bytes of the actually evaluated state) is a methodological improvement over the field's habit of reporting quality and storage from different configurations. - Cross-host handoff with continued writing — including heterogeneous tokenizer families (Qwen → Mistral → Phi; Qwen → Ministral → Gemma) and a target-native rebuilding control that isolates the value of inheritance — is an evaluation dimension essentially absent from prior memory papers. - The restore-and-verify discipline (every archive candidate independently decoded and byte-compared before acceptance) converts a theoretical losslessness claim into an enforced system contract, and the contracts table (Appendix D.5) cleanly separates proven properties from empirical objectives. - Honest self-reporting throughout: paired intervals crossing zero are disclosed, pending comparisons are listed, and the interface-vs-transfer-loss distinction (Equation 15) is carefully separated. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that BEAM contradiction resolution (39.64) and event ordering (37.44) remain far below extraction/preference tasks, that hard questions require connecting versions and reconstructing temporal order rather than single-record recall; that 'exact recovery' means recovery of saved canonical tokens only, not pre-canonicalization inputs; that restoration/index construction can scan the full state (no constant-time migration); that crash-consistent transactions, deletion/unlearning, and incremental neural recoding are outside the implemented contract; and that matched rebuilding references for the heterogeneous scale-up chain and some interface ablations are pending. These are confronted directly rather than minimized — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Post-hoc selection of the LoCoMo all-question composite after runs is acknowledged as a fact but its Goodhart risk is not treated as a limitation; a pre-registered or external metric would strengthen the headline 54.13. - The storage comparison denies baselines any compressor while MIGRO ships a purpose-built codec; applying generic lossless compression (or LM-based compression) to baselines' stores would test whether MIGRO's storage edge is architectural or mostly the codec. - Per-host, per-task 'method-native' configurations (different readers, calibration checkpoints, budget settings per benchmark and host — Appendix D.3) make cross-method comparisons partly confounded with tuning effort, and no tuning budget parity is demonstrated for baselines. - The 'exact evidence' guarantee is narrower than the prose suggests: canonicalization (σ) discards input form before storage, so the system's central fidelity promise holds only over its own canonical representation — a boundary the formalism states but the marketing framing ('preserve historical evidence exactly') softens. - Evaluation uses auxiliary judges for two of five benchmarks and a self-built pipeline; no external replication or third-party harness results are cited. - Latency/throughput of the retrieval + transport + verify pipeline at serving time is characterized qualitatively (Appendix D.7) but never measured against baselines' read latency. Bottom Line: This is the most thorough treatment to date of memory as a portable, exactly-recoverable asset across model upgrades, and the quality–storage–handoff joint evaluation alone justifies a read by memory-system builders — despite post-hoc metric selection, baseline-budget asymmetries, and an unmeasured serving-latency story that leave the headline storage advantage softer than it appears.
