Problem & Motivation: Teams training large language models — and the researchers who study them — face a transparency crisis: open-weight models ship final checkpoints while the data, intermediate states, and decisions behind them are "rarely released." This forces anyone wanting to study scaling behavior, data-mix effects, RL recipes, or training stability to run expensive ablations from scratch. A second problem is compute efficiency at mid-scale: making a ~37B-total-parameter MoE model match a 32B dense model would make self-hosted agentic assistants far cheaper. The work closes the gap between "open weights" and genuinely reproducible frontier model development, and simultaneously probes whether sparse attention-side scaling can substitute for dense parameter count. Key Idea: The single sharpest idea is Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA): route tokens sparsely over V=64 nonlinear value-expert projections (SiLU applied per projection to break linearity, since a mixture of pure linear projections collapses to one input-dependent linear map), selecting 4 per token, which adds a sparsity axis orthogonal to FFN-MoE while leaving the KV cache unchanged (only mixed values are cached). A second, arguably more consequential idea for the field: choose the pre-training data mix by predicted benchmark scores at production scale — fit per-validation-set scaling laws on a 33-model grid (36M–1.5B params, up to 59B tokens), extrapolate losses ~20× beyond the largest fitted model, then map losses to 13 benchmark scores with a LARS-Lasso sparse regression — which reversed the ranking obtained from measured 1.5B-run scores (web-heavy predicted best at 31.2B at 57.4 vs. 55.1 for SFT-heavy, which was best at 1.5B at 40.5 vs. 36.6). Methodology: The lifecycle is pre-training → mid-training → RL domain experts → weight merging → SFT (per model, with size-specific variations). Pre-training uses AdamW (β₁=0.9, β₂=0.95, clip 1.0), a fitted LR scaling rule η ∝ N^(−1/2), a shared AdamW timescale (τ_epoch·√T_PP ≈ 2.6–2.9), and — for all models except the 0.9B — no learning-rate decay, with decay realized implicitly by averaging final checkpoints before mid-training. Mid-training runs four stages (32k→128k→512k context, RoPE base 1M→10M, ~1.9T tokens) introducing agentic trajectories from the first context-extension stage. Post-training for the 375B trains five RL domain experts (search, knowledge work, tool use, scientific reasoning, instruction-following-with-abstention) in sandboxed verifier-scored environments, merges them via ISO-RAM weight merging, and applies targeted SFT; small models add FTPO on preference pairs mined from the model's own repetitive loops, and the 0.9B alternates math/code RL to avoid entropy collapse plus multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Data: ~10T synthetic pre-training tokens across math (250M problems, teacher–student Socratic dialogues from GPT-OSS-120B), code (259M synthesized tasks with 50.3M knob configurations), IF-constrained reasoning, and search-grounded "behaviors" (1.1B documents, 3.18T tokens via Search360, a FAISS index over 994M documents), with diversity verified by a custom compressor (WZIP) tracking natural-data compression trends. Infrastructure: xLLM (FSDP/ZeRO-3 + tied TP≡EP=8 intra-node, CP up to 4 at 512k, no pipeline parallelism) and RL360, run on H200 clusters with a 30-minute-cycle loss monitor triggering automated rollbacks. Uno adapters distill the AR models into diffusion decoders for up to 2.2× lossless decoding speedup without a draft model (details in §9, beyond the excerpt). Key Results: (1) The 36B-A4B MoVA model's pre-training loss closely tracks the same-data 32B dense model, trailing by only 1.2–3.7 points on MMLU, GSM8K, HellaSwag, and HumanEval at ~1/7 active parameters (4.7B vs. 32.2B). (2) The four shared-corpus models (3.7B/7B/32B dense, 36B-A4B MoVA) show nearly identical normalized loss curves across ~10× parameter range, empirically confirming Bergsma et al. (2026) scaling collapse at production scale. (3) The 375B-A23B flagship base model (after mid-training) scores MMLU 89.5, MMLU-Pro 82.6, GPQA Diamond 84.9, AIME 2026 92.5, GSM8K 95.1, MBPP 93.8, IFEval Avg 92.1, versus GLM-5.1 (754B-A40B), GLM-4.7, MiniMax-M2.7, and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B — leading on AIME 2026 and GSM8K, trailing ~3–4 points on MMLU/MMLU-Pro. The abstract additionally claims first or second place on most agentic/coding benchmarks among contemporaneous open models, Toolathlon-Verified 65.3 (above GPT-5.6 Terra), SWE-Atlas-QnA 48.4, and Uno speedups up to 2.2×; the 7B and 3.7B reportedly lead SWE-bench Verified "by wide margins" within their size class. Baselines are contemporaneous (GLM-5.1, Qwen3.5, MiniMax-M2.7, Nemotron 3 Ultra), i.e., current and strong, though evaluations are self-run in the authors' own harness. Notably, the flagship's admitted weakness is expert-level scientific reasoning (HLE, CritPt). A counter-intuitive operational finding: 43–67% of loss-spike episodes occur in the last 60% of training under constant-LR schedules (vs. front-loaded spikes under cosine decay), and gradient norm carries predictive signal only in the final ~10 steps before a spike. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the complete six-model open lifecycle release with 380 checkpoints, logs, and pipeline code — the fullest disclosure of its kind), NEW METHOD (MoVA; softplus attention gate with β=log 2 giving identity at init), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (production-scale confirmation of loss-curve collapse across dense/sparse architectures; demonstration that small-scale data-mix rankings invert at production scale; spike-timing analysis under constant-LR schedules). The MoE-FFN, DeepSeekMoE fine-grained experts, GQA, RoPE, SwiGLU, and SFT/RL merging are standard components competently combined; Uno extends existing diffusion-AR hybrid work rather than inventing it. Rigor & Reproducibility: Exceptional on reproducibility infrastructure: Apache 2.0 models, CC BY 4.0 web data, 17 code repositories (github.com/ifm-ai), public W&B logs (forge.coreweave.com/wandb/llm360), 380 versioned checkpoints loadable by revision tag, benchmark decontamination via 8-gram inverted-index matching over 208 registered benchmarks (197,149 matches removed from 88,625 documents; contamination rates ≤0.026% per dataset), and all external models evaluated in one open harness (Eval360). Ablations exist for the data mix (three candidates × scaling-law prediction) and LR sparsity transfer (six-layer MoE sweeps, 4–128 experts), but are small-scale proxies. Missing rigor markers: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are stated for any benchmark comparison; the MoVA result rests on a single (36B-A4B) configuration with one dense control; and the two-stage loss→score prediction pipeline is fitted and evaluated against the same benchmark suite used to justify the final mix, a moderate Goodhart risk. The provided excerpt cuts off mid-§5.5, so §6–11 (RL algorithms, post-training evaluation tables, safety) cannot be verified from the text given. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained models with measured benchmarks) with a SYSTEMS component (xLLM, RL360, Eval360, Uno). - Practical: Yes — six sizes spanning a 2.2 GB phone-scale model to a 758 GB multi-GPU flagship, with FP8/NVFP4/GGUF/MLX quantizations for consumer and mobile deployment. - Efficient: The 36B-A4B achieves 32B-dense-near performance at ~1/7 active parameters; Uno claims up to 2.2× decode speedup losslessly (claimed, with experiments deferred to the unseen §9.4); flagship training took ~120 days on H200 nodes. - Effective: Effective on math, coding, and agentic-tool benchmarks relative to contemporaneous open models, with self-run evaluations; effectiveness at the claimed frontier-agentic level rests on comparison tables not included in the provided text. - Scalable: Demonstrated from 0.9B to 375B and 22T tokens with consistent scaling behavior across four same-recipe models; claims about further scale are not tested but the released scaling laws support extrapolation. The work delivers concrete artifacts: six trained models, 380 checkpoints, ~21.6 TB of data, and 17 code repositories, plus reusable techniques (two-stage benchmark-score prediction; WZIP diversity metric; ISO-RAM merging). Strengths: - The most complete open release in the LLM360 lineage: not just weights but per-stage checkpoints (58 logged training runs), the actual data with regeneration pipelines, and honest failure documentation (40 rollbacks, deepest 4,217 steps, a documented case where training spiked at the same step across ten resumes and required a deep manual rollback). - MoVA is a genuinely new sparsity axis with a clean engineering argument: compatibility with FlashAttention/GQA and zero KV-cache overhead, plus a correct observation that SiLU per expert is required to prevent the mixture collapsing to a single linear map. - The predicted-at-scale data-mix decision is a methodological contribution in itself — the measured-vs-predicted ranking inversion (SFT-heavy best at 1.5B, predicted worst at 31.2B) is the kind of result that changes how practitioners run ablations. - The four-model controlled corpus (two pairs with identical batch orders) converts a model release into a scientific instrument for scale/sparsity studies. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state directly that the flagship's main gap is expert-level scientific reasoning (HLE and CritPt, §7.2); that most synthetic pre-training data is unverified (math solutions unchecked, code never executed), justified by a tokens-not-documents argument they flag openly; that >80% of collected math problems are procedurally generated with suboptimal diversity (the "Is it prime?" box: 4% of problems, 59–70% of over-budget generations); that the 0.9B's math-RL initially caused entropy collapse requiring a workaround; that the loss monitor has deliberately "no guard against resuming repeatedly from the same checkpoint"; and that unverified Socratic dialogues may contain teacher-missed correct attempts (50–80% first-try acceptance unexamined). They confront limitations candidly rather than minimizing them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting: single-run, single-seed benchmark numbers throughout, with no confidence intervals on the headline claims (e.g., "leads SWE-bench Verified by wide margins" is unquantified in the provided text). - The 32B and 36B-A4B are released pre+mid-training only (no post-training), so the MoVA-vs-dense comparison at deployment quality is incomplete; the dense model "maintains a modest lead" in loss that may compound after post-training. - The data-mix selection procedure is validated only by its final adoption — no post-hoc confirmation that the web-heavy mix actually beat SFT-heavy at 32B is reported in the excerpt. - Stage 2 of score prediction is fitted on checkpoints up to 7B and applied to extrapolated losses ~20×/340× beyond the fitted grid; extrapolation error is unquantified. - Heavy dependence on other vendors' models as teachers (GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3.5-397B, Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash) raises both a provenance/licensing question (partially addressed by license-compliant filtering) and a ceiling question: the fleet's reasoning distribution is downstream of Qwen/GPT-OSS teachers, confounding attribution of gains to MoVA or the recipe. - Training-dynamics findings (spike timing under constant LR) are observational with a stated hypothesis, not causally established. Bottom Line: Any team training or studying large models gains more per page from this report than from almost any contemporary LLM paper — the MoVA idea alone is modest, but the predicted-at-scale data-mix methodology, the fleet-level scaling-curve evidence, and the unprecedented release completeness make it essential reading, with the caveat that its competitive benchmark claims are vendor self-reported and should be treated as provisional until independent replication.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a cross-lingual poverty-of-stimulus (CPOS) experimental design showing that language models can partially transfer hierarchical syntactic generalization (subject-verb number agreement) from a source language L1 to a target language L2, but only when the L1 and L2 token vocabularies overlap. - Why it's important: It causally isolates whether cross-lingual transfer reflects abstraction of language-universal structure versus mundane artifacts like shared vocabulary or better initialization, which matters both for multilingual LM design (tokenizer choices) and for using LMs as models of human second-language acquisition. - How it does it: It counterfactually contrasts continued-pretraining scenarios where positive evidence for the hierarchical agreement rule (attractor-bearing sentences, deep clausal embedding) exists only in the L1 corpus while the L2 corpus is deliberately ambiguous between linear and hierarchical rules, then manipulates L1-L2 shared token IDs (FULL / 1K / NO overlap). - The good: The vocabulary-overlap intervention is decisive: transfer on CLAMS is credibly positive with overlap (Δhier = 0.121 log-odds [0.092, 0.150] overall) and not credible without it (0.025 [−0.025, 0.074]), established via a Bayesian mixed-effects model over 72 independently trained runs with item and run random effects. - The missing: All experiments use GPT-2-small with a frozen Transformer during L2 training and L2 fixed as English, so the central claim — that transfer is conditional on vocabulary overlap — is untested at scale, under full fine-tuning, and beyond one target language and one syntactic phenomenon. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in multilingual NLP, syntactic generalization, or LM-as-cognitive-model work who need to know that tokenizer vocabulary overlap gates even abstract syntactic transfer; skippable for practitioners seeking deployable multilingual methods, since nothing here is yet a training recipe.

Resilience (75) is good — claims are carefully bounded — though intermediate realistic overlap levels and full fine-tuning are untested. Impact (55) is the weak leg: a reusable experimental framework, but a laboratory phenomenon, not a deployable training recipe. Problem & Motivation: Language models transfer well across languages through continued pretraining, but the mechanism is unclear. One hypothesis is that LMs abstract language-universal properties — notably hierarchical structure — from source-language (L1) data and reuse them when learning a target language (L2). Competing explanations (sheer data-volume scaling, improved non-linguistic initialization such as position embeddings) coexist with any observed transfer. Prior work on hierarchical generalization (the poverty-of-stimulus line from McCoy et al. 2020 onward) is monolingual: the language supplying positive evidence and the language evaluated on coincide, so it cannot tell whether the acquired hierarchical bias is language-specific or a language-general abstraction. Someone needs a controlled, counterfactual design that isolates the causal flow of linguistic evidence from L1 to L2 — relevant to multilingual model builders, linguists probing learnability, and psycholinguists using LMs as references for human L2 acquisition. Key Idea: Make the L2 corpus deliberately ambiguous between a linear and a hierarchical agreement rule (no attractor sentences, no deep embedding) while positive evidence for the hierarchical rule exists only in the L1 corpus; any above-chance hierarchical generalization at L2 must then be transferred L1 evidence, and its dependence on confounds can be tested by ablating shared vocabulary (offsetting shared token IDs into disjoint ID ranges). The core trick is the cross-lingual transplant of the established monolingual POS paradigm, plus the vocabulary-overlap counterfactual borrowed from Kallini et al. (2025). Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Corpus construction: Wikipedia corpora for four L1s (English, German, Russian, Japanese) are parsed with Stanza and each sentence classified as positive-evidence (contains attractor NPs between subject and verb, embedding depth ≥ 1) or non-evidential (no attractors, depth 0); two matched 50M-token versions per language are built — Ambiguous data (evidence removed) and Disambiguating data (evidence enriched). (2) Training: GPT-2-small models are trained from scratch for 8 epochs (400M tokens) on L1, then the Transformer layers are frozen and continued pretraining runs 8 more epochs on an all-Ambiguous 50M-token English L2 corpus, in a 2 (HIER→LIN vs. LIN→LIN) × 4 (L1) × 3 (overlap: FULL / 1K / NO) × 3 (seeds) design; a byte-level BPE tokenizer with 64k vocabulary is trained on the concatenated corpora, and the overlap manipulation offsets L2-side IDs of shared tokens following Kallini et al. (2025). (3) Evaluation: minimal-pair accuracy (perplexity preference for grammatical sentence) on the English portions of CLAMS (50,400 synthetic pairs; primary) and MultiBLiMP (130 naturalistic pairs; directional check), with Δacc = acc_HIER→LIN − acc_LIN→LIN isolating transfer, plus a Bayesian Bernoulli-logit mixed-effects model (correct ~ L1_evidence overlap L1_language + random intercepts for run and item) over all 72 runs. Critical design decisions: freezing the Transformer during L2 (justified as isolating transfer from embedding adaptation, with an unfreezing ablation in Appendix E); a conservative evidence-removal criterion that deletes ALL intervening NPs regardless of morphological features (acknowledged as conservative but not directly ablated); the 50:50 L1 mixture of Disambiguating and Ambiguous data (motivation for the specific ratio not deeply justified). Key Results: Under LIN→LIN, L2 accuracy hovers near chance (51.07–56.04% on CLAMS), confirming the L2 data alone cannot induce the hierarchical rule. With positive evidence in L1 (HIER→LIN), transfer appears for all four L1s on CLAMS: En→En Δ+5.45 (61.49%), De→En Δ+1.68 (54.52%), Ru→En Δ+1.04 (52.11%), Ja→En Δ+0.53 (51.77%) — a gradient roughly tracking typological distance. On MultiBLiMP, only En→En is credibly positive (Δ+8.53, 69.92%); German reverses (Δ−2.54). Under NO OVERLAP, transfer nearly vanishes even for En→En (CLAMS Δ drops from +5.45 to +0.79; MultiBLiMP from +8.53 to +2.53), and no credible interval under NO OVERLAP excludes zero at the L1 level on CLAMS. Under 1K OVERLAP (1,000 shared tokens), transfer is retained (En→En CLAMS Δ+5.76) and, for En→En, recovers to FULL-OVERLAP levels by late training when extended to 16 epochs. Mixed-effects estimates on CLAMS: overall Δhier = 0.121 [0.092, 0.150]; overlap-present-minus-absent = 0.144 [0.083, 0.205]; NO-OVERLAP contrast = 0.025 [−0.025, 0.074], not credible. Scale is small and standard: GPT-2-small, 50M tokens per stage, 3 seeds per cell. Surprising finding: a lexical bridge of only 1,000 shared tokens suffices for full late-training recovery of syntactic transfer. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel contribution is the cross-lingual instantiation of the poverty-of-stimulus design — positive evidence supplied exclusively in L1, generalization evaluated in a evidence-ambiguous L2 — and the empirical demonstration that vocabulary overlap gates even abstract syntactic transfer (previously shown only for downstream-task performance). The individual ingredients (POS paradigms, attractor-based agreement evaluation, ID-offset vocabulary intervention from Kallini et al. 2025, continued-pretraining L2-LM setups from Oba et al. 2023 / Aoyama & Schneider 2024) are all established; the paper is a well-executed combination of them in a new, well-chosen setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and meaningful: three vocabulary-overlap conditions, an unfrozen-Transformer ablation (Appendix E), extended 16-epoch training for En→En, and per-L1 breakdowns. Uncertainty is handled unusually well for this literature — 3 seeds per cell with ±1 SD bands on trajectories, and a Bayesian mixed-effects model with 95% credible intervals over all 72 runs, with priors and convergence diagnostics (R-hat ≤ 1.01, no divergences) reported. Code (github.com/shin0729/cpos) and data (huggingface.co/datasets/shin0729/cpos) are publicly released. Methodological concerns: (a) the primary benchmark (CLAMS) is synthetic and generated by the same community whose operationalizations the paper adopts, while the naturalistic check (MultiBLiMP) contains only 130 items and fails to reproduce the language gradient — the authors flag this divergence but cannot adjudicate among three explanations; (b) the evidence-classification pipeline relies on Stanza parses, so parser errors could leak or remove evidence differentially across languages; (c) the tokenizer is trained on concatenated L1+L2 corpora, so FULL OVERLAP partly reflects this shared-tokenizer choice rather than natural conditions. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (controlled scientific experiments; no deployed system). - Practical: Yes in principle — GPT-2-small trains on single A100 GPUs (~1,116 GPU-hours total for all 72+ runs), trivially reproducible hardware. - Efficient: Very cheap by modern standards; the contribution is a controlled design, not an efficient method, so efficiency relative to alternatives is not the relevant axis. - Effective: The evidence convincingly shows conditional transfer of the specific agreement rule, but only as a laboratory phenomenon under frozen-Transformer continued pretraining — not evidence that real multilingual pretraining pipelines behave this way. - Scalable: Untested; the authors explicitly argue phenomena should be established at small scale first, but the vocabulary-overlap dependence at 10–100× model/data scale is a claim, not a measurement. The work delivers a released codebase and dataset (a reusable experimental framework) rather than a model or library; it stops at paper-plus-artifact form. Strengths: (1) The CPOS design is a genuinely clever causal-innovation move: by making L2 evidence-free by construction, any above-chance hierarchical accuracy at L2 is attributable to L1 transfer, cleanly separating linguistic-evidence transfer from scaling and initialization confounds that plague observational cross-lingual studies. (2) The vocabulary-overlap counterfactual converts a correlational claim from Kallini et al. (2025) into a causal one for syntactic abstraction — showing that even a phenomenon as structural as hierarchical agreement needs a lexical bridge is a non-obvious finding. (3) Statistical rigor exceeds field norms: mixed-effects modeling over item-level correctness across 72 runs, credible intervals, and explicit convergence diagnostics, rather than seed-mean accuracy alone. (4) Honest handling of the CLAMS/MultiBLiMP divergence, with three competing explanations laid out rather than buried. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (i) only GPT-2-small and four L1s with L2 fixed to English, so generalization to non-Indo-European pairs and to varied L2 is untested; (ii) the frozen-Transformer design does not extrapolate to standard multilingual or joint pretraining, and whether the overlap dependence survives full fine-tuning is open; (iii) hierarchy is operationalized only via attractor-based subject-verb agreement and embedding depth, excluding filler-gap dependencies and islands; (iv) the synthetic/naturalistic benchmark divergence is unresolved, with statistical power (130 MultiBLiMP items, 3 seeds) possibly too low to detect small effects. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The NO OVERLAP condition is acknowledged as "a somewhat extreme counterfactual" — in En→En, offsetting token IDs makes identical English text lexically disjoint, which never occurs in real multilingual training; the paper does not test intermediate, realistic overlap levels between 1K and FULL, so the practical relevance of the tokenizer-design implication is unquantified. (2) The 1K-overlap recovery claim rests mainly on the En→En extended-training case; per-L1 recovery behavior at 1K for De/Ru/Ja is relegated to appendix figures and appears weaker, so "a minimal bridge suffices" may be English-specific. (3) The unfreezing ablation (Appendix E) is reported only as figures without quantitative analysis in the main text, leaving the robustness of the headline overlap effect under full fine-tuning visually asserted rather than statistically tested. (4) Removing all intervening NPs regardless of morphological features (the conservative criterion) means the Ambiguous corpora also lose linear-rule-relevant distributional information; an ablation of the removal criterion's granularity is absent. (5) Position-embedding and other non-linguistic initialization confounds are motivating but never directly ablated — the frozen-Transformer design partially mitigates this, but embedding-layer updates during L2 (only position/layer-norm? unclear) are not dissected. Bottom Line: A rigorous, well-controlled scientific paper that any researcher in multilingual NLP or LM learnability should read for its decisive vocabulary-overlap finding, but practitioners seeking better multilingual training recipes will find stronger, more directly actionable alternatives (e.g., Kallini et al. 2025 for tokenizer design at scale).

#23 — Innovative (73)

Jailbreaking via Activation Dilution: Neuron-Guided Adaptive Decomposition of Language Models

J Wang, C Fu, X Du, B Luo · infinitywings.github.io · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Nadia, a jailbreak framework that RL-trains a 7B decomposer to split harmful requests into sub-questions and uses a neuron-based refusal-risk score from a reference model's activations to select the lowest-risk decomposition granularity before querying the target model. - Why it's important: Decomposition-based jailbreaks evade modern safety guardrails while incurring far fewer refusals than prior automated attacks, exposing a stealth/cost trade-off (refusal exposure, throttling, detection) that static attack evaluation ignores; the findings directly inform defense design for monitored commercial LLM APIs. - How it does it: The core trick is separating 'learning what to ask' (policy-gradient RL on sub-question tokens with reward = (1 − refusal rate) × helpfulness, trained against a fixed GPT-OSS-20B response model) from 'choosing which decomposition to execute' (ranking candidate granularities m ∈ {3,…,7} by mean activation-based risk score computed from safety neurons identified in GPT-OSS-20B MLP gate-up activations). - The good: The strongest evidence is the ASR–refusal trade-off: 92.0–94.0% ASR on four targets (GPT-OSS-20B, Qwen3-Next-80B, GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Flash) at 1.6–7.4% step-level refusal, versus 0–78% ASR and up to 100% refusal for TAP, DrAttack, KDA, and Crescendo, using only 3–7 target calls and 35–55 s per objective. - The missing: The entire activation-based scoring apparatus is built on and validated against a single reference model family (GPT-OSS-20B), with moderate discriminative power (AUROC 0.764), and the paper does not test any additional reference model family, leaving transferability of the scorer — the component enabling pre-execution selection — the least-evidenced claim. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM safety evaluation, red-teaming, or multi-query attack/defense modeling — it is the first paper to make refusal exposure a first-class optimization objective in decomposition attacks — but skip it if you only need the observation that decomposition jailbreaks work (DrAttack, 2024, already established that).
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (78) is strong — making refusal exposure a first-class optimization objective and using activation signals for pre-execution candidate selection is a new formulation, not just a new attack variant — and Non-Obviousness (80) is backed by a coherent dose-response mechanistic story across four conditions and four datasets. Rigor (72) is solid on ablations and scorer-stability splits but loses points for a single reference model (GPT-OSS-20B) carrying the entire scoring apparatus, no repeated training seeds, 100-prompt evaluation sets, and code available only on request. Completeness (75) is helped by unusually honest accounting (KDA reimplementation caveat, scorer-as-heuristic framing); Resilience (70) is capped by the untested monitoring-evasion motivation and absence of any defense evaluation. Impact (55) reflects a recipe rather than a released artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*55 = 73.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Aligned LLMs refuse harmful direct prompts, and prior decomposition-based jailbreaks (DrAttack, CKA-Agent, Jigsaw Puzzles) treat decomposition as a static, hand-crafted or template-based heuristic with no mechanism to learn better decompositions or control granularity per instance. Two failure modes exist: decompositions that are too coarse still trigger refusals, and ones that are too fine waste query budget on redundant sub-questions. In monitored commercial APIs, refusals are not free — they consume budget, add latency, and feed provider-side abuse monitoring that can throttle or ban accounts. The paper argues (and this is its genuine framing gap) that prior work optimizes only eventual attack success, not refusal exposure across the interaction, and offers no pre-execution selection mechanism that avoids burning target queries on refusals. Key Idea: Treat decomposition as an optimizable policy decoupled from inference-time granularity control: a single RL-trained weak decomposer learns (once, against a fixed response model) which sub-questions stay below the refusal boundary while remaining informative, and a neuron-derived risk score built from a reference model's safety neurons (activation-rate gap between direct-harmful and benign prompts, plus a directional term from answered→refused activation shift) ranks candidate decompositions before the first target call. The 'activation dilution' hypothesis — that spreading harmful signal across independent queries disperses safety-relevant activation patterns — explains both why decomposition works and why batching recomposition partially restores refusal. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Policy learning: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 + LoRA generates structured (step, sub-question) decompositions; each sub-question is queried independently against a fixed training-time model (GPT-OSS-20B); refusals are detected by a conservative regex detector validated on 2,000 annotated responses; helpfulness is scored 0–5 by GPT-5; the reward R(x) = (1 − avg_refused)·(avg_helpfulness/5) drives a masked policy-gradient update (gradients only on sub-question tokens) with an EMA baseline, advantage scaling, and KL regularization to the frozen base model. (2) Neuron-based risk scoring: MLP gate-up activations at the last token are z-scored against benign statistics (Alpaca); the top-N neurons by activation-rate gap between direct-harmful (AdvBench) and benign prompts form a safety-neuron set; a prompt's score combines a positive-part RMS magnitude term with a softplus-clipped projection onto the answered→refused mean-activation direction, calibrated by two benign-quantile cutoffs and squashed to (0,1) by a sigmoid. (3) Adaptive inference and aggregation: candidates at sizes {3,4,5,6,7} are ranked by mean sub-question score, the argmin is executed as independent target queries, and a two-stage hierarchical aggregation (rewrite then synthesize, restricted to reorganizing collected evidence) produces the final answer. Two propositions formalize when decomposition reduces average refusal probability (sigmoid calibration with margin κ) and when score-based selection is near-optimal (score ordering preserves refusal-probability ordering within ε); these are straightforward restatements of the assumptions rather than deep results, and the authors say so. Critical design decisions: RL against a fixed response model rather than the target (justified by one-time-training reusability, but conflates decomposer skill with the specific M_train's refusal behavior); the same scorer used cross-target as a pure ranking heuristic (explicitly framed as heuristic, not probability calibration); regex-based refusal detection (intentionally conservative, validated on annotations). Key Results: On a deduplicated 100-prompt AdvBench subset held out from RL training, Nadia achieves 94.0% (GPT-OSS-20B), 93.0% (GPT-5.2), 92.0% (Qwen3-Next-80B), and 92.0% (Gemini-3-Flash) ASR with 2.1%, 7.4%, 4.4%, and 1.6% refusal respectively, judged by the PAIR/TAP GPT-4 rubric (score 10 = success). Baselines on the same subset: CKA-Agent-32B reaches 86–94% ASR but with 9.3–22.4% refusal, 7.33–8.46 target calls, and 455–653 s/objective (vs. Nadia's 3–7 calls, 35–55 s); Crescendo averages 59.3% ASR; KDA (authors' reimplementation with the same Mistral backbone) 52–72% ASR at 65–77% refusal; TAP collapses to 0–23% ASR on three of four modern targets; DrAttack 0–31%. Component analysis: RL training cuts subtask refusal 10.8%→2.6% (75.9% relative) on GPT-OSS-20B and raises helpfulness 3.996→4.384; adaptive selection adds a further reduction (2.6%→2.2%, and 22.8%→7.4% on GPT-5.2 overall). Mechanistic evidence: average risk score on AdvBench drops ~1.00 (direct) → 0.56 (batched) → 0.35 (original decomposition) → 0.18 (RL+adaptive), with refusal 100%→27%→11%→2%; the same ordering holds on MaliciousInstruct, HEx-PHI, and StrongREJECT. Scorer discriminative power is AUROC 0.764 ± 0.006 across five random splits. Judge robustness: GPT-5.4 and Qwen3.5-397B judges agree with GPT-4 within 1 point on 92.5% and 89.75% of 400 responses. Scale is modest: 100-prompt evaluation sets, one 7B decomposer, one reference model. The relative weakness of TAP/DrAttack on 2025-26 targets is a notable secondary finding about template aging. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) formulating decomposition-based jailbreaking as a joint optimization of decomposition utility and refusal exposure, with refusal as an explicit objective rather than a post-hoc metric; (b) using internal activation signals for pre-execution candidate selection rather than diagnosis or intervention, repurposing mechanistic-refusal findings; and (c) the batched-vs-independent risk-score ordering supporting activation dilution. The individual ingredients — LoRA policy-gradient fine-tuning, decomposition attacks, refusal-direction analysis — are all established; the combination and the refusal-exposure framing are the contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: selector ablation against fixed sizes and random selection over the same candidate pool (Table 3), selected-size distribution showing the selector does not collapse to a fixed granularity (Fig. 6), data-efficiency curves (50–100 prompts saturate, Appendix G), five random 70/30 splits for scorer stability, and topic- and style-paired controls for the score with paired t-test/Wilcoxon p-values around 10⁻²⁴–10⁻²⁸. Standard deviations are reported over the 100-prompt evaluation set (prompt-level, not multi-seed training runs; no confidence intervals on the headline ASR numbers, though with binary outcomes on n=100 the margins over most baselines are large). Code access is 'upon request for research purposes' via https://github.com/JiahangWang/Nadia-CCS2026 — not openly released, an explicit dual-use mitigation that limits reproducibility. Concerns: (i) the KDA baseline is a reimplementation, not the original system; (ii) evaluation sets are 100 prompts from benchmarks whose harmful prompts are public and likely represented in modern models' safety training; (iii) the score-construction data and evaluation both derive from the GPT-OSS-20B reference-target pair (the scorer is developed on the regime it is first evaluated on), though cross-target results partially mitigate Goodhart concerns; (iv) helpfulness and ASR are LLM-judged (GPT-5 for reward, GPT-4 for ASR), introducing reward-model circularity in training, though judge-agreement checks and rule-based refusal detection reduce this. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (an attack pipeline run against live black-box targets). Practical: Yes — needs a 7B open-weight model with LoRA training, one 20B open-weight reference model for activations, and standard API access to targets; no exotic hardware. Efficient: Strong — 3–7 target calls and 35–55 s per objective after one-time training, versus 21–27 calls/370–576 s for Crescendo and 455–653 s for CKA-Agent-32B, though RL training (100 prompts × 5 runs against GPT-OSS-20B) is a real upfront cost. Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated objective (high ASR at low refusal across four targets and four datasets); whether 'low refusal' actually evades provider monitoring is claimed, not measured — no experiment touches real abuse-detection systems. Scalable: Untested beyond 100-prompt sets and four targets; the authors do not claim scale, and saturation/degradation beyond ~100 RL prompts (Appendix G) hints the policy may not improve indefinitely. Deliverable: research code available on request plus a reusable recipe (decomposer checkpoint, scorer construction procedure); no released weights or library. Strengths: - Refusal exposure as a first-class attack metric is a genuinely useful reframing — the ASR–refusal Pareto plot (Fig. 2) and per-method call/time budgets (Table 8) give defenders and evaluators a dimension most prior jailbreak papers omit. - Pre-execution candidate selection via internal activations transfers across three non-reference targets without target-specific tuning, an unusual and practically relevant form of scorer portability that the authors carefully frame as heuristic rather than calibrated. - The mechanistic story is unusually complete for an attack paper: dose-response evidence across four conditions (direct → batched → independent → RL+adaptive) on four datasets, PCA geometry in the safety-neuron subspace, and two external guard-model checks (Qwen3Guard-8B, Llama-Guard-4-12B) all cohere with the dilution interpretation. - Honest accounting: the KDA reimplementation caveat, the distinction between scorer usefulness as a ranking signal vs. refusal-probability calibration on non-reference targets, and the strict-inequality conditions under which the dilution ordering can fail are all stated rather than buried. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the risk scorer is built from offline activations of a single open-weight reference model family and flag extending it to other reference families and API-only systems as future work (though they assert this does not change the main behavioral results). They also note the score's meaning is limited to refusal-linked activation patterns in their dataset, that the dilution ordering can fail when one sub-question concentrates the full harmful signal, that the propositions' premises can fail under batching re-concentration, and (Appendix G) that RL performance saturates and can degrade beyond ~100 training prompts. The ethical considerations section confronts dual-use risk directly and explains the gated artifact release. Overall, limitations are confronted rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Single reference model: all activation machinery — neuron selection, direction, cutoffs — is GPT-OSS-20B-specific; the claim that 'reference–target similarity does not matter' rests on one reference model, and the authors' own future-work note concedes this without testing a second family. (2) AUROC 0.764 is moderate; the paper does not report how often the argmin-scoring selection picks a candidate whose true refusal risk is worse than the pool median. (3) The monitoring/throttling motivation is never tested against an actual abuse-monitoring or rate-limiting system — 'lower refusal exposure' is measured only as a proxy. (4) No adversarial evaluation: whether defenders can patch decomposition attacks (e.g., cross-query intent aggregation, sub-question correlation detection) is unexamined, so the 92–94% figures should be read as pre-defense numbers. (5) ASR judged by GPT-4 with 'rating 10 = fully complies' is a known-lenient proxy; the judge-agreement study checks cross-judge consistency, not ground truth of harmfulness. (6) RL reward is scored by the same GPT-5 class of model that could also be the target (GPT-5.2 is a target), raising a mild train-target stylistic overlap question not discussed. (7) Prompt-level standard deviations conflate prompt difficulty with method variance; no repeated training seeds, so RL-training stochasticity is unquantified. Bottom Line: This is the strongest current evidence that decomposition-based jailbreaking should be evaluated and defended as a refusal-exposure problem, and the ASR–refusal trade-off plus cross-target scorer portability make it essential reading for LLM safety researchers and API-defense engineers — though the single-reference-model scorer, absent defense evaluation, and 100-prompt scale mean its headline numbers are a snapshot against today's guardrails, not a stable result.

LoCoJAX: Host-Local Coordination for Small-Model RL on TPUs

L Chen, GB Rehm, Y Song, H Xie, M Lei, C Bai… · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LoCoJAX, a TPU reinforcement-learning post-training system that moves rollout control from a single Pathways controller to each TPU host, cutting per-step time by 1.3–3.6× for Qwen3-0.6B and reducing chip-hours to a quality target by up to 2.77×. - Why it's important: Small (<7B) models are increasingly trained with RL for latency-sensitive and embedded reasoning, but on TPUs the documented recipe's single-controller coordination costs — which do not shrink with model size or chip count — dominate the step, wasting most of the rented accelerator time. - How it does it: Each host runs its own JAX controller and vLLM rollout engine that admits its share of requests locally and keeps each GRPO response group on one host (eliminating cross-host rollout communication), while training remains globally sharded and synchronous; a Ray-managed disaggregated mode separates rollout and training hosts asynchronously. - The good: The attribution is concrete and measured, not anecdotal: profiling shows host orchestration is 36% of the 0.6B GRPO step versus 2% network, and two named Pathways mechanisms — ~1 s serial request admission per step and a 2.15 ms vs 0.90 ms per-decode-iteration premium (~2.25 s over ~1,800 iterations) — account for most of the gap, backed by a pre-registered chip-hours-to-target study. - The missing: The system is rigorously tuned and evaluated on essentially one model (Qwen3-0.6B); other models get descriptive, less-tuned comparisons, and the baseline is the authors' own assembly of Google's public Pathways recipe rather than any peer-reviewed TPU small-model RL result. - Read it or not: Read it if you run RL post-training on TPUs (especially for sub-7B models) or design RL training infrastructure — the characterization data and colocated-vs-disaggregated placement guidance are directly actionable; skip it if you work exclusively on GPUs, where prior systems work covers similar ground.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Rigor (78) is a major driver — pre-registered chip-hours-to-quality study, bootstrap CIs, per-lever ablations, and measurement-driven causal attribution — with Completeness (78) lifted by unusually direct disclosure of provisional cells and self-tuned baselines. Novelty (70) reflects the first TPU RL characterization and placement study, though the core mechanism was proposed in an unimplemented RFC. Impact (70) is capped by no stated public code repository and the self-referential baseline (authors' own upstream PRs tune the comparison). Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: RL post-training with verifiable rewards is increasingly applied to small (sub-billion to few-billion parameter) reasoning models, which serve as fast agents in latency-sensitive or embedded settings. On GPUs, small-model RL steps are known to be bound by incidentals outside the model computation (framework dispatch, kernel boundaries, launch latency, scheduling), but TPUs had not been studied: their stack (JAX/XLA, Pallas, MaxText/Tunix, vLLM TPU backend), 3D-torus ICI interconnect, and control model differ materially, and Google's documented multi-host RL recipes run everything under Pathways, whose single controller coordinates every host. A TPU device can host only one user-space process, so trainer and rollout engine cannot be trivially colocated in separate processes. The paper asks where small-model RL time actually goes on TPUs and whether the single-controller execution model is the right default at small scale. Key Idea: Replace the single-controller (Pathways) execution model with multi-controller JAX: give every host a local controller and rollout engine so request admission, GRPO grouping, reward, and advantage computation happen host-locally with no cross-host rollout communication, while training stays globally sharded (FSDP) and synchronous. The enabling observation is that host-orchestration overhead — flat ~1 s serial batch admission in the Pathways head plus a 2.4× per-iteration decode premium from lockstep SPMD rollout — does not amortize at small model sizes, so removing the controller from the rollout path is worth more than any compute-side optimization. Methodology: The paper has three phases. (1) A characterization/scaling study: GRPO on Pathways, 128 TPU v7x chips, dense models 0.6B–405B, decode-heavy workload (2,048 completions forced to 8,192 tokens), splitting each step into compute, network, and host orchestration; tensor-parallel (TP) degree swept per model. (2) LoCoJAX: two modes. Colocated (LoCoJAX-CO) runs one process per host containing a vLLM engine plus an FSDP trainer shard; each step is local request admission → generation → reward/advantage → synchronous training step → weight all-gather and engine reload. Disaggregated (LoCoJAX-DA) uses Ray to place rollout and training on separate host sets with one-step policy staleness and importance weighting. Four optional optimizations (O1–O4: off-barrier metrics export, frozen GC, length-balanced prompt sharding, single-call weight publish) define "LoCoJAX optimized." (3) Evaluation protocol: equal-work verification (matched prompts, output lengths within [0.8, 1.25]), 95% percentile bootstrap CIs over steady steps, a pre-declared 1.111 speedup verdict threshold, and a chip-hours-to-quality-target study (85% GSM8K accuracy at temperature 0.7, three seeds per cell, frozen target). Critical design decisions — keeping GRPO synchronous and on-policy in CO mode, keeping each GRPO group on one host, and using TP1 rollout for 0.6B — are each justified by measurement (e.g., TP1→TP2 at 0.6B saves 0.21 ms of weight streaming but adds 0.7–0.9 ms of collectives per iteration). Key Results: Characterization (128 chips, decode-heavy): host orchestration falls from 36.4% of step time at 0.6B to 1.4% at 405B, while network rises from 2.2% to 38.5%, crossing at ~8B (18.3%/18.5%). Stack comparison (Qwen3-0.6B, 8–64 chips, three workloads, tuned Pathways baseline): LoCoJAX optimized is 2.13–3.56× faster on GSM8K, 1.25–1.89× on NuminaMath-CoT, and 1.72–2.32× on SWE-agent; on GSM8K, LoCoJAX on 8 chips (5.07 s) beats Pathways on 64 chips (6.75 s). Against Google's published recipes: 5.3× on Qwen3-1.7B (Tunix, 4 chips) and 2.1× on Gemma4-26B MoE (MaxText, 64 chips). Attribution: Pathways head interval is 0.88–0.98 s flat from 8 to 64 chips (8%→14% of step), and the decode premium adds ~2.25 s/step. Cost-to-learn: Pathways needs 1.27–2.77× the chip-hours of LoCoJAX base to reach the 85% GSM8K target (4–128 chips), with held-out quality within ~0.65 pp (noise floor ~1 pp). Placement study (8–256 chips, three trainer/rollout splits): disaggregation wins only when rollout dominates and gets most hosts — NuminaMath at 256 chips with 75% rollout hosts cuts step time ~15% (0.85×) — while colocation wins on SWE at every size (1.14–1.30×) and on GSM8K below 128 chips. Baselines are Google's current public recipes, assembled from pinned upstream commits and themselves tuned with the authors' 20+ merged upstream PRs; no peer-reviewed TPU small-model RL baseline exists to compare against. Tested at genuine stress scale (up to 256 chips, models to 405B) for a systems paper. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the first characterization of LLM RL time breakdown on TPUs across a 0.6B–405B sweep, the first colocated-vs-disaggregated placement comparison for small-model RL on TPUs, and the chip-hours-to-quality-target methodology. The core mechanism (multi-controller JAX for post-training) was proposed in an unimplemented Tunix RFC (#706), which the authors credit; LoCoJAX implements it for the full RL loop. Colocation/disaggregation tradeoffs, FSDP training, and Ray-based disaggregation are all established techniques (HybridFlow, AReaL, RLinf on GPUs) applied to a new hardware/control regime — the value is in the measured evidence, not a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: per-optimization lever attribution (O1/O2/O4 save only 1.01–1.11× chip-hours), device-level TP sweeps isolated from head-placement noise, upstream PR-level accounting of the 20+ contributions to the baseline, and a fitted fixed-overhead model (R = 1 + Δ/T) with held-out checks and explicit statements of where it fails. Statistics include 95% bootstrap/Welch intervals, three launches per arm, a pre-declared verdict threshold, and a pre-registered 0.005 reward band for the disaggregation study. Everything runs on public models, datasets, and frameworks with pinned commits, and the authors merged their baseline improvements upstream, but no explicit code repository URL for LoCoJAX is stated in the text. Concerns: (i) the baseline is built by the authors and tuned with their own upstream fixes — a fair-faith but self-referential comparison, with no independent strong baseline; (ii) the concurrent Tunix distributed RL runtime (dist_rl, added October 2026) was not evaluated; (iii) step times are read from each stack's own clock with compile time excluded; (iv) several disaggregation cells are provisional (fewer than three launches) or post hoc; (v) the cost-to-learn study covers one model and one dataset. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built system evaluated by running it). Practical: Runs on commercial Google Cloud TPU v7x plus standard open-source components (JAX, vLLM TPU, MaxText, Ray), so it is deployable by any TPU tenant, but not on GPUs. Efficient: It is itself an efficiency contribution — 1.3–3.6× step-time and 1.27–2.77× chip-hour reductions — with the cost being trainer memory (no gradient accumulation, so it fails to fit SWE-agent at 8 chips, needing 157.6 of 94.7 GiB per device). Effective: Evidence covers both step time and, on one model/dataset, wall-clock-to-quality-target with quality within noise, so it demonstrably solves the stated problem on its primary configuration, with weaker evidence elsewhere. Scalable: Tested to 256 chips, where colocated GSM8K rollout stops scaling (1.77 s at 256 vs 1.73 s at 128 chips) — the paper measures this limit rather than claiming past it, and offers disaggregation as the partial answer. The work delivers a system (LoCoJAX-CO/DA) plus ~20 merged upstream PRs to tpu-inference, Tunix, and MaxText; a public code release is not stated. Strengths: (1) The causal attribution is measurement-driven and specific: two named controller costs (serial admission ~1 s/step; 2.15 ms vs 0.90 ms per decode iteration totaling ~2.25 s/step) with clean isolation experiments, not vague "overhead" claims. (2) The 0.6B–405B characterization produces a genuinely actionable crossover finding — host orchestration dominates below ~8B, network above — that redirects optimization effort by model class and is supported by a TP-sweep cost model (weight-streaming savings vs collective penalties). (3) The pre-registered, chip-hours-to-quality-target study ties a systems speedup to training outcome, which most RL systems papers omit entirely. (4) Unusual disclosure discipline: provisional cells marked hollow, post hoc cells flagged, cases where their fitted model fails are reported, and the authors state plainly that Pathways could not be tuned as heavily as their own system. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that the closed-source Pathways runtime could not be tuned to the same degree as LoCoJAX; that the characterization covers only a decode-heavy workload; that characterization and stack comparison use non-comparable setups; that bf16 (GSM8K) vs fp32 (NuminaMath/SWE) trainer weights may confound speedup magnitudes; that LoCoJAX's lack of gradient accumulation causes out-of-memory exclusions; and that only Qwen3-0.6B was tuned and rigorously evaluated, with other models only descriptively compared. This is direct, non-minimizing disclosure — a credibility positive. They also disclose evaluation quirks in the recipe comparison (13 of 16 Gemma baseline launches failed to reach the measured window for unknown reasons; shared sampling seeds limit some intervals to timing noise). Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The headline 1.3–3.6× speedups come disproportionately from the shortest-work workload (GSM8K), where fixed orchestration overhead looms largest; on the workload closest to production reasoning RL (decode-heavy NuminaMath), the advantage narrows to 1.25–1.89×, and per-token speedups on the Google recipe comparison are correspondingly lower (3.49–5.06× on 1.7B). (2) The strongest available baseline — Google's concurrently released Tunix distributed RL runtime (dist_rl), which also separates trainer and rollout workers — was not evaluated, so "best alternative on TPUs" is untested. (3) The baseline's performance partially depends on the authors' own 20 upstream PRs to the very components it is built from; a recipe without those fixes yields inflated "frozen recipe" ratios (up to 3.15×), which the authors report but which invites careful reading of which number is the fair one. (4) Quality evidence (cost-to-learn, accuracy parity) exists for exactly one model-dataset pair at ≤348 updates; no evidence that synchronous on-policy GRPO with one-step staleness in DA mode preserves quality on harder or longer-horizon tasks. (5) The 405B characterization runs use randomly initialized weights and a single run at the fastest TP, so the large-model end of the crossover curve rests on thin replication; network shares are self-described upper-end estimates. Bottom Line: For anyone training small reasoning models on TPUs this is currently the only rigorous public evidence on where the time goes and how to structure the loop, and its colocated-default recommendation plus placement guidance is worth adopting immediately; for GPU practitioners, RLinf/HybridFlow-style work covers the same design space, so this is a TPU-specific — though unusually well-measured — contribution rather than a general advance.

$π^4$: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion (13 ▲ )

Yifan Wang, Weiguang Zhao, Ni Yang, Haoyu Guo, Junting Dong, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 18 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces π4, a ~0.5B-parameter feed-forward foundation model that, from uncalibrated RGB inputs (single image, unordered image collection, or video), jointly predicts dense pointmaps, camera poses, metric scale, 2D/3D point tracks, and moving-object masks in a single forward pass per scene. - Why it's important: Robust 4D perception from in-the-wild RGB—without calibration, ordered inputs, or per-scene optimization—is the gateway capability for robotics, AR, and content capture; existing models split geometry and motion across separate systems or fail to generalize across input regimes. - How it does it: The core move is factorization: keep the frozen π3-style permutation-equivariant geometry branch, condition a separate motion decoder on detached geometry features via Spatial AdaLN, predict motion only as image-space correspondences, and lift tracks to 3D analytically by sampling the reconstructed target-view pointmap—so visible 3D track endpoints lie on reconstructed surfaces by construction. - The good: The evaluation is broad and current: best overall average rank (3.00 vs 3.10 for Pi3X) across 16 geometry settings against nine 2025–2026 baselines, best Oxford Spires long-sequence ATE (0.7337 m, a 47.2% reduction vs DVLT), and a detailed ablation section quantifying each design choice. - The missing: The paper acknowledges it does not match traditional geometric-optimization accuracy on sequences longer than the 64-view training context, and single-view long-baseline 3D tracking (ADT APD 72.90, AJ 66.30) beats baselines only by small margins; there is also no inference-time compute/memory cost reported for the 1,000+-image forward-pass regime showcased in Figure 1. - Read it or not: Read it if you build 3D/4D perception systems and need a single small model covering geometry plus motion, or if you design multi-task training/data recipes—the data-curation and gradient-routing details are transferable; skip it if you only need best-in-class monocular depth (Pi3X/DA3-Giant rank higher on that panel) or moving-object segmentation (GMOS scores 87.48 vs π4's 85.04 mean J&F).

Problem & Motivation Feed-forward reconstruction models (DUSt3R, VGGT, π3) recover geometry from RGB but handle motion poorly or not at all; feed-forward trackers (CoWTracker, TAPIP3D, ARROW, Track4World) handle motion but either assume video ordering or regress 3D endpoints whose error compounds with camera estimates. Practitioners in robotics, AR, and 3D content creation need one system that works on uncalibrated, unordered, arbitrarily numerous RGB observations in the wild—scene content, camera configurations, and observation counts all unconstrained. Prior feed-forward models are also parameter-heavy (baselines in this paper's tables span 1.14–1.72B parameters), limiting where they can be deployed. The specific gap π4 closes is joint, single-pass geometry-plus-motion estimation that matches specialized models on reconstruction while remaining competitive on tracking, at less than half the parameter count of most baselines. Key Idea The central trick is the division of labor between geometry and motion: the motion branch predicts only image-space correspondences U(q→i) (scale-independent, CoWTracker-style iterative warping without temporal positional embeddings), and 3D tracks are obtained by indexing the geometry branch's metric target-view pointmap at the predicted correspondence, Y(q→i)(u) = X(metric,i)(U(q→i)(u)). This removes the need for the motion head to learn scene scale or camera placement, and makes track–geometry consistency a structural guarantee rather than something to regularize. A secondary enabling trick is conditioning the frozen geometry backbone's features into the motion decoder through Spatial AdaLN, transferring cross-view spatial cues without co-training. Methodology The pipeline is: (1) a shared DINOv3 encoder (layers 11+17 combined) produces patch features; (2) a looped Transformer geometry decoder (frame attention + cross-view attention, weight-shared across L=8–16 training steps, L=16 at eval, with explicit loop-step conditioning) predicts per-view local pointmaps parameterized as depth × ray, relative camera poses (permutation-equivariant, no reference view), one shared log-scale, and a confidence map; (3) a MoGe3-style sparse 3D U-Net refiner iteratively updates log-depth in S refinement rounds; (4) a motion decoder with the same looped structure but independent parameters, conditioned on detached geometry features via Spatial AdaLN, runs a CoWTracker-adapted warping head to produce dense correspondences and visibility, plus a query-independent moving-object mask head fusing a frozen SAM 2 encoder. Training is staged: geometry (with point, relative-pose, relative-point, ray, patch-matching, and metric-scale losses) first; then motion (CoWTracker-style regression + BCE) with geometry frozen; then the confidence head. Notable loss details: sequence-wise point normalization with a stop-gradient on the camera-translation path (cuts camera loss 10.9% in ablation), ROE-solver scale alignment, and point-gradient matching for surface structure. Data engineering is a major component: ~10,000 scene assets from Funes/Sketchfab rendered with coverage-aware view selection, connected view chains, and natural-vs-counterbias camera sets (wide roll/focal variation); sequence-consistent lens/crop augmentation (identity/barrel/fisheye/pincushion); foreground-suppressed pseudo-labeling of Internet videos (inpaint moving foreground, reconstruct background with an earlier π4 checkpoint, keep only originally visible background pixels, pair labels with original frames); and the GameRealm game-engine dataset for native dynamic-scene tracks. Trained on 64×A800, ~300k geometry + ~100k motion updates, BF16, max 64 views per training context with stochastically sampled view counts. Three design decisions stand out: image-space correspondence + analytic lifting (well justified by the Figure 10 qualitative comparison against ARROW's XYZ regression and MoSE3's independent depth), freezing geometry during motion training (justified by the geometry-conditioning ablation, −7.17 px EPE), and the mixed short/long view-count training recipe (motivated but only qualitatively justified for the thousands-of-images extrapolation). Key Results Geometry: across 16 settings in four panels (mono depth, video depth, pose/trajectory, multiview reconstruction), π4 achieves the best overall average rank of 3.00 versus Pi3X's 3.10 (2nd) and DA3-Giant 1.1's 5.53 (4th); baselines include VGGT (1.26B), MapAnything (1.23B), VGGT-Ω, DVLT (117M), ARROW, Track4World (1.72B) — all current 2025–2026 models. Specific wins: Sintel video depth AbsRel 0.160 (vs 0.181 for Track4World, next best), Sintel mono depth Rel 0.256, DTU reconstruction accuracy 1.0452 mm (vs ARROW's 1.0613), ETH3D accuracy 0.1722. However, π4 loses the monocular-depth panel to Pi3X (rank 2.57 vs 3.50) and is worse than Pi3X on metric-scale error (mean 20.11% vs 16.92%). Long-sequence: on six Oxford Spires routes (361–800 frames, single forward pass), π4 completes 6/6 with ATE 0.7337 m, RRE 2.93°/100 m, CD 1.1573 m, F1 0.9392 — beating DVLT (ATE 1.3885) on all five metrics, while MapAnything (3/6), DA3 (2/6), VGGT (0/6), and Track4World (2/6) hit out-of-memory failures. Tracking: on Track4World's released ADT/PointOdyssey/PStudio subsets plus GameRealm (Long), π4 leads average 2D AJ (72.43) and 3D APD (57.33)/AJ (47.68), ranking second on most other entries behind CoWTracker (2D) and ARROW (3D on PointOdyssey). Multiview tracking: leads average 2D AJ (35.07), second in 3D. Moving-object segmentation: mean J&F 85.04, second to GMOS (87.48). Tested at standard benchmark scale plus a genuine stress-scale demonstration (800-frame routes; qualitative 1,000+-image scenes). No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported. Novelty Classification NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus NEW FORMULATION and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely novel element is the geometry-conditioned, image-space-correspondence-with-analytic-lifting formulation for joint 4D perception — prior joint systems either regress 3D endpoints directly (ARROW), predict UV+depth (MoSE3), or handle geometry and tracking separately. Most of the rest is competent composition of known components: π3's permutation-equivariant geometry, Déjà View's looped decoding, MoGe3's sparse refiner, CoWTracker's warping head, SAM 2 fusion à la GMOS, and VGGT-Ω-style matching supervision. The data pipeline (counterbias cameras, lens augmentation, foreground-suppressed pseudo-labeling) is a substantial but largely incremental data-engineering contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are a strength: Section 6 quantifies loop-step conditioning (−2.8% point loss, −10.2% camera loss), encoder layer choice (11+17), fine-tuning learning rate (10^-5 beats freezing by 8.1%/4.5%), gradient routing through shared normalization (−10.9% camera loss), relative-point loss weighting, geometry conditioning (−7.17 px EPE), and negative results for PixelDiT-style heads and unconditioned refinement (refiner with zero/noise features improves surface structure but raises XYZ error 8.77%/7.47%). No multi-seed error bars or significance tests are reported anywhere; several head-to-head margins (e.g., overall rank 3.00 vs 3.10) are small. Code and models are publicly released (Code | Project Page | Hugging Face links; GameRealm at github.com/weiguangzhao/GameRealm). Concerns: (1) 3D tracking evaluation uses scale-and-shift alignment fitted to ground-truth visible points, a protocol the authors disclose but which softens absolute 3D claims; (2) metric-scale results are reported separately and are mid-pack; (3) GameRealm (Long) is the authors' own dataset, and Track4World scores only 37/45 clips there (disclosed); (4) the paper is an arXiv preprint, as are several key baselines (VGGT-Ω, DVLT, ARROW, Track4World, MoSE3, CoWTracker), so the comparison table reflects fast-moving, unreviewed work on both sides. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained system with benchmark and in-the-wild evaluation; the shipped artifact is itself a tool). — Practical: Yes — the full system is ~0.5B parameters, runs inference in a single forward pass, and trains on 64×A800 80GB; released on Hugging Face with a demo. — Efficient: At inference, looped decoding with shared weights and a DINOv3 backbone is far lighter than the 1.14–1.72B baselines; training required ~300k+100k optimizer updates on 64 A800s, a mid-scale but non-trivial budget; long-input inference cost is not reported. — Effective: The evidence supports the stated goal — best overall geometry rank and complete 6/6 Oxford Spires routes where four baselines OOM — but not universal superiority: Pi3X wins monocular depth and metric scale, GMOS wins segmentation, and 3D tracking is competitive rather than dominant. — Scalable: Demonstrated up to 800-frame routes and qualitatively at 1,000+ images despite a 64-view training context; the authors explicitly warn that accuracy degrades beyond training-length sequences and do not provide quantitative reconstruction numbers past 800 frames. Delivers a concrete software artifact (code, weights, dataset), not just a paper. Strengths - The image-space-correspondence-plus-lifting formulation is a real insight, not engineering: it converts track–geometry consistency from a training objective into a structural guarantee, and the Figure 10 comparison against ARROW (drifting XYZ endpoints) and MoSE3 (off-surface independent depth) gives it a concrete mechanistic explanation. - Unusually honest and granular ablations, including negative results (PixelDiT head artifacts, refiner with zero/noise conditioning raising error) — most system papers report only favorable ablations. - The data recipe tackles identifiable coverage gaps with non-obvious moves: counterbias camera sets for roll/focal diversity, sequence-consistent lens warping with exact recomputed geometry targets, and foreground-suppressed pseudo-labeling that avoids supervising on inpainted pixels. - Clear efficiency claim backed by the evaluation table: 343M loaded geometry parameters (≈0.5B full system) versus 1.14–1.72B for joint baselines, with no accuracy collapse. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive: (1) camera–object motion ambiguity — the model can interpret a moving foreground as static when the background is weakly textured or the foreground dominates, conflating camera and object motion; (2) sensitivity of camera-position error to distance from the coordinate origin, implicating the numerical scale of absolute translations; (3) failure to consistently match traditional optimization-based accuracy, especially on sequences longer than the training context, with globally consistent trajectories under length extrapolation named as an open problem. These are stated plainly in a dedicated Limitations section without minimization. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No inference-time compute, memory, or latency measurements for the flagship 1,000+-image forward-pass regime — the headline Figure 1 capability has no cost accounting. - Several ablations use "model-development configurations" and validation-loss deltas rather than downstream benchmark metrics, so some claimed component benefits (e.g., relative-point weighting) are not tied to end-task accuracy. - The quantitative tracking comparisons mostly show π4 ranking second rather than first, and the GameRealm (Long) benchmark — where π4 does best relative to baselines — is the authors' own concurrently released dataset; a neutral long-sequence tracking benchmark is absent. - The foreground-suppression pipeline uses generative video inpainting (Wan2.1) whose failure modes (hallucinated background structure) could silently corrupt pseudo-labels; no analysis of pseudo-label noise is provided. - The geometry-conditioning ablation measures EPE on image pairs, but the claim that geometry features "provide useful context" for tracking more broadly is not tested against alternative conditioning (e.g., conditioning on raw images only at matching capacity). - Statistical rigor: single runs, no variance estimates, and rank comparisons with sub-0.1 margins (3.00 vs 3.10) could flip under re-evaluation. Bottom Line A practitioner building 4D perception should read this: it is currently the most complete and parameter-efficient single-pass geometry-plus-tracking system with public code, and its factorization insight and data recipe are transferable — but specialists wanting the best monocular depth, metric scale, or moving-object segmentation should still reach for Pi3X/DA3 and GMOS respectively.

Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers (49 ▲ )

Hyunjong Ok, Jaeho Lee · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 18 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows empirically that when three frontier LLMs write network weights without gradient training (weight-space programming, WSP), all three abandon Transformers and converge on sparse fact tables queried by a fixed procedure, and it proposes a hashed concept-pair associative-memory model that reaches 49.6–52.4% ARC test accuracy while running up to 17× faster on a GPU than a same-sized Transformer. - Why it's important: WSP is an emerging paradigm (LLMs author weights directly, no gradient descent), and the architecture criteria that favor Transformers (gradient flow, dense GPU matmul) simply do not apply there, so knowing what structure LLMs can actually write and edit line-by-line determines the paradigm's trajectory. - How it does it: The authors give each LLM only ten labeled examples and a sandbox, then analyze the written models as associative memories (Equation 1), showing sparse keys with hard top-k selection avoid the dense-key interference that plagues LLM-written Transformers, and design a fixed forward pass that reads 120 hashed pair-table rows plus one product with a concept table, making cost independent of fact count. - The good: The mechanistic analysis is controlled and quantitative — scoring each option from its single best-matching fact alone reproduces 49.1% of the full model's 50.8% ARC accuracy, removing one written line changes 0.5–1.8 test answers in table models versus 4.8 to 1,350.7 in LLM-written Transformers, and LLM-written Transformers trail BM25 over their own text by 8.0 points on average. - The missing: There are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests (most rows are single runs), and the headline result — 54.4% ARC accuracy — sits far below a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B at 82.1%, so the practical payoff of WSP itself remains unproven. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM-generated models, weight-space programming, neural memory, or interpretability of what LLMs can author; skip it if you need deployable QA accuracy, since prompted pretrained models dominate the written models everywhere.
