Problem & Motivation: Weight-space programming (Takehi et al., 2026) asks an LLM to write the weights of a target model by hand, with no gradient training and no data fitting. Transformers were selected by history because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs, but neither criterion applies when weights are typed line-by-line by an LLM. The authors ask whether WSP should keep the Transformer or whether gradient-free weight writing favors a different structure — a question no prior work addresses, since prior weight-construction work (Tracr, hand-built fact MLPs, model editing) all fixes the architecture first. Key Idea: The core insight is that writing weights without gradients imposes two requirements — traceability (each prediction traces to a few nameable written lines) and locality (editing one line changes only dependent predictions) — and these requirements select for sparse keys with hard selection over dense keys with soft selection. Formally, a Transformer layer and the LLM-designed table are both associative memories f(x) = Σ v_i σ(k_i^T x), but the LLMs choose σ = top-k with ~7-nonzero-entry keys over 3,368 concepts, eliminating the interference that dense overlapping keys cause; the authors' own model replaces full table scans with hashed addressing h(a,b) = (ap + b) mod H so per-question cost is constant in the number of written facts. Methodology: The pipeline has three regimes on ARC-Easy+Challenge (3,530 four-option test questions): (i) fixed architectures — the LLM writes weights over random initializations of 15 released models (Transformers, Mamba-2, RWKV-7, BERT variants) or a given two-layer Transformer; (ii) LLM-designed models — the LLM delivers an architecture file, plain-text knowledge files, and a build script compiled to CPU tensors, under a syntax check forbidding Python control flow; (iii) lineages — five-to-eight generations where each run inherits the better of two parent runs by a single validation accuracy. Writers see ten labeled examples and never see test data; a separate sandbox scores deliverables. The authors' model compiles written lines into a first-order concept table A (concept→concept recall) and a second-order pair table hashed to H rows (e.g., H = 2^20, up to 40 recalled concepts per row), scoring options via r = Σ_{(a,b)∈P(q)} q_a q_b t_{h(a,b)} + μA^T q and s_c = o_c^T r with J = 16 top concepts forming 120 pairs. Critical design decisions: (1) fixing the forward pass ourselves after LLM GPU rewrites stayed 6–33× slower than a same-sized Transformer — well justified by measurement; (2) hashed pair addressing over explicit search — justified by the traceability/locality analysis, though hash collisions are inherent (757 shared rows at H = 2^20, accuracy preserved down to 65,536 rows); (3) concept-based (not word-based) keys so morphological variants share one concept — justified by the worked example, ablated only implicitly. Key Results: LLM-designed models beat every released architecture written by the same LLM: Claude Opus 5.5's generation-5 model reaches 54.4% ARC test accuracy with 3.35M parameters versus 48.7% for its best written released architecture (Qwen3-1.7B, 1.72B parameters) — a 1,800× parameter reduction; the associative-memory-based model reaches 49.6–52.4% with 2.53–6.24M parameters and is 680× smaller. Gradient descent from random initialization stays at 24.6–32.7% even on the full 3,358-question training set, so WSP from ten examples beats training from scratch without pretraining. Speed: the associative-memory-based model answers all 3,530 test questions in 18 ms on one RTX 3090, 7× (gen-1) to 17× (gen-5) faster than a same-sized Transformer at its fastest input treatment; median LLM-designed model is 9.4× slower than a same-sized Transformer. Causal analysis: LLM-written two-layer Transformers score below BM25 over their own text in 20 of 23 runs (mean −8.0 points for Claude), while table models beat BM25 in 21 of 24 runs — evidence that structure, not content, drives the gap. Generality: SciQ transfers within ~4 points (50.1%); MMLU stays at chance; SQuAD F1 42.3 versus 33.2 for the written Transformer; CIFAR-10 raw pixels fail (21–28% versus 10% chance) but DINOv2-token tables reach 96.1%; on AG News, networks written with zero articles reach ~84%, which gradient descent needs thousands of labels to match. Pretrained fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B remains far ahead at 82.1% ARC. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (three independent frontier LLMs, given free architectural choice under WSP, converge on sparse fact tables rather than Transformers, with a controlled causal analysis of why) plus NEW METHOD (the hashed concept-pair associative-memory model with constant-cost lookup). The WSP setting itself is adopted from Takehi et al. (2026); the associative-memory framing of Transformers builds on Zhong et al. (2025) and Wang (2026); the pair-table design resembles product-key memories (Lample et al., 2019) and the Engram module (Cheng et al., 2026) but with LLM-written entries replacing gradient-learned ones — the genuinely novel move is studying architecture choice under authorship rather than trainability. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: forbidding practice questions costs ~1 point, forbidding fact rows costs ~5 points with 100× more non-zero values, keeping only the best fact per option recovers 49.1 of 50.8%, pair-table folding from 2^20 to 2^16 rows preserves accuracy, and a no-row-table control shows the LLM builds superposed random vectors instead. Contamination is addressed with four n-gram overlap rules, a deletion test (accuracy unchanged after removing flagged lines), and a masked-option recall probe (15.3% on test versus 16.3% on unseen training items). However: most rows are single runs, two runs where present, with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests; lineages stop on validation plateaus so multiple-comparison risk is small but generation selection is noisy. Code and a project page are linked from the first page, though no URL is printed in the text; released models are listed in an appendix. Methodological concerns: the primary benchmark is one dataset family (ARC), the LLM writers are proprietary and version-dependent (non-reproducible writers), and the 'same-sized Transformer' speed baseline uses random weights written to match non-zero counts — fair for timing but the accuracy comparison rests on the LLM's inability to write Transformers, which is itself the finding rather than an independent control. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component in the proposed model). Practical: Yes — all timing is on a single RTX 3090, and the model is CPU-buildable by construction. Efficient: 18 ms for 3,530 questions on a 3090 (CUDA-graph replay), constant in fact count, but time grows with concept count and overtakes a Transformer between ~15,000–32,000 concepts with a dense concept table (~100,000 with row lists); LLM API costs per lineage run $2–$490. Effective: It solves the narrow stated problem (more accurate and faster written models than LLM-written Transformers) but only on a proxy of practical utility — absolute accuracy (52–54% ARC) is far below prompted or fine-tuned small pretrained models (75–91%), and the authors concede pretrained LLMs remain more accurate. Scalable: Only partially tested — synthetic scaling to 1B non-zero pair-table values holds time flat at 0.012 ms/question, but accuracy at scale is untested and the models store only what the writer can state. Deliverable: code, project page, and released written models are indicated; the method stops at paper-plus-artifact form with no trained model of general utility. Strengths: - The convergent-design finding is a genuinely new empirical observation with an unusually well-controlled causal analysis: the BM25-over-own-text control cleanly separates content from structure, and the direct interference measurement on SciQ generation (F1 0.37 outside versus 0.24–0.25 inside a written Transformer) is direct evidence, not inference. - The two-property framework (traceability, locality) is an exportable design principle for any gradient-free weight-authoring system, backed by the line-removal experiments across 14 models and three writers. - The associative-memory-based model is a competent systems contribution: hashed second-order addressing with a fixed 120-row read is a clean solution to the full-scan bottleneck, and the scaling analysis honestly maps where the advantage ends. - Contamination controls (n-gram overlap, deletion tests, recall probes) exceed the standard of care in most LLM-as-writer papers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are candid and thorough: written models only recall stated facts and cannot chain or compose (ARC-Challenge stays near 38% versus 63% Easy); MMLU stays at chance; the Transformer claim is scoped to current LLMs writing from random initialization without data; the speed advantage holds only up to measured concept counts; only one GPU (RTX 3090) was tested and lookup-oriented hardware is unexplored; low-label domains are motivated but untested; and they explicitly flag the familiarity confound — LLMs may choose tables because retrieval is the classic training-free baseline they know, not because it suits weight writing, and their no-row-table control does not fully separate these. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No error bars or repeated seeds anywhere; with single-run lineages and generation-selection by validation accuracy, the 49.6–54.4% figures carry unquantified variance, and the claimed ~3-point accuracy gap between LLM-designed and associative-memory-based models is within plausible run-to-run noise. - The LLM-written Transformer is arguably a soft baseline: the finding that a specific LLM fails to write a Transformer does not establish that no prompt, scaffold, or writer could — the paper generalizes from three writers' first attempts under fixed prompts. - The speed comparison excludes optimized sparse/scatter kernels beyond CUDA graphs and torch.compile; the 7–17× margin against a batch-dense Transformer on dense-GPU hardware may shrink substantially under a sparse-aware runtime, and no CPU baseline for the table models is reported in the main comparison. - Practical impact is bounded by the elephant the authors address only in passing: a prompted Qwen3-0.6B scores 75.4% on ARC with zero training, dwarfing every written model, so the deployment case for WSP here rests entirely on the untested low-label/warm-start scenario (AG News warm-start shows +21 points over from-scratch training at 100 labels, but only one task, one writer). - Cross-writer variance is large (GPT-6 Astra's best lineage cost $490 versus $96 for Claude's), and the paper does not analyze why writer ability differs, which matters for predicting whether the finding survives future model releases. Bottom Line: For researchers in LLM-authored models, neural memory, and gradient-free learning, this is the most rigorous evidence yet on what architecture LLMs choose and why, and worth reading in full; for anyone else, the absolute accuracy gap to a prompted 0.6B pretrained model means the practical yield does not yet justify the paradigm.

Zixuan Huang, Yang Zhou, Guli Zhang, Sunzhu Li, Hongyan Xie, Zehao Chen, Fuzhen Zhuang, Kaixuan Wang, Xiaozhi Chen, Yikun Ban, Deqing Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 20 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ZeroVLN, a slow–fast vision-language navigation framework in which a VLM 'brain' issues natural-language tool calls to a trainable flow-matching action expert, achieving navigation competence with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM and joint closed-loop RL of both policies. - Why it's important: Standard VLN pipelines fine-tune the VLM on navigation data, which destroys the model's general visual/spatial capabilities (their SFT baselines drop to 0% on twelve general benchmarks); preserving the general-purpose brain while adding navigation skill removes a major deployment cost for embodied agents. - How it does it: The core trick is a semantic tool-call interface (target/where/plan in natural language) plus request-grounded supervision — a privileged mesh-based planner converts the frozen brain's own sampled requests into executable reference trajectories that train the action expert — followed by trajectory-level RLOO RL with process and outcome rewards shared across both policies via separate gradient paths. - The good: The capability-preservation evidence is convincing and multi-pronged: 0.01497% relative VLM weight displacement (vs 3.21% DualVLN, 7.67% NaVILA), 59.16% mean retained accuracy on twelve general benchmarks (base: 59.47%; skippable for readers needing practical path efficiency or real-robot results today.

Problem & Motivation: Vision-language navigation (VLN) agents must couple high-level movement decisions with precise continuous motion. Dominant approaches fine-tune a general-purpose VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals (pixel targets) or numerical motion commands for an action head. The authors observe — and quantify — that this adaptation displaces base VLM weights (3.21–7.67% relative L2) and catastrophically degrades general visual/spatial capabilities (SFT-adapted models score 0% across twelve benchmarks including CV-Bench, EmbSpatialBench, and MMSI-Bench). Practitioners who want a single embodied agent that retains general perception/reasoning while navigating currently face a destructive-adaptation dilemma. The gap: no prior slow–fast VLN framework trains navigation without SFT of the VLM brain. Key Idea: Replace the brain's geometric output interface with a natural-language semantic tool call (run_action_head(target, where, plan)) and make the base brain's own sampled requests executable, rather than teaching the brain new output formats. This works because (a) a general VLM already makes useful navigation decisions via tool use (their Direct Tool Use baseline achieves 39.5% SR on SAGE-3D with zero training), (b) a privileged trajectory planner can turn the brain's actual online requests into execution-verified supervision for a small flow-matching action expert, and (c) trajectory-level RLOO RL then improves both policies via return-weighted updates that reinforce or suppress the brain's existing token paths instead of fitting a prescribed distribution — the authors formalize this with a proposition showing the SFT gradient contains a return-irrelevant distribution-matching component (the orthogonal w in their minimum-norm analysis) that RL avoids. Methodology: Two training stages. (1) Request-grounded action-expert adaptation: with the brain and frozen Qwen3.5-4B visual encoder fixed, the brain samples movement calls on training episodes (34,445 episodes; 384,836 anchors; 65.6% retention after verification); a privileged planner grounds each request via dependency parsing, lexical/text-encoder retrieval, lexicographic candidate ranking (Eq. 13–14), clearance-aware A* (Eq. 15), spline smoothing, and simulator execution verification, producing reference trajectories paired with the originating requests. The 34.8M-parameter, 12-layer flow-matching action expert (DualVLN-style dual-stream conditioning: 16 learnable semantic queries contextualized by the VLM + 32 pooled visual tokens from reference/current RGB) is trained with flow-matching loss supervised only on the executed 4-step prefix of a 16-step horizon (Eq. 3), fixing the train-time/execute-time mismatch of full-sequence chunk supervision. (2) Joint agentic RL: 200 steps of REINFORCE-style updates with G=8 rollouts per episode, RLOO trajectory-level advantage (Eq. 4) shared by both policies but with separate gradient paths — the brain only via the text objective (Eq. 10), the action expert via Flow-SDE path likelihood gradients following Flow-GRPO/DPPO (Eq. 11), with action gradients flowing through the VLM to the queries but θ fixed on that path. Reward = terminal success + first arrival + bounded distance-progress potential + information-discovery (depth-verified new entities, capped at 0.05/episode). Key design decisions: trajectory-level vs round-level credit (ablated and justified), prefix-only flow supervision (ablated), and request-grounded vs constructed/GT-route supervision (ablated in Appendix D.2 — notably, direction-augmentation raises paired-direction accuracy to 95.9–96.3% yet yields no navigation transfer, SR 13.25% both ways, a well-executed negative result). Brain: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (MoE, A3B active). Key Results: Controlled same-backbone, same-episode comparisons: ZeroVLN achieves 51.3% SR / 32.0 SPL on SAGE-3D, 66.7% SR / 29.2 SPL / 29.2 NE on R2R-CE, and 64.6% SR / 28.1 SPL / 28.1 NE on RxR-CE, versus NaVILA at 23.5/42.4/55.6 SR and DualVLN at 21.2/15.4/17.7 SR — a >30-point SR gain over DualVLN on all three benchmarks and +27.8/+6.2/+2.7 over NaVILA. Against published results trained on far more data, ZeroVLN beats NaVILA-SAGE's 46.0% SAGE-3D SR using 1/14 the episodes (34.4K vs 500K), and exceeds Uni-NaVid OSR by 13.4/9.1 points on R2R/RxR, though it trails JanusVLN (65.2 SR, 60.5 SPL R2R) and NavFoM (64.9/56.2), which use ≥150K–182K+ episodes — ZeroVLN's SPL also lags these leaders. RL is the dominant driver: SR jumps from 36.9→51.3 (SAGE), 42.4→66.7 (R2R), 18.7→51.4 (RxR) over the no-RL checkpoint. Weight displacement is 0.01497% (ZeroVLN) vs 3.21% (DualVLN) vs 7.67% (NaVILA); general benchmark mean accuracy 59.16% (base 59.47%, SFT baselines 0.00%), confirmed at 62.00% vs 62.86% base under a format-free next-token readout (SFT baselines near the 32.48% random baseline). The reachability–efficiency trade-off is explicit: higher OSR than NaVILA (66.7/64.6 vs 51.8/55.6) but lower SPL (29.2/28.1 vs 41.8/43.0). Baselines are current and retrained under controlled conditions; published SOTA comparisons are not same-data, which the authors acknowledge by tabulating training-episode counts. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW FORMULATION with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component. Genuinely novel: the first slow–fast VLN framework where the VLM brain communicates through natural-language semantic tool calls rather than geometric targets, with zero navigation-domain SFT of the brain, and the first joint closed-loop agentic RL of a VLM brain plus continuous flow-matching action expert in VLN-CE; the request-grounded data-construction pipeline (planning trajectories from the frozen brain's own online requests) is a non-obvious enabling contribution, supported by the augmentation/GT-route negative results. Standard components reused: flow matching, DualVLN's dual-stream conditioning, RLOO/REINFORCE, Flow-GRPO/DPPO action-policy gradients, and privileged-planner imitation — the contribution is their composition around the semantic interface, not any single algorithmic primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: trajectory-level vs round-level credit (matched rewards), joint vs brain-only vs expert-only RL (including the interesting collapse of brain-only RL as the request distribution drifts from a fixed expert), removal of each of the four reward components, execution-prefix vs full-sequence flow supervision on identical trajectories, and three supervision-construction alternatives. The paper also includes a formal analysis (two propositions + a KL/Pinsker capability-retention bound) that, while using idealized local assumptions, is stated honestly as explanatory rather than predictive. Metrics: SR, SPL, NE, OSR on official evaluation sets with 200-round limits; RL monitoring on 100 fixed episodes every 4 steps. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for headline results (single runs); the augmentation experiments in Appendix D.2 explicitly note one training seed. Code (github.com/hzx122/ZeroVLN) and model weights (huggingface.co/hzxllll/ZeroVLN) are released. Methodological concerns: the privileged planner requires scene meshes and training-time geometry, so the method's data-generation story does not transfer directly to real environments; some published-baseline comparisons (SAGE-Bench rows) differ in training data and episodes; the RL budget of 200 steps raises questions about how conclusions depend on compute scale, though this also means results are achieved cheaply. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (simulation-trained, simulation-evaluated system with released artifacts). - Practical: The brain is a 35B-A3B MoE VLM (≈3B active) paired with a 34.8M expert and a frozen 333.5M vision tower, so inference runs on a single high-end accelerator-class node, though training used 128 devices for open-loop adaptation and RL; no real-robot deployment is shown. - Efficient: Data-efficient (34.4K episodes vs 80K–500K for published baselines) and 200 RL steps, but slow inference — semantic tool calls plus multi-cycle flow execution, with a 200-round evaluation budget, and the OSR/SPL gap implies ~40% longer paths than NaVILA-style shortcuts. - Effective: Strong evidence it solves goal-reaching in simulation (66.7% R2R SR, +14.9 OSR over Uni-NaVid), but path efficiency is worse than SFT baselines, so it partially solves the stated problem at a cost the paper discloses. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 34K episodes and 200 RL steps; the paper claims the paradigm extends to general embodied skills but provides no experiment at larger scale. Delivers a software artifact: released code and trained model weights, plus a reusable request-grounding data-generation recipe. Strengths: (1) The capability-preservation claim is validated at three levels — parameter displacement (0.01497% vs 3.21/7.67%), free-form benchmark accuracy (59.16% vs 0.00%), and a controlled next-token readout that eliminates answer-formatting confounds — a model of careful claim testing. (2) The request-grounded supervision design is genuinely non-obvious and empirically motivated: the authors ran the obvious alternatives (CAST-style augmentation, GT-route anchoring), showed they fail (95.9% template accuracy but zero navigation transfer), and built the method around the failure. (3) The controlled same-backbone/same-episode comparison of NaVILA and DualVLN isolates the interface choice from data and backbone effects, which most VLN papers skip. (4) The negative result that brain-only RL collapses (SR falls below initialization as requests drift from a fixed expert) is an honest and useful finding for anyone doing joint policy optimization. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly confront the reachability–efficiency trade-off — higher OSR but lower SPL than NaVILA on R2R/RxR due to exploration and recovery behavior — and analyze it rather than burying it. They note semantic/trajectory maps and mesh geometry are training-only, acknowledge that published-baseline comparisons involve differing episode counts, and the appendix reports seed limitations for the augmentation experiments ('one training seed and different training exposure'). They do not claim real-robot or sim-to-real results. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No confidence intervals, seeds, or significance tests on the headline benchmark numbers, which is material given margins of +2.7 SR over NaVILA on RxR. (2) The privileged planner's dependence on scene meshes and dependency parsing for grounding is a hidden dependency that constrains application to environments with mesh/semantic-map access — the paper frames the method as needing 'no dataset-provided expert trajectories' but the planner effectively is an expert trajectory generator. (3) Evaluation is confined to simulation benchmarks (SAGE-3D, R2R-CE, RxR-CE, Habitat-class); nothing tests whether the semantic-interface benefit survives physical execution noise, latency, or a non-simulator action expert. (4) The information-discovery reward depends on a depth-verified entity detector whose errors are not characterized. (5) The theoretical section's local linearization assumptions (Proposition 2) and the capability bound's curvature assumption M are idealized; the paper says so, but the gap between the 0.015% displacement and the bound's practical meaning is untested. (6) The RL stage's 200 steps vs the baselines' full-SFT budgets means compute-matched comparisons across paradigms are not provided. Bottom Line: For VLN and embodied-agent researchers, this is a substantive and well-controlled demonstration that a semantic tool interface plus RL can replace navigation SFT without wrecking the base VLM — read it despite the simulation-only setting and the SPL penalty, because the capability-retention evidence and the supervision-construction negative results are findings you will not get from the SFT-based literature it replaces.

FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency (23 ▲ )

Gene Chou, Guandao Yang, Fujun Luan, Lars Mescheder, Wei Dong, Stephan Richter, Vladlen Koltun · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 18 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of autoregressive video diffusion models (1.3B and 14B parameters) that achieve end-to-end per-frame latency of 36 ms and 45 ms respectively at 480p, entering the ≤50 ms interactive regime while matching the VBench quality of baselines 7.6–10.6× slower. - Why it's important: Prior autoregressive video diffusion models are 5–50× too slow for fluid human interaction (delay-detection threshold ≈50 ms), blocking their use in interactive world models, games, and camera/physics-conditioned applications. - How it does it: Profiling reveals that VAE decoding and KV-cache refinement — not diffusion denoising — dominate latency, so the paper replaces the VAE decoder with a ConvNeXt readout head (147× faster), the DiT-based KV refinement pass with a lightweight repair network (~10–20× faster), and applies hardware-aware systems optimizations plus 8-GPU context parallelism. - The good: The profiling insight is quantified and actionable: for the strongest baseline (Causal Forcing++), only ~30% of 272 ms wall time is diffusion sampling, and the paper shows 1.3B FastFrames retains 84.23 VBench Total vs. 84.11 for the same-weight baseline while being 7.6× faster. - The missing: Quality is evaluated almost exclusively via VBench on the authors' chosen prompts/seeds (no FVD, no human study, no long-video consistency metrics), and the interactive latency numbers depend on B200-class GPUs — at 720p latency roughly triples to 116–127 ms, outside the interactive regime. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or deploy autoregressive video diffusion systems or interactive world models — the latency decomposition and component replacements transfer to other models — skip it if you only care about offline generation quality, where it does not advance the frontier.

Non-Obviousness (78) is the paper's strongest dimension: the quantified finding that VAE decoding and KV refinement, not diffusion sampling, dominate end-to-end latency genuinely redirects the field's attention. Completeness (72) is helped by a direct, non-minimizing limitations section (720p, B200 dependence, long-horizon consistency named as open), but long-horizon drift through the lightweight decoder and repaired KV cache — the central interactive risk — is unmeasured. Problem & Motivation: Interactive video applications (world simulation, games, robotics predictive models) need autoregressive video diffusion models that respond to new inputs within ~50 ms, the human delay-detection threshold from HCI studies. Existing acceleration work reports FPS, which amortizes batch generation time and does not capture input-to-response latency; the fastest published baselines (e.g., Causal Forcing++ at 272 ms/frame, Krea-Realtime at 1,675 ms) fall far short of the 20 responses-per-second target. The paper observes that acceleration research has focused on distilling diffusion sampling steps, while profiling shows the true bottleneck lies elsewhere — VAE decoding alone (147 ms) exceeds the entire 50 ms budget, and a single KV-cache refinement DiT pass costs as much as a diffusion step. Key Idea: Treat two components usually considered fixed architecture — the VAE decoder and the clean-latent KV-cache refinement pass — as replaceable lightweight readouts. Because a two-step distilled DiT already produces rich, spatially contextualized features, pixel rendering becomes a cheap per-model head (three causal 3D ConvNeXt blocks at 21×30×52 token resolution plus one linear unpatchify, 63.9M params, 1 ms) rather than a general-purpose reconstruction problem, and KV cache repair becomes a small transformer adapter that predicts residual corrections to the noisy keys/values. The remaining DiT cost is then attacked with systems engineering (persistent KV buffers, fused QKV, segmented KV attention with softmax merge, CUDA graphs, context parallelism). Methodology: The pipeline starts from the Causal Forcing++ recipe: a Wan 2.1 bidirectional teacher is converted to an autoregressive model, distilled with distribution-matching distillation (DMD) into a two-step student that generates one latent frame per autoregressive step. Three components are then built/optimized: (1) Pixel decoder — three causal ConvNeXt-style 3D blocks with depthwise 3×3×3 convolutions at token resolution, ending in a linear projection to 4×16×16 RGB patches; trained first with a five-term reconstruction loss (L1, MSE, spatial gradient, temporal gradient, motion-weighted L1, λ's = 0.5/5.0/0.05/0.05/0.5) against frozen VAE outputs on 150K rollouts, then finetuned adversarially with a relativistic discriminator built on frozen DINOv3 ViT-S/16 features (six heads over layers 4/8/12), enabling end-to-end pixel-space GAN training (peak memory 5 GB vs. 68 GB for the VAE decoder). (2) KV refinement network — a shared stem (patch embed → 768 channels, four lightweight self-attention blocks) plus per-layer repair heads predicting residual corrections to the noisy K/V written by the final denoising pass, supervised by the original DiT refinement pass's K/V and attention outputs; value errors get ~3× the weight of key errors. (3) Systems optimizations — persistent KV buffers, precomputed RoPE/text/timestep tensors, fused QKV, splitting the 32,760-token KV cache into five parallel segments merged via softmax (13% latency reduction), CUDA graphs, and 8-GPU context parallelism with NVLink symmetric-memory gathers. DiT evaluation drops from 41.6 to 16.4 ms (1.3B, single GPU) and 75.6 to 20.3 ms (14B single GPU), then to 5.8/20.3 ms on 8 GPUs. The DiT is frozen throughout; finetuning it was tried and abandoned due to instability. Design decisions are justified by profiling and ablations (e.g., Fig. 6 shows removing KV refinement causes subject drift even after retraining). Key Results: On VBench (same prompts and seeds for all models, B200 GPU, ~480p): FastFrames-S (1.3B) reaches 84.23 Total at 36 ms/frame (27.8 RPS) on one B200 and 14 ms (71.4 RPS) on 8 GPUs, vs. Causal Forcing++ at 84.11 Total and 272 ms — a 7.6× speedup at equal-or-better Total score, though Semantic score slightly drops (79.92 vs. 80.20). FastFrames-L (14B) reaches 84.44 Total at 158 ms on one GPU and 45 ms (22.2 RPS) on 8×B200, vs. Krea-Realtime at 84.42 Total and 1,675 ms — a 37× speedup on the 8-GPU configuration. No baseline meets the 50 ms target; the fastest, CF++, reaches only 3.68 RPS, 5.4× short of 20 RPS. Component-level speedups: VAE decode 147→1 ms, KV refinement 41.6→2 ms (1.3B) / 75.6→6 ms (14B). Transfer experiments: LingBot 1.3B camera-conditioned model drops from 842 ms (official 2-GPU) to 52 ms (16×), RealWonder physics-conditioned from 1,141 ms to 51 ms (22×), LingBot 14B from 1,373 ms to 233 ms on 8 GPUs. At 720p, latency rises to 127 ms (FastFrames-S) and 116 ms (FastFrames-L, 8 GPU); H100s are 25–50% slower than B200s. The paper also reports that Self-Forcing's published latency averages over a sequence with a filling cache and thus understates steady-state latency, and that CF++ reports identical 270 ms for its 1/2/4-step variants without explanation. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the profiling result that non-denoising operations — VAE decode and KV-cache refinement — constitute the majority of end-to-end latency in few-step AR video diffusion) plus NEW METHOD (the lightweight pixel readout head with pixel-space adversarial training, and the KV cache repair network) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (context parallelism, CUDA graphs, segmented attention — individually standard techniques, but combined and validated on the steady-state per-frame critical path). The pixel head and repair adapter combine known ingredients (ConvNeXt, JiT-style linear readouts, relativistic GANs, DINOv3 features) in a new setting; the genuinely novel part is the demonstrated decomposition showing where latency actually lives and that the "accessory" components can be replaced without quality loss. Rigor & Reproducibility: Component ablations are present and load-bearing: Fig. 6 shows naive removal of KV refinement and even retraining without it cause subject drift and artifacts, justifying the repair network; Fig. 3 shows a pure linear projection is blurry but recognizable, motivating the ConvNeXt head. Error bars, multiple seeds, and significance tests are not reported for VBench scores, though evaluation uses fixed shared prompts/seeds. Code and model weights are promised on the project page (https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-fastframes/). Latency methodology is unusually careful — steady-state with full KV cache, per-operation breakdowns, cross-GPU (B200/H100) and cross-resolution (480p/720p) profiling, and a documented critique of Self-Forcing's amortized latency reporting. Concerns: (1) quality is judged almost entirely by VBench on the authors' chosen setup, with no FVD, no human preference study, and no long-horizon consistency metric, despite the adversarial decoder and interactive use case making temporal artifacts a live risk; (2) the adversarial pixel decoder is trained on an "internal dataset of 10K real videos" that is not released; (3) the 14B model is initialized and evaluated within the same Wan/CF++ ecosystem the authors optimize (baseline comparisons share the backbone, which is fair, but the interactive-application models LingBot and RealWonder are compared against "official" implementations the authors themselves tuned); (4) some latency-relevant baselines (e.g., CF++ step-count reporting) are flagged as opaque, and the paper re-measures rather than reproduces them. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a strong SYSTEMS component — released models, code, and optimized inference pipelines). Practical: Not on consumer hardware — the headline numbers require B200 GPUs (an 8-GPU node for the 14B variant), and the authors themselves flag accessible/on-device hardware as future work; H100 numbers are provided but still exceed 50 ms in several configurations. Efficient: Relative to alternatives it is the efficiency contribution — 7.6–37× lower latency at matched VBench, with the pixel decoder using ~5 GB vs. 68 GB peak training memory for the VAE. Effective: Evidence shows it meets the stated latency proxy (steady-state per-frame time) and matches VBench, but whether interactive sessions remain visually consistent over minutes (drift, error accumulation through the lightweight decoder and repaired KV cache) is shown only via qualitative side-by-sides, not measured. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: models, code, and an interactive demo on the project page, plus reusable training recipes for the pixel head and KV adapter. Strengths: - The profiling result is a genuine, quantified finding that contradicts the field's implicit focus: diffusion sampling is only ~30% of end-to-end latency in the fastest baseline, redirecting attention to VAE decoding and KV management. - The pixel-space adversarial decoder is a real methodological contribution, not just compression: bypassing the VAE enables end-to-end GAN training (5 GB vs. 68 GB memory), which the authors credit for FastFrames-S's quality gain over the same-weights CF++ baseline. - The KV repair network preserves an empirically necessary refinement (ablation in Fig. 6) at ~1/10–1/20 the cost, with an instructive detail that value corruption dominates key corruption. - Honest latency methodology: steady-state measurement with a full KV cache, per-operation breakdowns across GPUs and resolutions, and an explicit correction of how a competitor (Self-Forcing) reports latency. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: evaluation is at 480p only, and 720p latency (116–127 ms) leaves the interactive regime, requiring further optimization; measurements are on B200 GPUs, with on-device/accessible hardware unaddressed; applied to existing action-conditioned models (LingBot, RealWonder), extra diffusion steps and conditioning overhead keep even 1.3B models at ~51–52 ms and needing 8 GPUs, and they argue future base models should be designed for lower-latency conditioning (e.g., channel- rather than sequence-dimension camera poses); and they name long-term consistency and physical plausibility as open problems. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No human-subject evaluation despite motivating the 50 ms target with HCI literature; whether 36 ms renders "fluid" interaction is asserted via demo videos, not measured. - No long-horizon quantitative metric (drift, subject consistency, error accumulation through the repaired KV cache and adversarial decoder) — the paper's own conclusion names long-term consistency as future work, but for an interactive system this is the central unmeasured risk. - VBench is a short-clip benchmark; its Total score may not capture the temporal artifacts most relevant to streaming AR generation, and no statistical uncertainty is reported for the 0.1–0.3 score margins over baselines. - The adversarial pixel decoder is model-specific (acknowledged for the decoder but not as a general cost), and its GAN training data (10K internal videos) is not released, complicating exact reproduction. - Transfer results (LingBot, RealWonder) are compared against the vendors' official inference code; no independent optimized baseline (e.g., aggressive quantization or KV compression methods cited in related work) is run on these models to isolate how much of the speedup comes from FastFrames' components versus systems engineering alone. - Hardware constraints mean the "interactive regime" claim is currently contingent on top-tier datacenter GPUs; nothing in the paper demonstrates the approach on the hardware an interactive product would plausibly ship on. Bottom Line: For anyone building real-time or interactive video generation systems, this paper is worth reading for its latency decomposition alone — it convincingly shows the field has been optimizing the wrong third of the pipeline — but its quality evidence rests on VBench margins and qualitative demos, so treat the interactivity claim as demonstrated on hardware, not yet on humans.

On the Difficulty of Sequence-Level Supervised Learning for Autoregressive Language Models

M Blondel, ME Sander, G Vivier-Ardisson, T Liu… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proves that two natural sequence-level supervised losses for autoregressive language models — one built on greedy decoding, one on ancestral sampling — are unbounded below and therefore unusable, and that the stop-gradient 'moment matching' surrogate direction, while a valid descent direction in function space, is not the gradient of any loss and suffers from high variance. - Why it's important: Exposure bias — the train/inference mismatch of teacher forcing — has motivated 25+ years of attempts at decoding-aware sequence-level training; this paper explains why the most natural formulations of that idea are structurally broken, redirecting effort toward data-distribution fixes (on-policy distillation) or RL post-training. - How it does it: The core move is an autoregressive Gumbel trick showing the sampling loss equals the Gumbel-perturbed expectation of the greedy loss, plus a soft-Bellman 'AR-to-EBM' reparameterization proving the stop-gradient direction is the EBM functional gradient — hence a descent direction for the AR negative log-likelihood. - The good: The impossibility results are proven cleanly on minimal counterexamples (T=2, V=2), and the descent result (Proposition 7) is established via a contraction/positive-definiteness argument on the Jacobian of the AR-to-EBM mapping, giving a genuine structural explanation for the pathologies rather than just observed failure. - The missing: The paper contains no experiments whatsoever — even a small-scale empirical demonstration of the moment matching direction's high variance or of the divergence of the flawed losses would substantially strengthen the claims; all statements are in function space (tabular setting) with only an acknowledged caveat about parameter space. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on training objectives for sequence models, structured prediction, or the theory of decoding-aware learning — it is a short, rigorous negative result that should preempt future attempts; skip it if you want practical algorithms, since it delivers none.

Problem & Motivation: Supervised training of autoregressive (AR) language models uses teacher forcing: token-level cross-entropy conditioned on ground-truth prefixes. This is suspected of causing exposure bias — at inference the model conditions on its own predictions, potentially accumulating errors. Prior remedies split into (a) policy-gradient / minimum-risk methods that require external rewards, and (b) structured-prediction losses (perceptron loss, CRF negative log-likelihood, energy-based models) that require exact maximization or log-partition oracles, both intractable over the exponentially large sequence space Y = V^T. The paper targets the researchers and theorists who have repeatedly attempted the natural middle path: sequence-level losses that plug the inference-time decoding procedure (greedy decoding or ancestral sampling) into the cumulant slot of these classical losses. The gap it closes is explanatory: why does this middle path keep failing, and is there any salvageable update rule in its vicinity. Key Idea: The single core insight is that greedy decoding and ancestral sampling are two faces of one object, connected by an autoregressive Gumbel trick: sampling Y ~ p_AR(·|x) is equivalent to greedy decoding under i.i.d. Gumbel-perturbed scores q+Z, so L_sampling = E_Z[L_{q+Z}^greedy]. Both losses inherit their pathology from the dependence of the decoded sequence (and hence the cumulant A) on the model parameters: because the 'cumulant' is not a true log-partition function of a Gibbs distribution over the AR model's scores, the envelope theorem fails, and the loss can be driven to -∞ by enlarging a search error (greedy decoding a sequence that scores lower than the ground truth). Removing this dependence via a stop gradient yields a moment-matching direction that is the EBM gradient under the invertible AR-to-EBM soft-Bellman mapping M — mathematically the correct gradient with the non-stationarity term dropped. Methodology: The paper is purely theoretical, structured as a sequence of propositions with proofs in the appendix, using the function-space (tabular) representation where the score q itself is the parameter and R_q(x,y) = <q, φ(x,y)> with φ a feature map over visited state-action pairs. The pipeline is: (1) Background — unify EBMs and AR models by writing p_AR as a Gibbs form with a prefix-dependent 'log-partition' A_AR; (2) Section 3 defines L_greedy = A_greedy - R_q (O(VT) complexity vs O(V^T) for exact max) and L_sampling = E_{Y~p_AR}[A_AR(x,Y)] - R_q, and proves via explicit T=2, V=2 counterexamples that both are nonconvex, and unbounded below (greedy is additionally discontinuous); (3) Section 4 proves the autoregressive Gumbel trick (Proposition 4) unifying the two losses; (4) Section 5 analyzes the stop-gradient moment matching direction d_q = E_{Y~p_AR}[φ(x,Y)] - φ(x,y): Proposition 5 shows no loss has d_q as its gradient (Jacobian of the model mean is not self-adjoint for T≥2), Proposition 6 shows d_q equals the EBM functional gradient under the mapping r = M(q) and equals the AR gradient preconditioned by (∂M(q))^{-1}, and Proposition 7 proves -d_q is a descent direction via a contraction property of the soft-Bellman expectation operator and Cauchy–Schwarz. Critical design decisions: using the Blondel et al. (2025) AR-to-EBM mapping as the proof engine (well-justified, as invertibility gives the half-space condition for descent); restricting descent guarantees to function space (acknowledged as a real limitation — the Gram operator J(w)J(w) can deform inner products in parameter space); and the honest variance analysis — teacher forcing gives the exact gradient in one forward pass, while d_q requires Monte Carlo over V^T with correlated prefixes whose variance grows with T. Key Results: There are no quantitative or experimental results; the headline outcomes are the propositions themselves. Specifically: (i) L_greedy is discontinuous, nonconvex in q, and unbounded below (loss → -∞ as a logit parameter α → ∞ by inflating a search error where greedy decoding scores the ground truth below the decoded sequence); (ii) L_sampling is smooth but nonconvex and unbounded below, with a closed-form divergence rate ½log(1+e^α) - α → -∞ in the proof; (iii) the two losses are linked by L_sampling = E_Z[L_{q+Z}^greedy] under shifted Gumbel noise; (iv) d_q is not a gradient of any loss for T≥2, but -d_q satisfies ⟨-d_q, ∇_q L_AR^q⟩ < 0, a strict descent condition in function space. The scale of analysis is minimal toy settings (T=2, V=2) for the impossibility proofs, which is appropriate for negative results but means no behavior at realistic model scale is examined. No baselines, datasets, or benchmarks apply. The counter-intuitive finding worth highlighting is that the 'mathematically incorrect' stop-gradient reparameterization (which the paper shows cannot be justified by the standard pathwise-derivative argument) is nonetheless a certified descent direction — while the mathematically correct REINFORCE gradient targets a loss that provably diverges. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (theoretical): the genuinely novel contributions are the autoregressive Gumbel trick unifying greedy and sampling-based losses (Proposition 4, distinct from Kool et al. 2019's Gumbel-top-k for beam-search sampling), the proof that both decoding-aware losses are unbounded below, and the identification of the stop-gradient moment matching direction with a preconditioned AR gradient that is provably a descent direction despite not being a gradient. The building blocks — Gumbel tricks, Fenchel–Young/perceptron loss structure, EBMs, soft-Bellman mappings, stop gradients, scheduled sampling — are all established; the paper is largely a rigorous synthesis through the lens of the authors' own prior AR-as-EBM framework (Blondel et al., 2025), with the descent-direction analysis as the sharpest new element. Rigor & Reproducibility: The proofs are self-contained, short, and use explicit counterexamples rather than hand-waving; the appendix verifies each proposition, including a careful contraction/positive-definiteness argument for the Jacobian of the soft-Bellman mapping. Ablations, seeds, and error bars are not applicable (no experiments). No code, data, or model weights are released — none are needed, but also none exist to independently verify the practical claims (e.g., that the variance of d_q grows with T is argued, not measured). Methodological concerns: (a) the central descent guarantee (Proposition 7) holds only in function space; the authors correctly flag that parameter-space descent can fail even under linear parameterization, which means the practical relevance of the positive result is thin; (b) the fixed-length assumption T (with variable-length handling deferred to Blondel et al., 2025) excludes EOS/termination issues that are central to real LLM exposure bias; (c) the framework excludes reward-based and candidate-set-restricted losses, which are the methods actually used in practice — the paper discusses these honestly but they sit outside what is analyzed. There is no Goodhart/benchmark-gaming risk since there is no benchmark. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL — the paper proves results and runs no experiments, trains no model, and releases no artifact. Sound: Assumptions are explicit (fixed T, differentiable q_w, tabular function-space setting for the descent claims) and the proofs are complete; the main gap is the acknowledged function-space-vs-parameter-space divide. General: The impossibility results hold for T≥2 with minimal assumptions and are broadly applicable; the positive result (descent direction) holds only in function space and the variance limitation makes it broadly unrealistic to deploy. Tight: Not a bound-style paper, but the negative results are tight in the sense that explicit counterexamples achieve divergence, and the descent characterization is exact (equality of d_q with the preconditioned gradient, not merely inequality). Implementable: The moment matching direction is implementable (ancestral sampling plus stop-gradient), but the paper itself argues it is dominated by teacher forcing on cost and variance; no follow-up operationalization exists within the paper. The work delivers no software artifact — it stops at paper form, contributing a reusable proof technique (AR-to-EBM reparameterization for analyzing AR training directions) and a set of caveats for future loss design. Strengths: - The unification of greedy-decoding and sampling-based losses via the autoregressive Gumbel trick (L_sampling = E_Z[L_{q+Z}^greedy]) is a genuine conceptual contribution that collapses two previously separate research threads into one analysis. - The impossibility proofs are unusually concrete: divergence is exhibited by explicit two-token, two-symbol families q_α with closed-form rates (e.g., ½log(1+e^α) - α → -∞), making the pathology transparent — it comes from search errors where the decoded sequence scores below the ground truth. - The descent analysis via the soft-Bellman AR-to-EBM mapping cleanly explains why the stop-gradient trick works (it drops the non-stationarity term from ∇_q A_sampling, which the envelope theorem would kill in the EBM case but cannot in the AR case) — this is a real structural insight, not just a sufficient-condition certificate. - The paper confronts its own limitations head-on: it explicitly proves the direction is not a gradient, explicitly restricts descent to function space, and explicitly concludes against its own practical utility — a degree of intellectual honesty rare in this area. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: (1) the descent guarantee (Proposition 7) holds only in function space and does not transfer to parameter space, even under linear parameterization, because the Gram operator J(w)J(w)* deforms inner products; (2) the moment matching direction has high variance — it requires Monte Carlo estimation over the sequence distribution with correlated prefixes, with variance growing with sequence length T, whereas teacher forcing gives the exact gradient in a single forward pass; (3) constraining parameters to a bounded set does not fix the unboundedness pathology, only hides it at the constraint boundary; (4) the stop-gradient reparameterization does not transfer to RL post-training, where the reward is a separate function and REINFORCE remains necessary; (5) violation-fixing/margin methods (early updates, max-violation, beam-search optimization) avoid the pathologies but have sparse gradients and require teacher-forcing pre-training. This is a credibility positive: the limitations are stated directly and the final conclusion is calibrated to them, not minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the authors' own caveats, a critical reviewer would flag: (1) the fixed-length setting Y = V^T sidesteps termination and variable-length generation, which is where exposure bias arguably bites hardest in real LLMs; the deferral to Blondel et al. (2025) means the impossibility results are not directly stated for realistic decoders with EOS. (2) The claim that exposure bias is a real concern is treated as given and uncited against counter-evidence; since the paper concludes teacher forcing suffices, an empirical measurement of how much exposure bias actually costs at scale would have sharpened the practical takeaway — the paper proves losses are broken but never demonstrates the bias they were meant to fix matters. (3) The variance argument against d_q is qualitative; a small experiment (even on a toy HMM or tiny Transformer) quantifying variance growth and comparing one update of d_q versus teacher forcing would have closed the loop. (4) The analysis presumes the decoupling into 'supervised learning from static datasets' versus 'RL post-training' — the boundary is asserted rather than derived, and hybrid settings (e.g., sequence-level losses with learned rewards that share parameters, which would revive the stop-gradient trick) are not explored. (5) The descent result gives no step-size or convergence rate; a descent direction without a rate is weak assurance, and the paper does not discuss whether the preconditioned geometry makes practical step sizes pathological. These are gaps of scope and completeness, not errors — the core results appear sound. Bottom Line: Any theorist or practitioner tempted to design decoding-aware sequence-level supervised losses should read this paper first, because it rigorously closes the most natural design space and articulates exactly why on-policy distillation and RL post-training are the surviving alternatives; there is no stronger alternative covering this specific negative-result ground.

Deep Personalization: Continuous Context Observation for Local Proactive Agents

Y Shao, S Bian, J Guo, J Jiang, Z Dong, H Mao, D Yang… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Coco, a proactive desktop agent whose Observer Agent continuously watches screen activity, maintains a long-term proposition-observation memory, and adapts its intervention-timing decisions from implicit user feedback via prompt evolution or LoRA, released with OSWorld-Persona (a synthetic persona-conditioned benchmark of 6,558 key frames / 3,279 annotations from 108 OSWorld 2.0 sessions) and on-device deployment strategies running on a single RTX 5090 or DGX Spark. - Why it's important: Current agents only help users who already know when and how to ask, and the screen data needed to fix this is too sensitive to stream to cloud providers, so proactive assistance and privacy are in direct tension. - How it does it: A closed loop in which continuous observation supplies both context and supervision — engagement/dismissal/repeated-work/manual-AI-use events are converted into binary reward labels, revised by self-reflection, and fed back into the Observer Agent via ACE-style prompt evolution or LoRA, all scheduled locally with change-aware frame deduplication and idle-time personalization. - The good: Adaptation lifts macro F1 by 2.4–3.0× over direct prompting across three model backbones (best 0.483 on Qwen-3.5-9B) and beats an Oracle Persona baseline that hands the model the true persona, which is the strongest single piece of evidence that the loop learns real user-specific structure. - The missing: The benchmark's ground-truth labels are generated by a VLM simulator (Kimi-K2.6) conditioned on the same personas used for evaluation, so headline gains measure alignment with a simulator, not with humans, and the in-the-wild study is only 10 participants for one week with a proxy F1 the authors admit underestimates false negatives. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on proactive/personalized agents, on-device LLM serving, or memory systems — it is a rare fully-measured end-to-end system; Problem & Motivation: LLM agents are reactive: the user must recognize that AI could help and initiate the request, which excludes users who cannot identify those moments. Proactive agents must instead judge, per user and per moment, whether an interruption is welcome — a judgment prior work handles with static profiles or explicit configuration, which cannot capture situated, evolving preferences. Who has this problem: builders of desktop/OS-level assistants and HCI researchers studying mixed-initiative interfaces (a line running from Maes 1994 and Horvitz 1999 to recent proactive-agent benchmarks). Two additional gaps motivate the design: continuous screen observation is privacy-critical data that current cloud-centric personalization pipelines cannot safely process, and no existing benchmark measures persona-dependent intervention timing over real computer-use workflows (prior proactive-agent datasets are text-only). Key Idea: The core insight is that a continuous observation stream is simultaneously the context signal and the supervision signal: the same screenshots that tell an agent what the user is doing also yield free labels afterward (engaged = positive, dismissed = negative, later getting stuck / repeating an operation / manually invoking another AI assistant after the agent stayed silent = a missed opportunity penalized retroactively). Formalizing this as a closed loop — observe, decide y_t ∈ {0,1}, store structured output in a bipartite proposition-observation memory, retrieve as next-step context, and adapt from r_t — is the trick; everything else (LoRA vs. prompt evolution, frame dedup, idle-time training) is machinery to make the loop fit on one GPU. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Observation: a multimodal LLM maps (screenshots with timestamps, prior context h_{t-1}) to a structured output (incremental observation, user intent, rationale, binary need_support); memory M is a bipartite graph of timestamped observations and higher-level propositions synthesized with the General User Model, retrieved temporally and semantically to form h_t. (2) Feedback labeling: r_t = 1 for engaged interventions, 0 for dismissed ones; the same on-device model retrospectively scans the hidden-state history for missed-opportunity heuristics (repetition, stuckness, manual AI invocation) and assigns negative feedback to preceding silent decisions; self-reflection rewrites outputs o'_t for r_t = 0, producing training set D = {(s_t, h_{t-1}, o'_t)}. (3) Adaptation: either LoRA fine-tuning (rank 32, α=64, 1 epoch, vision encoder frozen) or ACE-style generate-reflect-curate prompt evolution over batches of 8 with a 50-bullet memory cap. On-device serving uses change-aware frame selection (retain a frame only when RGB MSE from the last retained frame exceeds τ, forwarding its actions to the next retained frame), observation-first preemptive scheduling with checkpointed idle-time personalization, DFlash block-diffusion speculative decoding, and a radix prefix cache in the CTI engine. The benchmark pipeline runs five stages: collect OSWorld 2.0 recordings → key-frame extraction → pair frames with 4 personas → two-stage labeling by Kimi-K2.6 with a temperature-0.4 self-consistency check and human validation of positive labels only → chronological 70/30 split per persona. Key design decisions: on-device placement (justified as a privacy principle, not just engineering), the missed-opportunity heuristic (acknowledged as inferred, not confirmed, preference), and the self-consistency label filter (only two additional runs — a weak filter). Notably the paper explicitly states no explicit loss function for the framework itself; the RL-style formulation in Eq. 1 is motivational, and adaptation is supervised distillation of self-revised outputs. Key Results: On OSWorld-Persona, vanilla prompting yields macro recall of 0.082–0.186 and F1 below 0.19 across three backbones (Qwen-3.5-9B, Qwen-3.5-35B-A3B, Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni), i.e., off-the-shelf models are near-silent. Coco-PE/Coco-LoRA reach best macro F1 of 0.483 (Qwen-9B, 2.6×), 0.433 (35B-A3B, 2.4×), and 0.349 (Nemotron, 3.0×), with per-persona F1 up to 0.86 (Nemotron Coco-LoRA, Learning-oriented); adapted observers beat the Oracle Persona baseline (0.16–0.39 macro F1) and improve precision, not just intervention rate, though false-alarm rates rise to 0.13–0.25 versus vanilla's near-zero rate. Context ablations: removing accumulated context drops Qwen-9B F1 from 0.483 to 0.388 (Coco-PE) and 0.455 to 0.285 (Coco-LoRA); decision-only output drops it to 0.305. On memory benchmarks (LLM-as-judge), Coco beats Mem0 everywhere: with GPT-5.5 judge, LoCoMo 0.951 vs 0.773, LongMemEval 0.822 vs 0.722, BEAM-100K 0.750 vs 0.675, BEAM-1M 0.679 vs 0.626; with Claude-Sonnet-4.6, BEAM-1M 0.833 vs 0.717. User study: 10 participants, 1 week, Qwen-3.5-9B on RTX 5090, F1 proxy rose 0.199 → 0.515, with 6/10 users at zero F1 on day 1 (cold start). On-device profiling: 9B on RTX 5090 mean latency 2.84 s / TTFT 1.22 s; 35B-A3B-FP8 on DGX Spark 7.52 s / 2.83 s; change-aware frame selection raises KV cache hit rate from ~27% to 45.2% and improves TTFT >1.7×. Baselines (vanilla, induced persona, oracle persona, Mem0) are reasonably current. Surprising finding: prompt evolution beats LoRA on the two Qwen backbones but loses on Nemotron, and both beat giving the model the true persona — evidence the adaptation captures more than the persona text encodes. Scale: standard (single-device, 108 sessions, 10 users), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM formulation (deep personalization = personalized intervention timing from continuous observation), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (OSWorld-Persona and its reusable synthesis pipeline), NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (Coco, including the unified inference+training CTI deployment). The individual mechanisms — LoRA, ACE prompt evolution, GUM-style propositions, Mem0-comparable memory, MSE-based frame deduplication, speculative decoding — are standard; the genuinely novel part is the closed-loop wiring of implicit feedback into on-device continual adaptation for proactive timing, plus the persona-conditioned benchmark recipe applied to computer-use data. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: context removal, decision-only output, and Oracle/Induced Persona baselines isolate which components matter, and Table 1 results are averaged over three random seeds. Code and benchmark data are released (https://github.com/NVlabs/deep-personalization, https://github.com/collaborative-agents/coco). Methodological concerns: (1) benchmark labels are self-labeled by a VLM simulator whose persona conditioning defines the ground truth — the benchmark measures simulator alignment, and human validation covers only need_support=true cases; (2) the adaptation pipeline uses the same model to detect missed opportunities and generate revised targets (self-distillation), with no label-noise quantification; (3) the user study has no in-the-wild control condition (e.g., a non-adapting observer) and the F1 proxy deliberately underestimates false negatives; (4) the latency replay workload is 30 minutes from a single author; (5) a numeric inconsistency exists — the intro claims "up to 0.77 F1" on one persona while Table 1 reports 0.81–0.86. None of these invalidate the results, but the benchmark numbers should be read as upper-bound estimates of real-user alignment. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, deployed tool with supporting benchmark experiments). Practical: Yes — runs interactively on a consumer RTX 5090 (Qwen-3.5-9B, 2.84 s mean latency) or DGX Spark (35B-A3B-FP8, 7.52 s). Efficient: Frame selection doubles KV cache hit rate to 45.2% and cuts TTFT >1.7×, and idle-time preemptive training avoids competing with serving, but always-on energy/thermal cost on battery devices is explicitly uncharacterized. Effective: Evidence supports improved intervention timing on synthetic persona labels and a coarse real-world proxy; effectiveness against actual user satisfaction is only partially evidenced by 10 thumb-based signals per user. Scalable: Not tested — months-long adaptation, preference drift, memory bloat beyond 50 bullets, and behavior across many users remain claims rather than experiments. The work delivers real artifacts: released code, the OSWorld-Persona dataset, a desktop app, and the CTI serving/training engine. Strengths: - The Oracle Persona result is the paper's best card: learned adaptation (macro F1 0.483) beating a baseline handed the true persona text (0.393 on the same backbone) shows the loop extracts situated signal that a static profile cannot express, not merely that more tokens were consumed. - The OSWorld-Persona synthesis pipeline is a genuinely reusable recipe — any computer-use dataset plus personas yields a privacy-safe proactive-agent benchmark, with chronological per-persona splits to prevent leakage. - Real systems measurement rather than vendor-style claims: TTFT, P50/P95 latency, and cache-hit rates on named consumer hardware, with an honest comparison of two hardware/model configurations. - The closed-loop framing cleanly resolves the personalization-privacy tension as an architectural principle (Observer stays on-device), which is a substantive design argument, not just an engineering note. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly (a credibility positive). Appendix A names: users want visibility/control over what is learned (inspection, editing, forgetting); risk of fostering dependence rather than augmentation; the execution agent's cloud-hosted context means privacy is reduced, not eliminated; and energy costs of the always-on observer are unmeasured. Section 3.3 concedes the missed-opportunity signal identifies potential rather than confirmed preferences, and footnote 4 concedes the study's false-negative count is underestimated. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Label circularity: the personas conditioning Kimi-K2.6's labels are the same 4 personas used to split and evaluate, so the benchmark partially rewards learning the simulator's persona definitions; no held-out persona or human-relabeled test slice exists. - Human validation is applied only to need_support=true examples; the (larger) negative-label population is unverified, and negative labels dominate the training signal for the missed-opportunity pathway. - The in-the-wild study includes an author whose local data is analyzed qualitatively (Figure 4c) — self-report contamination — and n=10 over one week cannot speak to long-run stability, prompt overfitting, or preference drift. - Coco-LoRA degrades sharply on the largest backbone (0.314 vs Coco-PE's 0.433 macro F1 on 35B-A3B) with no analysis of why, leaving the choice of adaptation strategy unexplained. - The memory-benchmark win over Mem0 is not ablated: Coco's gains may come from multi-turn agentic retrieval (up to 5 tool calls) rather than the bipartite proposition graph specifically. - Minor: intro's "up to 0.77 F1" per persona contradicts Table 1's 0.81–0.86 values. - No comparison on prior proactive-agent benchmarks (e.g., Lu et al. 2025) despite adopting their metrics, so cross-paper positioning is impossible. Bottom Line: A practitioner building proactive, personalized, or on-device agents gains a concrete, measured, open-source blueprint and a reusable benchmark recipe here — the synthetic-label circularity caps how much the headline numbers prove, but nothing else currently covers this ground end-to-end, so it is worth reading.

Market-Conditioned JEPA: Learning from Unpredictable Market Shocks

Y Wang, F Liu, M Li, H Luo, L Li, Q Liu · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MC-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture for financial time series that, during training only, conditions its predictor on a leave-one-out market factor built from other assets' future target embeddings, yielding a per-asset encoder that beats per-asset JEPA on nine financial prediction targets plus a trading backtest. - Why it's important: Per-asset self-supervised encoders treat market-wide shocks as irreducible noise and get no supervision for how an asset responds to them, which limits representations used for portfolio construction, risk, and liquidity estimation. - How it does it: A factor-structured predictor predicts each asset's future embedding as a base term plus a loading vector (computed from the asset's own representation) times a scalar market factor (the mean of other assets' future target embeddings in the same panel), mirroring a single-index model, with the condition used only during training. - The good: The gains are mechanism-specific and well-controlled: a placebo condition from a different date and an unfactored predictor both underperform MC-JEPA, paired Newey–West tests show significant gains on seven of nine targets (t up to 49.4), and a synthetic factor-model study with known parameters confirms conditioning improves recovery of both exposure and asset-specific components. - The missing: All real-data evidence comes from a single market (Chinese A-shares, 2015–2025) at a single minute-level frequency, return-probe gains are small and partly not significant (minute-return t-stats ≤ 1.8 vs. per-asset JEPA), and no comparison is run against the supervised cross-asset models (FactorVAE, conditional autoencoders) the paper positions itself against. - Read it or not: Worth reading for quantitative researchers working on self-supervised financial representation learning or privileged-information training, since the leave-one-out conditioning trick is transferable and the ablations are unusually careful; skippable for general ML readers, who will find the JEPA-plus-privileged-information recipe applied to one domain.
