Problem & Motivation: Quantitative portfolio managers and risk teams need estimates of return, volatility, liquidity, and market exposure (beta) from one representation. Self-supervised time-series encoders (PatchTST-style masked reconstruction, TS2Vec, CPC, time-series foundation models like Kronos, TimesFM, Chronos-2, MOMENT) encode each asset independently. Under a factor structure, much of an asset's future variation is driven by market-wide shocks unpredictable from the asset's own history; per-asset objectives therefore (i) give no gradient signal for market exposure — the optimal predictor only needs the conditional mean — and (ii) learn asset-specific signal against the market component as noise. Existing cross-asset models (HIST, MASTER, conditional autoencoders, FactorVAE) require cross-sectional inputs at inference or are supervised daily-feature models. The gap: incorporate cross-asset supervision into training while keeping a per-asset encoder at inference. Key Idea: Unpredictable market movements are observable at training time through the realized futures of other assets; conditioning the predictor on this realized factor converts market variation from irreducible noise into supervision for market exposure. Proposition 1 formalizes this under a linear latent factor model u = α + Bf + ε: unconditional prediction's minimum error is attained by any representation recovering the conditional mean α + Bm (exposure B need not be encoded), while conditioned prediction attains the floor E‖ε‖² only if B is recoverable from the representation, and conditioning also shrinks the noise floor. The single-index-structured predictor (loading from the asset's own representation, factor from peers) forces the condition to help only through exposure. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Per-asset JEPA: a 12-layer bidirectional Transformer (~10M params, D=256) patches 960 one-minute OHLCV bars into 96 patches of 10, producing a [CLS] representation zᵢ; an EMA target encoder embeds future 30-bar blocks at horizons {1, 60, 240} bars; the loss is normalized MSE against running-statistics-standardized target embeddings. (2) Market conditioning: for each scored asset, a leave-one-out mean of other assets' future target embeddings c₋ᵢ,h is standardized by running statistics and injected through a factor-structured predictor ûᶜ = a_φ(zᵢ,h) + b_ψ(zᵢ,h)·wᵀc̃₋ᵢ,h with a single factor (K=1); the objective is a λ-weighted combination (λ=0.75) of unconditional and conditional losses. (3) Evaluation: frozen encoders read out via ridge probes on 2019-01–2022-06, hyperparameters selected on 2022-07–2022-12, tested 2023-01–2025-12 on nine RankIC targets plus a long-only CSI300 backtest. Critical design decisions: leave-one-out exclusion (prevents answer copying — justified, and the placebo ablation validates alignment matters), factor structure with loadings from zᵢ (ablation shows the unfactored predictor underperforms on all nine targets), and privileged-information-only conditioning (justified by the channel-independence robustness literature and the deployment cost argument). The proof assumes f is independent of x and Σf ≻ 0; the paper honestly notes the real condition is a noisy estimate of f. Key Results: On 11 years of minute-level Chinese A-share data (pretraining ≤ July 2022; test 2023–2025), MC-JEPA improves over per-asset JEPA on all nine targets: Beta 20d RankIC 0.374 vs. 0.359, Vol 120m 0.517 vs. 0.444, Volume 120m 0.594 vs. 0.573, Ret 1d 0.0746 vs. 0.0712, Ret 20d 0.1389 vs. 0.1337 (three seeds, mean±std). It is best on all three liquidity targets and on returns from 120 minutes to 5 days; it loses Ret 20d to TS2Vec (0.1454 vs. 0.1389) and intraday volatility to CPC (0.552 vs. 0.517). Frozen foundation models (Kronos, TimesFM-2.5, Chronos-2, MOMENT) trail on all return horizons regardless of scale. Backtest: MC-JEPA achieves 0.135 annualized excess return, 1.19 Sharpe, 0.117 MDD vs. 0.117/1.11/0.132 for per-asset JEPA, net of 5/15 bp costs. Newey–West tests: gains significant at 5% on seven of nine targets vs. per-asset JEPA; minute returns show no significant gain. Ablations: placebo condition (other date) recovers volatility/liquidity gains but not return/exposure gains, confirming the mechanism; K>1 helps risk/exposure but hurts returns. The label-free loading-based beta estimate reaches RankIC 0.368 vs. 0.374 for a supervised probe, but trailing historical betas reach 0.525. On real data the condition removes only 4.5% of unconditional error — the paper itself flags this as modest denoising. Synthetic study: exposure probe R² improves from 0.51–0.68 to 0.69–0.80 and asset-specific R² from 0.62–0.78 to 0.79–0.85 across factor-predictability levels (five seeds). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (market-conditioned JEPA with leave-one-out future-embedding factor and factor-structured predictor) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (conditioning turns market shocks into exposure supervision, validated by placebo ablation and synthetic recovery). The genuinely novel move is importing the privileged-information factor structure of FactorVAE into self-supervised latent-space prediction while preserving channel-independent inference; the components (JEPA/EMA target encoder, patch transformers, ridge probes, single-index conditioning) are individually standard, and the theory is a straightforward proposition about linear factor regression rather than a deep result. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. Three seeds with mean±std for all trained encoders, five for the synthetic study; paired Newey–West t-tests with horizon-aware lag selection (Table 12); exhaustive ablations over λ, K (1–128), and pool size |Mₜ| (8–128) on both validation and test periods; hyperparameters selected on a validation window disjoint from the 2023–2025 test period, avoiding Goodhart on the test set. Code is released at github.com/OpenFinMind/MC-JEPA; no pretrained weights are mentioned. Baselines are current (TimesFM-2.5, Chronos-2, Kronos, MOMENT) and readout choices ([CLS] vs. mean pooling) were verified per-baseline. Concerns: (i) evaluation is confined to the authors' own market and data pipeline; (ii) the paper's own analysis shows trailing betas (0.525) substantially beat the learned exposure (0.374), which weakens the practical case for learned exposure estimates; (iii) return-probe gains are small in absolute terms (≤0.005 RankIC) and not significant on minute returns; (iv) the closely related supervised competitors (FactorVAE, conditional autoencoders) are discussed but not run as baselines. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent backtest). Practical: Yes — a 10M-parameter encoder trained on two H800 GPUs, with frozen-encoder ridge probes at deployment; no cross-sectional data needed at inference. Efficient: Overhead over per-asset JEPA is only the loading network plus target-encoder forward passes over a 32-asset condition pool; inference cost is identical to per-asset JEPA. Effective: The evidence supports exposure, risk, and liquidity gains strongly; return and economic-value gains are real but modest (1.8-point AER improvement, significant on only some return horizons), and the learned exposure signal underperforms a trivial trailing-beta baseline. Scalable: Not tested beyond ~4,000 A-share names and one frequency; pool-size and K ablations suggest diminishing returns to scaling the condition, and cross-market generalization is untested. The work delivers a software artifact (code) plus a training recipe; no trained model weights are reported as released. It is a preprint and has not, as far as the text states, undergone peer review. Strengths: - The core insight — using peers' future embeddings as privileged training-time supervision while preserving per-asset inference — is a clean, transferable trick that resolves a real tension between cross-asset modeling and channel-independence robustness. - The placebo-condition ablation is exactly the right control: it shows the return/exposure gains require temporal alignment with the realized market movement, not merely panel batching or extra conditioning capacity. - Proposition 1 is simple but does real work: it explains why per-asset objectives cannot supervise exposure and generates testable predictions the ablations confirm. - Honest self-measurement throughout: the paper reports that its condition removes only 4.5% of prediction error, that minute-return gains are not significant, and that its label-free beta estimate loses to trailing betas — disclosures many papers would omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that all real-data experiments are on Chinese A-shares at one bar frequency, so generalization to other markets, asset classes, or frequencies is untested (they note retail participation, price limits, and T+1 settlement may shape shock propagation). They acknowledge Proposition 1 assumes a linear factor model with the true factor while MC-JEPA uses a noisy estimated condition; that K=1 leaves industry/style structure implicit; and that per-window normalization makes loadings capture correlation rather than beta, requiring a scale-restoration step. They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No empirical comparison against FactorVAE or conditional autoencoders despite positioning the method against them; the claim that MC-JEPA's self-supervised route is preferable is asserted, not measured. - The exposure story is undercut by the paper's own Table 13/14: trailing betas (0.525) dominate both the supervised probe (0.374) and the label-free loading estimate (0.368), so a practitioner wanting beta would not use this model for it. - The backtest covers one strategy (long-only top-7/8 CSI300, 20-day holding) in one market over three years; robustness to transaction-cost assumptions, universe breadth, and regime is unexamined. - Hyperparameters (λ=0.75, K=1, |Mₜ|=32) are selected on a six-month validation window and by return targets specifically; the K trade-off between return and risk targets means the default configuration is optimized for the headline return metrics. - The 4.5% error-reduction measurement is on validation-period training losses (a training-time quantity) rather than a direct test-set quantity, and the paper concedes return gains are not explained by denoising; the precise source of the return improvement remains partially unexplained. - Two author affiliations include a commercial entity (Grace Investment Machine); no conflict-of-interest statement regarding the backtest is noted. Bottom Line: A practitioner in self-supervised financial ML should read this for the conditioning mechanism and its unusually honest evaluation — it is the strongest evidence yet that training-time cross-asset supervision can improve per-asset encoders — but the modest and market-specific return gains mean it complements rather than replaces simpler exposure and return baselines.

metalSPARSE: A 2: 4 Semi-Structured Sparse GEMV Kernel for Apple Silicon GPUs

TR Awasthi, B Awasthi · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the first 2:4 semi-structured sparse GEMV/GEMM kernel family and fused C++/Metal decoder for Apple silicon GPUs, plus a laptop-scale pruning recipe, and demonstrates 3.6× faster token decoding than PyTorch-MPS (HuggingFace eager) on an 8 GB M2 MacBook Air and 1.52× faster than MLX on a 16 GB M4 for Qwen2.5-1.5B. - Why it's important: Edge LLM decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound, and Apple GPUs have no sparse matrix hardware, so a decade of N:M pruning research has had no practical route to Macs — this work makes 2:4 sparsity deliver its theoretical byte-halving as wall-clock decode time on that platform. - How it does it: Weights are stored packed (two fp16 values + 4-bit metadata per block of four, ρ = 0.5625 of dense), streamed compressed, and expanded in registers inside Metal kernels tiered by batch size, paired with a quality-recovery recipe (Wanda mask → block-wise reconstruction with scaled calibration → jointly trained rank-308 low-rank correction quantized to NF4). - The good: The evaluation isolates the contribution cleanly: the authors' own dense-weight engine matches MLX within 1%, so the sparse speedup is attributable to the compressed format, and the 2:4 GEMV sustains 87.5 GB/s (96% of the M2's measured 91 GB/s STREAM bandwidth), converting sparsity to time at 98% of its byte ceiling. - The missing: The all-linear configuration reaches a 1.34× perplexity ratio to dense on WikiText-2 — still substantially degraded from dense (9.0 → ~12.05 PPL on the M4 harness) — and zero-shot task accuracy, larger models, and a 4-bit dense MLX baseline at matched bytes are all deferred to camera-ready. - Read it or not: Read it if you build inference runtimes for edge or Apple-silicon hardware or work on post-training pruning/low-rank correction; skip it if you need prefill acceleration or quality-preserving compression at larger model scales, since prefill gains nothing here and evaluation is confined to 1.3–1.5B models.

Problem & Motivation: Single-stream LLM decoding on edge devices is bound by memory bandwidth: Qwen2.5-1.5B in fp16 streams 3.09 GB of weights per token, which on an M2's 91 GB/s bus means decode time is essentially bytes over bandwidth (the compute takes 1.1 ms of a ≥33.9 ms floor). 2:4 semi-structured sparsity halves weight bytes and is a first-class hardware feature on NVIDIA, AMD, and Meta accelerators, but Apple GPUs expose no sparse matrix instructions, MLX has declined a sparse-matmul path (closed as wontfix), and no runtime ships a 2:4 weight-sparse route — leaving all N:M pruning research inapplicable to Macs. A second obstacle is quality: one-shot 2:4 pruning of Qwen2.5-1.5B (Wanda with a closed-form per-matrix refit) leaves perplexity at 3.01× dense, and the strongest closed-form low-rank corrections (SLiM-style) are designed for GPUs where adapter bytes and dispatches are nearly free — on a dispatch-latency-bound, bandwidth-bound Apple GPU an unadapted correction can cost more than it saves. The intended users are anyone running LLMs locally on fanless 8–16 GB Apple laptops. Key Idea: The core insight is that on a GPU with no sparse hardware, 2:4 pays entirely through bytes, not FLOPs — so the method streams weights in compressed form and expands blocks in registers, making sparsity's speedup identical to its byte reduction; the authors formalize this with an Amdahl-style byte ceiling (Eq. 1: speedup ≤ Σb_i / Σρ_i·b_i) and design the whole system — kernels, engine, adapter placement, even the measurement methodology — to convert format bytes to wall-clock time at near-100% efficiency while keeping the runtime itself at dense parity with MLX so the two gains are separable. A secondary insight on the quality side: after block-wise reconstruction, the pruning mask choice becomes statistically irrelevant, and a low-rank correction trained jointly with the surviving weights inside the block objective beats closed-form corrections at matched bytes; quantizing that correction to 4 bits is nearly lossless (98% of benefit retained) because its quantization noise enters second-order in the loss. Methodology: The system has an offline recipe and an online engine meeting at a packed model file. Offline, per decoder block with fixed 2:4 mask M, the objective (Eq. 2) minimizes block output error ||MLP_b(x; (W⊙M)+LR) − MLP_b^dense(x)||² over C4 calibration inputs: (1) a Wanda mask (|W_ij|·||X_j||₂) selects the 2:4 support from 32×1,024 tokens; (2) a per-row masked least-squares refit w_S = (H_SS + λI)⁻¹H_S:· w_dense warm-starts values; (3) masked Adam (fp32 copies, re-projection onto M each step) performs block-wise reconstruction, with calibration volume scaled to 256 sequences of 1,024 tokens and a do-no-harm gate; (4) a rank-308 low-rank correction, initialized from SLiM's diagonal-saliency closed form and then trained jointly with surviving weights; (5) MLP corrections are quantized to NF4 (L) and group-INT4 (R) with an activation-weighted clip, while attention corrections are folded into the dense weights at load time. Online, a C++/Metal engine runs: a simdgroup-per-row GEMV for B≤3 (one half2 load, nibble decode, register expansion, contiguous half4 activation load, four fp32 FMAs per block, simd_sum reduce); register-tiled and simdgroup-matrix variants for B=4–8; a P-GEMM prefill kernel that decompresses 2:4 tiles during tile load with adapter correction as extra K-steps and fused SwiGLU epilogue; split-K GQA attention with INT8 V-cache; an INT8 tied LM head; and zero per-token allocations with merged command encoders. Critical design decisions: (a) deliberately multiplying two zeros per block in the GEMV rather than skipping them — justified by measurements showing zero-skipping is operand-delivery-limited (only 1.14× over its dense twin at M=512); (b) folding attention corrections into dense weights — justified by a measured near-zero net (73 MB/token saved vs. 0.6–0.9 ms dispatch cost); (c) the diagonal (not Gram) saliency closed form as initialization — justified by showing the Gram form overfits calibration second-order structure and derails sink windows. Key Results: All quality numbers are paired, window-clustered perplexity ratios to dense on WikiText-2 test (146 non-overlapping 2,048-token windows, 298,862 tokens; dense PPL 9.265/14.625 depending on arm). The 50% all-linear row moves from 3.0103× dense (one-shot) → 1.9124× (block reconstruction) → 1.5909× (+closed-form r=154) → 1.5166× (+joint training r=154) → 1.3335× (r=308) → 1.3422× (INT4 corrections shipped), recovering 73.3% of the one-shot log-excess. The 32% hybrid row (24/28 MLPs pruned, attention dense, no correction) reaches 1.2167×. Speed: on M2 8 GB, both shipped rows decode 3.6× faster than HuggingFace eager on PyTorch-MPS (25.3 and 24.8 ms/token); on M4 16 GB, the 50% row hits 47.2 tok/s, 1.52× MLX and 1.55× oMLX, with the dense arms split as runtime 1.01× + INT8 head 1.08× + 2:4/INT4 1.39×. The 2:4 GEMV chain sustains 87.5 GB/s (96% of STREAM); sparsity realizes 98% of its byte ceiling. On OPT-1.3B under SLiM's protocol, the recipe reaches 1.2989 vs. SLiM-LoRA's 1.27 (+2.3% ratio) while decoding 4.45× faster than HuggingFace eager on the M4. Prefill does not speed up (0.73× MLX; 0.73–0.94× dense on M2), as predicted. Baselines are current for the platform (MLX 0.32, oMLX 0.6.4, PyTorch-MPS eager), but the strongest sparse-compression competitors (SLiM quality-wise) are compared on a different model, and a 4-bit dense MLX baseline at matched bytes is absent. The testing scale is a single 1.5B model primarily, with one transfer experiment at 1.3B — toy-to-standard scale, not stress-scale. A notable negative finding: zero-skipping kernels reach only 0.82–0.86 dense-equivalent TFLOP/s and skipping zeros yields just 1.14× over their dense twin, confirming prefill cannot benefit. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (first 2:4 weight-sparse kernel family and fused decoder for Apple GPUs — genuinely new, as prior platform work is CPU-side NEON or attention-only sparsification), NEW METHOD (the jointly-trained-in-block-objective low-rank correction with NF4 storage, and the matched-runtime decomposition measurement methodology), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (mask policy is irrelevant after block reconstruction; calibration volume, not optimizer sophistication, is the binding one-shot constraint; a correction tolerates 4-bit quantization at 98% benefit retention because its noise is second-order). The pruning recipe is a competent recombination of known components (Wanda, block reconstruction à la Wagner et al., SLiM's closed-form initialization, NF4 from QLoRA) — the novelty lies in proving which components matter on this platform and in the kernel engineering, not in the recipe itself. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: mask-policy tie (Wanda vs. SparseGPT, 0.24% ± 0.36%, 0.7 SE), calibration-scaling ladder (32→128→256 sequences, each step paired), closed-form vs. joint training at matched ranks (4.67%, 52 SE, on all 146 windows), rank sweep (77/154/308), INT4 vs. INT8 vs. fp16 corrections with a pre-registered shipping bar, and a zero-skipping kernel experiment that pre-registers a hypothesis the paper then confirms. Every quality comparison is paired on identical windows with cluster-robust standard errors (0.08–0.09% paired); every speed number is in-situ decode-only ms/token reproducible to 0.4%, with an explicit argument that isolated kernel microbenchmarks invert format rankings (INT8 wins by 0.43 ms in isolation, INT4 wins by 0.92 ms in-engine). Code (MSL kernels, C++ bindings, calibration scripts) is released at github.com/Tekraj15/metalSPARSE, and all experiments use public models and splits. Concerns: the primary speed baseline (PyTorch-MPS eager, 3.6×) is a known-weak, dispatch-bound reference — the honest comparison is the 1.52× vs. MLX; the headline quality recovery (73%) is calibrated on C4 and evaluated on WikiText-2, a cross-corpus protocol inherited from SLiM; some cited related work (SparseForge, SpenseGPT, BaseRT, vllm-mlx) carries 2026 arXiv identifiers and the footnote admits "issue and PR numbers to be verified" — signs of an unpolished preprint; and no significance testing on the speed side beyond replicate ranges (±7% short-generation variance on fanless hardware is disclosed). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built kernel family + decoder + recipe, evaluated by in-situ deployment on consumer hardware). Practical: Runs on a fanless 8 GB MacBook Air within Metal's 5,461 MiB working-set recommendation — the target hardware is commercially available and the recipe itself runs on the same laptop in single-digit hours. Efficient: Streams 1,992 MB/token vs. 3,101 dense (ρ=0.642) at 86–89% of STREAM bandwidth, though resident memory is 4.45 GB vs. MLX's 2.88 GB on the M4 (prefill buffers + dequantized corrections). Effective: It solves the stated decode-bandwidth problem with unusually clean attribution (dense-parity engine isolating the format's contribution), but the quality cost is real — 1.34× perplexity ratio means the all-linear row trades measurable perplexity for speed, and only the hybrid row (1.22×) approaches losslessness. Scalable: Not tested beyond 1.5B; the authors state "larger models, zero-shot task suites, and a 4-bit dense baseline at matched bytes" are next steps, and the correction bytes (140 MB/token at rank 308) and recipe runtime presumably grow with model size — the 10× scaling claim is asserted, not measured. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (kernels, engine, packed pruned models, benchmark harness) plus a reusable measurement methodology. Strengths: (1) The matched-runtime decomposition is the paper's most credible move — building a dense-weight twin of the engine that matches MLX within 1% converts an unattributable systems speedup into a clean format-only measurement, a discipline most kernel papers lack. (2) The negative result on zero-skipping prefill kernels (Table 4: only 1.14× over the dense twin, closing a 2.1–2.2× gap needed) pre-empts the obvious objection with data rather than argument. (3) The empirical finding that mask selection becomes a statistical tie once block reconstruction follows — with the cheap mask saving ~40 minutes per model vs. OBS — is a genuinely useful simplification for practitioners. (4) The measurement-methodology contribution (silent MPS defect above 1,024 rows against the 151,936-row LM head, per-op profiler mispricing of ATen ops by up to 8×, allocator heap granularity doubling resident memory) documents platform failure modes that will bite anyone doing serious Metal inference work. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state plainly that prefill is compute-bound and cannot gain from 2:4 on this hardware (all-linear prefill sits at 0.73–0.94× dense), that zero-shot task accuracy and a 4-bit MLX baseline at matched bytes are deferred to camera-ready, that the recipe does not beat SLiM on SLiM's own model (within 2.3%, attributed to rank being the remaining lever), that "low-rank" at rank 308 (20% of hidden size) is "being stretched," that the INT4 correction at rank 308 exceeds the pre-registered shipping bar by 0.15 points and ships as a disclosed override, and that rank is not directly comparable to SLiM's reported shares on a different model. This is an unusually direct confrontation with limitations — the pre-registered-bar-with-documented-override pattern and the paired-window instruments signal high measurement integrity. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The 3.6× headline is against PyTorch-MPS eager, a dispatch-bound strawman the paper itself implicitly concedes by building a 2.9×-faster runtime; the honest headline is 1.52× vs. MLX, and the ordering of the abstract invites over-reading. (2) All quality results are perplexity-only on one dataset pair — no downstream task accuracy, no long-context evaluation beyond the 512-token test prompt despite the model's 32K context, and no human-visible generation quality assessment. (3) Only one primary model (Qwen2.5-1.5B) with one transfer test (OPT-1.3B); nothing establishes whether the 73% recovery share or the mask-irrelevance finding holds at 7B+ or on modern architectures, though the recipes' compute cost grows with model size on the same laptop. (4) The engine's prefill at 0.73× MLX and higher resident memory (4.45 vs. 2.88 GB) are real regressions disclosed but not weighed against the decode gain in any net-utility framing. (5) The AI-use disclosure (Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro) is present, but the boundary of "template boilerplate" vs. analysis code is not auditable from the paper; combined with the unverified footnote and future-dated citations, the camera-ready should tighten provenance. Bottom Line: For anyone building local LLM inference on Apple silicon, this is currently the only working 2:4 sparse path on the platform and its measurement methodology alone is worth adopting; for the broader pruning and edge-inference communities, the jointly-trained-correction and calibration-scaling findings travel beyond Macs, but the perplexity-only, sub-2B evaluation means the quality story needs replication before it should guide anyone's production compression recipe.

Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation (45 ▲ )

Yuzhi Huang, Jie Wu, Fanding Huang, Junchao Lin, Weichen Zhang, Ziyi Xiong, Yang Li, Zhengwei Xie, Zhimin Wang, Zhen Liu, Jiazhen Huang, Yuzheng Zhang, Yuche Liu, Hongyi Yang, Chen Tang, Shixiang Tang, Hakan Aktas, Adam Wu, Duo Wu, Kangye Ji, Shuzhao Xie, Huanan Liu, Weijue Bu, Chenxin Li, Xinyuan Wang, Tianyi Bai, Yinan Mao, Jiawei Wang, Minglei Li, Heng Yu, Ehsan Adeli, Minchen Li, Yong-Lu Li, Cengiz Öztireli, Huazhe Xu, Chao Yu, Jing Zhang, Shanghang Zhang, Weitao Zhou, Wenwu Zhu, Cheng Chi, Jingyan Jiang, Zhi Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 20 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Mind2Act World, a simulation benchmark of 30 bimanual manipulation tasks organized into three diagnostic views — Mind (history-based reasoning), Act (precise/timely execution), and Mind2Act (their closed-loop composition) — plus a failure-diagnosis harness that attributes every failed episode to reasoning, execution, or their composition. - Why it's important: Existing manipulation benchmarks either entangle reasoning and execution in one success rate or test them separately, so practitioners cannot tell whether a deployed system forgot the task state, failed to execute, or failed to chain the two — this benchmark makes that attribution measurable and actionable. - How it does it: Tasks are designed so each view stresses one demand while keeping the others easy, success is judged only from environment-side physical predicates (never self-declared completion), and a three-layer pipeline (deterministic rules → LLM judge over video/tool logs → human review) labels the first unrecoverable error in each failed episode. - The good: The central result is clean and consequential across 56,700 scored episodes: the strongest agent (GPT-6 Astra) achieves 52.7% on Mind and 39.0% on Act but only 12.0% on Mind2Act, no end-to-end policy exceeds 3.6% on Mind2Act, and 8 of 30 tasks are never completed by any system. - The missing: The Mind/Act/Mind2Act comparison is correlational, not interventional — Mind2Act tasks are longer and differ in content from the single-view tasks, so the headline composition gap cannot yet be separated from horizon length; the authors acknowledge this and defer oracle and matched-pair interventions to future work. - Read it or not: If you build VLAs, world-action models, or embodied agents and want to know whether your failures are memory, motor control, or closed-loop composition — and want targeted data/harness fixes — read it; if you only need another general manipulation benchmark, LIBERO/RoboCasa-class suites already cover simpler ground.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Practical Impact (78) is the top driver — a genuinely open artifact suite with leaderboard, scorers, demonstrations, and diagnosis tooling — and Rigor (70) is strong for a benchmark (predicate-based scoring, scripted-feasibility upper bound, Wilson intervals, team-run evaluations). Novelty (72) reflects a real conceptual contribution in the decouple/recouple task structure and the striking composition-collapse finding. Completeness (72) benefits from unusually candid limitation disclosure, but Resilience (65) is held down because the central 'composition is the bottleneck' claim is correlational — Mind2Act tasks are longer, the LLM judge is unvalidated against human labels, and the promised oracle/matched-pair interventions are deferred. Weighted composite: 0.15*72 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*70 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.30*78 = 72.

Problem & Motivation: Developers of embodied systems face a diagnostic blind spot: when a robot fails a manipulation workflow, is it because the system cannot remember earlier observations (Mind), cannot produce the required physical effect precisely and on time (Act), or cannot use realized action outcomes to update subsequent decisions (Mind-Action Composition)? Existing benchmarks either fold all three into a single success rate (LIBERO, RLBench, RoboCasa), or test reasoning and execution in separate assessments without composing them (RMBench, RoboMME, GeoMind, RoboColiseum). The authors argue this prevents targeted improvement, since each research line (memory-augmented policies, contact-aware controllers, LLM agents) is typically evaluated where only its own demand is hard. The intended users are robotics and embodied-AI researchers comparing agents, VLAs, and world-action models on equal terms. Key Idea: The core trick is "decouple, then recouple": design triads of tasks with related semantics where Mind tasks make history-based decisions hard but execution routine, Act tasks make execution hard but state the operation explicitly, and Mind2Act tasks chain dependent operations so each physical outcome decides the next action. Because the separate demands are measured in isolation on comparable task semantics, the gap between isolated performance and composed performance becomes an interpretable diagnostic signal — provided success is verified from simulator-side physical predicates and every failed episode is logged with stage/event traces for attribution. Methodology: The benchmark runs in Isaac Sim with two ARX X5 arms (120 Hz physics, 30 Hz control/RGB, three 640×480 cameras), 30 tabletop tasks across five application domains and 12 capability categories, each at Easy/Medium/Hard and in Clean and Random scenes (clutter, 23 table materials, 6 light types), yielding 180 configurations. Two action interfaces share one information contract and evaluator: end-to-end policies (4 VLAs, 2 WAMs) fine-tuned on 4,500 scripted, quality-controlled demonstrations (75.8 h, avg. 60.7 s, up to 127.6 s for Hard Mind2Act) output action chunks; agents (3 frontier multimodal LLMs, zero-shot) issue structured tool calls (move_eef, wait_steps, memory_resolve, give_up) served by a fixed IK/motion-planning harness. Metrics are final success rate plus a 0–100 partial-progress task score, with Overall weighted 0.25 Mind + 0.25 Act + 0.50 Mind2Act and 95% Wilson intervals. The diagnosis harness assigns each failed episode one of 21 failure codes via deterministic rules (settling ~22–38% of failures), an LLM judge that cannot overturn rules, and human review of uncertain cases; results are summarized in per-model profile cards. Critical design decisions: (1) paused-clock timing (inference does not consume the simulated response window) — well-motivated for cross-interface fairness but explicitly acknowledged to inflate agent performance on timed tasks; (2) agents get 4× the physics budget and 150 decisions of end-to-end policies, with separate leaderboards — reasonable but limits cross-family claims; (3) environment-side predicate scoring with hidden state (target angles, gate timing) — well-justified against self-declared completion and action-repeat gaming. Key Results: Across 56,700 scored episodes (9 systems × 180 configurations; 900 episodes per agent, 9,000 per end-to-end policy), GPT-6 Astra leads every view: 52.7% Mind, 39.0% Act, 12.0% Mind2Act (34.6% Overall SR), while no end-to-end policy exceeds 3.6% on Mind2Act (π0.5) and best end-to-end Overall is InternW0 at 8.7%. The other two agents (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Gemini-4-Argon) score 0.0% on Mind2Act. Eight tasks (M1, DR4, PR5, PR6, CP03, CP04, CP07, CP09) have zero successes in all 56,700 episodes. Under scene randomization, the four VLAs retain 86–94% of their Act successes but only 28–41% of their Mind successes, whereas GPT-6 Astra's Mind rate drops only from 54.7% to 50.7%. Difficulty scaling shows Mind2Act collapsing hardest (GPT-6 Astra: 26%→3% Easy→Hard) while timed Act tasks barely change. Latency/cost: agents take 11.0–35.6 s per call (GPT-6 Astra costs $25.13/episode, $72.7/success) versus 77–488 ms for end-to-end policies. Diagnosis of 8,343 failed episodes from three systems attributes ~37–55% of failures to execution, ~28–33% to perception/reasoning for the end-to-end policies, and only 6–11% to composition — most workflows fail before composition is ever tested. A scripted simulator-state controller completes every task, ruling out task impossibility. Baselines are the strongest publicly identifiable current models in each family, evaluated by the benchmark team itself. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the deliberate three-view decouple/recouple task structure with matched semantics so composition failure becomes measurable, and (b) the episode-level three-layer failure-attribution harness producing profile cards with actionable failure codes. The individual ingredients — Isaac Sim simulation, scripted-demonstration collection, difficulty ladders, Clean/Random generalization splits, LLM-judge failure analysis — are standard techniques competently combined; the diagnostic framing and the negative composition finding are the contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for a benchmark paper: frozen shared instance lists across all systems, environment-side predicate scoring with documented anti-gaming rules, hidden-state handling, manifest-bound episode records, 95% Wilson intervals in the appendix, full training hyperparameters for every fine-tuned policy, and scripted-expert feasibility as an upper bound for every task/level. Ablation-style evidence exists at the system level (Clean vs. Random, Easy/Medium/Hard, per-view, per-task, latency/cost breakdowns), though there is no repeated-run variance estimate (the authors note intervals cover only instance sampling). Code, tasks, leaderboard, and documentation are open at mind2act-world.com; evaluations were run by the benchmark team on its own machines, mitigating self-report concerns. Methodological concerns: the LLM-judge layer's accuracy is never validated against a human-labeled gold set; only 3 of 9 systems get diagnosed profile cards; agents run only 5 episodes per configuration (300 per view), so per-difficulty agent numbers are coarse — the authors flag this themselves. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built benchmark/simulation suite with an evaluation service, plus a large empirical study run on it). - Practical: Runs in Isaac Sim on GPU hardware the authors already distribute; agent evaluation additionally requires paid frontier-model APIs. - Efficient: End-to-end evaluation of one policy takes 4,500 episodes (hours-scale on simulated clock, but agent runs cost $1,000s of API spend — GPT-6 Astra alone would be ~$22.6k for its 900-episode protocol at $25.13/episode), and GPT-6 Astra episodes average 22.2 wall-clock minutes. - Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark discriminates capability bottlenecks and yields actionable failure codes, but the diagnosis-to-improvement loop (change model per card → re-evaluate) is planned, not yet demonstrated. - Scalable: The suite is tabletop-bimanual only; extension to dexterous hands, mobile manipulation, and real robots is claimed as future work, not tested, and per-category task counts (1–6) are already too small for category-level statistical claims. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: an open simulation suite with 4,500 demonstrations, scorers, task specs, policy adapters, a public leaderboard, and diagnosis tooling. Strengths: - The three-view decouple/recouple design is a real conceptual contribution: it converts the vague question "why did the robot fail?" into a measurable contrast, and the paper honestly notes that view-level differences alone do not prove composition failure (matched interventions deferred). - The headline finding is robust and quantified: composition collapses (52.7/39.0 → 12.0% for the best agent; <3.6% for all end-to-end policies) while a scripted controller solves everything, cleanly locating the bottleneck in the models rather than the tasks. - The diagnosis harness with 21 failure codes and profile cards converts evaluation into engineering direction (e.g., 1,324 grasp failures for G0.5 vs. 1,132 fine-control failures for InternW0; breakpoint analysis showing 299/300 CP09 episodes end before board removal, motivating breakpoint-centered rather than full-trajectory data collection). - Unusually candid self-criticism: the paused-clock caveat on agent timed-task successes, the confound of view length, and the small agent episode counts are all stated by the authors, not extracted by reviewers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (1) limited causal attribution — views are task sets, not interventions, and Mind2Act tasks are longer/different in content; (2) the paused clock means timed results measure correct action choice in simulation time, not real-time capability, and the fixed agent harness means results do not reflect what a model could do with its own tools; (3) limited system coverage — no hybrid or memory-augmented systems, only 3/9 systems diagnosed, 10 episodes per agent task-level; (4) single embodiment (bimanual ARX X5 tabletop), one English instruction per task, no real-robot validation, and capability categories with too few tasks for per-category claims. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The LLM judge layer is central to attribution (settling ~62–78% of failed episodes for the diagnosed systems) yet has no reported inter-rater agreement or accuracy against human labels; a biased judge could systematically shift Mind/Act/Composition proportions, and the headline "only 6–11% of failures are composition failures" partially rests on it. - Agents receive a proprietary motion-planning harness whose failure modes (GPT-6 Astra stopping after planner pose rejections in 264 of 459 voluntary stops) are conflated with model capability; a joint-level agent interface or second harness variant would isolate this, but none is run in this report. - The Random setting randomizes appearance but all demonstrations are Clean-only, so the VLA Mind-memory collapse under randomization is partially a train/test distribution artifact rather than a pure generalization finding — a memory-augmented or randomization-augmented baseline is needed to separate these, and none is included. - Difficulty levels appear miscalibrated on at least some tasks (the authors note levels that "make no difference" will be recalibrated, e.g., X-VLA's 97%/1%/94% on PR4 Easy/Medium/Hard), which weakens the difficulty-scaling analysis where it matters most. - The composition gap could be substantially an error-compounding artifact of longer horizons (which the authors' own demonstration-length statistics support: 99.6 s vs. 23.9 s); the promised stage-conditional pass rates and oracle interventions are exactly the experiments needed to settle the paper's central claim, and their absence means the "composition is the main open problem" conclusion is, strictly, a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated mechanism. - Eight never-solved tasks make the Mind2Act view's effective sample much smaller than nominal, and per-cell Wilson intervals for agents (n=300/view) are wide (e.g., 8.8–16.2% for the 12.0% headline), so some cross-system rankings within a family are not statistically separated. Bottom Line: This is the most careful diagnostic instrumentation yet for the reasoning-vs-execution-vs-composition question in manipulation, and its negative result — that no current system composes the capabilities it has — is genuinely useful for anyone deciding whether to invest in memory, contact control, or closed-loop verification; read it as a benchmark-plus-diagnosis report whose causal story is promised but not yet proven, and expect the planned oracle/matched-pair follow-ups to determine whether its central claim survives.

#34 — Innovative (72)

Hierarchical Graph Representation Learning with Pooling-Induced Substructures

L Sbicego, X Dong, D Thanou · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PSA-GNN, an architecture that treats clusters produced by structure-based graph pooling as explicit induced subgraphs to be processed with message passing—rather than immediately collapsing them into supernodes—and proves and empirically demonstrates that this strictly increases WL expressivity and accuracy on hierarchy-dependent graph-level tasks. - Why it's important: Graph pooling has a decade-long record of inconsistent gains over flat MPNNs (sometimes matching randomized pooling), and the field lacks benchmarks that isolate when hierarchy matters; this work diagnoses why pooling underdelivers and supplies the controlled benchmarks to fix evaluation. - How it does it: The core move is reframing pooling as a subgraph-policy generator: each pooled cluster becomes an induced subgraph processed by a DSS-GNN-style layer (subgraph-internal message passing plus a graph-level branch over the original adjacency), with a padded edge-covering policy and core/halo node markings providing controlled overlap between neighboring substructures. - The good: A proven strict expressivity hierarchy (Pool-GNN < IP-GNN < PSA-GNN) with explicit separation constructions (P4 vs. K1,3 clusters, a halo-neighborhood argument for the strict PSA-GNN step), verified on BREC where PSA-GNN distinguishes up to 209/400 pairs versus 66/400 for matched Pool-GNN. - The missing: The nested-SBM hierarchy probe is validated by anecdotal correlation across roughly nine datasets rather than a statistical study, and the padded/markings machinery that drives the strict theoretical separation over IP-GNN shows effects within one standard deviation on most real-world datasets in the ablation (Table 7). - Read it or not: Read it if you work on GNN pooling, subgraph GNNs, or higher-order graph learning—the framing, theory, and released benchmarks are genuinely useful; skip it if you need maximum accuracy on molecular benchmarks, where DiffPool (ZINC MAE 0.147 vs. PSA-GNN's 0.177) still wins.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. This is the cluster's only substantive contribution: Novelty (75) is strong — pooling reframed as subgraph-policy generation with a proven Pool-GNN < IP-GNN < PSA-GNN expressivity hierarchy and two released diagnostic benchmarks — and Rigor (72) benefits from parameter-matched baselines, public code/data, and honest reporting of losses to DiffPool, though unadjusted Welch tests, no significance testing against flat GIN, and a main-text/appendix protocol inconsistency hold it back. Non-Obviousness (75) is driven by the halo-degree separation construction; Completeness (70) and Resilience (68) are dented by the thin, near-variance real-world margins over simply not pooling and the missing GPS comparison on real data. Impact (70) reflects genuinely reusable code, datasets, and the nested-SBM hierarchy probe. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*70 = 72.

Problem & Motivation: MPNNs and graph transformers have a locality bias: they must infer hierarchical organization (communities, multi-scale structure) implicitly from local node views, which is hard exactly when the graph-level label depends on relationships between substructures. Graph pooling was meant to solve this by coarsening graphs, but learned feature-based pooling performs on par with randomized assignments (Mesquita et al., NeurIPS 2020) and provably cannot exceed the base encoder's expressivity; only structure-based pooling can. Meanwhile, evaluation is broken: standard benchmarks (ZINC, NCI1) have unclear hierarchical content, and no synthetic datasets with controllable hierarchical signal exist. The gap is twofold: pooling discards the very substructures it discovers, and no tool exists to say when those substructures matter. Key Idea: Once a structure-based pooling scheme partitions the graph, each cluster's induced subgraph is a task-relevant substructure—so instead of collapsing clusters into supernodes (SEL-RED-CON), run message passing inside each induced subgraph and on the original graph in parallel, sum the two branches per node, and read out graph-level predictions with a DeepSets-style aggregation over subgraph embeddings. Optionally pad each subgraph with crossing edges and boundary (halo) nodes so neighboring substructures exchange information. This connects graph pooling directly to the Subgraph GNN literature, with the subgraph collection supplied by pooling rather than egonets or node deletion. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) precompute a structure-based partition via a policy π (Leiden community detection, CurvPool balanced-Forman-curvature clustering, or CliquePool maximal cliques, all with fixed untuned defaults); (2) build vertex-disjoint subgraph policy π or padded edge-covering policy π̂ with binary core/halo node markings; (3) apply L layers of the PSA-GNN update X'_i = L_sg(A_i, X_i) + (L_graph(A, X̄))_{π_i}, i.e., a GIN-based subgraph encoder plus a GIN branch on the original graph after scatter-aggregation; (4) pool each subgraph into s_i and apply ŷ = MLP_head(Σ_i MLP_sg(s_i)). Two theoretical results structure the design: Proposition 3 (IP-GNN, which adds within-subgraph message passing before RED-CON, is at least as expressive as Pool-GNN and strictly more for some partitions—proof by identity-map simulation plus a P4/K1,3 separation) and Proposition 4 (PSA-GNN with supergraph readout subsumes IP-GNN, and the padded policy with node markings is strictly more expressive—proof via a halo-degree-counting separation on two 4-regular diamond-partitioned graphs). Evaluation adds two SBM-generated synthetic datasets (MACRO-HIERARCHIES: ring vs. bipartite macro-community connectivity; GRANULAR-HIERARCHIES: even vs. uneven cluster sizes, both with difficulty knobs and degree-matched noise), a nested-SBM probe extracting substructure count and depth for real benchmarks, and matched depth/parameter-budget comparisons (~500K params) against Pool-GNN, IP-GNN, GIN, GPS, DiffPool, MinCutPool, SAGPool, ASAPool, and an egonet Subgraph GNN. Critical design decisions: the padded policy with markings (justified by the strict-separation proof, but ablations show ≤1σ effects on most real datasets); untuned policy defaults (justified by wanting policy-agnostic conclusions, but risks underestimating policies); DeepSets readout over supergraph readout (justified by hypothesis, acknowledged as a deviation from the theory's interface). Key Results: On BREC, PSA-GNN distinguishes 209/400 pairs with CliquePool-maximal (Pool-GNN: 66; IP-GNN: 77; egonet-PSA-GNN also 209). On the synthetic benchmarks, PSA-GNN with Leiden reaches 95.7% vs. GIN's 53.7% on medium GRANULAR-HIERARCHIES and 99.1% vs. 52.5% on MACRO-HIERARCHIES (featureless), degrading more slowly with difficulty, while GPS with random-walk SEs stays near chance on MACRO-HIERARCHIES. Appendix diagnostics show dense pooling (DiffPool, MinCutPool) never beats GIN on these tasks, SAGPool/ASAPool do well on MACRO but all learned pooling fails on GRANULAR. On real-world data (5 seeds, 80/10/10 splits), PSA-GNN achieves mean rank 1.36 across dataset–policy comparisons vs. 2.33 (IP-GNN) and 2.31 (Pool-GNN), e.g., COLLAB/CurvPool 76.8% vs. 71.1% Pool-GNN, REDDIT-12K/Leiden 50.0% vs. 44.7%, REDDIT-5K/Leiden 55.3% vs. 53.1% (Welch p<0.05 unadjusted). But against flat GIN the margins narrow: COLLAB 78.1–78.9% vs. 74.9%, REDDIT-12K 50.1% vs. 48.3%, MalNet 92.3% (CliquePool-max) vs. 91.0%. On structurally flat data, PSA-GNN does not win: ZINC MAE 0.177–0.182 vs. DiffPool's 0.147 and GIN's 0.172; NCI1 ~81.5% vs. GIN 80.9% and egonet 81.6%. The CO-RB vs. CO-ER contrast validates the hierarchy metric: +25.14% relative gain over GIN on hierarchical RB graphs (MAE 0.9345 vs. 1.4251) vs. −0.70% on flat ER graphs. Scalability: complexity O((1+c_π)(|V|+|E|)); pooled policies induce orders-of-magnitude fewer node occurrences than egonets; measured per-epoch cost is ~1.5–1.75× GIN (REDDIT-12K: 16.1s vs. 9.2s). Baselines are current (GPS, BREC protocol, recent GraphBench tasks) and comparisons are parameter- and depth-matched—a methodologically strong setup. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (PSA-GNN: pooled-substructure processing), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (MACRO-HIERARCHIES, GRANULAR-HIERARCHIES, and the nested-SBM hierarchy descriptors), NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (pooling gains align with measured hierarchical structure across datasets). The core mechanism is a well-executed combination of existing components—structure-based pooling policies, DSS-GNN-style subgraph layers, DeepSets readout—applied to a new interface; the genuinely novel elements are the pooling-as-substructure-exposure framing, the formal three-level expressivity hierarchy with explicit separation constructions, and the controlled benchmarks plus structural probe, which together constitute a substantive conceptual contribution beyond the sum of parts. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover padding, node markings (Table 7), number of pooling steps, and contextual node features at five informativeness levels; layer allocations and hyperparameters are fully tabulated. Mean±std over 3–10 seeds is reported throughout, with Welch tests (unadjusted for multiple comparisons—a flag) against matched Pool-GNN. Code and both datasets are public (https://github.com/lsbicego/PSA-GNN/), and all experiments run on a single A100. Strengths: parameter/depth matching, a strong BREC baseline (their Pool-GNN exceeds prior reported numbers, supporting fair hyperparameter choices), and honest reporting where baselines win (DiffPool on ZINC). Concerns: (1) significance is tested only against Pool-GNN, not against the flat GIN or GPS baselines that PSA-GNN's real-world margins over are within ~1–2 points; (2) the paper's central claim—that gains track hierarchical structure—rests on qualitative agreement across ~9 datasets, with no statistical validation of the SBM probe; (3) the main text states a single pooling step while Appendix E.3 says two steps are generally beneficial for hierarchical GNNs, an internal inconsistency in the protocol; (4) synthetic datasets were designed around the authors' hypothesis (developed and evaluated on the same construct), though the real-world and CO-task results partially mitigate this. Deployability: (EMPIRICAL profile, with a released artifact):* Practical: Yes—single NVIDIA A100, 10–70 minutes per training run, PyTorch Geometric implementation. Efficient: 1.5–1.8× the per-epoch time of flat GIN in measured settings, with a policy-dependent linear-complexity overhead factor c_π that stays small for pooled policies (unlike quadratic-risk egonet policies). Effective: Evidence supports the claim on hierarchy-relevant tasks (synthetic: up to +46 points over GIN; CO-RB: +25% relative MAE gain), but on flat real-world tasks it is competitive at best and loses to DiffPool on ZINC—the method solves the stated problem only where the problem exists, which the authors acknowledge. Scalable:* Claimed via linear complexity and node-occurrence analysis; experiments top out around 1,500-node average graphs (MalNet-Tiny) and very large REDDIT graphs are explicitly omitted from the scalability plot, so 10–100× scale is analyzed, not demonstrated. Delivers: public code repository, two reusable synthetic datasets, and the SBM hierarchy-probe methodology. Strengths: - The expressivity hierarchy (Props. 3–4) is backed by concrete, checkable separation constructions—including a genuinely non-obvious halo-degree argument showing padded substructure processing strictly exceeds unpadded—and is validated behaviorally on BREC rather than left as theory. - The two synthetic benchmarks have real diagnostic value beyond promoting the authors' method: they expose that dense pooling fails where node features carry no cluster signal, that sparse pooling succeeds on macro-structure but not granularity tasks, and that randomized-pooling null results (Mesquita et al.) do not extend to topology-driven tasks—all released for community use. - The nested-SBM probe reframes a murky evaluation culture: reporting ZINC/NCI1 as structurally flat and REDDIT/COLLAB/MalNet as hierarchy-rich gives the field a lens for interpreting pooling results, and the CO-ER/CO-RB pair is a clean validation. - Comparisons are matched in depth and parameters, the BREC baseline is strengthened beyond prior work, and losses to baselines (DiffPool on ZINC) are reported plainly. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that pooling helps only when graphs exhibit hierarchical structure, that the pooling policy must align with the task-relevant hierarchy and no single policy dominates (requiring validation-based selection), and that the structural characterization is a first step that does not assess whether detected hierarchy is predictive of the label. They confront these directly in the conclusion—a credibility positive—rather than minimizing them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No significance testing against the flat GIN baseline, against which real-world gains are 1.2–3.2 points on COLLAB and REDDIT-12K—within or near seed variance on several datasets; the paper's advantage over immediate coarsening is well-evidenced, but its advantage over simply not pooling is thinner than the framing suggests. - GPS is evaluated only on synthetic data (where it fails), not on the real-world benchmarks in Table 1, leaving the graph-transformer comparison incomplete exactly where the method's practical case is made. - The strict theoretical separation of PSA-GNN over IP-GNN depends on padding plus node markings, yet the Table 7 ablation shows these components change real-world results by at most ~1σ in most policy–dataset combinations; the theory's strictness is not visibly realized in practice. - The hierarchy metric's predictive validity is asserted from agreement across a small, partly self-selected set of datasets; no held-out or statistical test of the metric's correlation with pooling gains is provided. - Pooling-policy hyperparameters are deliberately untuned, which is principled for architecture comparison but may disadvantage policies (e.g., Leiden resolution, CurvPool thresholds) that are sensitive to defaults. - The main-text protocol (single pooling step) and the appendix (two steps generally better for hierarchical GNNs) appear inconsistent; the actual configuration for headline real-world numbers is ambiguous. - Learned (feature-based) pooling operators are never combined with PSA-GNN's substructure processing, so the framework's reach beyond structure-based policies is untested. Bottom Line: A graph-ML researcher gains real value here—the pooling-as-substructure-exposure framing, the proven expressivity hierarchy, and the released hierarchical benchmarks are durable contributions—even though a practitioner chasing leaderboard gains on molecular or flat benchmarks should stick with existing alternatives.

Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth (28 ▲ )

Peiyun Hu, Marko Mihajlovic, Lyndon Duong, Lahav Lipson, Wei Dong, Amaël Delaunoy, Stephan R. Richter, Vladlen Koltun · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 20 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Depth Pro 2, a family of transformer models (24M–872M parameters) that predicts dense metric depth for both single images and video at native resolution, simultaneously achieving sharp occlusion boundaries, temporal consistency, and metric accuracy — collapsing the sharpness-vs-stability trade-off that splits prior single-frame and multi-frame depth methods. - Why it's important: Applications like depth-guided bokeh, novel-view synthesis, and video production need depth maps that are sharp at object boundaries AND stable across frames; prior work forced practitioners to pick one, with multi-frame methods oversmoothing and single-frame methods flickering. - How it does it: A DINOv3-initialized ViT processes a flexible number of frames jointly at native resolution by converting a subset of self-attention blocks into alternating within-frame/cross-frame attention (with no frame-order encoding), and a new multi-view consistency loss warps predicted depth between frames via ground-truth camera poses to penalize flicker during training on 1–32-frame clips. - The good: Depth Pro 2-H+ ranks first on zero-shot metric depth (avg. rank 1.0–1.2 on video benchmarks), boundary F1 (DyDToF 34.4, Sintel 43.4), and temporal jitter (Sintel 1.39, Spring 0.86) against ~25 baselines, with thorough controlled ablations (Table 19) attributing gains to specific design choices. - The missing: Temporal consistency is only quantified on synthetic benchmarks (Sintel, Spring) with ground-truth flow; the training mix relies on ~27M frames of proprietary internal data (the ablation shows removing it costs 45.2 points of δ1 on ARKitScenes), so full reproduction is impossible from public data. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or deploying monocular/multi-view depth or 3D reconstruction systems — it is the new reference point for the sharpness-consistency Pareto frontier — but skip if you only need the single-image metric-depth literature at a conceptual level.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Practical Impact (80) is the strongest dimension — released weights across four model sizes, measured runtimes, and a demonstrated downstream task make this the new reference for the sharpness-consistency frontier. Problem & Motivation: Monocular depth estimation has bifurcated: single-image methods (Depth Pro, InfiniDepth, MoGe) produce sharp boundaries but flicker when applied frame-by-frame to video, while multi-frame methods (VGGT, π3, DepthCrafter, video-diffusion approaches) are temporally stable but operate at reduced resolution, blurring boundaries. The paper documents this empirically: on Sintel and Spring, single-frame and multi-frame methods occupy opposite corners of a sharpness-vs-jitter plot (Figure 2). Consumers of depth — video editing, bokeh rendering, AR — need both properties plus metric scale, and prior work offered no single model achieving all three. The domain is zero-shot monocular/multi-view depth estimation; the beneficiaries are downstream graphics, robotics, and video-production pipelines. Key Idea: Train one network jointly on clips of 1–32 frames (images are length-1 clips) at native resolution, where cross-frame attention supplies temporal stability and native-resolution processing preserves sharpness — with temporal consistency enforced not by architecture alone but by a multi-view self-consistency loss that reprojects predicted depth between frames using ground-truth poses and penalizes inverse-depth mismatch, filtered to static, unoccluded pixels via ground-truth depth warping. A secondary trick: restricting the first third of transformer blocks to within-frame self-attention and omitting frame-order encoding makes the model permutation-equivariant over frames, allowing direct reuse of single-image pretrained attention weights and flexible clip lengths. Methodology: The pipeline is (1) a multi-view ViT backbone (DINOv3 ViT-S/B/L/H+ at patch 16) where blocks 0–L/3 do within-frame self-attention and the remaining 2L/3 alternate within/cross-frame attention; tokens get 2D rotary embeddings with coordinates normalized by the longer side (preserving aspect ratio); (2) a DPT decoder per frame that reassembles intermediate tokens at 1/4–1/32 resolution and outputs focal-normalized inverse depth; (3) a separate 23.5M-parameter FoV estimator (finetuned DINOv3 ViT-S on ~92M Flickr EXIF images) converting focal-normalized disparity to metric depth. The loss is an unweighted sum L = Lmae (trimmed L1 on metric inverse depth) + Lssi (scale-shift-invariant trimmed L1) + Lmge (3-scale multi-scale gradient matching on synthetic data) + Lmvc (pose-based reprojection consistency, Eq. 3.2, trimmed at τ). Training uses 19 datasets (heavily synthetic), token-budget batching (73,728 tokens/GPU), 100K steps on 128 B200 GPUs, no ground-truth interpolation to avoid flying pixels. Critical design decisions with ablation support: native-resolution/varied-aspect training (square 1536² crops cost 46.6 δ1 points on Waymo), DINOv3 over DINOv2 init (−12.8 δ1 on ARKitScenes), and rejecting confidence-weighted losses (costs 6.8 boundary-F1 points). Inference supports buffered streaming (overlapping clips, linear blending) and unbuffered causal streaming with a FIFO key/value cache; recommended defaults are N=16/K=4 and C=16. Key Results: Zero-shot metric depth (video setting, 50-frame clips, δ1): Depth Pro 2-H+ averages rank 1.0 (GT intrinsics) / 1.2 (predicted) over KITTI, Sintel, Spring, DyDToF — e.g., Sintel δ1 51.2/41.4 vs. 36.4/37.0 for UniDepthV2-L and 36.5/30.1 for Depth Pro; DyDToF 86.2/94.8. Boundary F1 (single-image): best avg. rank 1.6 (DyDToF 31.6, Middlebury 21.9) vs. InfiniDepth at 3.0. Jitter (temporal consistency): 1.39 (Sintel) and 0.86 (Spring), avg. rank 1.5, vs. 4.0 for VGGT-Ω — a large margin. Focal-length estimation: mean δ25 of 88.6% across six photo benchmarks vs. 71.7% for Depth Pro, ranking first on all six. Runtime (B200, bf16, eager): Depth Pro 2-S at 347 fps VGA / 44.8 fps 1080p buffered (paper claims 53 fps 1080p unbuffered); H+ at 5.3 fps 1080p buffered (claim: 8 fps unbuffered). Baselines are current (2025–2026: DA3-NGL, MoGe-3, π3, VGGT-Ω, MapAnything, MetricAnything) and evaluated from released checkpoints under a unified protocol. Downstream: bokeh rendering on RealBokeh (220 scenes) improves PSNR to 23.95 dB (+0.50 over the strongest baseline); novel-view synthesis is qualitative only. Counter-intuitive finding: confidence-weighted losses — standard in feed-forward reconstruction — actively hurt boundary sharpness. Tested at standard benchmark scale; long-video evaluation covers 300-frame DynamicReplica sequences. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component (the lightweight FoV estimator). The genuinely novel core is the joint recipe: variable-length clip training at native resolution with pose-based multi-view self-consistency, demonstrating empirically that the sharpness/consistency dichotomy is a training and resolution artifact, not a fundamental trade-off. The cross-frame attention blocks, DPT decoding, focal-normalized depth, and Depth Pro's FoV-estimator pattern are existing ideas (the authors candidly note token-sharing variants appear in video transformers and Depth Anything 3); the contribution is the specific combination plus the evidence that it dissolves the trade-off rather than a fundamentally new mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: a controlled-experiment table (Table 19) sweeps model size, data mixture, cropping, backbone, and losses, with 3 seeds and mean±std for the baseline condition (though 1 seed for all other conditions — unquantified seed variance for the deltas). Statistical rigor elsewhere is thinner: the main benchmark tables (Tables 2–5) report no error bars or significance tests, using average ranks instead. The evaluation protocol is exceptionally careful — unified 50-frame clips, explicit zero-shot flagging (gray non-zero-shot entries excluded from ranks), trimmed affine alignment, documented baseline configurations, and a candid critique of the TAE metric including a blurred-depth reference row. Methodological concerns: (1) the jitter metric is computed only on synthetic data with dense GT flow (Sintel, Spring); (2) ~27M of ~57M training frames are proprietary internal data; the D4 ablation shows external data alone loses 45.2 δ1 points on ARKitScenes, so the reported zero-shot numbers partly reflect non-public data — the strongest reproduction barrier; (3) AbsRel results show large failure spots the δ1 ranking hides (DIODE AbsRel 2.418, Booster with predicted intrinsics 0.675), which the authors explain but which complicate the "best everywhere" narrative; (4) a runtime discrepancy: Table 13 measures 5.3 fps at 1080p for H+ (with FoV estimation) vs. the headline 8 fps (without). Code/model release is announced via the project page (https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/); internal data and full training data are not releasable. This is an arXiv preprint (Nov 2026), not peer-reviewed; Apple industrial-lab provenance with 128-GPU training warrants standard confidence in self-run comparisons, though baseline execution appears even-handed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained model family with measured runtimes, memory, and downstream applications; also SYSTEMS-adjacent since released models are the artifact). - Practical: Runs on a single B200 GPU in eager PyTorch; B200-class hardware is high-end but commercially available, and smaller variants (24M/96M) target modest hardware. - Efficient: 2-S processes 1080p at ~45–53 fps with 8 GiB peak — real-time for streaming; H+ at 5–8 fps 1080p / 114.6 GiB peak is research-grade only; OOMs at 4K for H+. - Effective: Strong evidence it solves the stated problem on synthetic and standard benchmarks plus a real downstream task (bokeh), but temporal-consistency quantification rests entirely on synthetic sequences; real-world video stability is shown qualitatively (Figures 8–9). - Scalable: Long-video behavior is tested to 300 frames (jitter saturates at N=64/C=32, roughly constant per-frame cost for cached frames); beyond that, memory scales with clip length and cache size, and 4K already OOMs for large variants — 100× scale is untested, though the streaming modes bound cost by design. The work delivers released model weights and code (per the project page), spanning four model sizes; the training data mixture is only partially reproducible. Strengths: - The central empirical claim is validated on the axes where prior methods fail simultaneously: it is the first model shown to top the rankings on metric accuracy, boundary F1, AND jitter in one unified protocol, turning Figure 2's observed dichotomy into a falsifiable target and then beating it. - The causal analysis goes beyond correlation: attention-dropout experiments (Table 20) show jitter rises monotonically from 0.24 to 0.84 as cross-frame connections are removed, directly implicating the mechanism; resolution sweeps (Table 21) show boundary F1 more than doubles from 360px to native. - Honest metric engineering: the paper defines jitter against ground truth to circumvent TAE's demonstrated pathology (non-zero TAE for ground-truth depth, reward for blur), and includes a blurred-depth reference row — a self-critical evaluation practice few papers match. - The permutation-equivariant, frame-order-agnostic design that lets single-image pretrained weights transfer to multi-frame processing with zero extra parameters is a clean, reusable architectural move. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly flag: TAE's unreliability on sparse/low-quality annotations (ScanNet, Bonn, KITTI) and its bias toward blurry predictions; the DIODE AbsRel artifact (sky vs. bare branches); the exclusion of Kinect-sensor datasets for noisy ground truth; that D1 (added real data) smooths boundaries; FoV estimator degradation outside 384–768px short sides; jitter's dependence on synthetic GT flow (implicitly, by only reporting it on Sintel/Spring); and the static-scene assumption in Lmvc, handled by GT-depth occlusion filtering. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Temporal consistency is never quantified on real video; Sintel and Spring are synthetic. A real-video jitter proxy (e.g., tracks from a learned tracker on handheld footage) is absent, leaving the headline claim partially unvalidated outside the domain where ground truth is cleanest. - Main tables lack error bars/significance tests; with ~25 baselines and average ranks, several rank-1 margins (e.g., boundary F1 vs. InfiniDepth) may be fragile. Only one ablation condition is seed-replicated. - The zero-shot advantage is entangled with proprietary data scale: external-data-only training loses 45.2 δ1 points on ARKitScenes, so a public-data reproduction cannot be expected to match, and "zero-shot" for Depth Pro 2 covers a broader effective training distribution than any competitor's. - The δ1-average-rank presentation can mask large per-dataset weaknesses (DIODE AbsRel 2.418; Booster with predicted intrinsics δ1 43.1 vs. 74.8 for UniDepthV2-family methods) — the predicted-intrinsics column shows real regressions the rank summary softens. - Runtime claims mix configurations: the 8 fps / 53 fps headline figures exclude FoV estimation while Table 13 (fair-comparison protocol, estimator included) shows 5.3 / 44.8 fps. - Training data heavily skewed to synthetic depth (sharp GT), yet deployment targets real video; the boundary-sharpness advantage may partly reflect this mixture rather than the method, and the D2/D1 ablations hint the sharpness gain is partly a synthetic-data effect. Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying depth estimation gains something concrete and currently unmatched — one model family covering sharp, metric, temporally stable, streamable depth with released weights — and this is the new reference for the sharpness-consistency frontier; the caveats (synthetic-only temporal metrics, proprietary training data, no significance testing) temper but do not overturn that verdict.

MovieRoll: A Systematic Framework for Rolling Out Long-Form Videos (11 ▲ )

Yunyang Ge, Weijie Kong, Ryan Xu, Yue Wu, Qi Tian, Jiangfeng Xiong, Bin Lin, Mingzhe Zheng, Shenghai Yuan, Zheyuan Liu, Jianwei Zhang, Li Yuan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 17 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds MovieRoll, an 8.3B-parameter streaming video generation system (base 50-step model plus 5-step distilled model) that generates up to 60-second videos with sequential event prompts, via window-wise teacher forcing, hierarchical KV-cache compression, cumulative long-rollout distillation, and CFG annealing. - Why it's important: Streaming video generation degrades beyond the training horizon due to exposure bias, unbounded KV-cache growth, and guidance-induced drift; fixing this enables minute-scale, prompt-controllable video output rather than isolated 5-second clips. - How it does it: The core move is a rolling-window formulation where chunks at progressive noise levels attend bidirectionally within a window and causally to clean cached history, combined with gradient accumulation across an entire self-generated rollout before each distillation update (CuLT-DMD). - The good: Thorough ablations isolate each component — window-wise teacher forcing beats chunk-wise (6.321 vs 5.001 total score at 721 frames), KV recomputation beats full-history and sliding-window caching (6.873 vs 6.519), and HieraKV cuts KV memory from 48.7 to 10.8 GiB while improving quality. - The missing: All automatic evaluation runs on prompts rewritten by the authors' own prompt-rewriting skill, which encodes their model's preferred conventions (static/tracking camera, centered subjects), and no error bars or seed variance accompany the headline HeliosBench ratings; training data is confidential and unreleased. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building autoregressive or streaming diffusion video systems — the ablation design and the rollout-level gradient accumulation trick are directly reusable — but skippable if you only need a general-purpose video generator, since it is not real-time (2.04 FPS on one H20 GPU).
