Problem & Motivation: Practitioners deploying video generation need continuous, minute-long output with evolving prompts, but bidirectional diffusion models jointly denoise whole clips, delaying first output and scaling computation with duration. Existing streaming approaches have gaps: Self Forcing and LongLive target only few-step generators; Resampling Forcing and Rolling Forcing evaluate at ≤15s; Helios-Base uses bidirectional continuation without KV caching. Long generation additionally faces three coupled problems — exposure bias from conditioning on self-generated history, extrapolation beyond the training horizon, and KV caches that grow without bound — and history management schemes (sliding windows, retrieval, learned memory) each discard context or add mechanisms. MovieRoll addresses all three within one base-to-distilled pipeline. Key Idea: Treat the autoregressive streaming model as a window of chunks at progressively increasing noise levels — bidirectional within the window, causal to cached clean history — so multiple training windows can be supervised in parallel under different event prompts, and couple this with the insight that distillation gradients from an entire long self-rollout should be averaged into a single parameter update rather than updating per supervision window (CuLT-DMD), which combines supervision across temporal positions while holding only one local computation graph in memory at a time. Methodology: Three stages. (1) WinTF streaming fine-tuning: a pretrained bidirectional model (HunyuanVideo-1.5-480P-T2V, 8.3B MMDiT, 54 blocks) is trained with flow matching where each rolling window of ≤5 chunks (4 latent frames each) receives monotonically increasing timesteps sampled via sorted uniform splits plus a shared logit-normal relative position, with phase offsets covering prefill and full decoding windows; history is noise-perturbed with p=0.9, σ∈U(0,0.15). (2) CuLT-DMD distillation: a 5-step student is ODE-initialized from the base, then trained on 241-frame (Phase 1) and 721-frame (Phase 2) self-generated rollouts; per supervision window k, a local DMD loss (frozen bidirectional teacher with CFG 4 vs. conditional fake-score critic, normalized by max-mean deviation) is backpropagated with K-fold scaling, graphs released, and gradients averaged over K=3 (or 9) windows before one optimizer step (Eq. 3). (3) Long-horizon inference: threshold-triggered KV recomputation (at 18 chunks ≈12s, and at prompt switches) causally re-encodes sink, event-middle, and recent chunks at t=0 without text; AnnealCFG sets w(t) = 1 + (wmax−1)t, linearly annealing guidance 4→1 toward the clean endpoint, motivated by a measured "extrapolation impulse" |Δσ|(w−1)‖vc−vu‖ concentrated in late denoising steps (47–60% of total impulse in the last 20% of steps under constant CFG). Infrastructure: FBCA packs visible keys/values for varlen FlashAttention with budget-bounded grouping (gradient-correct gather with FP32 accumulation); PS-VAE streams decoding with cached conv suffixes, first-frame phase indicators, and causal bottleneck-attention KV, plus row-sharded spatial parallelism with halo exchange. Critical design decisions: bidirectional-within-window attention (justified by ablation vs. chunk-wise and self-resampling variants); the 6-global/48-local HieraKV split (justified by layer-wise attention entropy analysis and a 5-way allocation ablation); fixed-parameters-per-rollout gradient accumulation (justified by head-to-head comparison against LongLive-style per-window updates from the same checkpoint). Key Results: On HeliosBench (200 single-event prompts from MovieGen/VBench sets; 100 multi-event MemFlow prompts; all rewritten by the authors' skill), MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total weighted rating at every tested duration among 11 baselines including CausVid, Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, Rolling Forcing, MemFlow, LongLive, Echo-Infinity, Krea, and both Helios variants — all from 2024–2026, so current and strong: 7.515 (10s), 7.260 (30s), 7.032 (60s) single-event and 7.044 (30s, 3-event), 6.492 (60s, 6-event) multi-event. MovieRoll-Base scores 7.485 (10s) and 6.903 (30s) and stays competitive at 30s despite training only on ≤15s videos. A user study (59 professionals, 2,616 judgments, 350 pairs) shows 67.0–90.3% win rates single-event and 62.3–81.9% multi-event against every baseline. Efficiency: HieraKV reduces KV memory up to 78% (48.7→10.8 GiB at 18 chunks) and peak CFG denoising-step latency ~53% (33.8→15.8s); FBCA reaches 1,878 ms fwd+bwd vs. 2,790 (FlexAttention) and 6,803 (SDPA) for 3 windows; PS-VAE decodes 1,441 frames at 40.46 dB PSNR with 3.97× speedup on 8 H20 GPUs where full-sequence VAE decoding OOMs. End-to-end, MovieRoll-Distilled runs at 2.04 FPS on one H20 GPU (SageAttention) and 9.47 FPS on eight — below the 24 FPS real-time threshold, and slower per-GPU than 1.3B baselines like CausVid (6.21 FPS). Notable negative result honestly reported: base-model semantic/drift ratings degrade at 60s, where only the distilled model is evaluated. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (CuLT-DMD rollout-level gradient averaging and WinTF parallel multi-window supervision) + ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (FBCA, PS-VAE, HieraKV, KV recomputation) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (layer-wise attention depth structure in video diffusion motivating hierarchical cache retention, and the late-stage CFG extrapolation impulse analysis). The rolling-window-with-causal-history attention pattern exists in Rolling Forcing/Magi-1; DMD distillation on self-rollouts is Self Forcing/LongLive; KV compression by layer role follows PyramidKV. The genuine novelty is the combination into a coherent base-to-distilled pipeline for multi-step models — especially CuLT-DMD's "one optimizer step per rollout" training rule and threshold-triggered cache re-encoding for horizon extrapolation — rather than any single component being unprecedented. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a strength: five separate ablation families (autoregressive formulation, extrapolation strategy, HieraKV allocation, CuLT-DMD vs. LongLive-style, CFG schedule) all use matched checkpoints, data, and inference settings, with total scores and per-metric ratings reported. The AnnealCFG analysis reports 95% bootstrap CIs over 32 paired prompts with matched seeds. However, the main HeliosBench tables show no error bars, no significance tests, and no multi-seed generation variance; many headline gaps (e.g., 7.260 vs. 7.131 for CuLT-DMD vs. LongLive-style, or 7.515 vs. 7.485 for Distilled vs. Base at 10s) are small relative to integer-granularity rating noise. The evaluation pipeline itself is partially self-constructed: prompts are rewritten by the authors' own skill applied to all methods, naturalness is scored by Gemini-2.5-Pro (evaluator choice justified by a GPT-5.2 cross-check, Spearman ρ=0.930), and rating thresholds are hand-set. Code (github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/MovieRoll) and weights (Hugging Face yunyangge/MovieRoll) are released, but the training corpus is internal and confidential, preventing full reproduction. Methodological concern: HieraKV is motivated by attention analysis of the authors' own WinTF-trained model and evaluated on their own benchmark — an acceptable but self-referential loop. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS — a built, released system evaluated by benchmark and user study. Practical: Runs on NVIDIA H20 GPUs (8.3B params, BF16/FP16); weights and code are public, but the resolution (480×864) and GPU class are enterprise-grade. Efficient: Not real-time — 2.04 FPS single-GPU, 9.47 FPS on 8 GPUs vs. 24 FPS needed; slower than smaller distilled baselines, though HieraKV and FBCA provide substantial internal savings. Effective: Evidence covers 60s generation with sustained naturalness (rating 10 across durations) and majority user preference, but only on rewritten prompts and proxy metrics; interactive/online use is untested. Scalable: Context cost is bounded by design (recomputation at 18 chunks, bounded RoPE positions), and 60s/1,441-frame generation is demonstrated; beyond 60s is claimed-feasible but unmeasured. Delivers a concrete software artifact: code, model weights, and reusable infrastructure (FBCA kernel packing, PS-VAE), not just a paper. Strengths: - CuLT-DMD's "fix parameters, average gradients across the rollout" training rule is a clean, well-motivated twist on Self Forcing/LongLive distillation, and the direct comparison against LongLive-style per-window updates from an identical checkpoint is the paper's most convincing experiment (7.260 vs. 7.131, with visibly better long-range consistency in the moon example). - The layer-wise attention analysis (Fig. 4) grounding HieraKV turns a cache-compression heuristic into an empirically observed property of the trained model, and the 78% memory reduction with quality improvement is a rare free lunch, verified across a 5-point allocation sweep. - The AnnealCFG "extrapolation impulse" decomposition gives a quantitative, mechanistic account of why constant guidance hurts streaming generation (47–60% of latent-update magnitude concentrated in the final 20% of denoising steps), elevating a schedule tweak into an analysis tool. - Honest negative reporting: the paper states plainly that the base model is unstable at 60s, that real-time is unmet, and that distilled-model semantic ratings decline at 60s — the limitation section matches the measured tables. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (1) MovieRoll-Distilled is not real-time (9.47 FPS at 8 GPUs vs. 24 FPS required); (2) MovieRoll-Base is insufficiently stable at 60s and is not evaluated there; (3) the distilled model's semantic and drifting-naturalness ratings drop at 60s relative to 10s; (4) joint window denoising, periodic KV recomputation, and VAE decoding remain costly; and (5) training data is confidential and cannot be released. They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them, which strengthens credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Every quantitative comparison runs on prompts rewritten by the authors' own Streaming Video Prompt Rewriting Skill, which enforces conventions (static/tracking camera, centered subject, no camera pans/zooms) that plausibly align with their model's training distribution — an untested confound favoring MovieRoll over baselines whose native strengths may include dynamic camera work. (2) No error bars, seed variance, or significance tests on HeliosBench totals; several claimed wins are within 0.1–0.4 rating points on a 1–10 integer scale aggregated from ~200 videos. (3) The dynamics metric is raw optical-flow magnitude, rewarding motion quantity over correctness — MovieRoll's "active motion" advantage could partly reflect flow-heavy artifacts. (4) HieraKV's motivating attention analysis is done on their own WinTF model, so the 6/48 split's transferability to other video diffusion architectures is unverified. (5) Interaction latency and online/reactive generation — the stated motivation for streaming — are never measured (no keystroke-to-first-frame latency); the user study only judges offline videos. (6) The KV recomputation ablation compares against a sliding-window baseline with the same cache length, but not against training-horizon-extended fine-tuning or retrieval-style memory baselines (e.g., MemFlow's mechanism) under matched compute. Bottom Line: For anyone engineering long-horizon or interactive streaming video diffusion, this is one of the most complete and honestly ablated system papers in the current wave and worth a careful read; general readers can safely rely on its released weights without reading past the ablation tables, and should treat the benchmark margins as small and prompt-rewriting-confounded.

Problem & Motivation: Obtaining closed-form white-box models from measured data requires expert decisions on model class, estimation criterion, prior-knowledge integration, and validation — decisions that symbolic regression (SR) and sparse regression automate only partially and within fixed search procedures. Existing agentic equation-discovery systems (ASIA, SR-Scientist, KeplerAgent, LLM-SR) either fix the toolset, lack support for user-specified physical requirements and their independent verification, allow implicit test-data leakage, or produce no auditable record distinguishing fitted, fixed, and tied parameters. Practitioners in control engineering and robotics who need interpretable, physically consistent, embeddable models currently lack an agentic framework that combines free method choice with verifiable guarantees. This is a preprint (arXiv:2611.13114, cs.RO), not stated as peer-reviewed. Key Idea: The core insight is an architectural separation of powers: let the LLM agent choose and implement any identification method it likes, but strip it of evaluative authority — the harness alone computes all errors on sealed test data, independently verifies formal physical requirements, fixes the agent's recommendation before test results exist, and retains full execution logs so every claim in the delivered model record can be checked against what the agent actually did. Trust comes from the harness, not from constraining the agent. Methodology: ASPIRE comprises (1) task intake — the harness generates a task brief (by fixed rules, no LLM) from compulsory inputs (training data, model form, evaluation mode, budget) and optional inputs (descriptions, intended use, physical requirements); (2) identification rounds — the agent (an LLM behind a provider API, optionally with helper agents) inspects data, writes and runs estimation code (it may use SciPy, gplearn, PySINDy, or its own code), and delivers a pool of up to 10 structurally distinct closed-form candidates under default budgets of 60 turns, 3600 s, and $10; (3) checks — record completeness/consistency validation; (4) evaluation — prediction or free-run simulation (RK4 with one step per sampling period, optional horizon-H segmented simulation), RMSE ranking on test data, and verification of nine formal requirement types (symmetry, monotonicity, parity, exact value, inequality, curvature, limit, equation, relation) with outcomes of proof / counterexample / inconclusive; and (5) record/report — HTML reports with per-turn command logs. Each candidate carries a parameter table (fitted/fixed/tied types), an estimation record, and a discussion interpreting every term. Interactive operation adds a task interview (agent proposes the task specification from raw data files), agent questions, user feedback rounds labeled test-informed. Evaluation uses simulation error with test trajectories; recommendation is made without test access, and oracle-based selection is reported separately with pool sizes. Key Results: Three measured systems, each run as described and blind task, five runs per task (30 runs total), agent = gpt-6.1-sol at medium reasoning effort, cost $0.96–$3.38 per run ($61.10 total, $0.48 per candidate). All 30 runs delivered passing pools; all 126 candidates were eligible; no budget limit was hit. Test scores (RMSE, mean ± SD over 5 runs): mobile robot 0.0430 ± 0.0010 m (described) / 0.0401 ± 0.0015 m (blind); friction system 0.0417 ± 0.0070 / 0.0408 ± 0.0079 rad; fermenter 0.0232 ± 0.0006 / 0.0225 ± 0.0010 bar. Baselines: PySINDy and PySR at default and matched settings, evaluated by the same harness on the same test data. Agent models beat or match all tool baselines on the mobile robot and fermenter; on the friction system, PySR matched (0.0363 ± 0.0039 rad) but all 12 tool models violated requirement R2 (direction of gravity torque at rest) and would have been excluded for an agent candidate. Description withholding did not increase test error but changed model form: described tasks yielded physically named structures with fewer parameters (e.g., 2.4 ± 0.9 vs. 9.6 ± 5.9 for the robot; 5.6 ± 1.1 vs. 19.0 ± 2.2 for the fermenter), while blind fermenter models were cubic polynomials. Model-record assessment: 132/150 items fully satisfied, 18 partly, 0 no; the most common discrepancy (9 records) was inaccurate claims about how the model structure originated, detectable only via execution logs. A sealed-test-data scan found 16 coincidental number matches across 7 runs, all benign. Notably, the agent never used the installed gplearn or PySINDy packages, writing its own estimation code instead. Baselines are standard and current for closed-form identification, but the authors deliberately did not run competing agentic systems (ASIA, SR-Scientist, KeplerAgent), arguing adaptations would confound results. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus NEW FORMULATION of evaluation protocol. Genuinely novel: the harness architecture combining agent-selected identification methods with sealed test data, independent formal-requirement verification, structured model records (fitted/fixed/tied parameters), pre-test recommendation freezing, and quantified run-to-run variability — no prior agentic system combines these. The LLM-agent-writes-and-runs-code mechanism itself is a standard combination of existing agentic patterns (FunSearch/ASIA-style); the requirement taxonomy consolidates known physics-aware SR constraint types. Rigor & Reproducibility: Exceptional for this area: five runs per task with per-run and cross-run statistics (mean ± sample SD) reported; oracle-based selection reported separately from agent recommendation with pool sizes; PySR run with five seeds; a pre-registered median-run selection rule for figures; an explicit audit of test-data leakage; and a manual assessment of all 30 model records with per-item evidence published. Code, task specifications, data, complete run records, HTML reports, baseline scripts, and the record-assessment evidence are released at https://github.com/erik-derner/aspire-sysid (CC BY 4.0). Methodological concerns: (1) the authors developed the framework against these same three systems and their test data — a development/evaluation overlap they acknowledge; (2) a single LLM without a dated snapshot, so runs are not reproducible at the model level; (3) the record assessment was partly automated (Claude Code with Opus 5.5) then manually verified by the authors, who are also the framework's developers — no independent evaluators; (4) no statistical tests applied to the agent-vs-baseline comparisons, and the fermenter test score rests on a single trajectory; (5) competing agentic systems were not run head-to-head. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built framework evaluated on measured physical data, with code and run records released). - Practical: Runs on commodity hardware with any LLM provider API; the only external dependency is token pricing. - Efficient: $0.96–$3.38 per identification run, 9–21 minutes of execution time — cheap relative to expert effort and comparable to a single-core PySR search of 4–31 minutes per fitting target. - Effective: Evidence covers the stated goal on three real systems — accurate simulation models that satisfy physical requirements baselines violate — but the sealed-evaluation and record-trust guarantees are demonstrated by design and audit, not by adversarial stress-testing. - Scalable: Not tested beyond three small systems (13–3500 training samples, 1–3 states); behavior on high-dimensional, noisy, or multi-output systems (excluded by assumptions A1–A3) is unknown and unclaimed. Delivers a software artifact: the harness, task specifications, data, all 30 run records, and reports in a public repository. Strengths: - The sealed-evaluation architecture is a concrete, reusable answer to the test-leakage problem that ASIA's own authors identified in agentic system identification, and the paper audits its own seal (16 coincidental number matches examined and explained). - The model-record format with fitted/fixed/tied parameter provenance and execution-log cross-checking is a substantive contribution to auditability of agent-produced scientific artifacts; the finding that records document methods more reliably than decision provenance (9/30 discrepancies, all in item (b)) is a genuinely useful empirical observation about LLM agents. - Honest, quantified reporting of negative and neutral results: prior knowledge did not reduce test error (and slightly increased it in all three systems), the agent ignored the provided SR packages, and requirement verification was inconclusive (sampling-only) for 36 of 66 checks rather than claiming symbolic proof. - The interactive case study demonstrates capabilities competitors lack: task interview from raw data files (15 turns, $0.46), agent questions tied to specific modeling decisions, and user feedback that reshapes the pool with test-informed rounds explicitly labeled. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) test data were sealed against the agent but not against the authors, who used them during framework and task development; (2) only one language model was used, with no dated snapshot, so cross-model performance is unestablished (preliminary experiments with other models are mentioned but not reported); (3) evaluation scale is small; (4) assumptions A1–A3 restrict the framework to a single scalar scored output, fully measured states, and a given measurement equation, excluding multi-output scores and state estimation. They confront limitations directly and specifically, including quantified record-assessment failures — a strong credibility positive. Future work plans (multi-output, unmeasured states, multi-model comparison, independent users, agent-guided data collection, natural-language requirement checking) are stated rather than claimed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No head-to-head comparison with any competing agentic system (ASIA, SR-Scientist, KeplerAgent); the stated excuse (adaptations would confound) is defensible but leaves the central claim — that agent method-freedom plus the harness beats fixed-pipeline agents — untested against alternatives; the honest comparison is against non-agentic tools only. - The formal-requirement verification is weaker than the framing suggests: only 30 of 66 verifications ended in proof; the rest were inconclusive sampled checks, and the agent itself performed pre-delivery sampling checks on the same requirements, so the independent-verification guarantee partially reduces to sampling with 10,000 points — a demonstrated violation excludes, but absence of violation is not assurance. - Blind-task models on the friction system all violate R2, yet the paper does not report the magnitude of those violations as it does for PySR, making the practical cost of omitting requirements hard to judge. - The record assessment was performed by the authors (with an LLM assistant) on their own system with no inter-rater reliability or independent evaluator; the 'fully satisfied 132 of 150' figure is self-reported. - The three systems are small and low-dimensional (1–3 states); the $10 default budget, single-output scoring, and RK4 fixed-step integration have unknown behavior on stiff, high-dimensional, or partially observed systems. - The harness's value proposition over a general coding agent with the same model is argued qualitatively (Section 7.3) — 'we have no evidence that the harness changes the error' — not measured with even one control session. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or evaluating agentic modeling systems should read this for its harness architecture and unusually honest evaluation protocol, which set a standard the field should adopt — but the empirical evidence rests on three small systems, one unversioned LLM, self-assessed records, and no competing-agent baseline, so the accuracy claims are suggestive rather than settled.

Do Language Models Know What Compelling Scientific Evidence Looks Like?

C Igoe, G Grand, Z Koch, A Bou, E Moss, MM Hinks… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EDB-Bio, a 96,000-episode benchmark of calibrated probabilistic forecasting over real biological evidence (drug-perturbation transcriptomics, CRISPR dependency screens, GWAS), and uses it to show that frontier LLMs are systematically underconfident — scoring no better on Brier than a constant base-rate forecaster — while a post-trained 30B model (Ibis0) closes the calibration gap and a factored expected-information-gain (EIG) estimator built on it extracts ~2.5× more information per selected experiment than prompted frontier models. - Why it's important: LLM-driven autonomous discovery systems must decide which hypotheses to pursue and which experiments to run, and poorly calibrated probabilistic judgments feed directly into wasted experiments and overconfident scientific claims. - How it does it: Each episode holds out a target experiment, gives the model a graded-relevance pool of up to 16 related evidence "stubs," and asks for p(supported); belief revision is analyzed as log Bayes factors (decibans), and calibration is fixed by post-training against strictly proper scoring rules (negative-Brier RL and a BCE-trained classifier head). - The good: The strongest evidence is the separation of calibration from discrimination — frontier models achieve AUROC 0.737–0.752 yet Brier scores statistically indistinguishable from 0.25, and the belief-update calibration slope β exposes quantitative overreaction (untrained Qwen3 β = 0.13, i.e., updates ~8× larger than outcomes justify; Ibis0 non-thinking β = 0.89) — a diagnosis simple accuracy benchmarks cannot produce. - The missing: The benchmark is built from structured, threshold-defined labels with a forced 50:50 base rate, and the fine-tuned models are trained on the same distribution they are evaluated on; 53.2% of GWAS test targets also appear as training evidence stubs (measured and mostly attributed to selection effects, but not eliminated), and only two frontier baselines at one reasoning setting are compared. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate agentic scientific-reasoning systems and care about calibration, sequential belief updating, or LLM-based experimental design; skip it if you need evidence about free-text literature deliberation or non-biological domains, since the task is deliberately structured and synthetic in its evidence presentation.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (72) is strong — the relevance-graded, leakage-audited EDB-Bio benchmark plus the calibration-vs-discrimination dissociation and the β-based belief-update diagnostic are genuinely new contributions, even if proper-scoring post-training itself is known. Rigor (68) reflects exemplary audit culture (Platt-scaling controls, overlap quantification, clustered bootstraps, full artifact release) undercut by the self-referential structure — same organization builds the benchmark, trains the model on it, and reports the win — the 53.2% GWAS overlap, and the fine-tuned-vs-zero-shot baseline asymmetry. Non-Obviousness (75) is high: the finding that frontier models rank evidence well yet calibrate no better than a base-rate forecaster, and that aggregate calibration coexists with 8× overreaction in updates, is surprising and reveals hidden structure. Completeness (80) is boosted by a direct limitations section; Resilience (65) is capped by the thin frontier comparison and the pooled 2.5× EIG headline that vanishes on Tahoe. Impact (80) reflects a fully released benchmark, weights, code, and logs. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*68 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*80 = 72.

Problem & Motivation: Autonomous research agents increasingly make decisions — which hypothesis to pursue, which experiment to run, how confidently to report conclusions — that depend on weighing heterogeneous empirical evidence of variable quality and relevance. Prior LLM-calibration work concentrates on factual QA, mathematics, and commonsense reasoning, where the evidence structure differs fundamentally from multi-study scientific deliberation. The gap: no benchmark measures whether a model's stated belief tracks the strength and relevance of experimental evidence, as opposed to merely ranking claims correctly. The motivating users are builders of AI-scientist systems (the authors' own Kosmos/Edison Scientific among them) and anyone deploying LLMs for evidence-based forecasting in biology. Key Idea: Reframe scientific evidence deliberation as a sequential probabilistic forecasting problem with a controlled evidence pool: hold out the experiment that directly tests a hypothesis, reveal related experiments one at a time, and score the model's stated probability with proper scoring rules. Because the evidence pool is relevance-graded by domain experts and the target is always excluded, one can decompose performance into calibration vs. discrimination and measure per-stub belief updates as log Bayes factors — turning "does the model find this evidence compelling?" into a measurable quantity. A secondary trick is the factored EIG estimator: marginalize over the local hypothesis label θ′ to split EIG into supportive and non-supportive branches, costing 3 belief calls + 2 simulator calls per candidate instead of a nested Monte Carlo loop. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Dataset construction: 3 domains × 32,000 training / 256 validation / 2,000 test episodes from Tahoe-100M (pseudobulk RNA-seq, DESeq2 readouts), DepMap (CRISPR Chronos scores), and the GWAS Catalog, each with hypotheses like "Drug D downregulates gene G in cell line C" and binary labels from domain-specific significance thresholds; five design principles enforce artifact exclusion (P1), 50:50 balance and diversity (P2), expert-defined graded relevance hierarchies (P3), sufficiency strata (P4), and target-leakage exclusion (P5). (2) Model training: starting from Qwen3-30B-A3B, three Ibis0 variants — two GRPO-style RL policies with reward r = 1 − (p − θ)² (thinking and non-thinking) and a full fine-tuned classifier with a scalar linear head trained on BCE — plus an SFT outcome simulator for experiment selection; training on 8×B200 nodes with prime-rl. (3) Evaluation: Brier score, sMECE (a smooth-ECE calibration error), AUROC, Murphy decomposition, weight-of-evidence calibration slope β, order/composition consistency tests, and a sequential Bayesian experimental-design task on 512 episodes per domain comparing random, naive-prompting, and EIG-based policies. Critical design decisions: expert-curated (not automated) relevance hierarchies — well-justified; forced 50:50 base rate — justified for clean calibration analysis but acknowledged as possibly explaining cross-domain calibration transfer; i.i.d. splits — acknowledged as a weakness given the measured GWAS overlap. Notably, calibration analysis is careful: episode-clustered bootstraps, cross-fit Platt scaling as a recalibration control, and a quantified overlap audit (App. A.7). Key Results: Out of the box, GPT-5.6-sol (AUROC 0.737) and Claude Opus 5 (AUROC 0.752) rank supported above unsupported hypotheses, but their macro Brier scores (0.288, 0.277) are not significantly better than the 0.25 base-rate forecaster; untrained Qwen3 is worse (0.297–0.334). All three Ibis0 variants beat 0.25 in every domain: the classifier achieves Brier 0.177 and AUROC 0.820; the RL policies are best calibrated (sMECE 0.032 vs. 0.066 for the classifier; 0.24–0.31 for zero-shot models). Verbalizing models emit fewer than 100 distinct probability values; the classifier emits ~1,742 (18–50× finer resolution). On belief updates, every model overreacts (β < 1): untrained Qwen3 non-thinking β = 0.13, frontier models in between, Ibis0 non-thinking β = 0.89 (the only model whose interval includes 1). All models under-weight same-mechanism evidence and over-weight aggregate summaries relative to the expert hierarchy; all show primacy effects (classifier worst, +1.01 dB). In experiment selection, EIG-simulate gains 0.155 bits on the first experiment vs. 0.062 for the best prompted frontier policy (non-overlapping 95% CIs; ~2.5×), though on Tahoe the top EIG and frontier policies are statistically tied. Cross-domain transfer: calibration transfers (reliability retention 58–86%) but discrimination does not (Brier retention 70.0% Tahoe → 26.3% GWAS). Baselines are current frontier models at high reasoning effort with a 24,000-token budget, though only two are tested. Scale is standard benchmark scale (30B MoE, ≤16-stub contexts), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (EDB-Bio: relevance-graded, leakage-audited scientific forecasting episodes across three domains) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (systematic underconfidence of frontier LLMs on scientific evidence despite good discrimination; quantified overreaction via β) + NEW METHOD (factored EIG estimator with a trained outcome simulator for sequential experiment selection). The proper-scoring post-training itself is a known technique (Damani et al., Bani-Harouni et al., Leng et al.) applied to a new setting; the log-Bayes-factor update analysis adapts classical tools (Good, Mantel–Haenszel) rather than introducing new statistics. The genuinely novel pieces are the controlled-evidence benchmark design and the demonstration that calibration and discrimination dissociate, and that aggregate calibration does not imply correctly sized or order-invariant updates. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: three Ibis0 variants isolate output-head vs. objective effects, leave-one-domain-out classifiers test transfer, Platt-scaling controls show the trained models' calibration edge is not just a monotone remap, and the overlap audit (Table 4, Fig. 6) recomputes all metrics with contaminated episodes removed. Uncertainty is handled with 95% bootstrap intervals (2,000 draws for headline tables; episode-clustered for per-stub analyses), and the appendix candidly flags positively-biased intervals near zero. Multiple seeds are not reported for training runs, though decoding uses 4-draw averaging at fixed temperature. All artifacts are released: dataset and test sets on Hugging Face (EdisonScientific/EDB-Bio), Ibis0 weights, code on GitHub (EdisonScientific/ibis0, Apache-2.0), and full training logs — a best-practice reproducibility package. Methodological concerns: (1) the benchmark is authored and evaluated by the same organization, which also sells AI-scientist systems, so the task framing favors their calibration-training recipe; (2) trained models are tuned on the same distribution they are scored on, while frontier baselines are zero-shot — a train/test asymmetry that partly explains the headline gap; (3) 53.2% GWAS test-target overlap with training evidence is measured but not eliminated (authors attribute residual effects to selection, and the DepMap pattern is "consistent with memorization" at ~0.004 Brier). These are disclosed, which raises credibility, but the industry-source and self-benchmark structure warrants moderate caution on the frontier-comparison claims. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — released models and benchmark). - Practical: Yes — everything runs on a 30B-A3B open-weight model (8×B200 for training; inference is single-GPU-class), and the released weights and code are Apache-2.0. - Efficient: The factored EIG estimator costs 3 belief + 2 simulator calls per candidate — cheaper than nested Monte Carlo but more expensive than naive prompting; the authors state this cost trade-off explicitly. - Effective: The evidence shows calibrated forecasting and higher per-experiment information gain on the benchmark itself; whether this transfers to real deliberation over free-text literature is untested — the effective claim holds for the proxy, not the ultimate use case. - Scalable: Not tested — evidence pools cap at 16 stubs, one model family at one scale is trained, and the authors flag the fixed-cost, uniform-experiment assumption; 10× context growth is unexamined. The work delivers concrete artifacts: a dataset, trained model weights, an outcome simulator, and an evaluation harness, all publicly released. Strengths: - The controlled-evidence design (held-out target, expert-graded relevance hierarchy, P1–P5 principles) is a real methodological contribution: it converts the vague question "do models weigh evidence well?" into decomposable measurements, and the calibrated-update slope β is a genuinely informative diagnostic that no accuracy-style benchmark yields. - The audit culture is exemplary: quantifying its own test/train overlap (53.2% of GWAS targets), cross-fit Platt recalibration as a competing explanation, and Murphy decomposition showing that calibration transfers across domains while discrimination does not — the latter is a substantive finding about what post-training actually buys. - The factored EIG estimator is a practical algorithmic contribution with a clean efficiency argument (one outcome sample per branch, parallelizable), validated against empirical exemplar sampling and a nested-MC alternative. - Full artifact release (data, weights, code, logs) with a detailed reproducibility statement exceeds typical benchmark-paper practice. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: evidence stubs are structured summaries rather than free-text literature; hypotheses are binary and domains are forced to a 0.5 base rate (which may explain cross-domain calibration transfer); only one model family (Qwen3) at one scale is post-trained; the factored EIG estimator costs more than naive prompting; beliefs are collapsed to a single probability; experiments are assumed uniform-cost; and the i.i.d. split causes test-target/train-evidence overlap (quantified in App. A.7 with a promised fix in a future revision). This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No human-expert baseline: the paper benchmarks models against a curated relevance hierarchy and a base-rate forecaster, but never against working biologists doing the same task, so "expert-level" claims are implicit rather than measured. - The frontier comparison is thin (two models, one reasoning setting, one evaluation date) and confounded by the fine-tuning asymmetry — a frontier model few-shot prompted with in-domain calibration examples, or with the EIB policy applied to its own verbalized beliefs, is not tested (Ibis0-with-EIG is, but only with the trained belief model). - Label validity is threshold-based: "supported iff |log2FC| > 0.5, padj < 0.05" conflates statistical significance with scientific truth, so the benchmark measures agreement with assay readouts, not with biology; the "GWAS has no refuting stubs" asymmetry also makes domains non-comparable in the directional analyses. - LD leakage in GWAS is explicitly deferred, and given 53.2% overlap plus high-LD near-duplicates, the GWAS domain numbers should be read with the most caution. - The 2.5× EIG headline pools domains; on Tahoe the advantage vanishes (statistically tied), and the paper does not surface this per-domain heterogeneity in the abstract framing. - Goodhart exposure: the same organization defines the task, builds the data, trains the model on it, and reports the win; an independent replication on the released artifacts would materially strengthen the calibration-training claim. Bottom Line: For anyone building LLM-driven scientific agents, this is worth reading in full — the benchmark, the calibration-vs-discrimination dissociation, and the β-based update diagnostics are tools you can adopt immediately — but treat the frontier-vs-Ibis0 margins as one team's self-referential evaluation pending independent replication and free-text-evidence follow-up.

TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs (22 ▲ )

Xuwei Ding, Skylar Zhai, Linxin Song, Jiarui Feng, Dongqi Fu, Huajun Xi, Junnan Li, Jingcheng Liang, Jieyu Zhao, Yinglong Xia, Hong Li, Jian Kang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 20 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 program-generated interactive spatial CAPTCHAs solved via real GUI actions (clicks/drags on screenshots), which serves both as a benchmark (TuringSpace-Bench) and as an unlimited trajectory generator for training (TuringSpace-Gym). - Why it's important: Existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and non-spatial, while spatial benchmarks are mostly multiple-choice, so there is no testbed that measures whether MLLMs can close the act-observe-adjust loop that grounds 3D spatial understanding — a capability gap that currently separates frontier models from humans. - How it does it: Each of the 125 tasks is a generator program that synthesizes fresh instances from random seeds with a programmatic checker and an oracle solution; replaying oracle solutions yields verified action-trajectories, and fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 55,000 such trajectories (cross-entropy on oracle tool calls, vision encoder frozen) yields TuringSpace-9B. - The good: Humans solve 94.1% of tasks while the best model (GPT-6 Astra) reaches only 74.1% pass@1 and 58.4% pass^3; training in the gym lifts Qwen3.5-9B from 1.6% to 33.1% and improves it on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including +9.9 points on real-world video (VSI-Bench). - The missing: All transfer results come from a single base model (Qwen3.5-9B) trained with SFT on oracle trajectories only — no second model, no RL comparison, no data-scale ablation, and no equal-sized control dataset to attribute the transfer gains to spatial reasoning rather than generic multi-turn GUI supervision. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on MLLM spatial reasoning, computer-use agents, or verifiable synthetic training environments; skip it if you only need frontier-model spatial scores, which existing multiple-choice spatial benchmarks already cover more cheaply.

Problem & Motivation: MLLMs now handle 2D perception well but remain far behind humans on 3D spatial understanding (perspective taking, mental rotation, predicting how actions change a scene). The authors argue that spatial cognition is a closed loop — read the scene, act, observe, adjust — and that benchmarks testing it fail in one of two ways: CAPTCHA benchmarks are solved by computer-use agents and mostly test non-spatial puzzles, while spatial benchmarks pose multiple-choice questions about static images, letting models guess without ever acting. Where interactive spatial environments exist (iVISPAR, VisGym, ESI-Bench), models act only through text commands, and several CAPTCHA benchmarks expose the page DOM or rely on timing/animation that screenshots cannot convey. The gap: no benchmark requires spatial reasoning expressed through pixel-level GUI actions with verifiable, regeneratable instances, and no training environment supplies verified demonstrations for that format. Key Idea: Make every spatial puzzle a program, not a puzzle: a generator G(z, M) maps a seed and an asset pool to a full instance (initial state, instruction, checker, oracle action sequence). The checker gives automated verification of model submissions (no human grading, no answer leakage), the oracle gives unlimited verified training trajectories in the exact action format of evaluation, and disjoint train/test seeds plus disjoint asset pools plus a configuration-hash rejection step give leakage control. This single design turns one set of 125 hand-reviewed task types into both a stable benchmark and a scalable gym. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Task construction: 125 seed task programs across five categories (spatial relation, closed-loop manipulation, multi-step planning, mental transformation, spatiotemporal reasoning) are written by a coding agent (Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5) on a shared page runtime, drawing assets from Open Images, COCO, Poly Haven, and ambientCG. Each task passes a review loop: 100-seed programmatic checks (renders, deterministic regeneration, oracle solves, random clicking fails), a Sonnet 5.5 trajectory reviewed by authors for shortcuts, and two authors playing the task. (2) Benchmark/gym split: three random test seeds per task with a held-out asset pool form Dtest; up to 500 instances per task (200 for spatiotemporal) form Dtrain (55,000 trajectories total). (3) Training: full fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-9B's language model (vision encoder and aligner frozen) with token-averaged cross-entropy on oracle tool-call tokens in the thinking-off setting, 1,000 steps (~2.3 epochs) on 32× H200, batch size 128, LR 5e-6 cosine. Evaluation uses each model's official OSWorld computer-use implementation at 1920×1080, ≤50 steps, pass@1 over three seeds (375 attempts) with standard deviation, plus pass^3 for stability. Critical design decisions: programmatic checkers instead of human grading (well justified — deterministic and scalable); screenshot-only interaction with no timing dependence (justified — isolates capability from interface artifacts); oracle-trajectory SFT rather than RL (a limitation, not justified against alternatives). Key Results: Humans (3 non-author authors) solve 94.1% pass@1 (84.8% pass^3) in 33.1 s/task. GPT-6 Astra leads models at 74.1% pass@1 (58.4% pass^3); Claude Opus 5.5 65.3%, Gemini 4 Argon 57.9%; Kimi K3 32.0% and Qwen3.8-Max 30.7% despite 2.4–2.8T parameters; specialized GUI agents score ≤3.5%. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B (1.6%) to 33.1% (±6.1) surpasses Kimi K3, Qwen3.8-Max, and Gemini 3.8 Flash. Spatiotemporal tasks are hardest (GPT-6 Astra 52.0%). Zero-shot transfer of TuringSpace-9B: +17.2 on ReCAP (73.6%), +10.0 on Open CaptchaWorld (36.9%), +19.8 on RefSpatial-Bench (58.1%), +9.9 on VSI-Bench (60.4%), +6.1 on SpatialViz-Bench, +7.4 on VABench-Point, +12.2 on RoboAfford-Eval. Analysis: perception causes 57.1% of the 380 failures of the three strongest models (depth misjudgment 34–46% each), with zero grounding errors and 85 of 129 closed-loop/planning failures still perceptual despite per-action visual feedback. In 293 failed attempts of open-weight models, the decisive wrong belief forms within the first two steps in 68% of cases; reasoning doubts it 89.4% of the time but abandons it only 7.5%; fabricated observations (74%), hallucinated priors (66%), and blind submissions (55%) defend the belief and increase with reasoning length. Thinking amount negatively correlates with pass@1 (r = −0.75), but hard-task thinking allocation correlates positively (r = 0.82). Baselines are current frontier models as of the paper's date; scale is standard (125 task types, 375 eval attempts), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (programmatic interactive spatial CAPTCHA environment doubling as a verifiable training gym), plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the wrong-belief-propagation and hallucinated-evidence analysis; the observation that spatial CAPTCHA training transfers to conventional CAPTCHAs but not vice versa). The training method itself is standard SFT on oracle demonstrations; the genuinely novel element is the benchmark-plus-gym design and the human-model gap it exposes, not the learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: reasoning-effort sweeps across four models and a thinking-token analysis are informative, but there is no ablation over training-data size, no RL-vs-SFT comparison, no alternative-data control, and no second base model. Error bars are reported (per-seed standard deviations for pass@1, e.g., 74.1±1.7 for GPT-6 Astra, 33.1±6.1 for TuringSpace-9B); no significance tests. Annotation reliability is checked: 92% agreement on 50 sampled wrong-belief labels and 90.3% agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.88) on root causes, though both judges are Claude Opus 5.5 plus one human author. Leakage is addressed seriously (disjoint seeds, disjoint asset pools, hash-based configuration rejection). Code and data are stated as "We will release TuringSpace" with project/GitHub/HF links referenced, but the release is promised, not confirmed in the text. Concerns: frontier-model evaluation depends on vendor APIs with self-reported behavior and default sampling; the error-analysis judge is itself a frontier model from a vendor whose models are being evaluated; the human baseline is only 3 people, each on one seed; and only 3 test instances per task type. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a built artifact). Practical: Yes — tasks run in a browser and evaluation uses the standard OSWorld CUA harness; inference needs only API access or an open-weight 9B model. Efficient: Training required 32× H200 for ~2.3 epochs, a moderate but non-trivial cost; inference cost matches standard computer-use agents. Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark separates humans from models and that training improves both in-domain and OOD scores, but the trained model still solves only 33.1% versus 94.1% human — the stated problem is exposed, not solved. Scalable: Unlimited instance generation is architectural, but nothing beyond the 125 task types and 55,000 trajectories has been tested; a 10× task-type scale-up is unverified. Deliverable: a software artifact (benchmark environment, gym, and a fine-tuned 9B model checkpoint, promised for release). Strengths: - The program-as-task design (generator + checker + oracle + seed/asset-pair leakage control) is a genuinely useful reusable pattern that makes the same artifact serve as benchmark, training gym, and automatic grader. - The wrong-belief analysis is the paper's most interesting empirical contribution: quantifying that open-weight models doubt their initial wrong belief 89.4% of the time but abandon it only 7.5%, and that hallucinated evidence increases with reasoning length, is a specific, falsifiable, non-obvious finding. - Evaluation discipline: 16 models including specialized GUI agents under their official harnesses, pass^3 stability metric, human timing baseline, and OOD transfer across seven heterogeneous benchmarks (CAPTCHA, video, robot pointing) rather than in-domain numbers alone. - The asymmetry finding — spatial CAPTCHA training improves conventional CAPTCHAs while conventional-CAPTCHA-trained agents (UI-Venus-2, ReCAP-32B) solve almost nothing in TuringSpace — cleanly demonstrates the direction of transfer. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Explicitly stated: the ethics statement acknowledges dual use — agents trained in TuringSpace-Gym could be used to bypass deployed CAPTCHAs protecting real websites. The paper also notes that Gemini 4 Argon repeatedly refused to answer five attempts (excluded from root-cause analysis) and that Kimi K3 and Qwen3.5-9B run at different reasoning-effort settings for compatibility reasons. Beyond these, the visible text does not contain a dedicated limitations section; the authors do not directly confront the single-base-model, SFT-only scope of the training claims, which is a modest credibility deduction. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No equal-sized control dataset: the +31.5 in-domain and OOD gains could partly reflect generic multi-turn GUI/screenshot-action supervision rather than spatial content; a control fine-tune on 55,000 trajectories from conventional CAPTCHAs or non-spatial GUI tasks is missing. - All training and transfer results use one base model (Qwen3.5-9B) at one scale; the claim that "spatial understanding grounded in screen actions transfers to real-world scenes" is supported by a single 9B data point. - The error analysis of frontier-model failures is performed by Claude Opus 5.5 acting as judge — a model from a lab whose products are among the evaluated systems — with human verification on only a 50-attempt sample (92% agreement); the root-cause taxonomy distribution (e.g., 57.1% perception) is therefore not fully independent of vendor systems. - The human baseline is 3 authors on one test seed each; human variance across a broader population is unmeasured. - Oracle-trajectory SFT teaches only one solution path per instance, potentially teaching shortcut behaviors rather than generalizable spatial reasoning; no analysis of whether the fine-tuned model's failures still stem from perception (the diagnosis motivating the work). - Frontier-model scores depend on API behavior at a fixed (medium) reasoning effort; the effort sweep shows up to ~16-point swings for some models, so the ranking of proprietary models is effort-sensitive. - Preprint (arXiv, November 2026), not peer-reviewed; vendor self-reported model capabilities underpin the frontier comparison. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or evaluating spatial/computer-use agents gains real value from the programmatic benchmark-plus-gym design and the wrong-belief analysis, but the training-side claims rest on one model, one algorithm, and no control dataset, so read it as a strong benchmark paper with a promising but under-ablated training result.

Large Flow Language Models

A Chavan, C Lee, U Bamba, J Yoo, S Hong… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Lafa, a blockwise continuous flow language model adapted from pretrained autoregressive checkpoints (0.5B–8B parameters, <30B training tokens) that matches autoregressive quality while enabling 2.54× decoding throughput via self-speculative decoding. - Why it's important: Autoregressive LLMs generate one token per forward pass, making inference latency a bottleneck, and prior continuous flow language models had not been demonstrated at billion-parameter scale with practical inference speed. - How it does it: It casts generation as a block-autoregressive factorization where each block is denoised by an asynchronous flow (tokenwise time schedules learned from denoising loss) over vocabulary embeddings, trained jointly with the original AR objective on a Qwen checkpoint, and then uses the retained AR predictor to verify one-step flow drafts within the same model. - The good: Controlled comparisons against identically trained MTP, block-parallel, and discrete diffusion baselines (matching initialization, data, and budget) show Lafa's single-token AR accuracy exceeding matched AR SFT at all three scales (e.g., 60.9% vs 58.4% six-benchmark average at 7B), plus 2.54× wall-clock throughput at comparable quality on a single H100. - The missing: Full flow decoding requires many Euler steps (quality still trails AR at ≤8 steps at 7B), flow map distillation leaves a quality gap, throughput is measured only at batch size 1 on one GPU, and no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on parallel decoding or diffusion/flow language models — it is the first credible demonstration of a continuous flow LM at 7–8B scale with controlled baselines; skip it if you only care about serving-scale throughput with batched workloads, which is untested here.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Practical Impact (75) is the strongest driver — released code plus 0.5B/7B/8B checkpoints, <30B adaptation tokens, and a demonstrated 2.54× throughput gain — and Rigor (72) is anchored by the controlled-baseline protocol (retraining MTP, block-parallel, and diffusion baselines under matched budgets) and systematic 0.5B ablations, though single runs without seeds and batch-1-only wall-clock measurements temper it. Novelty (72) and Non-Obviousness (70) reflect the self-speculative decoding insight (flow training yields an in-model AR verifier) rather than a fundamentally new formulation. Completeness (68) and Resilience (68) are reduced by the flow-map quality gap, the confounded cross-checkpoint comparisons, and the IFEval prompt-format concern at 8B. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*75 = 71.

Problem & Motivation: Parallel text generation is pursued via multi-token prediction (MTP), discrete diffusion, and continuous flow language models. Continuous flows are attractive because they admit tools from continuous generative modeling (flow maps, guidance, distillation) unavailable to discrete diffusion, but existing flow LMs were demonstrated only at small scale on simple tasks, and a prior scaling attempt (Gulrajani & Hashimoto's likelihood-based diffusion LMs) reported training inefficiency. The open problem: build a flow language model at billion-parameter scale that (a) trains cheaply by reusing pretrained AR checkpoints, (b) preserves AR quality, and (c) generates fast. The stakeholders are anyone deploying LLMs where inference latency dominates cost. Key Idea: Combine block-autoregressive factorization with an asynchronous continuous flow inside each block: prefix tokens get causal attention and time-1 conditioning (clean), while each noisy block denoises with tokenwise time schedules (earlier positions progress faster, learned as the inverse CDF of per-position denoising loss). The single trick that makes everything cohere: training the block denoiser jointly with the AR loss on the prefix preserves — and per their results improves — the AR predictor, so the same network can both draft blocks via one-step flow and verify drafts autoregressively, enabling self-speculative decoding without a separate draft model. Embedding norms are frozen at pretrained values (only directions are learned) to prevent the model from shrinking effective noise scale. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) initialize from Qwen2.5 Instruct 0.5B/7B or Qwen3 8B Base; (2) train a block denoiser with adaLN time conditioning, block-bidirectional attention (bidirectional within the noisy block, causal toward the clean prefix), learned tokenwise time τ updated via an EMA'd loss histogram, and a composite loss: prefix AR cross-entropy + denoising cross-entropy + embedding squared error (Eq. 6), with all blocks of a sequence trained in one forward pass via a clean/noisy-replica attention mask; (3) optionally distill the flow into a two-time flow map via semigroup-based distillation with KL losses extended to asynchronous schedules (Propositions A.2–A.3 prove the population minimizer recovers the teacher flow); (4) decode either by Euler integration (with self-conditioning and prefix guidance), by flow-map jumps (down to one step), or by self-speculative decoding where a one-step flow draft is verified against the model's own greedy AR predictions, with a fused single forward pass that simultaneously verifies the previous draft and drafts successor blocks for every possible acceptance length. Design decisions — bidirectional vs causal block attention, learned vs synchronous time, norm-frozen vs frozen/unconstrained embeddings, joint vs denoising-only loss — are each justified by ablation at 0.5B. Key Results: Tested at 0.5B, 7B, 8B on IFEval, BBH, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, GSM8K, HumanEval via lm-evaluation-harness. Single-token AR accuracy: Lafa 7B averages 60.9% vs 58.4% for matched AR SFT and 60.0% for matched DeepSeek-MTP; Lafa 8B reaches 63.1% vs 56.8% matched AR SFT and 63.5% for Efficient-DLM (a released checkpoint trained with ≥18× more tokens). Self-speculative decoding: Lafa 7B with B=16 achieves 2.54× wall-clock throughput of 7B AR SFT (100.2 vs 39.5 tokens/sec on one H100, batch size 1) at 74.5% vs 73.9% average accuracy on IFEval/GSM8K/HumanEval; ~2.5–5 tokens-per-forward across scales. DeepSeek-MTP and MARS cap at ~1.4× AR throughput; diffusion baselines (Dream, Fast-dLLM v2, Efficient-DLM) fall below AR SFT accuracy at their fast settings. Flow map distillation helps few-step regimes (two-step 7B student approaches four-step teacher) but a gap to multi-step flow decoding persists. Baselines are a mix of controlled (authors-trained, matched-budget, marked †) and released checkpoints with different data/budgets — the controlled comparisons are current and reasonably strong; note that at 7B, released Dream and Fast-dLLM v2 checkpoints score below Lafa's, but those were trained on different data. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the asynchronous blockwise flow formulation adapted from pretrained AR checkpoints with norm-frozen embedding updates and learned tokenwise time, and the self-speculative decoding scheme that exploits the MTP-like side effect of flow training to verify flow drafts within one model. The components are assembled from known ideas — block diffusion's factorization, flow matching, tokenwise time from prior asynchronous diffusion work, semigroup flow-map distillation from the authors' and related prior work (refs 13, 27, 38), speculative decoding (Stern et al. 2018) — applied to a new setting (8B-scale flow LMs); the scaling result itself is the contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations (Table 3, 0.5B, B=4, 32 steps) isolate each training and inference choice and show consistent effects: block-bidirectional attention 38.0% vs 32.7% causal, asynchronous vs synchronous time 38.0% vs 36.2%, norm-frozen embeddings 38.0% vs 34.4% frozen / 36.9% unconstrained, and AR loss added to denoising CE&MSE 38.0% vs 35.8%. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere. Code (github.com/lafa-gh/large-flow-lms) and model weights (huggingface.co/lafa-hf/models) are released, and controlled baselines are retrained under matched budgets — a credibility strength. Concerns: wall-clock throughput is measured only at batch size 1 on a single H100 (batched serving, the realistic deployment regime, is untested); some headline comparisons (e.g., vs Efficient-DLM's 18× token budget) conflate training-budget differences with method differences; the AR-gain claim rests on single runs; and the 8B comparison uses Qwen3 Base while 7B uses Qwen2.5 Instruct, so the scale axis mixes base/instruction variants. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact). Practical: Runs on a single H100 with bfloat16; architecture is a standard Qwen transformer with adaLN, so hardware requirements are ordinary. Efficient: Training is the headline efficiency claim (<30B tokens vs up to 500B for comparable discrete diffusion adaptations) and inference reaches 2.54× AR throughput, though flow decoding needs prefix-guidance passes (one extra block-only forward per step) and self-conditioning. Effective: Evidence shows quality parity with greedy AR for self-speculative decoding (output provably matches AR verification) and near-parity for multi-step flow decoding; flow-map one-step decoding does not yet reach AR quality, so the fastest mode is quality-degraded. Scalable: Untested beyond 8B and 512–1024-token sequences; batch size 1 only for wall-clock; claims about scaling are extrapolation. Delivers a software artifact: released code and 0.5B/7B/8B checkpoints on Hugging Face. Strengths: - The controlled-baseline protocol (retraining MTP, DeepSeek-MTP, MARS, SBD, BD3-LM, Fast-dLLM v2 from the same initialization, data, and budget) makes the quality comparisons genuinely interpretable, which most parallel-decoding papers skip. - The self-speculative decoding insight — that flow training's MTP effect yields an in-model AR verifier, enabling provably greedy-AR-consistent fast decoding without a separate draft model — is a clean, useful mechanism, backed by a fused single-pass verify-and-draft implementation. - The asynchronous flow machinery is given full theoretical treatment: the velocity-denoiser identity (Prop A.1) and flow-map well-posedness (Props A.2–A.3) are proved, so the distillation objective is principled rather than heuristic. - Honest accounting of training cost (<30B tokens) and per-benchmark numbers in the appendix rather than cherry-picked aggregates. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that a quality gap remains between flow-map decoding and multi-step flow decoding (attributed to self-conditioning and prefix guidance not yet being incorporated into distillation) and flag improving distillation as future work. They also note that further training of the post-trained Qwen3 8B Instruct checkpoint degraded performance, so the 8B model uses the Base checkpoint. They acknowledge that confidence-threshold acceptance trades accuracy for speed versus AR verification. They confront these directly rather than minimize them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-run, no-seed experiments throughout: the AR-improvement claim (e.g., 60.9% vs 58.4%) is within plausible seed variance for some benchmarks, and no variance is quantified. - Wall-clock throughput at batch size 1 is a weak proxy for serving; MTP and diffusion baselines may fare differently under batching, and prefix guidance doubles per-step block evaluations only cheaply because blocks are small — batched behavior is unknown. - Sequence lengths are capped at 512–1024 tokens; long-context behavior of blockwise flow with prefix caching is untested. - The '18× fewer tokens' comparison against Efficient-DLM/LLaDA/Dream compares authors' SFT-style adaptation against those models' full training pipelines; the fair statement is about adaptation cost, and cross-method quality comparisons against released checkpoints with different data are inherently confounded (the authors do mark controlled vs uncontrolled, but Figure 1 and the abstract blur this). - IFEval accuracy at 8B (38.1% for AR SFT) suggests a prompt-format mismatch with Qwen3 Base, making the 8B row less trustworthy than the 7B rows. - The learned tokenwise time is estimated with gradient-free forward passes every 100 steps using an EMA histogram — the paper does not report the overhead or sensitivity of this estimation. Bottom Line: For anyone working on parallel decoding or flow/diffusion language models, this is currently the strongest evidence that continuous flows can be adapted from AR checkpoints at 7–8B scale cheaply and decoded faster than AR without a separate draft model — it substantially advances the subfield, though serving-scale (batched, long-context) validation is left to future work.

VibePrevisBench: Evaluating Agentic Coding for 4D Scene Generation in Blender (84 ▲ )

Yuzhe Chen, Muxi Diao, Lele Yang, Wenbin Xu, Xuyang Liu, Qile Su, Changyi Liu, Jiankang Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Haoyu Zhang, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Bingyi Li, Xu Wang, Xuanyu Zheng, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Jiale Cao · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 16 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VibePrevisBench, a 242-task benchmark that scores coding agents on 4D scene generation in Blender — requiring agents to turn scripts, photos, continuations, or reference videos into executable 4D scenes rendered as graybox proxy videos — using a deterministic rule-based Scene Check against hidden ground-truth facts plus a VLM-based Screen Check of on-screen recognizability. - Why it's important: Proxy videos condition controllable real-world video generation, so agent errors in layout, motion, and camera propagate into final generated videos; no prior benchmark jointly tests multi-shot, multi-person, timed 4D scenes with both scene-level and screen-level checks (Table 1 claims VibePrevisBench is the only one covering all columns). - How it does it: Each task pairs a brief with hidden GT facts; the delivered program is re-run from scratch in a sandbox, the exported 4D scene (per-frame oriented boxes, cameras, cuts) is scored against the facts across nine rule dimensions (chance-corrected per block), and a VLM judge blind to agent identity rates only rule-passing items for recognition, action readability, visibility, and story beats. - The good: The evaluation is validated unusually thoroughly — deterministic rescoring of 2,786 deliveries, injected-defect tests showing monotone score drops in intended dimensions, three VLM judges correlating at Spearman 0.94–0.96 at agent level, and a human study on 242 pairs correlating at 0.90–0.92. - The missing: Ground truth for video/continuation tasks comes from an automated 4D reconstruction pipeline (SAM 3, MapAnything, GVHMR) whose own errors set the scoring ceiling, tasks were pruned post hoc for agent-discrimination (a benchmark-construction-on-eval-distribution concern), and each task is run only once per agent. - Read it or not: Read it if you build coding agents or controllable video generation pipelines and need a rigorous, reproducible evaluation of long-horizon 3D scene code; skip it if you only care about final video quality metrics, which the paper explicitly defers to future work.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (72) is unusually strong for a benchmark paper — injected-defect validation, paired bootstrap, 18 scoring variants with rank invariance, a 242-pair human study correlating at 0.90–0.92, and checksum-frozen scoring — and completeness (78) benefits from direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment of pruning, model-assisted ground truth, and the unmeasured link to final video quality. The composite is tempered by the post-hoc task-pruning on the very agents evaluated and reconstruction-derived ground truth (resilience 68), single runs per task, and an impact (70) bounded to a benchmark artifact that measures proxy quality rather than end-video outcomes. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*70 = 71.
