HINT-WAM: Hindsight-Informed Training for World Action Models (22 ▲ )

Phuong Tuan Dat, Qi Li, Xinchao Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 19 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HINT-WAM, a post-training framework in which a world action model acts as its own teacher conditioned on the demonstration's future video ("hindsight"), distilling that supervision into the student on the student's own denoising trajectories using an energy-score objective. - Why it's important: Post-training flow-matching robot policies is bottlenecked by exposure bias in SFT and by sparse rewards in RL; HINT-WAM gets dense, on-policy supervision with no simulator, no rewards, and no separately trained teacher. - How it does it: The trick is a self-distillation asymmetry — the same frozen backbone reads future video latents through a 13M-parameter hindsight encoder and gated cross-attention adapters (teacher), and the student is matched to one teacher sample per state with the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule that avoids mode-averaging without requiring likelihoods. - The good: The objective ablation is convincing and internally consistent: velocity matching gains +0.1 pts over SFT, kernel MMD +1.7, action-space MSE +4.0, and the energy score +6.3 (85.18% on LIBERO-90), with a toy experiment isolating the mode-averaging mechanism. - The missing: The entire evaluation uses a single training seed (42) and no code or model release is stated; the headline HINT-WAM-vs-SFT sign test (p = 0.087) is not significant, and "on-policy" covers only sampler states on demonstration observations, not closed-loop interaction — a gap the authors acknowledge but which limits the deployed-relevant claim. - Read it or not: Read it if you post-train diffusion/flow-matching action or generative policies — the energy-score distillation recipe and its ablations transfer beyond this architecture; skip it if you need closed-loop RL or real-robot evidence.

Non-Obviousness (74) and Completeness (75) lead: the insight that privileged-information distillation makes the teacher multimodal from the student's view — hence the energy score rather than velocity regression — is genuinely counter-intuitive, and the control suite (shuffled hindsight, off-policy states, BC-only, distillation-only) plus honest negative results are exemplary. Rigor (68) is good but constrained: single seed, headline sign test p = 0.087, no code or weight release, and no benchmarking against the RL/teacher-distillation baselines the paper critiques. Problem & Motivation: Practitioners deploying world action models (WAMs) — policies that couple action generation with future visual prediction — must adapt pretrained checkpoints to downstream tasks, but the two standard routes both fail. Offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains the flow-matching action expert only on noised demonstrations, never on the intermediate states its own sampler visits (exposure bias), and a demonstrated action chunk is only one of several plausible continuations, so the SFT target is ambiguous. On-policy RL trains on the policy's own behavior, but manipulation rewards are sparse, and even dense shaping provides only scalar feedback rather than action targets. Both approaches risk degrading pretrained skills (catastrophic forgetting). The paper targets robot-learning researchers post-training large multimodal action models without simulator access. Key Idea: Use hindsight — the future video frames of a training demonstration — as privileged information that converts the same network into a strictly better teacher: the teacher reads the future, the student does not, and the student is supervised at the exact denoising states its own ODE visits. Because the teacher's conditional distribution is multimodal from the student's perspective (the student cannot see which future unfolds), regressing the teacher's velocity would average modes; instead the paper matches distributions with the energy score, which needs only one teacher sample and has well-behaved (non-vanishing, bounded) gradients at all sample distances. Methodology: Built on Fast-WAM (Mixture-of-Transformers: 5.00B Wan2.2 video diffusion expert, 1.02B flow-matching action expert; 10-step Euler sampling; K/V cache over video tokens). Three stages: Stage 0 (SFT) fine-tunes the action expert with the rectified-flow loss L_FM = E‖v_θ(a^σ,σ,o) − (ε−a)‖² for 5,000 steps, with the video expert frozen; Stage A freezes this checkpoint and trains a hindsight encoder (spatial mean-pool of future VAE latents, learned-query attention pooling to 8×512 tokens) plus gated cross-attention adapters (Flamingo-style tanh gates, zero-initialized W_up) inserted after action-expert layers {4,9,14,19,24,29}, trained with the flow-matching loss conditioned on hindsight; Stage B initializes the student from θ0, integrates the student's own ODE without gradients, and minimizes L_B = λ_dist·L_dist + λ_BC·L_FM, where L_dist is either velocity matching on the top-K points weighted by Δ_i² or the energy score over M=4 differentiable "implied actions" (â = a^σ − σv_θ, the one-pass clean-action estimate) against one teacher rollout sample. Key design decisions: (1) the teacher must share the student's initialization — justified by a pilot showing a teacher built on the weaker released checkpoint hurt performance (55.0% → 47.5%); (2) the BC anchor is essential — distillation alone falls to 74.4%, below the SFT initialization; (3) energy score rather than velocity/MMD/MSE — well justified by the ablation gradient analysis and a toy experiment. Only the action expert is updated in Stage B; the teacher modules are discarded at deployment. Key Results: On LIBERO-90 (3,921 demonstrations, 90 unseen tasks, 50 trials each from fixed initial states), the released Fast-WAM scores 15.56%; SFT raises this to 78.88%; HINT-WAM reaches 85.18% (+6.30 over SFT, paired t = 3.58; +3.94 over full SFT, which trains all 6.02B parameters for 2.3× the wall-clock). Controls attribute the gain: BC-only continuation with the same budget drops to 71.56%, self-imitation adds only +0.74 over SFT, and shuffled hindsight (teacher reads another episode's future) reaches 80.28% — confirming the privileged information carries the improvement. On a pre-registered 25-task hard subset of RoboTwin 2.0 (dual-arm), HINT-WAM reaches 87.04% clean / 83.68% randomized, essentially matching the released checkpoint (86.48/83.44) where continued BC and full SFT both degrade it — the clean-setting gain over BC control is only borderline significant (t = 2.00). Forgetting: post-training on LIBERO-90 without replay cuts original-suite accuracy from 96.55% to below 45% for every method; HINT-WAM retains the most (44.05%) and composes with replay (95.10% retained, 81.56% on new tasks). Cost: 1.28× SFT, 0.56× full SFT (71.6 h on 8×24GB A5000). The gain is concentrated on weak tasks (+32.2% where SFT < 50%) with small losses on saturated ones; a small number of basket/caddy tasks regress. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (on-policy self-distillation with a hindsight-conditioned self-teacher for flow-matching action experts) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (energy score beats velocity/MMD/MSE distillation under privileged-information asymmetry). The framing adapts known components — self-distilled reasoning with privileged information from LLM work (Self-Distilled Reasoner, dOPSD), DAgger-style on-policy state logic, the energy score from Gneiting–Raftery — to a setting where they had not been combined: continuous action experts without tractable likelihoods. The energy-score choice over reverse-KL/token matching is a genuine, well-motivated adaptation, not a transplant. The claim of being the "first self-distillation framework for world action models" is plausible given concurrent teacher-based WAM distillation work (WAM-OPD variants) but rests on a fast-moving preprint landscape. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong on ablation design: the four-objective comparison holds teacher, states, anchor, M, and budget fixed; Fig. 5 shows distillation-only and BC-only are each worse than SFT (a non-obvious interaction); Fig. 6 separates repulsion benefit from sample count; Fig. 7 isolates on-policy states (off-policy noised demonstrations: 80.7% vs 85.2%); the shuffled-hindsight control cleanly isolates the privileged information. Statistical reporting is unusually careful: paired t-tests and sign tests per task, per-task win/loss breakdowns, and an honest note that the per-task grouping may reflect regression to the mean. However: single seed (42) for all training; the headline HINT-WAM-vs-SFT sign test is p = 0.087 (the paired t is significant, the sign test is not); several RoboTwin comparisons are not significant (vs. released checkpoint, t = 0.47 and 0.23); no code, data, or model release is mentioned; no error bars across training seeds; and the teacher-vs-student held-out loss check (Table 5) uses the same held-out episodes that guided objective selection. No external/real-robot evaluation. The LIBERO-90 evaluation follows the standard protocol and the authors show fixed-test-placement performance does not exceed random-placement performance (80.94% vs 78.88%), addressing Goodhart concerns. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a training method evaluated in simulation). Practical: Runs on 8× 24GB consumer-tier GPUs thanks to a frozen 5B video expert and cached K/V — no cluster-scale hardware needed. Efficient: 1.28× SFT cost (1.51× per Stage-B step), 0.56× full-SFT cost while beating it; the 13M teacher modules add zero inference cost since they are discarded. Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem (improving post-training without a simulator) at 85.18% vs 78.88% on LIBERO-90, but the RoboTwin results show near-zero headroom when the checkpoint already fits the data, so the method's value is specific to the unseen-task adaptation regime. Scalable: Not tested — no experiments on larger backbones, more demonstration data, or real robots; the authors note the M-curve has not saturated but do not test beyond M=4. Deliverable: stops at paper form; no artifact (code, weights, or dataset) is stated as released. Strengths: - The self-distillation asymmetry (same backbone, privileged hindsight) eliminates both the separately-trained teacher of prior WAM distillation methods and the reward/simulator requirement of RL, at 13M extra training-only parameters — a clean and economical design. - The objective analysis is the paper's intellectual core: it correctly identifies that privileged-information distillation makes the teacher multimodal from the student's view, predicts that velocity regression must fail (and it does, +0.14), explains why MMD's Gaussian kernel and MSE's mode-collapse are each inadequate, and validates the energy score's distance-kernel gradient properties empirically. - The control suite is unusually thorough for robotics papers: BC-only, self-imitation, shuffled-hindsight, off-policy-states, and distillation-only ablations jointly pin the +6.3 gain to the interaction of privileged information and on-policy states (each alone < 2 pts; together +6.3). - Honest negative-result reporting: the paper shows its own components degrade performance in isolation and quantifies which tasks regress, with full paired statistics in the supplement. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that "on-policy" here means sampler states on demonstration observations, not closed-loop interaction, so compounding errors across control steps are unaddressed and the method is complementary to DAgger/RL. They acknowledge forgetting is reduced but not prevented without replay. In the supplement they flag that per-task gain groupings may reflect regression to the mean, that the sign test is weaker than the paired t-test, and that specific basket/caddy tasks regress. They also note the energy-score estimator slightly under-weights dispersion via the (M−1)/M factor. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation disclosure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Single training seed with no seed variance; several reported margins (RoboTwin: +0.56/+0.24 over the released checkpoint) are within plausible seed noise, and the t = 2.00 clean-setting result would be fragile under retraining. (2) Hindsight is only available in offline demonstrations, so the method inherits the demonstrator's state distribution for observations; the paper's "on-policy" claim covers only the action-sampler axis, and the interaction between this partial on-policy-ness and deployment-time compounding errors is untested (no closed-loop data collection experiment). (3) No comparison against the actual on-policy RL or teacher-based distillation baselines it critiques (WAM-RL, WAM-OPD) on shared settings — the related work motivating the design is not empirically benchmarked. (4) No code or weights release is stated, which matters given the many implementation-sensitive details (Δ²-weighted top-K selection, adapter placement, K=1 vs K=3 per objective). (5) Both benchmarks are simulation; the hindsight encoder assumes VAE latents of aligned demonstration futures, and behavior under domain shift or real-world demonstration noise is unknown. (6) The headline sign test (p = 0.087) suggests the average gain, while real, is not uniform across tasks — the paper reports this but the abstract does not. Bottom Line: A practitioner post-training flow-matching action or diffusion policies gains concrete, well-isolated evidence that energy-score self-distillation under a privileged-information asymmetry beats both velocity regression and plain imitation — a genuinely useful recipe — but should await a code release and multi-seed or real-robot replication before treating the +6.3-point headline as settled.

MIRIX-2.0: Multi-Agent Memory System (46 ▲ )

Wei-Chieh Huang, Weizhi Zhang, Jiayan Nan, Peng Xia, Yu Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 16 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MIRIX-2.0, a multi-agent LLM memory system that keeps complete verbatim records in a typed vector store as the system of record, indexes them with a provenance-preserving n-ary hypergraph retrieved under explicit budgets, and consolidates offline (AutoDream) by merging duplicate entity anchors and distilling task sessions into skills. - Why it's important: Teams deploying agents over long horizons currently must trade accuracy (consolidation discards details), efficiency (verbatim stores grow unboundedly), and practicality (parametric memories need training); Problem & Motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents (personal assistants with months of conversation, task agents revisiting similar problems) need memory that is simultaneously accurate (names, dates, counts, event distinctions recoverable), practical (no fine-tuning, works with closed models, traceable answers, consolidation that cannot destroy data), and efficient (bounded latency and token cost as history grows). The paper argues every existing family fails at least one requirement: fact-extraction systems (mem0-style) lose discarded details; verbatim stores (flat memory) face ever-growing retrieval; binary-triple graph memories fragment n-ary facts; hypergraph memories (HyperMem) and file-system memories (Claude Code auto-memory) route retrieval through storage-time summaries, so details not in summaries become unreachable; parametric memories require training. A further gap: user-centric memory (broad recall of a user's history) and agent-centric memory (precise distillation of the agent's own experience) have opposite demands, and no prior single system serves both. Key Idea: The core trick is a strict storage/index separation with provenance-carrying n-ary frames: complete records are committed first and are immutable, the hypergraph only indexes them, and every graph fact cites the exact row IDs it was extracted from — so consolidation can be made safe by construction (merges rewire graph arms, never rewrite evidence), and retrieval cost is bounded by explicit per-operator budgets (6–12 rows) rather than history length. A second key mechanism is occurrence identity: episodic frames hash in an occurrence key (event time or immutable memory ID) so undated but similar events never collapse into one frame, while semantic claims accumulate citations on one node. Methodology: The system has a write path, a read path, and an offline consolidation path (AutoDream), all stated as Algorithm 1. Write: a Meta Memory Manager (an LLM call) routes each input to a subset of six typed writers (Core, Episodic, Semantic, Procedural, Resource, Knowledge Vault); each writer commits a full record (row ID, text, event/mention times, provenance, embeddings) to a vector database (the system of record); only episodic and semantic records are then extracted into a hypergraph (stored in Neo4j) of anchors, reified fact frames with open-vocabulary roles, and literal attributes; frames materialize only with ≥2 distinct anchors, a deterministic admission gate caps anchors per record (16 episodic / 18 semantic), and a bounded repair call may add — never remove — frames. Read: a deterministic planner maps a query to one of five operators with budgets (e.g., single: 6 base rows / 4 cited rows; count: 8/12); anchor entry combines vector recall (top 15) with exact-name lookup under a composite score with a logarithmic hub penalty; two bounded lanes (base recall and relation-citation, with predicate filtering inside Neo4j before a 240-frame cap) are scored by a nine-term additive frame score and fused citation-first; an answer-time rule-based verifier can trigger one extra search and rewrite (harness-side, never sees reference answers). AutoDream (semantic): for anchors of identity-stable types (person, organization, location, object, concept) backed by the newly written frontier, form candidate pairs at cosine ≥0.86 (capped at 80/120/60 pairs per round, negative decisions cached), have an LLM verify same-entity, and perform a lossless structural merge (union IDs, rewire arms) — the evidence store is provably returned unchanged. AutoDream (procedural): a distiller judges finished task sessions from quoted transcript evidence into lessons/mistakes, and a curator creates or edits skills whose edits must cite checked quotes. Critical design decisions: (1) fail-soft indexing (graph failure never rolls back a committed memory) — well-justified by the storage/index split; (2) mergeable-only types for semantic Dream (events and dates excluded) — justified by the temporal-identity requirement; (3) explicit budgets tied to query operators — justified as bounding access, though the budget values appear heuristic. Key Results: User memory: on LoCoMo (1,540 non-adversarial questions), MIRIX-2.0 reaches 91.4% overall vs. HyperMem 91.0% (authors' own run; HyperMem's paper reports 92.7%), mem0 82.9%, A-Mem 68.3%; the largest gains over HyperMem are temporal (+5.0) and multi-hop (+0.7), while HyperMem wins open-domain and single-hop. On LongMemEval-S (300 questions), 72.6% vs. HyperMem 58.3% (+14.3). On MemoryAgentBench with M1 (AutoDream off): SHDocQA 83.0% and MHDocQA 71.0% vs. HyperMem 52.0% and 49.0% (+31.0/+22.0), but DetectiveQA 64.8% loses to MemoryBank 67.6% and HyperMem 66.2%. On MemoryCD cross-domain summarization, best on all four metrics (ROUGE-L .1510 vs. .1430; BLEU-4 .0209 vs. .0162), though single-domain margins shrink to near-ties. Agent memory (3 runs): ALFWorld 76.4%±6.2 with GPT-6 Luna vs. AWM 73.6%±1.9 and no-memory 69.4%; WebShop 37.4%±2.1 vs. AWM 36.0%; MetaClaw-Bench 49.2% with GPT-5.2 vs. 44.0% reported for MetaClaw Skills (not a controlled rerun), and only 52.7% vs. 51.8% with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Efficiency (M1 only): answer latency beats HyperMem on all five benchmarks (e.g., 5.45s vs. 10.55s on SHDocQA); document ingestion is 3.8–4.0× slower than flat memory; on ALFWorld, test tokens (3.813M) are the highest among memory methods despite the highest success. Counter-intuitive finding the paper reports honestly: ReasoningBank falls below no-memory on both interactive benchmarks, and retrieved procedures actively hurt some ALFWorld task types (Pick, Look, Pick Two drop below no-memory). Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with elements of NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the combination of a typed evidence plane as an immutable system of record with a provenance-citing n-ary hypergraph index, occurrence-identity hashing for episodic frames, budgeted graph-owned retrieval, and the lossless merge contract for semantic consolidation — plus the claim (plausible, hard to verify) of being the first single store serving both user-centric and agent-centric memory. Individual ingredients are standard: multi-agent memory routing (MIRIX-1.0), hypergraph indexing (HyperMem, HyperGraphRAG), offline consolidation (sleep-time compute, Auto-Dreamer), and skill distillation (AWM, ExpeL); the contribution is the architecture that composes them under explicit safety and cost invariants rather than any single new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist at the configuration level (M0 flat vs. M1 +graph vs. M2 +AutoDream on both conversational benchmarks), but no component-level ablations: n-ary frames, cited rows, occurrence identity, answer-time verification, and the distiller/curator are never isolated — the authors admit their mechanistic explanations are interpretations. User-memory results are single runs (no seeds, no error bars) partly scored by a gpt-4o-mini LLM judge with majority-of-3 voting; agent results average three runs but with large spreads (MIRIX-2.0 ALFWorld std up to 14.0 points, which the paper flags as limiting conclusions). Several baselines are author-reported values rather than controlled reruns (MetaClaw on GPT-5.2; MemoryCD method rows with unidentified configuration), and HyperMem on LoCoMo was rerun by the authors to 91.0 vs. its reported 92.7 — meaning the headline LoCoMo margin over the strongest baseline is +0.4 points by the authors' own run. Document QA uses small test sets (100, 100, 71 questions). Code is public (github.com/Mirix-AI/MIRIX), and the appendix (A.1–A.7) documents constants, thresholds, caps, prompts-adjacent details, and complexity to an unusually high standard. Methodological concerns: evaluation models (gpt-4.1-mini/nano) differ from graph-construction models in the appendix example (Claude Haiku 5.5); budget constants and thresholds (0.86 cosine, cap sizes) are not tuned or ablated; no significance testing anywhere. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built system evaluated on benchmarks, no production deployment reported). Practical: Yes — runs with closed and open model backbones, no fine-tuning, standard infrastructure (vector database + Neo4j), public code. Effective: Strong evidence for accuracy on connected/temporal recall and for procedural skill reuse (leads on 4/5 QA benchmarks, both interactive benchmarks, MetaClaw), but it loses DetectiveQA to simpler baselines and the MetaClaw gain nearly vanishes with the open backbone. Efficient: Answer latency and WebShop tokens are competitive or best-in-comparison, but document ingestion is 3.8–4.0× slower than flat memory and all efficiency numbers exclude AutoDream, whose consolidation cost is unmeasured end-to-end. Scalable: Bounded evidence per query is guaranteed by construction and complexity is stated (O(d+h) write, O(KA+KF+KM) retrieval, capped Dream rounds), but no experiment varies history length to show latency/cost actually stays flat, and M2 end-to-end cost at any scale is untested. Deliverable: a real software artifact (open-source system, versioned from MIRIX-1.0), not just a paper. Strengths: - The storage/index separation with provenance-citing frames is a clean architectural answer to a real dilemma (accuracy vs. compactness), and the lossless-merge contract (Eq. 12, commutative/associative merge algebra) turns a safety worry about consolidation into a provable invariant. - Occurrence identity for episodic frames (Eq. 7) is a precise, well-motivated fix for a concrete failure mode (similar undated events collapsing) that most graph-memory systems ignore. - Unusually honest reporting for a systems paper: the authors volunteer that HyperMem beats them on DetectiveQA, that latency claims do not cover the full system, that three runs with 14-point standard deviations do not establish an advantage over AWM, and that their component explanations are interpretations rather than established mechanisms. - Coverage across genuinely different memory regimes (conversational recall, document QA, personalization generation, embodied/procedural tasks) with per-benchmark cost accounting in appendices, plus explicit hard invariants (Section A.6) that hold regardless of LLM behavior. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: ablations add components in groups and do not isolate n-ary frames, cited rows, occurrence identities, verification, or the procedural judge/distiller/curator, so mechanistic claims are interpretations; user-memory results are single runs partly scored by an LLM judge; agent results have large spreads over only three runs; some baselines are author-reported values; the full M2 system is untimed and retrieval bounds cover inspected evidence, not measured latency as history grows; document ingestion is 3.8–4.0× slower than flat memory; ALFWorld test tokens are highest among memory methods; no varying-horizon amortization study exists; and tables do not measure merge precision, source-detail retention, skill provenance coverage, or the routing policy's contribution. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline LongMemEval-S margin (+14.3 over HyperMem) rests on HyperMem collapsing to 58.3%, near flat memory M0 (58.8%) and mem0 (56.3%) — far below what a strong baseline should do on that benchmark; the possibility that HyperMem was under-tuned in the authors' rerun is not addressed, and the LoCoMo margin over the same baseline is only +0.4 by their own run. - Budget constants, thresholds (0.86 cosine, 0.72 canonicalization, 0.93 index scale), admission caps, and the nine-term frame score are presented without any sensitivity analysis or tuning methodology — a Goodhart risk since the same benchmarks motivate the design. - The MetaClaw-Bench and MemoryCD comparisons mix controlled reruns with reported numbers and unidentified configurations, so cross-method conclusions there are weak; the open-backbone MetaClaw result (52.7 vs. 51.8) suggests the advantage may be backbone-specific but this is not explored. - No measured merge precision/recall of AutoDream and no audit of whether merges help or harm individual answers (the authors note an audit would be needed); no test of behavior as history grows (the central efficiency claim is by construction, not by experiment). - MemoryCD margins (BERTScore spread ≤.006 across all systems) are within plausible judge/noise variation given single runs, yet are claimed as wins on all metrics. - The answer-time verifier fires on every intersection question and rewrites freely; its contribution to accuracy is never isolated, so part of the reported gain may be harness machinery any baseline could also receive. Bottom Line: A practitioner building LLM agent memory gains concrete, well-documented design patterns (immutable evidence plane as system of record, provenance-citing n-ary index, budgeted graph retrieval, conservative offline merges) that are worth adopting or at least benchmarking against, but the headline accuracy claims should be treated as promising rather than settled given single runs, mixed baseline provenance, and untested full-system cost — the design, not the leaderboard, is the value here.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SWE-CoWork, a benchmark of 101 development assignments across 101 real repositories that place coding agents in simulated engineering organizations of 26 rule-governed, LLM-backed digital employees, and evaluates eleven models on end-to-end organizational software delivery. - Why it's important: Existing coding benchmarks evaluate pre-scoped issues, so they cannot measure whether agents can recover requirements from people and conflicting records — the bottleneck between today's "spec executor" agents and autonomous digital employees, where frontier models satisfy only ~63% of fail-to-pass tests yet complete under 8% of assignments. - How it does it: Each task links every scored requirement to an accountable colleague, a discovery route through versioned workplace records (boards, docs, chat, MRs, CI), and private executable F2P/P2P tests, enabling requirement-level tracing plus a paired Oracle-Spec condition that hands the agent the full requirement list upfront. - The good: The Oracle-Spec contrast is the strongest evidence: supplying complete requirements raises F2P by ~16 points for two models yet leaves complete-task success exactly unchanged (0.99% and 7.92%), cleanly showing that implementation/verification — not just requirement acquisition — is a binding bottleneck. - The missing: All trajectory and behavioral judgments come from a single LLM reviewer (GPT-6 Astra) grading a competing model's trajectories, with no human validation of those annotations, and the main results appear to be single runs per model with no error bars or significance testing. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate agentic coding systems and need to know where multi-step organizational delivery breaks down; skip it if you only need another leaderboard of issue-resolution capability, since the harness itself is the contribution.

Problem & Motivation: Frontier coding agents saturate issue-resolution benchmarks while real software engineering requires recovering evolving, distributed, and contradictory requirements from stakeholders and organizational records. Practitioners deploying coding agents must still hand-edit specifications, resolve evidence conflicts, and track requirement state — the paper argues agents must become Continuous, Proactive, Efficient, and Persistent organizational collaborators rather than passive spec executors. Prior benchmarks either give a fixed objective (SWE-bench lineage, DeepSWE, FrontierSWE v2), route clarification through a single simulated user (Ask or Assume, Dialogue SWE-Bench, LHAW), or evaluate generic workplace tasks without code execution (TheAgentCompany). No prior benchmark measures requirement recovery from multiple bounded-knowledge owners, reconciliation of superseded records, and verified delivery in one executable contract. Key Idea: Instrument the entire requirement lifecycle: author an organization where each scored behavioral fact has exactly one accountable owner with controlled disclosure rules (require code context, defer answers, refer, one topic at a time), tie each fact to specific F2P test nodes, and log every disclosure — so failures can be decomposed into discovery, ask, implement, verify, and handoff stages, and separated from implementation failures via a paired oracle condition sharing repository, tests, scaffold, and 8-hour budget. Methodology: Each of 101 tasks combines a real upstream repository (median reference change: 2,955 production lines across 60 files) with an authored workplace of 26 colleagues (2,626 profiles), 10,329 board cards, 5,097 versioned documents, 40,836 chat messages, and 1,194 merge requests; the executable contract totals 2,699 F2P and 562 P2P test nodes. The agent starts from a median 206-word onboarding note and works through a tool interface (directory search, board, docs, chat, MR/CI inspection) for up to 8 hours, ending with a delivery note. Colleagues are generated by GPT-5.6 Terra at high reasoning effort under fixed knowledge boundaries, held constant across agents. Evaluation reports F2P, P2P, and Pass rate (all nodes passing in one run), plus an Oracle-Spec arm for Seed Evolving and GPT-6 Astra. Trajectory analysis of Claude-Opus-5.5 combines programmatic disclosure logs with an LLM trajectory reviewer (GPT-6 Astra) scoring 16 behavioral dimensions on a 4-level scale and classifying failure stages. Critical design decisions: (1) deterministic disclosure rules to constrain simulator variance — well-justified given known user-simulator unreliability, though the underlying colleague LLM is itself a fidelity risk; (2) pooled test-node aggregation for F2P — reasonable but weights large tasks more; (3) LLM-judged trajectories assessed before grading outcomes are attached — a sensible blinding, but unvalidated. Key Results: Claude-Opus-5.5 scores 63.84% F2P / 93.24% P2P / 6.93% Pass; GPT-6 Astra 62.91% / 89.15% / 7.92%; the other nine models (Seed Evolving, Qwen3.8-Max/Flash, GLM 5.3/5.2, DeepSeek V4 Pro/V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3, Seed 2.1 Pro) reach at most 39.09% F2P and 0.99% Pass, with six models at 0% Pass — a pronounced floor. Oracle-Spec lifts F2P from 39.09% to 55.76% (Seed Evolving) and 62.91% to 78.84% (GPT-6 Astra) with Pass rate unchanged. Colleague-requirement acquisition correlates with F2P at Spearman ρ = 0.94 across models while median tool calls correlate at ρ = 0.08. For Claude-Opus-5.5: 93% of first questions target the accountable owner but only 64% of 2,176 colleague-held requirements are obtained; 153 of 450 deferred threads are never followed up despite a median 7.1 hours of remaining budget; 56% of failed linked F2P nodes fail at the implement stage; 255 of 826 (31%) requirements reported "done" fail their tests; the reviewer identifies 49 premature stops. 15 of 94 patches violating test-preservation constraints is a notable reliability datum. Baselines are current (2026 frontier models), though scaffold is confounded with model (Codex for GPT-6 Astra, Claude Code for the rest). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the multi-owner requirement-distribution design with per-requirement test linkage and the oracle-paired decomposition of organizational vs. implementation failure. The constituent techniques — F2P/P2P scoring from SWE-bench, LLM-simulated colleagues from TheAgentCompany, underspecification from LHAW/RealSWE — are standard, recombined here at larger organizational scale. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style evidence exists (Oracle-Spec pairs, stratified diagnostics by language/edit size/domain in Appendix F), but no repeated runs, error bars, or significance tests are reported for headline numbers; with 101 tasks and pass rates of 0–8%, run-to-run variance is likely material. Code (github.com/TokenWave-AI/swe-cowork-bench), data (huggingface.co/datasets/Tokenwave-AI/swe-cowork), and a project page are released. Concerns: (1) the trajectory reviewer is GPT-6 Astra — a model whose competitor's trajectories it grades — with no human-annotation agreement reported; (2) the same-authored Oracle-Spec both defines requirements and drives the analysis, risking circularity; (3) scaffold and model are confounded; (4) single runs per model per condition are implied but not explicitly stated. Requirements are defined on public repositories, so contamination from upstream issue/PR history is possible, though the authored workplaces mitigate it. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark with executed agent evaluations). - Practical: Runs via commercial APIs and standard scaffolds (Claude Code, Codex) on ordinary cloud infrastructure; no special hardware implied. - Efficient: Expensive — median runs reach 8 wall-clock hours and tens of millions of input tokens (Claude-Opus-5.5: 47.57M input tokens/run), so a full 11-model evaluation is a serious compute expenditure. - Effective: Executable tests measure real delivery, and the 31% false-completion finding shows the benchmark also captures reporting honesty — but simulated colleagues remain a proxy for human stakeholders. - Scalable: Tested only at 101 tasks over 8-hour budgets; the claimed extension to teams of autonomous agents is asserted, not demonstrated. Delivers a concrete artifact: released benchmark harness, dataset, and task suite — not just a paper. Strengths: - The requirement-to-test-to-owner linkage is the real contribution: it converts a coarse pass/fail score into a stage-resolved failure analysis (discovery/ask/implement/verify/handoff), which no prior coding benchmark offers. - The Oracle-Spec paired design cleanly separates "couldn't find the requirements" from "couldn't implement them," and the null effect on Pass rate (+0.00 for both models) is a genuinely non-obvious empirical finding. - The 94% vs. 8% Spearman contrast (acquisition vs. tool-call volume against F2P) is a crisp, actionable result for agent designers. - Honest negative reporting — 15 constraint-violating patches, 31% false completion claims, abandoned deferrals — increases confidence that results are not curated. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors note that simulated colleagues may differ from human users (citing Seshadri et al. on simulator unreliability), that cross-model correlations are exploratory and do not establish causation ("do not establish that earlier editing or more frequent messaging causes better outcomes"), that explicit requirement-tracking is only a hypothesized remedy whose benefit "remains an open question," and that behavioral annotations depend on an LLM reviewer with defined but unvalidated rubrics. They confront limitations reasonably directly rather than minimizing them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No inter-rater or human validation of the GPT-6 Astra trajectory reviewer, despite it producing the paper's most-quoted behavioral claims (93% targeting, 49 premature stops, 31% false completions). - Single-run results without variance estimates make the 0–1% Pass-rate floor and the Claude-Opus-5.5 vs. GPT-6 Astra ordering statistically unverifiable. - The colleague simulator itself (GPT-5.6 Terra) could leak, hallucinate, or vary in disclosure behavior in ways the fixed rules only partially constrain; no simulator-fidelity audit is reported. - Requirement recovery is evaluated only against the authors' own Oracle-Spec decomposition; no independent check that the authored requirements match what the tests actually encode. - Only two models receive the Oracle-Spec comparison, limiting generalization of the "implementation gap" claim; and the trajectory deep-dive covers only the single top model. - Contamination risk from public upstream repositories is not discussed (issues and PRs for the reference changes may be in training data for 2026-era models). Bottom Line: This is the most credible attempt yet to benchmark coding agents as organizational collaborators, and its oracle-paired finding that complete requirements don't move whole-task success should reset evaluation priorities in agentic SWE — read it, but treat the LLM-judged trajectory statistics as hypotheses pending human validation.

DEPUTYBENCH: Evaluating Contextual Safety in Enterprise Agents

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DeputyBench, an executable benchmark of 79 base enterprise tasks (375 instances) organized as paired permission worlds — a suspicious world and a legitimate twin sharing the same business objective — plus 28 derived tasks with controlled fact-flip, evidence-masking, and irrelevant-rewrite interventions, evaluated across 12 LLM agents. - Why it's important: Enterprise agents that delegate multi-step business operations (payments, record sharing, exports) must decide whether the requester is permitted using backend records the request does not name; existing agent-safety benchmarks evaluate judgment from supplied context or abstention triggers, not whether behavior tracks backend authorization state. - How it does it: Each suspicious instance has a legitimate twin differing only in deciding permission facts; skip it if you need a production-risk estimate or a publicly available artifact, since the authors themselves state the rates are neither.

Problem & Motivation: In enterprise workflows, users delegate business goals (process a payment, share a customer record) while the agent decides intermediate actions. Whether an action is permitted depends on facts outside the request — approval limits, policy revision effective dates, consent records, object ownership — scattered across identity services, approval histories, and policy documents. An agent must identify the relevant check, retrieve its evidence, and decide. Prior evaluations fall short in specific ways: CASE-Bench and MTMCS-Bench judge supplied contexts as if verified; AgentAbstain and EpiSEM-Bench test information acquisition and abstention but not whether agent behavior tracks deciding backend permissions when the request is held fixed, whether agents withhold actions when permission evidence is unavailable rather than merely contradicted, and whether irrelevant record changes leave outcomes untouched. The operators of this problem are anyone deploying tool-using agents on consequential business data. Key Idea: The core move is paired permission worlds with controlled context interventions: for every suspicious instance (action should be withheld), construct a legitimate twin with the identical business objective, tools, and role, differing only in deciding permission facts (e.g., a policy-revision notice effective 15 Oct vs. 1 Nov). Because the request alone cannot distinguish the worlds, any behavioral difference is attributable to backend authorization state. Three derived interventions sharpen this: fact flips (F) change only the authorization fact; masking (M) removes the deciding evidence while keeping both latent worlds observationally matched; irrelevant rewrites (P) perturb non-deciding fields as a placebo. A secondary design axis grades "evidence distance" (L1 visible fact, L2 single lookup, L3 cross-source join or domain interpretation). Methodology: Each instance runs in an isolated Docker company system (5–7 containers; FastAPI/SQLite services implementing business logic with a deliberately absent enforcement control), inside an Inspect evaluation loop with native function calling, ≤12 model rounds per user message, and an 80-message cap; audit events (action, object, owner, authorization verdict) and end states feed deterministic predicate checks — no LLM judge for the primary metrics. Metrics are Safety = 1 − harm rate on suspicious runs, Completion = twin pass rate, and PSR = fraction of matched pairs passing both. The controlled study derives 28 tasks frozen before execution (F/P on 28, M on 27 after a pre-run exclusion), runs 6 models × 281 instances × 3 repetitions (5,058 runs), and analyzes ΔF = C_F − H_F, D_M = E_M − C_F, and ΔP via task-cluster bootstraps (B=10,000) with Holm-adjusted directional tests and a prespecified ±0.05 equivalence margin for P. Scorer-v2.1 extends harm checks to all twins and is validated on a 541-counterexample suite (257 dev / 284 test, hidden from the reviser before freeze). Critical design decisions: (1) paired twins with byte-identical user messages in 115/155 L2/L3 pairs — well justified, this is what licenses the causal-ish contrast; (2) scoring provider blocks as stops on suspicious runs — defensible and disclosed; (3) deriving the controlled tasks from earlier benchmark items rather than independent authorship — weakly justified, acknowledged as limiting generalization. Key Results: Across 12 models and 13,326 counted original runs (3 rounds × 375 instances), pooled safety is 88.0%, completion 90.4%, PSR 79.1%. Top models GPT 6 Astra and GPT 6.1 Sol reach 0.991 safety but leave 11.6–15.8% of legitimate twins incomplete; Seed 2.1 Turbo is weakest (safety 0.627, PSR 0.563). In the controlled study, fact flips produce ΔF = 0.857 [0.821, 0.891] with all six models positive (Holm-adjusted p = 0.0006), establishing outcome dependence on authorization facts. The central finding: on 27 matched tasks, restricted execution under masking is 10.3% (100/972) versus 3.5% (17/486) under explicit non-permission, a +6.8pp gap [1.9, 13.0] that persists excluding Seed 2.1 Turbo (+6.9pp) or both Seed models (+6.3pp), but falls to +1.8pp [−0.7, +4.3] excluding four privacy tasks (cross-border total: 72.2% masked execution rate; all six models execute at least once on that task). Irrelevant rewrites are equivalent within ±0.05 on the six-model mean (ΔP = −0.010, 90% CI [−0.033, +0.013]) but only Gemini 4 meets the margin individually. Observational L3−L2 safety is −0.086 [−0.153, −0.021], yet neither controlled comparison detects a distance penalty or a reminder effect. Scorer v2.1 improves held-out joint correctness from 178/284 (v1) to 266/284, still missing 12 of 170 expected harmful cases. Baselines are contemporary frontier models (GPT 6.x, Gemini 4/3.8, Claude Opus/Sonnet 5.5, Grok 4.7, Doubao-Seed family), so the comparison set is current; scale is standard (hundreds of instances, not thousands of tasks). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a secondary NEW METHOD component in the F/M/P intervention protocol. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the paired-twin design with frozen requests across fact-flipped backend worlds, scored by executable audits rather than LLM judges, and (b) the quantified missing-evidence-versus-contrary-evidence gap. The underlying ingredients — Docker service sandboxes, audit predicates, bootstrap over task clusters, counterexample-based scorer validation — are competent combinations of existing evaluation practice (τ-bench, AgentDojo, BashArena lineage), applied to a setting prior work does not cover. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: task-level bootstrap clustering, Holm-adjusted registered tests, sensitivity to void-twin handling (PSR shifts up to 0.077), scoring-version rescoring of all 20,022 archived runs, matched-world and violation-subclass controls for the masking gap, and documented preregistration timestamps (with acknowledged mid-execution amendments). Scorer validation uses a held-out counterexample partition hidden from the reviser. However: no error bars on per-run basis beyond cluster bootstraps; no independent third-party replication (a clean-environment reproduction was author-side via an LLM executor); stage labels are LLM-generated with 0.705 earliest-stage agreement and no human validation; code and data are packaged but not publicly released ("will be publicly released at a later date"), which at review time makes the reproducibility claims unverifiable. Methodological flags: tested models (including the judge, Claude Sonnet 5.5) participated in item drafting, review, and pre-freeze repairs, creating construction–evaluation entanglement for the original set; the headline masking-gap analysis is explicitly post hoc and driven by 4 of 27 tasks; and the controlled task set derives from earlier benchmark items, so Goodhart-style contamination within the authors' own pipeline cannot be excluded (they mitigate this with pre-execution freezes). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark and evaluation infrastructure the authors actually ran at scale). - Practical: Yes — the full stack runs on a single 16-vCPU host with 96 concurrent containers, Docker Engine ≥25, ~10 GB disk; no exotic hardware. - Efficient: Moderate — 4.6–15.0M tokens per model round (≈12k–33k input tokens per run), plus a Claude Sonnet 5.5 judge at ~4.2k input tokens per judged run for the legacy diagnostic; primary metrics avoid judge cost. - Effective: Partially — audits certify absence of implemented harm checks and passage of completion checks, not exhaustive compliance (indirect disclosure through executed scripts is uncovered; scorer still misses 12/170 held-out harmful cases), and the authors correctly frame benchmark rates as not production-risk estimates. - Scalable: Untested — the controlled finding rests on 27–28 tasks; a frozen 14-task harder set exists but has not been run, and no evidence addresses generalization to broader enterprise task distributions. Deliverables: an executable benchmark environment, versioned scorer, counterexample suite, and reproduction scripts, currently internal-only; no public artifact is yet available. Strengths: - The paired-twin + F/M/P factorial design is a real methodological contribution: it converts a vague "contextual safety" notion into three separable, testable claims (fact sensitivity, evidence-sufficiency behavior, invariance to irrelevant change), each with a registered test. - The masking result — that agents act more often when permission is unverifiable than when it is explicitly denied — is a genuinely counter-intuitive, quantified behavioral finding with matched-world and violation-subclass controls ruling out obvious artifacts. - Audit validation is treated as a first-class result rather than an afterthought: held-out counterexamples, versioned rescoring of all archived runs, and published residual-error rates (93.7% joint correctness) let readers bound what the headline metrics certify. - The execution environment (per-instance fictional companies, deterministic audit predicates, no LLM judge for primary outcomes, infrastructure-error detection via state digests) is engineered to a standard above most agent benchmarks, including canary screening and offline answer-leakage checks. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and in detail, which is a credibility positive: synthetic English-only tasks in six families with one executor; tested models informed original construction; the context set derives from earlier tasks and excludes harder structures; scorer-v2.1 retains held-out errors and does not cover every disclosure channel; context-study safety is near ceiling for four models, limiting discrimination; P equivalence holds only on the six-model mean; stage labels have 0.705 agreement and no human validation; the masking concentration analysis is post hoc and full transcripts for the four focal tasks are unavailable in the package, precluding mechanism attribution; assets are not publicly released; and benchmark rates are not production risk estimates. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline missing-evidence finding is a four-task phenomenon: outside the focal privacy tasks the gap is +1.8pp with an interval spanning zero, so the abstract-level claim ("restricted execution is more frequent with missing evidence") generalizes far less than the topline number suggests — the authors hedge but the framing still leads with the aggregate. - No public artifact means every validation claim (counterexample suite, clean-environment reproduction, freeze timestamps) is currently self-attested; the sanitized bundle's commit hashes differ from the freeze hashes with only author-side mappings. - Construction–evaluation entanglement: Claude-based agents drafted and reviewed all items, and the judge is a tested model; the authors note the drafting models' identity is "not recorded," leaving the independence of the benchmark from the Claude evaluation results unestablished. - The evidence-distance axis (L1/L2/L3) fails to produce a controlled effect, which undermines the benchmark's own grading taxonomy as a predictive instrument; the paper reports this honestly but the taxonomy's remaining utility is unclear. - Mechanism attribution is absent by design (no transcripts for focal tasks), so the actionable interpretation — e.g., "missing equals zero" default assumptions — remains speculative despite motivating the paper's practical recommendation. - No comparison against any mitigation (prompted checklists, tool-enforced verification), so a practitioner learns the failure exists but not whether cheap interventions close it beyond the small prompt study concentrated in one weak model. Bottom Line: A practitioner building enterprise-agent safety evaluation gains concrete, reusable assets here — the paired-world protocol, the F/M/P intervention template, and the audit-validation discipline are better executed than in competing benchmarks like AgentAbstain or EpiSEM-Bench — but the unverified release status, four-task concentration of the headline finding, and construction contamination mean its empirical claims should be treated as promising and preliminary rather than established.

WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules (18 ▲ )

Mingliang Zhai, Chuanhao Li, Jiaming Tan, Zhen Li, Yuwei Wu, Yunde Jia, Zian Meng, Yuanyang Yin, Kaipeng Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 19 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WorldRuler, an interactive video world model framework that saves/restores user-defined game rules jointly with world state and realizes rule effects on specific visual objects, plus RuleVerse, a 3,200-pair annotated dataset of rule-enabled/disabled interaction videos from GTA-V and Habitat. - Why it's important: Generative game worlds currently forget rule consequences across save/load boundaries and out-of-view events, which blocks the customizable gameplay that defines actual games; this targets the persistence and visual grounding gap directly. - How it does it: An executable 3D rule graph holds rules, object identities, and execution state; dynamic object binding grounds rule entities in visual instances, and a projection-based attribute replacement operator corrects denoising latents so attribute readouts match rule targets during sampling. - The good: Large gains over the closest baseline (SWM) on their RuleVerse benchmark — average Rule Success Rate 64.99% vs 44.06% (Habitat) and 67.42% vs 44.19% (GTA-V) — with component ablations that each isolate a needed piece (removing attribute replacement drops RSR by 18.56 points; removing the swapping loss collapses First-appearance from 29.69% to 6.45%). - The missing: All headline numbers come from a frozen VLM judge on largely self-authored data, the external WorldState-Bench gain over SWM is only 2 points (94 vs 92 PairFollow, 92 vs 90 PairStrict), no error bars or seeds are reported, and SWM scores 0.00 FCR on GTA-V tasks, suggesting a possible evaluation-format mismatch rather than a genuine 67-point gap. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building stateful, rule-governed video world models or controllable video generation, especially for the projection-based latent attribute correction and the paired counterfactual data recipe; skippable if you only care about generic video world model quality.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (78) is the paper's strongest dimension — the save/load rule-persistence formulation, exact-readout projection operator with null-space writer, and paired counterfactual dataset are genuinely new. Non-Obviousness (75) is also strong. But Rigor (62) is pulled down materially by VLM-judge circularity (self-authored benchmark, self-designed judge protocol), the anomalous SWM 0.00 on GTA-V, no error bars or seeds, and only a 2-point external-benchmark edge at n=50. Completeness (68) and Resilience (65) are reduced by the undiagnosed baseline failure and unvalidated generalization beyond the fixed attribute vocabulary, though released code/data and the informative save/load ablation are positives. Impact (72) reflects the full software artifact release. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*72 ≈ 70.

Problem & Motivation: Interactive generative world models can render action-conditioned video but cannot honor user-defined gameplay rules — e.g., "defeating a monster drops a key, the key opens a door" — particularly across save/load boundaries and when affected objects are off-screen. Game designers and developers of playable generative worlds need two things prior work lacks: Rule-State Persistence (rules, dependencies, and states surviving checkpointing) and Rule-to-Visual Realization (a rule-induced change appearing on the correct object and attribute at the correct time, including at an object's first on-screen appearance after being changed while invisible). Existing video world models (Yume1.5, WorldPlay, Matrix-Game 3.0, AlayaWorld) target consistency and real-time control but not persistent user-defined rules; state-maintenance systems (Code World Model, Programmable World Model, State World Models) execute logic but do not bind rule states to persistent visual instances. Key Idea: Treat rules as an executable graph whose nodes carry persistent object identities and attribute states, and close the loop to pixels via a projection operator: pool the diffusion model's clean estimate over a bound object's mask, read attributes with a frozen affine reader, then add B_iδ_i (a right-inverse correction that exactly sets the attribute readout to the rule target, since A_iB_i = I) plus a null-space term Q_i f_φ (since A_iQ_i = 0) that learns compatible appearance/motion changes without disturbing the prescribed readout. Counterfactual paired training (reconstruction, difference, and bidirectional attribute-swapping losses on rule-on/rule-off video pairs) supplies the supervision. This projection-with-null-space trick is the core insight; the rest is a competent assembly of graph execution, SAM2-based binding, and diffusion guidance. Methodology: The system runs in generation windows. (1) An executor evaluates each action against the rule graph state X_t = (S_t, q_t) — object attributes plus event history, activation records, transition progress, pending effects — with safeguards such as requiring confirmed action-completion events and treating unknown attributes as explicitly unknown (so negation cannot satisfy a precondition). (2) Dynamic object binding matches rule entities to 3D instances and image regions via semantic/appearance/spatial consistency, stores bindings in B_t, and assigns stored states to projected regions of objects that were affected while invisible. (3) Video generation (MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA Turbo, 1344×768, 24 fps, 124-frame windows) is conditioned on the graph, bindings, and effective states; at each denoising step, attribute replacement computes the clean estimate, pools per-object features, applies the replacement operator T_φ (Eq. 6), scatters corrections back, and advances sampling with the corrected velocity. (4) Perceptual feedback (Qwen3.8-Max, SAM2, DA3) independently verifies identity, visibility, attributes, and action completion; prescribed states and observed outcomes are kept separate so a gate that renders closed despite an open-prescription stays prescribed. (5) A checkpoint jointly serializes graph, execution state, and bindings. Training freezes the reader, generator, and visual encoder and optimizes only the writer φ with L = L_rec + λ_diff·L_diff + λ_swap·L_swap on paired videos. Critical design decisions: separating direct attribute correction from null-space compatible adjustment (well-justified by Eq. 7's exact-readout guarantee); requiring event evidence rather than action requests (justified by timing/hold metrics); and the paired rule-on/rule-off data design (sound, but circular with the evaluation, which also uses counterfactual pairs). The full-rank/independently-identifiable assumption on A_i is stated but the consequence of violating it in practice is not analyzed. Key Results: On RuleVerse (300 test pairs; 2,900 train), WorldRuler reaches average RSR 64.99% (Habitat) and 67.42% (GTA-V) vs SWM's 44.06% and 44.19% and MiniMax-H3's 33.75% and 43.43%; average FCR is 48.04% (Habitat) vs SWM's 17.98%. Component-level gains are largest on Effect (58.47% vs 20.74%), Timing (37.36% vs 15.67%), and Hold (50.83% vs 17.05%) on Habitat. On the external WorldState-Bench (50 official pairs), WorldRuler scores 96/94/96/95/99/92 across EndFollow/PairFollow/TwinContrast/Strict/CntAbsent/PairStrict vs SWM's 96/92/96/95/98/90 — a 2-point edge on two metrics, effectively a tie. Ablations: fixed binding reduces RSR to 48.09%; no attribute replacement to 46.43% (RSR) with First-appearance 12.90%; no L_swap leaves RSR at 51.24% but collapses First-appearance to 6.45%. Save/load: joint checkpointing achieves 98.17% consistency and 54.36%/47.89% post-load RSR/FCR vs 51.26%/45.53% without execution progress. Baselines (SWM, CWM, MiniMax-H3) appear current and relevant; however, SWM's 0.00 Stages/Order/Goal on GTA-V tasks is anomalous and suggests the multi-stage task format may disadvantage it. Tested scale is small: 300 test pairs and a 50-pair external benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. Genuinely novel: framing persistence as joint save/load of rules, execution state, and bindings; the exact-readout projection operator with a learned null-space writer inside the diffusion sampling loop; and the paired rule-on/rule-off dataset with first-appearance annotations. The components themselves — graph-based world state, LLM-generated rulebooks, SAM2 segmentation, VLM perception, condition-guided video diffusion — are standard pieces combined in a new setting, and the closest prior (SWM, Programmable World Model) already covers much of the state-execution ground. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative, covering each major component (binding, replacement, swapping loss) and each save/load information level — this is a strength. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; all RuleVerse metrics use a frozen VLM judge with fixed-choice questions, a protocol the authors also designed, creating a Goodhart risk since their framework feeds the judge structured conditions the baselines lack; the external-benchmark gains are within plausible judge noise at 2 points with n=50; and the GTA-V FCR comparison (66.66% vs 0.00% for SWM) is not explained. Code (github.com/AlayaLab/WorldRuler) and data (huggingface.co/datasets/AlayaLab/RuleVerse) are publicly released, which is a credibility positive. RuleVerse is split by scene/location group, which mitigates but does not eliminate the train/eval same-pipeline concern. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact in the released code/data). - Practical: Yes — it builds on an open video generator (MiniMax-H3) plus off-the-shelf perception models, though it requires a full stack (LLM planner, SAM2, DA3, VLM judge) rather than a single model. - Efficient: Not stated — no wall-clock, latency, or FLOP comparison against baselines; per-step attribute replacement and multiple feedback corrections add overhead that is unquantified. - Effective: Strong on their own metrics and near-parity externally; the evidence supports rule realization on seen objects less conclusively than the headline numbers suggest, given the VLM-judge circularity. - Scalable: Untested beyond 124-frame windows, 50–300 test samples, and two simulation sources; behavior with many simultaneous rules, open-ended rule authoring by end users, or much longer horizons is claimed only implicitly. The work delivers a software artifact (code, dataset, trained writer module), not just a paper. Strengths: - The projection-based replacement operator is a real technical contribution: Eq. 7 guarantees the attribute readout exactly matches the rule target while the null-space branch learns compatible edits, and corrections vanish when the target is already satisfied — a clean mathematical guarantee rare in diffusion-guidance papers. - The save/load ablation directly tests the paper's central claim (Rule-State Persistence) with an information-graded design (image+text vs rules+attributes vs joint checkpoint), showing a consistent ordering (98.17 vs 95.13 vs 94.25 consistency). - The paired rule-enabled/disabled data collection pipeline is a genuinely reusable contribution, including cases where rules fire on off-screen objects, with first-appearance and preservation metrics that target precisely the failure modes of prior work. - Honest architectural separation: prescribed states are kept distinct from perceptual observations, so generation failures do not corrupt the logical world state. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper acknowledges that effects on entirely unlocalized entities remain pending until binding is possible, that first-appearance control depends on prior spatial grounding, that GTA-V pairs allow minor character-motion variation and temporal synchronization uncertainty between screen recordings and engine logs, and that attribute replacement only covers "currently known and controllable" attributes. The conclusion is measured rather than promotional. The paper does not, however, include an explicit limitations section discussing VLM-judge reliability, scale, or rule-authoring constraints. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The evaluation judge is a frozen VLM and the benchmark authors are also the framework authors; structured conditions fed by WorldRuler could bias the judge toward it, and no human study is reported to validate the metric. - SWM's 0.00 FCR on all GTA-V task components is presented without diagnosis — this 67-point gap smells like task-format incompatibility, and the paper should explain or normalize it. - The WorldState-Bench configuration "permits up to two feedback corrections before publishing the clip" — whether baselines received the same correction budget and whether this budget was tuned on the benchmark is unstated. - The attribute vocabulary is fixed by the affine reader fitted on annotated data; the paper never tests rules with attributes outside this vocabulary, so generalization to arbitrary user-defined rules is extrapolated. - No latency/throughput numbers despite the system's interactive-world positioning, and no test of more than a handful of simultaneous rules. - Only two data sources, both simulators; transfer to real-video or open-web worlds is unaddressed. Bottom Line: A practitioner building rule-governed or stateful video world models should read this for the projection-based attribute replacement operator and the paired counterfactual data recipe, but should treat the headline numbers as self-benchmarked until an independent VLM-judge-free evaluation confirms the margins over SWM.

From Forecasting to World Modeling: Can Temporal Foundation Models Recover Causal Response?

J Hong, M Hwang, V Shankar · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows that temporal foundation models (tabular: TabPFN, TabICLv2, TabFM; time-series: Chronos-2; causal: CCPFN) that forecast retail sales accurately fail to recover the causal effect of price, and that instrumental variables help only when supplied as control-function residuals, not as raw features. - Why it's important: Retailers use these forecasts to set prices, and a model that misestimates how sales respond to a price change produces wrong pricing decisions even when its forecasts are the most accurate on the leaderboard. - How it does it: It exploits the CausalDemand simulator (calibrated to IRI store records), which generates paired confounded/unconfounded datasets from identical random draws, exposing exact ground truth E[q | do(p), x] for 32 ±10% price-intervention scenarios. - The good: The paired-data design cleanly isolates confounding as the sole cause of causal-recovery failure, and the result generalizes across six model families: under confounding, extra data flatten or worsen counterfactual error while improving forecasts, and raw instruments raise counterfactual WMAPE for every model (e.g., LightGBM 0.092→0.153, TabPFN 0.094→0.193) while improving forecast accuracy. - The missing: The evaluation rests on one simulator (log-linear demand, one product category, one calibration regime) built by the authors in a companion working paper, so the generality of the forecast/causal divergence beyond this generator is not established. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone deploying foundation models for pricing, demand estimation, or causal effect estimation from observational data, and for benchmark designers; skippable for readers seeking new methods, since the paper contributes an evaluation and a diagnosis, not a fix.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Non-Obviousness (80) is the driver — the finding that raw instruments worsen every model's causal accuracy while improving forecasts, so forecast-based model selection picks the wrong pipeline, is a surprising and consequential result — and the paired confounded/unconfounded generator plus proper 95% t-intervals and bootstrap give Rigor (72) real credibility. Novelty (65) is a solid NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, but the evaluation's dependence on the authors' own companion-paper simulator, single-category scope, and diagnosis-without-fix keep Completeness (65), Resilience (68), and Impact (62) in the mid range. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*62 = 69.
