Problem & Motivation: Retailers and analysts use sales forecasts to make pricing decisions, but forecasting targets E[q | p, x] — the sales that typically accompanied observed prices — while pricing decisions require E[q | do(p), x] — the sales that would follow an intervention. These diverge because retailers set prices in response to demand conditions (e.g., anticipated high demand before deep discounts) that are unrecorded in transaction data, so price endogenously correlates with the omitted demand shock ξ. The paper asks whether released foundation models, including causal foundation models pretrained specifically for intervention prediction (CCPFN, whose pretraining assumes no unobserved confounding), resist this endogeneity bias, and whether more data or the econometric remedy of instrumental variables closes the gap. Key Idea: Use a simulator that generates two versions of the same retail panel — identical in every random draw, differing only in whether price responds to the unobserved demand shock (δ = 0.30 vs δ = 0) — so that any degradation in causal recovery between the two versions is attributable to confounding alone, while the simulator's knowledge of ξ yields exact interventional ground truth. The key insight from the econometrics side (Equation 2) is that the OLS-style bias term δ·Var(ξ)/Var(log p) sharpens, rather than shrinks, with more data from the same pricing policy, which explains why data-scaling helps forecasts but not counterfactuals. Methodology: Three experiments over the CausalDemand benchmark (40 facial-tissue products, 731 stores, 156 weeks; 140 training weeks, 16 test weeks; five seeds). (1) Real-data check on Dominick's snack-cracker and breakfast-cereal panels (60 products, 81–82 stores): forecast WMAPE plus "own-sign accuracy" — the fraction of rows where a +10% price increase predicts lower sales, the law-of-demand sanity check. (2) Context-scaling: nested training samples from 100 to 102,340 store-weeks (model-dependent caps: TabFM 400, CCPFN 1,600, TabPFN/TabICLv2 6,400), scoring forecast WMAPE and counterfactual WMAPE over 32 intervention scenarios on confounded and unconfounded panels. (3) Instrument-form ablation: models receive instruments as (a) nothing, (b) control-function residuals (least-squares residuals of price components on instruments and controls, per Petrin–Train/Wooldridge), or (c) eight raw instrument columns (log supply cost, promotion-cost polynomial, cross-product averages). Scores are WMAPE with 95% t-intervals across five datasets; the counterfactual metric applies the predicted percentage change to true sales so level errors cannot offset response errors. Models are used with released weights, no fine-tuning, no tuning; LightGBM and a Double ML (Chernozhukov et al.) implementation with cross-fitting serve as supervised and econometric references. Critical design decisions: paired confounded/unconfounded generation (well justified — it isolates confounding), scoring the response ratio rather than the counterfactual level (well justified — decouples the two tasks), and restricting the simulator to the log-linear demand variant of CausalDemand (stated but weakly justified given the discrete-choice variant exists). Key Results: On real Dominick's data, the best forecasters predict the wrong direction of the price effect on a substantial share of rows: Chronos-2 (forecast WMAPE 0.368 crackers) has own-sign accuracy of 0.834 (crackers) and 0.942 (cereals), TabPFN 0.844/0.788, TabFM 0.844/0.869, whereas Double ML — with higher forecast error (0.463/0.442) — achieves 1.000 on both categories. On simulated data under confounding (δ = 0.30), additional context reduces forecast error (roughly 0.30–0.55 WMAPE range across models) but leaves counterfactual error flat or rising for every model without instruments (roughly 0.06–0.10 vs a 0.144 no-change baseline and 0.042 rounding floor); without confounding, data improve both errors. With instruments supplied as residuals, counterfactual error drops for most models (e.g., LightGBM 0.092→0.064, TabPFN 0.094→0.052, TabICLv2 0.077→0.052); as raw instruments, counterfactual error rises for all six models (LightGBM 0.153, TabICLv2 0.179, TabPFN 0.193 — all worse than predicting no change at 0.144) even though raw instruments improve forecast accuracy for the tabular models, so model selection by forecast error would pick the worse causal input form. Double ML with instruments reaches counterfactual WMAPE 0.046 (confounded) and 0.048 (unconfounded), an order of magnitude better than the foundation models. CCPFN, the causal foundation model, shows no advantage: 0.075 counterfactual WMAPE without instruments, and residuals do not help it (0.080). Baselines are current (2025–2026 model releases); scale is a mid-sized retail panel (~2.3M training rows full panel), not a stress test. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (forecast–causal divergence and the raw-instrument hazard in released foundation models) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK usage (CausalDemand, though introduced in the authors' companion working paper). No new method, model, or algorithm is proposed — the control-function residual input is a standard econometric technique (Petrin–Train 2010, Wooldridge 2015) repackaged as a feature-engineering recipe for in-context models, which is a useful but non-novel move. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and load-bearing: the paired confounded/unconfounded design, the three-form instrument ablation, and the nested context-scaling curve each isolate one factor. Uncertainty is handled properly — 95% t-intervals across five datasets for simulations and store-clustered percentile bootstrap (1,000 draws) for the real-data table. Full implementation details (package versions, seeds, sampling procedure, hyperparameter search ranges, per-model runtime and GPU specs) are in the appendix, and the benchmark is released on Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/jean-jsj/CausalDemand). Methodological concerns: (1) the primary evaluation is on the authors' own simulator from a companion working paper (Hong et al., 2026, cited as "Working paper"), so simulator design and evaluation are not independent; (2) the real-data experiment measures only sign, not magnitude, of the causal effect (unavoidable, but it weakens the headline claim); (3) foundation models are frozen at package defaults while LightGBM/Double ML are tuned on the real data — a mild asymmetry, though the paper argues this reflects "standard use"; (4) the preprint is not peer-reviewed, and one compared model (TabFM) is cited to a Google Research blog rather than a paper. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement/diagnosis study over existing models; no new system is built). - Practical: Yes — all evaluated models run on a single 24 GB A10 GPU (one configuration needed an 80 GB A100/H200), and baselines run on CPU. - Efficient: Cheap — full runs take 1–21 minutes per model; the finding costs almost nothing to reproduce. - Effective: The evidence shows foundation models fail to solve the stated causal-response problem under confounding, and that only Double ML (a non-foundation econometric baseline) recovers the effect — the paper demonstrates a problem rather than a solution. - Scalable: Not tested beyond one 731-store panel; the paper claims nothing about larger catalogs, more categories, or higher-frequency data, and context-length caps (400–6,400 store-weeks for several models) suggest real scaling limits it does not probe. Deliverable: a public benchmark and scorer (Hugging Face dataset) plus evaluation code details; no new model, library, or trained artifact. Strengths: - The paired-generation design (identical random draws, δ toggled) is a genuinely clean identification of confounding as the failure cause — most benchmark papers cannot isolate a single mechanism this precisely. - The raw-instrument result is the most non-obvious finding: supplying valid instruments as raw features strictly worsens every model's causal accuracy while improving its forecast accuracy, meaning forecast-based model selection actively picks the wrong pipeline — this contradicts the naive "more information is better" intuition for in-context learners. - Honest evaluation of released, unfine-tuned model weights at package defaults, including a causal foundation model (CCPFN) that the results show is not helped by its causal pretraining under unobserved confounding — an unflattering result the authors could have softened. - The framing connects an econometric theory result (bias grows with more endogenous data, Eq. 2) to a concrete ML failure mode, and the data-scaling experiment confirms the theory's prediction. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the compared models differ in training objective, capacity, and pretraining, so the study characterizes currently available models under standard use rather than architectural capabilities. They also note real-data counterfactual error cannot be computed (sign-only check). This is stated briefly in the conclusion — acknowledged directly but minimally, without discussing simulator-dependence or the single-category scope. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single simulator, single demand model (log-linear only; the discrete-choice variant is acknowledged but unused), single product category (facial tissue), and single calibration to IRI 2001–2007 data — the forecast/causal divergence is near-certain to be real in principle, but its magnitude on other retail settings, other industries, or non-log-linear demand is unmeasured. - The benchmark and this paper share authors (CausalDemand is Hong, Hwang, Shankar — the same three), so simulator choices (e.g., the 10% intervention size, the discount mechanism as the sole confounding channel, the two specific instruments) were made by the evaluators; a third-party generator would strengthen the claims. - No fix is proposed or tested beyond control-function residuals — the most actionable result (residuals work, raw instruments hurt) is left as a recipe without exploring alternatives (front-door, negative controls, fine-tuning CCPFN on confounded pretraining data), and residuals fail for CCPFN and barely move Chronos-2, which is not explained. - No comparison against fine-tuned models, larger foundation models, or causal methods beyond Double ML (e.g., deep IV, GAN-based IV methods), so the boundary of the failure is uncharted. - The own-sign accuracy of Double ML being exactly 1.000 on real data, while reassuring, is presented without discussing that Double ML was tuned on those same real datasets — a mild in-sample circularity in the one real-data result. Bottom Line: Practitioners pricing with foundation-model forecasts or reaching for causal foundation models should read this — it documents, with unusually clean evidence, that forecast leaderboards actively select against causal validity and that raw instruments backfire in-context — but method researchers will need to look elsewhere for solutions beyond control-function residuals.

LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny

W Wesselink, K Huizing, H van de Wetering · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a ten-step workflow in which an LLM coding agent (Claude Code, called the Verification Construction Agent) produces complete machine-checked Dafny verifications of published algorithms, evaluated on 37 algorithms totaling 74,539 lines of Dafny code and 2,371 lemmas. - Why it's important: Machine-checking a complex algorithm normally takes expert proof engineers weeks-to-months per algorithm; the paper reports verified proofs delivered in hours to days, which, if generalizable, changes the cost calculus of formal verification. - How it does it: The workflow locks a human-reviewed contract, generates dual Python/Dafny implementations, empirically tests candidate loop invariants (truth tests, counterexample-to-induction tests, drop tests) before proving, then uses solver-resource measurements to guide proof restructuring (opaque predicate bundles, lemma decomposition, per-declaration assertion isolation) under static guardrails that prevent specification weakening. - The good: The corpus includes genuinely hard targets — a machine-checked Hopcroft–Tarjan triconnectivity test (9,731 LoC, 370 lemmas, 226.4s verification) and Edmonds' blossom algorithm verified with minimal human involvement — targets the authors state have no prior machine-checked verification, and the artifact is publicly released (https://10x10.org/dafny). - The missing: There is no controlled comparison against unassisted or differently-assisted verification, and all 37 algorithms are classic published algorithms likely well represented in LLM training data, so neither the speedup nor the generality claim is measured (the authors admit both). - Read it or not: Read it if you work on automated reasoning, proof engineering, or LLM agents for formal methods — it is currently the most substantial demonstration of end-to-end LLM-assisted Dafny verification; skip it if you want controlled experiments or techniques transferable outside Dafny/Z3.

Problem & Motivation: Formal verification of complex algorithms (nested loops, mutable data structures, global graph/LTS properties, non-trivial termination measures) requires expertise in specification, invariant construction, and managing SMT-solver behavior; even when the mathematics is understood, expressing it so Z3 can discharge the obligations is a proof-engineering bottleneck. Prior LLM-assisted verification work targets narrow subtasks (invariant generation, annotation synthesis, specification inference, repair) or assumes an existing implementation; the gap addressed is the complete pipeline from a published pseudocode description to a fully verified Dafny program, where the solver must verify the entire artifact under Dafny's native batched configuration, not just isolated obligations. Key Idea: Treat LLM-assisted verification as a workflow-design problem rather than a proof-synthesis problem: the core move is to gate formal proof construction on empirical invariant validation — an instrumented Python execution tests whether invariant clauses hold in reachable states, are inductive (CTI tests with state perturbation), and are necessary (drop tests) — combined with a resource-guided optimization loop in which solver resource-consumption measurements, not intuition, decide between proof-engineering interventions (lemma decomposition, opaque specification bundles that hide contract predicates behind revealing lemmas, and selective `{:isolate_assertions}` annotations). Methodology: The pipeline is ten steps in three phases. (1) Specification: the agent transcribes the publication into LaTeX pseudocode, flags ambiguities, and formalizes pre/postconditions; the human approves and the contract is locked (a lock records the contract plus every transitive definition, since weakening a definition silently weakens the contract). (2) Code generation and contract testing: Python and Dafny implementations are generated from the same pseudocode; randomized Python tests check pre/postconditions. (3) Proof development (the main loop): the agent writes invariants and termination measures, validates them empirically via the Python checker, drafts lemmas and ghost code, then iterates through resource-restricted subagent loops — Step 8 verifies obligations in isolation, Step 9 drives the complete file to verify under Dafny's batched native configuration using bottleneck-profiling tools — followed by an audit for unjustified assumptions. Guardrails (static file checks) forbid non-ghost code changes, axioms, and `assume` statements. The framework is Dafny's verification-condition generation over Z3; the invariant checker explicitly proves nothing, it only finds counterexamples. Critical design decisions: contract locking (justified — closes a real soundness hole); isolated-then-batched verification strategy (justified by the observation that obligations passing in isolation can still time out batched); opaque-predicate bundling applied consistently (empirically justified: partial opacity in Lengauer–Tarjan left 36 timeouts at 2,098M resource units, the complete design eliminated all timeouts at 144M). Key Results: The corpus comprises 37 verified algorithms (31 graph, 5 LTS, 1 geometry) totaling 74,539 LoC, 2,371 lemmas, 4,922 declarations, and 1,221.7s aggregate verification time on an i7-13700 (16 cores, 12 GB memory cap per run, Dafny 4.10.0 with bundled Z3). Headline targets: Hopcroft–Tarjan triconnectivity test (9,731 LoC, 370 lemmas, 794 declarations, 226.4s, 14 calendar days) — claimed to have no prior machine-checked verification — and n-dimensional Quickhull (5,137 LoC, 170.4s, with a general-position input restriction), likewise claimed first. Lengauer–Tarjan restructuring cut main-routine obligations from 644 to 271 and Z3 resources from ~2.1B to 144M units. Assertion isolation on bron_kerbosch2 dropped 113.2M to 5.2M resource units. Edmonds' blossom was verified largely autonomously (>1,100 obligations) after the authors were informed by the Abdulaziz–Mehlhorn Isabelle proof. Of all attempted algorithms, only Hopcroft–Tarjan's triconnected-components companion remains unverified (16,658 LoC ongoing). All baselines are the authors' own pre-optimization measurements — there is no comparison against human-only verification effort or competing LLM tools; the calendar-day column ranges 1–123 days and is acknowledged as a rough, confounded proxy. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the ten-step workflow with locked contracts, empirical invariant validation, and resource-guided proof engineering) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (first reported machine-checked verifications of the Hopcroft–Tarjan triconnectivity test and n-dimensional Quickhull). The individual ingredients — Dafny, Z3, LLM agents, randomized testing, assertion isolation, lemma decomposition — are all existing; the genuine contribution is their integration into a repeatable pipeline and the demonstration that it scales to verification targets of this difficulty, not any new verification technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist only as informal post-hoc case studies (e.g., opaque-bundle application in Lengauer–Tarjan, the seven post-optimization failures that turned out to be false statements); there is no controlled ablation isolating each workflow component's contribution, which the authors acknowledge. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported — though the verification outcomes themselves are binary and machine-checked, which is inherently more objective than typical empirical claims. Source code, verification models, and experiment instructions are released at https://10x10.org/dafny, a major reproducibility positive. Methodological concerns: (1) training-data contamination — all targets are canonical published algorithms the LLM plausibly saw during training; (2) the "Days" metric confounds stalled development waiting for new tooling with actual effort; (3) correctness is conditional on human review of the reconstructed pseudocode and contract, an unquantified failure mode; (4) techniques were developed and evaluated on the same corpus (the ~25 proof-engineering techniques' effectiveness figures are self-described as "indicative"). Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built workflow/toolchain evaluated by producing verification artifacts). Practical: Yes — runs on a single desktop (16-core CPU, 128 GB RAM) with Dafny 4.10.0/Z3, though it requires a paid frontier LLM (Claude Opus 5/5.5 via Claude Code). Efficient: Verification is bounded to 6 cores/12 GB; the dominant cost is LLM-agent interaction time (hours to days of interactive development per algorithm), which is not quantified in tokens or cost. Effective: The evidence (37 fully verified files, including first-ever machine-checked proofs of two hard algorithms) shows it solves the stated problem for published pseudocode, but only a proxy for the broader goal of verifying arbitrary or unseen algorithms. Scalable: Untested beyond ~10K-LoC single files; the one attempt at a larger target (triconnected-components at 16,658 LoC) is stalled, and the authors claim rather than demonstrate scalability to unseen problems. The work delivers a real software artifact (workflow tooling, domain libraries, 37 verified proof files) at the released URL, not merely a paper. Strengths: (1) The empirical invariant-validation layer (truth tests, CTI with state perturbation, drop tests) is a genuinely useful intermediate checks-before-proving mechanism that catches false statements before solver effort is wasted — supported by the observation that all seven post-optimization failures examined this way were false claims. (2) The resource-guided proof-engineering discipline — measuring Z3 resource units to choose between restructuring options and requiring verification under Dafny's native batched configuration, not just isolation — addresses a real, often-overlooked gap between per-obligation and whole-file verification. (3) The target selection is credibly hard: blossom, Lengauer–Tarjan, and Hopcroft–Tarjan triconnectivity are established stress tests for verification, and two targets plausibly have no prior machine-checked proof in any system. (4) Guardrails (contract locking including transitive definitions, ghost-code-only edits, no axioms/assumes) directly address the most dangerous failure mode of LLM-driven verification — silently weakening what is proven. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that: correctness rests on human review of the reconstructed pseudocode and contract, which may contain undetected errors; all algorithms are published and likely represented in LLM training data, so generalization to unseen algorithms or arbitrary source code is unestablished; no controlled comparison with conventional human-led verification was performed; the evaluation does not isolate individual workflow components; and all correctness claims are conditional on Dafny's and Z3's soundness. Section 9.4 confronts these directly rather than minimizing them, which strengthens the paper's credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No cost accounting of the LLM usage (tokens, API cost, wall-clock agent time per algorithm), so the "hours to days" claim cannot be compared against expert-effort baselines on any axis. (2) No comparison against the obvious competing baselines the paper itself cites — DafnyPro, Dafny-annotator, or even a plain unstructured Claude Code session — so the workflow's contribution over raw LLM capability is unquantified; the cross-case claim that proof-engineering techniques transfer between domains rests on exactly two LTS examples, which the authors concede. (3) The two "first-ever verification" claims are backed by "to our knowledge" rather than a systematic search, and the triconnectivity test relies on the Gutwenger–Mutzel correction of the original algorithm, so what is verified is a corrected variant. (4) The claim that the human role has shifted to "supervision" is supported only by narrative; the degree of human proof-idea contribution in the hardest cases (e.g., the proof-dependency-graph idea during the stalled triconnected-components run) suggests the human contribution remains material and unmeasured. (5) Provenance of each algorithm relative to the specific models' training cutoffs is unknown even to the authors and untested. Bottom Line: For anyone doing proof engineering or building LLM agents for formal methods, this is essential reading — it is the strongest published demonstration that a structured agent-plus-verifier workflow can produce first-of-a-kind machine-checked proofs of hard algorithms — but its headline efficiency claim (hours-to-days versus expert months) is unmeasured, so treat it as a capability demonstration, not a validated productivity result.

One Table, Many Queries: Benchmarking Generalist Tabular Models Across Generation, Imputation, and Prediction

Y Wang, K Li, X Li, Z Li, Y Lu, X Zhang, P Cui · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OTBENCH, a 56-dataset, 46-method, 20-capability-axis benchmark that aligns tabular data generation, imputation, and prediction under shared splits and explicit task contracts, and uses it to run rank-alignment, controlled objective-intervention, and fixed-model profile analyses. - Why it's important: These three tasks are evaluated in separate silos despite querying the same joint distribution, so practitioners building unified or foundation tabular models have no evidence about which capabilities transfer, whether multi-objective training helps or hurts, and when a generalist beats a specialist portfolio. - How it does it: The core move is formulating all three tasks as probabilistic queries (O, Q, C) against one joint distribution, then combining observational rank correlations on aligned method support with a factorial intervention study (5 backbones × 7 objective combinations × 5 datasets × 3 seeds = 525 trained systems) that defines single-addition (SAE) and cross-addition (CAE) effects on normalized rank scales. - The good: The intervention study is the most credible element: matched backbone–dataset–seed comparisons show self-inclusion of the recipient's own objective gives the largest gains on all 19 displayed axes, generation has the broadest positive auxiliary coverage, and objective benefits are demonstrably sub-additive and context-dependent. - The missing: The factorial study rests on only 5 datasets (1 regression) and 5 backbones, most off-diagonal auxiliary effects fail the authors' own cross-backbone robustness criterion (e.g., the headline P→G TSTR effect of +0.092 has CI [−0.041, +0.225]), and the categorical-fidelity portfolio comparison uses only 3 datasets. - Read it or not: Read it if you build tabular foundation models, generative/imputation methods, or benchmarks — it delivers the first controlled cross-task evidence base — but skip the fine print on auxiliary effects if you only want a leaderboard, since the paper deliberately refuses to pool one.
Why this rank

Impact (70) reflects that concrete artifact plus a reusable SAE/CAE analysis protocol; this dimension carries 30% weight and lifts the composite. Novelty (72) for the three-task conditional-query formulation and the rank-alignment-vs-intervention separation; Non-Obviousness (72) for the sub-additivity finding. Rigor (68) is above the benchmark-paper bar — three seeds, 2,000-draw bootstrap, LOMO diagnostics, metric-redundancy audit, public code — but is held back by the 5-dataset/5-backbone factorial scope, no tree-ensemble baseline, and authorship overlap with the winning generalist family (LimiX). Completeness (72) from the candid limitations; Resilience (62) is reduced by the headline P→G claim whose CI includes zero and the untested fine-tuned unified model. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Tabular generation (sampling full rows), imputation (recovering masked features), and prediction (inferring a target) all query aspects of the same joint distribution, yet each has its own benchmarks, metrics, and modeling traditions. Practitioners choosing or building tabular models — especially the recent wave of tabular foundation models (LimiX-2, TabICLv2, TabPFN-3) — cannot tell from task-wise evaluations which capabilities co-occur across tasks, whether training one objective helps another, or whether one fixed model can serve all three uses of a table competitively. The gap is threefold: observational rank similarity does not establish objective transfer, and existing benchmarks (TabArena, Synthcity, Shades-of-Null, etc.) cover at most one or two tasks. No prior benchmark aligned all three tasks on shared data splits with explicit information-access contracts and capability-level (rather than task-level) metrics. Key Idea: The central insight is the conditional-query formulation: generation, imputation, and prediction are queries q = (O, Q, C) to a single joint P*(Z), which permits (a) shared train/test splits and capability axes across tasks, and (b) a clean separation between observational evidence (do method rankings agree across tasks?) and interventional evidence (does enabling an objective change another recipient task within a fixed model?). The SAE/CAE factorial design — averaging the gain from adding objective s with and without a third objective u present — is the trick that turns benchmark infrastructure into causal-style transfer measurement. Methodology: Three complementary analyses on a common 56-dataset suite (50 OpenML datasets selected from 492 literature-sourced candidates via method-independent meta-features, PCA to 41 components, k-means with k=50, nearest-to-centroid selection, same-source duplicate suppression; plus 6 TabStruct SCM datasets) with one fixed 80/20 train–test split shared by all tasks. (1) Task Rank Analysis: 9 multi-task-capable methods are run under their default protocols; 45 metrics are reduced to 20 semantic capability axes via a redundancy audit (common-support percentile ranks, correlation clustering with ρ ≥ 0.85/CI ≥ 0.70 thresholds, reliability-checked via rank ICC); pooled Spearman correlations between axis scores across task pairs are computed on aligned method–dataset support, with leave-one-method-out (LOMO) sign-stability diagnostics. (2) Controlled Transfer: Gaussian Copula, Forest-VP Joint, TabDiff, TabSyn, and TabDDPM are trained under all 7 non-empty objective subsets of {G, I, P} on 5 datasets × 3 seeds; SAE (Eq. 2) averages the rank gain from adding one objective; CAE (Eq. 3) tests additivity conditional on an anchor objective; uncertainty from 2,000 crossed backbone–dataset bootstrap draws; imputation evaluated under MCAR/MAR/MNAR/mixed at rates {0.1, 0.3, 0.5}. (3) Fixed-Model Generality: 9 generalist identities are compared against declared specialist portfolios via fractions of specialists beaten per axis and paired worst-task-percentile gaps, with Pareto frontiers at ε = 0.05. Critical design decisions: method-independent dataset selection (defensible and pre-specified); member-complete, equal-weight axis aggregation (conservative but means axes are composites of non-interchangeable estimands, e.g., authenticity is kept despite opposing global utility at ρ = −0.881); and target-observed imputation (MCAR, 0.3) for the rank study versus target-hidden imputation in the intervention study (acknowledged as a contract mismatch). Key Results: (1) Rank alignment is capability-dependent: imputation–prediction agree through numerical point accuracy, association, and utility gap (pooled ρ 0.35–0.59, direction-preserving under LOMO), while distributional axes show unstable or opposing relations (neither distribution axis preserves direction against classification). Generation–imputation is the most LOMO-stable pair (36/42 axis pairs), with TSTR gap and global-utility compromise positive on all six imputation axes; fidelity and C2ST have negative direction-preserving correlations with all classification axes (e.g., fidelity vs. hard-decision ρ = −0.19). (2) Interventions: self-inclusion effects range +0.122 to +0.445 (G), +0.159 to +0.317 (I), +0.098 to +0.456 (P); adding G improves all six imputation axes and 5/7 prediction axes; adding P improves all six imputation axes (e.g., numerical point accuracy +0.080 vs. G's +0.007) and raises the P→G TSTR-gap score by +0.092 pooled (CI [−0.041, +0.225], positive for 4/5 backbones, Forest-VP Joint at −0.033). CAE shows systematic sub-additivity for G×I|P and G×P|I (e.g., fidelity −0.47, numerical point −0.48) while I×P|G is positive but crosses zero. (3) Profile analysis: the practical Pareto frontier for objective arms is {G, GI, GP, IP, GIP}, with GIP at 94% exact-frontier bootstrap membership; LimiX-2 leads every displayed prediction axis and beats 84–98% of specialists on prediction, TabPFN-3 leads TSTR gap (90% beaten), Gaussian Copula leads fidelity (87–90%); generalists exceed their utility portfolios (TabICLv2 +0.157, CI [0.078, 0.229]) but lose on fidelity (categorical portfolio gaps −0.396 to −0.261, all CIs below zero, on a 3-dataset cohort). Scale is standard (datasets of 106–53,940 rows, ≤126 features), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the three-task conditional-query benchmark with aligned splits and contracts, and the SAE/CAE factorial intervention design that distinguishes rank co-occurrence from objective transfer — the sub-additivity finding and the utility-vs-fidelity split between generalists and portfolios are new empirical results. Individual metrics (C2ST, α-precision/β-recall, TSTR, KS, Wasserstein, MIA diagnostics) are standard constructions assembled competently; the generalist methods evaluated are existing models, not contributions of this paper. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is above the bar for benchmark papers: three seeds per factorial arm with bootstrap uncertainty (2,000 crossed draws), a pre-specified robustness criterion for SAE/CAE that the authors report rather than hide when effects fail it, LOMO sign-stability diagnostics for every rank correlation, a full metric-redundancy audit with repeatability (rank ICC 0.592–0.963) and winner-agreement analyses, and stress-test examples showing metric-specific responses to column shuffling, row replay, and probability rescaling. Code, configurations, and evaluation routines are public at https://github.com/limix-ldm-ai/OTBench. Concerns: (a) the factorial study's 5-dataset/5-backbone scope with one regression dataset limits external validity of pooled effects, and the authors concede none of the off-diagonal SAE effects meets the complete robustness criterion; (b) the categorical fidelity portfolio comparison rests on 3 datasets; (c) rank-based effect sizes are unitless and hard to translate into practical magnitudes — the paper itself flags that a higher TSTR-gap score is not a raw-accuracy change; (d) the benchmark and several highlighted foundation models (LimiX-2, TabICLv2) share authorship overlap (StableAI/Tsinghua with the LimiX authors), so the favorable frozen-foundation-model findings warrant independent replication. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a reusable benchmark suite with code and configs) with strong EMPIRICAL content. Practical: Yes — datasets are capped at 100k rows/160 features, and all 46 methods run under a controlled compute budget on standard hardware. Efficient: The rank protocol requires member-complete support, which shrinks usable method pools (e.g., 9–10 methods per task pair), but the suite itself imposes modest cost relative to re-running ad hoc task-specific evaluations. Effective: The evidence convincingly supports the descriptive claims (capability-specific rankings, sub-additivity) but the prescriptive guidance for unified-model design remains correlational; frozen-model results are inference-system capabilities, not attributions to pretraining. Scalable: The dataset selection pipeline is method-independent and re-runnable at larger candidate-pool scale, but the paper has not tested whether rank alignments or objective effects hold beyond 56 datasets / 5 backbones, and the categorical cohort (3 datasets) would not survive even 2× expansion without new data collection. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (benchmark code, configs, evaluation routines) plus a reusable SAE/CAE analysis protocol. Strengths: - The rank-alignment-versus-intervention separation is a real methodological contribution: it cleanly demonstrates that correlated method rankings across tasks (e.g., TSTR gap ↔ imputation) do not by themselves license claims about objective transfer, and then supplies the intervention the field was missing. - The metric-space audit is unusually honest for a benchmark: it documents which metrics are redundant (NMAE–NRMSE ρ = 0.947), which genuinely conflict (authenticity vs. global utility ρ = −0.881), and which are noisy (MIA TPR@1% ICC 0.592), rather than averaging everything into one leaderboard. - The sub-additivity finding (CAE negative across G×I|P and G×P|I despite individually positive SAEs) is a non-obvious, actionable result for multi-objective tabular training design. - The refusal to collapse results into a single cross-task score, including per-axis frontier membership and profile-specific Pareto sets, reflects a mature understanding of benchmark gaming risks. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront: dependence of conclusions on the chosen capability axes and contracts; the target-observed vs. target-hidden imputation mismatch between the rank and intervention studies; the small factorial scope (5 backbones, 5 datasets, 1 regression, unavailable evaluations); the exploratory, non-robust nature of auxiliary SAE effects; the rank-scale (not mechanism-identifying) character of SAE/CAE, including confounds from conditioning-policy switches and fixed-budget update redistribution; the 3-dataset categorical profile cohort; and the fact that frozen-model results cannot isolate pretraining contributions without matched pretraining/inference ablations. This is a candid limitations section — credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Potential conflict of interest: the benchmark originates from groups overlapping with LimiX/LimiX-2, one of the best-performing generalists; no independent-party validation is offered. (2) The headline P→G utility claim ("prediction can improve synthetic-data utility") is supported by a pooled effect whose 95% CI includes zero and by "inconclusive" localization contrasts — the paper's framing slightly outruns its evidence here. (3) The 5-dataset factorial omits any dataset with native missingness and high-cardinality categoricals beyond the suite's range, yet imputation conclusions are drawn from only 4 classification + 1 regression tasks. (4) No strong tree-ensemble baseline (XGBoost/CatBoost) is included in the multi-task-capable rank pool, so cross-task rank relationships are characterized almost entirely among neural/generative/foundation models. (5) Rank-based effect sizes on a normalized 7-arm scale have no calibrated practical meaning; a practitioner cannot tell whether a +0.16 rank change matters in production terms. (6) Not evaluated: any fine-tuned (non-frozen) unified model, so the paper's central motivation — building models that share conditional information — remains untested by construction. Bottom Line: This is the most rigorous cross-task tabular benchmark published to date and essential reading for anyone building unified tabular or foundation models — its intervention design and non-additivity findings will not be found in task-wise alternatives like TabArena or Synthcity — but its headline transfer claims are under-powered, its generalist winners come from an author-adjacent model family, and every quantitative effect should be treated as exploratory until replicated at broader scale.

FOE-Dreamer: Deployment-Efficient Learning of Cyber Defense Policies in Operational Networks

Y Du, C Kiekintveld · arxiv.org · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FOE-Dreamer, a model-based RL framework with a factored world model and an opponent model that trains a cyber-defense policy directly on a live 8-host OpenStack emulation, cutting episode loss by roughly 2× against Rainbow and IQN under a matched 3-day, single-GPU budget. - Why it's important: Training RL defenders in simulators creates a fidelity gap that causes transfer failures (the CybORG lineage reports success rates as low as 66% moving sim→emulation), but training directly in a running network makes every interaction costly, so sample efficiency is the binding constraint for deployable autonomous defense. - How it does it: A Dreamer-style world model splits the latent state into an action-conditioned controllable factor, an action-independent exogenous factor for user traffic, and an opponent embedding inferred from defender-observable history, so most policy updates happen on imagined latent rollouts instead of real network interactions. - The good: Latent-disentanglement diagnostics directly verify the factoring claim — user activity decodes from the exogenous latent with R² 0.72–0.79 but only 0.14–0.18 from the controllable latent, and defender actions decode from z_t at 0.71 accuracy versus 0.21 from u_t. - The missing: Evaluation covers only two scripted, fixed-class attacker profiles on a single 8-host topology, with no adaptive adversaries, no zero-shot attacker generalization, and no demonstration that the approach survives at enterprise scale or transfers beyond the authors' own testbed. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on RL-based cyber defense or sim-to-real-style RL in live infrastructure; anyone else can skip it, as the technical machinery is standard Dreamer plus two conditional components whose value is specific to noisy, partially observable operational environments.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations deploying autonomous network defense face a dilemma: RL defenders trained in abstract simulators (CybORG, CyberBattleSim, Yawning Titan) fail to transfer because simulators omit authentication delays, real CVE exploit paths, and human-behavior-correlated user traffic, while training directly in a production or emulated network makes each exploratory action (isolate, reboot) operationally expensive. The paper defines a middle rung on a "realism ladder" — high-fidelity emulation with real software and real CVEs — and asks how to make RL sample-efficient enough to train there. The motivating episode (an Equifax-style kill chain through WordPress exploitation, SSH pivoting, and cron-based root escalation, obscured by concurrent GHOSTS user activity) grounds three challenges: entangled observations (C1), profile-dependent optimal responses (C2), and the interaction budget of live training (C3). Prior model-based RL in security exists only on the attacker side (MEME); no prior work applies Dreamer-style world models to the defender or trains one in-network. Key Idea: The core insight is that a live network's observations are the joint product of three distinct variance sources — defender actions, benign user activity, and attacker behavior — and that architecturally factoring the latent state along exactly these lines reduces policy-gradient variance during imagined rollouts, making model-based RL tractable under a live-network interaction budget. The action gate entering only the controllable posterior (qϕ(z_t | h_t, s_{t−1}, a_{t−1}) vs. qψ(u_t | h_t, s_{t−1})) is the single asymmetric commitment that drives the separation. Methodology: The problem is cast as a POMDP with a 5-second polling interval, per-host observations (alert counts, honeypot status, availability, trap indicators), five defender actions (Isolate, Disrupt, Monitor, Deceive, Null), and 100-step (~8 min) episodes. Four components are trained jointly: (i) an observation encoder fθ producing h_t; (ii) a factored world model with action-conditioned controllable and action-free exogenous posterior/transition heads, an observation decoder gη(z_t, u_t), and a reward predictor hζ(z_t, u_t, τ); (iii) a recurrent opponent encoder fξ mapping a K-step window of defender observations/actions to an embedding τ, supervised (privileged information, training only) by cross-entropy on the attacker's next action and target host; and (iv) an actor-critic updated on H-step imagined rollouts in latent space. The world model uses the Dreamer-family ELBO (reconstruction + reward terms plus per-factor KL, Eq. 6); the combined loss weights policy and opponent terms (Eq. 8). Training iterates Collect (8 parallel testbed episodes) → Fit → Imagine → Optimize. Critical design decisions: the action-gate asymmetry separating z_t from u_t (well-motivated by credit-assignment arguments and validated by diagnostics); conditioning the reward predictor on all three latents including the opponent embedding (justified by reward dependence on attacker behavior); and privileged attacker-action targets for opponent supervision while excluding them from policy inputs (a clean deployment-consistency argument, though the asymmetry between training and deployment conditions is a subtlety). The authors honestly state the factoring assumptions (action-independent user dynamics, additive user reward) and that containment actions violate them, treating factoring as an inductive bias rather than a claim of true independence. Key Results: On the 8-host OpenStack testbed against two scripted profiles (Avoidant, Enticed) with GHOSTS user activity (U-rand and U-burst), after 3 days of single-GPU training across 5 seeds: FOE-Dreamer achieves episode loss −48 ± 7 (Avoidant) and −38 ± 5 (Enticed), versus Rainbow at −102 ± 20 / −76 ± 17 and IQN at −118 ± 26 / −84 ± 21 — roughly 2× better, with gaps exceeding one standard deviation in every cell. It also beats a hand-designed Expert-Inspired heuristic (−138 / −88), Random (−152 / −242), and Sleep (−178 / −285). Nested ablations show factoring contributes ~14 (Avoidant) / 10 (Enticed) points and the opponent model a further 16 / 10 points, with opponent modeling mattering most against the probe-and-withdraw Avoidant profile. Latent diagnostics: ridge regression decodes ground-truth user activity from u_t at R² 0.72 (U-rand) / 0.79 (U-burst) versus 0.14 / 0.18 from z_t; multinomial classifiers decode defender actions from z_t at 0.71 accuracy versus 0.21 from u_t (0.17 random baseline); t-SNE shows clear profile separation in the opponent embedding. Baselines Rainbow and IQN are standard but not the strongest modern candidates (e.g., no PPO, despite the paper's own related-work section citing PPO as a frequent ACND baseline). Scale is deliberately small: 8 hosts, 4 CVE classes, 2 attacker profiles, 2 user profiles — a depth-over-breadth testbed smaller than MHBench (20–50 hosts). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (factored controllable/exogenous/opponent world model applied to defender-side model-based RL) and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the integrated OpenStack + real-CVE + GHOSTS + gRPC RL testbed). The genuine novelty is the first Dreamer-style defender trained in-network without a simulator stage, plus the testbed integration that no prior artifact combines. The constituent techniques are standard: Dreamer's ELBO and imagination-based actor-critic are used essentially unchanged, and the opponent encoder follows the established Papoudakis et al. encoder-decoder pattern for agent modeling under partial observability — the contribution is a well-motivated architectural factoring of known components for a new, demanding setting rather than a new learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is notably rigorous for a systems-security RL paper: 5 seeds with mean ± standard deviation reported, per-seed raw losses released for independent bootstrap CIs, a documented hyperparameter grid search with explicit bounds (Appendix B) showing selected values are not at search boundaries, a nested ablation with an explicitly stated justification for excluding the missing cell (Factor+No-Opponent), and — unusually — a dedicated latent-probing section (linear decoding, t-SNE) testing whether components do what they claim rather than only whether they help. Code, configurations, and reproduction recipes are at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FOE-DREAMER-5117. Methodological concerns: the ablation is nested, not a full 2×2, so no factorial main/interaction effects; the evaluation environment, the validation set for hyperparameter selection, and the test set are the same testbed; the Expert baseline is self-designed rather than drawn from prior literature; no significance tests beyond the std-vs-gap comparison; and a hyperparameter sensitivity sweep and failure-mode prevalence counts are explicitly deferred. No error bars are missing, but claims of robustness rest on two attacker profiles only. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — the testbed — as supporting contribution). - Practical: Yes — the full training run fits a single GPU for 3 days alongside an 8-VM OpenStack tenant on commodity cloud infrastructure; all deployed CVEs are patched public vulnerabilities. - Efficient: Model-based training is the point — it achieves useful policies in a 3-day budget where model-free methods (millions of interactions) are infeasible, though the Collect phase dominates wall-clock cost and snapshot-restore per episode reset takes 35–90 seconds. - Effective: The evidence shows it beats model-free and heuristic baselines on its own testbed against scripted attackers — a proxy for the stated goal of defending operational networks, which remains untested. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — the authors state that scaling to 50+ hosts is an open deployment question and argue the factoring should remain useful because the underlying problems intensify, but no experiment addresses it. The work delivers a software artifact (defender code, testbed configurations, reproduction recipes) plus a reusable evaluation methodology (latent linear-decoding probes); the paper does not ship a standalone library or trained model weights. Strengths: - Honest and unusual epistemic discipline: the paper separates claims from evidence throughout — e.g., stating that separate transition heads are an inductive bias that does not establish process independence, labeling deployment notes as observations rather than empirical claims, and gating its headline factoring claim on direct latent probes (R² 0.72–0.79 user decoding from u_t vs. 0.14–0.18 from z_t). - First-mover position on a genuinely important gap: to the authors' (credible) knowledge this is the first defender-side Dreamer-style world model trained in-network, addressing the sim-to-real problem that the field's own survey (Vyas et al.) names as a top open problem. - The integrated testbed (OpenStack substrate + real CVE exploit paths + GHOSTS user emulation + 5 s gRPC RL polling) is a substantive contribution independent of the algorithm — the paper's axis-by-axis comparison against MHBench/Incalmo, CSLE, Cyberwheel, and Kyoushi makes the gap-filling claim verifiable. - The threat model is carefully scoped with explicit out-of-scope lists (no adaptive adversaries, no adversarial ML, no zero-days, no credentialed insiders), and four concrete failure modes are documented rather than hidden. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly (a credibility positive). They state: training happens in emulation, not production, and the 3-day budget does not imply production sample requirements; evaluation covers only two scripted fixed-class attacker profiles with no zero-shot or adaptive-adversary transfer; four documented failure modes (early deception-budget exhaustion against Enticed, Isolate/Disrupt oscillation while τ is uncertain, exogenous-prediction degradation under U-burst regime shifts, and the one-cron-period blind window on cron escalation); a hyperparameter sweep and failure-mode prevalence counts deferred for compute reasons; and scaling to 50+ hosts unaddressed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Only two scripted attacker profiles bound the evaluation; since the opponent model's value depends on attacker behavioral diversity, results against more heterogeneous or mid-spectrum profiles are unknown, and the claim that the two profiles "bracket the spectrum" is asserted from field-study citations rather than demonstrated. - The nested ablation omits the Factor+No-Opponent cell; the stated reason (opponent supervision supports attacker/user separation) is plausible but means component interactions are not established, and the opponent model itself depends on privileged attacker action/target labels during training — a training condition that may not exist when defending a real network where such labels are unavailable. - No PPO baseline despite the paper's own related work calling it the most frequent ACND baseline; Rainbow and IQN are 2018-era algorithms, so "2× better than model-free" is against a somewhat dated field. - Hyperparameters were selected on a validation set drawn from the same testbed and same attacker/user profiles used for evaluation, so some Goodhart-style overfitting to the testbed cannot be excluded; generalization to a different topology is untested entirely. - The headline metric (episode loss of magnitude ~−48) has no externally interpretable scale; absolute defender quality (e.g., containment rate, exfiltration prevented, user-disruption minutes) is not reported, making cross-paper comparison impossible. - The paper is a preprint (arXiv:2611.14880) and has not, as far as stated, undergone peer review. Bottom Line: A practitioner in RL-for-cyber-defense gains something real from this paper — both a working recipe for sample-efficient in-network training and an unusually honest evaluation template — but the narrow attacker coverage and untested scalability mean it is a strong proof of feasibility on one testbed, not yet evidence of a deployable defender, and anyone needing production-ready evidence should treat it as a promising first step rather than a settled result.

Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long - Horizon Real-Time Game Agent

R Luo, K Zhang, Q Deng, Y Chen, Z Yang, Y Zhang… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Gamer, a vision-language-action foundation model that plays diverse commercial 3D games through raw screen pixels and native keyboard/mouse actions, combining continued pre-training on gameplay trajectories, sparse-reasoning instruction tuning, memory-linked reinforcement learning (TA-GRPO), and a custom low-latency serving engine (Streaming-vLLM). - Why it's important: Real-world embodied agents are expensive to train and evaluate, and modern games offer visually complex, long-horizon, real-time environments without APIs or privileged state — a setting prior game agents (built on game-specific APIs, action spaces, or paused evaluation) do not address. - How it does it: The core moves are (1) a unified device-level action serialization (5 Hz observations, six 33 ms key/mouse blocks per step), (2) segmenting long rollouts with the same memory-compaction summaries used at inference so that GRPO can be applied to finite, verifiable-scored segments without restoring game states (TA-GRPO), and (3) a serving engine with stateful KV-cache reuse, incremental RoPE refresh, and FSM-guided speculative decoding that cuts end-to-end latency from ~1.31 s to 65 ms (20.1×). - The good: The staged ablation across the full pipeline on held-out Honkai: Star Rail content is convincing: on two side quests (30 and 55 milestones), accuracy rises from 0.0%/13.9% (base Qwen3-VL-8B) to 34.4%/47.9% (CPT), 72.2%/69.1% (SFT), and 80.0%/83.6% (RL), and the paper shows concretely that low-latency rollouts prevent reward collapse in online RL that occurs with a 0.6-FPS control. - The missing: Almost all headline evaluation is on the authors' own game (HSR) with self-built, engine-instrumented verifiers and held-out tasks within a familiar game rather than unseen games; there are no error bars or significance tests (3 attempts per task), and no ablation isolating the contribution of TA-GRPO's temporal credit-assignment weights or the CPT debiasing tricks. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building real-time interactive/embodied agents or serving systems for agentic inference — the TA-GRPO formulation and the latency-versus-RL-quality finding are directly transferable — but skip it if you want unbiased cross-game generalization evidence, since the strongest results are on the publisher's own title.

Problem & Motivation: Game-playing agents that matched humans on Atari, Minecraft, and StarCraft II rely on privileged internal states, tailored action spaces, or dedicated APIs, and generalize poorly beyond their training domain. Modern commercial 3D games (e.g., Honkai: Star Rail) instead demand pixel-only perception, native keyboard/mouse control, partial observability, delayed feedback, and tasks lasting hours — conditions under which conventional inference latency causes actions to arrive after the game state has changed, degrading both deployment performance and the quality of online RL rollouts. The authors (a game studio's AI R&D team) want a single generalist agent that transfers across games and supports real-time interaction and online learning without invasive game modifications. The specific gaps addressed are: unified transferable control across heterogeneous games, long-horizon task execution beyond a finite context window, and stable online RL under real-time constraints. Key Idea: The central insight is that the same memory-compaction mechanism used at inference (periodically summarizing evicted interaction history into a persistent task memory) can also partition long online rollouts into finite, memory-linked segments, allowing GRPO-style group-relative advantage estimation over verifiable segment outcomes without fitting an entire trajectory into context or restoring intermediate game states — with a temporal decay weighting (β-discount, weights normalized to mean 1) distributing each segment's advantage across its steps. A second, arguably equally load-bearing idea is that inference latency is not just a deployment metric but a training-quality variable: delayed actions bias collected trajectories and cause reward collapse, motivating a heavily engineered real-time serving path shared by training and deployment. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages sharing one autoregressive policy (no action head; actions serialized into the LM vocabulary). (1) CPT trains on ~2.4K hours of cross-game trajectories (VPT, D2E, OpenP2P pools) plus ~15% general vision-language data (~6.3B tokens total), using a unified action format (accumulated mouse Δ plus six key/button sets per 200 ms interval, 30 Hz control), a per-game control specification in the prompt, random key remapping (a sampled bijection over rebindable keys applied consistently to spec, history, and targets, to break key-identity shortcuts), and repeat-aware loss decay (ωt = γ^(nt−1), γ=0.9, down-weighting the >85% of steps that repeat the previous action). (2) SFT on ~1K hours of GPT-5.6-Luna-annotated HSR gameplay (1.2M think annotations, 63K task segments, 223K memory summaries) at three instruction levels (operation/subgoal/task), training sparse reasoning (rt ∈ {∅, current reasoning, memory summary}) and summary-based cross-context memory within a single autoregressive objective. (3) TA-GRPO samples G=8 rollouts per task, partitions them into segments linked by generated memory summaries, scores segments by environment-verifiable outcomes (game-engine-side verifiers; no learned reward model or critic), normalizes within-stage groups, and applies the temporally weighted clipped token-level GRPO objective. (4) Streaming-vLLM serves training rollouts and deployment: paged KV-cache reuse with incremental RoPE refresh after compaction, GDN state carryover for hybrid backbones, all-layer megakernels, selective W8A8 quantization, FSM-drafted speculative decoding with BF16 verification, and streaming dispatch of the first action blocks before the packet completes. RL uses 64 H200 GPUs serving 32 parallel Windows game clients, 128 rollouts per iteration. Key design decisions: segment grouping by task stage rather than identical states (justified by avoiding game-state restoration, but acknowledged to mix state distributions); temporal weighting as a prior (explicitly noted not to imply later actions cause outcomes); verifier access to privileged game state kept strictly environment-side (the policy sees only pixels). Key Results: On four public benchmarks (MCU, ViZDoom, OmniGameArena, GameWorld) under real-time evaluation, CPT-only checkpoints score 29.5 (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 31.5 (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE) average versus 17.6 for the strongest general-purpose baseline (GPT-5.6-Sol), with 65.3 vs 8.7 on MCU; baselines are current frontier models (GPT-5.6/6.1, Gemini-3.8-Flash, Claude-Opus-5.0, GLM-5.3-Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision), and RT-vs-TP deltas show baselines losing 21–35 points when the game runs during inference while Gamer loses little (the MoE policy gains +3.4). On held-out HSR side quests, Gamer-RL reaches 80.0% and 83.6% pooled milestone accuracy (vs 28.1%/41.8% for GPT-5.6-Sol); on the 40-instance, 7-type minigame suite the macro-average goes 3.2% → 15.0% (CPT) → 39.2% (SFT) → 49.7% (RL), though Janus's Maze drops from 52.4% to 23.8% after RL. The GameScaling companion study (120 CPT configurations, ~45K H200 GPU-hours) fits a composition-aware scaling law (R²=0.982/0.995 within-mixture for Minecraft/training-game validation) and shows distant unseen games do not keep improving with more CPT data (b→0). Streaming-vLLM scores 83.29 StreamingBench / 62.3 OVO-Bench on Qwen3-VL-8B at 0.08 s latency versus 0.53 s for DSCache at matched accuracy, and the cumulative system ablation shows 1,306 ms → 65 ms end-to-end latency (20.1×) on H200 with the 35B-A3B MoE. Scale tested is substantial on infrastructure (64 H200s, 32 concurrent game clients) but the eval tasks are 2 side quests and 40 minigames from one game, plus 4 external benchmarks. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (Gamer + Streaming-vLLM + the engine-instrumented HSR RL sandbox), with NEW METHOD components (TA-GRPO's memory-linked segment-level RL with temporal credit assignment) and an EMPIRICAL FINDING (low inference latency is a prerequisite for stable online RL in non-pausable environments). Genuinely novel: connecting inference-time memory compaction to RL trajectory segmentation so long-horizon online RL works within finite contexts without state restoration; the RT-vs-TP evaluation methodology exposing that frontier MLLMs' game performance largely evaporates in real time. Standard combinations applied to a new setting: CPT→SFT→RL recipe, GRPO (from DeepSeekMath), speculative decoding, paged KV caches, D-CPT-law-style scaling fits, repeat-aware decay (adopted from Game-TARS), and LLM-annotated instruction data (following GameHorizon) are all existing techniques; the 5 Hz/6-block device-level action format follows prior keyboard-mouse agents (Lumine, Game-TARS). Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present for the serving stack (a clean cumulative configuration ablation, Table 9) and the training stages are ablated sequentially (base→CPT→SFT→RL on every eval suite), but component-level ablations are missing for random key remapping, repeat-aware loss decay, the temporal weighting in TA-GRPO (β), and sparse-vs-dense reasoning — the paper attributes gains to stages, not mechanisms. The 120-configuration scaling study provides R², RMSE, block-wise holdouts, and 300 bootstrap resamples, but that study lives in a companion paper (GameScaling, arXiv:2610.28698, same team) and is summarized here. No error bars or significance tests on game evaluations (3 attempts per task, averaged); no seeds reported. Release is partial: the inference engine and CPT-scaling checkpoints are open, but — explicitly for data-security reasons — no HSR data and no HSR-trained model checkpoints, meaning the headline side-quest and minigame results are not reproducible. Methodological concerns: the flagship evaluation is on the authors' own commercial title with self-built, engine-instrumented verifiers and GM-scripted initial states (a Goodhart-style risk since the verifiers define both RL reward and reported success); frontier baselines on HSR are evaluated zero-shot against a fine-tuned specialist; the "tens of thousands of hours" framing in the abstract overstates the ~2.4K-hour CPT corpus plus 11K hours of raw HSR video from which only ~1K hours survive filtering. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a strong SYSTEMS component). Practical: Runs on commercially available A800/H200 GPUs, but the RL configuration (64 H200s serving 32 game environments, plus separate CPT/SFT clusters) is far beyond individual-lab scale, and the 35B-A3B serving target needs datacenter hardware. Efficient: Streaming-vLLM is genuinely efficient — 0.08 s query latency and 22 GB peak memory on Qwen3-VL-8B, a 20.1× end-to-end latency reduction for the MoE model — and the paper shows this efficiency is load-bearing for RL stability, not just deployment. Effective: The evidence shows it solves held-out tasks within a familiar game and transfers control (not tasks) to unseen games; zero-shot transfer to visually and mechanically distant games remains weak per the authors' own scaling analysis. Scalable: Only claimed, not tested, beyond 32 concurrent environments and one game's task distribution; the paper's own scaling law warns that gains from more gameplay data saturate without target-relevant coverage. The work delivers a partial software artifact (inference engine + scaling-study checkpoints on the project page, mihoyo-gamer.github.io); the trained generalist agent itself stops at paper form due to unreleased HSR components. Strengths: (1) The RT-vs-TP paired evaluation is a genuinely clarifying methodological contribution — it quantifies that frontier MLLMs lose 21–35 points when the game does not pause for inference, reframing latency as a capability variable rather than an engineering footnote. (2) TA-GRPO's memory-linked segmentation is a clean, well-motivated solution to a real problem (finite context vs. hour-long rollouts in online RL) that reuses one mechanism (compaction) across training and inference rather than bolting on a separate memory model. (3) The staged evidence chain (base→CPT→SFT→RL on identical held-out tasks, with per-interaction-type milestone breakdowns) is unusually transparent for an industry system paper. (4) The honest negative results in the scaling analysis — distant unseen games plateau or degrade with more CPT data, and a high nominal R² can mask within-mixture R² of 0.079 — show unusual willingness to report where scaling does not help. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that evaluation covers a selected set of environments and task structures; that Streaming-vLLM's serving cost limits wider deployment; and that fast, continuous interaction does not guarantee deep deliberation, proposing future System-1/System-2 hierarchical agents. They also acknowledge within the scaling analysis that distant unseen games do not benefit from additional CPT data and that the scaling relation is an empirical description of the measured regime, not a universal law. This is a reasonably direct confrontation of limitations, though the framing stays constructive and does not dwell on the evaluator-in-the-loop concern. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Reward/eval verifier circularity: the same engine-side verifiers define the TA-GRPO reward and the reported success metric, so RL could partially optimize the verifier rather than the task, and there is no independent human or external check of verifier validity. (2) No statistical treatment: 3 attempts per task with no variance, seeds, or significance testing is thin for headline claims of +7.8/+14.5 point RL gains. (3) The minigame RL regression on Janus's Maze (52.4%→23.8%) is reported but not analyzed — a dog-not-barking signal about TA-GRPO's temporal weighting or reward hacking on timing-sensitive tasks. (4) No ablation of the CPT debiasing tricks (key remapping, repeat-aware decay) or of sparse reasoning versus always-think, so the paper's mechanism claims rest on stage-level attribution only. (5) Annotation quality from GPT-5.6-Luna (1.2M think labels, 223K memories) is never validated against human annotation, yet the entire SFT signal derives from it. (6) Frontier baselines on HSR are zero-shot with no tooling or fine-tuning budget parity, making the 80%+ vs ~28% gap partly a statement about specialization rather than agent quality. (7) The abstract's "tens of thousands of hours" and "cross-domain (physical and virtual)" framing outruns the evidence: only ~1K hours are annotated, and no physical/embodied environment is actually evaluated. Bottom Line: A practitioner building real-time interactive agents should read this for the TA-GRPO formulation, the RT-vs-TP evaluation methodology, and a credible demonstration that serving latency determines RL training stability — but should treat the headline HSR numbers as a specialist evaluated by its own publisher on its own game, with no stronger public alternative currently covering the same ground.

WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection (49 ▲ )

Yipeng Du, Yuxi Li, Ying Zhang, Chong Sun, Chen Li, Jing Lyu, Ying Tai · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 20 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WeVisForensics, an agentic AI-generated video detector in which an RL-trained investigator adaptively dispatches temporal-scoped inspections to a library of forensic sub-agents that co-evolve with it via a dual-timescale algorithm (DTPO), supported by a new role-structured dataset (ForenCue-30K) and agentic benchmark (AgenticCue). - Why it's important: Synthetic video is becoming indistinguishable from real footage, and prior detectors either reason in one holistic pass (missing brief/localized artifacts) or run static multi-agent workflows whose frozen experts cap what better routing can recover; verdicts also need localized, auditable evidence rather than free-form rationales. - How it does it: The investigator is updated on every rollout batch with GRPO using a correctness reward, a tool-coverage F1 bonus, and CLUE — a per-call credit score measuring how much each inspection shifted a frozen reference model toward the true label — while inspectors are slowly refined by on-policy privileged distillation from an EMA teacher on exactly the calls the investigator issued, plus reflector-revised "skill card" rules refreshed every 20 steps. - The good: The ablations cleanly isolate the claim: co-evolution reaches 95.2% average accuracy versus 91.3% (SFT), 93.2% (investigator-only RL), and 92.0% (inspectors-only), and sub-agent evidence F1 rises by up to 31.3 points (physical role on GenBuster), directly showing the inspectors improve, not just the routing. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests on any headline number; the AgenticCue role-relevance labels come from the authors' own VLM annotation pipeline (the same technology and taxonomy as their training data), and there is no evaluation under compression, re-encoding, or adversarial perturbation — standard stresses for deployed forensic detectors. - Read it or not: Read it if you build MLLM-based forensic agents or multi-agent RL with evolving tools — it is the most complete documented instance of coordinator–tool co-evolution — but skip it if you need a lightweight detector, since each verdict costs a multi-turn loop of ~2.2 VLM sub-agent calls.
