Problem & Motivation: Media-forensics platforms and misinformation defenses need reliable detection of AI-generated video as commercial generators (the paper cites Veo 3, Kling, Sora 2, Seedance) approach photographic fidelity. Two gaps in prior MLLM-based approaches motivate the work: (a) chain-of-thought detectors judge the whole video in one pass, so artifacts confined to a brief interval or small region get missed or explained away, and their claims cannot be supervised or audited individually; (b) agent-based detectors either fix the entire workflow or train only the coordinator over frozen specialists (e.g., ARGUS freezes its four observers), so an inspector that misses a subtle artifact bounds the whole system regardless of how well the judge is trained. Existing forensic datasets also supervise only a single verdict or holistic rationale, providing neither role-specific evidence with temporal intervals nor executed coordination trajectories. Key Idea: The investigator's own RL rollouts double as the training curriculum for the inspectors. Because updating coordinator and experts simultaneously makes each a moving target for the other, updates are split across two timescales: a fast process (GRPO on the investigator every batch, against a fixed inspector snapshot) and a slow process (inspectors distilled on-policy from an EMA teacher, grounded in annotated artifact intervals, every H=20 steps), after which the refined library re-enters subsequent rollouts. This closes the loop so the system's interaction experience — not an external annotator at training time — drives both what is asked and what is reported. Methodology: The system formalizes detection as a POMDP-style investigation: an investigator policy π_θ sees ~1-FPS overview frames (≤16) and at each turn either calls one of six sub-agents with a role and temporal scope, or emits a real/fake verdict; at most 4 calls, no repeated calls, and no audio tools on silent videos are allowed, and invalid trajectories score zero reward (Eq. 4). The Forensic Sub-agent Library has four trainable visual inspectors (appearance, physical consistency, commonsense, OCR — the last a three-stage PaddleOCR-plus-crop pipeline on a chosen timestamp) and two fixed audio tools (voice profile, ASR timing). Training has two stages. Stage I is SFT on ForenCue-30K (30,000 videos; 117,552 role-specific records; 33,896 executed trajectories; 7,500-row RL pool), with a masked next-token loss over model-authored tokens; all five models are rank-64 LoRA adapters on a shared frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone. Stage II, DTPO, runs GRPO (G=4 rollouts) with advantages augmented by CLUE (Eq. 10: clipped log-ratio of the frozen reference's correct-label probability before/after each inspection report, group-centered, λ=0.2) and a tool-coverage F1 bonus (weight 0.3). The slow process keeps calls whose scope overlaps annotated artifact intervals (Eq. 12), partitions them into hits/false-alarms/misses/hedges (a correct-but-inconclusive low-CLUE answer is relabeled a hedge, κ=−0.05), and optimizes a privileged-distillation loss (Eq. 14): an EMA teacher sees the ground-truth label/intervals the student does not, trained by on-policy distillation KL plus a two-way verdict-token contrast. A frozen reflector LLM proposes skill-card rule edits accepted only if they improve held-out correctness monotonically. All design choices are justified — frozen audio tools (label scarcity, measurement stability), execution-grounded rather than imagined trajectories, and monotone card acceptance — though the H=20 cadence is justified mainly empirically (Table 7). Key Results: WeVisForensics-DTPO reaches 97.7% on in-domain GenBuster, 97.5% on GenBuster++, 88.0% mean on the six unseen-generator MintVid categories, and 97.0–98.8% on the five AgenticCue categories, averaging 95.2% — 9.0 points above the strongest prior detector (VideoVeritas, 86.2%) and 19.0 above ARGUS (76.2). Baselines are current per the paper's timeline (NeurIPS'25/26, CVPR'26, ICML'26, COLM'26 methods; Gemini-3.1-Pro), and binary detectors were retrained on the authors' data, though they sit near chance (46.4–57.0% on GenBuster++). Process-level evidence: invocation precision of 94.3–99.7% against base rates of 21.5–91.1% (2.19 calls/video, 12.4% fewer than SFT), physical sub-agent F1 rising from 66.5% to 97.8% on GB with inconclusive rate falling from 26.9% to 0.3%, and a paired blind human review preferring evolved evidence 65–20 with flawed responses cut from 30.5% to 8.0%. A notable negative control: GRPO alone gains 2.9% in-domain but only 0.4% on AgenticCue, showing that frozen experts bottleneck the coordinator. Tested scale is standard benchmark scale (hundreds to ~2,300 videos per split); no stress-scale or long-video stress tests are reported. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (DTPO, the dual-timescale co-evolution of a tool-calling coordinator with the tools themselves) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (ForenCue-30K's role-decomposed, interval-grounded supervision; AgenticCue's invocation-precision metric). The surrounding machinery — ReAct-style tool loops, GRPO, EMA mean-teachers, on-policy distillation, Voyager-style skill cards — is a competent combination of existing techniques; the genuinely new element is the closed-loop schedule in which investigator rollouts are curated by annotation overlap into the inspectors' curriculum, and the empirical demonstration that this beats both staged and every-step alternatives. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a strength: component-wise (Table 6), schedule-wise (Table 7: every-step refresh costs up to 4.8% on unseen generators; staged training 2.4% on the six-generator mean), a 2×2 investigator×inspector crossover showing super-additive gains (+3.9% vs 1.3% summed single-level gains), and role-level evidence scoring against annotations. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests appear anywhere; all results appear to come from single training runs. Human audits exist but are small (340 annotations, 100 trajectories, 200 paired comparisons). Code, weights, project page, and datasets are linked for release (github.com/Tencent/WeVisForensics, huggingface.co/tencent/WeVisForensics). Methodological concerns: the annotation pipeline and the AgenticCue relevance labels both come from the authors' own VLM annotators and role taxonomy, so the benchmark partially rewards the training taxonomy; the CLUE reference is the same model family as the agent backbone (base Qwen3.5-4B), a mild circularity risk for credit scores; in-domain evaluation overlaps training sources (GenBuster-200K feeds both training data and the in-domain benchmark); and this is a company-lab (Tencent WeChat Vision) self-reported evaluation, albeit with promised public artifacts. The paper is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2611.21373), not peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built agent system run end-to-end, evaluated on benchmarks). Practical: Yes — a single frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone plus five LoRA adapters served via vLLM is commodity-hardware feasible. Efficient: Inference costs ~2.2 multi-turn sub-agent calls per verdict plus investigator turns — substantially costlier than single-pass detectors, and no latency/GPU-cost per verdict is reported; training completes in about a day, but the cluster size is unstated. Effective: On the authors' benchmarks it both detects and grounds verdicts in localized, timestamped evidence with measured invocation precision, but effectiveness against compression, re-encoding, and deliberate evasion — the deployment threats that matter in forensics — is untested. Scalable: Untested beyond ~15–30 s clips and current generator diversity; the skill-card/LoRA refresh cadence (every 20 steps, manual-length rule lists) is an untested bottleneck if the generator distribution shifts faster. Delivered artifacts: code, trained weights, datasets, and benchmark, i.e., a full software artifact, not just a paper. Strengths: - The core contribution is real, not cosmetic: the 2×2 crossover (Table 9) and the GRPO-vs-DTPO ablation show that inspector evolution — not just adaptive routing — drives out-of-domain transfer (+2.3% MintVid, +2.7% AgenticCue from the slow process alone), which is the paper's central and otherwise-unclaimed point. - CLUE is a clean, cheap solution to per-call credit assignment in tool-use RL: it scores the informativeness of each report against a third-party frozen reference rather than the policy's own belief, avoiding self-reinforcing credit. - The data design avoids a known failure mode of forensic SFT: real videos contribute "no-issue" records under every role, and generated videos get "no-issue" under roles without visible artifacts, preventing inspectors from learning "generated ⇒ my artifact type is present." - Evaluation goes beyond verdict accuracy to process quality — invocation precision against base rates, role-level evidence F1, blind paired human review, and training-time visualization of miss rates and skill-card evolution — which most agent papers omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: There is no dedicated limitations section or failure-mode discussion in the paper. Limitations are acknowledged only implicitly and locally: audio tools stay fixed because labeled audio forgeries are scarce; inconclusive reports are treated as genuine evidence limitations rather than hidden decisions; invocation precision is read jointly with accuracy to prevent gaming by skipping inspections. The authors do confront competing training schedules head-on (Table 7) rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive, but scope boundaries such as robustness to post-processing or adversarial evasion are never raised. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical uncertainty anywhere: with ~500–1,000 videos per split, 9-point margins survive noise, but 0.5–2-point ablation gaps (e.g., CLUE adding 1.4% only in combination) could plausibly fall within seed variance. - Circular annotation risk: training records, CLUE groundings, the tool-coverage reward, and AgenticCue's role-relevance labels all derive from the same VLM-annotation taxonomy and tooling; the benchmark may partially measure fit to the authors' taxonomy rather than open-ended forensic skill, and human review is sampled, not exhaustive. - No robustness evaluation under compression, transcoding, resolution changes, or adversarial perturbation — the first thing a deployed forensic detector faces — and no discussion of generators deliberately trained to evade semantic/physical-implausibility checks. - Inference efficiency relative to single-pass baselines is never quantified (latency, cost per verdict), despite the 9% accuracy margin being paid for with a multi-turn agent loop. - The near-chance binary-detector baselines (46–57%) despite retraining on the authors' data invite scrutiny of the retraining protocol; either these models are genuinely hopeless on curated data (a finding worth analyzing) or the protocol disadvantages them. - "Real" videos come from stock platforms (OpenVid, Koala, Pexels, Pixabay), which may not represent in-the-wild phone footage, VHS transfers, or heavily edited broadcast content. - The CLUE reference shares its pretraining lineage with the agent backbone; the paper does not test sensitivity to the choice of reference model. Bottom Line: For anyone building MLLM-based forensic agents or, more broadly, multi-agent RL systems where the tools must learn from the coordinator's queries, this paper is worth reading in full — the co-evolution result and its ablations are convincing and the artifacts are released — but practitioners seeking a deployable detector should weigh the untested compression/adversarial robustness and multi-call inference cost before adopting it over a strong single-pass alternative like VideoVeritas.

ForceHarness: Turning Force into Action and Physics for Frozen Frontier Models (39 ▲ )

Ke Sun, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Yike Zhang, Yanzhe Chen, Mike Zheng Shou · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 18 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ForceHarness, a three-layer middleware (force calibration, self-terminating force primitives, physics translation layer) that lets API-only frozen frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra perform contact-rich manipulation using force, with no demonstrations or weight updates, and contributes HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. - Why it's important: Many manipulation tasks (screwing, USB insertion, weighing objects) are impossible from vision alone, and existing force-aware policies require per-task demonstrations and weight updates, which is incompatible with API-only frontier models that increasingly act as zero-shot robot policies. - How it does it: Contact control is closed beneath the model at controller rate via admittance-based primitives that terminate on contact events, while each primitive's force trace is translated by fixed estimators into physical quantities with uncertainties (payload mass, friction, contact height, insertion advance) returned as tool results. - The good: On a real Franka FR3 with no wrist force/torque sensor, GPT-6 Astra improves from 2/60 to 54/60 across six tasks (3.3% → 90.0%), and on HiddenPhys both tested models reach 135/140, matching a hand-written expert force controller and beating Diffusion Policy, π0.5, and ForceVLA trained on ~200 demonstrations per task. - The missing: Tools and perception thresholds were tuned on ForceBench evaluation seeds, real-robot results use only 10 episodes per task without repeating ablations on hardware, and no code or benchmark is released yet (promised "upon publication"). - Read it or not: Read it if you build LLM/VLA robot harnesses or study force-aware manipulation — the primitive-plus-physics-quantities interface pattern and the surprising ablation that small models need computed quantities rather than raw force readings are directly reusable; skip it if you only want a new learned force policy, since it trains nothing.

Problem & Motivation: Frontier multimodal models now act as zero-shot robot policies behind an API with frozen weights, but manipulation tasks involving contact — driving a screw, inserting a plug, sorting bottles by weight — depend on forces invisible to cameras. Prior solutions require either learned force-aware policies trained per task on demonstrations (incompatible with frozen API models) or harnesses that pass raw wrench/tactile streams or ask the model to write force-control code, leaving the model to parse raw sensor numbers. The target problem: give a frozen, slow (seconds-per-decision) API model a usable sense of force without any training or weight access. Key Idea: Split force handling into two time scales and two interfaces: (1) self-terminating primitives regulate force beneath the model at controller rate, ending on contact events (contact, stall, resistance drop, force cap) so the seconds-latency model never needs to react during contact; and (2) a physics translation layer converts each primitive's force trace into a handful of calibrated physical quantities with propagated uncertainties and status flags — deliberately excluding any task thresholds — so the model reasons over "payload mass 0.637 ± 0.033 kg" rather than raw force samples. A third enabling trick: on position-controlled arms, force is produced purely by leading the measured pose with a clamped target (−F ≈ K(p* − p)), so all compliance rides on the stock impedance controller. Methodology: Three layers. (1) Force sensing and calibration: wrench at the flange from a wrist F/T sensor or from external joint torques via least squares w = (Jᵀ)⁺τ_ext; because the torque-based zero drifts with pose, calibration controls when it reads (tare at rest before empty-hand primitives, settle and average after each call, report within-episode changes) rather than filtering. (2) Twelve self-terminating force primitives (probe, push, slide, search, insert, wiggle, screw, press_turn, lift, hold, pull, plus turn/rotation tools) all sharing one loop: each tick a small control law (admittance, v = clip(k_f(F_d − F_u))) updates a clamped target pose, and fixed event detectors with hysteresis stop the call; a fixed guard beneath everything caps force (25 N), torque, speed, and workspace independently of the model. (3) Physics translation layer: fixed estimators (means with standard errors, ratio error propagation, least-squares stiffness fits) pick a meaningful window, remove tares, and return value ± σ plus flags (lost contact, stick-slip, dropped-in), with mass accuracy validated against simulator ground truth (mean error 0.004 kg, σ 0.03 kg matching printed σ). The model issues one tool call per turn from images/instruction/history; primitives like search combine an Archimedean spiral under constant normal force with drop detection. Key design decisions — event-based self-termination, reporting physical quantities instead of raw values, no task thresholds in estimators — are each tested in ablations. HiddenPhys is a seven-task robosuite/MuJoCo benchmark (Weight, CoM, Wipe, Stack, Peg, Latch, Lock) where a seed-drawn hidden variable (mass, CoM offset, table height, hole position, unlock angle, locked/stiff class) decides success, shipped with expert force controllers, position-only controllers, and retrained Diffusion Policy, π0.5, and ForceVLA baselines on identical seeds. Key Results: Real robot (Franka FR3, no wrist F/T sensor, six tasks, 10 episodes each): GPT-6 Astra improves 2/60 → 54/60 with ForceHarness (all tasks differ at p < 0.01, Fisher's exact); GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 47/60. Sorting and soft/hard tasks go from 0/10 to 10/10. ForceBench (8 tasks, Isaac Lab, 10 seeds/task): Astra and Sol both reach 87.5% vs 70.0% and 65.0% without force, versus 35.31% for the best trained policy from the ForceBench paper (not reproduced by authors); force's paired gain concentrates on Drawer Pull (0/10 → 10/10, McNemar p = 0.001). HiddenPhys (7 tasks, 20 seeds/task): Astra 87/140 → 135/140 and Fable 96/140 → 135/140 with zero handle damage, matching the expert force controller (136/140) and far exceeding learned policies at 65–83/140 trained on ~200 demos each; adding force to learned policies gives no consistent gain. Under distribution shift on four tasks, ForceHarness rows drop only 5–8% relatively while learned policies lose 17–25%. Ablations (simulation only): event words alone lift smaller GPT-5.x models from 0.18 to 0.54 success and cut Lock damage 25 → 3 episodes; L2 physical quantities raise small-model decision accuracy from 0.57 (no force) to 0.85 vs 0.69 for raw numbers (McNemar p = 0.023), while Sol does well on any numeric form; turn-by-turn calling reaches 91% vs 77% for one-shot Code-as-Policies programs over the same interface. A notable negative control: ForceBench gains are partly model-driven (70% no-force baseline is already strong), which the authors state explicitly. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (a training-free force harness for frozen API models, combining calibration-by-read-timing, event-terminating primitives, and physics-quantity tool results) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (HiddenPhys with hidden physical variables, expert/learned baselines on identical seeds) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (frozen models with the right force interface match hand-written expert controllers and beat demonstration-trained force policies; smaller models specifically need computed quantities rather than plots or raw samples). The primitives themselves are classical admittance/impedance control and guarded moves from 1980s robotics, and the tool-calling loop is Code-as-Policies-style — the novelty is the interface contract (what is computed, what terminates a call, what the model is told), not the control theory. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong statistical hygiene: paired seeds across all rows, exact McNemar and Fisher tests, Wilson intervals, no dropped test seeds, dev/tuning seeds disjoint from test seeds, damage tracked as a separate safety metric, estimator accuracy validated against simulator ground truth, and honest protocol notes (ForceBench tools and thresholds tuned on 8 of 10 evaluation seeds; two tasks revised after initial runs; the public ForceBench evaluator omits release/clearance checks on three tasks — a generous evaluator favoring their numbers; the no-force control retains kinematic force leaks like 2–3 mm sag). Ablations isolate primitives, feedback form, and loop structure. Concerns: real-robot sample size is 10 episodes/task with an operator labeling success; learned baselines use one training seed each; ForceBench trained baselines are quoted, not reproduced; the component ablation (Table 6) runs only in simulation; code and benchmark are promised "upon publication" and are not yet available (project page: showlab.github.io/ForceHarness). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built system evaluated on real hardware and two simulators). Practical: Yes — runs on a stock Franka FR3 via Polymetis plus commercial API access, needing no wrist F/T sensor; the guard runs on the real-time computer. Efficient: ForceHarness cuts Astra's per-episode API cost by 45% on HiddenPhys (e.g., $0.61 → $0.36) by reducing tool calls; Sol achieves similar success at roughly a fifth of Astra's cost; the seconds of model latency between primitives are the binding cost. Effective: Evidence covers real-robot quasi-static contact tasks, ForceBench, and HiddenPhys — it demonstrably solves the stated problem for the tested task class, though the no-force baseline retains kinematic force leaks, so some margins may be slightly overstated. Scalable: Not tested beyond single-arm tabletop with a parallel gripper; the authors state that multi-second API latency precludes reactive coordination during dynamic motion, and the fixed primitive menu limits transfer to tasks needing new motion laws — 10× task diversity is untested. The work delivers a system artifact (harness + HiddenPhys benchmark + web monitor for episode replay), promised for release on publication; currently paper-only. Strengths: - The core insight — the model decides what and how hard, the primitive decides when to stop, and a fixed guard enforces limits — cleanly resolves the rate mismatch between contact dynamics (ms) and API latency (seconds), and is validated by the event-words ablation (primitives alone cut small-model Lock damage from 25 to 3). - The physics-translation interface is well-motivated and empirically dissected: the finding that GPT-5.x models fail with force plots (0.56) and raw numbers (0.69 decision) but succeed with computed quantities (0.85, p = 0.023) is a genuinely useful, non-obvious result for anyone designing perception channels for LLM agents. - Calibration-by-read-timing (tare near the contact pose, settle-then-read, within-episode comparisons) is a practical answer to drift in torque-derived force estimation, demonstrated on hardware with no wrist sensor at 0.08 N median consecutive-reading difference. - HiddenPhys is a well-designed contribution: hidden variables drawn per seed, identical seeds across expert/learned/frozen-model rows, code-checked success, a damage metric, and distribution-shift tests without retraining. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that model queries add seconds between primitives, precluding reactive replanning during dynamic motion; that the primitive menu and estimators are hand-specified with hand-written per-task instructions (automatic primitive synthesis left to future work); that evaluation covers single-arm tabletop manipulation with a parallel gripper across two API providers; and that component ablations run only in simulation, not on real hardware. They also disclose the ForceBench tuning-on-evaluation-seeds issue and the public evaluator's missing checks. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline real-robot comparison (3.3% → 90.0%) compares against a control that is arguably weaker than a fair no-force baseline in spirit: the no-force condition still leaks force through kinematics (sag, duration), yet the more informative comparison — a trained force-aware policy on the same real tasks — is absent entirely; the real-robot evidence is harness-vs-nothing only. - Real-robot success is operator-labeled (with an external web monitor for review) rather than code-checked, and 10 episodes per task per condition is small for the 86.7-point claim; no confidence intervals are given for Table 3 (only Fisher's test). - The strongest learned-baseline comparison (HiddenPhys) uses noisy text poses instead of images for the frozen models while learned policies see cameras — a perception asymmetry deliberately introduced to isolate force, but one that also flatters the harness on Peg, where the authors note learned policies' cameras reveal the hole. - The two strongest models (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol) both come from OpenAI; the third-party model (Claude Fable 5.2) trails by 12.5 points on ForceBench, so the "any frontier model" framing rests partly on one provider's models. - Development history on ForceBench (tasks revised after seeing initial runs, tools tuned on evaluation seeds) means the 87.5% ForceBench number should be read as development-on-benchmark, and the trained baselines were evaluated under a stricter (unreproduced) original protocol. - No code, weights, or benchmark files are available at review time, so none of the numbers are yet independently checkable. Bottom Line: A practitioner building LLM-driven manipulation should read this: the self-terminating-primitive-plus-physics-quantities interface pattern is immediately reusable and the small-model ablation alone justifies the read, but the ForceBench results deserve discounting for on-benchmark tuning, and the headline real-robot gap needs replication — ideally once the code and HiddenPhys are actually released.

Third Eye: Beyond Immediate Gains in Recursive Self - Improvement

S Dutta, PI Sneha, K Mahitha, S Vanga, N Choudhary · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Third Eye, a paired measurement protocol that evaluates a verified self-generated LoRA update both immediately and after a further native self-update, showing that immediate utility can reverse sign under continuation. - Why it's important: Recursive self-improvement pipelines (STaR, SEAL-style loops) currently judge an update by its immediate checkpoint score, and this paper shows that metric can be misleading — the same selected candidates lose a further 1.78–4.26 pp of utility after one more self-update in several backbones. - How it does it: From each parent model it grows three equal-budget LoRA correction candidates, continues every candidate through three native correction-and-update draws, and scores all checkpoints on development-independent item sets against the unchanged parent with a no-update baseline and frozen, pre-declared statistical tests. - The good: The pre-registered, multiplicity-corrected paired contrast is decisive where it matters — a −1.776 pp continuation decrement with simultaneous 95% interval [−2.876, −0.679] and Holm-adjusted p = 0.0012 — plus a candid selection-effect control (candidate-averaged immediate utility is already −0.686 pp). - The missing: The update recipe is tiny and possibly pathological (two corrections, 50 steps, 400 presentations per update), so the central question of whether real recursive self-improvement regimes suffer the same second-step loss remains untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or evaluating self-improving/self-tuning LLM loops, because it supplies a concrete evaluation protocol and a sobering negative result; skippable for readers seeking a mechanism or a fix, since the controls explicitly resolve neither.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Problem & Motivation: Practitioners building recursive self-improvement loops — where a model generates training data from its own failures, updates its parameters, and repeats — currently assess each update by scoring the resulting checkpoint. Verification (answer checks, execution tests) certifies individual corrections but not the value of training on them, and that value can change after the next update, when the modified model both generates new data and absorbs it. The gap the paper closes is the absence of any measurement framework distinguishing an update's immediate value (H1) from its value after a further native update (H2); prior work like SEAL uses post-adaptation feedback but does not pair horizons with independent scoring and an explicit no-update baseline. The relevant audience is anyone deploying self-generated-data fine-tuning, where silent capability erosion after the first step would otherwise go undetected. Key Idea: Treat a self-update not as a checkpoint but as an adaptation transition: score the parent, every candidate, and every descendant on the same frozen independent item sets under a composite utility (equal-weight mean of target, out-of-distribution, and retention accuracy changes), and report the paired H2−H1 difference. The second key move is decoupling selection from evaluation — candidates are chosen on development items, scored on disjoint final items, and compared against uniform candidate weights to separate the update procedure's effect from the selector's optimism. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) a parent M0 attempts training problems (GSM8K, MBPP); failed problems get up to eight verified correction attempts (answer matching for math, sandboxed execution tests for code); (2) three compositionally distinct two-problem batches form three LoRA candidates (rank 16, 50 AdamW steps, lr 1e-4, 400 presentations, optimizer reset per update), each trained from a restored parent — equation (1); (3) every candidate, selected or not, undergoes three native continuation draws where it generates and verifies its own correction batch before a further identical update — equation (2); (4) all 13 checkpoints per run are scored on fixed dev/final/OOD/retention sets (utility = equal-role mean accuracy change, eq. 3), with the immediate selector's endpoints G1 (eq. 4) and G2 (eq. 5) and paired difference Δ as primary statistics. Critical design decisions: (a) disjoint development and final items to avoid selection optimism — well-justified, backed by an Appendix D diagnostic showing 2.09 pp optimism at K=3 with same-outcome selection; (b) continuing all candidates, not just the selected one — justified as isolating procedure effects from selection; (c) the two-example/50-step update budget — weakly justified, and the paper's own 10/25/50-step controls cannot rule out that this recipe is the problem. Uncertainty uses 5,000 bootstrap replicates resampling parent runs within model/task strata and shared items jointly, with pre-declared test families, simultaneous intervals, and Holm correction. Key Results: Across 64 fresh runs, 192 candidates, 576 continuations, and 832 scored checkpoints on five backbones (Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, SmolLM3-3B): in the balanced 32-run Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility is +0.016 pp ([−1.319, 1.326]) but continued utility is −1.760 pp ([−3.105, −0.420]); the paired decrement is −1.776 pp with adjusted interval [−2.876, −0.679], Holm p = 0.0012. SmolLM3-3B declines 4.262 pp ([−6.163, −2.581]) and Llama-3.1-8B 2.501 pp ([−4.411, −0.583]); Qwen3-8B is inconclusive at −0.681 pp ([−1.914, 0.629]). Candidate-averaged (uniform-weight) immediate utility is already negative at −0.686 pp, showing selection inflates the first-step mean. Role decomposition shows target and OOD losses dominate retention: for Llama-3.2-3B, target −6.45 pp, OOD −3.88 pp, retention −0.01 pp. The REPLAY admission gate commits 21.9% of selected mass and yields −0.27 pp ([−0.80, 0.21]) versus holding — abstention is not a demonstrated fix. Controls on 16 follow-up parents (272 scored cells) find no resolved mitigation: 10-step (+0.47 pp), 25-step (−0.28 pp), and pooled-correction (+0.29 pp) contrasts all cross zero, and the crossed recipient×donor design cannot isolate a mechanism (interaction −0.63 pp [−2.79, 1.56]). A gold-solution arm is 11.56 pp worse than self-generated solutions ([−14.45, −8.64]), attributed to 41–61% fewer assistant-label tokens and elevated syntax failures (e.g., Llama code syntax failures 1.66% → 18.55%), not to reference solutions being intrinsically inferior. Baselines are the current released checkpoints of the tested models, and scale is standard small-model academic scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus a NEW FORMULATION (measuring self-updates as two-horizon adaptation transitions with paired independent scoring). The genuinely novel element is the paired immediate/continued contrast with native correction regeneration and an explicit no-update baseline — no prior work the paper cites separates these horizons for persistent weight updates. The individual machinery (LoRA, self-generated verified corrections, bootstrap pairing, Holm correction, selection-optimism controls) is a competent combination of standard techniques; the gold-solution control is a known-style data-substitution check whose token-count confound the authors honestly surface. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and substantive: uniform vs. selected candidate weights, role decomposition (target/OOD/retention), step-count and pooled-correction controls, a crossed recipient–donor design, and a selection-optimism diagnostic. Statistical practice is unusually careful: pre-declared test families frozen before outcomes, joint run/item bootstrap respecting shared items, simultaneous 95% intervals, Holm-adjusted p-values, and explicit separation of confirmatory from descriptive analyses. The paper distinguishes fresh runs from reused inspected parents and treats checkpoints/draws as repeated measures, not independent units. Concerns: (a) no evidence of a public code/data repository URL — Appendix F says "the accompanying source includes analysis code" and checksums, but no link is stated in the provided text; (b) the study is designed and evaluated around its own measurement objective (equal-role utility), so Goodhart-style concerns apply to the metric itself, though the authors acknowledge the weights are a "specified objective"; (c) Qwen3-8B ran on A100 while other models ran on GH200, and the authors flag that hardware, family, and size are not independently randomized; (d) the 8B models have only four fresh runs per task, limiting precision. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement study with no proposed method or built system). - Practical: Yes — everything runs on single-GPU hardware (GH200/A100) with LoRA rank 16 on 3–8B models, within reach of most labs. - Efficient: Each update is only 50 AdamW steps on two examples, so the protocol's compute cost is dominated by the 832 checkpoint evaluations (128 target + 128 OOD + 256 retention items each), which is substantial but bounded. - Effective: The evidence shows the measurement works and that the stated problem (immediate scores misrepresent update value) is real for four of five backbones; it does not show a fix, and REPLAY fails to beat holding. - Scalable: Untested beyond 3–8B models, two-example updates, and exactly one continuation step (H2); the authors state that transfer to larger batches, full fine-tuning, or longer loops is untested — the claim of broader relevance is asserted, not measured. The work delivers an evaluation protocol and analysis code/checksums as its reusable artifact, not a trained model, library, or tool with a stated public release URL. Strengths: - The paired two-horizon design is a genuinely new empirical question for self-improvement loops, and the headline contrast (−1.776 pp, p = 0.0012) is statistically decisive under conservative multiplicity control. - The selection-effect decomposition is a real insight: the near-zero immediate mean partly reflects selector optimism over an already-negative candidate-averaged utility (−0.686 pp), which reframes how first-step results in this literature should be read. - The role decomposition (target/OOD loss dwarfing retention loss, e.g., −6.45/−3.88/−0.01 pp for Llama-3.2-3B) is actionable: it shows a retention-only safety gate would miss most of the damage. - Unusual candor: the paper reports its failed mitigations (REPLAY, step reduction, gold solutions) as negative results, discloses the gold-arm token-count confound, and pre-declares tests rather than mining the five-model matrix. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state coverage is limited to five 3–8B backbones, two tasks, two-example LoRA updates, and one continuation horizon; transfer to larger batches, full fine-tuning, or longer loops is untested. They concede the recipe may over-specialize, that 8B models have fewer runs and less precision, that hardware and parameter count are confounded, that fixed item sets may overlap pretraining data, that code's dev/final OOD domains differ (MBPP validation vs. HumanEval), that intervals condition on only three averaged continuation draws, and that the control parents reuse inspected runs without establishing a mediator. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central ecological-validity question is unaddressed: a two-correction, 50-step update with 400 presentations is far from any realistic recursive self-improvement regime, and the paper's own controls admit better recipes exist; the finding may partially be an artifact of an aggressive small-batch recipe rather than a property of self-updates generally. - Only one continuation step is measured (H2); whether the observed loss compounds, plateaus, or reverses at H3+ is unknown, which limits the "recursive" framing. - No release URL or repository is given in the text; without the training pipeline and manifests, exact reproduction depends on an "accompanying source" whose availability is unverifiable from the paper. - The equal-role utility weighting is a design choice that determines the headline numbers; no results are reported under alternative weightings, so sensitivity of conclusions to the metric is unknown. - The 16 control parents are not fresh replications, and the donor D0/D1 comparison confounds generation runtime with data composition — the authors note this, but it means the mechanistic section largely produces null results rather than bounds, despite the framing. - The paper measures only greedy pass@1 and conditional-likelihood scoring; no pass@k or sampling-based evaluation is reported, leaving capability loss estimates tied to a single decoding regime. Bottom Line: A practitioner building self-improving LLM pipelines gains a concrete, statistically disciplined evaluation protocol and a genuinely useful caution about first-step scores, but anyone expecting a mechanism or remedy — or evidence at realistic update scales beyond two examples and one extra step — will need to wait for follow-up work.

The good: Independent reproduction of eight shortlisted benchmarks on a fixed eight-model panel is unusually rigorous for a benchmark survey — it empirically demonstrated saturation (three knowledge benchmarks with top models ≥85) and limited discrimination (HealthBench SD ≤ 4), justifying exclusions rather than asserting them. - The missing: The headline 'inclusive healthcare' framing is not delivered by the artifact itself: the release covers only 3 of 9 Atlas cells, has zero patient-facing benchmarks, is 94% US-context and ~93% English text-only tasks, and its one new benchmark (InclusionMed-DxFiles) is private and scored by an LLM judge. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building medical AI evaluation suites or selecting models for healthcare deployment (the role/capability and cost–score analyses are directly actionable), but skippable for methodologists seeking new measurement techniques — there are none.

Problem & Motivation: Teams deploying or building medical AI need to know which model works for which healthcare use case — a clinician's workflow differs from a payer's prior-authorization process and from a patient's health questions — but existing benchmarks concentrate on English exam questions and clinician-style QA. Composite rankings (e.g., Artificial Analysis Healthcare & Medical Index) inherit the coverage biases of their constituent benchmarks, so a high score can say little about the populations, roles, or settings a deployment actually cares about. The paper targets evaluators and healthcare AI adopters who need coverage-aware, context-specific model comparison. Key Idea: The single organizing insight is to make benchmark portfolio composition itself the object of analysis: map every candidate benchmark to a cell in a role-by-capability matrix, audit and reproduce candidates before trusting them, and let the resulting coverage map (including its empty cells) qualify what any aggregate score can mean. This is a measurement-framework contribution, not an algorithmic one — the index is a simple equal-weight mean, and the tagging scheme is a flat annotation layer. Methodology: Three phases. (1) Collection and curation: 388 candidate benchmarks (May 2023–Sep 2026) from literature, platforms, and community submissions, distilled into structured benchmark cards via LLM-assisted curation. (2) Auditing and reproduction: six sequential criteria filtered 388 → 8 shortlisted; independent reproduction of all 8 on a fixed 8-model panel (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen3.8 Max, Qwen3.8 27B, GLM-5.3, Grok 4.3), with pre-specified exclusion rules (saturation: three top models ≥85; limited discrimination: SD ≤ 4), yielding 4 public benchmarks (HealthBench Professional, PhysicianBench, ALE-CLI v1.0 Health & Medicine, CHI-Bench) plus the authors' private InclusionMed-DxFiles (312 NEJM case-record diagnostic reasoning tasks). (3) Index evaluation: 22 models across 11 families run under benchmark-native protocols (API calls, FHIR EHR agent, CLI agent harnesses), each benchmark scored 0–100 and equally weighted at 20%; role/capability sub-scores are cell means; task-level tagging (8 attributes) supports stratified analysis; inference cost is estimated from recorded token usage and published prices. Critical design decisions: equal benchmark weighting (asserted, not justified against alternatives; acknowledged as needing sensitivity analysis), exclusion thresholds of 85/SD 4 (arbitrary but pre-specified), and LLM-judge scoring of DxFiles using GPT-6.1 Sol (questionable — see Gaps). Key Results: Overall InclusionMed Index scores span 17.5–49.1/100 across 22 models; Gemini 4 Argon leads (49.1), followed by Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 (48.9). Rankings diverge by cell: Claude Opus 5.5 leads healthcare professionals (55.6), GPT-6 Astra leads reasoning (58.7), Claude Fable 5.1 leads agency (46.1); GPT-6 Luna ranks 8th in reasoning but 20th in agency. Within-benchmark tagging shows all top-10 models score higher on patient communication (median 69.1) than clinical decision-making, and treatment planning/implementation trails assessment/diagnosis in both HealthBench Professional and 8 of 10 models on PhysicianBench. Cost analysis finds a ~24× per-task cost gap between Kimi K3 ($1.51) and GPT-5.6 Luna ($0.064) at near-identical Index scores (37.9 vs 36.9), with five models on the observed Pareto frontier. Benchmarks are small: 22–525 tasks each; PhysicianBench pass@1 requires all checkpoints to pass, making the 100-case scale a real constraint on precision. Baselines are current frontier models, which is a strength; there is no external validation that Index scores predict downstream clinical utility (acknowledged by the authors). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (InclusionMed-DxFiles) + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the Atlas taxonomy, audit pipeline, and Index as ongoing infrastructure) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (documented saturation of three medical knowledge benchmarks and rank instability across roles/capabilities). The genuinely novel element is the audit-then-reproduce portfolio construction with explicit coverage accounting; the taxonomy, equal-weight composite index, and cost–performance Pareto analysis are competent assemblies of known ideas (HELM/MedHELM-style harnesses, OECD composite-indicator practice, AI-agent cost analysis), applied to a healthcare coverage framing. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style evidence is indirect but real: the reproduction panel empirically demonstrates which candidate benchmarks fail discriminability, and checkpoint-level failure analysis (e.g., 51.4% of 912 failed PhysicianBench checkpoints were clinical reasoning; action execution had the highest within-category failure rate at 17.4%) isolates which capabilities drive scores. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for the 22-model evaluation (CHI-Bench averages 3 runs; other benchmarks are 1 run per task), so adjacent-rank differences (e.g., 49.1 vs 48.9) are statistically unsupported. Code and benchmark materials are on GitHub (github.com/panuvi/inclusionmed) with results on inclusionmed.ai, but the fifth Index component, DxFiles, is private and not independently verifiable. Methodological concerns: (a) DxFiles is graded by GPT-6.1 Sol, itself an evaluated model, against reference diagnoses with an unstated inter-grader agreement check; (b) exclusion criteria were tuned on the same reproduction runs used to select the portfolio (mild Goodhart risk); (c) two of five Index benchmarks map to the same Atlas cell (professionals × agency), so equal weighting does not yield equal cell coverage. The audit pipeline itself is LLM-assisted with human spot-checking, described but not quantified for reliability. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (an evaluation infrastructure/index, evaluated by running it). - Practical: Yes — everything runs via commercial APIs and standard agent harnesses (Codex, Gemini CLI, Claude Code) on ordinary infrastructure; no special hardware. - Efficient: The evaluation itself costs non-trivially (per-task inference up to ~$4 for frontier models), and the paper's own contribution is showing 24× cost spreads at equal quality, which is the practical payoff for adopters. - Effective: It demonstrably ranks models and surfaces coverage gaps, but effectiveness for the stated inclusive-healthcare goal is only a proxy — no patient-facing or non-US evaluation exists in this release, and clinical benefit is explicitly not established. - Scalable: The pipeline is periodic-by-design, but scaling to 9/9 cells and more benchmarks is claimed via community contribution, not demonstrated; only 26.8% of the 388 candidates were even reproducible. The work delivers a live artifact: a website with results, a GitHub repository, a versioned benchmark pool, and the private DxFiles benchmark; it stops short of releasing the full evaluation harness details for all five benchmarks. Strengths: - The independent-reproduction gate is the strongest execution element: excluding saturated benchmarks (XLingHealth, NEJMQA-Exams, PubHealthBench) with published score distributions (Figure S3) is a concrete, verifiable contribution that most composite leaderboards lack. - The coverage accounting is honest and quantified — 388 candidates with country (US 37.1%, China 32.0%), language (English in 87.9%), and reproducibility (only 104/388 fully reproducible) statistics turn the 'inclusion' framing into checkable claims. - Rank instability across roles and capabilities, plus the cost–score decoupling, is a genuinely useful empirical finding for deployment decisions that single-benchmark papers cannot show. - The authors consistently separate what the Index measures from what it does not (e.g., 'improvements on the current portfolio therefore do not establish whether model performance has improved for these populations'), which is unusually disciplined framing. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length: only 3 of 9 Atlas cells are covered; no patient/public benchmark is included; 318 of 338 geographically identifiable tasks are US-based; 99.8% of tasks are text-only; the Index reflects only this portfolio with equal weights (sensitivity analyses deferred to future work); cost estimates exclude judge, tool, sandbox, and retry charges; benchmark scores are not comparable across categories; and clinical deployment requires separate validation. This candor is a credibility positive, though it means the release's scope is far narrower than its title. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - InclusionMed-DxFiles, 20% of the Index, is private, constructed and scored by the authors, with an LLM judge (GPT-6.1 Sol) that is itself a ranked model; no human-expert grading agreement, no judge-robustness check, and no contamination analysis for NEJM-derived cases are reported. - No statistical uncertainty for any headline ranking; with 22 tasks in ALE-CLI and pass-all-checkpoints scoring on 100 PhysicianBench cases, several rank orderings are likely within noise. - Equal weighting is undefined in justification: two benchmarks occupy one cell while three other cells (including all of knowledge and patients-and-public) receive zero weight, so the 'Index' structurally over-weights professional agency work relative to the stated inclusivity mission. - The eight-model reproduction panel doubles as the saturating set for discriminability decisions, and the SD ≤ 4 / ≥85 thresholds are not validated against any downstream consequence. - Model names omit date suffixes 'for readability' while full releases are relegated to an appendix table, and the evaluation is entirely API-based with vendor-default generation settings, limiting strict reproducibility even for the public benchmarks. Bottom Line: A practitioner selecting or evaluating medical LLMs gains real, actionable evidence here — especially the saturation results and the role/capability/cost decomposition — but methodologists should read it as a v0.5 infrastructure report whose inclusivity ambitions materially exceed its five-benchmark, three-cell, US-centric first release, with no stronger existing alternative that audits coverage this systematically.

On the Limits of Sufficient Explanations

K Weinbauer, PF Stadler, T GÃĪrtner, S Malhotra · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a formal framework (instance space + classifier + select relation) that fully characterizes when sufficient sub-instance explanations — e.g., subgraphs for molecules, substrings for text — can exist for a classification task, and derives dataset-level statistics that upper-bound the best any explainer can achieve. - Why it's important: Sufficiency-based explanation methods (Anchors, sufficient input subsets, fidelity-based GNN explainers) are routinely scored as if low scores indicate a poor explainer; this work shows that on most real structured datasets no explainer — not even the trivial whole-instance explainer — can ever be sufficient, so the ceiling is a property of the task, not the method. - How it does it: The core move is the "co-bound" — an instance that can be selected as a sub-instance of a differently labeled instance — plus the theorem that a sufficient explainer exists iff no co-bounds exist; a variant of this argument yields a task-level upper bound (1 − c_t(x)(1 − m_t(x))) on probabilistic sufficiency for every explainer. - The good: The empirical survey is concrete and checks directly on the data: 9 of 10 datasets (AIDS, MCF-7, MUTAG, Mutagenicity, NCI1, ENZYMES, PROTEINS, ToxinPred3, SST-2) contain co-bounds, ruling out sufficient explainers for those tasks outright. - The missing: All analysis is performed against ground-truth dataset labels, not against trained classifiers' predictions — yet practical post-hoc explainers explain model predictions, and the paper does not measure co-bound prevalence under realistic model-induced labelings or trained models. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or benchmark sufficiency-style explainers (rationales, subgraph explainers, Anchors); skip it if you want heavy machinery — the main theorem is nearly trivial, and the value is in the framing and the empirical prevalence tables.

Problem & Motivation: Post-hoc sufficient explanations select a part of the input (subgraph, substring, feature subset) that alone ensures the predicted label. Formal analyses of sufficiency to date (Darwiche & Hirth 2020, Barceló et al. 2020, Marques-Silva et al. 2021) assume constant-size instance spaces like {0,1}^d, where sufficiency is always achievable and the question of existence never arises. For structured data — graphs and strings of unbounded size — one instance can be contained in another with a different label (a mutagenic molecule whose every subgraph also appears in a non-mutagenic molecule; "great" inside "not great"), and no unified analysis existed of when sufficient explainers can exist at all, or how much sufficiency is attainable when existence fails. Practitioners evaluating explanation methods need to know whether failures are the explainer's fault or intrinsic to the task. Key Idea: The single core insight is the co-bound characterization: given a selection order (which sub-instances an explainer may pick) and a classifier, define a co-bound as an instance x that is selectable from some x′ with a different label. Theorem 4.1 shows a sufficient explainer exists iff the task is co-bound free — sufficiency is a joint property of the classifier and the selection formalism, and its absence is an in-distribution obstruction checkable on the dataset, distinct from the out-of-distribution perturbation problems usually blamed for low fidelity. Methodology: The paper defines an instance space X with a sub-instance partial order ⊑, a selection domain of selectable sub-instances, and a select relation ⪯ (a partial order under two mild assumptions: selection is instance-independent, and every element selects itself). An explainer e : X → X must satisfy e(x) ⪯ x; sufficiency (Dasgupta et al. 2022) requires e(x₁) ⪯ x₂ ⟹ f(x₁) = f(x₂). The analysis proceeds by: (i) proving the co-bound iff-existence characterization (Theorem 4.1, two-paragraph proof); (ii) recovering prior existence results as corollaries — antichain/constant-size instance spaces (Theorem 4.2) and monotone classes for class-wise sufficiency (Theorem 4.3), connecting to forbidden-substructure graph characterizations and positive existential FO formulas; (iii) extending to probabilistic sufficiency with the bound mₑ(x) ≤ 1 − c_t(x)(1 − m_t(x)) relative to the trivial explainer (Theorem 4.4); and (iv) showing deletion sufficiency (the perturbation-based criterion used in practice) is always achievable but can be vacuous — on monotone classes even the empty explanation passes. Empirically, the paper computes three dataset statistics from pairwise sub-instance/substring relations (transitive closure via an O(n²) pairwise-check algorithm): co-bound prevalence, minimum accuracy loss from relabeling to make the task co-bound free, and the minimal upper bound M(D) on local probabilistic sufficiency, across 7 graph datasets and 3 string datasets. Critical design decisions: restricting to sub-instance (not similarity/counterfactual) explainers — justified by unifying subgraph/substring formalisms, but acknowledged as excluding whole explanation families; and using ground-truth labels f* rather than a trained classifier's labels — not explicitly justified. Key Results: Main theoretical result: sufficient explainers exist iff the task is co-bound free; every constant-size instance space admits one (Corollary 4.3), while connectedness classification (graphs) and character-majority/sentiment classification (strings) do not (Corollaries 4.1–4.2). The probabilistic-sufficiency bound holds for every explainer; on PROTEINS some instance has probabilistic sufficiency upper-bounded at 58%, on MUTAG at 73%, versus >99% on Mutagenicity and ToxinPred3. Empirically (Table 1): 9/10 datasets contain co-bounds; SST-2 has 14,105 co-bounds (21% of 66,973 instances); AIDS has 47% of sub-instance relations spanning different classes; ToxinPred2 has zero co-bounds. The most interesting finding is that co-bound counts understate the damage: ENZYMES has only 2.2% co-bounds (13/595) yet making it co-bound free requires relabeling 82% of instances, whereas MUTAG at 14% co-bounds needs only a 23% accuracy loss. These are dataset-level measurements against idealized sufficiency, not benchmark scores for competing explainers, so there are no baseline explainers to compare. Tested scale is modest: 183–66,973 instances, with co-bound search taking 14 seconds (MUTAG) to 5 hours (PROTEINS/MCF-7) single-threaded on an i9-12900KF. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM and NEW FORMULATION: the existence question for sufficient explainers on variable-size structured data is genuinely new, and the select-relation/co-bound formalism unifying subgraph, substring, and feature-subset explainers is a real conceptual contribution. The proofs themselves are elementary (the main theorem follows almost immediately from the definitions, and the authors say so), the probabilistic bound is a short measure-concentration argument on nested applicability sets, and the empirical section is a straightforward pairwise-relation census of public datasets — competent execution of the new framing rather than technical depth. Rigor & Reproducibility: Proofs for all claims are included in the appendix and are correct as far as verifiable from the text; theorems are simple enough that this is credible. Empirically, the pipeline is deterministic (no seeds or error bars needed for the combinatorial statistics, and none are relevant). Ablations in the ML sense do not apply, but the paper does disentangle which statistic carries which information (co-bound count vs. minimum accuracy loss vs. probabilistic bound) — e.g., the ENZYMES vs. MUTAG contrast. No public code repository URL is stated; Appendix C lists software packages and versions (PyTorch 2.11, torch-geometric 2.7, NetworkX, etc.) and dataset licenses, which aids but does not guarantee reproduction. Methodological concerns: (a) all statistics are computed against ground-truth labels, not the predictions of any trained classifier, though the motivation is post-hoc explanation of classifiers; (b) the evaluation is entirely on the authors' chosen datasets with no trained models at all, so no learning-based experiment validates that the bounds matter in practice; (c) runtime is only reported on a consumer CPU with no parallelization — not a methodological flaw, but scalability of the O(n²) subgraph-isomorphism checks is untested beyond ~27k graphs. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL with a supporting EMPIRICAL analysis (no trained models, no system artifact). - Sound: Assumptions are explicit and minimal (select relation is acyclic/instance-independent), and proofs are complete; the main gap is a modeling gap — real explainers explain model predictions, not ground truth — not a gap in the proofs. - General: Results hold for any acyclic select relation (they show acyclicity fully characterizes select relations) and any classifier, which is broad; but the framework excludes similarity-based, prototype, and counterfactual explainers by construction. - Tight: The existence characterization is exact (iff), and the probabilistic bound is attained by instances in the surveyed data (values as low as 58% and 18% for ENZYMES), so it is not vacuous; no matching lower-bound formalism is discussed. - Implementable: Yes — the co-bound search and three statistics are simple algorithms (O(n²) pairwise relation checks with transitive closure), directly usable as an audit step for any new structured dataset, though subgraph isomorphism checking is NP-hard in general and costs up to 5 hours for ~27k graphs here. The work delivers reusable analysis machinery (Algorithm 1 plus three metrics) described at implementation level, but no released library, CLI, or packaged dataset is mentioned; it stops at paper form plus enumerated public datasets. Strengths: - A genuinely new question — when do sufficient explainers exist at all — posed and answered exactly, with an iff characterization that cleanly separates what the explanation formalism permits from what the classification task allows. - The co-bound notion converts a philosophical worry ("maybe low fidelity is the task's fault") into a concrete, checkable, in-distribution data condition, with worked witnesses from MUTAG, AIDS, SST-2, etc. - The empirical finding that co-bound count and required relabeling diverge sharply (ENZYMES: 2.2% co-bounds but 82% accuracy loss) is a non-obvious result with direct practical use for interpreting explanation benchmarks. - The paper correctly recovers prior positive results (propositional logic, constant-size spaces, monotone classes) as corollaries of one framework, and honestly proves its own main theorem is technically trivial rather than overselling it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion explicitly states the formalism "does not cover every possible way of explaining decisions" — similar-instance explainers, prototypes, and counterfactuals are excluded and left to future work. The authors also note that the probabilistic analysis assumes a distribution over instances (empirically, the dataset distribution) and that deletion sufficiency, while always achievable, can be vacuous. They confront these limitations directly and do not minimize them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The largest unacknowledged gap: every statistic is computed against ground-truth labels, but the motivating use case is post-hoc explanation of trained models; a classifier trained on a co-bound-laden dataset will typically fit or label those instances consistently, and the paper never measures co-bound prevalence or M(D) under model predictions, so the practical severity for deployed explainers is extrapolated rather than measured. (2) The select relation is assumed given and binary, but for real graph explainers (e.g., GNNExplainer's soft masks) "subgraph" selection is graded and architecture-dependent; sensitivity of the statistics to this choice is not explored beyond the node/edge-induced/any-subgraph taxonomy. (3) No trained model, no explanation method, and no fidelity score is ever run, so the paper cannot demonstrate that the claimed task-level ceiling actually explains observed low fidelity scores in any existing benchmark — the bridge from bound to practice is asserted. (4) Dataset-scale ceiling: O(n²) subgraph-isomorphism checks (5 hours for 27k graphs) make the audit infeasible for web-scale corpora without indexing tricks the paper does not discuss. (5) The SST-2 analysis conflates phrase-level parse-tree fragments with instances (the paper footnotes this), which inflates substring co-bound prevalence relative to how substring explainers are used on full sentences. Bottom Line: Anyone designing or interpreting sufficiency-style evaluation for graph or text explainers should read this — the co-bound check is a cheap, useful pre-audit and the ENZYMES/MUTAG contrast alone justifies it — but readers seeking evidence that these dataset-level bounds predict real explainer failure on trained models will need to run that experiment themselves.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds Agency, a Valgrind-inspired interposition platform (ptrace + cgroups) that transparently monitors and rewrites context, tool calls, and LLM requests of unmodified off-the-shelf agent harnesses (Claude Code, Codex CLI), and uses it to deploy five cost-optimization techniques that cut end-to-end agent cost to 0.77× baseline on average (up to 35% reduction) with a 0.97× accuracy ratio. - Why it's important: LLM API costs are dominated by re-reading cached context on every turn — cache reads reach 73% of total execution cost on long sessions — and harness choice alone swings cost by up to 2.6× at equal accuracy, so anyone running coding or retrieval agents at scale pays a large, avoidable harness tax. - How it does it: The core move is cost-aware context management: a closed-form savings model (Eq. 2: cache-read savings minus compression cost minus extra-turn cost) gates three context-compression tiers (lossless tool-output compaction, LightGBM-predicted context garbage collection, a subtask 'stack machine' that pops finished subtask contexts) plus SQLite metadata tables that replace filesystem-search tool-call chains, all inserted between the harness and its environment without touching harness or model. - The good: The characterization is quantitatively concrete and the evaluation includes real per-technique ablations (e.g., metadata-assisted search alone cuts cost 32% on OfficeQA; Problem & Motivation: Agent harnesses (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, SWE-agent-style ReAct loops) impose large per-run costs through system prompts, tool schemas, and the turn-by-turn re-reading of the full context, yet recent evidence (Pan et al., 2026, plus the authors' own 100-task study across four harnesses and five models) shows harness choice barely affects task accuracy on frontier agentic models — a bare ReAct harness with only a bash tool matches Claude Code's accuracy. Cost, however, varies up to 2.6× for the same model and task, and long-horizon sessions cost 10–100× more than short ones. The gap the paper closes: existing token/context-reduction work (observation masking, ACON, Context-Folding, LLMCompiler) targets long-context capability or latency, requires fine-tuning or model cooperation, and does not optimize end-to-end dollar cost under provider pricing models (cache reads vs. cache writes vs. uncached input vs. output). The intended beneficiaries are users and platform teams running commercial coding/retrieval agents who cannot modify closed-source models or vendor harnesses. Key Idea: The key insight is that agent cost under provider pricing is a linear function of per-call context reads, writes, and outputs (Eq. 1), so every optimization decision — compress, delete, batch, index — reduces to a simple break-even calculation (Eq. 2: net saving = pr·N·Δ cache-read savings − compression cost − extra-turn cost), and that this calculation can be enforced by an OS-level interposition layer (ptrace/cgroups, hash-list context representation with lookup-table rewriting) that transparently manipulates any black-box harness without modifying it. This reframes harness optimization from an accuracy problem (where harnesses don't matter) to a cost problem (where they matter a lot). Methodology: The paper has two phases. Phase 1 — characterization: cost-decompose ~23K traces (own runs on 100 tasks across SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 2, OfficeQA Pro, plus 18K public TraceLab/FreeInference traces) into cache-read/new-input/output components per call; classify tool-output tokens as used/unused by checking whether the agent later references each line; build turn-dependency graphs labeled by GPT-6-Luna and replay traces with unneeded subtask contexts pruned; vary OfficeQA filesystem layouts (flat/tree, plaintext/UUID names) to isolate search cost. Phase 2 — system: Agency runs a host engine and a sandbox engine bridged by a Unix Domain Socket; the sandbox engine wraps the harness in ptrace/cgroups, translates provider-specific LLM-call formats into a shared representation (message blocks as hash lists with lookup tables), logs to SQLite, and applies user hooks that rewrite context, batch tool calls, or gate tool execution on resource availability. The five techniques: (1) near-lossless tool-output compaction (whitespace/format stripping, deduplication, cross-output line pointers) applied before caching; (2) LightGBM-based context garbage collection predicting per-line reuse probability and remaining turns, firing only when Eq. 2's predicted saving is positive; (3) a subtask stack machine that phase-classifies turns, groups them into segments, and every T=6 segments replaces the popped subtask's turns with a summary block (91% token reduction per firing, fires once per ~20 turns); (4) metadata-assisted search via offline-extracted SQLite tables (files + per-line-range entries, rule-based AST/heading extraction) exposed in the user prompt; (5) tool-call batching via a user-prompt instruction. Critical design decisions: compression must happen before cache writes land (justified by the cache-invalidation analysis); GC is deliberately conservative/mechanical rather than LLM-based (justified because LLM output cost outweighs savings — stated, not quantified); batching via prompt rather than harness forcing (justified by failed alternatives on small models, though it is the least 'systematic' of the five). Key Results: End-to-end across 100 coding tasks and 100 OfficeQA retrieval tasks, 4 frontier models, 3 harnesses: cost ratio 0.65–0.85 vs. baseline (average 0.77, i.e., 23% savings; headline max 35% on OfficeQA Pro tree/UUID layout, 0.51–0.66), accuracy ratio 0.97 average (0.98–0.99 for Sol/Sonnet/Opus; 0.93 for GPT-6-Luna, which misuses the SQLite metadata tables). Ablations (Basic-full, GPT-6-Luna, coding tasks): tool output compaction 0.95 cost ratio, context GC 0.88, subtask stack machine 0.94, metadata-assisted search 0.68 on OfficeQA (32% cost cut, 42% fewer cache reads, steps 16.7→13.5) — and tool call batching 1.02, a 2% cost increase despite 19% fewer steps, because Luna issues 11% more tool calls when told to batch. Savings grow with run length (0.93 for <100K-token runs vs. 0.67 for >1M-token runs). 17–29% of individual tasks cost more than baseline; savings concentrate in the longest, most expensive runs. Baselines are current commercial harnesses and pricing (AWS Bedrock +10% surcharge), though comparison against prior compression tools (Headroom, RTK, ACON) is qualitative, not experimental. Tested at standard benchmark scale (traces 2–3× shorter than real-world traces, which the authors note understates benefits). The counter-intuitive finding is that SOTA agents already know common repository structures from training, so metadata search helps retrieval tasks far more than coding tasks (0.2 lookups/run on coding vs. 4.8 on OfficeQA). Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the Agency interposition platform) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the cost-accumulation decomposition: cache-read dominance, tool-call cost gradients, tool-output sparsity, filesystem-search share, subtask breadth). The five optimization techniques are individually competent recombinations of known ideas — line-pointer deduplication resembles existing tools (Headroom/RTK), turn-batching echoes LLMCompiler, stack-based subtask summarization echoes Context-Folding — but the genuinely novel element is the cost break-even model (Eq. 2) governing when each is safe to fire, plus applying them transparently to unmodified commercial harnesses and closed models, which no prior work does. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and individually reported per technique with token-class breakdowns (cache read/new input/output/steps/cost), which is better than most systems papers of this type. Error bars are sparse: the transparency test gives a proper 95% CI, but end-to-end results in Figs. 8–10 are single-run distributions (quartiles/whiskers across tasks, not across seeds); agent runs are inherently stochastic and no repeated-seed variance is reported. The dependency-graph ground truth is LLM-labeled (GPT-6-Luna) and never validated against human labels — a quiet circularity risk for the Sec. 3.6 headroom numbers. Methodological concerns: (a) the model used for labeling is also one of the evaluated models; (b) pricing assumptions (AWS Bedrock rates, caching behavior, 5-min cache TTL) are baked into every number and, as the authors admit, may change; (c) the analysis is retrospective while deployment is online, so observation-based upper bounds (73% cache-read share, 27% output utilization) cannot be achieved live; (d) batching is evaluated via a prompt addition, which is not deterministic or 'system-level' in the sense the paper claims. No public code, model, or dataset release is mentioned. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built interposition platform evaluated by deployment on commercial harnesses). Practical: Yes — it runs unmodified Claude Code and Codex CLI on Linux with ptrace/cgroups, hardware available to anyone. Efficient: Near-zero overhead measured directly (mean −1.50% cost change, 95% CI [−4.69%, +2.04%]); GC trees are cheap (LightGBM) and the metadata extractor is rule-based with no LLM calls. Effective: The evidence shows real dollar-cost reduction at 0.97× accuracy on standard benchmarks, but only a 23% average realization of the theoretical headroom, and 17–29% of tasks regress. Scalable: Not directly tested beyond benchmark traces that are 2–3× shorter than production traces; the authors argue savings grow with length (0.67 ratio at >1M tokens in their data) but this is extrapolation onto a regime their benchmarks under-sample. Delivers a software artifact (the Agency platform plus five implemented technique hooks), though no release URL is stated in the provided text. Strengths: (1) The cost-decomposition methodology is genuinely useful and replicable: expressing agent cost as cache-read/write/input/output components and deriving the linear cost-gradient of tool calls gives the field a shared vocabulary for why 'token reduction' does not imply 'cost reduction' — the batching ablation (fewer steps, +2% cost) is a memorable demonstration. (2) The interposition design (ptrace/cgroups wrapping of black-box harnesses, hash-list context with lookup-table rewriting that survives across LLM calls) is a real systems contribution that sidesteps the fine-tuning/model-cooperation requirements of prior context-management work. (3) Honest calibration of claims against evidence: the paper explicitly labels Sec. 3's headroom numbers as retrospective upper bounds and Sec. 5's results as proof-of-concept, and reports the negative result for batching on small models. (4) The filesystem-layout experiment (flat/tree × plaintext/UUID on OfficeQA) is a clean controlled study isolating search cost, showing 22–50% of run cost spent on search and a 42% repeat-listing rate across sessions. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that (a) their analysis depends on the current provider pricing formula, which may change; (b) some techniques (context recovery steps, batching prompts) may behave differently with future models; (c) the Sec. 3 analysis is hindsight-based, so its savings are theoretical maxima not fully exploitable live; and (d) the field lacks a dedicated cost benchmark for agent-optimization techniques, which they leave to future work. This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive — though they do not address the LLM-labeled dependency graphs, the missing seed variance, or the lack of comparison experiments against existing compression tools. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No validation of the GPT-6-Luna turn-dependency labels or the 'used tool output' heuristic (a referenced-value match), which underpin the tool-sparsity and subtask-breadth headline numbers; measurement error here propagates everywhere. (2) No experimental comparison against the cited prior systems (Headroom, RTK, ACON, Context-Folding) despite claiming complementarity — the reader cannot tell how much of the 23% is attributable to Agency's novel techniques versus generic output compression that off-the-shelf tools already provide. (3) The tool call batching result contradicts the paper's framing: a technique that costs +2% in isolation is included in a paper about cost reduction, and the 'simple user prompt' mechanism undermines the transparency/determinism claim central to the system's pitch. (4) Accuracy on OfficeQA Pro is presumably self-graded against known answers, but per-model accuracy levels in Fig. 1 are shown without absolute numbers, making the 0.97 accuracy-ratio hard to sanity-check against absolute pass rates. (5) No release of Agency, the trace datasets used, or the trained GC models is stated, limiting reproducibility of the exact pipeline. (6) The metadata index is built offline on a static filesystem; behavior under agents that create, move, or rename files mid-task (common in coding work) is unexamined. Bottom Line: A practitioner running commercial coding or retrieval agents should read this for the cost-decomposition analysis and the interposition architecture, which together define the emerging 'harness tax' problem better than any prior work — but the optimization techniques themselves are early-stage, partially self-defeating (batching), and unvalidated against existing compression tools, so treat the 23% average savings as a lower bound on opportunity rather than a deployable recipe.

Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks

D Zhang, Q Bai, D Min, X Mu, Z Chen, J Yin · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Veritas, a harness that automatically generates executable verifiers for agent tasks by adding three mechanisms to a stock coding agent — an evidence header stating what the verifier will observe at judgment time, a browsable library of unstated domain rules, and nine authoring principles that substitute for tests the agent cannot run. - Why it's important: Self-improvement loops are bottlenecked by verifiers; most real-world tasks ship without one, hand-writing them does not scale, and even expert-audited benchmark verifiers are flawed (61.1% of original SWE-bench tasks were flagged, and an exploit scored 100% on three benchmarks by tampering with test containers). - How it does it: It reframes verifier generation as a harness-design problem, injecting the answer-side constraints the writing agent cannot see (verifier-input evidence, latent domain obligations, no-candidates-to-test) as structured prompt mechanisms, with a probe-and-single-repair stage and a 32-round self-improvement loop over fit/validation tasks. - The good: With the model fixed at GLM-5.2 and a five-gate certification procedure making official verdicts trustworthy labels, Veritas achieves the best agreement with official verdicts among eight harnesses on all four execution-scored benchmarks (e.g., κ*=0.787 vs. 0.726 for the best plain harness on τ²-bench; skip it if you only care about pairwise LLM judging, where the mechanisms are near-irrelevant by the paper's own analysis.
