Problem & Motivation: Every recursive self-improvement or agentic RL loop selects its next iteration via a verifier's verdict, but verifiers are hand-written, expensive, and frequently absent for tasks collected from real use. Even shipped benchmark verifiers are defective: the paper cites the SWE-bench Verified audit (61.1% of 1,699 tasks flagged, 68.3% discarded), 26 of the 500 verified tasks later shown to accept wrong patches, and a container-tampering exploit scoring 100% on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, and Terminal-Bench. Naively asking a general-purpose coding agent (Claude Code, Codex CLI) to write the verifier fails for three structural reasons the paper identifies: the agent conflates what it can see now with what the verifier will see at judgment time; the obligations a verifier must check extend beyond the task text into unstated domain policy; and the agent has no candidates or labels to validate against because they do not exist yet. The domain is agentic AI evaluation and self-improvement; the gap closed is that no prior work generates executable per-task verifiers for agent tasks with dialogue and environment-state evidence, closed-book (no reference solution, no candidate in view). Key Idea: The core insight is that verifier generation fails on the answer side of the information asymmetry, and each answer-side failure has a targeted, cheap fix inside the writing harness: (E) an evidence header that declares, before generation, exactly which inputs (trajectory τ, initial state E₀, final state E_f) the verifier will receive, with a precedence rule that state comparisons must gate and dialogue evidence cannot overturn them — because the trajectory is the evidence a candidate can most easily fake; (R) a 19,603-entry domain rule library (four domains from PRBench, plus airline/banking rules from τ²-bench tasks outside the evaluation set), browsed as a filesystem so only relevant rules enter the verifier; (H) nine benchmark-agnostic authoring principles that stand in for the unit tests a verifier-writer cannot run. The state-precedence rule in E is the single most non-obvious design choice, and the paper defends it with a concrete failure case. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages, identical for all eight harnesses: (1) Packaging — a per-benchmark adapter converts a task into a container spec; a code-layout separation between generation and scoring sides enforces the no-labels information boundary by construction. (2) Generation — the chosen agent runs in the task environment on the Harbor framework and must write the verifier artifact to a contract-specified path. (3) Probe and one repair — a benchmark-specific probe classifies the artifact; a crash or a verifier that accepts a known-wrong candidate (e.g., the no-op) triggers exactly one regeneration, adopted only if its own probe is clean. (4) Delivery — verdicts computed later by the scoring side. Veritas differs only in the three prompt-level mechanisms of E, R, H. Evaluation uses a metric κ, Cohen's κ against certified official labels with missing verdicts charged as errors. Label trust is established by a five-gate certification (G1 reference passes, G2 suite separates, G3 single-check deletion is exposed, G4 hand-adjudication of every mismatch, G5 three-run stability) applied to candidate suites built mechanically from reference solutions (gold patch, no-op, one-line-dropped patch; oracle, no-op, truncated/corrupted final states via six generic corruption operators). A 32-round self-improvement loop with a mechanical anti-overfitting lint and task-clustered paired permutation tests (later phases) kept 4 of 32 edits, only two of which affect the scored benchmarks. Critical design decisions: state-over-trajectory precedence (well-justified by the faked-dialogue case study), filesystem-mounted rather than inlined rule library (justified by scale: 19,603 entries), and delivery as a first-class scored quantity via κ (well-motivated, since non-delivery dominated losses on Terminal-Bench). Key Results: With GLM-5.2 fixed and seven plain harness baselines (Codex CLI, OpenCode, pi, Terminus 2, Hermes, Claude Code, Gemini CLI — all current, named versions), Veritas leads on all four execution-scored benchmarks: κ 0.787 on τ²-bench (58 certified tasks, +0.061 over Claude Code), 0.720 on SWE-bench Verified (138 tasks, +0.027 over pi), 0.465 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (33 tasks, +0.078 over Codex CLI), 0.548 on TB-Science 0.1 (39 tasks, +0.074 over OpenCode); on pairwise LLMBar (75 pairs, 0.920, one pair behind Terminus 2) and JudgeBench coding subset (51 pairs, 0.980, tied best) it is at or near ceiling. With model varied, Veritas beats the vendor's own harness on all four execution benchmarks for Qwen3.7-Plus and Gemini 3.5 Flash (margins up to 0.206), but loses to Codex CLI on GPT-5.6-sol on three of four benchmarks. Mechanisms added unchanged to Codex CLI and Claude Code improve 5 of 8 execution-scored harness-benchmark pairs, never dropping any pair by more than 0.050; Claude Code gains +0.348 on Terminal-Bench, largely via delivery. Ablations show H is critical on τ²-bench (0.787→0.250 without it, below the plain baseline), E secures SWE-bench delivery (missing verdicts 15→46 without it), and R is inert on SWE-bench by construction. Three findings beyond the ranking: plain harnesses span κ 0.16–0.73 on τ²-bench with the same model (harness matters as much as model); plain harnesses lose mainly on delivery in heavy environments (pi: best judged-subset agreement 0.671, yet 67/189 candidates unjudged, κ* 0.048); and generated verifiers err mainly by false rejection (Veritas oracle TPR 0.45 on Terminal-Bench) whereas official verifiers err mainly by false acceptance. The audit appendix additionally confirms defects in official verifiers of six benchmarks (e.g., 27/82 Agents' Last Exam tasks, 36/106 DeepSWE tasks accepting a one-hunk-removed gold patch, MCP-Atlas judge flipping verdicts on identical input at temperature zero on 72/500 tasks). Scale is modest and standard, not stress-scale: 33–138 tasks per benchmark, single-run for most configurations. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (a verifier-generation harness with the E/R/H mechanisms, the first closed-book generator of executable verifiers for agent tasks with dialogue-plus-environment evidence, judged without reference solution or candidate in view), plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (with the model fixed, harness choice alone moves verifier quality by as much as model choice; delivery failures dominate in heavy environments; generated and official verifiers have opposite error profiles) and a substantial methodological contribution in the certification-gate/audit protocol (G1–G5 plus executed-counterexample auditing of official verifiers). The rule library is a competent repackaging of existing rubric sources (PRBench, τ²-bench policy assertions), and the probe-repair and self-improvement loops are standard mechanisms; the genuinely new part is the evidence-header abstraction and the systematic demonstration that harness design, not just model choice, determines verifier quality. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative — each mechanism is removed individually on OpenCode across four benchmarks, and the paper is careful to note where a mechanism is structurally inactive (R on SWE-bench) and to run a matched ablation-series configuration for SWE-bench where Table 2 and Table 4 differ (0.720 vs. 0.741) for the same nominal system. Error bars/significance tests are largely absent for the headline comparisons: each configuration runs once, with repeats reported only in an appendix showing run-to-run κ variation of 0.083 (plain Claude Code) and 0.040 (Claude Code+ERH) on τ²-bench — the same order as the +0.027 SWE-bench margin, though permutation tests are used in phase 3 of the self-improvement loop. No public code, data, or artifact release URL is stated for Veritas itself (the Harbor framework and several baselines are open source). Methodological concerns to flag: (1) the mechanisms were designed on τ²-bench and SWE-bench fit/validation tasks and are also scored on those benchmarks' test tasks — a partial Goodhart exposure, partially mitigated by the terminal benchmarks being added after the mechanisms were frozen; (2) ground truth is the official verifier on certified candidates, so κ measures agreement with a possibly-wrong judge, which the paper acknowledges and mitigates with gates but cannot eliminate; (3) most candidates are constructed (no-ops, corrupted states) rather than real agent attempts; (4) the rule library includes τ²-bench-derived airline assertions, adjacent to (though disjoint from) the evaluation tasks; (5) the model may have memorized public benchmarks. The label-certification work is a rigor strength: the audit of official verifiers is backed by executed counterexamples with a refuter agent and planted-defect controls, not static claims. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (and SYSTEMS — Veritas is a harness built on Harbor, but the evidence is benchmark agreement, not production deployment). - Practical: Yes — it runs as prompt-level additions to stock coding agents (OpenCode, Codex CLI, Claude Code) on standard agent infrastructure with a 7,200-second generation limit; no special hardware is implied. - Efficient: No added cost — on τ²-bench Veritas used 97.0M prompt / 2.5M completion tokens vs. 104.5M / 2.6M for plain OpenCode, with comparable cache hit rates (93–94%); the mechanisms are essentially free. - Effective: The evidence shows higher agreement with certified official verdicts, which is a proxy — the paper does not yet show that higher agreement produces better self-improvement rounds, and explicitly defers this to future work. - Scalable: Not tested — per-benchmark scale is 33–138 tasks, the rule library is fixed at six domains, and behavior on tasks from domains absent from the library or on far larger task distributions is claimed only implicitly. The work delivers a reusable harness design (three transferable prompt mechanisms plus a probe/repair pipeline) and an audit methodology, but no stated public artifact release; it stops at paper form as far as the text indicates. Strengths: - The evidence-header abstraction is a real, transferable insight: naming what the verifier will observe at judgment time — and the state-precedence rule within it — directly fixes the faked-trajectory failure mode, demonstrated concretely (banking task 23: plain OpenCode accepts a run whose database records no identity check). - The κ* metric that charges non-delivery as an error exposes a failure axis (pi: best judged-subset agreement, worst effective score on Terminal-Bench) that standard judged-subset metrics hide; the delivery-versus-judgment decomposition is a genuinely useful analysis tool. - The five-gate certification plus executed-counterexample audit of official verifiers is rigorous and independent of the main contribution's success — it confirms defects across six benchmarks (e.g., 36/106 DeepSWE tasks accepting an incomplete gold patch; MCP-Atlas judge nondeterministic on 72/500 tasks at temperature zero) with refuter/planted-defect controls. - Honest ablation reporting, including mechanisms that are inert by construction (R on SWE-bench), mechanisms that hurt when added to a stronger harness (−0.063 on τ²-bench for Claude Code+ERH), and a self-improvement loop where 28 of 32 proposed edits were rejected. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Limitations section is direct and specific: single runs per configuration due to compute budget; 33–138 execution-scored tasks; only GLM-5.2 compared against all seven plain harnesses (other model families only versus their vendor harness); mechanisms added to only two other harnesses and ablated on four of six benchmarks; most candidates are constructed (reference solutions, empty runs, corrupted outputs) so real agent attempts may be harder to judge; official verdicts on certified candidates are treated as ground truth despite gates that may miss defects, and κ* counts a correctly-stricter generated verifier as wrong when the official verifier is too lenient; and the model may have seen public benchmarks during training despite the closed-book harness. The authors confront limitations squarely rather than minimize them, which is a credibility positive. They also flag that verifier defects reported in the audit could be exploited for score inflation, and disclose them for repair. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline comparison is partially self-referential: τ²-bench and SWE-bench are the benchmarks whose fit/validation tasks shaped the mechanisms, and the certified test tasks still share task style, candidate-construction scheme, and (for τ²-bench airline) rule-library provenance with the design loop. The two post-freeze terminal benchmarks are cleaner evidence, and Veritas does win there, but on the smallest task counts (33 and 39). - Ground truth circularity has a directional bias the paper under-weights in the headline numbers: official verifiers are shown to be lenient (accepting near-misses ~53% of the time on 33 τ²-bench tasks), while generated verifiers are strict; κ* against a lenient judge systematically penalizes the stricter system, so "agreement with official verdicts" and "verifier correctness" can diverge — the paper states this in Limitations but the abstract frames the result as reliability. - No statistical treatment of the main Table 2 comparisons: with single runs and documented 0.083 run-to-run variation, several margins (+0.027 SWE-bench, small cross-model margins of 0.012–0.014) are within noise, and the GPT-5.6-sol reversal — where Veritas loses to Codex CLI on three benchmarks and delivers zero verifiers on 47 τ²-bench banking tasks — receives no failure analysis. - The rule library's coverage is the mechanism least stress-tested: six domains, two of which are tailored to τ²-bench; there is no experiment on tasks from a domain with no library coverage to isolate how much of the R gain is domain-general priors versus leakage-adjacent task-family knowledge. - Effect on downstream self-improvement is untested — the entire motivating loop (better verifiers → better improvement rounds) remains a claim, not a measurement. Bottom Line: For anyone building agent benchmarks, verifiers, or self-improvement loops, this is worth reading for the evidence-header idea, the delivery-aware κ* metric, and the certification/audit methodology — the strongest alternatives (test-generation work like SWT-Bench or Otter) cover only code tasks and none cover the harness-vs-model question — but the cross-harness margins should be read with single-run caution and the self-improvement payoff remains unproven.

#64 — Innovative (68)

A rigidly-convected, lifting-line vortex model in the optimal control of airborne wind energy systems

R Leuthold, J De Schutter, C Crawford, S Gros, M Diehl · wes.copernicus.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a formulation that embeds a rigidly-convected, lifting-line (RLL) vortex-filament wake model into an airborne wind energy (AWE) optimal control problem (OCP) and solves it, by lifting wake-node positions, average circulations, and induced velocities into the algebraic decision variables with matching equality constraints and a dedicated induction-homotopy step. - Why it's important: AWE performance predictions from OCPs have historically ignored or crudely approximated wake induction; the paper shows this omission inflates predicted harvestable power by 20–30%, which directly distorts early-stage system design and levelized-cost-of-electricity estimates. - How it does it: The core trick is algebraic variable "lifting" — representing wake geometry and circulation as OCP decision variables pinned by convection and Kutta-Joukowski constraints (rather than forward-simulating the wake), combined with a predictor-corrector homotopy that gradually enforces the highly nonlinear Biot-Savart induction. - The good: The model's predictions were verified against independently published Large Eddy Simulations (Haas & Meyers 2017 steady case; Haas et al. 2019 dynamic case) and reproduce the expected induction structure with E = 963 vortex elements versus ~14.2 million LES control volumes. - The missing: The demonstration is a single two-kite (Ampyx AP2), single-winding test problem; there is no quantitative error metric against LES, no comparison against cheaper actuator-type wake models within the same OCP, and the power-maximizing solution is heavily homotopy-initialization dependent (a cheaper tracking-based solution finds 7.65 kW vs 6.25 kW via the full homotopy path). - Read it or not: Read it if you work on AWE trajectory optimization or wind-farm OCPs with vortex models — it is the first demonstrated solution of a vortex-filament wake model inside an inequality-constrained AWE OCP and documents cost scaling and optimizer-exploitation pitfalls in unusual depth; skip it if you need a turnkey efficient wake model, since the method costs ~62 GB memory and ~7.8×10⁶ CPU-seconds per solve.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (70) is strong for the domain — first demonstrated solution of a vortex-filament wake model inside an inequality-constrained AWE OCP, plus a new 20–30% power-prediction finding — and Rigor (68) is helped by released code and replication scripts, convergence studies diagnosing optimizer exploitation, and LES verification, but held back by purely qualitative (no quantitative error-norm) verification. Completeness (75) and Resilience (72) are the paper's best dimensions: limitation acknowledgment is unusually direct (local-minimum sensitivity, cost scaling, initialization dependence are all confronted head-on). Non-Obviousness (65) reflects the lifting-plus-homotopy reformulation being a competent but recognizable OCP move. Impact (55) is capped by a released-but-impractical artifact: ~62 GB and ~7.8M CPU-seconds per solve, demonstrated on a single two-kite configuration. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*68 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*55 = 68.

Problem & Motivation: Designers of multi-kite airborne wind energy systems use offline optimal control to predict maximum harvestable power for early-stage design decisions. Existing wake treatments force a bad trade-off: actuator-surface models assume regular rotor-like geometries that cannot be defined for the irregular, non-planar, non-circular trajectories AWE OCPs produce, while LES-in-the-loop optimal control is prohibitively expensive (e.g., 35,000 core-hours per 300 s, 16-turbine case in Munters 2017). Prior AWE OCPs with wake models used low-fidelity actuator representations, and the broader question — how to include a vortex-filament model in an OCP with an irregular trajectory and many inequality constraints — had few successful precedents (e.g., van den Broek et al. 2024 for turbines without the trajectory irregularity of AWE). The gap is whether the power-prediction difference between assuming negligible induced velocity and modeling momentum conservation persists under a mid-fidelity vorticity model. Key Idea: Reformulate the wake as lifted algebraic decision variables inside a monolithic discretized OCP: wake-node positions are fixed by rigid freestream convection constraints (Eq. 10), per-shedding-interval average circulations are fixed by a Kutta-Joukowski-derived circulation constraint (Eq. 15), induced velocities are fixed by a regularized Biot-Savart superposition (Eqs. 17–20), and periodicity recycles the current trajectory as pre-history wake. A new induction-homotopy parameter (Eq. 16) gradually transitions from zero applied induction to full Biot-Savart enforcement, keeping the NLP tractable despite the near-singular Biot-Savart nonlinearity. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) a baseline AWE OCP from the open-source awebox toolbox (De Schutter et al. 2023) with 6-DOF kite dynamics, tether model, path inequalities (tether stress, airspeed, aerodynamic validity, anti-collision, yaw limits), periodicity, and a tracking-to-power homotopy objective; (2) a RLL wake structure of 3KA finite filaments per kite (one bound filament, shed filaments, two trailing helices) plus two semi-infinite far-wake filaments per kite, discretized with A wake nodes coupled to the OCP control grid (Radau-IIA collocation, D = 4); (3) three lifted variable groups — wake-node positions, time-averaged circulations, and both applied and computed induced velocities — each with a corresponding equality constraint so no spurious degrees of freedom are introduced; (4) solution via IPOPT with exact-Hessian Newton steps, Metis ordering, and the MA86 linear solver, along a multi-step predictor-corrector homotopy (fictitious forces, interior-point, induction, power). Critical design decisions: uniform spanwise circulation (single lifting line) to match the geometry-free kite model; coupling the vortex-shedding grid to the control grid so constraints are enforced where vorticity is shed (explicitly justified against the optimizer "cheating physics"); cut-off vortex-core regularization at 5% of mean aerodynamic chord rather than element-size-based; and time-averaged (rather than instantaneous) circulation at shedding to prevent exploitation at control nodes. Each decision is argued in detail, mostly via footnoted practical experience rather than systematic ablation. Key Results: Verification against LES: for the rotationally-steady three-kite case (Haas & Meyers 2017, Lockheed C-5a geometry, v∞ = 10 m/s), the RLL model reproduces the qualitative axial-induction-factor structure (downwash annulus, upwash before the kites) with the main discrepancy being the tangential extent of the a = 0.2 region (RLL cuts off at y ≈ R/4 vs LES extending to y = 0). For the dynamic single-kite case (Haas et al. 2019, I = 80, P = 4, E = 963 elements, V ≈ 3.8×10⁵ total), temporally-averaged velocity deficits match LES well near the wake origin but the inviscid rigid-convection model over-predicts and over-concentrates deficits downstream. Convergence study (two Ampyx AP2 kites, single winding): optimal power converges once the tracked wake covers roughly one optimization period plus the reel-out phase (P ≳ 1 + t⬗switch/t⬗final); fewer than 20 control intervals per winding lets the optimizer exploit the discretization. Headline comparison (I = 30, P = 1.86): baseline no-wake OCP predicts 9.32 kW average power vs 6.25 kW with the RLL model (−33%), with the optimization period dropping 48% (23.1 s → 11.9 s) and secondary tether length dropping 31%; a tracking-based comparison at matched local minima gives −17% to −19% (9.23 kW anticipated vs 7.65/7.49 kW harvestable). Cost: with V = 51,642 total vortex elements, memory (62.1 GB) scales ≈ linearly in V and processor time (7.84×10⁶ CPU-s) scales ≈ V^2.4, dominated by the KKT linear solves rather than Biot-Savart evaluation. The RLL solution finds a qualitatively different trajectory (two partially overlapping "Venn" loops vs the baseline's tight-turning pattern) that avoids kite-over-wake overflights. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel contribution is the first demonstrated solution of a vortex-filament wake model inside a monolithic, inequality-constrained AWE OCP with an irregular trajectory, achieved via the lifting-plus-induction-homotopy reformulation and an honest cost-scaling characterization; the finding that a mid-fidelity wake model changes predicted power by 20–30% and qualitatively reshapes the optimal trajectory is new for AWE. The individual ingredients — lifting-line theory, Biot-Savart with cut-off regularization, direct collocation, predictor-corrector homotopy, IPOPT — are all standard; the contribution is their combination and the OCP-specific reformulation, not any new aerodynamics or optimization theory. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style evidence is present in two forms: a convergence study over wake resolution (I × P grid) that shows which resolution choices matter and explicitly diagnoses where the optimizer exploits discretization (the "power dip-then-recovery" at I = 15, absent at I = 20, cross-checked against De Schutter et al. 2026's vorticity-patch results), and a homotopy-order reversal check that confirms the headline comparison is not an artifact of step ordering. No error bars or significance tests are reported for the power comparisons, though the authors report tight clustering of optimization-period values (e.g., 11.832 s ± 0.0017 s) across resolutions. Verification is qualitative (contour and profile comparisons); no quantitative error norms against LES are computed. Code is public: awebox v1.0.1 (tag "v1.0.1-wes-2026") at https://github.com/awebox/awebox with the paper's scripts in awebox/examples/Leuthold_2026_RLL_paper_scripts; full replication tables (system properties, constraints, initial guesses) are in Appendices B–C. Methodological concerns: the headline −33% comparison is between different local minima of a non-convex problem (the authors acknowledge this and partially mitigate with the tracking study); the verification uses the authors' own Simulation-OCP construction rather than an independent forward-simulation code; and the dynamic verification requires reproducing a known-idiosyncratic tether-drag implementation ("equivalence-buggy") to match the reference. This is a peer-review-track preprint (Copernicus WES discussion paper, submitted 12 November 2026), so results should be treated as not yet peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a computational method with numerical experiments; also a SYSTEMS-adjacent artifact since it ships in the awebox toolbox). - Practical: Runs on a single workstation (62 GB peak memory, IPOPT/MA86 on commodity hardware), but at the edge of a personal computer as the authors themselves note in motivation. - Efficient: Very expensive relative to alternatives — ~630× more optimization CPU time and ~9.9× more memory than the baseline no-wake OCP (7.84×10⁶ vs 1.24×10³ CPU-s; 62.1 vs 6.27 GB) — though the authors argue the V^2.4 time scaling leaves room for algorithmic improvement since Biot-Savart evaluation itself is cheap here. - Effective: The evidence supports the paper's actual claim — that wake modeling materially changes OCP predictions — but does not establish that the RLL-optimal 6.25 kW trajectory is the true optimum, since a tracking-based solve recovers 7.65 kW under the same model, indicating the homotopy path finds only a subset of local minima. - Scalable: Not tested beyond two kites and a single-winding trajectory; the V ∝ I² (roughly) and time ∝ V^2.4 scalings imply multi-kite, multi-winding, or free-wake extensions will be severely memory- and time-limited, and the authors only claim (not demonstrate) that better-tuned algorithms could reduce cost. The work delivers a software artifact: the RLL model is implemented in the open-source awebox toolbox (v1.0.1) with released replication scripts, not merely described on paper. Strengths: - The lifting-plus-homotopy reformulation is a real methodological contribution: it makes a previously unsolved problem class (vortex filaments inside inequality-constrained AWE OCPs) solvable, with a clean argument that the appended constraint block has an invertible Jacobian in the lifted variables. - The convergence/expense study is unusually honest and diagnostic: it identifies, with cross-evidence, exactly where and why the optimizer exploits the coupled shedding/control grid (the I = 15 power-recovery artifact), and derives empirical cost scalings (memory ≈ V, time ≈ V^2.4) that contradict forward-simulation heuristics. - Verification against two independently published LES datasets (steady and dynamic), using the Simulation-OCP device to test the model exactly as implemented in the OCP, is a thoughtful validation design. - Unusual transparency: footnoted documentation of failed approaches, solver non-repeatability, the deliberately uncorrected "equivalence-buggy" tether-drag model used for reproduction, and explicit acknowledgment that the −33% figure compares different local minima. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: the method is expensive (memory linear in V, time ≈ V^2.4 in total vortex elements); the power-maximizing solution is heavily influenced by the homotopy-initialization strategy (a cheaper tracking solve harvests 7.65 kW vs 6.25 kW via the full path, so initialization locks in the local minimum); rigid convection is inconsistent with the strong induction (a = 1/3) in the steady verification case, explaining discrepancy with LES; the inviscid model over-predicts and over-concentrates velocity deficits downstream; the uniform single-lifting-line circulation distribution is a deliberate low-information choice; solutions require ≥20 control intervals per winding to limit optimizer "trickery"; and non-periodic trajectories need modifications to the pre-history construction. They confront limitations directly and at length — a strong credibility positive — and clearly frame free-wake convection, vorticity-patch near-wakes, and actuator-model hybrids as future work rather than claiming them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the authors' acknowledgments: (1) no quantitative verification metric (e.g., RMS induction-factor or velocity-deficit error vs LES) — all model-quality claims rest on visual/qualitative agreement, so "consistent with LES" is a claim, not a measurement; (2) the headline −33% comes from comparing solutions at different local minima of a non-convex problem, and the paper does not rule out that a better global solution of the RLL OCP lies between 6.25 and 7.65 kW, making the precise loss figure uncertain within the authors' own model; (3) the demonstration system is a single two-kite, single-winding configuration with one kite model (Ampyx AP2) — the generality of the 20–30% finding across architectures, winding numbers, and wind speeds is untested; (4) no comparison against a cheaper actuator-type wake model inside the same OCP, so the reader cannot judge how much of the 20–30% effect the expensive vortex model uniquely captures versus what a cheap model would already reveal (the authors pose this as a future question but it bounds the practical value of the current result); (5) the "equivalence-buggy" tether-drag reproduction, while transparently documented, means the dynamic verification baseline is matched to a known numerical error rather than to physics; (6) solver repeatability is flagged (MA86 heuristics) but no multi-start study is reported to characterize the local-minimum landscape of the RLL OCP. Bottom Line: For researchers building AWE trajectory-optimization tools or attempting vortex models in OCPs, this is essential reading — it proves feasibility, quantifies the wake-modeling stakes at 20–30% of predicted power, and documents cost and optimizer-exploitation pitfalls no other paper covers — but practitioners wanting production-ready performance prediction should treat the current formulation as a proof of concept whose expense and initialization sensitivity leave substantial work before routine use.

SAB: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Startup Research and Ranking

M Kalpin, A Zhuravlev, D Golomidov, S Bilich, V Li · mento.vc · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SAB, a benchmark from a venture fund that evaluates LLM research agents on 960 startup-research tasks with deterministic grading of answers and citations, and on 101 ranking cohorts of 100 companies scored by Spearman correlation against realized subsequent growth in web traffic and headcount. - Why it's important: Venture funds are delegating company research to LLM agents whose errors (stale figures, confident hallucinations, size-biased screens) can flow directly into investment memos, and no prior benchmark scored citations, abstention, and outcome-based ranking together. - How it does it: Agents work in frozen per-task corpora through budgeted MCP search/fetch tools against private answer keys, with a scoring rule that credits "unknown" on 221 withheld facts and checks cited source IDs, while ranking tasks are graded against outcomes the models could not have been told. - The good: The best model (Claude Opus 5.5) scores 97.2/100 with a 96% strict pass rate, yet every model gives a value for 9–33% of withheld facts, and all 13 ranking models fall below a trivial headcount-growth heuristic (ρ = −0.16 to −0.003 vs. +0.058) — a sharp, well-powered separation of what agents can and cannot be trusted to do. - The missing: The ranking target ("operating momentum") is deliberately never defined to the model, so the negative correlations cannot be separated from a different reading of the objective, and the keys were corrected after the authors saw model answers via an audit that by construction finds only too-strict errors. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or deploy deep-research/agents for financial or screening workflows — it is a model for how to benchmark citation discipline and abstention — or skip it if you only care about model ranking ability, where the undefined-target confound weakens the headline claim.

Problem & Motivation: Venture investors review roughly a hundred companies per investment and increasingly hand the research to AI agents (a vendor survey reports 64% of investors use AI for company research). Before trusting an agent, a fund needs to know: does it find relevant evidence in a corpus of mostly distractors; does it cite real, sufficient sources; does it abstain when evidence is missing; and can it rank companies better than a simple rule? Existing work covers pieces only: startup-success studies score predictions from given profiles, deep-research benchmarks (GAIA, BrowseComp, BrowseComp-Plus, FinSearchComp) score search on general or financial corpora but score abstention only partially, and commercial deal-sourcing platforms publish no held-out evaluations of their agents. Key Idea: Combine a frozen, distractor-heavy corpus with deterministic grading that (a) verifies cited source IDs against the supporting documents each answer needs, (b) pays explicitly for abstaining on facts the generator deliberately made unanswerable (a utility where answering beats "unknown" only if expected accuracy exceeds 0.6), and (c) scores zero-tool rankings of masked companies against realized future growth — so search, citation discipline, calibration, and forecasting are each independently measurable in one private harness. Methodology: The benchmark has two parts. Research: 960 tasks across six analyst workflows (product, market, competition, team, traction, sourcing), 80 synthetic + 80 real-world per family; synthetic environments hold a median of 49 documents with ~5.5% supporting the answer, and the real-world track freezes 8,000 warehouse records (30,529 documents total). Tasks fix a JSON schema with per-field "unknown"; grading covers 4,560 criteria via exact match, numeric tolerance, or set F1, worth 80 content points plus 20 evidence points (score = Σwⱼaⱼ + ¼Σwⱼaⱼeⱼ − min(20, 10f) for nonexistent citations), with 1,735 critical criteria gating a strict pass rule. For every fifth task the generator tries to remove a document and label a criterion unanswerable (111 of 192 attempts succeed; 221 withheld criteria in 95 tasks). Ranking: 101 cohorts of 100 masked companies across five monthly waves plus a recent cohort; the target is 0.625·F(Δtraffic) + 0.375·F(Δheadcount) percentile growth at 90/180 days, scored by Spearman ρ. Fourteen models from four vendors ran once each, zero-shot, at high reasoning effort, with paired stratified-bootstrap statistics, Holm-corrected permutation tests, and list-price cost accounting. A post hoc key audit corrected eight defect classes (raising scores 4.8–7.5 points and pass rates 5.7–17.6 points). Critical design choices: frozen corpora with private keys prevent contamination (justified); an undefined ranking target prevents look-ahead but creates an objective-interpretation confound (acknowledged); post hoc key corrections applied uniformly to saved answers (defensible but asymmetric, as the authors note). Key Results: Research: Claude Opus 5.5 leads at 97.2/100 (95% CI [96.9, 97.5], 96% strict pass), followed by Claude Fable 5.1 (96.8) and Opus 5 (96.2); only 3 of 13 adjacent model differences are significant after Holm correction. Nonexistent citations are rare (≤2 tasks per model), but every model answers 9–33% of withheld facts instead of abstaining; weaker models over-abstain on answerable fields (7–10%). Closed-book controls score 7.49–7.56 vs. 7.53 for the all-unknown reference. Cost per task ranges from $0.003 (GPT-6 Luna) to $0.359 (Claude Fable 5.1), a >100× spread. Ranking: the headcount-growth heuristic scores ρ = +0.058 [0.041, 0.075]; all 13 models score −0.160 to −0.003, 12 below the 95% random range, and every model's ranking correlates positively with baseline traffic (+0.35 to +0.70) while the target correlates at −0.24; a post hoc smallest-first rule scores +0.242. Under size-controlled partial correlation, 12 of 13 models are positive and 4 significantly exceed the heuristic — reported as exploratory. Baselines are current (2025–2026-era frontier models); tested at benchmark scale, not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK with a NEW FORMULATION of agent evaluation (content + evidence + abstention utility + outcome-scored ranking in one harness). The genuinely novel elements are the withheld-fact utility, strict citation checking against sufficient supporting documents, and cohorts scored against realized growth; the components themselves (frozen corpora à la BrowseComp-Plus, Spearman scoring against outcomes à la ForecastBench) are standard techniques combined in a new domain with unusually careful statistics. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong: paired bootstrap intervals with shared draws, permutation tests with Holm correction, a closed-book control, per-family/per-track breakdowns, full run logs (interruptions, restarts, invalid answers), and honest treatment of a selected-subset artifact (DeepSeek-V3.2's 87.3 on finished tasks). No multiple seeds — each model ran once, which the authors acknowledge. Ablations exist at the key level (Table 5 isolates each correction's effect). The release (sab-v0.7.0) has a hash-committed manifest; corrected keys and the underlying fund data remain private, and the correction code is promised with v0.7.1 — so full external reproduction is not possible. Methodological concerns flagged by the authors themselves: key corrections were made after seeing model answers; the audit finds too-strict keys but by construction misses too-lenient ones; cohorts are selection-conditioned (companies lacking positive traffic/headcount at any horizon are excluded, 28–37% of eligible companies). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark and evaluation study, no new model). Practical: Yes — all evaluation runs through commercial provider APIs; the harness is a standard MCP server. Efficient: Per-task inference costs $0.003–$0.359; the expensive part is building the benchmark, not running it. Effective: The evidence credibly shows agents can gather and cite evidence (research scores 79.8–97.2) but cannot rank startups against realized momentum; the ranking verdict is partially confounded by the undefined target. Scalable: Not tested — 960 tasks and 101 cohorts spanning five months from one fund's warehouse; 10× more outcome waves would be needed to separate signal from period effects. Deliverable: a frozen benchmark release with private keys and partially private data; a reusable evaluation protocol (utility, citation rules, audit procedure) rather than a public software artifact. Strengths: - The abstention-scoring utility and withheld-fact construction turn "does the model hallucinate when evidence is missing" from an anecdote into a measurable rate (9–33% of withheld facts), and the all-unknown reference score (7.5) anchors the scale. - The key audit is unusually honest: the authors released scores 4.8–7.5 points lower than their own released keys would give after finding defects in their own answer keys, and document every correction with per-correction effect sizes. - The ranking finding is a genuinely useful negative result: every frontier model systematically prefers larger companies, and the size-controlled partial correlation (positive for 12 of 13 models, labeled exploratory) cleanly separates "cannot rank" from "misreads the objective." - Statistical practice is above the bar for agent benchmarks: paired tests, rank intervals, power analysis (~1.6-point detectable difference), and explicit statements of which orderings the sample cannot resolve. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: single runs per model with no cross-run variance; no human-analyst or fitted-model baselines; one fund's non-releasable data; post hoc, asymmetric key corrections; no evaluation of investment returns; an undefined ranking target that prevents separating forecasting error from interpretation; possible training-data overlap with the outcome period (2.3% of descriptions still name the company); synthetic-track generator artifacts; research tasks near ceiling for the best models; and cohort selection excluding unmeasurable companies. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headcount-growth heuristic uses past headcount series that appear in the models' own signal panels, so "models lose to a heuristic" partially measures whether the model ignored or mis-weighted an input it could have applied mechanically; a fitted baseline (e.g., a simple regressor on the signal panel) is absent and would make the ranking comparison much sharper. - The traffic-growth and smallest-first rules were defined after seeing results, and the authors themselves note that the strong negative traffic-growth vs. size correlation (ρ = −0.32) may be largely regression to the mean and measurement noise in percentage growth — meaning the "smallest-first scores +0.24" headline may partly reflect a denominator artifact rather than a genuine model bias diagnostic. - Model version identifiers and API behavior are vendor-controlled and checkpoint drift is acknowledged but untestable; the paper's leaderboard cannot be re-frozen by third parties. - Only three models got the closed-book control; the leakage audit for ranking relies on a name-in-description heuristic that may under-detect contamination. - The "recent cohort" (n = 1 cohort, 100 companies) is too small to support the contamination-mitigation claim it is designed for. Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying research agents — especially in finance or any evidence-gathering workflow — gains a great deal from the protocol, the abstention findings, and the honest key-audit method, and can reasonably skip nothing; the ranking half is interesting but the undefined-target confound means it should be read as a diagnostic of size bias rather than a verdict on forecasting ability, and no existing benchmark covers the same ground as well.

FlexCast: Flexible Context Learning for Time Series Foundation Models

Z Shen, L Gong, F Fan, B Wang, X Ao, Y Wei, M Liu… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FlexCast, a masked-prediction time series foundation model that reformulates forecasting as variable-length imputation over patches, and uses it to show that the benefit attributed to autoregressive time series foundation models comes from flexible training-time context diversity rather than from sequential rollout at inference. - Why it's important: Autoregressive TSFMs pay a real latency and error-accumulation tax for multi-step decoding; if single-pass masked forecasting matches their accuracy, practitioners get the same generality at a fraction of the inference cost, and researchers stop over-crediting the AR mechanism itself. - How it does it: During pretraining it dynamically samples a single contiguous masked span (random position, mask rate r~U(0.1, 0.3)) over patch tokens, so the model sees diverse context-target geometries under one objective, and at inference the same checkpoint supports one-step, confidence-ordered iterative (MaskGIT-style, using quantile interval width as confidence), and blockwise-AR reveal schedules. - The good: The controlled attribution is the strongest element: with architecture, data (BLAST), and objective held fixed, the Flexible Context/Flexible Target variant beats the Rigid/Rigid variant (e.g., average MSE ~0.362 vs ~0.420 on the six-benchmark average shown in Figure 4), while an NTP variant with the same backbone trails even tail-aligned masking on every dataset, directly supporting the central claim. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, and zero-shot evaluation is confined to six datasets (ETTh1/ETTh2/ETTm1/ETTm2/Weather/GlobalTemp) that do not include the broader GIFT-Eval suite where modern TSFMs are usually stress-tested, so the win counts (11/18 MSE, 13/18 MAE) may not be robust. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or evaluating TSFMs — the decomposition of 'AR success' into context flexibility versus rollout is a genuinely useful diagnostic — but skip it if you only need another forecasting model, since the accuracy numbers are competitive rather than clearly leading.

Scored using Empirical profile. Problem & Motivation: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) pretrain on heterogeneous corpora and transfer zero-shot, but the dominant autoregressive (AR) paradigm couples two factors that are hard to separate: (i) variable-context conditioning — next-token prediction exposes the model to histories of every length and composition — and (ii) factorizing the horizon into prediction units that are rolled out sequentially with predictions fed back as input. Because AR training creates flexible contexts through sequential decoding, strong AR performance cannot tell practitioners which factor drives generalization. This matters for anyone deploying TSFMs (cloud provisioning, traffic, monitoring), since sequential rollout multiplies inference latency and exposes long horizons to accumulated error, while conventional non-AR forecasters avoid this only by fixing one context-length-to-horizon mapping per model. The gap the paper closes is diagnostic: no prior work isolates whether AR TSFMs generalize because of flexible training distribution, sequential inference, or their combination. Key Idea: Make the context-target geometry an explicit random variable rather than a byproduct of decoding: by sampling a single contiguous masked span with random position and random length during pretraining, a bidirectional patch Transformer acquires the same diverse context distribution that AR training induces — but without ever decoding sequentially — so that inference schedule (one-pass vs. confidence-ordered vs. left-to-right AR) becomes a free, controllable knob on one pretrained checkpoint. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) per-channel instance normalization (RevIN computed over context-visible positions only) plus asinh stabilization; (2) non-overlapping patching (patch length 16) where each patch is concatenated with a binary mask indicator and embedded via a residual block; (3) a pre-norm Transformer encoder with RoPE and an additive attention bias that sends padding keys to −∞, with bidirectional attention over all non-padding patches; (4) a quantile head that predicts a base value plus softplus offsets cumulatively summed to guarantee monotone quantiles (99 levels), with point forecasts from a triangularly weighted quantile combination. Training minimizes the quantile pinball loss (Eq. 8), computed only at prediction positions in normalized asinh space; masks partition patches into mutually exclusive context/prediction/padding sets (Eq. 2), and the mask ratio is drawn from U(0.1, 0.3) with a uniformly sampled span start, covering forecasting (tail target) and imputation (interior target) as special cases. Inference supports three reveal schedules sharing one checkpoint: single-pass (K=1), confidence-ordered iterative reveal (confidence = negative quantile-interval width, ~N_pred/K patches revealed per round, revealed patches fixed, MaskGIT-inspired), and blockwise AR reveal of the leftmost unit (96 or 192 steps). Critical design decisions: (a) a single random contiguous span instead of TiRex-style multi-block CPM — justified by ablation (Figure 5, random-rate beats CPM, tail, fixed-rate, and NTP); (b) a deliberately standard backbone to keep attribution clean — well justified; (c) quantile-width as confidence to avoid a separate confidence estimator — reasonable but unvalidated against other confidence measures. Pretraining: 10k steps, batch 2048, AdamW lr 3e-4, BF16, 8×A100, on BLAST (~19.8M sequences of 4096 steps, ~81B time points). Key Results: Zero-shot on ETTh1/ETTh2/ETTm1/ETTm2/Weather/GlobalTemp at horizons 96/192/336/720, FlexCast (131.4M params, BLAST-pretrained) posts 11 best MSE and 13 best MAE results out of 18 dataset-horizon pairs against PatchTST-FM (260M, ~230B-observation corpus), Sundial-l (444M, trillion-scale TimeBench corpus), and TimeMoE/MOIRAI/Chronos variants retrained on the same BLAST corpus; FlexCast leads the BLAST-retrained group most clearly (e.g., ETTh2 average MSE .328 vs .334–.361 for all baselines). Latency on one A100 (batch 1, 512-step context): FlexCast's single-pass latency grows only moderately with horizon while sequential Sundial/TimeMoE/Chronos scale upward, though some baseline points and the 3-step FlexCast curve are extrapolated from measured 720-step endpoints. Ablations: context flexibility is the dominant factor (rigid/rigid worst; flexible-context/flexible-target best, avg MSE ~0.362 vs ~0.420); NTP-style causal supervision with identical mask rates trails even tail masking on all six datasets; blockwise AR inference increases MSE relative to one-step in nearly all settings (e.g., up to +6.0% on ETTm1 with 192-step units), while confidence-ordered K=3 inference is within a few percent of one-step except ETTh2-horizon-720, where it improves MSE by 4.7%. Scaling is monotone over 15M→40M→131.4M (avg MSE .360→.332→.308, ~14% relative reduction). Sensitivity: patch 16, mask interval [0.1, 0.3], 99 quantiles, and ~3376-step context are optimal; the full 4096-step context slightly degrades MSE. Baselines are current and strong (2024–2026 TSFMs), and the same-corpus retraining protocol partially removes the data-scale confound. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a NEW METHOD component. The genuinely novel contributions are (a) the explicit decomposition of AR-TSFM success into context flexibility versus prediction-unit rollout, turned into a testable attribution question via one checkpoint with interchangeable inference schedules, and (b) the empirical finding that chronological rollout adds nothing once flexible contexts are learned. The model itself is a competent combination of known parts — MaskGIT-style confidence-ordered decoding, Mask-Predict iterative refinement, MOIRAI/PatchTST-FM-style masked patch pretraining, quantile heads from TiRex/Chronos — applied to time series with a single random contiguous span (an incremental refinement of TiRex's CPM), so the method-level novelty is modest even though the scientific claim is not. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are the paper's strength: four context-target geometry variants (Table 2/Figure 4), five masking strategies including an NTP-in-the-same-backbone control (Table 3/Figure 5), three inference schedules on one checkpoint (Figure 6), three model sizes, and one-factor-at-a-time hyperparameter sweeps. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests appear anywhere, and given that many zero-shot comparisons differ in the third decimal place (e.g., ETTh1 avg MSE .407 vs .395 for TimeMoE-l), some win/loss splits may not be robust. Code is released at https://github.com/BenchCouncil/FlexCast; no model weights are stated as released. Concerns: evaluation is confined to the six BLAST-associated benchmarks rather than the broader GIFT-Eval suite, the latency study uses batch size 1 and extrapolates some baseline points, baselines released only as weights (Sundial, PatchTST-FM) trained on larger corpora are compared at unequal data scale (the authors acknowledge this favors FlexCast being 'conservative,' but it still muddies accuracy attribution), and the latency gap to other single-pass models is attributed to design differences the authors admit they did 'not isolate.' Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained model with zero-shot benchmarks, latency measurements, and ablations). - Practical: Yes — 131.4M parameters trained and evaluated on 8×A100 80GB with PyTorch 2.5.1; inference runs on a single A100 at batch size 1. - Efficient: Single-pass inference is O(1) model calls regardless of horizon, giving it a clear latency edge over sequential TSFMs whose rollout cost grows with horizon; it is also faster than other single-pass baselines (MOIRAI, PatchTST-FM), attributed to a fixed patch size and direct quantile aggregation, though training still wastes compute on padding for variable lengths (acknowledged). - Effective: The evidence shows it matches or beats baselines on the six tested benchmarks, with the same-corpus comparisons most convincing; effectiveness on more diverse or out-of-distribution tasks is untested. - Scalable: Untested beyond 131.4M parameters and the ~81B-time-point BLAST corpus; the monotone 15M→131.4M scaling trend is suggestive, but the authors explicitly note that larger models may need different mask-rate curricula and that larger, more heterogeneous corpora were not evaluated. The deliverable is a software artifact (code repository); trained weights are not stated as public. Strengths: - The core attribution experiment is well designed: by holding architecture, corpus, and objective fixed and swapping only the reveal schedule on one checkpoint, the paper converts a folk claim ('AR works because of sequential generation') into a measured result, and the NTP-with-same-backbone control (Figure 5) is exactly the right dog-not-barking test. - The finding that blockwise AR inference typically increases MSE (+1% to +6%) relative to one-pass prediction, with larger units worse, is a concrete, actionable negative result for anyone choosing inference schedules. - The monotone-quantile head (cumulative softplus offsets) with quantile-width confidence reuses the probabilistic output as a free ordering signal for MaskGIT-style decoding — a clean, parameter-free connection between uncertainty estimation and generation schedule. - Honest experimental hygiene in places: the same-corpus retraining protocol to remove data confounds, extrapolated latency points labeled as estimated, and a conservative framing of comparisons against larger-corpus baselines. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state three: (1) the padding-based batching for variable lengths wastes compute, with Patch-n'-Pack-style packing proposed as a fix; (2) inference schedules were compared only under a fixed protocol (K=3, fixed unit sizes), and adaptive schedules keyed to predicted uncertainty spread remain unexplored; (3) the study covers only BLAST-style pretraining, and the optimal mask-rate distribution may shift with model size, data mixture, and token budget. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. The authors also concede the latency gap to other single-pass models is not fully decomposed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting of any kind: single runs, no seeds, no confidence intervals, which is particularly problematic because many baseline margins are small and win counts are used as a headline metric. - Evaluation breadth is narrow for a foundation-model claim: six datasets, several of which (ETT family, Weather) are small, well-worn, and possibly represented in pretraining corpora of the weight-only baselines; the absence of the GIFT-Eval suite that PatchTST-FM's own corpus draws from is a conspicuous omission. - The central negative claim ('AR rollout offers no consistent gain') is established at one pretraining scale (131.4M, 10k steps, one corpus); whether larger models or longer training change the context-flexibility-vs-rollout trade-off is acknowledged as open but untested, so the conclusion is broader than the evidence. - The confidence measure (quantile interval width) is never compared against alternatives (e.g., prediction entropy, ensemble variance), and the K=3 schedule was hand-picked; the 4.7% ETTh2-720 improvement could be schedule-tuning luck. - Some strong single-pass baselines are missing from the latency-accuracy frontier (e.g., TiRex, Chronos-2, which the related-work section cites as supporting variable-length non-AR forecasting), limiting how much the efficiency claim generalizes. - Ablation variants are trained with filtering steps ('all variants remove samples whose effective sequence length is shorter than 4096'), which changes the effective training set between variants in ways that are not quantified. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or selecting TSFMs should read this for the controlled disproof of the 'AR rollout is necessary' assumption and the practical one-pass-vs-sequential latency argument, but should treat the accuracy tables as single-run evidence on a narrow benchmark set rather than proof of a new state of the art.

Problem & Motivation: Weather machine learning has matured along separated axes: forecasting (future states, fixed grid), spatial downscaling (finer grid, fixed time), and temporal downscaling (denser time, fixed grid). Real applications — minute-scale wind-power forecasting, sub-hourly precipitation nowcasting, aviation turbulence guidance — need all three at once: predict a future, spatially finer, temporally denser trajectory from coarse history. The paper also targets the practical constraint that modern weather foundation models (WFMs) are too large to fully fine-tune per task, so adaptation must happen under a small trainable-parameter budget, and asks whether low-rank adaptation can support this coupled task shift. Key Idea: The core trick is twofold. (1) Task-level: decompose PSWD into a spatial stage (backbone predicts a high-resolution endpoint at the final lead) and a temporal stage (linear interpolation between the upsampled present state and that endpoint, plus a learned residual), so fixed numerical scaffolds carry the bulk of the structure and lightweight heads learn only what interpolation cannot. (2) Adaptation-level: under a fixed rank budget r = rp + ro, allocate part of the rank to a principal branch initialized from the top singular components of W0 (PiSSA-style, function-preserving via residualization) and the rest to an orthogonal branch with fixed projectors onto the complement of the principal subspaces (OPLoRA-style), then rescale each rank-1 optimizer update by α = r · sg(ρ·π), where ρ (branch score) and π (component score) are gradient-magnitude-based, normalized signals with unit mean — reallocating update strength without changing trainable parameter count. Methodology: The pipeline: (a) fixed bilinear upsampler U_s lifts two coarse inputs (t−6h, t at 5.625°) to the 1.5° grid; (b) the PEFT-adapted Aurora backbone predicts a spatial scaffold at the 6h endpoint; (c) spatial correction head C_s (depthwise 3×3 conv + pointwise SwiGLU, zero-init output) adds a residual; (d) fixed linear interpolator U_t forms per-lead scaffolds between ˜x_t and the endpoint; (e) lead-conditioned temporal head C_t (softmax-gated residual basis maps) adds residuals for leads 1h–6h. Training is end-to-end with Aurora's variable-weighted L1 pretraining loss averaged over leads; the spatial endpoint receives no auxiliary loss (supervision flows through the temporal stage). PROLA's effective weight is W_eff = W_res + s_p·B_p·A_p + s_o·P⊥·B_o·A_o·Q⊥, with W_res = W0 − ΔW_p,0 preserving the pretrained function. Gradient-guided scaling is applied post-optimizer per rank-1 component, with stop-gradient scores and a mean-preserving normalization. Critical design decisions, each ablated: the scaffold-and-correct decomposition vs. direct joint prediction (Table 4: full pipeline 50.30 vs. 53.13 Z500 3h RMSE); the balanced 4+4 rank split vs. 6+2/2+6 (Table 5); and combining both branch and component scores vs. either alone (both-scored 50.30 vs. 76.06/75.45 at 6h Z500). All three are justified by controlled experiments. Key Results: Main benchmark: Aurora on WeatherBench 2, 5.625°→1.5°, inputs every 6h, targets 1h–6h, 2018 test, 68 channels, three seeds. PROLA (3.92M trainable, <0.4% of Full FT) achieves Z500 RMSE 50.58/72.35 at 3h/6h vs. best baseline AdaLoRA 53.40/77.51 (5.3%/6.7% lower) and beats 1.26B-parameter Full FT on Z500 at both leads and on T850/T2M at 6h (Full FT 106.68 vs. PROLA 72.35 Z500 6h). Ablations: removing both correction heads raises 3h Z500 RMSE to 87.73; the temporal head matters more than the spatial head at intermediate leads (84.53 vs. 53.35 when removed). Update-geometry diagnostic: PROLA places 34% of update energy in the orthogonal block vs. 16% for PiSSA (Full FT: 93%). Transfer: ERA5→CERRA (PROLA reduces Z500 RMSE 4.7% vs. PiSSA, best on all five variables, both leads); regional 6h precipitation (SEEPS 0.590 vs. 0.605 for OPLoRA at 12h); second backbone (ArchesWeather-M, best Z500/T2M at all four leads); additional resolution gap (5.625°→2.8125°); and text-to-SQL on BIRD with Qwen3.5-9B (52.87% EX vs. 51.96% PiSSA, 45.50% pretrained). Notably, the paper shows PROLA still under-predicts fine-scale variance (spectral power ratios <1 at short wavelengths, though less so than baselines) and that Full FT retains an edge on wind variables at some learning rates. Regional and transfer experiments use seed 0 only. Baselines (LoRA, DoRA, AdaLoRA, PiSSA, OPLoRA) are current and representative of the low-rank PEFT literature; no non-PEFT downscaling baselines (e.g., generative/diffusion downscalers) are compared. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (PSWD as a unified forecasting + spatial + temporal downscaling formulation and benchmark) + NEW METHOD (PROLA). The genuinely novel elements are the PSWD task formulation with its scaffold-and-correct evaluation protocol, and the specific composition of PiSSA-style principal initialization, OPLoRA-style orthogonal projection, and gradient-magnitude-guided, mean-preserving scaling of rank-1 optimizer updates — the latter being the most original mechanism. Each individual ingredient derives from existing work (PiSSA, OPLoRA, importance-scored update ideas), so the method is a new combination with a new scaling mechanism rather than a from-scratch framework; the update-geometry analysis (orthogonal energy share) is a useful new diagnostic. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. Main comparisons report mean ± standard deviation over three seeds; code is released (stated in the NeurIPS checklist, "We release the code"); training details (2× RTX 3090, 10 epochs, AdamW, schedules, per-method hyperparameters, parameter counts) are fully specified, including a training-cost table (PROLA 67m18s/epoch vs. LoRA 54m38s, same 15.56 GiB peak memory). Ablations isolate the pipeline, branch composition, rank split, and both scaling components; a full-FT learning-rate sweep guards against a weak Full FT baseline; rank-128 comparisons address rank sensitivity; spectral, seasonal, spatial-tail, tendency, and wind-derivative diagnostics go beyond RMSE. Concerns: (1) the regional and transfer experiments (CERRA, precipitation, ArchesWeather, BIRD, Table 12) are seed-0 only; (2) the method is developed and primarily evaluated on the same WeatherBench 2 setup, so Goodhart risk on the benchmark is not fully eliminated; (3) no significance tests, only std over 3 seeds; (4) no comparison against dedicated downscaling or generative weather models — only against other PEFT adapters within the authors' own pipeline, so the pipeline's competitiveness against the broader downscaling literature is unmeasured. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-flavored pipeline, but the claims are experimental). - Practical: Yes — all PEFT experiments run on two consumer RTX 3090 GPUs with ~15.6 GiB peak memory each, well within commodity hardware. - Efficient: Mostly — 3.92M trainable parameters (0.3% of Full FT) but training is ~23% slower per epoch than LoRA (67m vs. 55m) due to gradient-score computation and scaling overhead. - Effective: The evidence shows it improves PEFT-based PSWD on reanalysis benchmarks; it does not establish skill against real observational targets or against non-PEFT downscaling systems, so "solves PSWD" is only demonstrated relative to a within-pipeline proxy. - Scalable: Not directly tested — the main setting stops at 6h leads and 1.5° targets; a 5.625°→2.8125° gap and rank-128 runs exist, but nothing approaches km-scale targets or long rollout horizons (a 6–240h relative-RMSE figure exists but normalizes against Full FT rather than testing absolute skill). Deliverable: a software artifact (released code implementing the pipeline and PROLA); no released dataset or model checkpoints are stated. Strengths: - The PSWD formulation is a genuine conceptual contribution: it names and operationalizes a task regime (joint future + spatial + temporal refinement) that existing benchmarks treat separately, and the scaffold-and-correct pipeline is a sensible, well-ablated inductive bias for it. - The gradient-guided, mean-preserving rank-1 update scaling is a technically interesting mechanism with a clean unit-average property, and the blockwise update-energy diagnostic (34% vs. 16% orthogonal share vs. PiSSA, 93% for Full FT) provides mechanistic insight into why the method works, not just that it does. - The evidence that PROLA beats 1.26B-parameter full fine-tuning on several variables at 0.3% of the trainable parameters — checked across a full-FT learning-rate sweep — is a persuasive result for the implicit-regularization value of constrained low-rank adaptation. - Transfer breadth (two backbones, three weather tasks, plus BIRD text-to-SQL) is unusually thorough for a PEFT paper, partially defending against weather-specific overfitting of the method. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: In Appendix J, the authors state that PSWD is constrained by atmospheric chaos and the limited fine-scale information in coarse inputs; that evaluation covers a global reanalysis benchmark plus regional tasks; and that future work should extend to broader regions and target sources and add physical constraints and probabilistic prediction. They confront limitations directly but briefly — notably they do not acknowledge the absence of comparison against non-PEFT downscaling baselines or the single-seed nature of the regional/transfer results. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - All ground-truth "high-resolution" targets are reanalysis products (ERA5 at 1.5°, CERRA, conservatively remapped 2.8125°), i.e., spatially smooth fields; the paper never evaluates against genuinely observed fine-scale data, so the claim of resolving "local atmospheric patterns" is tested only against interpolated references — the same criticism the field levels at downscaling-to-reanalysis work. - No baselines from the spatial/statistical or generative downscaling literature (e.g., residual corrective diffusion downscalers cited in the related work); the comparison universe is entirely LoRA-variants inside the authors' own pipeline, so it is impossible to tell whether the scaffold-and-correct pipeline or PROLA itself is competitive with the state of practice for downscaling. - The main benchmark's forecast horizon is ≤6h with a 6h-cadence backbone; the claimed motivation (nowcasting, minute-scale wind, turbulence) involves different regimes, and the long-rollout figure (up to 240h) only shows relative-to-Full-FT ratios without absolute skill or comparison to the backbone's native use. - Regional, ArchesWeather, resolution-gap, and BIRD results are single-seed with no variance estimates, weakening the generality claims exactly where the sample size is smallest (e.g., the 0.91-point BIRD margin over PiSSA is within typical seed noise). - Gradient-guided scaling costs ~20% extra training time vs. LoRA; no analysis of whether the gain justifies this at larger rank/scale beyond the single rank-128 data point. - The orthogonal branch's fixed projectors are tied to the top-rp singular directions of the pretrained weight; no experiment probes sensitivity to how well the pretrained spectrum aligns with the target task (e.g., a poorly aligned backbone), so the method's robustness to the key assumption — that principal directions of W0 are meaningful for the new task — is untested. Bottom Line: A PEFT researcher or weather-ML practitioner building adaptation pipelines for weather foundation models gains real value here — a well-executed new task benchmark, a genuinely useful adapter design with mechanistic diagnostics, and strong matched-budget evidence — while anyone seeking competitive operational downscaling must look elsewhere, since the paper never benchmarks against dedicated downscaling systems or non-reanalysis targets.
