Problem & Motivation: Multi-humanoid teams are needed when objects (tables, sofas, stair carries, truck-bed handovers) exceed one robot's payload or geometry. Three coupled challenges exist: (1) interaction forces through a shared object make each robot's balance depend on partners it cannot observe; (2) long-horizon tasks (e.g., rotate the object to fit a door narrower than the object) require grounded planning; (3) mistimed lifts or steps destabilize the load. Centralized policies avoid these issues only by growing observation/action dimensions with team size, requiring retraining and networked inference; prior decentralized humanoid work largely targets single-robot skills or human-humanoid dyads, and cooperative multi-character manipulation is simulation-only. The paper targets real, physically coupled humanoid teams acting from local sensing alone, with fixed per-robot interfaces that scale to arbitrary team sizes. Key Idea: The core trick is a two-level decomposition with a deliberately narrow interface: all team skills are defined to start and end at one of two hub poses (empty-handed standing, holding object), so any skill composes with any other, each robot maps the shared team skill to its own frame via a fixed role map, and partners influence each robot only through forces in the shared object — which makes the shared, egocentric policy team-size-agnostic by construction. Synchronization is then solved by separating what (one discrete token decided by a leader) from when (a coarse shared slot grid that absorbs acoustic-delay jitter), so spoken commands replace network packets. Methodology: Low level: a frozen SONIC foundation tracker produces joint targets; a shared residual actor πθ learns corrections a_i = π_base(o_i) + πθ(o_i, π_base(o_i)), trained with MAPPO (centralized critic over concatenated observations, one value per agent; coupled terminations end the episode for the whole team). Rewards cover reference tracking for body and object, hand-loaded contact, and gait quality. References come from human video retargeting plus procedural IK, cut into hub-to-hub skills conditioned on the object spec c=(L,W,H,m) with ±10% size and ±20% mass perturbation; training uses long random legal skill chains, random waits at hubs, domain randomization (friction, pushes, actuation delay), and a teacher-student privileged-learning distillation (teacher trained with privileged observations, student adaptation module predicts the privileged latent locally), fine-tuned closed-loop with MAPPO over 4096 parallel two-robot teams at ~10^9 environment steps. High level: Qwen3-VL-2B fine-tuned with LoRA (~140M trainable params) outputs one token from K ∪ {HOLD, DONE} per leader camera image; 24 real teleoperated episodes or 1000 simulated episodes per task; decisions are made at hub poses only. Speech sync uses a spoken skill token, on-board microphones, and slot-grid scheduling with leader-side acoustic-delay offset. Design decisions are mostly well-justified by ablations (shared vs. independent actors, with vs. without SONIC), though the fixed skill length/angle discretization is asserted rather than ablated. Key Results: Low level (sim, 12 tasks, 3 seeds × 512 teams): HEAVE-HO 94.41% mean success, 18.62 cm body / 19.59 cm object error; baselines Pure SONIC 0.22%, Multi-HDMI 28.56%, ablations w/o SONIC 16.78%, independent actors 22.05%. Baselines are current and reasonable (SONIC [42] is the foundation model itself; Multi-HDMI extends HDMI [67]; CHORUS [16] is the closest decentralized VLA system). High level (5 tasks, 10 trials each): HEAVE-HO planner 86% average (6/10 real narrow door, 7/10 real corridor, 10/10 on all three sim tasks) vs. zero-shot GPT-6 (Astra) 42%, CHORUS 12% (fails every trial except 6/10 handover), human operator 98% upper bound; planner latency 52.5 ms on one RTX 4090 (5.3 GiB) vs. 78 ms CHORUS and ~6.46 s GPT-6 API (~120×). Real world: 92/100 successes across 10 team/task configurations; hardest is stair carry with a human (7/10). Scalability: policy trained on two G1s runs, without retraining, 4/8/10-G1 table carries in sim and 4-G1, 3-G1+human, PM01+human, and G1+PM01+human table carries in the real world. Testing scale is standard for humanoid RL training (Isaac, 4096 parallel teams) with a genuinely stress-scale deployment test at 10 robots; sim and real success rates are explicitly flagged as not directly comparable (wider initial-position sampling in sim). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (multi-agent residual post-training of a frozen humanoid foundation tracker for physically coupled decentralized collaboration), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (HH-BENCH, 12 tasks, 2–10 humanoids), and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the full speech-synchronized leader–follower stack). The genuinely novel elements are the hub-pose skill interface that makes a two-robot policy team-size-agnostic, and acoustic slot-grid synchronization replacing network sync; the underlying machinery — MAPPO with centralized training/decentralized execution, LoRA fine-tuning of a small VLM, domain randomization — is a competent combination of known techniques applied to a new and harder setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are strong: shared vs. independent actors, with vs. without frozen SONIC, and two external baselines, each with three seeds, 512 teams per seed, and per-seed standard deviations reported per task (Table 7), including body and object tracking errors. The high-level comparison uses 10 trials per task with a human-operator upper bound. However: no code, weights, or HH-BENCH release URL is stated anywhere (only a project page with videos is referenced), which limits reproducibility given the teleop data collection burden. Methodological concerns: the planner is fine-tuned on 24 episodes (real) or 1000 episodes (sim) per task of the same five tasks it is evaluated on, so its 86% vs. GPT-6's 42% partly measures task-specific training, not planning ability — a Goodhart-style confound the authors do not discuss; the zero-shot GPT-6 baseline is structurally disadvantaged. Real-world trials start from nominal configurations with small perturbations, so robustness claims rest mostly on simulation. Speech robustness (noise, misrecognition) is acknowledged qualitatively but never measured. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a strong SYSTEMS component — real hardware deployment). - Practical: Yes — runs on Unitree G1 on-board computers at 50 Hz, with the planner on a single RTX 4090 (5.3 GiB), all commercially available hardware. - Efficient: Two-robot training is compute-heavy (~10^9 env steps × 4096 teams), but inference is cheap and the planner is ~120× faster than the API-based LLM alternative; no retraining needed to change team size or add a human/PM01. - Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem for the tested tasks — 92/100 real trials, including a door narrower than the carried object — but success depends on a quiet acoustic environment and the follower's reliable speech recognition. - Scalable: Tested to 10 robots in simulation and 4 robots + human + alternate platform in the real world; growth beyond that is claimed by construction (shared egocentric policy, object-mediated coupling) rather than experimentally demonstrated, and the centralized-critic training phase scales with team size in observation length. Deliverable: the work stops at paper + project-page videos; no software artifact, trained model, or benchmark distribution is stated. Strengths: - The hub-pose skill interface is a real insight: by constraining every skill to shared start/end configurations and a common displacement profile, long-horizon composition reduces to discrete choice and the two-robot policy transfers to 10 robots and heterogeneous bodies with zero retraining — demonstrated, not just claimed. - The speech-based slot-grid synchronization is a clever, cheap mechanism that sidesteps networking entirely and, unusually, lets humans join or lead the team through the identical interface. - The low-level evaluation is unusually thorough for a systems robotics paper: 3 seeds × 512 teams × 12 tasks with per-task error bars, body/object error metrics, and ablations that isolate each claimed ingredient (frozen tracker, shared actor). - Real-world heterogeneous deployments (G1 + PM01 + human carrying a table; stair carry with a human) at 37/40 success show the sim-to-real and team-composition generalization is genuine rather than simulated. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state two limitations directly: (1) speech-based synchronization requires a reasonably quiet environment and reliable sound pickup; (2) training the planner for a new task requires manually collected teleoperation demonstrations, which is time-consuming. This is a candid but partial accounting — both limitations are real and the authors do not minimize them — but they omit the planner's task-specific fine-tuning confound and the absence of released artifacts. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The planner comparison conflates fine-tuning with planning ability: HEAVE-HO's Qwen3-VL-2B is trained on the evaluation tasks; GPT-6 is zero-shot. A fairer missing baseline is a fine-tuned GPT-6 or a trained planner on held-out task compositions. - The benchmark is developed and evaluated by the same authors on their own tasks, with no external tasks or third-party baselines beyond CHORUS and Multi-HDMI; HH-BENCH's value as a community benchmark depends on artifacts that are not stated as released. - No speech-channel robustness quantification: recognition error rate under noise, command confusion (e.g., 'left' vs. 'right'), or failure recovery when a follower mishears — a single misrecognized skill token during a coupled carry could drop the object. - Safety is not addressed: coupled multi-humanoid carrying near humans with no network, no stop mechanism discussion, and no discussion of what happens when the leader errs mid-task. - Real-world evaluation starts from nominal configurations with small perturbations, while the sim evaluation samples broadly; the claimed real-world robustness is therefore narrower than the sim numbers suggest (the authors flag incomparability but not the asymmetry). - The paper reports simulated scaling to 8–10 robots only for the table-carry task; whether the 10-robot claim holds for other task types is not evaluated. Bottom Line: A practitioner in humanoid or multi-robot manipulation gains concrete, transferable recipes — residual post-training of a frozen foundation tracker, hub-pose skill composition, and acoustic slot-grid synchronization — backed by unusually careful low-level evaluation and real heterogeneous deployments, making this one of the strongest demonstrations of decentralized physically-coupled humanoid collaboration to date despite the task-specific planner evaluation and unreleased artifacts.

Breath-Dx: A Time Series Classification Benchmark for Disease Screening with eNose (32 ▲ )

Ivan Poddiakov, Ivan Kruzhilov, Galina Zubkova, Svetlana Erofeeva, Andrey Savchenko, Pavel Blinov · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 18 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Breath-Dx, a benchmark built on the Scent of Health (S-OH) dataset — the largest public clinical electronic-nose collection (1,234 patients, 9 diagnostic groups, 17-channel breath time series, 13 weeks, 2 clinical sites) — and systematically evaluates 10 time series classification methods under drift-aware temporal splits. - Why it's important: Clinical eNose research has been stuck on small (<100–250 patient), private, single-pathology datasets with incomparable evaluation protocols, so reported results (often from random cross-validation) badly overestimate real-world screening performance. - How it does it: The core move is explicit temporal train/test separation by collection week (with disease-specific held-out test segments and no patient leakage), which converts sensor drift — a known but rarely quantified failure mode — into a measurable benchmark condition. - The good: The drift quantification is concrete and reproducible: all methods drop 0.05–0.12 AUC under temporal vs. random validation, and a CatBoost model predicts the measurement day from raw sensor data with 2–3 days median absolute error, directly proving a strong non-stationary signal in the sensor traces. - The missing: There is no external or cross-device validation (both sites used the same sensor hardware), no benchmarking of drift-correction methods, and the headline 0.05–0.12 AUC drop is tabulated for only a selected subset of method–disease pairs rather than the full grid. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on breathomics, gas-sensor ML, or medical time series under distribution shift — the dataset and drift-aware protocol are immediately reusable — but skip it if you want a new method, since no architecture here is novel and most AUCs are modest.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Practical Impact (80) is the strongest dimension — the S-OH dataset, temporal splits, and demographic-confounder protocol are released (Hugging Face + GitHub) and are an order of magnitude larger than any prior public eNose collection, making them immediately reusable. Novelty (70) is anchored by NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus the first quantified drift penalty, though all methods are off-the-shelf. Rigor (68) is limited by a drift claim tabulated for only four method–disease pairs, unablated channel selection, and hyperparameter asymmetry favoring deep models; Completeness (65) is dented by unexplained sub-0.5 AUCs and an unflagged one-vs-rest comparability caveat. Resilience (62) suffers because the headline 0.05–0.12 AUC drop is extrapolated from a selected subset, and peak AUCs of 0.70–0.77 do not support clinical screening claims. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*68 + 0.15*62 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*62 + 0.10*80 = 67.

Problem & Motivation: Electronic noses promise portable, non-invasive disease screening from exhaled breath VOCs, but the field lacks systematic comparisons under realistic conditions. Prior clinical studies evaluate one method on one pathology with tens to a few hundred patients (e.g., asthma n=38, tuberculosis n=224), almost never release raw data or code, and use inconsistent protocols that ignore sensor drift. Consequently, basic questions — which classifier families survive drift, whether reported gains beat simple baselines, whether breath signals carry information beyond demographics — remain unanswered, blocking clinical deployment. Key Idea: The key idea is not an algorithmic trick but a benchmark-design decision: preserve sensor drift as a first-class evaluation axis by splitting data temporally (train and test weeks disjoint, disease-specific test segments, no patient leakage), then quantify both the drift itself (day-of-measurement prediction from raw signals, MAE 2–3 days) and its cost (AUC drop under temporal vs. random validation). A secondary insight is treating demographic-only models (age/gender) as mandatory confounder baselines for any eNose screening claim. Methodology: Each patient contributes a 17-channel series (358 time steps at 0.4 Hz over 895 s); each of nine groups (healthy controls + 8 ICD-10 diseases) is framed as one-vs-rest binary classification, scored by ROC AUC over 16 random training splits with 15% validation/early stopping and a fixed temporal test set. Ten methods span four families: (i) feature-based tabular learners (CatBoost, XGBoost, HistGradientBoost, RandomForest) over four engineered feature sets — Stats 5 (min/max/mean/median/std), LogFit 2/4 (logistic growth-curve kinetic parameters via scipy curve_fit), and wavelet-smoothed polynomial features; (ii) convolution models treating series as images (shallow CNN, ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18 on polynomial feature matrices); (iii) Graphormer on a complete 8-node graph of stable channels with 9-dim node features (stats + kinetic + Chebyshev coefficients) and 3-dim edge features; (iv) raw-series models (3-layer LSTM with 128 hidden units, InceptionTime ensemble, TS2Vec unsupervised pretraining + logistic head). Time series are clipped to gas-flow windows, median-filtered, and min-max normalized per channel (or per-channel normalization preserving channel ratios for Graphormer). A flattened L2-regularized Logistic Regression serves as the linear lower-bound baseline. Critical design decisions: (1) disease-specific temporal splits — justified as mimicking realistic deployment, though the exact week-assignment rationale is not given; (2) deliberate exclusion of drift-correction techniques from the core benchmark — justified as establishing baselines, but it leaves the drift problem unsolved rather than addressed; (3) using only 8 of 17 channels for feature-based/graph methods based on manufacturer stability pre-screening — justified only by a priori criteria, not ablated. Key Results: Under temporal validation, the best per-disease results are Graphormer on COPD (AUC 0.767±0.061), InceptionTime on lung cancer (0.746±0.030), and CatBoost+Stats 5 on hepatitis (0.698±0.011); diabetes (E11) and tuberculosis (A15) stay near chance (0.45–0.55) for all 10 methods. Random vs. temporal splits show 0.05–0.12 AUC degradation for all methods (e.g., InceptionTime on lung cancer 0.812→0.746; Graphormer on COPD 0.831→0.767), though Table V reports only four selected pairs. No single method dominates: LSTM is most consistent (average AUC 0.598, top-3 for 5/9 diseases), while Graphormer and InceptionTime show peak-but-unstable behavior (Graphormer std up to ±0.118 on Z00). The Logistic Regression baseline is competitive — best on gastritis (AUC 0.718) and strong on hepatitis (0.687) and tuberculosis (0.688) — beating several deep methods. Demographics confound strongly: age-only AUC reaches 0.803 for tuberculosis and 0.678 for lung cancer (rivaling sensor models), while for liver disease (K76) and gastritis (K29) demographic-only models sit at AUC≈0.5 but sensor models exceed 0.65, evidence of genuinely independent breath signal. Subgroup effects are large: hepatitis AUC is 0.763 in women vs. 0.552 in men. Scale is moderate — 1,234 patients, largest public eNose collection but still small by ML standards, hence the ±0.01–0.12 standard deviations. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel contributions are the S-OH dataset (first large, multi-pathology, multi-site public clinical eNose collection with temporal annotations) and the first quantified drift penalty under standardized temporal splits. The 10 methods are entirely off-the-shelf; the Graphormer-over-sensor-channels construction is a reasonable adaptation, not a new formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: the paper compares feature sets against each other, temporal vs. random splits, and demographic-only vs. sensor models, but does not ablate channel selection (8 vs. 17 channels) or preprocessing choices. Error bars are reported as mean±std over 16 training splits with a fixed temporal test set; no significance tests are run. The dataset is released on Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/ivanpodd/S-OH) and code at https://github.com/ivanpodd/Breath-Dx, which is a major reproducibility asset. Methodological concerns: the drift-severity claim (0.05–0.12 AUC) is only tabulated for four method–disease pairs while being claimed as a universal finding; hyperparameters for ensembles are library defaults while deep models get moderate tuning, an asymmetry that partially explains why the linear baseline is competitive; and the paper is a self-described ICDM 2026 submission/acceptance (Best Paper Runner-Up per the title page), so the award status is self-reported. Baselines against prior eNose literature are qualitative (citation of their reported metrics), not re-run, which is defensible given those datasets are private. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark dataset plus methods actually run), with a SYSTEMS-adjacent artifact (released dataset, splits, code). - Practical: Yes — models are small; CNN/ResNet18 inference runs under 1 second on CPU, and feature-based methods are trivially deployable. - Efficient: Ensembles and CNNs are cheap relative to the 358×17 input size; Graphormer and InceptionTime cost more for little average gain (LSTM, cheapest raw-series option, has the best average rank). - Effective: Evidence supports useful signal for COPD, lung cancer, and hepatitis (AUC 0.70–0.77), but the proxy question — whether temporal-split AUC predicts prospective clinical screening performance — is untested; the authors themselves say temporal splits "approximate but cannot fully replace" prospective validation. - Scalable: Untested at 10× scale; Graphormer's high variance and the authors' own note that graph methods "may require larger datasets" suggest current scale limits some architectures, and cross-device generalization is unexamined. The work delivers a real software/data artifact (dataset, temporal splits, evaluation protocols, code), not just a paper. Strengths: - The dataset itself: 1,234 patients across 9 groups, 2 sites, 13 consecutive weeks with temporal metadata and auxiliary readings (temperature, pressure, humidity, CO2) — roughly an order of magnitude larger than the prior largest public eNose disease dataset (n=78) and the only one with drift-aware splits. - The drift quantification is done properly: day-of-measurement prediction (MAE 2–3 days) establishes drift independently of the classification task, and the random-vs-temporal AUC comparison turns an anecdotal failure mode into a measured number. - The demographic-confounder analysis is a genuine methodological contribution to the field: showing age-only AUC of 0.803 for tuberculosis while sensor models sit near chance, versus the reverse pattern for liver disease and gastritis, gives the community a concrete template for honest eNose evaluation. - Honest negative results: near-chance performance on two diseases and a linear baseline beating deep models are reported prominently rather than buried, which raises trust in the positive numbers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (i) both clinical sites used the same eNose device, so cross-device and cross-batch generalization is unassessed; (ii) no drift-correction techniques were applied — the benchmark establishes baselines only; (iii) temporal splits approximate but cannot replace prospective validation on new cohorts; (iv) diabetes performance may be confounded by treated patients normalizing breath profiles, and tuberculosis patients were enrolled at a dedicated treatment center, possibly normalizing VOCs. They confront limitations directly and enumerate three future directions (drift-robust learning, multi-disease models, prospective validation) — this is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline "0.05–0.12 AUC drop" is extrapolated from a four-row selected table (Table V) to all methods and diseases; the full grid comparison is not shown. - Only 8 of 17 channels are used for feature-based and graph methods based on manufacturer pre-screening; no experiment tests whether the excluded 9 channels carry diagnostic information. - The one-vs-rest design means the healthy group (Z00) is itself a classification target and every disease model's negative class mixes healthy + 7 other diseases, so AUCs across diseases are not directly comparable to single-pathology literature results — a comparability caveat the paper does not flag. - Graphormer's standard deviations (up to ±0.118) are large relative to the gap between methods, yet method rankings are discussed without significance testing; several LSTM entries also exceed ±0.10. - Some AUCs fall well below 0.5 (e.g., Logistic Regression on K76 = 0.302), indicating label-flipping inconsistencies in reporting that are not explained. - The tuberculosis cohort comes from a different site, device-era window (weeks 12–13), and disease profile than the rest, so its near-chance result conflates site shift, drift, and biology; the authors mention cohort normalization but not the confounded site/week structure. - No calibration or operating-point analysis (sensitivity/specificity at clinically meaningful thresholds) despite framing the work as screening-oriented. Bottom Line: A practitioner in breathomics or sensor-drift-aware medical ML gains real, reusable value — the dataset, temporal splits, and demographic-baseline protocol should become the community default — even though the methods compared are stock and the achieved AUCs (0.70–0.77 peak) suggest eNose screening is not yet clinically deployable; there is no stronger alternative resource covering the same ground.

Training-Free Character-Length Control in Summarization with Diffusion Language Models

S Castle, N Feldhus, C Ebert, L Hennig, S Möller · aclanthology.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DELTA, a training-free inference-time algorithm for masked diffusion language models (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B) that estimates expected character length at each denoising step and dynamically inserts or removes mask positions to hit an exact character-count target in summarization. - Why it's important: Publishing pipelines, notification previews, subtitles, and UI text require outputs that fit fixed character slots, and autoregressive LMs can only approximate such budgets via prompting or task-specific fine-tuning — even a few excess characters cause truncation or layout overflow. - How it does it: The core trick is an expected character-length estimator that combines exact lengths of committed tokens with probability-weighted expected lengths over remaining masks, then greedily adds/removes low-confidence masks between commitment steps to steer the denoising buffer toward the target. - The good: The length-control gain is large and cleanly isolated: mean absolute character-length error drops from 44.9–112.2 characters (best autoregressive/API baselines on arXiv) to 2.3–3.1 characters across three benchmarks, with >98% of outputs within 10 characters of target, and the fixed-buffer ablation (Appendix C) directly attributes this to the dynamic buffer adjustment. - The missing: There is no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis — the confidence thresholds (τ, τ_low) were grid-searched per dataset and per model on validation sets, and the initial buffer size itself is estimated from validation reference statistics, so plug-and-play applicability to new domains is untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on controllable generation or diffusion language models, and for practitioners who need hard character budgets in production pipelines — skippable if you only care about autoregressive decoding or unconstrained summarization quality.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (70) is solid — the expected-character-length estimator over mask distributions is a genuine new formulation of length control inside diffusion decoding — and Completeness (70) benefits from the honest accounting of the quality trade-off. Rigor (65) is held back by absent seeds/error bars, per-dataset grid-searched hyperparameters on the evaluation benchmarks, and unevaluated closest competitors (DreamOn, ρ-EOS). Practical Impact (60) reflects a released code artifact but 4–7× slower inference than autoregressive decoding. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*62 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*60 = 66.

Problem & Motivation: Summarization for fixed display slots (headlines, article previews, notification previews, subtitles, UI text) requires outputs fitting an exact character budget. Training-based autoregressive solutions (CTRLsum length bins, Miculicich et al.'s joint length-predictor decoding, Belligoli et al.'s EOS-loss upweighting) need task-specific fine-tuning; zero-shot strategies (Retkowski & Waibel's length-approximation with sampling/filtering, Xie & Lee's countdown markers) achieve only approximate compliance and degrade as target length grows. Both families operate under left-to-right decoding where already-emitted tokens cannot be revised within a generation pass, so decoded character length cannot be corrected mid-generation. Masked diffusion LMs, which iteratively refine a buffer of masked tokens, offer a structurally different opportunity that no prior method exploits for character-level budget steering. Key Idea: Because a masked diffusion LM produces a full predictive distribution q_i over the vocabulary at every masked position at every denoising step, one can compute a running expected decoded character length — committed positions contribute exact token lengths, masked positions contribute probability-weighted expected token lengths — and use the gap between this estimate and the target to insert or delete mask tokens mid-denoising. This works precisely because diffusion models tolerate occasional buffer-length perturbations during refinement, an operation that is structurally unavailable to autoregressive decoders. Methodology: DELTA is an inference-time decoding loop wrapped around a standard masked diffusion LM (LLaDA-8B-Instruct or Dream-7B-Instruct), with no fine-tuning or architectural change. Each iteration: (1) forward pass yields per-position distributions q_i and confidence scores c_i (max predicted probability, MaskGIT-style); (2) expected character length L̂ is computed by summing exact lengths of committed tokens and Σ_v q_{i,v}·ℓ(v) over masked positions, with zero-length special tokens masked out of the logits; (3) if L̂ > L, the lowest-confidence masks (below threshold τ_low) are greedily removed until the expected-length deficit is minimized; if L̂ < L, new masks are inserted adjacent to least-confident positions, with insertion count estimated as (L* − L̂)/ℓ̄ using the current mean expected characters per token; (4) otherwise, positions with c_i > τ are committed via argmax, with at least one commitment per step guaranteeing progress. To prevent oscillation between insertion and removal, buffer adjustment is permitted only immediately after a commitment step. Critical design decisions: (a) probability-weighted expected length rather than sampling — sensible and cheap, well-justified by the ablation showing fixed-buffer decoding fails (MAE 15.6–113.9 vs. 2.3–3.1); (b) the anti-oscillation rule (adjust only after commitment) — plausible but justified only informally, with no analysis of convergence; (c) per-dataset/per-model grid-searched thresholds — effective but not adaptive. Key Results: On XSum, CNN/DailyMail, and arXiv test sets (11,334 / 11,490 / 6,440 examples; average reference lengths 125 / 312 / 969 characters), DELTA achieves MAE of 2.3–3.1 characters and 98.3–99.7% of outputs within 10 characters of target, versus LA-SF-AR (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, the strongest length-control baseline) at MAE 5.2 (XSum), 10.3 (CNN/DM), 44.9 (arXiv) with only 22.9% within-10 on arXiv; GPT-4o-mini prompting reaches MAE 13.1–112.2. Quality stays competitive: DELTA+Dream posts the best ROUGE-1 (0.333 XSum) and BERTScore (0.890) on XSum and best BERTScore on arXiv (0.853), second only to fine-tuned BART on CNN/DM (ROUGE-1 0.409 vs. 0.441); autoregressive baselines score higher on G-Eval (e.g., GPT-4o-mini: 4.53 relevance vs. 3.97 for DELTA+Dream on CNN/DM), a trade-off the authors acknowledge. A blind human evaluation on 50 CNN/DM examples with two annotators rates DELTA+Dream at 4.27 average vs. 4.32 (LA-SF-AR) and 4.31 (GPT-4o-mini). Fixed-buffer ablation confirms the mechanism (MAE 15.55 vs. 2.3 on XSum). DAEDAL, the closest training-free diffusion baseline, fails badly on character budgets (MAE 74.5–6337.5). Baselines are reasonably current (LA-SF-AR from NAACL 2025, GPT-4o-mini, DAEDAL from ICLR 2026), though no comparison to DreamOn or ρ-EOS is run in the main table. Runtime is a real cost: 8.59 s/summary on CNN/DM and 20.75–22.80 s on arXiv vs. 2.19 s and 13.22 s for LA-SF-AR, due to repeated full-sequence forward passes without KV caching. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with an EMPIRICAL FINDING component. The genuinely novel element is the expected-character-length estimator over uncommitted mask distributions combined with in-loop buffer insertion/removal to hit a decoded character budget — prior diffusion work (DreamOn, DAEDAL, ρ-EOS) addresses variable-length generation but not targeting a specified decoded character count. The building blocks are standard: MaskGIT-style confidence decoding, greedy mask sorting, and the models themselves; the contribution is a new formulation of the control target within the diffusion decoding loop rather than a new model or training procedure. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes a well-designed fixed-buffer ablation (same model, prompt, confidence schedule, initialization) that isolates the mechanism, a comparison to the closest training-free diffusion alternative (DAEDAL), a Lead-3 diagnostic distinguishing the character-budgeted extractive baseline from standard Lead-3, and a judge-sensitivity analysis (GPT-4o-mini vs. GPT-5-mini G-Eval scores differ substantially, particularly for extractive baselines). No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported for the length/quality metrics; runtime reports mean ± std only. Code, evaluation scripts, prompts, hyperparameters, and seeds are released at https://github.com/DFKI-NLP/delta-diffusion. Methodological concerns: τ and τ_low are grid-searched per dataset and model on validation sets, and the initial buffer size uses average characters-per-token from validation references — a modest Goodhart risk since hyperparameters are tuned on the same benchmark family used for evaluation; the human evaluation is small (50 examples, two annotators, 91.5% within-one-point agreement); DAEDAL on arXiv is evaluated on only a 100-example diagnostic subset. The evaluation is honest about the quality/length trade-off rather than gaming it. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact). - Practical: Yes — runs on open-weight 7–8B diffusion models; GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3.1-8B baselines are also commercially/locally accessible hardware, though no GPU specification is given. - Efficient: No — 8.6–22.8 s per summary on CNN/DM/arXiv (roughly 4–7× slower than LA-SF-AR's 2.19–13.22 s) because bidirectional diffusion attention precludes standard KV caching; only on short targets (XSum, 0.67–0.69 s) is it faster than the autoregressive baseline. - Effective: Yes on the stated problem — near-exact character compliance (MAE ≤ 3.1, >98% within 10 chars) with quality competitive to baselines per ROUGE/BERTScore/human eval, though G-Eval favors autoregressive baselines on quality. - Scalable: Not tested — all evaluation is English summarization with two 7–8B models; effectiveness on much longer targets, other languages, other tokenizers, and smaller/larger diffusion models is explicitly unvalidated. Delivers a software artifact: public implementation, evaluation scripts, and configuration. Strengths: - A clean conceptual insight: the per-step predictive distributions over masks double as a free, differentiable-in-expectation character-length signal, turning the diffusion buffer into a controllable budget rather than a fixed canvas. - The fixed-buffer ablation is the right experiment — it uses identical models, prompts, confidence schedules, and initialization, so the 15.55→2.3 MAE (XSum) and 113.94→2.8 MAE (arXiv) deltas are directly attributable to the buffer-adjustment mechanism, not to prompting or model choice. - Testing across three datasets with 6–969-character targets shows the method's error is roughly length-invariant (MAE 2.3–3.1), while the strongest autoregressive baseline's error grows 5.2→44.9 — a genuinely structural advantage, not a tuned lucky result. - Honest accounting of the trade-off: autoregressive baselines win on G-Eval quality scores, and the paper says so plainly rather than burying it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Limitations section confronts the paper's weaknesses directly (a credibility positive): (1) inference is slow — 8.59 s (CNN/DM) and 20.75–22.80 s (arXiv) per summary vs. 2.19 s and 13.22 s for LA-SF-AR, since diffusion LMs cannot use standard KV caching; (2) LLM-judge scores are judge-sensitive (GPT-4o-mini vs. GPT-5-mini differ substantially on Consistency/Coherence, especially for extractive baselines); (3) the human evaluation covers only 50 CNN/DM examples with two annotators; (4) evaluation is English-only, limited to two 7–8B models, and character-length estimation depends on the tokenizer's token-to-character mapping; (5) τ and τ_low are grid-searched per dataset/model with no sensitivity analysis or adaptive setting, limiting plug-and-play use. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical rigor around headline numbers: single runs, no seeds, no confidence intervals on MAE or ROUGE; given MAE gaps as small as 2.3 vs. 5.2 (XSum vs. LA-SF-AR), variance matters. - The initial buffer size is estimated from validation reference statistics (average characters per token) — meaning the method partly leans on dataset-derived priors rather than being fully zero-shot at the document level; no experiment shows robustness when this prior is miscalibrated. - No sensitivity analysis of the anti-oscillation rule or the confidence threshold on termination behavior; worst-case non-convergence to the target length (relying on a maximum-iteration cap of ⌊L*/2⌋) is never characterized. - Quality measurement is partly confounded: DELTA outputs are conditioned on exact-length prompts, but the diffusion models' G-Eval relevance scores are notably lower than autoregressive baselines on arXiv (3.71/3.09 vs. 3.98), and the paper does not probe whether hitting an exact length forces content compression that a length-tolerant system avoids. - No comparison with DreamOn or ρ-EOS (both cited, both ICLR 2026/arXiv), leaving the strongest diffusion-side competitors unevaluated; the DAEDAL arXiv comparison rests on 100 examples. - Human evaluation has no reported inter-annotator statistic beyond within-one-point agreement (91.5%) and no significance testing; 50 examples across three systems is thin for claiming quality parity. Bottom Line: A practitioner or researcher who needs hard character budgets in generation should read and likely reuse DELTA — it is the first convincing demonstration that masked diffusion LMs natively support exact decoded-length control that autoregressive decoders structurally cannot match, and the code is public; anyone optimizing for summary quality per unit of latency should stick with autoregressive baselines, since DELTA's quality is competitive rather than superior and its inference cost is 4–7× higher on long inputs.

BypassGym: A Benchmark for Evaluating AI Agents ' Endpoint Defense Evasion Capabilities

W Yuan, Z Chen, Y Zhang, F Dong, P Gao, H Wang · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces BypassGym, the first benchmark that measures whether LLM agents can autonomously build and iterate a shellcode loader that executes a C2 payload on a real Windows endpoint protected by a deployed EDR product. - Why it's important: AI-assisted malware that evades endpoint defenses is already observed in the wild (LAMEHUG, PROMPTFLUX, Anthropic-documented ransomware abuse), so model providers, EDR vendors, and policymakers need a repeatable measurement of this capability rather than anecdotes. - How it does it: The benchmark fixes a C2 shellcode payload and an iteration budget, lets an agent compile loader candidates in a Docker toolchain, and evaluates them on snapshot-restored Proxmox VE Windows VMs — first without EDR for functional validation, then against one of six commercial EDRs — returning structured pass/fail check feedback to the agent. - The good: Across 90 runs (5 models × 6 EDRs × 3 payloads), 71 (78.9%) produced a working, EDR-evading loader, with even the cheapest model (DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash) at 17/18 — a systematic, execution-based demonstration that low-cost EDR evasion is broadly available to current agents. - The missing: Every cell is a single run with no repeats, seeds, or variance estimates, and RQ2/RQ3 ablations cover only 2 of 5 models, so the headline percentages carry no uncertainty quantification and the ablation conclusions may not generalize. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on AI cybersecurity risk assessment, EDR engineering, or model safety/policy evaluation; skip it if you want novel agent architectures or rigorous statistics, since the core contribution is the benchmark and its measurement results.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. The benchmark's first-mover value is real — an execution-based oracle on snapshot-restored VMs with commercial EDRs and a delayed-replay study is a substantively harder measurement than scanner-verdict prior work (Novelty 72), and the knowledge-dependence finding is genuinely actionable (Non-Obviousness 65). Rigor (55) is the dominant drag: one run per model-EDR-payload cell with no variance estimation anywhere, RQ2/RQ3 models selected post hoc on the same benchmark, and a harness-EBR contamination at Bitdefender that is unquantified. Impact (68) is limited by post-review-only release and EDR licensing constraints on reproduction; Completeness (72) is a positive — limitations are confronted directly and quantified. Resilience (60) suffers from the self-defined 'non-blocking' scope being narrower than the title implies. Weighted composite: 0.15*72 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*65 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*60 + 0.30*68 = 66.

Problem & Motivation: EDR is the primary deployed defense against malware, and LLM agents can now autonomously write, compile, and debug offensive tooling, but existing evaluations do not answer whether an agent can produce a functional loader whose payload actually runs on a real endpoint under a deployed EDR. Prior malware-evasion work (MalGEN, LLMalMorph) checks scanner verdicts or sandboxes offline; Obfusc8 only rewrites PowerShell scripts; Dante-7B generates loaders but never tests execution against an EDR; agentic security benchmarks (Cybench, AutoPenBench, CyberGym, AgentCyberRange, CyberSecEval 3) target penetration testing, CTF, or vulnerability reproduction, where EDR evasion is at most one step in a chain, often judged by LLM evaluators rather than real endpoints. The gap: no standardized, comparable, execution-based measurement of agent-driven endpoint defense evasion. Key Idea: Close the evaluation loop with a real, snapshot-restored Windows VM running a commercial EDR and return structured, check-level failure feedback to the agent — i.e., treat EDR evasion as an iterative, feedback-guided compilation task with an execution-based oracle (payload executes, process survives, and a working C2 session completes command and file-transfer checks), rather than a one-shot generation task judged by scanners or LLM heuristics. Methodology: BypassGym has three modules. (1) Evasion Task Setup pairs a fixed shellcode payload from an open-source C2 framework (Havoc 0.7, Sliver 1.5.43, AdaptixC2 1.2) with one target EDR and a curated evasion-knowledge skill (37 techniques, 3 reference loader projects — AceLdr, gargoyle, BOAZ — and 6 DLL-hijacking templates, packaged as a native Codex-style agent skill with full/partial/none availability conditions). (2) Shellcode Loader Development gives the agent (Codex CLI, Claude Code, or OpenCode scaffolds; GPT-6 Luna, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, GLM-5.3 Flash, DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash, or Qwen3.7 Plus backends) a Windows compilation toolchain and up to 10 iterations; each submission is a ZIP with exactly one PE32+ entry executable and encrypted shellcode. (3) EDR Evaluation and Feedback runs the candidate on a NoEDR Windows 11 VM (Endpoint Execution Check: static, process survival after 10 s, outbound traffic within 60 s, delayed survival after another 10 s), then on the target EDR VM where it must additionally pass a C2 Functionality Check (communication, command execution via whoami, bidirectional file transfer) driven by a common playbook. The oracle is functional execution and survival; detection alerts are deliberately excluded because vendors do not expose consistent alert telemetry. Critical design decisions: (a) alerts excluded from the verdict — justified operationally (attackers care whether code runs, and alert telemetry is not uniformly accessible), but it narrows "evasion" to non-interference; (b) snapshot restoration before each test — well justified for comparability; (c) fixed payload with open loader design — well justified as the standardization/capability trade-off, though it limits payload-side evasion analysis. Key Results: RQ1 (90 runs, one per cell, Codex CLI scaffold): 71/90 (78.9%) passed. DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash was strongest at 17/18 (94.4%), Qwen3.7 Plus weakest at 10/18; GPT-6 Luna 14/18, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite 15/18, GLM-5.3 Flash 15/18. Windows Defender passed all 15 submissions; Bitdefender allowed only 5/15 (33.3%); all five models failed Havoc-on-Bitdefender. Payload difficulty: Sliver 27/30, Havoc 24/30, AdaptixC2 20/30. A default-C2 baseline confirms the task is non-trivial: 15 of 18 default executables failed their EDR. 50/71 passing submissions used DLL side-loading via the signed ssvagent.exe host. Delayed replay 1–4 weeks later (after 24-hour EDR update windows): 62/71 (87.3%) still passed, with Trend Micro, Sophos, and Bitdefender at 100% survival and Kaspersky an outlier at 61.5% (5/13 losses). RQ2 (DeepSeek and GLM only, 18 runs per condition): removing the knowledge skill caused the largest drop (GLM 15/18 → 9/18; DeepSeek 17/18 → 13/18); all three scaffolds achieved 15/18 for GLM and 16–17/18 for DeepSeek with model-dependent repair costs; reasoning effort was non-monotonic (GLM 11→14→14; DeepSeek best at Low, 17/18). RQ3: detailed check-level feedback raised success to 15/18 (GLM) and 17/18 (DeepSeek) versus 14/18 one-shot; binary pass/fail feedback added nothing. Refusals occurred in 4 runs (135 turns, 97 in one GPT run). All results are preprint, self-reported by the authors. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (1) the first execution-based benchmark measuring whether agent-built loaders survive deployed commercial EDRs on real endpoints, and (2) the systematic finding that cheap flash-tier models achieve 78.9–94.4% evasion success with a common DLL side-loading pattern. The individual ingredients — iterative coding agents, snapshot-restored VMs, known evasion techniques from public repositories — are standard combinations applied to a new evaluation setting; the knowledge skill is a curated aggregation of public material, not a new technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present for knowledge richness, scaffold, and reasoning effort, and the RQ3 feedback ablation cleanly isolates the value of detailed verdicts — these are the paper's strongest experimental elements. However, there is one run per model-EDR-payload cell with no repetitions, no error bars, no significance tests, and no confidence intervals anywhere; conclusions like "Bitdefender is hardest" rest on n=1 per cell. RQ2/RQ3 cover only the two best models, selected post hoc on the same benchmark, which risks selection bias in the ablation conclusions. The functional baseline (Table 3) is a good control showing defaults fail. Exact versions for every EDR, OS, tool, and payload are documented (Appendix C). Code and data are promised for release after review, with the caveat that licensed EDR installs, credentials, and C2 shellcode cannot be redistributed — so full reproduction requires users to supply their own authorized EDR environments, weakening out-of-the-box reproducibility. Methodological concerns: evaluation only on the authors' own benchmark; the Bitdefender Guest Agent deletion failure mode contaminates some results (the harness itself gets quarantined); and the oracle's exclusion of alerts means "evasion" is really "non-blocking," a choice the authors defend but which understates silent-detection outcomes. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built benchmark/evaluation infrastructure, evaluated by running it), with an EMPIRICAL component (agent experiments). - Practical: Runs on Proxmox VE with consumer/enterprise Windows VMs and Docker containers — realistic for any security lab that holds EDR licenses, but not trivially for academic groups without licenses. - Efficient: Successful runs typically cost 8–30 minutes and 0.1–3M tokens; failures can burn 2–48M tokens and 1–3 hours, so worst-case cost is 10–100× the typical success case. - Effective: The evidence shows agents solve the stated operational problem (payload executes, C2 session completes command + file transfer) — a direct outcome measure, not a proxy — though 12.7% of successes were retroactively caught by delayed cloud telemetry. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 5 models × 6 EDRs × 3 payloads; scaling to more EDRs, OSes, and payload types is claimed as future work, and per-run VM restoration cost is unexamined at 10× scale. The work delivers a benchmark framework (source code and data promised post-review); no trained model or defense artifact. Strengths: - First execution-based oracle for agent EDR evasion on real, snapshot-controlled endpoints with commercial products — a substantively harder and more realistic target than VirusTotal/sandbox verdicts used by MalGEN and LLMalMorph. - The delayed-replay study (62/71 surviving 1–4 weeks with EDR cloud updates enabled) adds a temporal dimension to evasion measurement that no prior agentic benchmark reports. - The knowledge-condition experiment cleanly demonstrates that supplied domain knowledge, not raw model capability, is the binding constraint (GLM 83.3% → 50.0% without it), a directly actionable finding for both agent developers and safety evaluators. - Honest decomposition of the oracle into independent endpoint and C2 vantage points, plus a functional baseline proving the task is not trivially passable. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: only six commodity EDRs on Windows are covered; evasion applies to the loader, not the payload itself; the knowledge skill is deliberately narrow so absolute success rates are lower bounds; and the design cannot separate loader detection from payload detection, so payload-level differences should not be read as loader-evasion ability. They also note the feedback-detail trade-off (precise block reasons help attackers localize the interception point) and that the benchmark is intended for vendor and policy use with responsible disclosure to all six EDR vendors. These limitations are confronted directly and quantified where possible — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single run per cell with no variance estimation: a 1-run 17/18 versus 15/18 difference across models is not distinguishable from noise at this sample size, yet the paper ranks models on it. - RQ2/RQ3 models were selected because they won RQ1 on the same benchmark, so ablation findings (e.g., knowledge dependence, reasoning-effort non-monotonicity) are unverified for weaker or frontier-tier models. - The harness's Python Guest Agent being deleted by Bitdefender means some Bitdefender "failures" measure harness stealth, not agent capability; the number of affected runs is not reported. - Alert telemetry is excluded, so a defender's view (was the sample flagged for human triage?) is invisible; the paper's "evasion" claim is narrower than the title implies. - No frontier-tier open-weights or largest commercial model is tested (all backends are Flash/Lite/Plus tier plus mid-tier GPT-6 Luna), so the policy-relevant question of frontier model capability is extrapolated, not measured. - The dual-use uplift risk of releasing a curated, tested evasion-knowledge skill plus check-level feedback loop is discussed only briefly in the ethics statement; the skill's marginal uplift over public repositories (its source material) is not quantified. Bottom Line: For anyone benchmarking AI cyber-offense risk or hardening endpoint defenses, this is the first credible, execution-grounded measurement harness for agent-driven EDR evasion and worth reading closely despite its single-run-per-cell statistics; model-risk and policy audiences should treat the headline capability finding (cheap agents evade deployed EDRs ~79–94% of the time) as real, and the model rankings as provisional.

RPEG: Training Reasoning Language Models Scalably and Cost-Effectively

M Besta, L Schmidt, P Pang, P Okanovic… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RPEG, a property-graph intermediate representation and optimization framework that jointly searches over reinforcement-learning pipeline structure (bounded asynchrony, actor–critic sharing) and execution plans (placement, 3D parallelism, microbatching) for reasoning-LLM post-training, backed by a calibrated analytical time/memory model and a completion-driven distributed runtime. - Why it's important: RL post-training of reasoning models couples multiple large models across heterogeneous generation/assessment/training stages, consuming millions of GPU-hours at frontier scale, so a few-percent utilization or throughput gain translates into large dollar and energy savings on expensive HPC hardware. - How it does it: A cyclic steady-state graph (vertices = model invocations, typed edges = data and cross-step weight publication with per-model staleness budgets) is unrolled, lowered to a hardware-aware DAG with explicit COMM/RESHARD nodes, scored with an analytical performance model, and optimized via simulated annealing over both structural variants and execution plans. - The good: The analytical model is validated against measurements (15.5% MAPE for latency, Spearman ρ=0.990; 15.1% MAPE for peak memory, ρ=0.972 over 123 configurations), and the measured end-to-end results are concrete: up to 2× over ReaL on A100s, 1.024×–2.477× (median 1.488×) over VERL on GH200s up to 256 GPUs, and 1.250×–1.471× over fully colocated baselines on the same runtime. - The missing: Training-quality evidence is thin — only a single mean-rollout-reward comparison against synchronous VERL (within 0.47% relative difference) at unspecified scale and task, and no comparison against modern asynchronous baselines (AReaL, AsyncFlow, Laminar) in measured head-to-head runs. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or select RL post-training systems or cost models for multi-model LLM pipelines; skip it if you only need ML algorithmic contributions, since the RL algorithm itself is untouched.

Problem & Motivation: Teams post-training reasoning LLMs with PPO/GRPO face a pipeline where each RL step runs up to six heterogeneous model invocations (actor generation, reward/reference/critic inference, actor/critic training) with different compute profiles: latency-bound autoregressive decoding, throughput-bound teacher-forced inference, and memory-heavy training. Existing systems optimize only slices of this design space — ReaL and VERL search execution plans for a fixed pipeline; RLHFuse and AReaL hand-craft fusion or asynchrony; none jointly search pipeline structure and execution, and few model hierarchical rack/node/GPU communication costs. The gap: structure choices (staleness, actor–critic sharing) and execution choices (placement, parallelism, microbatching) interact — fixing one degrades the other — and greedy schedules either leave GPUs idle in bubbles or split GPUs so thinly that per-operator latency erases the overlap benefit. Key Idea: Represent the entire RL post-training pipeline as a compact cyclic property graph C = (G°, P) in which both the graph structure (including bounded-staleness publication edges and actor–critic sharing) and its execution plan are first-class search variables, so a simulated-annealing optimizer evaluates structural and hardware-mapping choices jointly through a fast calibrated analytical model rather than searching a materialized multi-step DAG. The staleness map τ(m) makes asynchrony a one-line structural edit (re-unroll rather than rewire), and the compact cyclic form keeps the search space at ∏ q_v instead of ∏ q_v^(K_eval). Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) Unroll the cyclic G° over a K_eval-step horizon into an acyclic graph, instantiating publication edges per staleness budget (publisher selection s_m(k) = k − τ(m) − 1), with acyclicity proven (Lemma A.1); (2) Lower onto an execution plan P = (σ, Π, mb) — per-invocation device allocation, DP/PP/TP degrees, microbatch count — inserting explicit COMM and RESHARD nodes, performing response-length-quantile splitting of generation and inference into Q sub-nodes for gen–inf overlap, and detecting "shadow pairs" (staleness + disjoint allocations → persistent weight copies, no intra-step reshard); (3) Locally evaluate with an analytical model: α–β communication costs tiered by rack/node/GPU hierarchy, roofline GEMM throughput with calibrated shape-efficiency factors (η from γ_M, γ_K), separate prefill/decode terms for generation, and a memory model with persistent (ZeRO-2 sharded Adam state, shadow/frozen weights) plus worst-case transient per device against M_eff = 0.9·M_GPU; (4) Schedule with a greedy list scheduler (earliest-feasible-start, comm-first then downstream-rank tie-breaking) producing makespan MS(Ĝ); (5) Score as Score(C) = K_eval·B·R·(L_p+L_r)/MS(Ĝ) with a soft exponential OOM penalty and an optional throughput×utilization objective; (6) Optimize via simulated annealing — outer loop over structural tuples y = (ac, τ), inner loop over execution plans with single-invocation (60% critical-path-biased) and two-invocation donor/receiver moves, caching, warm restarts, and a final greedy coordinate-descent polish; (7) Execute on persistent distributed workers with completion-driven dispatch over PyTorch/Megatron, NCCL/Gloo, plus hash-based plan verification that the runtime faithfully realizes the optimized plan. Key design decisions: cyclic-not-flat search representation (justified by combinatorial argument), analytical-not-profiled scoring (justified by calibration results and caching needs), and explicit plan verification (justified by the risk of predicted-vs-actual divergence). Three critical decisions — searched structural space limited to {AC sharing, τ}, greedy scheduler, and no CPU offloading — are argued but the first is admittedly a small subset of possible structure changes. Key Results: (1) Model validation on GH200s over 123 configurations (LLaMA 3B/7B/13B, B∈{32..2048}, 1–128 GPUs, 25 parallel strategies): latency MAPE 15.5%, Spearman ρ=0.990, 95.4% pairwise ranking accuracy; memory MAPE 15.1%, ρ=0.972. (2) Predicted weak scaling (8–128 GPUs, LLaMA-2, up to 70B/70B actor/critic): 5–60% throughput gain over the concurrent heuristic, with RPEG finding feasible plans where baselines OOM; utilization-aware plans trade 1–3% throughput for up to +25pp scheduled GPU utilization. (3) Predicted strong scaling (13B, B=1024): 20–49% over greedy, reaching 104,930 tokens/s at 128 GPUs. (4) Ablations (200 runs, 5 seeds × 4 scenarios × 9 ablations): disabling bounded asynchrony costs 16.1% on average, gen–inf overlap 9.2%, microbatch tuning 4.3%; search-heuristic ablations <3%, so gains come from the search space, not the search algorithm. (5) Measured end-to-end: vs ReaL on A100s, faster in 11/13 configurations, 1.4×–2× throughput, up to 30% higher utilization, plus one feasible plan where ReaL OOMs; vs VERL on GH200s (Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.3 70B, up to 256 GPUs), 1.024×–2.477× step-latency reduction (median 1.488×); within-runtime comparisons of optimized vs colocated baselines: 1.250×–1.471× (mean 1.365×) across 20 measured comparisons. Structural results: τ=1 asynchrony speeds separate-model execution 1.346×–1.429× (8B) and 1.217×–1.662× (70B); AC sharing 1.14×–1.51×; stage fusion 7% on one topology-matched test but reversible under resharding cost. (6) Optimizer: ~14–19% makespan reduction over the initial plan; within 300 s the best plan is within 5% of a one-hour search even at 2048 modeled GPUs; run-to-run coefficient of variation 0.27–2.31% over 200 seeds. Training-outcome check: mean final rollout reward within 0.47% of synchronous VERL. Tested scale is substantial (256 GPUs measured; 2048 modeled) but still below frontier training scale. Baselines ReaL and VERL are current, widely used systems; the fully colocated and concurrent heuristics are internal controls. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (joint structural-plus-execution search over an RLM pipeline via a property-graph IR) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (optimizer + runtime + analytical model). The genuinely novel pieces are: (a) making pipeline structure (staleness, AC sharing) an optimizer variable alongside placement/parallelism, (b) a calibrated memory model with co-residency-aware device peaks for multi-model RL pipelines, and (c) hash-verified plan execution. Individual mechanisms — simulated annealing, α–β communication models, quantile-based rollout splitting (closely related to RLHFuse fusion), shadow copies for asynchrony (present in AReaL), Megatron parallelism — are standard; the contribution is their unification under one searchable, verifiable representation, which is a real but incremental synthesis. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative (Table IV isolates search-space features from search heuristics, with the honest finding that heuristic tweaks matter <3%). Multi-seed evidence is provided for the optimizer (200 runs/configuration, CoV reported) though the end-to-end system comparisons appear to be single runs without error bars or significance tests. The performance model is validated against hardware rather than merely asserted, a rigor positive, and 15.5% MAPE is disclosed plainly rather than hidden. Code is released at https://github.com/spcl/RPEG. Methodological concerns: (a) the weak-scaling and strong-scaling "advantages" in Figures 6–8 are predicted by the authors' own model, not measured — the model is validated, but using it as the headline comparison tool for its own optimizer's decisions risks circular self-confirmation; (b) the training-quality check (0.47% reward difference) follows AsyncFlow's methodology but is a single configuration, single run, on an unspecified task — thin evidence that bounded asynchrony preserves learning across settings; (c) the VERL comparison uses separate actor/critic models (the "controlled synchronous comparison"), while the headline 2.48× is the max over configurations, with median 1.488×; (d) no measured head-to-head against asynchronous systems (AReaL, AsyncFlow, Laminar, StaleFlow) despite those being the closest competitors — Table VI is a feature checklist, not an experiment. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built optimizer and distributed runtime, evaluated by deployment on two HPC platforms, with an EMPIRICAL component in model validation). Practical: Yes — runs on commodity A100 and GH200 clusters via Slurm, PyTorch/Megatron, NCCL/Gloo; no exotic hardware. Efficient: Optimizer overhead is negligible (amortized 1.3–2.5% over 1,000 PPO updates for a 300–600 s search); memory model reserves 10% HBM headroom; system gains 20–30% utilization over baselines. Effective: Evidence shows throughput/latency/utilization wins on real hardware and a reward-preservation check, but "solves the problem" rests partly on model-predicted rather than measured schedules for the scaling studies. Scalable: Measured to 256 GPUs and modeled to 2048; the paper claims but does not measure behavior at 10× beyond that (multi-rack communication is modeled, and rank/node hierarchies are explicit, which is encouraging but unverified at frontier scale). The work delivers a real software artifact (code released) plus a reusable calibrated-model methodology; it does not stop at paper form. Strengths: (1) The cyclic-graph-with-staleness-budget abstraction is a clean formulation that makes asynchrony a structural parameter edit instead of a systems rewrite, and the acyclicity argument for unrolled graphs is simple and correct. (2) The co-residency-aware memory model (persistent per-model state + max transient per device, with shadow-pair vs. reshard cases enumerated) addresses a real, often-ignored failure mode in multi-model RL pipelines — the OOM results for baselines at 8 GPUs (strong scaling) demonstrate it matters. (3) The evaluation discipline is above average for systems papers: analytical model validated separately from end-to-end wins, an ablation that honestly shows the search space (not the search algorithm) drives gains, and a case study showing the optimizer deliberately makes locally suboptimal choices (Peff 1.8–1.9, 17–22% makespan reduction) — a non-obvious empirical finding. (4) Plan hash-verification closes the predicted-vs-executed gap that plagues plan-optimizing systems. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: stage fusion's benefit can reverse under resharding costs; the utilization objective is scheduled resource occupancy, not arithmetic utilization (an honest distinction); the memory model underpredicts by the ~2–3 GB CUDA context overhead, covered by the ε_rt margin; the searched structural space is limited to AC sharing and staleness ("Additional execution refinements... enlarge the executable design space without treating arbitrary graph topology as an outer-loop search variable"); GPU-hours are traded explicitly in the utilization objective; and ChatGPT was used as an editorial tool. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No measured comparison against any asynchronous baseline system — the closest competitors (AReaL, AsyncFlow, Laminar, StaleFlow) appear only in a feature table, so the claim of superiority over "existing systems" rests on synchronous ReaL/VERL comparisons. (2) The weak/strong-scaling headline figures are model predictions of the same model used to guide optimization — a Goodhart-style circularity the authors do not flag for those specific figures (they do validate the model independently, which mitigates but does not eliminate this). (3) Training-quality preservation is tested once (one task, one scale, τ=1); no evidence for multi-step staleness, agentic/long-horizon workloads, or reward-model-based objectives, despite the motivation citing agentic token inflation. (4) Response-length quantiles are profiled from the current checkpoint — no analysis of how distribution drift during training degrades sub-node splitting or plan quality over a long run. (5) The searched structural space is small (AC sharing × a few staleness values); the "pipeline structure as an optimization variable" framing promises more than the implementation delivers, e.g., no search over reward-model placement strategies beyond standard roles, no EP, no multi-model heterogeneous graph variants beyond PPO/GRPO/DPO hand-instantiations. (6) Gloo for semantic data transfers in the principal campaign is unusual for the claimed performance numbers on Clariden-scale systems, and the NCCL/Gloo split's effect on the measured comparisons is not ablated. Bottom Line: Practitioners building or operating multi-model RL post-training pipelines should read this — the joint structure/execution search, validated analytical model, and honest ablations deliver measurable wins (median 1.488× over VERL) over the strongest available synchronous baselines — but treat the async-system superiority claim as unproven until a head-to-head with AReaL/AsyncFlow-class systems exists.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Reconfigurable Action Theories (RAT), a formal action-language extension in which actions can load and unload modules of the action description itself (its vocabulary, causal laws, and initializer), plus preservation theorems, complexity results, and translations to causal theories and ASP. - Why it's important: Modern agent harnesses (DeepSeek Harness, Pi, OpenHands) change their tools, providers, and policies at runtime, and designers currently lack a formal way to reason about how such changes affect which actions are available, enabled, or which goals remain reachable. - How it does it: A RAT configuration pairs the active module set K with a world state s; load/unload are ordinary actions under the source description D[K], while the target state is causally explained by the target description D[K'], with module initializers supplying values for newly introduced private fluents. - The good: The paper proves RAT collapses to standard C+-style causal semantics when the module set is fixed (Proposition 1), gives a full complexity map (transition checking in P; successor existence and bounded reachability NP-complete; unbounded reachability PSPACE-complete), and validates hand-built RAT models of three real harnesses against 67 recorded operations with zero prediction errors. - The missing: The empirical validation consists of small, single-module, hand-authored models of scripted workflows; there is no empirical comparison against a designer plainly encoding module switching as guarded fluents in an ordinary causal theory, and the ASP experiments are run on synthetic models with no alternative encodings or solvers as baselines (acknowledged by the author). - Read it or not: Worth reading for KR researchers working on action languages, modular theories, or formal verification of agent tooling; agent-systems practitioners seeking ready-to-use verification infrastructure will find it a specification paper with a prototype, not a deployable tool.
