Problem & Motivation: Agent harnesses — the scaffolding around LLM agents that constructs context, exposes and validates tools, selects providers, and enforces policies — increasingly support runtime changes to their components: loading a tool introduces new callable actions, replacing a provider or toggling a policy changes when calls are permitted. Conventional action theories (C+, situation calculus, STRIPS-style formalisms) fix their vocabulary and causal laws, so they cannot natively describe an execution step that changes which laws govern subsequent steps. The paper targets designers of such harnesses who want to ask, before deployment, whether a tool can be loaded, whether adding a module breaks existing behavior, or whether a goal remains reachable after a component change. Prior modular action languages (MAD, ALM) assemble reusable descriptions at design time, and theory-change formalisms revise laws, but neither treats module selection as an executable action within the theory with explicit initialization semantics. Key Idea: The core move is to separate, per action, which description governs the action's executability and direct effects (the source description D[K]) from which description governs static consequences in the resulting state (the target description D[K']), and to supply values for newly introduced private basic fluents via per-module initializers — functions from the pre-loading state to permitted complete assignments. Loading adds laws and vocabulary without the module contributing executability or direct-effect laws to its own loading step; unloading removes fluents and disables any dynamic law whose head or after-condition mentions a removed fluent ("target applicability"). Once this split is fixed, everything downstream — preservation theorems, complexity, ASP encoding — follows from the standard nonmonotonic causal reduct semantics (McCain–Turner) applied unchanged. Methodology: The formal framework is the Boolean, literal-headed, single-action fragment of C+ built on nonmonotonic causal theories (a rule F ⇐ G makes F caused when G holds; an interpretation is explained iff it is the unique classical model of its reduct). A RAT system is a fixed module catalogue, an always-active core, and per-module descriptions with disjoint private basic fluents plus initializers. Transitions (Definition 4) require the action to be enabled in D[K], the target module set to follow NextK(a), and the target state to be causally explained by a single-step theory combining target static laws, source dynamic laws with target-applicability filtering, inertia over surviving fluents, and initializer facts. On this base the paper proves: reduction to ordinary semantics for fixed K (Prop 1, Cor 1); unique successor under acyclic dependency ordering and singleton initializers (Props 2–3); behavior preservation when adding an independent (vocabulary-disjoint) module (Thm 1) or a read-only module that reads shared fluents without causing, blocking, or constraining them (Thm 2); commuting of two jointly independent loads (Thm 3); and a five-task complexity analysis via reductions from SAT and STRIPS planning (Thm 4). Finite systems are translated to a time-indexed causal theory Γh (Thm 5: exact execution correspondence) and then, via the Ferraris et al. literal-headed causal-to-ASP translation using double default negation, to answer set programs (Thm 6, Cor 4), enabling bounded planning in clingo. Key design decisions — one action per step, initializer-owned private fluents, target-applicability disabling rather than blocking — are each justified with counterexamples showing what fails without them (e.g., the ordering counterexample with the law "caused x if x"). Key Results: Formal: transition checking is in P; successor existence, possible goal satisfaction, and sequence execution are NP-complete; necessary satisfaction is coNP-complete; bounded reachability is NP-complete; unbounded reachability is PSPACE-complete. Empirical validation on three harnesses: a DeepSeek Harness file-editing workflow with load/unload of an observation-policy plugin (39 attempted operations across 4 recorded sequences, 31 executed, 8 refused; direct causal evaluation and ASP each predicted every outcome and resulting configuration correctly); three Pi workflows (dynamic tool disabling, planning-mode restrictions, MCP internal-vs-direct tool calls; 24 attempts, 18 executed, 6 refused, all predicted correctly); and an OpenHands tool-removal workflow (13 attempts, 12 executed, 1 refused, all predicted). ASP scaling on synthetic model families (Mac mini M4, 24 GiB, clingo 5.8.2, 1200 s / 8 GiB limits, 137 cases, 211 runs): tool-sequence configuration computation reaches n=128 at a median 112.18 s while planning times out at n=128 (194.84 s median at n=64) and grounding exhausts memory at n=256; provider-choice planning is grounding-bound (median grounding 202.44 s at n=240, only 1 of 10 cases finishes); infeasible resource-allocation planning times out for n≥12 despite ≤102,341 ground rules, even though resource counting proves infeasibility trivially. A separate checker validated all 140 returned SAT executions (12,756 transitions) directly against the RAT laws. All harness agreement numbers are from hand-authored single-module models of scripted workflows, not autonomous modeling of arbitrary harness behavior. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component (the ASP translation). The genuinely new element is treating module selection as first-class actions with initializer semantics, private-fluent ownership, and target-applicability rules, plus preservation and load-commutation theorems stated over module declarations rather than encoding internals. The underlying machinery — nonmonotonic causal reducts, C+ transition semantics, the Ferraris et al. ASP translation, and the complexity techniques (SAT and STRIPS reductions) — is entirely standard; the contribution is a clean, well-motivated composition in a new setting, and the paper itself concedes RAT adds no expressive power over plain causal theories for finite catalogues and bounds (Section 9.1). Rigor & Reproducibility: Proofs are detailed and self-contained; the semantic core (unique-model-of-reduct for literal-headed theories) is used consistently, and counterexamples are supplied for each dropped sufficient condition. The complexity proofs include both membership and hardness arguments. However, there are no stochastic elements, so error bars are not applicable and none are claimed; the harness agreement results have no repetition variance because each operation is deterministic. Reproducibility is strong: the project page (http://staff.ustc.edu.cn/~jianmin/rat/) provides models, ASP evaluators, harness observations, query inputs, per-run records, checking scripts, pinned dependencies, and source hashes; a separate checker validated all 140 SAT executions. Methodological concerns: (1) the harness "validation" is the author modeling systems he also observed and formalized — agreement demonstrates internal consistency of the modeling exercise, not that RAT was necessary or that a competing formalism would fail; (2) the scaling benchmarks use generated models with no baseline encodings, solvers, or alternative approaches, so the timings characterize one implementation, not the approach (the author states this); (3) the 12 provider UNSAT results lack independent certificates; (4) the harness ecosystems cited (DeepSeek Harness, Pi, and the Cordis-related reference) cannot be independently verified from the paper text alone. The author discloses that OpenAI Codex assisted with ASP encodings, scenarios, and manuscript preparation, with verification procedures described in supplementary Section S8. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a formalism with proofs plus executed prototype evaluation; no deployed system). Practical: Yes — the prototype runs on a Mac mini with an M4 and 24 GiB RAM using clingo/clingo 5.8.2, so it needs no special hardware. Efficient: Transition checking is polynomial and cheap, but ASP grounding dominates for planning (millions of ground rules; 342.46 s and 3,282,605 rules for a single n=240 provider case), and 34 of 211 runs hit time or memory limits. Effective: The evidence shows RAT correctly predicts recorded tool-call outcomes and module changes in three harnesses on small scripted workflows — a proxy; it does not show the formalism catching real design errors or scaling to models of production harness complexity. Scalable: Tested to n=256 tools and n=320 providers on synthetic models, where grounding and search become the bottleneck; the paper does not claim and has not tested scaling on realistically sized harness models. Deliverable: a software artifact (code, RAT models, ASP encodings, checking scripts) at the project page, positioned as a specification and prototype rather than a production tool; a proposed LLM-assisted modeling workflow (Section 9.3) is explicitly unevaluated. Strengths: - The semantic core is genuinely well designed: the source/target description split, initializer-owned private fluents, and target-applicability of dynamic laws form a minimal, coherent mechanism, and each design choice is defended with a concrete counterexample (e.g., the ordering-sensitivity example motivating Theorem 3's condition (iv), and the shared-fluent policy example motivating read-only conditions). - The complexity analysis is complete and correctly calibrated: finite module selection provably does not raise worst-case bounds beyond ordinary finite causal planning (PSPACE for unbounded reachability via STRIPS reduction), which is the right sanity result for a formalism claiming to be a "minimal extension." - Validation against three independently developed, real harness implementations (DeepSeek Harness, Pi, OpenHands) with recorded commits, 67 operations, and zero prediction discrepancies is unusually grounded for a pure KR paper, and the distinction the framework draws — removing a tool's blocking laws (DeepSeek policy plugin) versus removing an action outright (OpenHands) versus changing a fluent under fixed laws (Pi disable) — is a real conceptual contribution to talking about harness reconfiguration. - Exceptional reproducibility practice: pinned commits, per-run records, an independent transition checker, and honest reporting of timeouts, memory overruns, and missing UNSAT certificates. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The author states: RAT handles one action per step and cannot represent concurrent/overlapping tool calls without explicit start/finish actions; it cannot load modules outside a fixed catalogue; it has no account of unfinished requests, resource commitments, or recovery when a component disappears (deferred to a proposed HAT extension); writing a faithful RAT model requires information beyond tool interfaces and cannot be verified as matching the software; reasoning is hard in the worst case; and the ASP measurements evaluate one encoding and solver without comparison to alternatives. The paper also candidly notes RAT adds no expressive power over direct causal encodings and positions its LLM-assisted workflow as unevaluated. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation discussion — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central empirical claim — that RAT's explicit module structure aids harness design — is never tested against the obvious alternative: a designer hand-encoding module activation as guarded fluents in an ordinary causal theory. Section 9.1 argues this qualitatively (RAT states preservation conditions over declarations, not encoding internals), but no study measures modeling effort, error rates, or verification cost for either approach. - The harness validation uses models with exactly one optional module each, so the two-module load-commutation result (Theorem 3) and the multi-module interaction scenarios most distinctive to RAT go untested against real systems. - All harness experiments are scripted by the author, who also wrote the models; there is no independent modeler, no adversarial case, and no report of modeling disagreements or failed first attempts, leaving the practical cost of producing faithful RAT descriptions unquantified. - The complexity results concern finite ground systems with explicitly listed signatures; realistic harnesses with parameterized tools and unbounded string/file states would require the schematic grounding layer, whose cost is only touched via the synthetic benchmarks. - Several cited artifacts (DeepSeek Harness repository and its observation-policy plugin, the Pi SDK, the Cordis/DeepSeek-Harness "context paradigm" preprint) are central to the motivation but cannot be assessed from the paper; the empirical claims inherit this dependence. - The infeasible resource-allocation timeouts are acknowledged as not isolating the allocation check's cost, but the paper offers no diagnosis of whether the encoding or the solver is at fault, which limits what the scaling study teaches. Bottom Line: For a KR/action-language researcher, this is a solid, honest, and reproducible formalization of a timely problem whose theorems and counterexamples are worth studying, but practitioners seeking verified tooling for real agent harnesses will not find here either a demonstrated advantage over naive causal encodings or a system that scales beyond toy-and-medium models — read it for the formulation, not for deployable verification infrastructure.

AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models

Z Zhang, R Hu, J Peng, S Li, S Bhatt, S Zeng, M Hong · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AutoScaffold, a framework in which a frozen teacher LLM (GPT-5.5) periodically reads a student model's RL training experience, diagnoses failure patterns, writes class-level strategies and instance-level hints into training prompts, validates its proposals on held-out tasks, and withdraws support as the student improves. - Why it's important: Outcome rewards collapse each rollout to a single number, so hard tasks where all rollouts fail produce zero gradient (the "learning cliff"), and existing scaffolding methods require hand-designed, domain-specific hints or fixed withdrawal schedules that do not track the student's changing abilities. - How it does it: Every K=10 training steps, the teacher queries training statistics, trajectories, and rollout groups through interactive tools plus a memory of its past decisions, then edits a two-level scaffold (class strategies with per-class injection probability q[C] capped below 1, and instance-level hints for zero-success tasks), keeping only class-level edits that beat both no-scaffold and current-scaffold on held-out tasks. - The good: The ablation study is decisive and each component is shown to matter — removing held-out validation drops ALFWorld success from 93.9% to 79.8% (below the 86.7% GiGPO baseline), replacing query tools with a fixed failure sample drops it to 85.3%, and reusing Skill0's published skill bank as a static scaffold drops it to 78.6% — directly supporting the paper's automaticity and adaptivity claims. - The missing: Several headline baselines (SkillRL, Skill0, QuestA, SAGE, DAPO) are quoted from their original papers rather than re-run under identical conditions, the teacher is a proprietary closed-source model (GPT-5.5) with no released prompt-pipeline artifact stated, and the math gains (+1.4 points over GRPO, on par with SAGE at 70.0% vs 70.1%) are thin. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone working on RLVR post-training, curriculum/hint design, or LLM-driven training automation, because it is the first demonstration that a teacher LLM can autonomously and adaptively manage training-time scaffolding across four heterogeneous domains with scaffold-free evaluation — skip it if you only care about math reasoning, where the gain over the strongest baseline is within noise.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (70) is strong — an LLM teacher autonomously designing, validating, and withdrawing two-level scaffolds across four heterogeneous domains is a new method with cross-domain unification — and Rigor (72) is anchored by exemplary ablations where every component's removal is individually consequential, with 3-seed error bars. Completeness (68) benefits from candid limitation discussion, but Impact (45) is held back by the closed-source GPT-5.5 teacher, transcribed (not re-run) baselines, and no stated code or artifact release, while Resilience (65) is dented by the thin math margin (tied with SAGE) and the unflagged oracle requirement of instance-level scaffolds. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*45 = 66.

Problem & Motivation: In RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR), a rollout group on a task the student rarely solves yields all-failure outcomes, zero advantage under group-relative methods like GRPO, and therefore no learning signal — the "learning cliff." Training-time scaffolds (hints, partial solutions, skills appended to training prompts, removed at evaluation) can restore signal, but prior methods are (i) hand-designed per domain before training, (ii) adapted only through predefined schedules or fixed pipelines, and (iii) tied to one scaffold form per domain. The people who suffer this problem are RL post-training practitioners; the gap AutoScaffold closes is removing the human researcher from the loop of diagnosing student failures and deciding what support to give, when, and how much. Key Idea: Let a frozen teacher LLM act as the scaffolding designer inside a live RL run: it interacts with the training log through query tools (class statistics, individual trajectories, per-task rollout groups) and its own decision memory, then manages a two-level scaffold — class-level strategies injected with a per-class probability q[C] ≤ qmax < 1 (so the student keeps practicing without help), and instance-level hints (e.g., solution prefixes) for tasks the student cannot solve at all — revising both every K steps. The theoretical backbone is a set of propositions showing group-relative learning signal (probability of a non-degenerate group, u(p) = 1 − (1−p)^G − p^G, and expected within-group reward variance) peaks at success probability p = 1/2, so a good scaffold pulls success toward 1/2, not beyond it; class-level scaffolds help iff sC < σC < 1 − sC, and instance-level scaffolds are needed for zero-success tasks. Methodology: The pipeline is scaffold-augmented group-relative RL (GRPO/DAPO/GiGPO/rubric-based GRPO, left unchanged except that prompts are augmented) plus a periodic teacher update (Algorithm 2) every K=10 steps with query budget B=15: (1) gather evidence — held-out success rates with/without current scaffold, then multi-turn tool calls over the block's training log and the teacher's memory M of its last three diagnoses; (2) propose edits ΔS = (ΔSclass, Δq, ΔSinst); (3) validate each proposed class-level scaffold by running the current checkpoint on held-out tasks VC with no scaffold, the current scaffold, and the proposal (n rollouts/task, matched seeds), and the teacher adopts, keeps, combines, or drops each edit; (4) deploy for the next block. The teacher's instructions contain no domain-specific rules — only the two analysis-derived principles (target low-success/all-fail classes; withdraw support once success without scaffold exceeds 50%) plus a short domain description and class list. Critical design decisions: the Bernoulli injection probability q[C] with cap qmax = 0.5 (justified by privileged-information dropout and the qmax=1 ablation, which falls below the RL baseline); holding out VC from training for validation (justified by the largest ablation, −14.1 points); and restricting instance-level scaffolds to math where verified reference solutions exist (partially justified — instance hints are unvalidated because they are solution prefixes, and they require oracle reference solutions the paper does not discuss as a limitation). Key Results: All results are scaffold-free evaluations, mean ± std over 3 independent runs. ALFWorld (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, GiGPO): 93.9% vs 86.7% (+7.2), beating 7B SkillRL (89.9%) and SkillC (90.6%); largest per-class gains Look +19.7, Cool +16.2, Pick2 +15.3. Search-based QA (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, trained on NQ+HotpotQA): 46.1% average EM vs 42.1% GiGPO (+4.0), beating same-scale SkillRL (38.9) and Skill0 (40.8) and even 7B Skill0 (44.4); out-of-domain gains (+4.1 avg on 5 held-out benchmarks) match in-domain gains (+3.8). Math with Qwen3-4B-Instruct: 70.1% avg vs 68.7% GRPO (+1.4), statistically tied with SAGE (70.0%); with Nemotron-1.5B: 62.4% vs 60.4% DAPO and 61.1% QuestA, using 350 training steps versus QuestA's 1,100 (~1/3 the steps), surpassing DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B (58.1%). KernelBench (Qwen3-8B, rubric-based GRPO vs StitchCUDA): correctness 63 vs 59 (Level 1), 54 vs 50 (Level 2), 33 vs 32 (Level 3); Fast1 up to 25 vs 20 on Level 2 (up to +5.0 points). Baselines are recent (2025–2026 methods), though several numbers are transcribed from the original papers rather than re-run. The branch-training analysis (Figure 6) shows the updated scaffold beats keeping the old scaffold and vanilla RL at every tested checkpoint (steps 20–80), directly evidencing that adaptation — not just scaffolding — drives learning. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (AI-teacher-in-the-loop scaffold design with interactive evidence gathering, held-out validation, and injection-probability control) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (a single unified scaffolding procedure transfers across agentic, QA, math, and kernel-generation domains). Relative to closest prior work — SAGE (rule-based hint strength tuning), SkillRL (teacher revises skills from a fixed failure sample, keeps skills at eval), SLIM (leave-one-skill-out validation, retains some skills at inference), QuestA (fixed prefix schedule) — the genuinely novel elements are the teacher's free choice of what evidence to inspect, the two-level scaffold taxonomy grounded in the p=1/2 analysis, scaffold-free evaluation of a fully adaptive text scaffold, and cross-domain unification including KernelBench. The RL training itself, the GRPO machinery, and privileged-information dropout are standard components; the propositions in Appendix A are direct extensions of Liao et al. (2026) analysis (Propositions 1–2 are cited as theirs). Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong on ablations — five ablations on ALFWorld (tools & memory, validation, static scaffold, K=5/20, qmax=1) each isolate a component and each one is consequential. Results report mean ± std over 3 seeds in the authors' own runs; no significance tests are given, and for the +1.4-point math margin over GRPO the ±0.3–0.5 std bars suggest the SAGE comparison is a tie, which the authors do acknowledge. Methodological concerns: (1) mixed provenance of baseline numbers — many are copied from original papers with potentially different training data, prompts, and compute, and the 7B scaffold-method comparisons are labeled "reference only"; (2) the teacher is GPT-5.5, a closed, non-versioned commercial model, so the exact teacher behavior is not reproducible and no code/data release URL is stated anywhere in the provided text; (3) no published baseline is re-run by the authors end-to-end, so some gains may reflect implementation differences; (4) validation itself consumes student rollouts (11–21 min per update on top of 3–5 min teacher time), a cost borne by training throughput that is only partially itemized. The Goodhart risk is low — scaffolds are designed and validated on training/held-out training tasks, never on evaluation tasks, and the teacher never sees evaluation data. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a training method run and measured across four domains, with a SYSTEMS flavor in the teacher tooling). - Practical: Yes — the student side uses 4–8 H200 GPUs with unchanged standard RL algorithms, and the teacher is an external API call requiring no special hardware. - Efficient: Teacher API cost is $2.35–$5.57 per run (a few dollars), but validation adds 11–21 minutes of GPU wall-clock per update (every 10 steps), and the framework reduces student steps substantially in the QuestA comparison (350 vs 1,100 steps), so the intervention roughly pays for itself where baseline comparisons exist. - Effective: Yes for the claimed goal — scaffold-free evaluation improves over RL baselines in all four domains and matches or beats human-designed scaffolding, with the branch-training experiment isolating the adaptation effect; effectiveness is proven on standard benchmarks, not a downstream product. - Scalable: Untested beyond 1.5B–8B students and 600–12,506 training tasks; the paper does not address how teacher diagnosis scales with log size (the B=15 query budget may become the bottleneck at 10× data) or whether a frontier teacher remains necessary for stronger students — scale claims are not made, and none are tested. - The work delivers a method and documented procedure (Algorithms 1–2, prompts in spirit via instructions), not a released library, dataset, or trained model — no artifact release is stated. Strengths: - The unified cross-domain result is real and non-trivial: identical teacher instructions (differing only in domain description and class list) produce sensible, domain-appropriate scaffolds for embodied planning, tool-use QA, math, and CUDA kernels — evidence the framework captures something general about scaffolding, not a domain-specific recipe. - The ablation design is exemplary: every component (interactive queries, memory, validation, adaptation, injection cap) is removed independently and each removal is individually catastrophic or clearly degrading, including the striking result that Skill0's published skill bank as a static scaffold (78.6%) underperforms even the no-scaffold baseline (86.7%). - The theoretical analysis, though simple, is load-bearing: the p=1/2 peak in non-degenerate group probability and the sC < σC < 1 − sC condition directly generate the design principles given to the teacher, rather than being decorative theory. - The branch-training experiment (Figure 6) cleanly separates "scaffolding helps" from "adapting scaffolds helps" — a comparison most related work omits — and the case-study logs (Appendix B) provide unusual transparency into actual teacher behavior, including a dropped Pick2 proposal that validated below no-scaffold. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly states that its analysis "does not model how improvements under scaffolds transfer to the unscaffolded policy" and calls characterizing this transfer future work; it acknowledges instance-level scaffolds are not validated (they are verified solution prefixes, not teacher-written text); it concedes the math result ties SAGE rather than beating it; it acknowledges Level 3 KernelBench gains are small (+1 point); and future work includes reducing teacher intervention cost and characterizing when scaffolded learning improves independent capability. The authors confront limitations reasonably directly, particularly in the theory's scope paragraph — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The transfer question the theory defers is the actual question: why does succeeding under a scaffolded prompt improve the unscaffolded policy? The qmax<1 cap and the qmax=1 ablation show that some transfer happens, but nothing measures whether scaffolded successes produce gradient that helps unscaffolded behavior versus merely teaching scaffold-conditional behavior; the mechanism is asserted, not analyzed. - The instance-level scaffold requires verified reference solutions with a truncatable prefix — this is an oracle signal unavailable in most real RLVR settings (and arguably a form of distillation from ground truth), yet it is never flagged as a scope limitation. - Single-teacher dependence on GPT-5.5 is unexamined: no ablation varies teacher capability (e.g., an open-weight teacher), so it is unknown how much of the framework's success rides on the frontier model's diagnostic ability versus the framework design; this matters for both reproducibility and cost claims at scale. - Validation on held-out tasks uses the current checkpoint with n rollouts per task, but no analysis quantifies validation reliability (variance of the three-way comparison, probability of adopting noise-level scaffolds); the step-30 case study shows a proposal accepted on a 30%-vs-30% tie, suggesting the decision rule may be brittle. - Some baseline comparisons inherit confounds: ALFWorld prompting and RL baseline numbers are taken from Feng et al. (2025) and scaffold-method numbers from third-party papers, so the +7.2-point headline is a cross-paper comparison, not a controlled re-run. - The B=15 query budget and K=10 interval are tuned on ALFWorld ablations (K=5/20 tested only there) and applied everywhere else; no cross-domain sensitivity analysis is given. Bottom Line: A practitioner doing RLVR post-training should read this: it is the most convincing demonstration yet that an LLM teacher can replace hand-designed hint/skill engineering with an adaptive, validated, cross-domain procedure, and its ablations tell you exactly which pieces you would need to reimplement — but treat the cross-paper baseline comparisons and the closed-source teacher as reasons to verify the gains in your own setting before adopting it, and note that no code release is stated.

s3

Kunal Jha, Gonçalo Faria, Shuyue Stella Li, Scott Geng, Faeze Brahman, Noah A. Smith, Yulia Tsvetkov, Max Kleiman-Weiner, Natasha Jaques · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces s3, a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which a shared LM policy, instantiated as N agents with private histories and free-form message/read tools, learns to coordinate (or not) entirely from a shared team reward with no prescribed roles, turn order, or communication structure. - Why it's important: Multi-agent LLM systems today depend on hand-designed harnesses (orchestrators, debate rounds, assigned roles) that are fixed guesses which duplicate work and break down; s3 offers a path where organization is learned, potentially making agent swarms that scale at inference without retraining the harness. - How it does it: It applies GRPO-style group-relative advantages at the team level — sampling 8 independent team attempts per problem, normalizing the single shared team reward (success minus a token-cost term), and assigning every generated token of a team the same advantage, so communication and task actions are trained jointly through an asynchronous Dec-POMDP harness. - The good: The ablation story is unusually thorough: on the private-information aggregation task, shared-reward RL reaches 93% success versus 35% for online SFT on successful teams and 13% for individual rewards (6 seeds, paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction), and removing communication costs 19 points in exploration — cleanly isolating that the gains come from learned coordination, not extra compute. - The missing: The headline exploration result — beating best-of-N by 9.4 points at the training size of 4 agents — is not significant after Bonferroni correction, and all results come from two synthetic tasks, tiny models (Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B), 32 held-out problems, and a single training run per condition. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on multi-agent LLM training, RL for agentic behavior, or emergent communication — the team-relative GRPO formulation and the social-dilemma analysis are directly reusable; skip it if you need evidence the approach works on realistic tasks or frontier-scale models, which is not yet here.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Non-Obviousness (72) and Novelty (72) lead: the team-relative GRPO reformulation sidesteps per-agent credit assignment, and the demonstration that individual rewards create a measurable public-goods dilemma causing learned silence is a new empirical finding. Rigor (70) is strong for the field — 6 evaluation seeds, paired t-tests with pre-specified Bonferroni correction, matched solo-learner controls — and the honest reporting that the flagship exploration gain does not survive correction is a credibility positive. However, Completeness (65) is reduced by the abstract's 'emergent roles' overclaim and the SFT-embedded communication protocol confound, Resilience (65) by single training runs and only two synthetic tasks, and Impact (40) by the absence of any released artifact and the gap to the realistic workloads motivating the paper. Problem & Motivation: Multi-agent LLM deployments (orchestrated subagents, debate, role-played teams) get their organization from static, designer-specified harnesses. These fixed guesses duplicate work, flood agents with updates, and fail when the imposed structure mismatches the task — and prior learned-structure work (workflow search, trained orchestrators) still centralizes design rather than letting coordination emerge from the agents themselves. The paper targets practitioners who want swarms whose members decide what to share, with whom, and when sharing is not worth the token cost. A second, subtler motivation is benchmarking honesty: a swarm of N agents trivially looks better than one agent, so the field needs comparisons against best-of-N sampling from solo policies with matched training and token budgets, which most prior multi-agent RL work omits. The closest prior work (Avalon-M1) trains collective-reward agents but builds in a CEO that assigns roles and does not establish a matched-budget gain over best-of-N. Key Idea: The core trick is team-level group-relative advantage: instead of solving per-agent credit assignment (difference rewards, counterfactual baselines, centralized critics), the paper compares whole independent team episodes on the same problem — every token generated by every member of a successful-but-cheap team gets a positive advantage, tokens of failed teams get negative ones, and behavior common to both cancels out. This makes communication learnable without any special reward for messaging: an agent is implicitly reinforced for sending its private number because successful teams contain such sends. The enabling infrastructure decision is asynchrony with 1,024-token generation chunks, so message notifications interleave with a partner's ongoing generation and discoveries can be acted on while still useful. Methodology: The setting is formalized as a Dec-POMDP with N agents sharing one policy; each agent gets its own task copy, an 8,192-token allowance, a `message(to, text)` tool, and a `read_messages()` tool; agents never see each other's reasoning or tool results, only messages they choose to read. The team reward is R = S·(1 − λ·min(1, Σ|τᵢ|/(NL))) with λ = 0.25 — a token-cost penalty charged only on success, so failures don't reward quitting and the max-over-agents success avoids rewarding teams merely for size. Training samples G = 8 teams per problem, normalizes team rewards into advantages (Eq. 2), masks loss to generated tokens only (received messages and tool outputs are not training targets), and applies masked importance ratios with IcePop plus Monte-Carlo score centering for the off-policy asynchronous runs (K = 32 samples). Exploration learners start from 50 updates of SFT on scripted depth-first-search demonstrations that include claim/report message templates; aggregation starts from the base model. Controls include individual-reward swarms, communication-disabled teams, online SFT on successful swarms, and solo learners matched on trajectories (512 per update) and token allowance. Design decisions are largely well-justified in Appendix D (one normalization per team, equal team weighting, no per-agent credit estimation), though the SFT demonstrations' embedded message conventions mean exploration "emergence" is partly scaffolded. Key Results: Information aggregation (Qwen3-0.6B, trained at N=4, 200 updates): s3 reaches 93.3% held-out success vs 28.7% for online SFT and 8.5% for individual reward (corrected p < 0.001; dz = 5.72 and 11.15); at 8 agents s3 succeeds more than 20× as often as the strongest control (abstract claims over 25×), retaining an advantage through 12 agents, with all methods collapsing at 16. Decentralized exploration (Qwen3-1.7B): room overlap of communicating swarms is roughly half that of the communication-disabled control (dz = −10.01); s3 beats solo best-of-4 by 9.4 points at N=4 (significant before but not after Bonferroni) and best-of-6 by 7.3 points at N=6 (corrected p < 0.05, dz = 1.71), with no detectable token-efficiency loss; gains vanish by N=8–16 as independent search saturates. Without SFT, the swarm has no significant advantage over solo RL (dz = −0.48) and both fail badly. Mechanistic findings: s3 converges to one broadcast per agent (~4.2 messages/team, Gini 0.30→0.04), while individual-reward agents learn to go silent — a public-goods social dilemma where never-sending agents are individually correct 5.6% vs 1.8% while their teams fail 6.1 points more. Communicating swarms succeed uniformly regardless of which door hides the exit; non-communicating ones degrade sharply as the exit moves to later-listed branches. Baselines are current and well-matched; testing scale is toy-to-standard (391-room mazes, number-sorting). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the first demonstration of cooperative MARL training asynchronous, role-free LM swarms that beat budget-matched best-of-N, and the empirical account of the individual-reward social dilemma causing learned silence in information-sharing tasks. The algorithmic machinery is a competent recombination of known pieces — GRPO applied at team granularity, IcePop/score-centering from prior work, Dec-POMDP framing, and classical learned-communication ideas — applied to a new setting (language-model agents with voluntary natural-language messaging). The claimed "emergent roles" is the weakest novelty claim: the observed behavior is a symmetric broadcast protocol, not differentiated roles. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for the field: 6 evaluation seeds, paired two-sided t-tests with pre-specified Bonferroni families, Cohen's dz effect sizes, matched training/token budgets against solo learners, and ablations isolating communication, reward structure, SFT, and demonstrations. The honest reporting of which comparisons survive correction (the flagship N=4 exploration gain does not) is a credibility positive. Concerns: one training run per condition (the authors admit seeds may not capture training variance); only 32 held-out problems per task; evaluation at exactly the training configuration with no cross-model or cross-task transfer tests; and the exploration task's demonstrations bake in claim/report conventions, so the RL result there is "RL improves a scaffolded start" rather than emergent communication from scratch — though the aggregation task (no SFT, base model start) does show genuine emergence. No code, data, or weights release is mentioned in the provided text. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained policies evaluated in custom environments). Practical: Yes in principle — runs on 2 trainer + 2–6 H200 GPUs with open-weight Qwen3 models at 0.6B/1.7B, well within commercial hardware. Efficient: Team-relative GRPO costs the same as solo GRPO at matched trajectories, but inference carries the swarm's KV-cache and sequencing overhead, which the paper engineers around rather than eliminates. Effective: Evidence supports effectiveness on the two proxy tasks (93% aggregation, ~90% exploration), but these are synthetic puzzles far from the real coordination workloads (research, software) the motivation invokes. Scalable: Only partially tested — evaluation to 16 agents shows aggregation degrades badly by N=16 and exploration gains saturate by N=8; scaling claims beyond that are extrapolation. Deliverable is currently paper-form; no artifact release is stated. Strengths: - The team-relative advantage reformulation of GRPO is a clean, reusable idea that sidesteps per-agent credit assignment in language-agent teams and is trivially portable to other cooperative settings. - The benchmarking discipline — matched solo learners, online-SFT and individual-reward controls, communication ablations — directly addresses the field's most common failure mode (swarms that win only by spending more compute) and makes the central claim defensible. - The mechanistic analysis of training trajectories is genuinely informative: the shift to one-broadcast-per-agent, the disappearance of read-before-send, and especially the demonstration that individual rewards create a measurable public-goods dilemma (silent agents profit individually, teams lose) constitute a new empirical finding about LLM multi-agent dynamics. - The asynchronous harness (chunked generation, mid-generation notification insertion) is a substantive systems contribution that future MARL-for-LLM work will likely need regardless of method. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state plainly (Section 7) that experiments cover only two tasks, small models, and one training run per condition, that additional runs may change findings, and that all methods struggle at 16 agents in aggregation. They identify concrete failure modes — submitting wrong answers despite having all information, retracing teammates' searches, trusting unverified reports — and propose epistemic tracking of partner knowledge as next steps. This direct confrontation with limitations is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline "25× more coordination problems" framing rests on the 8-agent comparison where controls collapse to near-zero; the absolute difference at the largest sizes is small in problem counts, and the training-size exploration gain (9.4pp) does not survive the paper's own multiple-comparison correction — a reader skimming the abstract could over-weight the robustness of the exploration result. - The exploration task's SFT demonstrations embed the exact communication protocol (claims and exhausted-branch reports as broadcasts) that the swarm later uses; the paper does not test RL from base-model communication on exploration except in the failing no-SFT condition, so the degree of genuinely emergent communication in exploration is undercharacterized. - Task generality is narrow: information aggregation has a single optimal protocol (broadcast once, submit) and exploration has one shared environment type with identical tree shapes; nothing shows the learned policy transfers to heterogeneous tasks, tool sets, or a second model family. - All agents share one policy, so "emergent roles" and heterogeneity of behavior are bounded by what one policy can express from different histories; the paper's evidence shows a uniform broadcast protocol, not differentiated roles, despite the abstract's "emergent roles" claim. - No comparison against prompted multi-agent baselines (debate, orchestrator) or test-time-communication methods at matched budgets on these tasks, leaving the learned-vs-prompted-organization question open even within the paper's own environments. - No released code, data, or checkpoints are mentioned, which limits verification of the intricate asynchronous training setup. Bottom Line: This is the most rigorous demonstration to date that cooperative MARL can make LLM swarms learn their own coordination and beat matched best-of-N — worth reading for anyone building multi-agent training methods, but the tiny models, two synthetic tasks, and single-run results mean practitioners should treat it as a promising formulation, not yet a deployable alternative to designed or prompted multi-agent systems.

VoxMel TTS Technical Report (22 ▲ )

Wenhao Guan, Jiaxin Ye, Haitao Li, Yifan Duan, Junxi Liu, Wangjin Zhou, Lin Li, Qingyang Hong, Xie Chen · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 17 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VoxMel, a tokenizer-free autoregressive TTS framework that applies a fixed, exactly invertible two-axis Haar wavelet transform to mel spectrograms, autoregressively generating only a coarse (Coarse-Mel) sequence while predicting temporal and frequency residuals with non-autoregressive tiers kept out of the autoregressive history. - Why it's important: Continuous autoregressive TTS currently depends on learned encoders (VAE latents, codec tokens) whose reconstruction fidelity caps output quality; a fixed, lossless mel-based target removes that encoder bottleneck and keeps the acoustic target upgradeable independently of the generator. - How it does it: A single-level Haar split along frequency and then time partitions the mel spectrogram into Coarse-Mel (92.9% of coefficient variance, 25% of coefficients), a temporal residual, and a frequency residual; an LM backbone with a flow-matching head autoregressively samples Coarse-Mel, and the residuals are generated in dependency order without feeding back into the AR history. - The good: The 0.6B model trained on 100K hours of Emilia reaches 1.51% WER / 0.738 SIM on Seed-TTS test-en and 1.29% CER / 0.755 SIM on test-zh (improving to 1.15%/0.753 and 1.17%/0.776 with frozen-head GRPO), competitive with or better than comparably sized learned-latent systems, and the decomposition ablations directly support the design (full-band mel AR collapses to 30.35% WER vs 1.90% for the fully split model at 0.15B). - The missing: No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported on any headline number; SIM of the distilled 4-step student degrades sharply (0.752 to 0.693 test-en), and the DiTAR-style transfer experiment explicitly uses unmatched configurations so it cannot isolate the target representation's contribution. - Read it or not: Worth reading for TTS researchers working on continuous autoregressive generation or acoustic target design — the variance/autocorrelation analysis and residual-feedback ablations are genuinely informative — but skip it if you only need a production-ready TTS recipe, since the mel target still trails the strongest Chinese baselines on CER and no human preference win over IndexTTS 2/VoxCPM is established.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Non-Obviousness (72) leads: the finding that residual feedback (not target compression) is the root cause of full-band mel AR instability — isolated by the 30.35%→1.90% WER ablation and text-reliance probes — is a data-driven, transferable insight, and the design decisions (Haar split, frozen-head GRPO) are each empirically justified. Rigor (65) reflects strong targeted ablations, released code/checkpoints/demo, and controlled GRPO comparisons, docked for zero seeds/error bars on headline margins of 0.1–0.3 WER and ablations run only at 0.15B. Novelty (65) is a solid new method plus new empirical finding, though composed of standard ingredients. Completeness (62) benefits from direct limitations but the unmatched DiTAR comparison and unexplained distilled-student SIM drop remain gaps; Resilience (58) is limited by proxy-metric reliance and Goodhart risk on guidance tuning. Impact (75) reflects real released model weights and code. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*62 + 0.15*58 + 0.10*75 = 66.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Zero-shot TTS systems built on language-model backbones must choose an acoustic target. Dominant choices are learned compressed representations — discrete codec tokens (AudioLM, VALL-E, CosyVoice) or continuous VAE latents (DiTAR, VoxCPM, VibeVoice) — where synthesis quality is partly bounded by the learned encoder's reconstruction. Mel spectrograms avoid a learned tokenizer and allow independent vocoder upgrades, but direct autoregression over full-band mel fails in practice: strong temporal redundancy (lag-one autocorrelation 0.944 on LibriSpeech test-clean) lets the model lean on acoustic history instead of text under teacher forcing, and every sampled frame — including its fine details and its errors — enters the autoregressive history where mistakes compound. Prior mitigations (frame patching, low-frame-rate latents, token-wise coarse-to-fine) all still feed reconstructed full-band content back into the history. The open problem is whether a fixed, lossless mel representation can be made tractable for autoregressive modeling. Key Idea: Factorize the mel spectrogram with a fixed, exactly invertible two-axis Haar wavelet transform so that only the small, text-predictive coarse stream (Coarse-Mel, half the frames at half the channel resolution) enters the autoregressive history, while the two residual bands — which measurements show carry little temporal autocorrelation (only 0.28 dB prediction gain from their own past) — are generated by parallel non-autoregressive flow-matching tiers in dependency order (temporal residual conditioned on Coarse-Mel, then frequency residual conditioned on the reconstructed Frequency-Averaged Mel). Because the transform is fixed and invertible, the change-of-variables determinant is constant and no information is lost; because residuals never re-enter the history, autoregressive error accumulation is confined to the coarse stream. This is a clean, well-motivated trick grounded in explicit statistics (Coarse-Mel holds 92.9% of variance in 25% of coefficients). Methodology: The pipeline has three tiers plus reconstruction. (1) A fixed Haar transform decomposes the log-mel into Coarse-Mel (T/2 × M/2), temporal residual D(t), and frequency residual D(f); the mean-form (averaging) split keeps coarse coefficients on the mel-value scale so existing normalization applies. (2) A decoder-only transformer backbone (initialized from Qwen2.5-0.5B, 494M params in the 0.6B model) consumes text tokens plus projected Coarse-Mel history; each step's hidden state conditions a conditional flow-matching head trained with the standard LCFM objective (E||v(z_s,s,g) − (a−ε)||², z_s = (1−s)ε + sa), plus a stop head for termination. (3) A bidirectional-attention non-autoregressive tier predicts the temporal residual from Coarse-Mel; a frame-wise (per-frame MLP) tier predicts the frequency residual from the reconstructed Frequency-Averaged Mel; the inverse Haar transform and a frozen Vocos vocoder produce waveforms. Inference uses nested text-first condition dropout (three condition states) enabling two-scale classifier-free guidance, v = v(∅,∅) + γ_text[v(T,S) − v(∅,S)] + γ_spk[v(∅,S) − v(∅,∅)] with (3.5, 3.0). Post-training applies GRPO with a frozen flow head (only the backbone updates, KL β=0.01, G=8 guided rollouts per prompt, reward = equal-weight speaker similarity + ASR accuracy). Distillation compresses the guided 32-step head into a guidance-conditioned 1/2/4-step student that absorbs classifier-free guidance into its weights, with 30% of batches drawn from student rollouts. Critical design decisions: (a) one Haar split per axis — justified by the measured first-order redundancy (93% variance reduction from one lag, diminishing returns beyond two); (b) excluding residuals from the AR history — justified by both probes (R² analyses) and the Section 4.4 ablations; (c) freezing the flow head during GRPO — justified by a controlled comparison showing trainable-head GRPO degrades all metrics (test-en WER 3.21% vs 1.15%). All three are empirically supported. Key Results: Benchmarks: VoxMel-0.6B (100K hours Emilia) achieves 1.98% WER / 0.721 SIM on LibriSpeech test-clean, 1.51% WER / 0.738 SIM on Seed-TTS test-en, 1.29% CER / 0.755 SIM on test-zh. Frozen-head GRPO improves to 1.95%/0.736, 1.15%/0.753, and 1.17%/0.776 — the highest SIM in their comparison table. Baselines are current and strong (CosyVoice 2/3, MaskGCT, FireRedTTS 2, IndexTTS 2, DiTAR, VoxCPM, OmniVoice, Qwen3-TTS, MOSS-TTS): VoxMel beats DiTAR (1.69%/0.735) on test-en but trails VoxCPM (0.93% CER) and OmniVoice-Emilia (0.89% CER) on test-zh, and several competitors use 5×–8× more training data (VoxCPM 1.8M hours, Qwen3-TTS 5M). A five-point listening test (20 native raters per language) shows VoxMel at 3.89/3.97 N-MOS/S-MOS (ZH) and 3.96/4.11 (EN) — competitive but not uniformly best; IndexTTS 2 leads several cells. Decomposition ablations (0.15B): full-band mel AR yields 30.35% WER / 0.493 SIM versus 1.90% / 0.667 for the fully split model, with text-reliance probe rising from 1.10% to 4.53% when both residuals leave the history — direct evidence for the core hypothesis. Scaling: 0.15B→0.6B improves test-en WER 1.90%→1.51% and SIM 0.667→0.738. Distillation: 4-step student cuts NFE per coarse frame from 96 to 4 (24×), reaching 1.49% WER / 0.693 SIM on test-en (vs 1.15%/0.752 for the guided GRPO teacher) — WER nearly matches supervised but SIM drops ~0.06–0.08. A surprising non-monotonicity: 8 solver steps beat 32 on test-en (1.38% vs 1.51% WER). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (wavelet-factorized autoregressive mel modeling with history-restricted coarse stream) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (residual feedback, not merely target compression, is what makes full-band mel AR unstable — supported by the text-reliance probe and exposure-gap analysis). The genuinely novel elements are the fixed Haar factorization that keeps residuals out of the AR history, and the frozen-head GRPO result for AR–flow hybrids. The constituent techniques — flow-matching heads, classifier-free guidance, GRPO, guidance distillation, MAR-style continuous AR generation — are standard; the contribution is their specific composition around a fixed invertible transform, which is a real but incremental formulation rather than a new learning principle. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and directly target the central design choice (Section 4.4 compares full-band mel, each residual alone, and both, plus text-reliance probes and exposure-gap metrics); GRPO frozen-vs-trainable head is a controlled comparison; solver-step and distillation sweeps quantify the quality–compute frontier. Weaknesses: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere; ablations run only at 0.15B, leaving open whether the decomposition effects hold at 0.6B; the DiTAR-style transfer comparison uses explicitly unmatched configurations, so it is directional only. Evaluation relies on ASR-based WER/CER (faster-whisper large-v3, Paraformer-zh) and WavLM-large SIM — standard but proxy metrics; the human listening test covers only 4 baselines and does not establish superiority. The authors tuned guidance scales on the evaluation-language benchmarks they report on (a mild Goodhart risk), though Seed-TTS-eval is a community benchmark, not their own. Code, demo page, and checkpoints are publicly released (github.com/VoxDance-Lab/VoxMel, huggingface.co/VoxDance-Lab, voxdance.github.io/voxmel-demo), which is a strong reproducibility positive. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — released models and demo). Practical: Yes — 0.6B-parameter model, Qwen2.5 backbone, frozen Vocos vocoder; nothing suggests exotic hardware, and 0.15B/0.3B variants exist for smaller budgets. Efficient: The autoregressive loop costs 96 head evaluations per coarse frame at 32 solver steps with two-scale guidance; distillation reduces this to 4 (24×) at a measurable SIM cost, and 8 solver steps without distillation actually improve WER — so inference cost is manageable but not better than non-autoregressive baselines like ZipVoice (16 NFE, 0.1B params). Effective: The evidence supports the claim on short-form zero-shot cloning for English and Chinese (WER/CER/SIM plus MOS), but long-form synthesis, expressiveness, and dialogue are untested. Scalable: Only 0.15B–0.6B tested; no evidence at 10× scale, and the non-monotonic Chinese CER scaling (0.3B best at 1.17%) hints scaling behavior is not yet clean. Delivers a real software artifact: released checkpoints, code, and a demo page, not just a paper. Strengths: - The motivating analysis is unusually concrete: measured lag-one autocorrelation (0.944), variance decomposition (92.9%/1.9%/5.2% across coarse/temporal/frequency bands), and linear-probe R² values directly predict which residuals can be excluded from the AR history — the design is derived from data, not asserted. - The Section 4.4 ablation is the paper's most valuable experiment: full-band mel AR collapsing to 30.35% WER while the split target reaches 1.90% isolates residual feedback as the failure mode, a transferable insight for any continuous AR speech model. - The frozen-head GRPO finding (trainable head degrades test-en WER from 1.51% to 3.21% while frozen head improves it to 1.15%) is a clean, controlled, practically useful result for AR–diffusion/flow hybrid post-training. - Guidance-aware distillation with student-rollout batches (30%) addresses exposure bias in the distillation itself; the authors show the head degrades severely without it, and the guidance-scale-as-input design keeps scales tunable post-distillation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: only one Haar split per axis was tested, with no evaluation of transform depth or other wavelet families; evaluation is limited to English and Chinese, short single-speaker utterances, with tonal languages beyond Mandarin, long-form synthesis, multi-speaker dialogue, paralinguistic control, singing, and code-switching all out of scope; only speech was tested, with no evidence the factorization transfers to music or general audio. They also concede the DiTAR-style transfer comparison is not configuration-matched and therefore does not establish target superiority. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical rigor: every headline number is a single point estimate without seeds or variance, and differences as small as 0.1–0.3 WER (e.g., 1.51% vs 1.69% vs DiTAR) are interpreted as meaningful. - The core ablation is run only at 0.15B; the claim that residual exclusion is what enables stable mel AR is never verified at the scale where the headline results are reported, and the 0.6B model was developed and evaluated on the same benchmarks (Seed-TTS-eval) used for guidance-scale selection. - The distilled 4-step student's SIM drop (0.752→0.693 test-en, ~0.06) is substantial and unexplained; the paper reports it but offers no analysis of whether SIM degradation comes from head distillation, guidance absorption, or student-rollout training. - Missing efficiency baseline: the paper does not report end-to-end wall-clock RTF (real-time factor) or total NFE including the residual tiers, making comparison with ZipVoice (16 NFE total, 0.1B params) or F5-TTS impossible from the reported numbers. - The text-reliance and exposure-gap probes are measured under the authors' own definitions; no external validation that the 4.53% text-reliance of the split model corresponds to genuinely better text adherence in human listening, where VoxMel does not clearly win. - REINFORCE-style GRPO reward uses ASR transcription accuracy, which risks the RL stage gaming the Whisper/Paraformer recognizers rather than improving perceptual quality — the MOS test does not separately evaluate the GRPO checkpoint. Bottom Line: A practitioner in speech generation should read this paper for the residual-feedback analysis and the frozen-head GRPO result — both are reusable findings — but VoxMel itself is not yet the strongest available TTS recipe, as VoxCPM, OmniVoice, and IndexTTS 2 match or beat it on accuracy at comparable or smaller data scales, and the mel target's fidelity advantage over learned latents is asserted rather than demonstrated in matched comparisons.

From Code Completion to Agentic Development: A Survey of AI Coding Agents, Ecosystems, and Evolving Software Engineering Practice

Y Wang, C Yang, S Hou, X Xu, B Cui, Y Jiang, T Yang · link.springer.com · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a structured scoping survey of AI coding agents that organizes the field along a new five-dimensional taxonomy (interaction paradigm, computational architecture, deployment form, orchestration mode, human-oversight mode) and, unusually for the genre, adds commercial-ecosystem, developer-workflow, interoperability, and societal analyses under an explicit evidence-stratification scheme. - Why it's important: Practitioners, researchers, and policymakers currently face a field flooded with vendor claims, contested productivity evidence, and surveys that cover only technical architecture, leaving no calibrated map of what is actually demonstrated versus marketed. - How it does it: The core move is separating human-oversight mode from computational architecture (resolving the conflation of, e.g., single-agent systems with approval gates in prior taxonomies) and enforcing source-type-stratified claim calibration: benchmark scores support only benchmark-specific statements, vendor reports only product descriptions, news only dated events. - The good: The methodology is unusually transparent and self-limiting for a survey: a reproducible search (29,784 records from arXiv/Semantic Scholar/DBLP, 18,261 after deduplication), a complete 154-source evidence corpus with a supplementary citation ledger, and explicit admission that no screening log was retained, hence "scoping survey, not systematic review." - The missing: The taxonomy is applied to only 12 illustrative systems by the authors' own single coding pass with no inter-rater reliability or Cohen's kappa reported, and the survey offers no quantitative synthesis (effect sizes, pooled evidence) across the studies it covers. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone entering or evaluating the AI-coding-agent space — especially SE researchers, tooling evaluators, and decision-makers who need the capability/adoption distinction and the benchmark-contamination analysis (SWE-bench Verified's documented flaws, the 19% METR slowdown finding) — skimmable for specialists already fluent in SWE-agent, MCP/A2A, and the benchmark landscape.
Why this rank
Scored using EMPIRICAL profile (meta-research survey). Completeness (75) and Resilience (75) are the paper's strongest dimensions: direct confrontation of the missing screening log and absent inter-rater reliability, explicit refusal to inflate to 'systematic review,' and tier-bound claims that resist the field's worst citation pathologies. Novelty (65) rests on the oversight-versus-architecture decoupling and the four-layer interoperability model — a real formulation contribution — while Rigor (65) is capped by single-coder taxonomy with no kappa and a 12-system validation sample. Non-Obviousness (65) reflects the evidence-stratification scheme's genuine analytical value over prior surveys; Impact (50) is limited to paper, scripts, and a citation ledger with no reusable instrument validated at scale. Problem & Motivation: LLM-based systems have moved software-development assistance from token-level completion toward agents that plan, edit files, run tools, and iterate on test feedback, but the literature lacks a map that (a) classifies these systems without conflating orthogonal design choices and (b) separates technical capability evidence from business and adoption claims. Five prior surveys (2024–2026, including two in ACM TOSEM) cover agent architectures and code generation but, per the authors' own 9-dimension coding (Table 1), none gives sustained treatment to commercial ecosystem, developer workflow, productivity evidence, agent interoperability, or societal impact. The people with the problem: researchers positioning new work, practitioners choosing tools, and educators/policymakers confronting workflow and governance changes with only vendor or anecdotal evidence available. Key Idea: The key intellectual move is a two-part reframing rather than a technical method: (1) a five-dimensional taxonomy in which each dimension asks exactly one question with mutually exclusive values and an "undisclosed" escape hatch — critically, human oversight (continuous steering / approval-gated / review-at-completion / exception-only) is coded independently of architecture (fixed pipeline / single-agent / multi-agent), because oversight can coexist with any architecture; and (2) evidence stratification, where the claim type a source is allowed to support is pinned to its evidence tier. This converts an otherwise standard literature review into an auditable claim-calibration exercise. Methodology: The paper self-identifies as a structured scoping survey, not a systematic review. Pipeline: (1) reproducible queries against arXiv, Semantic Scholar, and DBLP for 1 Jan 2021–28 Feb 2026 (full query strings and scripts in supplementary materials), re-run on 9 Aug 2026, yielding 29,784 unique within-database records and 18,261 after cross-database deduplication; (2) purposive selection of representative methods, systems, benchmarks, and studies against ten topic codes (architecture, repository context, planning/tool use, multi-agent coordination, SDLC application, human–agent interaction, evaluation, security, commercial context, societal/legal implications), producing a final corpus of exactly 154 cited sources with a CSV ledger recording citation key, source type, evidence tier, and first citation location; (3) narrative synthesis across background (pre-LLM synthesis, statistical code models, APR), the taxonomy, six technique groups (code understanding/generation, repository context, planning, tool integration, multi-agent collaboration, learning/adaptation), SDLC phases, commercial ecosystem, developer workflows, benchmarks, and open problems. No objective function or algorithmic framework applies. Critical design decisions: (a) coding human oversight as a separate dimension — well justified by the cross-tabulation in Table 5 showing all four oversight modes co-occurring with architectures; (b) refusing a PRISMA flow, exclusion counts, or Cohen's kappa because the original process did not retain screening records — an honesty-positive that caps rigor; (c) refusing to infer "benchmark gaming" from the SWE-bench Verified–Pro score gap alone — well argued, since the benchmarks differ in distribution and difficulty. Key Results: As a survey, its "results" are syntheses and coding outputs, not new measurements. Headline items: best published SWE-bench Verified result rose from 74.9% to 80.9% in the six months to 23 Feb 2026 (OpenAI-reported, treated as a dated benchmark-specific observation, not a model ranking); the METR randomized trial found experienced open-source developers took 19% longer with early-2025 agent tools on familiar repositories while predicting a speedup; SWE-agent's interface ablations showed resolve-rate differences up to 40% across agent–computer interface designs; the Stack Overflow 2025 survey reports 84% of respondents using or planning to use AI tools versus 46% actively distrusting accuracy; the coded 12-system sample shows single-agent architectures dominating (6 of 12) and exception-only oversight appearing in zero documented systems. The comparative coding of five prior surveys (Table 1) shows none covers commercial ecosystem, developer workflow, productivity evidence, or interoperability as dedicated sections. Baselines here are the five prior surveys; the comparison is scope-conditioned and explicitly not a ranking. The scale of evidence synthesis is moderate (154 sources) and the taxonomy validation sample is small (12 systems). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (the five-dimensional taxonomy with oversight decoupled from architecture, plus the four-layer interoperability decomposition of tool access / agent collaboration / orchestration / governance) combined with a genuinely broader synthesis scope than prior surveys. The technical content itself (ReAct, RAG, FIM, MCP/A2A, SWE-bench family, multi-agent patterns) is a standard, well-executed aggregation of existing material; what is genuinely new is the taxonomy's non-redundancy rules, the evidence-tier claim-calibration scheme, and the insistence on treating capability, business performance, and adoption as incommensurable quantities. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations do not apply, but the survey analog is present: decision rules, boundary cases (Agentless as fixed pipeline, Devin coded "undisclosed"), a complete bibliography-as-corpus, and a supplementary CSV ledger with search scripts and API fields make the coding auditable and reproducible in principle. Weaknesses the authors concede: no manual screening log was retained, so no PRISMA flow or inter-coder reliability (Cohen's kappa) can be reported; selection is purposive; English-only sources; the taxonomy reflects author judgment, not ground truth. The 12-system taxonomy sample is illustrative, not exhaustive, and closed commercial systems are coded "undisclosed" where evidence is missing — appropriately, but it limits the taxonomy's coverage of the most-deployed products. Published in Data Science and Engineering (Springer), with received/revised/accepted dates of March–August 2026; the paper is a peer-reviewed journal survey, though much of its underlying evidence is preprint or vendor material, which the authors flag tier-by-tier. The evidence-stratification discipline is the survey's main rigor asset: it systematically resists the field's worst citation pathology (using funding, GitHub stars, or vendor demos as capability evidence). Deployability: Profile: this is a survey, so the EMPIRICAL/THEORETICAL/SYSTEMS trichotomy fits awkwardly; treated as EMPIRICAL in the meta-research sense (a structured synthesis of literature evidence), with the four-property check adapted. Practical: N/A for a method; the survey's artifacts (search scripts, CSV ledger, supplementary materials) are reproducible on standard hardware. Efficient: The protocol covers three databases and 18,261 deduplicated records with a 154-source final corpus — a moderate, defensible screening load for a scoping survey. Effective: It delivers a calibrated map and taxonomy, which it demonstrably supports; it explicitly does not deliver pooled effect estimates or a validated maturity model. Scalable: Taxonomy coding over hundreds of systems or continuous re-coding as products change is untested; the authors themselves note the commercial snapshot is dated and fast-rotting. Deliverables: paper plus supplementary search scripts and citation-ledger CSV; no library, trained model, or dataset artifact. Strengths: - The oversight-versus-architecture separation is a real conceptual correction: prior classifications could not express that a single-agent system might be approval-gated or review-at-completion, and the Table 5 cross-tabulation makes the non-redundancy concrete rather than asserted. - The evidence-stratification methodology (Table 2) is the most disciplined handling of mixed academic/vendor/news evidence this reviewer has seen in an agent survey — every quantitative claim is tier-bound, and commercial metrics are explicitly barred from supporting capability or preference conclusions. - The benchmark section adds genuine analytical value beyond cataloguing: it correctly argues that the Verified–Pro score gap cannot diagnose gaming without direct contamination audits, and it incorporates OpenAI's February 2026 audit and retirement of Verified reporting as dated evidence. - Honest scoping: labeling itself a "structured scoping survey" rather than inflating to "systematic review" despite reproducible search numbers is a credibility-positive that most surveys in this space lack. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly (Sect. 11) rather than minimizing: no retained screening log hence no PRISMA/kappa; purposive, English-only, partly non-peer-reviewed selection; commercial archetype table as a February 2026 snapshot; reliance on single anecdotal incidents (curl bug-bounty closure, matplotlib agent incident) that cannot establish prevalence; no causal employment estimates and no legal analysis; taxonomy and survey-comparison dimensions are author-chosen coding decisions, not ground truth. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-coder taxonomy: with no reported inter-rater agreement even on the 12-system sample, the taxonomy's reliability as a reusable instrument is unverified — the "auditable" ledger mitigates but does not replace a second coder. - The 12-system coded sample skews toward academic and open systems (SWE-agent, Aider, OpenHands, MetaGPT); the highest-deployment commercial agents are coded "undisclosed" on 2–4 of 5 dimensions, so the taxonomy's practical grip on the products developers actually use is thin. - No quantitative synthesis anywhere: the productivity section correctly refuses to pool the Peng et al. 55% speedup with METR's 19% slowdown, but stops at declaring heterogeneity — a reviewer would want at least a structured moderator analysis (population, task familiarity, oversight policy) across the small set of controlled studies. - The survey cites its own institutions' framing heavily (PKU/Zhejiang authors) and its Table 1 comparison dimensions are self-defined, making the "prior surveys miss these topics" claim partly circular, as the authors half-acknowledge. - The interoperability four-layer model (Fig. 10) is offered as a hypothesis but never tested against even one concrete cross-vendor composition; several sections (multi-agent shared state, incident response, legacy modernization) correctly note absent evidence but thereby leave large parts of the synthesis at "more research needed." - Unusual dating: the paper's timeline (2026 cutoff, ICLR 2026 citations, received March 2026) is internally consistent but means much load-bearing evidence is months-old at best in a field where the authors themselves note product half-lives are short. Bottom Line: For anyone who needs a single, epistemically careful entry point into AI coding agents — particularly the capability-versus-hype separation and the benchmark-validity analysis — this is currently the best-calibrated survey available; specialists seeking quantitative synthesis or a validated taxonomy instrument will find it descriptive rather than decisive.

Mobile AI Factory: Building Specialized Language Models for Your Mobile Device (19 ▲ )

Evan Li, Krishna Deshpande, Wen Cheng, Shyamnath Gollakota · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 16 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Mobile AI Factory, an agentic system that takes a task specification and a target Android phone and automatically produces a fine-tuned, quantized small language model plus its inference engine and backend, meeting the task's accuracy goal and the phone's resource budgets. - Why it's important: Today this pipeline requires repeated expert tuning for every phone model (Facebook's app runs on 10,000+ device models), which is impractical outside the largest companies; automating it makes private, offline on-device LLM applications accessible to ordinary developers. - How it does it: An orchestrator LLM (Claude Sonnet 5) picks one intervention per iteration (hyperparameters, mined data, or targeted synthetic data) while deterministic rules handle rollback and escalation over buckets of model+quantization combinations, all constrained by measured per-phone profiles of prefill/decode speed, memory, and energy across llama.cpp and MNN on CPU/GPU. - The good: The phone-measurement study is decisive: across 364 profiled configurations, rankings flip per phone (GPU prefill is 5.4× faster than CPU on a OnePlus 15 but 7.4× slower on a OnePlus 8 Pro), and Claude Opus 5.5 with full spec sheets still misses the app's requirements in 60% of hard cases — proving measurement cannot be replaced by reasoning. - The missing: Each configuration is a single run with a self-estimated ±0.015 noise floor and no seeds or significance tests; the exhaustive-sweep comparison is run on only one of ten tasks; and synthesis was evaluated on seven tasks where the system's own teacher-quality gate would have disabled it. - Read it or not: Yes, if you build or deploy on-device/edge LLM systems — the profiling findings and the phone-in-the-loop design are immediately actionable; if you only care about agentic ML engineering generically, MLE-bench-style work covers that ground more directly.

Scored using Systems profile. The composite is lifted by solid Practical Impact (70 — released code plus independently valuable per-phone profiling data) and Non-Obviousness (70 — engine/backend rankings flipping per phone and spec-sheet reasoning failing 60% of hard cases). Rigor (63) is capped by single-run experiments throughout, a one-task exhaustive-sweep comparison, and the self-contradictory synthesis configuration, while Completeness (68) is helped by unusually honest gain accounting (admitting 88% of interventions fail and two unseen-set losses). Novelty (62) reflects a disciplined recombination of standard parts around one genuinely new constraint (phone-in-the-loop). Weighted composite: 0.15*62 + 0.15*63 + 0.10*70 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*62 + 0.30*70 = 66.
