Problem & Motivation: Mobile developers want task-specialized small language models that run on-device (for privacy and offline use), but producing one requires jointly choosing a base model, quantization level, inference engine, and backend, then fine-tuning and iterating on accuracy — a process repeated per phone model. The paper motivates this with measured cross-device variance: Qwen3-4B at 8 bits decodes 12.6–13.8 tokens/s on a OnePlus 15 but 0.7–4.8 tokens/s on a OnePlus 8 Pro; prompt-processing throughput spans 94× across four phones (3.3 to 309 tokens/s for Qwen3-0.6B at 4 bits). Prior agentic fine-tuning systems (Pioneer Agent, PostTrainBench, Slemify) assume server deployment where accuracy is the only objective; none treats device feasibility as a search constraint or scores accuracy post-quantization on the exact deployment artifact. Key Idea: Treat (base model, quantization, engine, backend) as one atomic choice, bucket these combinations into five size tiers, and search small-to-large with an LLM orchestrator constrained by deterministic rollback/escalation rules — using a once-per-phone measured hardware profile to prune configurations before any training, and scoring every model after quantization on the exact artifact the target engine will run. Methodology: The system runs in two stages. (1) Setup: the frozen phone profile plus developer budgets (latency, memory, energy per request) prune infeasible variants and pick the fastest engine/backend per surviving variant; the orchestrator writes a task brief; a held-out set (up to 1,000 rows) is frozen behind four contamination firewalls; the accuracy goal is set to the teacher model's five-shot (or zero-shot) score with a floor of 0.80 and cap of 0.99. (2) Search loop: LoRA fine-tuning (Unsloth/PEFT on 4-bit bases) with loss on answer tokens only; each iteration the orchestrator (Claude Sonnet 5, $2.62–8.46/task) makes exactly one intervention — hyperparameters (LoRA rank, α/rank, LR, weight decay, epochs), mining more real data, or teacher-generated synthetic rows (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 25–600 rows per failure category, gated by programmatic verifiers) — after which the merged adapter is exported to 4/8-bit deployment format and scored in the actual engine. Training restarts from the base model each time, so rollback exactly restores the best state; 88% of interventions in the most-iterated run hurt and were rolled back. Escalation to the next tier triggers after <0.02 gain over 15 evaluations or 30 evaluations without reaching the goal; the orchestrator can raise the goal after a quick win. Each run uses two NVIDIA L40S GPUs (one training, one teacher), with state checkpointed to SQLite. Design decisions are mostly well-justified with inline ablations (e.g., the watchdog added after an 8-hour wasted run; MNN's default 4-bit export loses up to 0.19 accuracy, justifying HQQ). Key Results: Across ten tasks (BC5CDR, calendar JSON, TOPv2, MultiCoNER, BFCL, CLINC150, SMS spam, GoEmotions, BEA-19, DialogSum), factory models beat the better of five-shot Claude Sonnet 5 / DeepSeek v4 Flash on seven tasks by 0.037–0.357 on the held-out set; on unseen test sets, five wins hold (up to +0.342 on TOPv2 exact match: 0.562 vs 0.221) with three ties and two losses. On biomedical entity extraction, a 517 MB Qwen3.5-0.8B at 4 bits scores 0.828 vs Claude's 0.652. The tiered search reaches the 0.80 goal in 8.6 GPU-hours/$2.62 vs 165 GPU-hours/$31.81 for an exhaustive 27-variant sweep (19× less GPU time), landing within 0.03 of the sweep's ceiling (0.830 vs 0.859 on the task where they were compared). Search adds a median 0.082 over the first fine-tune on the smallest tier but only 0.023 on the largest; the first fine-tune accounts for a median 82% of total improvement. Baselines are current frontier models (late-2026 naming) but only two, both via API with reasoning disabled; no comparison against cheaper cloud small-model APIs or prompt-optimized frontier models. Scale is modest but realistic: 135M–4B parameters, 2,600–5,000 real training rows per task, four Android phones (OnePlus 15, Galaxy S23, OnePlus 8 Pro, Redmi 9A). A counter-intuitive finding: 76 of 364 phone configurations failed to run, and only 35 of those failures are predicted by weight size — the rest crash, swap, or hit GPU-driver gaps invisible on a spec sheet. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the phone-in-the-loop constraint on agentic model-building (measured profiles as a hard feasibility filter and post-quantization scoring on the deployment artifact) and the cross-device profiling study showing backend/engine/precision rankings flip per phone. The individual techniques — LoRA fine-tuning, LLM-driven synthetic data targeting failure modes, quantization, latency benchmarking, tiered/progressive search — are standard; the contribution is their disciplined combination under device budgets, which the paper states fairly. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong on ablation and honesty: the paper decomposes gains into first-fine-tune vs search vs per-intervention (hyperparameters 41%, synthesis 40%, mining 19% of search gains), compares tiered search against both a one-shot pick (better on 8/10 tasks, by >noise on six) and an exhaustive sweep (one task only), quantifies run-to-run noise (±0.015 held-out, 0.1–5% timing, up to 38% for one MNN configuration), and validates on unseen test sets in Appendix A, admitting two losses there. It also self-reports that synthesis accounted for 67% of its credited gains on tasks where its own quality gate should have disabled it. Concerns: every run is a single execution with no seeds or significance tests; the held-out set guides all search decisions (selection leakage, partially addressed by unseen-set evaluation, though spam detection could not be checked on unseen rows); the exhaustive-sweep comparison rests on one task; and the goal-setting mechanism ties student targets to the teacher's own score, with a Qwen3.6 teacher and Qwen3/Qwen3.5 students (possible family synergy). Code is released at https://github.com/evanly-gh/SLM_Factory. This is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2611.13509), not stated as peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS — a built, evaluated agentic pipeline. - Practical: Yes for inference — the output runs on consumer Android phones including a $100-class Redmi 9A; building the model requires a two-L40S server plus a paid frontier-model API. - Efficient: Tiered search costs 8.6–286 GPU-hours and $2.62–8.46 of orchestrator API per task (663 GPU-hours total across ten runs, two GPUs each), roughly 19× cheaper than exhaustive search, but a run can take days. - Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated problem on-device — on a Galaxy S23 hard requirement it returned a 0.6B model within 0.013 of the accuracy of the smallest model that otherwise fits, and server-vs-phone accuracy differs by ≤0.016 — though only for the ten tested tasks with hand-built verifiers. - Scalable: Not tested beyond four phones and ten tasks; profiling is slow (thermal cooling between runs), and the paper only claims (does not demonstrate) prediction-based shortcuts for new phones; the ambition of covering thousands of phone models is extrapolation. The work delivers a software artifact (released code) and reusable per-phone profiling data; it does not ship trained models or a library of profiles beyond the four phones. Strengths: - The hardware profiling study (Section 3, 364 configurations on four phones) is independently valuable: it documents that the best engine/backend flips per phone, that quantization recipes labeled "4-bit" differ by up to 0.19 accuracy (MNN default vs Q4_K_M vs HQQ), and that 41 of 76 configuration failures are unpredictable from spec sheets. - Disciplined agent design: the paper quantifies that 88% of orchestrator interventions fail and therefore hard-wires rollback, escalation, and watchdogs in deterministic code — a credible answer to why the loop makes progress. - Honest gain accounting: it reports that the first fine-tune delivers a median 82% of improvement and that search gains shrink with model size (0.082 → 0.023 median), rather than overselling the agent loop. - Phone-measurement necessity is tested against a real alternative (Claude Opus 5.5 with full specs and high reasoning effort: 25% miss rate on easy/moderate requirements, 60% on hard), not just asserted. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the developer-supplied output verifier is the most hand-engineered part and the biggest autonomy bottleneck; the model pool is fixed (decoder-only, 135M–4B); training is LoRA-only (no preference optimization, RL, or distillation); synthesis rounds are small (hundreds of rows from a 35B teacher); NPUs are not profiled; measurements assume a cool, idle phone at one prompt length and four threads, so concurrent/thermal-realistic deployment may change which configurations qualify; and profiling is slow though paid once per phone. They confront these directly, including data on where synthesis backfired (quality-control pass rates of 3–24% predicted the largest drops under data scarcity), which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-run experiments throughout: with a ±0.015 noise floor and margins as small as 0.024 on unseen sets, several headline wins are within plausible seed-to-seed variance; no repeated runs or confidence intervals are provided. - The synthesis intervention was enabled on 7 of 10 tasks where the system's own 0.80 teacher gate would have turned it off — the reported 40% synthesis contribution reflects a configuration the factory would not ship. - Only two frontier baselines; no cheap cloud small-model API (e.g., GPT-4o-mini-class) baseline, which is the practical alternative for non-private or latency-tolerant use, and no prompt-optimization baseline on the frontier models, which could capture much of the gap at zero training cost. - The goal-setting mechanism uses the teacher's five-shot score as the target; with a Qwen-family teacher and Qwen-family students, target calibration and synthetic-data quality may not transfer to non-Qwen student models, and this is not ablated. - The exhaustive-sweep validation of the bucketed search exists for one task only; the one-shot-pick comparison across ten tasks is a weaker substitute since the pick's quality depends on the same orchestrator. - Server-side scoring uses the same engine but different hardware/kernels; on-phone validation of accuracy was done only on the OnePlus 15, so cross-device accuracy drift is checked on one phone. - The "first agentic system" claim is difficult to verify and rests on distinguishing the scope from Pioneer Agent. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or deploying LLMs on Android/edge hardware gains concrete, hard-to-find value here — the per-phone profiling findings and the demonstration that spec-sheet reasoning fails 60% of the time justify the read even if the agentic-search layer itself is a competent assembly of known parts.

Sequential-Halving Switchback

P Missault, B Mason, D Eswaran, H Li · cdn.amazon.science · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proposes Sequential-Halving Switchback (SHS), a two-phase adaptive A/B testing design that combines sequential-halving arm elimination with daily re-randomization (switchback) across many candidate treatments, ending in a confirmatory A/B on the finalists. - Why it's important: Online experimentation platforms need to screen many treatment arms at once without sacrificing statistical power or calendar time, and standard fixed-allocation A/B tests split traffic so thinly across arms that they are underpowered. - How it does it: It exploits the observation that best-arm selection needs only correct rankings, not unbiased effect estimates, so daily re-randomization (which biases conventional effect estimators under strict assumptions) is tolerable during exploration; traffic is split evenly across active arms each day, the worst half is eliminated per round, and data is pooled across rounds. - The good: The paper derives a closed-form bias-variance condition for pooling across rounds — pooling is worse only when an arm-specific shock exceeds roughly half the gap to the best arm — and validates this break-even (predicted 0.570, measured 0.576 and 0.570 at λ=2) over 600,000 Monte Carlo replications per cell. - The missing: The proof-of-concept study does not directly validate arm selection (the authors admit this would require a multi-way non-adaptive experiment across all 9 arms), and the variance inflation from non-independent unit-day re-triggers is explicitly left out of scope. - Read it or not: Worth reading for experimentation-platform practitioners and industrial statisticians designing multi-arm tests, particularly for the pooling-across-rounds analysis; skip it if you need deployable code, formal guarantees for the combined design, or large-scale empirical evidence.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (72) rests on the non-obvious insight that adaptive selection tolerates biased estimators as long as rankings are preserved, plus a closed-form pooling condition validated against 600k-replicate simulations — but the machinery itself (sequential halving, switchback, confirmatory A/B) is standard. Rigor (62) is pulled down by a single-run proof-of-concept with no error bars, no direct validation of arm selection, no released code, and preprint/abstract-level review status. Completeness (65) and Resilience (65) benefit from direct limitation acknowledgment but are capped by untested single-scenario assumptions and no comparison against alternative adaptive designs; Practical Impact (50) reflects a design recipe with no artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*50 = 66.

Problem & Motivation: Teams running A/B tests on online platforms often want to compare many candidate treatments simultaneously. A fixed-allocation design forces a trade-off between calendar time and power: either each arm gets enough traffic to be powered (long run time) or traffic is split across more arms (underpowered arms). Adaptive designs that shift traffic toward promising arms address this, but the standard practice of requiring unbiased estimators inside the adaptive loop imposes strict assumptions, especially when assignments are re-randomized daily (switchback designs), where carry-over effects bias conventional difference-in-means estimators. Key Idea: The core insight is that an adaptive selection procedure is robust to estimator bias as long as the bias preserves the ranking: writing E[τ̂ₐ] = τₐ + sₐ, selection succeeds if E[τ̂_best] > E[τ̂ₐ] for all arms. Because uniform daily re-randomization makes any carry-over shock common to all arms (canceling in the contrast), only arm-specific shocks matter — so the design can tolerate the bias that switchback re-randomization introduces and still pick the right arm. The second key idea is a closed-form bias-variance analysis showing that pooling observations across halving rounds (usually discouraged due to selection bias) is beneficial unless an arm-localized shock exceeds roughly half the arm's gap to the best arm. Methodology: SHS runs in two phases. (1) Exploration: sequential halving (Karnin et al.) with R = ⌈log₂ K⌉ rounds; each day's traffic is split evenly across still-active arms with daily re-randomization of units; at each round end the worst half is eliminated on that round's (pooled) sample means of a single primary metric. (2) Validation: survivors face control in a conventional single-randomization A/B. The authors model user triggering with a base rate b and retrigger rate r, showing unit-day sample counts grow linearly (slope r) versus the saturating concave growth of unit-level randomization. For pooling, they derive the precision gain G = √(n₁:R/n_R) < √2 under exact halving, and a closed-form misranking probability Φ(−λₖ) with λₖ = λ(1 − s·w_J/Δ) under pooling versus λ/G under per-round estimation, yielding the condition s·w_J > Δ(1 − 1/G) for when pooling loses. Simulations use an additive normal-outcome model with 8 arms, 3 rounds, a shocked runner-up arm, 600,000 replications per cell, sweeping shock ratio s/Δ ∈ [0,1] and gap-to-noise λ ∈ {0.5, 1, 2, 3}. A proof-of-concept run on an experimentation platform used 9 arms (control + 8 treatments), pooled data, two halving rounds to two finalists, then a 3-week validation A/B. Critical design decisions: (a) ending with a confirmatory A/B — well justified as a guard against exploration mistakes; (b) pooling across rounds despite common-practice discouragement — justified analytically and by simulation; (c) assuming correct variance estimation for re-randomized data is left out of scope — a noted but unaddressed gap. Key Results: Simulation: the predicted pooling/per-round break-even at s/Δ = 0.570 was measured at 0.576 (λ=2) and 0.570 (λ=3); at low noise (λ=0.5) pooling remains dominant even at a shock equal to the full gap; the closed-form Φ(λ(1−s·w_J/Δ)) matches simulated selection probabilities within 0.019 across all cells (400,000 replications each). Proof-of-concept (9 arms, metrics reported in units of standard error σ): exploration and validation estimates agree in sign on 13 of 14 comparisons (7 metrics × 2 treatments), the one disagreement being non-significant in both designs; no exploration estimate differs significantly from its validation counterpart; significance verdicts nest (validation-significant implies exploration-significant, never reverse); median absolute point-estimate disagreement 0.18σ, largest 1.63σ (p=0.10). Pooling cut mean exploration standard error by a factor of 1.4, and both pooled and non-pooled schemes eliminated the same 4 arms in round 1 and returned the same 2 finalists. The observed 2.6× sample-size increase from re-randomization bought only ≈1.4× standard-error reduction (vs. ≈1.6× under independence), quantifying the dependence shortfall. Baselines are the per-round (non-pooled) variant in simulation and a conventional A/B in the field study — appropriate, not outdated, but limited in number. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the SHS design combining sequential halving with daily re-randomization plus a validation phase) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the closed-form condition under which pooling across adaptive rounds is preferable despite selection bias). The components are standard — sequential halving (Karnin et al. 2013), switchback designs (Bojinov et al. 2023), and a validation A/B — so the genuine novelty lies in the observation that selection tolerates biased estimators and in the quantified pooling bias-variance trade-off, not in the machinery itself. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present in simulation: the pooling-versus-per-round comparison is swept over shock ratio and noise level, and the closed-form prediction is validated cell-by-cell with large replication counts (600,000 and 400,000 per cell). No error bars or multiple-seed variance are reported for the field study (a single proof-of-concept run, 14 comparisons), and no significance tests of the design-level agreement are given. No code or data release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (a) the field validation uses the authors' own platform and withholds metric identities, making independent verification impossible; (b) arm selection is never directly validated — the authors assume agreement between pooled exploration and validation estimates proxies selection correctness; (c) the paper is labeled an abstract/short paper, so this is preprint-level evidence, not full peer-reviewed treatment. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (simulation plus one field proof-of-concept run on a production experimentation platform). - Practical: Yes — the design runs on a standard experimentation platform with daily re-randomization and requires no specialized hardware or algorithms beyond sample-mean comparisons. - Efficient: Favors efficiency — pooling cut exploration standard error 1.4× and re-randomization grows effective samples linearly in horizon, though true error shrinks slower than √n due to within-unit dependence (measured 1.4× vs. ideal 1.6×). - Effective: Partially — the field study shows estimates agree between exploration and validation, but arm selection itself is assumed correct rather than tested, so effectiveness is demonstrated on a proxy. - Scalable: Claimed but not tested — the theory suggests advantages grow with arm count and horizon, but the field evidence covers only 9 arms and one platform; behavior at 10× arms or with strong non-additive carry-over is untested. The work delivers a design recipe and analysis but no released software artifact, library, or dataset; it stops at paper form. Strengths: - The framing that selection requires ranking consistency, not unbiasedness, is a genuinely useful relaxation that unlocks switchback re-randomization inside adaptive designs — a non-obvious conceptual move. - The closed-form pooling condition (pooling loses only when s·w_J > Δ(1 − 1/G), i.e., a shock exceeding roughly half the gap) is derived, has a memorable rule-of-thumb form, and matches simulation to within 0.019 in selection probability — a rare analytically-validated practical guideline for a question (pooling across adaptive interim looks) where conventional advice is a flat prohibition. - Honest quantification of the re-randomization dependence shortfall (2.6× samples bought 1.4× standard-error reduction) rather than overstating switchback gains. - The two-phase structure with a confirmatory A/B is a pragmatic safeguard that reflects operational experimentation practice. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that arm selection is not directly validated (a direct check would require an underpowered multi-way experiment over all 9-arm pairs), that the study of the re-randomization shortfall illustrates that true error shrinks by less than 1/√(rT), and that variance estimation for re-randomized data is left out of scope (citing [9]). They also withhold metric identities for confidentiality. They confront these limitations directly, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Only one simulation scenario shape is tested (one best arm, one runner-up at gap Δ, six arms at 3Δ, equal variances, normal outcomes, equal-length rounds); robustness to unequal variances, non-normal outcomes, multiple strong contenders, or time-varying effects is untested. - The field proof-of-concept has no error bars, no repeated runs, and only 14 comparisons; agreement in sign and nested significance on a single run is weak evidence for the design's general reliability. - The bias analysis assumes a constant, arm-localized shock; realistic carry-over in switchback experiments is often time-decaying and arm-pair-specific, and no such structure is modeled. - The validation phase does not correct for the adaptive selection (no post-selection inference), so effect estimates for the finalists may inherit selection bias; the paper does not discuss this. - No comparison against alternative adaptive designs (e.g., Thompson sampling or successive elimination with validation), so it is unknown whether SHS is the right adaptive baseline, only that it works. - No released code or simulation scripts, and the preprint/abstract format means the work has not undergone full peer review. Bottom Line: A practitioner designing multi-arm experiments on an online platform gains a concrete, analytically-backed design and a genuinely useful rule of thumb for pooling across adaptive rounds, but the thin single-run validation and absent artifacts mean most teams will need to replicate the simulations internally before trusting it at scale.

Understanding Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Beyond Expert Boundaries

Z Zhou, M Zheng, M Song, Q Li, K Wang, J Fang · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Routing-Aware Magnitude Profiling (RAMP), a neuron-importance measure for MoE LLMs that weights activation magnitudes by routing coefficients and down-projection norms, uses it to show that domain specialization lives at the neuron level across expert boundaries, traces this organization through training, and builds RAMPr, a neuron-level MoE pruning method. - Why it's important: It resolves a live controversy — whether MoE experts are domain specialists or whether routing merely reflects token identity — and converts that understanding into memory and throughput savings for serving MoE models, whose expert parameters are otherwise hard to compress without whole-expert removal. - How it does it: RAMP scores each expert-neuron coordinate as the root of summed squared routing-weighted activations times the down-projection column norm; aggregating these domain-wise scores across a shared calibration pool yields a single cross-domain neuron set retained per layer during pruning. - The good: Causal ablation backs the correlational analysis: zeroing a domain's top-10% RAMP neurons collapses matched tasks (e.g., HumanEval/MBPP to ≤0.40% after code ablation across all six models), while random removal of the same count costs at most ~16 points. - The missing: Evaluation tasks come from the same datasets used for calibration (GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval/MBPP sources), and no recovery fine-tuning, no comparison against cited neuron-level pruning baselines (HEAPr, TENP), and error bars on benchmark scores are absent; decode speedup is essentially 1×. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on MoE interpretability or MoE compression — the neuron-level reframing and the control experiments are genuinely useful — skip it if you only need a production pruning recipe, since the headline speedups are memory/prefill-bound and the field moves fast.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (70) is solid — the neuron-level reframing that dissolves the expert-specialization debate and the neuron-vs-expert training-dynamics dissociation are new empirical findings, though RAMP itself is a routing-weighted extension of known magnitude pruning. Rigor (62) is the main drag: the Fisher baseline collapses (making that comparison uninformative), cited neuron-level baselines (HEAPr, TENP) are never run, REAP wins on one of its two models, benchmark scores lack error bars, and — critically — pruning is calibrated on the same datasets used for evaluation, a Goodhart risk the paper does not address. Non-Obviousness (75) is high: the routing-only overlap bound and causal ablations rule out specific null explanations, and the finding that specialization lives inside experts despite stable expert aggregates is genuinely surprising. Completeness (65) is mixed — honest ablation reporting but unaddressed calibration-eval overlap, an abstract-table inconsistency, and no recovery fine-tuning. Impact (60) is limited: code referenced but no released checkpoints, and the decode speedup is ~1×. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*62 + 0.10*60 = 66.

Problem & Motivation: MoE LLMs (DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM, gpt-oss, OLMoE) route tokens to a subset of experts, and two incompatible accounts of expert behavior coexist in the literature: one line reports domain-associated expert preferences and builds architectures around expert specialization; another shows routing is largely explained by token identity and hidden-state geometry, questioning whether experts are domain specialists at all. Practitioners compressing MoE models (via expert pruning) and interpretability researchers both lack a definitive account of where domain-dependent computation actually lives. The paper argues the unit of analysis — the whole expert — is wrong, and that specialization must be probed at the neuron level within and across experts. It also addresses the follow-on engineering question: if capabilities are carried by specific neurons inside experts, MoE models can be compressed below the whole-expert granularity that prior pruning (REAP, expert dropping) is restricted to. Key Idea: Measure neuron importance as the routing-weighted contribution magnitude — RAMP, Equation (3): the square root of summed squared products of the router probability p_e(t), the gated activation a_e_i(t), and the down-projection column norm ‖w_e,down_i‖₂ — and treat the resulting domain-wise neuron rankings, not expert-level routing statistics, as the signature of specialization. Because RAMP mixes dispatch (which tokens reach the expert) with within-expert activation order, the paper can show that domain selection inside experts exceeds what routing alone can produce, reconciling both sides of the expert-specialization debate. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Static analysis: six open MoE models (Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, GLM-4.7-Flash, Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat, OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct) are profiled with 1152 calibration documents across nine buckets (chat/code/math/medical/Chinese × generation/MCQ), split 64/64 into discovery/validation. Top r% neuron sets (r ∈ {1, 3.125, 6.25, 12.5}%) per domain per layer are compared via same- vs cross-domain overlap, concentration (top-10% expert coverage), count-preserving overlap baselines, domain-enrichment ratios F with BH-adjusted hypergeometric tests, and Spearman correlation between discovery-side enrichment and validation-side dispatch preference. Controls include a routing-only overlap bound, a dispatch-count-normalized importance variant, a token-type-restricted analysis (6–11 shared token types), and an unweighted (no routing-magnitude) score. (2) Training dynamics: neuron vs. expert importance rank correlations between adjacent checkpoints across the OLMoE trajectory (34 pre-training + post-training checkpoints) and an OpenMoE-pretrain/Instella-posttrain combination — 7,458 domain-layer-pair cells — plus a decomposition of importance change into within-expert vs. between-expert components and a near-stable-routing transition filter (≤5% load shift). (3) Pruning (RAMPr): layer-wise selection of the top k_l = r·E·N_l routed neurons by either summed (RAMPr-L) or per-domain-normalized max (RAMPr-D) importance, removing gate/up rows and down columns; compared against Fisher-magnitude neuron pruning (calibrated on GSM8K or MBPP) and REAP whole-expert pruning on 13 knowledge/generation benchmarks. Design decisions worth noting: a single shared neuron set across domains (justified by the overlap analysis), layer-wise rather than per-expert quotas (justified by uneven domain concentration), and no recovery fine-tuning (stated as retraining-free, not ablated against fine-tuning). Key Results: At 6.25% selection, same-domain neuron-set overlap is 57.77–74.33% versus 15.23–23.68% cross-domain (random expectation = selection rate); at 1% it is 50.79–68.07% vs. 8.47–12.64%. Top-10% of experts hold 53.27–83.70% of a domain's selected neurons at 1% selection; observed overlap exceeds the count-preserving baseline by 22.39–40.11 pp at 6.25%. Enriched experts (13.39–23.26% of experts) carry 66.40–83.40% of domain-exclusive neurons, and enrichment correlates with validation routing preference at median Spearman ρ of 0.3682–0.6668 across models (Table 1). Pre-training neuron-rank correlations between adjacent checkpoints are 0.9393 (OLMoE) / 0.8418 (OpenMoE) versus expert-level 0.9898 / 0.9164; over full pre-training, first-to-last neuron correlation drops to 0.337 (OLMoE); post-training correlations are 0.997–0.998 at both levels, with the largest post-training change at Base-to-SFT. Pruning: at 75% retention RAMPr preserves 89.91–98.20% of full performance (per Table 2); RAMPr-D beats REAP by 2.91 points on GLM-4.7's 11-task macro-average (71.90 vs 68.99) but REAP wins on Qwen3 at 50% (76.74 vs 52.66/40.18). Both RAMPr variants beat both Fisher baselines in every model at 50% (e.g., Qwen3: 52.66 L / 40.18 D vs 29.25–29.37 Fisher). At 50% retention, resident GPU memory drops 36–43% and batched prefill throughput rises 17–39% (geometric mean 1.27×); decode speedup is 0.94–1.10× — effectively nil. REAP checkpoints exist for only two of the six models. Baselines are recent (REAP is ICLR 2026) but the Fisher baseline performs catastrophically (29–58 macro-average vs base scores of 45.92–85.20), so its comparison value is limited. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (neuron-level domain specialization spanning mixed experts; neuron reorganization during pre-training despite stable expert aggregates) + NEW METHOD (RAMP importance score and RAMPr cross-expert neuron pruning). The core measurement is a competent extension of known magnitude-importance pruning scores with a routing-weight factor; the genuinely novel part is the systematic demonstration that domain specialization is real but lives inside experts, plus the training-dynamics dissociation between neuron and expert stability. The pruning method is a straightforward application of the analysis rather than an algorithmic advance. Rigor & Reproducibility: Unusually strong control suite for an interpretability paper: count-preserving overlap baselines, a routing-only upper bound on cross-domain overlap (observed overlap is 20.39–74.95% of the bound, so selection is not routing-determined), per-dispatch normalization, shared-token analysis, unweighted-score control, document bootstrap with standard errors for the routing-association estimates, matched random-removal baselines, and calibration-size ablations for pruning. The causal ablation (Appendix A.14–A.15) elevates the correlation claims to necessity claims. However: benchmark scores are reported without seeds, error bars, or significance tests; the Fisher baseline's near-collapse makes the pruning comparison partly unfavored-foe; REAP is only compared on models where checkpoints exist; the calibration pool contains the evaluation datasets themselves (GSM8K, MATH, MetaMathQA, Magicoder sources feed calibration, and GSM8K/MATH-500/HumanEval/MBPP are evaluation tasks), so pruning is calibrated on the domains it is evaluated on — a Goodhart risk the paper does not address; and no fine-tuning-after-pruning comparison. A GitHub link is referenced (§ marker) but no URL appears in the provided text; no weights or pruned checkpoints are stated as released. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (measurement studies plus pruning experiments actually run). Practical: Yes — all profiling and pruning run on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU in BF16 with FP32 statistics accumulation. Efficient: At 50% retention, memory falls to ~60.68% of original and prefill speeds up 1.27× on average, but decode throughput is unchanged (~1.01×), so the benefit is memory/prefill-bound, and the pruned model's speedup lags the 50% parameter reduction because routing and shared experts are preserved. Effective: Evidence supports capability retention (91–98% at 75% retention) but on benchmarks overlapping the calibration domains; real out-of-domain generalization of the pruned models is untested. Scalable: Tested on 1B–35B-total-parameter MoEs (A3B active); behavior at much larger expert counts (e.g., 256-expert models are included) is covered, but 100× scale and proprietary MoEs are untested and only implied. Deliverable: a method plus referenced code repository; no released pruned model checkpoints mentioned. Strengths: (1) The neuron-level reframing genuinely dissolves a standing disagreement — the paper shows domain-enriched neurons concentrate in a few experts and that this enrichment predicts routing preferences, while mixed-expert composition explains why expert-level profiles look non-specialized; both prior camps' observations are accommodated. (2) The control experiments are unusually thorough for interpretability work: the routing-only bound, count-preserving baselines, and shared-token analysis each rule out a specific null explanation, and the ablation study converts correlational rankings into a causal claim. (3) The training-dynamics dissociation (neuron reorganization during pre-training with near-stable expert aggregates, 209/240 OLMoE transitions with <5% routing shift yet neuron ρ<0.90) is a new, non-obvious empirical finding with implications for anyone interpreting MoE checkpoints. (4) The pruning result — cross-expert neuron retention beating both whole-expert (REAP) and expert-local gradient (Fisher) pruning on multi-domain retention — is a practical validation that the analysis captures something real. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly label the overlap/spatial/enrichment results as correlational and add the ablation study to close that gap (Appendix A.14). They acknowledge that enrichment could follow from dispatch frequency and address it with per-dispatch normalization, and they candidly dissect the Qwen1.5 PubMedQA anomaly (a label-preference shift, not medical ability) rather than hiding it. They note checkpoint-spacing differences across the training-dynamics families and that the two trajectories are not matched. No dedicated limitations section exists in the main text, and the Impact Statement is generic; the calibration-evaluation overlap and the negligible decode speedup are not confronted. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Calibration–evaluation contamination: pruning importance is estimated from data drawn from the same datasets used as benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH/MetaMathQA, Magicoder for code), so retention numbers may overstate out-of-domain robustness; no held-out-domain pruning experiment is reported. (2) The Fisher baseline is calibrated only on GSM8K or MBPP and collapses to 26.89–58.26 macro-average — a weak or misconfigured comparator; no neuron-level baseline of comparable recency (e.g., HEAPr, TENP, both cited by the authors) is actually run. (3) REAP, the strongest baseline, is compared head-to-head on only two models, and it wins one of them (Qwen3 at 50%), which the text downplays. (4) Decode throughput — the metric that matters most for autoregressive serving — is unchanged, so the practical win is narrower than the abstract implies. (5) The abstract's claimed enrichment–routing correlation range (0.42–0.71) does not match Table 1's 0.3682–0.6668; a small but checkable inconsistency. (6) No recovery fine-tuning is attempted, leaving the 50%-retention degradation (61–88%) untested against a trivially stronger retrained baseline. (7) No seed variance or significance testing on benchmark scores despite single-run evaluations. Bottom Line: For researchers in MoE interpretability and compression this is one of the more convincing recent accounts of where specialization actually lives, with controls that most peers lack, but practitioners seeking immediate serving speedups should note the decode-side inaction and calibration-eval overlap and treat the pruning gains as promising rather than settled.

Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents

F Copty, N Haiby, M Braitmaiere, J Korsunsky · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Intent-Aware Security, a framework that represents a deployed agent's trusted purpose as a structured Intent Profile and shows that conditioning four security mechanisms (pre-execution detection, post-execution detection, input alignment, and system-prompt hardening) on this profile substantially improves detection of out-of-scope, abusive, and malicious agent interactions. - Why it's important: Existing agent defenses classify interactions by attack patterns or permissions, missing the case where a request is attack-free and technically authorized but inconsistent with what a specific agent was deployed to do — a gap that grows as agents gain enterprise data access and autonomy. - How it does it: The core move is extracting an agent-specific Intent Profile (mission, permitted workflows, tool constraints, data boundaries, prohibited behaviors) from organizational, role, and developer intent with a fixed precedence order, then feeding that profile as the security reference into every protection point instead of relying on the raw interaction or system prompt. - The good: The post-execution result on external, independently-labeled AgentDojo trajectories (0.949 AUROC for profile-based detection vs. 0.909 for LlamaFirewall's AlignmentCheck over >10,000 executed trajectories with environment-derived ground truth) provides out-of-pipeline evidence that the profile improves drift detection, not just classification of the authors' own synthetic benchmark. - The missing: The headline Out-of-Scope/Abusive results rest entirely on a synthetic, LLM-realized and LLM-validated benchmark where both profile extraction and detection use frontier LLMs; no real enterprise policy corpora, no white-box or open-weights replication, and the hardening/alignment experiment measures simulated rather than executed agent behavior. - Read it or not: Worth reading for security researchers and agent-platform builders working on guardrails, policy extraction, or deployment-time enforcement — it reframes agent security around a persistent intent reference and reports a credible external-benchmark result; skippable if you only care about attack-generation or training-time injection defenses.

Rigor (70) earns credit for agent-level cluster bootstrap CIs, the raw-context ablation cleanly isolating the value of structuring, and the external AgentDojo validation, but loses ground to judge-correlation risk (MAI judge + MAI extraction), synthetic-only Out-of-Scope/Abusive evidence, and closed-weights models with no artifact release (Impact 45). Non-Obviousness (62) is moderate — 'structured trusted context beats raw context' is intuitive once stated. Completeness (72) is strong due to a direct, non-minimizing limitations section; Resilience (65) is capped by the untested adversarial pressure on the profile itself and the unexamined precision asymmetry. Weighted composite: 0.20*68 + 0.25*70 + 0.15*62 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*45 = 65.

Problem & Motivation: Enterprises deploying LLM agents currently rely on defenses that detect prompt injection, harmful outputs, or suspicious behavior, plus permission systems that gate tool use. Both miss a distinct failure mode: a request can contain no attack signature and require only granted capabilities yet conflict with the agent's specific purpose — e.g., a travel-planning agent being handed a prompt-injection payload it was never meant to analyze, or a user repurposing an HR agent's authorized tools for an unauthorized workflow. The authors argue the security interpretation of an interaction depends on the receiving agent, and no existing benchmark or protection conditions on a persistent, agent-specific representation of intended purpose. The stake is enterprise agent governance at scale, where limited human oversight means scope violations and agent repurposing go undetected by attack-pattern classifiers. Key Idea: Treat the agent's trusted intent (organizational ≻ role ≻ developer precedence) as a first-class security object: distill heterogeneous policy sources into a structured five-part Intent Profile, then use that profile — not the interaction content, the system prompt, or the current user request — as the reference against which every protection decision is made. The formal distinction between attempted drift (a non-benign request) and completed Intent Drift (observable behavior violating the profile, C(a_t, h_t, P) = 0) lets the same object serve both request classification and trajectory monitoring. Methodology: The paper formalizes an execution τ = (u, h₀, a₁, ..., a_T) and a consistency predicate C(a_t, h_t, P) ∈ {0,1}; intent preservation requires C = 1 for all steps. Request-level operationalization uses an ordered decision rule over S (scope consistency), A (attack objective), and D (deliberate repurposing) to assign four labels: Benign, Out-of-Scope, Abusive, Malicious. The benchmark is built by a two-stage pipeline: deterministic construction fixes agent (from a domain/pattern/purpose/workflow/capability grid, 35 agents), action, target label, difficulty, attack family, and delivery mode before any generation; then a sample-realization LLM (GPT-5.4) produces the policies, agent configurations, and interactions, with labels never assigned by the generator. Validation runs deterministic checks plus a distinct judge LLM (MAI-Thinking-1) scoring five criteria at ≥4/5, run twice with the lower score kept; 887 of 1,000 candidates survived (88.7% acceptance). Four protections are evaluated: (I) pre-execution four-class classification (DeepSeek-V4-Pro detector) against input-only, PIGuard, and raw-context baselines; (II) post-execution binary drift detection on 10,536 executed AgentDojo v1.2.2 trajectories (GPT-4o agent) where ground truth comes from environment state — 2,480 successful attacks vs. 7,959 failed attacks plus 97 benign runs — against trajectory-only, agent-configuration, and modified AlignmentCheck monitors; (III) input alignment vs. DataFilter and system-prompt hardening vs. PPA and StruQ-style format hardening, scored by a simulate-then-evaluate protocol where success requires full refusal for non-benign classes and full achievement for Benign. Design decisions generally well-justified: label-before-realization defeats label leakage; a non-Microsoft-family classifier model rules out same-family effects in Exp. I; agent-level paired cluster bootstrap gives CIs. Weaker justification: organizational/role intent as unstructured text summaries is admittedly an abstraction, and the Exp. III LLM evaluator is a single model with a 95%-agreement manual spot check. Key Results: (1) Pre-execution four-class classification on the 887-sample benchmark: Intent Profile-based detection reaches 79% macro-F1 vs. 45% for a raw-context LLM (same base model, same inputs unstructured) and 43% input-only; Out-of-Scope F1 jumps from 8% to 76% (a 68-point gain); binary Malicious F1 is 72% vs. 50% raw-context and 36.8% for PIGuard. The 34-point macro-F1 gain has a 95% cluster-bootstrap CI of [29.5, 39.0] pp. (2) Post-execution on AgentDojo: profile-based monitor achieves 0.949 AUROC vs. 0.909 AlignmentCheck, 0.897 agent-configuration, 0.843 trajectory-only; at the 0.5 threshold AlignmentCheck has higher precision (95.9% vs. 75.9%) and F1 (93.5% vs. 83.8%) while the profile-based monitor has higher recall (93.3%); the profile curve dominates at low false-positive rates. (3) Input alignment: 85% macro protection success vs. 78% DataFilter and 69% unprotected baseline, with Out-of-Scope 85% vs. 67% and Benign slightly below the unprotected baseline (91% vs. 97%); hardening gives 83% macro vs. 81% PPA and 80% StruQ-style — a small margin with a 3-point Benign over-refusal cost. Baselines (PIGuard, DataFilter, AlignmentCheck, PPA, StruQ) are recent and reasonably strong; the strongest comparison is arguably the raw-context LLM ablation, which cleanly isolates the value of structuring the context. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (intent preservation/drift as agent-specific security properties with a precedence-ordered profile) + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the 887-sample, four-class, label-before-realization Intent-Aware benchmark) + NEW METHOD (four profile-conditioned protection mechanisms). The genuinely novel element is conditioning protection on a persistent, structured, agent-specific intent reference rather than the interaction, system prompt, or current task; the individual mechanisms are standard guardrail patterns (LLM classifier, input sanitizer, prompt rewriting) whose novelty is the reference object, and profile extraction is prompted LLM summarization rather than a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are effectively built in — the raw-context vs. profile-based comparison isolates the contribution of structuring the same information, and trajectory-only vs. agent-configuration vs. profile conditions do the same for Exp. II. Statistical rigor is above average for this area: agent-level paired cluster bootstrap with reported 95% CIs in Exp. I, threshold-independent AUROC as the primary Exp. II metric, and a 98%-accurate manual audit of 100 benchmark labels plus 95% evaluator agreement in Exp. III. Methodological concerns: (a) the primary Out-of-Scope/Abusive results are on the authors' own synthetic benchmark, generated and judged by LLMs — the judge model family (MAI) and profile extraction model (MAI-Thinking-1) are both Microsoft, though the classifier is not; (b) Exp. III measures simulated responses, not executed agents; (c) the AgentDojo evaluation covers only four agents, one agent model (GPT-4o), indirect injections only, and only 97 benign runs, so benign-vs-attack discrimination is under-sampled there; (d) Exp. II is binary, so the profile's four-class advantage is untested on executed trajectories; (e) all experiments use closed-weights models and no code, data, or benchmark release is mentioned — reproducibility is limited to the described procedure. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — the mechanisms are production-shaped guardrails but evaluated in simulation). Practical: Yes — all mechanisms are LLM-prompting pipelines runnable via API on commercially available hardware, no white-box model access required (explicitly contrasted with activation-based detectors). Efficient: The authors argue the once-per-agent profile extraction amortizes the expensive step and that runtime detection is a narrower task suited to a smaller model, but the accuracy–cost trade-off is hypothesized, not measured, and every reported condition runs frontier-class LLMs on each request/trajectory. Effective: Evidence supports improved classification and detection, but Exp. III's protection effect is measured on simulated agent behavior with an LLM evaluator — real-world effectiveness against live adversaries is untested. Scalable: 35 agents and one external benchmark suite; behavior at hundreds of agents, real heterogeneous policy corpora, or adversarial pressure on the extraction pipeline is only claimed, not tested. Deliverable status: paper only — no released library, benchmark download, trained model, or tool is stated. Strengths: - The raw-context vs. profile-based ablation is the paper's most convincing experiment: identical base model, identical underlying information, only the representation differs, yielding +34 pp macro-F1 with a tight bootstrap CI — this cleanly supports the central claim that structuring intent, not merely providing context, drives the gain. - Independent validation on AgentDojo with environment-derived ground truth, an externally-generated benchmark, and a modified open-source baseline (AlignmentCheck) guards against the benchmark self-confirmation that plagues most LLM-generated-security-dataset papers. - The label-before-realization benchmark methodology (fix agent/action/label/difficulty deterministically, then have an LLM realize it, judge it with a different model, reject rather than relabel) is a sound and reusable construction pattern for intent-dependent ground truth. - Careful conceptual hygiene: separating attempted drift from completed drift, request classification from trajectory monitoring, and detector accuracy from protection effectiveness are distinctions most agent-security papers blur. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly acknowledge: organizational/role intent is synthetic text summaries rather than production policy corpora; benchmark samples are LLM-realized and LLM-validated (mitigated by label fixing, judge/generator separation, and 98% manual audit); Exp. III uses simulated behavior and an LLM evaluator; AgentDojo covers only four agents, GPT-4o, 97 benign runs, and indirect injection only, so Out-of-Scope, Abusive, and user-side attacks are evaluated solely on their synthetic benchmark; the smaller-model hypothesis for runtime detection is unquantified future work; and closed-weights models limit exact reproducibility. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Adversarial pressure on the Intent Profile itself: the paper assumes trusted intent sources are uncompromised and the profile is held fixed, but never tests an adversary who probes or exfiltrates the profile (e.g., via indirect injection leaking its constraints) to craft boundary-respecting-but-malicious requests, or tests extraction robustness to incomplete/contradictory real policies — the O ≻ R ≻ D precedence is asserted, never exercised with genuinely conflicting sources. - Potential judge-correlation in the primary benchmark: the realization judge and Exp. III profile extraction/hardening both use MAI-Thinking-1, and all benchmark labels reflect a judge LLM's notion of scope/abuse; a systematic judge bias aligned with the profile representation would inflate Out-of-Scope/Abusive gains, and no inter-judge or human-labeled calibration beyond the 100-sample spot check is reported. - Precision asymmetry unaddressed: at the 0.5 threshold the profile-based monitor's precision (75.9%) trails AlignmentCheck's (95.9%) by 20 points; for a deployment guardrail, false-alarm rate on benign enterprise traffic may dominate total cost, and the paper does not analyze this operating point or report benign-only false-positive rates. - No baseline combining profile with an attack detector: the framing claims complementarity with attack-focused defenses, but no experiment stacks profile-based detection with PIGuard or an injection detector to test whether gains add rather than overlap. - Dogs not barking: no release of the benchmark, extraction prompts, or detector prompts despite reproducibility being a stated concern, and no latency/cost measurements for any protection despite a deployment-cost discussion. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agent guardrails or enterprise agent-governance policy should read this for its well-instrumented core finding — that structuring trusted deployment context into an explicit per-agent profile beats raw context by large margins on intent-dependent security decisions, validated on an external benchmark — while treating the synthetic-benchmark Out-of-Scope/Abusive numbers and the unreleased artifacts with appropriate caution; there is currently no stronger alternative covering the same formulation, but the paper's practical recipe is not yet reproducible from its text alone.

VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context (19 ▲ )

Yancheng Long, Xuanyu Zheng, Wei Chen, Luoyuan Zhang, Haoyang Xu, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 18 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VideoNexus, a training-free video-agent framework in which a text-only planner delegates all video/audio perception to short-lived sub-agents that return compact, temporally grounded 'Findings' plus small evidence cards, so the reasoning context never carries the video stream. - Why it's important: Hour-scale videos produce hundreds of thousands of visual tokens, and agentic systems that return frames or per-frame descriptions to the planner re-read that media at every reasoning step, inflating both cost and context burden; bounding what each observation adds to the context directly attacks this cost-accuracy trade-off. - How it does it: The planner controls where to look, what to ask, and sampling density; each perception call runs in an independent, discarded context on native audio-video (addressed by file offsets on the source timeline) and returns a bounded structured report (status, conclusion, timestamped evidence), decoupling report size from the amount of media perceived (measured log-log slope 0.00 for Overview, 0.18 for Inspect). - The good: On full LVBench (1,549 questions) with a shared Gemini 3.8 Flash backbone, it reaches 88.6% at $0.140/question versus 87.5% at $0.319 for Gemini's built-in agentic mode and 85.0% for static ingestion, with a per-call measurement study over 5,504 perception calls showing reports grow sub-linearly with perceived media while a VideoSeek re-run returns 28-63 tokens per frame read. - The missing: The headline claims rest on non-significant paired differences — the core decoupling ablation (86.5%→89.0%, p=0.23) and the win over Gemini Agentic (+1.1, p=0.10) — ablations were run on a 200-question subset used for development, and the Video-GAIA gain (+8.5) was measured on the same questions used to develop the tools, with acknowledged baseline misalignments. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building video or multi-agent systems where tool outputs accumulate in the reasoning context — the observation-size measurements and honest cost accounting are broadly transferable — but skippable if you only want a statistically airtight accuracy win.

Problem & Motivation: Long-video question answering requires locating evidence, resolving visual details, and integrating observations, but static ingestion forces all three into one multimodal context (a 1-hour video at 1 fps yields hundreds of thousands of tokens), and existing video agents that delegate perception still leak observation size into the planner's context: coupled agents append retrieved media to the reasoning history, and per-frame-description agents like VideoSeek return roughly one description per frame read (measured at 28 returned tokens per frame for VideoSeek's overview, 63 for its skim), so increasing sampling density increases what the planner must carry forward. The authors target practitioners of agentic video understanding who need dense, on-demand inspection without the context growth that dense sampling normally causes. Key Idea: Treat every perception call as a bounded evidence-gathering task whose output size is decoupled from the media it consumed: the planner chooses interval, frame rate, and a neutral local task; an ephemeral sub-agent reads native audio-video in its own context; and the planner receives only a compact Finding anchored to absolute source timestamps (plus at most a 6-frame evidence card). The critical enabling trick is native timeline addressing — passing file offsets rather than pre-cut clips so all Findings, transcripts, and Overview candidates share one clock (validated by a 12-response probe: 12/12 absolute times with offsets, 6/6 relative times with cropped clips) — combined with report schemas (capped candidate lists, task-specific conclusions) that make output size grow sub-linearly with perceived media. Methodology: The system is a training-free harness on a stock agent runtime (headless Claude Code session) with Model Context Protocol tools; no model weights are touched. Four tools: Transcribe (cached ASR, question-independent), Overview (query-conditioned global scan, ≤1 fps, ≤1,024 frames, full audio, returns ≤8 candidate intervals with relevance and uncertainty notes; a locator, forbidden from answering), Inspect (interval [s,e] at planner-chosen fps with an open-ended local task, returns a JSON Finding with status ∈ {ok, absent, uncertain, failed}, one-sentence conclusion, and evidence items {claim, [t0,t1], modality} validated by the harness for temporal containment), plus optional crops and web tools. Each perception call is an independent model invocation whose context is discarded. Design decisions with varying justification: (1) planner tasks are prompted to be 'neutral' but not enforced — 8.8% of Inspect tasks name answer options verbatim, a known leak; (2) the ≤6-frame evidence card is justified by an ablation (+5.0 points for Gemini 3.0 Flash, +1.0 for 3.8, the latter with only aggregate counts and no significance test); (3) cumulative frame limits (2,048) are enforced in the direct-media path but bypassed in the delegated path, which the authors show is moot empirically (max observed 1,624). The formal framing (equations for coupled vs. decoupled context growth) is descriptive, not a theorem. Key Results: On full LVBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash: VideoNexus 88.6%, Static ingestion 85.0% (+3.6, McNemar p=5×10⁻⁷), Gemini Agentic 87.5% (+1.1, p=0.10, not significant) at 44% of its measured cost ($0.140 vs $0.319/question), VideoSeek re-run 81.4% (+7.2, p=5×10⁻¹⁶, but with an acknowledged audio-access asymmetry), blind control 40.5% (revealing a substantial LVBench text prior). It reads 621 frames/question vs 2,035 (Static) and an estimated 464 (Agentic, derived from token accounting, not directly measured). Paired dev-200 ablation: decoupling cuts planner input 32% (18.1M→12.3M tokens) and raises accuracy 86.5%→89.0% (not significant, p=0.23); capping perception at VideoSeek's frame budget drops accuracy 90.0%→87.0% (p=0.11) while costing slightly more due to extra planner turns — evidence of a real density-interaction trade-off. Video-GAIA with Kimi K3: 60.2% vs 51.7% for the official ReAct agent (+8.5), LLM-judged once, with acknowledged development overlap. Transfer: +6.4 (Gemini 3.0 Flash, full LVBench), +6.5 (Kimi K3, dev-200 subset); margins shrink as the static baseline strengthens. Per-call measurement across 5,504 calls: Overview returns 740 tokens for 141k perceived (191× reduction, slope 0.00); Inspect returns 401 tokens for ~62 frames, growing 1.67× when frames grow 16.8× (slope 0.18). Baselines are current and same-backbone; the strongest comparator (Gemini Agentic) is a closed server-side mode, so its cost gap cannot be attributed. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new elements are the Finding protocol with harness-validated temporal grounding on a shared absolute timeline, and — most valuable — the direct measurement of observation-size scaling (log-log slopes of returned vs. perceived tokens) across competing agent designs, which no prior work reports in this form. Delegated perception, planner-directed tool use, and evidence cards are each established ideas (the authors themselves note the design parallels Anthropic's multi-agent research system, VideoSeek, AVP, and LAVE); the contribution is a careful, measured assembly of them with an interface contract that bounds context growth. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strengths: paired McNemar tests with discordant-pair counts on the main comparisons, a blind control, cold-start cost accounting with explicit cache repricing, a pricing-sensitivity analysis for the VideoSeek baseline, per-call instrumentation over the full run, and an unusually candid appendix (duplicate-run variability: 7 of 55 re-answered questions changed answers; a repeated dev configuration moved by 3 questions). Weaknesses: the headline decoupling ablation and the Agentic comparison are not statistically significant, yet the abstract and conclusion present them as headline findings; all ablations are on a 200-question development subset (acknowledged as 'not held-out results'); the Gemini 3.8 card ablation has aggregate counts only; the Video-GAIA comparison has four misaligned settings including a bounding-box bug in the authors' favor and a single-draw LLM judge; LLM-judged scoring introduces its own noise; the VideoSeek comparison confounds audio access, transport pricing, and report format (partially dissected in slices, not causally separated). No code, data, or artifact release URL is stated in the provided text. Ablations exist and are informative (tool granularity is worth 5.5 points; audio+ASR 2.5; several prompted policies hurt by 3-5 points and are honestly reported as null results). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built system evaluated by benchmark runs, not deployed in production). Practical: Yes — runs entirely on commercial APIs (Gemini, Kimi) via MCP with no training or weight access, though it depends on a specific vendor runtime (Claude Code) and provider token-pricing quirks. Efficient: Cheaper than both agentic alternatives measured ($0.140 vs $0.188-$0.319/question) and 2.6× cheaper than Static per its accounting, but per-question latency is not matched-compared (only 22 of 160 median seconds are API time; the rest is local decode/upload). Effective: It solves the LVBench-style long-video QA problem on this evidence, including overcoming a 40.5% text prior, but the two tightest head-to-head claims (vs. Gemini Agentic, and decoupling itself) are within noise. Scalable: Not tested beyond hour-scale benchmark videos; 10× longer media would stress the 1,024-frame Overview budget and the single-call global scan, and the paper only claims, not measures, scaling behavior. Deliverable: a described harness and protocol; no released artifact is mentioned. Strengths: - The observation-size measurement study (Figure 4, Table 7) is the paper's most original and reusable piece: it converts a vague intuition ('context bloat') into measured slopes (0.00 for Overview, 0.18 for Inspect vs ~1.0 for per-frame-description baselines) over all calls of a full benchmark run. - Native timeline addressing by file offset, with a small probe validating that models report absolute times only when given offsets, is a simple, well-verified design choice that makes multi-call evidence composable. - Exceptional disclosure quality: negative ablations, dev-set contamination, baseline bugs in both directions, duplicate-run variance, and the LVBench text prior are all surfaced by the authors rather than hidden — this is above the norm for systems papers, vendor-adjacent or otherwise. - The density ablation (4.6) is a genuine finding: cutting perception to a frugal budget loses 3 points while increasing cost, demonstrating that sparse perception forces more planner interaction rather than saving money. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: no wall-clock comparison; the LVBench text prior (40.5% blind); provider-specific dollar costs and the image-tier pricing confound for VideoSeek; the audio-access asymmetry in their favor with no-speech slices reported (margin 3.9 vs 8.7 points); ablations on non-held-out dev questions; aggregate-only counts for one card ablation; duplicate-run answer variability; perception errors persisting (overconfident 'absent' findings, inconsistent counts); API version dependence; static ingestion remaining competitive on short clips and global-order questions. They also flag the Video-GAIA development overlap and misaligned settings, and that the Gemini 3.0 rows do not isolate a backbone swap. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central scientific claim — that decoupling perception improves accuracy, not just cost — is supported only by a non-significant paired difference (p=0.23, 8 corrected vs 3 regressed); the framing in the abstract ('higher accuracy') outruns the evidence. - The +1.1 win over Gemini Agentic, the cost-effectiveness headline, is also not significant (p=0.10), and Agentic's frame count is estimated from token accounting rather than observed, so the '44% of the cost' comparison inherits an unverified quantity. - Neutral-task prompting is not enforced (8.8% of Inspect tasks leak options), and the measured effect of this leak is not quantified; the validation harness checks structure and time ranges but cannot check whether Findings echo the planner's hypothesis. - All dollar figures are single-vendor list prices with a self-acknowledged pricing confound; the accuracy-neutral reprice of VideoSeek to the cheapest image tier was never actually run. - The coverage analysis (Table 4) models uniform sampling, not the agents' realized adaptive trajectories, so its connection to VideoNexus's accuracy lead is correlational by the authors' own admission. - Single-run, single-judge evaluation on both benchmarks with demonstrated run-to-run answer variability (7/55 flips) means differences of 1-3 points — where several headline claims live — cannot be distinguished from noise; no multi-seed or repeat-run error bars are provided. - No evaluation on videos beyond ~2 hours or on streaming settings, though the framework's premise is long-video scalability. Bottom Line: A practitioner building long-video or evidence-heavy agents should read this for the observation-size measurements, the timeline-addressing trick, and a model of how to report agent evaluation honestly, but should treat the accuracy-win claims as provisional — the cost and context-growth case is solid, the accuracy case is not yet statistically established, and no stronger alternative measures the same quantity.

SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models (13 ▲ )

Jiachun Jin, Zetong Zhou, Haonan Wang, Zhijie Deng · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 17 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SALA, a latent action model that aligns human and robot latent actions through language supervision from atomic-action descriptions of unpaired videos, enabling robot policies to be trained on action-free human video along two scaling axes (general human-video pre-training and task-specific human-demo post-training). - Why it's important: Teleoperated robot demonstrations are expensive and hard to scale, while egocentric human video is cheap and abundant; a mechanism that converts human video into control-relevant supervision attacks the core data bottleneck of vision-language-action (VLA) models. - How it does it: The key trick is turning CLIP/Qwen text-embedding similarities between atomic-action descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips into soft neighborhood targets (a cross-entropy over softmax similarity distributions) that pull human latent actions toward robot latents anchored by robot action reconstruction, with a stop-gradient keeping robot latents fixed as control anchors and SoftVQ (soft, distributional quantization) enabling graded alignment. - The good: The ablations directly validate the mechanism: removing the alignment loss drops RoboTwin 2.0 average success from 64.4% to 36.8% in the randomized setting, and alignment shifts the variance explained by action vs. scene in the latent space from 0.41/0.14 to 0.67/0.04. - The missing: The pre-training scaling claim rests on a proxy metric (validation action L1 error decreasing by only ~2.2–4.1% relative, from roughly 17.1×10⁻³ to 16.4×10⁻³ over 2,678 hours), not on task success rates, and there are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests; real-robot evaluation is 20 trials per task on only 4 tasks, all on the authors' own robot. - Read it or not: Worth reading for robotics/embodied-AI researchers working on human-video pre-training or cross-embodiment transfer, since the language-relational alignment idea and the ablation methodology are directly reusable; practitioners outside robot learning can skip it.
