Problem & Motivation: Embodied foundation models (VLAs) need diverse interaction data, but teleoperated robot data is costly to collect. Egocentric human videos are a cheap, scalable alternative, but using them requires bridging the human-to-robot embodiment gap: differing kinematics, control mechanisms, and scenes. Latent action models (LAMs) infer pseudo-actions from video transitions, but latents trained purely by clip reconstruction cluster by visual appearance (scene) rather than by action semantics, so semantically similar human and robot behaviors land far apart in latent space and human-video supervision fails to transfer. The open problem is aligning latent actions across embodiments without paired human-robot data. Key Idea: Use language as relational supervision between unpaired videos: a human clip rarely has an exact robot counterpart, but its atomic-action description (e.g., "grasp the cup") is graded-similar to several robot clip descriptions. Encode these similarities as soft neighborhood distributions over robot clips in a batch (P = softmax of language similarities) and supervise the latent-space neighborhood (Q = softmax of latent cosine similarities) with cross-entropy — anchoring on robot latents grounded by action reconstruction (stop-gradient on robot side), and using SoftVQ rather than hard VQ so tokens vary smoothly with the pre-quantization latents and can express graded alignment. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Tokenizer training: an inverse-dynamics encoder maps two endpoint observations into 8 latent tokens, quantized by SoftVQ (256 codes) over frozen DINOv2 features; losses are visual reconstruction on human and robot clips (L_Hvis + L_Rvis)/2, a robot-only action-decoder Huber loss L_act reconstructing action chunks from latents plus initial state (grounding robot latents in control), and the language-alignment loss L_align = E[CE(P_i, Q_i)] with temperature-scaled softmaxes and stop-gradient through robot latents; total L_tok weights these by λ_act and λ_align (e.g., 5 and 0.005 in the real world). (2) Policy training: a frozen tokenizer labels both human and robot clips with token distributions y; a π0-style policy (Qwen3-VL-4B VLM plus a 0.6B flow-matching action expert with learnable latent queries) predicts ŷ supervised by KL divergence L_LA for both data types, with an additional flow-matching loss L_FM on robot data only. (3) Staged recipe: pre-training on human video with L_LA alone, mid-training on robot teleoperation with L_FM + λL_LA, optional post-training on task-specific teleoperated plus human demonstrations. Critical design decisions: the stop-gradient (well-justified by ablation — bidirectional alignment drops Clean success 80.2%→73.5%); the SoftVQ choice (well-justified — hard VQ leaves the alignment loss near its initial uniform-prediction value despite comparable reconstruction); and one-way human→robot alignment (sensible given human latents lack action grounding). Atomic-action annotations come from a scripted motion planner in simulation and a VLM (Doubao-Seed-2.0-Pro) with 15 predefined action labels in the real world. Key Results: On RoboTwin 2.0 (50 bimanual tasks, 100 rollouts/task, ARX-X5 videos as stand-in "human" data, 27,000 non-target + 2,500 target trajectories), SALA achieves 80.2% Clean / 48.6% Random / 64.4% average, beating π0.5 (58.7 avg), LingBot-VA (57.1), InternVLA-A1.5 (54.0), RotVLA (51.2), UniVLA (27.1), and OpenWAM (45.4, collapsing to 3.9% under domain randomization) — despite baselines π0.5, X-VLA, UniVLA, and RotVLA being initialized from robot-pretrained checkpoints while SALA starts from a general VLM only. On a real 63-DoF wheeled humanoid (two 22-DoF hands), over four tasks at 20 trials each, SALA reaches 72.5% average success vs. OpenWAM-α 63.75%, GR00T N1.7 41.25%, and a vanilla VLA of identical architecture without latent actions at 27.5%. Pre-training on 0/473/1,103/2,678 hours of human video monotonically reduces validation action L1 error (relative reduction of 2.21% vs. 0 h and 4.10% vs. vanilla VLA) with robot data held fixed; post-training with 10%/50%/100% of task human demonstrations raises average success from 53.75% to 60.00% to 72.50% with teleoperated demos fixed. Cross-embodiment retrieval improves from 41.3% to 78.2% same-atomic-action on RoboTwin and from 3.8% to 34.2% same-task in the real world. Baselines are recent (2025–2026) and mostly strong; the headline effect sizes in simulation are convincing, while the pre-training scaling effect is real but small in absolute terms. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with a supporting NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING on dual-axis scaling). The genuinely novel element is language-only relational supervision of cross-embodiment latent alignment from unpaired clips via soft neighborhood distributions anchored on control-grounded robot latents; prior LAM alignment work relies on paired demonstrations, recorded robot actions alongside videos, hand action labels, or contrastive action-category priors. The surrounding machinery — inverse-dynamics latents, SoftVQ, π0-style flow-matching action expert, staged pre/mid/post-training — is a competent combination of existing components. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a strength: each tokenizer component (alignment loss, stop-gradient, quantizer) is individually removed with matched policy training, and mechanistic analyses (variance decomposition, k-means clustering, retrieval metrics, alignment-loss curves for SoftVQ vs. hard VQ) support the claims rather than only end-task numbers. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; real-robot comparisons rest on 80 total trials per method (20 × 4 tasks), where the SALA-vs-OpenWAM-α gap (72.5% vs. 63.75%) is within plausible sampling noise; the pre-training scaling trend is measured only on validation L1 error, a proxy not shown to predict success; and a project website exists (https://sala-vla.github.io/) but no code, data, or model weights release is stated. Methodological concerns: the real-robot platform (Sharpa North) is the authors' own company robot, real-world atomic-action annotations are generated by a VLM with unquantified label noise, and the simulation comparison mixes baselines with and without robot-pretrained initialization in SALA's favor. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (methods trained and evaluated in simulation and on a real robot; the system is a full training recipe plus a deployed policy rather than a released tool). - Practical: The policy builds on open, commercially available components (Qwen3-VL-4B, DINOv2, SoftVQ) and ran on a commercial humanoid, so the compute and hardware are accessible in principle — though the data pipeline (VLM annotation of 983 hours of video) is nontrivial. - Efficient: The paper claims substantially lower training cost than OpenWAM-α and avoids pixel prediction (the stated LAM advantage), but gives no quantified training hours, FLOPs, or memory comparisons. - Effective: The evidence supports effectiveness on four real tasks and one simulation benchmark, with a same-architecture vanilla VLA control isolating the contribution of latent actions; effectiveness beyond these tasks and this embodiment is untested. - Scalable: Tested to 2,678 hours of human video pre-training — the largest axis of the paper — and the trend is monotonic, but the marginal gains shrink and the authors concede the trend at larger scales is open; no evidence at 10×–100× beyond that point. The work delivers a recipe and a project page, not a public software artifact; no library, CLI, dataset, or trained weights are stated as released. Strengths: - The language-relational alignment loss is a genuinely new supervision mechanism for cross-embodiment latent actions that requires no paired data, and the design (soft neighborhoods, stop-gradient anchoring) is argued and ablated rather than asserted. - The ablation and analysis suite is unusually complete for this area: component-wise tokenizer ablations tied to end-task success, latent-variance decomposition (action R² 0.41→0.67, scene R² 0.14→0.04), quantitative retrieval on held-out tasks, and a controlled same-architecture vanilla VLA baseline. - The dual-axis scaling evaluation is well-constructed: robot data is held fixed across pre-training budgets, and the post-training axis varies only the cheap human demonstrations, cleanly isolating what human video adds. - Real deployment on a 63-DoF dual-dexterous-hand humanoid with fine-grained tasks (gear assembly, flower insertion) goes beyond the typical single-gripper tabletop evaluations in this literature. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state two limitations explicitly: the tokenizer requires atomic-action descriptions for its training clips (though the policy itself consumes only video frames), and the pre-training scaling analysis covers at most 2,678 hours so whether the trend holds at larger scale remains open. They state these directly in the conclusion rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive; they do not, however, acknowledge the small sample sizes or the proxy-metric issue in the pre-training scaling claim. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical treatment anywhere: 20 trials per task is too few to separate 72.5% from 63.75% reliably, and the monotonic L1 trend over four pre-training budgets is presented without variance or seed repetition. - The pre-training scaling benefit is measured only as validation action L1 error on held-out teleoperated demonstrations — a proxy whose connection to real-task success at each budget is never shown (success is only reported at the 2,678-hour endpoint). - Real-world evaluation is confined to one embodiment (the authors' own robot), four tasks, and baselines that are post-trained open models; no comparison against other cross-embodiment LAMs (UniVLA, RotVLA) on the real robot, and no human-video baseline from the WAM family on the real platform other than OpenWAM-α. - VLM-generated atomic-action annotations in the real world introduce unquantified label noise and possible circularity: the alignment targets come from a text encoder whose biases (e.g., toward mentioned objects over motions) are not analyzed. - The simulation "human video" is actually another robot arm's videos with shared viewpoint and workspace — acknowledged implicitly but meaning the hardest part of the real human→robot gap (viewpoint, morphology, background) is only exercised in the real-world experiments where controlled comparison is weakest. - Only one codebook size, token count, and one text-encoder per setting; no sensitivity analysis for λ_align, batch composition, or the neighborhood temperature, all of which plausibly matter for a loss with a 0.001–0.005 weight. Bottom Line: A researcher working on human-video pre-training for robot manipulation should read this for the language-relational alignment mechanism and its unusually clean ablations, but should treat the scaling claims cautiously given the small margins, absent statistics, and proxy-metric evaluation — cross-embodiment LAM work is moving fast enough that a stronger consolidated comparison will likely appear soon.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

S Chung, W Du · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows that the n-gram embedding tables used in modern lookup-memory language models can be stored at 2–4 bits per value (with Lloyd–Max codebooks and per-embedding scales), saving 47–80% of table memory while retaining 97–99%+ of the validation-loss benefit, and that the saved memory can be reinvested in larger tables to beat full-precision baselines. - Why it's important: N-gram memory tables are a rapidly adopted capacity-scaling axis (DeepSeek's Engram allocates 196B parameters to them in V4.1-Flash), so table memory is now a first-order deployment cost, not a rounding error. - How it does it: Scalar quantization of trained table embeddings — each component becomes a b-bit index into a small shared codebook, multiplied by a 16-bit per-embedding scale — plus mixed-precision allocation across bigram/trigram/four-gram tables and a short post-compression fine-tune to recover lost performance. - The good: The study is systematic and externally validated: five from-scratch models across three architectures with 3 seeds and error bars, plus post-hoc compression of two large open-weight models (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) showing <1.2% perplexity change on three held-out corpora and ≤0.93% average downstream accuracy drop. - The missing: There is no measurement of actual serving cost — dequantization overhead, kernel support, or end-to-end latency/throughput — and no head-to-head comparison against alternative table-compression schemes (e.g., the factorized n-gram embeddings the paper itself cites), so 'savings' are computed on paper, not on hardware. - Read it or not: Read it if you are deploying or training models with hashed n-gram/embedding memory, where the precision-allocation guidance and the 'compress then reinvest in 4× more embeddings at 2 bits' recipe are directly actionable; skip it if you want new quantization theory — the techniques are 40+ years old.

Problem & Motivation: Lookup-based n-gram memory (Over-Tokenized Transformer, DeepSeek Engram, DSE) adds model capacity cheaply in compute but expensively in memory: tables must hold embeddings for enormous hashed key spaces (e.g., 262k–1M embeddings per table, four tables per model; 196B parameters in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash). Practitioners deploying such models face the same table-memory wall that motivates weight quantization for the backbone. Prior work reduced table size by shrinking the number of shared (hashed) embeddings, which forces unrelated n-grams to collide; the alternative axis — how many bits each stored value needs — had not been studied for this component. Key Idea: Treat n-gram embedding tables as a quantization target distinct from model weights: because tables are looked up (not matmul'd), the design space differs from standard weight quantization — a tiny shared codebook plus one 16-bit scale per embedding suffices, and precision can be allocated non-uniformly across n-gram orders. The counter-intuitive enabling insight is that most of a table's benefit survives 2–4-bit storage, so saved memory is better spent on 4× more embeddings (reducing hash collisions) than on precision. Methodology: Setup follows the Over-Tokenized Transformer: two bigram and two trigram tables; at each position, hashed bigram/trigram keys retrieve four embeddings (width d/4 each) that are concatenated and added to the token embedding. Compression represents each embedding component ŵ = s_r · c_{q} with a b-bit index q, a per-embedding 16-bit scale s_r, and a shared codebook c of ≤2^b values. Three codebook families are compared (uniform, normal-quantile, Lloyd–Max fitted per table via RMS-normalized components) and three scale rules (max-based, RMS, error-fitted by minimizing reconstruction MSE over a candidate sweep). Pipeline: (1) train models with/without 16-bit tables to establish the improvement baseline; (2) compress trained tables and measure retained improvement; (3) ablate codebooks, scales, and all 9–64 mixed-precision allocations; (4) fine-tune after compression or quantize throughout pre-training (straight-through estimator on a BF16 master copy, codebook refitted periodically); (5) reinvest savings by scaling tables to 1M embeddings at low precision; (6) post-hoc compression of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (bigram/trigram/four-gram, FP8 baseline) and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. Critical design decisions: error-fitted scales (justified — max-based scaling loses 28+ points of retained improvement at 2 bits: 58.04% vs 86.52%); per-table precision allocation (justified — 4-bit-bigram/3-bit-trigram retains 98.9–99.4% vs 95.2–95.7% for the reverse at equal cost); post-compression fine-tuning (justified with a control — fine-tune-then-compress underperforms compress-then-fine-tune at 1 bit, 44–63% vs 97–111%, showing recovery comes from low-bit adaptation, not extra training). Key Results: From-scratch models (nanochat 26M/50M, GPT-2-family 30M, Llama-family 31M/322M, trained on ClimbMix, 3 seeds): 4-bit tables save 74–75% of table memory and retain 99.3–99.6% of the validation-loss improvement; 3-bit save ~80% and retain 97.1–98.1%; 2-bit save 86–87% but retain only 85.9–91.0% (and 1-bit is destructive without adaptation, including negative improvement of −5.7% and −27.3% on the Llama models). Mixed precision 4/3 (bigram/trigram) retains 98.9–99.4% at 77–78% savings. Large models: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 4/5/4-bit and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 4/3-bit save 47–55% of table memory (relative to the models' FP8 tables) with perplexity changes within ±1.2% on WikiText-2, Penn Treebank, and C4, and average downstream accuracy changes of −0.93% (DeepSeek) and −0.27% (Qwen) on HellaSwag, ARC-Challenge, WinoGrande (most per-task bootstrap 95% CIs cross zero). Reinvestment: 1M-embedding tables at 2 bits deliver 122–126% of the original 16-bit 262k tables' improvement using 46–48% less memory (129–145% with fine-tuning). A notable negative-control finding: scale choice matters far more than codebook choice, and the optimal precision allocation differs between DeepSeek (favoring trigram/four-gram) and Qwen (favoring bigram). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. The genuinely novel content is the empirical characterization: that hashed n-gram tables tolerate extreme scalar quantization far better than one might expect, that scale fitting dominates codebook design, that optimal precision allocation is model-dependent, and that low-bit tables + 4× embeddings beat full-precision smaller tables at lower memory. The mechanisms themselves — Lloyd–Max quantization (1960/1982), per-embedding scales, straight-through fine-tuning, mixed precision — are standard techniques competently applied to a new component; no new algorithm is proposed. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: three codebook families, three scale rules, complete mixed-precision sweeps (all 9 combinations from-scratch, all 64 for DeepSeek), four training/compression orderings, and three hashing variants (Appendix C.6). Three seeds with sample standard deviations are reported for from-scratch results; large-model evaluations use paired bootstrap 95% CIs over 100k resamples. Code is released at https://github.com/dualverse-ai/lowbit-ngram. Concerns: (1) the headline 'improvement retained' metric normalizes by the tables' effect over the no-table model, which is small in absolute terms (e.g., 0.018 of 1.72 bits/byte total gap for nanochat 26M at 4 bits), so 99% retention coexists with negligible absolute loss — appropriate but easy to over-read; (2) for DeepSeek/Qwen, savings are relative to an FP8 baseline, not FP16, making the 47–55% figure less impressive than it first appears; (3) precision allocations for large models are selected on WikiText-2 validation, though transfer to PTB/C4 is checked; (4) the work originates from the authors' own autonomous research agent and is company-affiliated (DualverseAI), though the human-verified reproduction and released code mitigate this. It is a preprint; no peer review status is stated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent artifact). - Practical: Yes — from-scratch experiments run on a single RTX 5090 (10–25 min for small models, ~6.5 h for 322M), and large-model compression/evaluation uses 4× H200. - Efficient: Table memory drops 47–87% depending on bit width, but the paper never measures dequantization overhead or inference throughput, so end-to-end efficiency is unquantified. - Effective: For the stated problem (preserve table benefit at lower memory), evidence is strong on validation loss and perplexity; downstream evidence rests on only three tasks with mostly statistically insignificant deltas. - Scalable: Post-hoc compression of 100B+-parameter open-weight models is the best available scale evidence, but the reinvestment/fine-tuning recipes were tested only up to 322M parameters trained on ≤1B tokens — far from frontier pre-training scale, and the paper claims rather than demonstrates transfer of the training-time recipes. The work delivers a released code artifact; no library, trained checkpoint, or quantized model release beyond the repository is mentioned. Strengths: - The memory-reinvestment result is the paper's real intellectual contribution: showing that 1M-embedding tables at 2 bits outperform 262k tables at 16 bits (122–145% of baseline improvement at ~52% of the memory) reframes quantization from a lossy necessity into a capacity-reallocation tool. - The fine-tuning-order control (compress→fine-tune vs fine-tune→compress at matched budget) cleanly attributes recovery to adaptation to low-bit embeddings rather than extra training — a comparison many quantization papers omit. - Complete precision-allocation sweeps with an honest finding that the optimal allocation is model-specific (bigram-favoring for Qwen, longer-n-gram-favoring for DeepSeek) rather than forcing a universal rule. - Transparent disclosure of the autonomous-agent origin (Section 6) with independent human reproduction and extension. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that savings percentages describe table memory only, not total model memory, and that baselines differ (16-bit for scratch models, FP8 for DeepSeek/Qwen). They scope the same-column/random-component hashing findings as preliminary ('deserves further investigation... beyond the scope of this study'). They do not extensively discuss failure modes at 1–2 bits beyond reporting the numbers (including the negative improvements), which the appendix tables make visible — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No serving measurements: table lookups now require index-into-codebook + scale-multiply reconstruction; whether this is free, slower, or faster (smaller memory → better cache behavior) than FP16 lookup is never measured, yet it determines whether the memory savings translate to real deployments. - No comparison against alternative compression baselines the paper itself cites (TensoEngram factorization, FactorEngram, X-GRAM, simply using 4× fewer embeddings at 16 bits as a memory-matched control in the main comparison), so 'fewer bits' is never shown to dominate 'fewer embeddings' head-to-head at fixed memory in the from-scratch setting. - The 'improvement retained' metric rewards settings where the absolute table benefit is small; reporting absolute loss deltas alongside would let readers judge practical significance, especially for the 322M model where tables contribute only ~1.25% of loss. - From-scratch training budgets are tiny (≤1B targets, models ≤322M); whether 2-bit tables survive long pre-training at scale — where table utilization and collision patterns differ — is extrapolated, not shown. - The large-model downstream evaluation uses three tasks; reasoning, multilingual, and long-context behavior after table compression are untested. Bottom Line: For anyone building or serving models with hashed n-gram memory, this is the reference measurement for how hard these tables can be quantized and how to spend the savings, and it is worth reading despite standard techniques — but it is an empirical guide, not a method paper, and its deployment claims remain unverified without throughput numbers and memory-matched compression baselines.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a benchmark that directly evaluates table-level embeddings through four desiderata (partial-view consistency, multi-granularity discriminability, robustness, efficiency) and proposes a self-supervised loss called SCDM for learning compositional rules over frozen tabular foundation model states. - Why it's important: Corpus-scale operations like deduplication, retrieval, and data curation need one reusable embedding per table, but current tabular foundation models are evaluated only through row-level prediction, leaving table-level embedding quality unmeasured and potentially poor under default pooling. - How it does it: The benchmark samples controlled partial views of source tables and measures whether embedding similarity tracks partition overlap (IoU), discriminability across label granularities, robustness to perturbations, and throughput; SCDM matches the distribution of embedding similarities to the distribution of partition overlaps via a KL-divergence objective over local and global supports. - The good: Across all 15 learned-head configurations, SCDM raises the Spearman correlation between embedding similarity and partial-view overlap from 0.04 to 0.43–0.50 on synthetic data with frozen ConTextTab, and a downstream parent-table retrieval task confirms the benchmark ranking (Spearman 0.82–0.95 with D2). - The missing: The learned-composition experiment changes both the aggregation architecture and the training objective simultaneously, so it cannot separate which ingredient drives the improvement; only one backbone (ConTextTab) is tested for learned composition, and the gap to simple fingerprints persists on real data. - Read it or not: Practitioners building table retrieval, deduplication, or curation systems should read this to understand that simple hashing fingerprints beat tabular foundation model states pooled by fixed rules, and that learning a lightweight compositional head can recover most of the gap — but the finding that fingerprints win is itself the most actionable takeaway.

Problem & Motivation: Many large-scale table operations — indexing, deduplication, overlap estimation, source recovery, data curation, and table selection for tabular RAG — require a single reusable embedding vector per table that stays meaningful when only part of the table is observed. Existing evaluation of table representation methods relies on row-level prediction accuracy or supervised downstream tasks, which measures predictive quality but not whether the resulting table-level embedding is fit for corpus-scale operations. The gap: no prior benchmark directly measures whether a table-level embedding preserves overlap-sensitive similarity between partial views, discriminates across multiple equivalence relations, stays robust to benign perturbations, and is cheap to compute — all under a shared interface. Key Idea: The core insight is to decompose table-level embedding quality into two separable components: the information content of local encoder states (rows or cells), and the compositional rule (fixed pooling or learned head) that aggregates them into one vector. The benchmark evaluates the interface formed by an encoder, a compositional rule, and cosine similarity — not the encoder in isolation. This decomposition enables the key experimental move: freeze a tabular foundation model (ConTextTab), train only a lightweight head over its cell states using SCDM (a self-supervised loss that matches the distribution of embedding similarities to the distribution of partition overlaps via KL divergence over two supports: same-table partitions and the full batch), and attribute any improvement purely to the learned compositional rule. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Data preparation: 100 source tables per corpus (synthetic families with known generative factors from TabICL-style SCM, physics formulas, geometry, temporal sequences; real tables from CARTE, OpenML-CC18, OpenML-CTR23), with 10 partitions sampled per table under a shared observation budget, and four labeling schemes (Direct identity, Semantic, Semantic+Difficulty, Stat). (2) Embedding: each partition maps to a single vector, either directly (fingerprints, specialized encoders) or by composing local states with mean/max/sum/min/std pooling (TabPFN, ConTextTab) or with three learned head families (Attention, GatedAttention, GatedMLP) trained with SCDM: L = α·D_KL(T‖P_local) + (1−α)·D_KL(T‖P_global), where T is the IoU-based target distribution over partition overlaps, P_local normalizes over same-table candidates, and P_global over the full batch. (3) Evaluation: four desiderata measured by Spearman correlation between IoU and cosine similarity (D1), triplet ranking/clustering/retrieval/linear probing under four label types (D2), cosine similarity after permutation/masking/noise (D3), and tables-per-second throughput (D4). A downstream parent-table retrieval task with 100 candidate tables and 1000 queries validates the benchmark. Critical design decisions: (a) freezing the encoder and learning only the head isolates composition from representation learning — well-justified; (b) training heads on real data only, with a different partition sampler than the benchmark, so synthetic results measure transfer — well-justified; (c) the confound that SCDM changes both architecture and objective simultaneously — acknowledged but not resolved by the authors. Key Results: On synthetic data, HashingSchema achieves the best D1 consistency (0.59±0.01) and overall average rank (3.75); HashingText achieves the best D2 retrieval (R@5 = 1.00) and linear probe (0.90). Pooled TabPFN and ConTextTab rank lowest: D1 Spearman between −0.17 and 0.04, well below 0.54–0.59 for HashingText/HashingSchema. On real data, the pattern holds: HashingText leads (D1 = 0.41, overall rank 3.67) while pooled TabPFN (D1 = 0.06) and ConTextTab (D1 = 0.19 under mean) trail. Five parameter-free pooling rules over the same TFM states do not change the conclusion. Learning a compositional rule with SCDM over frozen ConTextTab states: on synthetic data, D1 rises from 0.04 to 0.48–0.50 across all 15 configurations, retrieval from 0.70 to 0.88–0.89; on real data, D1 rises from 0.19 to 0.24–0.27 and retrieval from 0.76 to 0.95–0.96. Parent-table retrieval: HashingText achieves R@1 = 0.98 on synthetic; HashingSchema achieves R@1 = 0.67 on real; the best learned head (ConTextTab-R GatedAttention) reaches R@1 = 0.35 on real vs. 0.10 for pooled ConTextTab, but does not close the gap to fingerprints. Learned heads rank first on synthetic and second on real in the augmented leaderboard. The Spearman correlation between benchmark D2 ranking and downstream retrieval MRR is 0.82 (synthetic) and 0.95 (real). All results reported with mean ± 95% CI over 10 evaluation seeds. Novelty Classification: NEW BENCHMARK (the evaluation pipeline with four desiderata, controlled partial views, and the encoder/composition decomposition), NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (lightweight fingerprints outperform pooled tabular foundation model states; weak pooled embeddings do not imply weak encoder states), and NEW METHOD (SCDM, a distribution-matching loss over frozen states for learning compositional rules). The learned heads themselves are standard attention/gated architectures; SCDM builds on listwise distribution matching (ListNet) applied to partition overlaps — a non-obvious but incremental combination. The genuinely novel element is the controlled decomposition of table-level embedding quality into encoder states vs. compositional rule, enabled by the frozen-state protocol. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are thorough: five pooling rules over identical states (Appendix A.7), column-name anonymization to test schema reliance (Appendix A.6), a full α-sweep for all three head families (Appendix A.10), and a linear-probe stratification analysis distinguishing label-stratified from source-group-disjoint folds (Appendix A.5). 95% confidence intervals over 10 evaluation seeds are reported throughout. Code is provided as an anonymized supplementary ZIP with a stated plan for a public repository upon acceptance; no public URL is given. Concerns: (1) the benchmark and the SCDM training signal share the same IoU overlap notion, so D1 improvements partly reflect optimizing the training objective on the evaluation signal (Goodhart's Law risk, partially mitigated by different partition samplers and transfer to synthetic data); (2) the downstream retrieval task shares the Direct-identity signal with the training objective, making it a consistency check rather than an independent test for the learned heads (acknowledged); (3) confidence intervals reflect evaluation sampling only, not variation across training runs (acknowledged); (4) no statistical significance tests beyond CIs. Deployability: (EMPIRICAL profile):** - Practical: Yes — learned heads run on a frozen ConTextTab backbone; the controlled throughput study used an NVIDIA T4 GPU, a widely available inference card. - Efficient: Learned heads add <5% cost over pooled ConTextTab (geometric mean 1.65–1.71 tables/s vs. 1.72 for pooled), but ConTextTab itself is among the slowest methods (1.72 Tbl/s vs. 5748 for HashingSchema), and fingerprints are 3–4 orders of magnitude faster. - Effective: The evidence shows learned composition recovers most of the partial-view consistency gap on synthetic data (D1 from 0.04 to 0.50 vs. fingerprints at 0.59) but only partially on real data (0.27 vs. 0.41), and simple fingerprints still dominate on both quality and cost. - Scalable: The efficiency study stress-tests encode throughput at 2048×64 tables, but the quality benchmark uses only 100 source tables with 10 partitions each; retrieval is tested on a closed corpus of 100 tables, so open-world behavior at 10–100× corpus size is untested. The work delivers a benchmark harness with a shared encode_tables interface, a self-supervised training loss, and reproducible configurations as supplementary code; it stops short of a production-ready library or trained model artifact release. Strengths: - The controlled frozen-encoder/learned-head experiment cleanly separates encoder-state information content from compositional-rule quality — an experimental design that prior benchmarks conflate. - The finding that lightweight hashing fingerprints outperform pooled tabular foundation model states is counter-intuitive, well-controlled (identical inputs, seeds, budgets across poolings), and survives multiple ablations (anonymization, five pooling rules). - The SCDM loss requires no external labels — it extracts supervision from the benchmark's own partition sampling — making it directly applicable to any encoder that exposes local states. - The parent-table retrieval validation with Spearman correlations of 0.82–0.95 against the benchmark's D2 ranking provides external construct validity for the benchmark design. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (1) the benchmark covers only cosine similarity under a shared observation budget; (2) fixed-composition findings concern only two TFMs (TabPFN, ConTextTab); (3) learned-composition uses a single backbone; (4) parent-table retrieval is a closed corpus of 100 tables, not open-world; (5) the learned-head experiment changes architecture and objective together, so neither ingredient is isolated; (6) confidence intervals reflect evaluation sampling, not training-run variation; (7) D3 robustness saturates for permutation-invariant methods; (8) learned-head gains averaged over label types are not decomposed. The authors confront these limitations directly and at length — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The learned-head improvement on D1 may be partly circular: SCDM trains to match the distribution of embedding similarities to IoU overlaps, and D1 measures Spearman correlation between similarity and IoU. The transfer to synthetic data mitigates but does not eliminate this concern, since the overlap notion is shared across corpora. - Only two tabular foundation models are tested under fixed composition; the claim that "states of tabular foundation models trail fingerprints" generalizes from a sample of two, and neither is tested with the SCDM protocol (only ConTextTab), so the generality of the learned-composition finding across backbones is unknown. - The benchmark's real-data semantic labels are derived from benchmark source and dataset identifier metadata, which may correlate with schema style or provenance rather than genuine semantic content; no analysis of what the semantic labels capture is provided. - No comparison to Starmie, TabSketchFM, or other contrastive table encoders trained specifically for table discovery, despite these being cited as related specialized methods — their absence from the twelve-method benchmark is unexplained. - The observation budget (partitions are 20–50% of rows/columns, minimum 10×5) may not reflect realistic partial-view sizes in production caching or context-window scenarios; no sensitivity analysis on partition size is reported. Bottom Line: A practitioner building table retrieval, deduplication, or curation pipelines gains immediately actionable evidence that lightweight hashing fingerprints remain the strongest and cheapest table-level embeddings, while the learned-composition contribution — though cleanly designed — is a research result with unproven generalization beyond one backbone, so the benchmark methodology is the more durable contribution than the SCDM method itself.

LogT: Logically Think with Images for Visual Search (12 ▲ )

Yanjun Fu, Quanzeng You, Jiadong Guo, Yujie Lu, Sai Charitha Akula, Haiping Wu, Miao Liu, Sanghamitra Dutta, Lu Yuan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 19 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LogT, a fully automated SFT data synthesis engine that generates 7.1k logic-chain-guided question-answer pairs and tool-use reasoning traces, showing that Qwen2.5-VL-7B fine-tuned only on this data (59.59 avg pass@1 across seven test sets) beats prior open-source models trained with both SFT and RL, and that adding a plain outcome-reward RL recipe reaches 67.28 avg, +9.59 over the best prior RL model. - Why it's important: Training VLMs to reason with a Zoom-in tool currently demands expensive tool-specific RL (e.g., >120× more GPU hours than LogT's SFT stage); if SFT data quality is the real bottleneck, practitioners can get better tool accuracy and efficiency for a small fraction of the compute. - How it does it: The engine generates hard, object-grounded QAs from SA1B crops using contextual+focused crops and a VLM-as-a-Judge filter, then builds per-question 'logic chains' (direct answer / multi-hop / exhaustive search) that act as skeletons guiding a VLM to write structured, tool-efficient reasoning traces. - The good: The controlled evidence that SFT data quality drives the RL ceiling — applying the same off-the-shelf RL recipe to baselines' SFT checkpoints makes them plateau at or below zero-RL, while LogT-SFT keeps improving — directly supports the paper's central claim rather than just a leaderboard win. - The missing: No error bars, single-seed runs, and no explicit code/data release URL; tool-call accuracy is measured only on V (the sole benchmark with ground-truth boxes), and the RL validation set draws from V/VisualProbe/HR-Bench — the same benchmarks used for headline evaluation. - Read it or not: Read it if you build post-training pipelines for tool-using VLMs and want a concrete, ablated recipe for high-quality agentic SFT data at ~120–960 GPU-hour cost; skip it if you only care about pushing absolute benchmark numbers, since o3 and frontier models remain far above.

Problem & Motivation: VLMs lose fine-grained visual detail through visual-encoder compression, so 'thinking with images' — interleaving reasoning with an external Zoom-in tool — has become the standard fix for fine-grained visual search on high-resolution images. Prior open-source approaches (Pixel Reasoner, DeepEyes, Chain-of-Focus, Mini-o3) use SFT cold-start plus increasingly complex, tool-specific RL, but models still make inaccurate or redundant tool calls (OpenAI's o3 blog cites 'redundant or unnecessary tool calls' as a known limitation). The paper targets the gap that prior SFT datasets contain easy questions and traces lacking human-like logical structure, and argues — against the field's trend — that SFT data quality, not RL sophistication, is the binding constraint. Practitioners training tool-using VLMs on 7B-scale open models are the intended audience. Key Idea: The core trick is decoupling trace synthesis into (i) abstract logic chains and (ii) chain-following trace generation. A text LLM (GPT-OSS-120B) writes a compact skeleton — ordered steps of the form 'noun-phrase (image-id)' specifying what region to inspect and which image to zoom into — chosen between a multi-hop and an exhaustive-search chain, and only then does a VLM expand the skeleton into a full interleaved text/image reasoning trace. Combined with a difficulty gate (questions the base model answers perfectly at avg@8=1 get no-tool direct-answer traces; only 24% of LogT questions are 'easy' vs. far higher in prior datasets), this yields traces that teach when not to call the tool as well as how to call it accurately. The insight is that this decoupling sidesteps current open VLMs' weak instruction-following for long structured generation, replacing the need for a visual process reward model. Methodology: The pipeline has two phases. Phase 1 (QA synthesis): from SA1B images, filter bounding boxes to <1% of image area, pick one or two boxes, build contextual crops (IC, several× larger) and focused crops (IF, exact box); prompt Qwen2.5-VL-72B to generate two candidate QAs of controlled types (perception, counting, OCR, reasoning); filter via format rules plus a 106B open VLM judge run twice with order reversal to mitigate positional bias, keeping only consistently validated pairs. Phase 2 (trace synthesis): questions the base model solves at avg@8=1 get single-turn direct-answer traces; otherwise GPT-OSS-120B generates multi-hop (LM) and exhaustive-search (LE) chains from the QA plus a caption, the judge-VLM selects one, and the judge-VLM expands it turn-by-turn into Zoom-in calls with predicted bounding boxes, with early stopping once the target is found. Training: 3-epoch SFT on Qwen2.5-VL-7B (lr 1e-5, batch 128) and on InternVL3.5-8B; then modified GRPO (no KL, clipping-higher at 0.315, 8 rollouts, 100 steps in veRL) with only correctness + 0.5 format rewards and no tool-specific reward shaping. Critical design decisions: (1) difficulty-controlled QA generation — justified by an ablation showing the harder half gains +4.72 on VisualProbe-Hard; (2) logic-chain guidance — justified by ablation (+2.87 avg after RL vs. fixed in-context examples); (3) VLM-as-a-Judge instead of humans — partially justified by a sampled error audit (12%/2%/7% error rates at QA/chain/trace stages), though 12% QA-stage error is non-trivial. Key Results: Evaluated greedy pass@1 on seven test sets (V, VisualProbe Easy/Medium/Hard, HR-Bench 4K/8K, MME-RealWorld-Lite). LogT-SFT (7.1k samples) averages 59.59, beating all open-source baselines including RL-trained ones: Mini-o3-RL at 57.69 (avg 4.3 tool calls/question vs. LogT-SFT's 2.7× fewer), Chain-of-Focus-RL 55.85, DeepEyes-RL 57.35. SFT took 3.2 hours on 8×A100 — >120× fewer GPU hours than Mini-o3-RL; data synthesis costs 960 GPU hours (or ~120 with smaller synthesis models, ablated to lose only 0.12 avg points). LogT-RL averages 67.28 (+9.59 over Mini-o3-RL), with HR-Bench-4K at 51.89 vs. baselines ≤36.79; the only regression is MME-RW-Lite (−0.47 vs. best baseline). Tool-call accuracy on V: 94.21% for LogT-RL vs. 72.09% for Mini-o3-RL, with most SFT baselines (e.g., Pixel Reasoner 6.15%) below the zero-shot prompted base model (69.70%). RL ablation: applying the same recipe to baselines' SFT checkpoints plateaus at or below zero-RL, while LogT-SFT climbs steadily — the strongest causal evidence. Generalization: InternVL3.5-8B +14.00 avg; zero-shot use of an unseen rotation tool on V-Rotated gives 68.06 vs. base 46.07. Human eval (100 V questions, 3 annotators): LogT-RL preferred 59%, tie 14%, vs. Mini-o3-RL. Baselines are current (2025 models, same 7B base family) and reasonably strong; o3 numbers are partial vendor-reported. Tested at standard academic scale (7–8B models, 7.1k SFT + 6.4k RL samples), not stress scale. arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the LogT data engine with logic-chain-decoupled trace synthesis) plus NEW DATASET (7.1k traces). The genuinely novel element is the abstract logic-chain layer separating 'what to inspect' planning from trace writing, plus the difficulty-gated direct-answer mechanism; the surrounding components — VLM-as-a-Judge filtering, GRPO with clipping-higher, outcome rewards, SA1B-sourced crops — are standard combinations of existing ideas applied to visual search. The framing claim (SFT data quality > RL complexity) is an empirical finding more than a new formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: question difficulty (Table 4), logic chains vs. fixed exemplars (Table 5, +2.87 after RL), and synthesis-model scale (Table 6, 59.55 vs. 59.43 avg with 8B/32B/20B substitutes), plus a per-stage data error audit (Table 7) and equal-data-budget comparisons (4k/5.4k/7.1k). Concerns: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests on any headline number; the human evaluation covers only 100 questions from V with all three annotators apparently affiliated; tool-call accuracy relies on IoG≥0.8 on V alone, the only benchmark with ground-truth boxes; the RL validation set is drawn from V*, VisualProbe, and HR-Bench — the same benchmarks used for final reporting, a mild Goodhart exposure; one baseline (Li et al.) is scored from its own paper rather than re-evaluated; the authors raise LogT's image-resolution budget (8192×28×28) above Mini-o3's default and justify it by noting Mini-o3 also improves under it, but this is still an evaluation-protocol asymmetry. The paper does not state a public code or dataset release URL. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (methods trained and evaluated; no new theory). - Practical: Yes — 7B–8B open models, SFT in 3.2 hours and RL data synthesis in ~120–960 GPU hours on A100s, all commercially available hardware. - Efficient: Strongly — >120× fewer GPU hours than Mini-o3-RL for the SFT stage and 2.3× fewer tool calls at inference than the best RL baseline, though synthesis of the full 7.1k set with large models (960 GPU-hours) is the main cost. - Effective: Evidence supports accurate and efficient Zoom-in use on visual-search benchmarks (67.28 avg, 94.21% tool accuracy), but gains on out-of-domain perception (MME-RW-Lite 53.00 vs. DeepEyes 53.47) show the effect is largely search-specific, not a general reasoning upgrade. - Scalable: Untested beyond 7.1k SFT samples and 7–8B models; the authors claim extensibility to other structured-reasoning domains and tools but run no experiment at 10× data or model scale. Deliverable: a synthesized 7.1k-sample dataset and trained checkpoints (release URL not stated in the provided text); the engine is described procedurally with prompts, not shipped as a library. Strengths: - The RL-ceiling experiment (same RL recipe across baselines' SFT checkpoints, Figure 4) is the paper's strongest contribution: it isolates SFT data quality as a causal variable rather than merely winning a leaderboard against differently-tuned systems. - The logic-chain abstraction is a real, reusable design idea — it converts hard structured trace generation into an easy planning step plus an easy expansion step, and the ablation (+2.87 after RL) plus the synthesis-model-scale ablation (performance invariant from 120B to 8B/20B generators) suggest the framework, not distillation of a big teacher, drives the gains. - Honest measurement of tool-use behavior: exposing that most prior SFT/RL baselines have worse tool-call accuracy (e.g., 6.15% for Pixel Reasoner-SFT) than zero-shot prompting the base model (69.70%) is a genuinely useful negative finding for the field. - Thorough ablation coverage (difficulty, logic chains, synthesis models, data budgets, second base model, unseen-tool generalization) at unusually low compute cost. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly confront two limitations: (1) centrality of Zoom-in — the method is trained for one tool, though they show out-of-domain gains on MME-RW-Lite and zero-shot transfer to an unseen rotation tool (+21.99 on V*-Rotated), and they position extension to other domains as future work; (2) reliance on VLM-as-a-Judge, which they mitigate with a double-evaluation protocol and a 100-sample manual audit (12% QA-stage error, 2% chain, 7% trace), while arguing annotation noise is unavoidable even with humans. This is direct, credible limitation handling rather than minimization, though the 12% QA error rate is presented more reassuringly than it perhaps warrants. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - RL monitoring and final evaluation share benchmarks (V*, VisualProbe, HR-Bench appear in the RL validation set), so model selection could leak into headline numbers; an untouched held-out visual-search benchmark would settle this. - Single-seed training and evaluation throughout; with 7.1k SFT samples, run-to-run variance is plausibly non-trivial relative to some reported margins (e.g., +1.9 over Mini-o3-RL for SFT-only). - The QA synthesis draws from SA1B high-resolution images of everyday scenes, overlapping in distribution with VisualProbe/HR-Bench content; a domain-shifted evaluation (e.g., documents, medical, remote sensing at high resolution) is absent despite MME-RW-Lite containing such tasks — where the model ties rather than wins. - The paper claims logic chains produce 'human-like' reasoning but validates logical coherence only via a small 3-annotator preference study (59% on 100 questions) and qualitative cases; no automatic faithfulness metric or larger study. - No public code/data URL is stated, so the engine itself — the paper's main artifact — cannot currently be independently rebuilt or audited. Bottom Line: For anyone post-training tool-using VLMs, this is worth reading and imitating: it delivers a concrete, cheaply reproducible demonstration that logic-structured SFT data buys more than tool-specific RL, and its data-engine recipe is directly actionable — but its benchmark wins are at 7B open-model scale, its evaluation protocol has mild leakage exposure, and frontier-model relevance remains unproven.

Problem & Motivation: VLMs applied to remote sensing scenes can name objects but fail at task-conditioned judgments that require inspecting local attributes, spatial relations, and visibility limits — e.g., deciding which waterfront supports vehicle staging before ship loading. Practitioners specializing models to a scene type (harbors, urban areas) face scarce high-quality annotations, and answer-only RL gives no feedback on whether observations actually support the conclusion. Prior relational approaches (MiCo, Fine-R1) reward agreement/disagreement on jointly processed inputs or category labels; the gap is that visually distinct scenes can warrant the same answer under a shared question, so the supervision must assess whether paired descriptions justify agreement or change, not whether outputs match. Key Idea: Separate verification of visual fidelity (is what the model says in the image?) from conditional reasoning (does the conclusion follow from what it described?), score both with rubric-based LLM judges, and couple the two responses of a task-matched image pair through a single shared pair-level advantage — so a response is rewarded or penalized partly based on how its judgment relates to its partner's given the described evidence. This pair-level shared advantage over independently generated single-image responses is the reconstructible core; the rest is a competent assembly of GRPO, LoRA SFT, and rubrics-as-rewards. Methodology: Stage 1 (EoT-SFT) trains on 1,008 distilled demonstrations over 888 CPRS harbor images, each structured as description → analysis ⊕ answer, minimizing a masked token-averaged NLL (Eq. 2); demonstrations carry 7,745 observation and 1,411 uncertainty annotations produced by a three-step distillation (scene observation into an "Evidence Card," task interpretation, consistency review). Stage 2 (RTPO) uses 500 Anchor–Bridging pairs (372 decisive-change, 77 invariance, 51 visibility-scope), each with per-image Evidence Cards and a shared Boundary Card. For each unit, the policy samples K=6 responses per image, randomly matches them into 6 candidate pairs, and computes: Gravity scores G1 (fidelity, 0–3, over all visual claims) and G2 (description coverage, 0–3, against the card); Flight scores F1 (evidence use, 0–5, per response) and F2 (paired adaptation, 0–5, per pair, jointly scored); plus Task Check correctness C against side-specific answer contracts. The pair reward is R_k = 0.5·Σv_i·C_i,k + ½Σ_i v_i(λ_G·G_i + λ_F·F_i), normalized within the unit into a shared advantage (Eq. 8), applied via a clipped GRPO-style objective with KL regularization to the frozen Stage-1 policy (Eq. 9). All verification runs through a single fixed DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash judge with view-specific prompts and information separation (the judge never sees private answer contracts for Flight). Critical design decisions: (1) shared pair-level advantage — justified by the shuffled-F2 control; (2) single-image rather than joint-input generation — justified by the joint-input control (66.49 vs 69.12); (3) random one-to-one matching (6 of 36 possible combinations scored for F2) — stated as a cost choice, not ablated against exhaustive matching. Key Results: On the mean of six harbor evaluation sets (HarborEval, OpenEval, harbor subsets of VRSBench, RSVQA, OmniEarth, VLRS-Bench), G&F (Qwen3.5-4B + LoRA) scores 69.12 overall vs 59.36 for the backbone (+9.76) and 64.56 for EoT-SFT alone (+4.56); the strongest remote sensing baseline, RS-EoT (7B), averages 56.26, and RSThinker (9B) 55.02. G&F wins five of six sets; RSThinker leads VRSBench (67.67 vs 54.19). Ablations: removing Flight costs 4.01 points, removing Gravity 2.80; task-only RL (63.34) underperforms the SFT checkpoint. Matched controls: single-image RL 65.12 → paired RL w/o F2 66.79 (+1.67) → full G&F 69.12 (+2.33 from F2); shuffled F2 feedback 64.71 (worse than omitting F2); joint-input RL 66.49. Token-level analysis on six sampled cases shows evidence density 38.48% vs 21.53% (G&F vs Base), mean length 179.50 vs 355.50 tokens, and 6/6 vs 3/6 agreement with reference judgments. Urban transfer (160 demos, 60 pairs from EarthVLSet) gives +1.93/+2.08/+4.67 points over the SFT-only model on EarthVQA/VRSBench/RSVQA-HR urban subsets, but urban absolute scores are low (e.g., 31.43 on EarthVQA). Training costs 16.69× the Stage-1 wall time (~26.7 GPU-hours on 2× RTX A6000s). Note the arXiv ID and references (CVPR'26, ICLR'26, Qwen3.5) indicate a late-2026 preprint; several cited baselines are contemporaneous rather than established. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the shared pair-level advantage coupling policy updates from independently generated responses under decoupled rubric verification) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (aligned relational feedback beats both its omission and shuffled feedback). The ingredients — GRPO, rubrics-as-rewards, image-pair contrastive supervision, LLM-judge verification — are existing; the genuinely novel element is the pair-advantage formulation and the information-separated Gravity/Flight verifier decomposition. The EoT-SFT stage is a competent execution of known structured-CoT distillation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well designed: reward-component removals, matched single-image/paired/shuffled/joint-input controls at equal image–question exposure, and a training-trace audit of realized advantages across 100 units (Table S5). However: (1) every run uses seed 42 with no error bars or significance tests, and the headline F2 contribution (+2.33) is small relative to the measured judge instability (F2 repeat-change rate 29.17%, human agreement 83.33% on 24 units — the authors honestly report this but do not propagate it into significance claims); (2) the token-level analysis covers six sampled cases with hand annotation; (3) HarborEval and OpenEval originate from FBA (ref [13]), whose author list overlaps with this paper's, and the OpenEval scores for several models were re-judged by the authors with a different judge (MiMo-v2.6-Flash) than the expert protocol used for FBA's original baselines — a mixed protocol within one table column; (4) the verifier reliability audit is small and the authors themselves state it "supports an indication of reliability rather than a precise estimate." A GitHub repository URL is given (https://github.com/Z0ngL1ng/Gravity-and-Flight); trained weights are not stated. The leakage audit for evaluation-image disjointness is a credibility positive. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a systems flavor via the online-verifier training loop). - Practical: Yes — full training ran on 2× RTX A6000 (~27 reserved GPU-hours), within reach of academic labs, though it requires API access to a fixed LLM judge (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash). - Efficient: Relatively — LoRA with frozen vision encoder on a 4B model, but RL wall time is 16.69× the SFT stage due to 27,000 verifier assessments per pass; removing verification terms cuts cost roughly proportionally (8.15×–15.83×). - Effective: The evidence supports improved grounded judgment on harbor benchmarks (69.12 vs 59.36 backbone), but gains over the SFT checkpoint on held-out urban transfer are modest (+1.93 to +4.67 on subsets where absolute scores remain ≤56.25), so effectiveness beyond the specialized domain is only partially demonstrated. - Scalable: Not tested — the method is demonstrated at 500–1,000 annotation scale on two scene types; behavior with more pairs, multiple seeds, larger backbones, or a different judge model is claimed only implicitly. The work delivers a method paper with a stated code repository; no released dataset, model weights, or library are confirmed in the text. Strengths: - The shared pair-level advantage is a real methodological contribution: it converts relational judgment (do two independently generated responses warrant agreement?) into a scalar training signal without joint-input generation, and the shuffled-F2 control (64.71 vs 69.12) is exactly the right test that alignment, not mere pair structure, drives the gain. - The matched-control ladder (single-image → paired w/o F2 → full; plus joint-input) isolates each mechanism at matched exposure — a design most rubric-reward papers skip. - Information separation in verification (Gravity sees image + card; Flight sees only descriptions + public task; Task Check sees only answers + contracts) enables genuinely distinct diagnoses (a false described fact vs an invalid inference from a described premise) and is documented at implementable depth (Tables S2–S3, score anchors). - Honest self-auditing: the verifier reliability study reports unflattering numbers (F2 agreement 83.33%, repeat-change 29.17%), and the advantage-trace audit exposes that 57.9% of pairs with one full-credit side received negative shared advantage — the paper shows its machinery's warts rather than hiding them. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: judging errors may remain correlated through the shared judge model; the reliability study is too small for precise estimates and "neither rate validates the rubric itself"; Overall is a study-specific unweighted aggregate whose per-set scores retain different task-specific meanings; geographic overlap and backbone pretraining exposure are outside the leakage audit's scope; the data-scale comparison across models uses incommensurate accounting scopes; and run-to-run variation dominates wall-time differences below a few percent. They confront these directly, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-seed results throughout: with judge repeat-change rates up to 29% and a +2.33-point headline contribution from F2, seed variance alone could plausibly reorder the paired-RL conditions; no variance estimate is offered. - Two of the six evaluation sets (HarborEval, OpenEval) are the authors' own benchmark from a self-cited prior paper, and the OpenEval column mixes expert scores (for FBA's original baselines) with the authors' own LLM-judge re-scoring (for six other models, including their own) — a within-column protocol inconsistency the paper documents but does not flag as a comparability threat. - The random 1-of-6 matching for F2 is never compared against exhaustive K² matching, even though the shared advantage makes partner choice matter (their own Table S5 shows it can flip advantage sign). - Hyperparameter sensitivity (λ_G=0.35, λ_F=0.15, β=0.04, and the mid-run learning-rate change from 10⁻⁶ to 2×10⁻⁶) is unexamined; the urban experiments reuse harbor weights without justification. - The token-level analysis (six cases, hand-annotated, one response pair per case) is presented as evidence of representational improvement but has the statistical weight of an anecdote. - No comparison against simply scaling EoT-SFT data (e.g., 2× demonstrations instead of adding RTPO at 16× cost), which is the natural practitioner question. Bottom Line: For researchers designing RL post-training with LLM-judge rewards, this paper's pair-level advantage formulation and unusually honest matched-control methodology are worth studying in detail; as a remote sensing solution, its gains are real but narrow, seed-unverified, and partly measured on the authors' own benchmarks, so treat the headline numbers as promising rather than settled.

#88 — Innovative (64)

MMFlash: Faster Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models (35 ▲ )

Sicheng Feng, Zigeng Chen, Song Wang, Gongfan Fang, Xinchao Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 16 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MMFlash, a diffusion-based speculative-drafting framework for vision-language models that upweights visually dependent tokens during drafter training and adopts sparse attention for video inputs, achieving lossless decoding speedups of up to 3.58×. - Why it's important: VLM inference is bottlenecked by autoregressive decoding, and the paper shows that existing diffusion drafters (DFlash) systematically fail on image-dependent tokens — the acceptance rate drops from 46% to 22% between the least and most visually dependent token quartiles — so multimodal acceleration currently leaves substantial speedup on the table. - How it does it: The core trick is turning a diagnostic metric (KL divergence between the target VLM's next-token distributions with vs. without the image, scaled by target confidence) into a per-token training weight that boosts gradient on hard, visually grounded tokens only while the drafter still predicts them poorly. - The good: The motivating empirical study is convincingly quantified — the most visually dependent quartile accounts for 44% of first rejections vs. 7% for the least dependent, a 2.1–2.4× acceptance gap that persists after multimodal fine-tuning — and MMFlash consistently outperforms retrained DFlash and EAGLE-3 across 7 image and 3 video benchmarks, 4 target models, 2 temperatures, 2 serving frameworks, and concurrency up to 32. - The missing: Each benchmark is evaluated on only 200 randomly selected samples with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests, and the offline cost of scoring visual dependence (running the target model twice per training token) is not reported. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on inference acceleration for multimodal models — the diagnostic metric and loss-reweighting scheme transfer directly to any block-diffusion drafter — but skip it if you only care about text-only speculative decoding, where DFlash and D-PACE already cover the ground.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (55) and Resilience (60) pull the composite down: 200-sample single-run evaluations with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests leave several reported margins (e.g., +4.7% from sparse attention alone) within plausible noise, and the entropy-gating factor and key hyperparameters are never ablated individually. Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (70) are genuinely good — the quantified failure localization of diffusion-drafter acceptance on visually dependent tokens is a real finding — but the method is a targeted training signal on DFlash rather than a new architecture. Practical Impact (65) reflects stated code/checkpoint releases that are not verifiable via any concrete URL. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*65 = 64.
empirical Novelty 70 Rigor 55 Non-Obv 70 Completeness 65 Resilience 60 Impact 65
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by having a lightweight drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Diffusion drafters like DFlash generate an entire token block in one forward pass, but DFlash and its variants were developed and validated on text-only LLMs. Practitioners serving VLMs (Q&A, document understanding, video understanding, STEM reasoning) lack a validated diffusion-drafting recipe for multimodal targets, and it is unknown where a text-style drafter loses acceptance when the target's predictions depend on images. The gap this paper closes is identifying and fixing the token-level failure mode of diffusion drafting on VLMs. Key Idea: Measure each token's "visual dependence" as the KL divergence between the target model's next-token distribution with and without the image (same textual prefix), then use this target-computable, offline-scoreable quantity — gated by target confidence and modulated by the drafter's current error — to reweight the DFlash block cross-entropy loss, so training capacity flows to image-determined tokens the drafter has not yet learned and recedes as it does. This diagnostic-to-training-signal conversion is the one insight from which the method follows. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Diagnosis: for each training token, run the target VLM twice (with/without image), compute d = KL(p(·|x<t, I) ‖ p(·|x<t)), bucket tokens into corpus-wide quantile ranks g̃_t, and gate by target entropy: g_t = g̃_t · exp(−H_t). (2) Training: replace DFlash's positional weight w_k = exp(−(k−1)/γ) with a three-factor product w_k = b_k(1 + α·g_k·(1 − sg(q_k))), where b_k = Π_i ((1−λ)sg(q_i)+λ) is a verification-aware chain-survival weight (smoothing λ=0.5 keeps later block positions from being silenced), the (1 − sg(q_k)) factor fades the visual boost as the drafter fits the token, and the objective remains a weighted cross-entropy against the target's own choices. The visual scores are precomputed offline; training follows the official DFlash recipe (block size 16, 512 anchors, batch 2, 6 epochs, LR 6.0×10⁻⁴ cosine, 8×H100, ~900K samples from LLaVA-OV-1.5 regenerated by the target). (3) Video extension: attention analysis shows the most recent 256 positions (0.8% of context) receive 50.1% of drafter attention on ~41K-token video inputs; the drafter uses a fixed sparse pattern (4 sink tokens, visual tokens at stride 32, all text tokens, 256-token local window) at both training and inference, plus 3 epochs of fine-tuning on 2K LLaVA-Video samples. Critical design decisions: deriving visual dependence from the target rather than drafter or attention maps (well justified — acceptance is defined by target behavior); entropy gating to skip flat, unpredictable distributions (reasonable, though unvalidated in isolation as an ablation); and coupling the sparse pattern across train/test (sensible, standard). Key Results: On Qwen3.5-4B/9B across seven image benchmarks (ChartQA, CharXiv, MMStar, MMBench, DynaMath, MathVista, MathVerse), MMFlash (block 16) achieves average speedups of 3.00–3.05× at T=0 and 2.54–2.70× at T=1, exceeding a same-data retrained DFlash by 6.7–10.9% and EAGLE-3 by much larger margins (EAGLE-3 averages only 1.58×/1.44×); the headline peak is 3.58× on Qwen3.5-9B/ChartQA. Native MTP reaches only 1.19–1.64×. On three ~40K-token video benchmarks (LongVideoBench, MVBench, Video-MME), sparse attention alone adds +11.1% acceptance length and +4.7% speedup without retraining; with fine-tuning, speedups reach 2.33–2.71×, 11.2–23.2% above DFlash. Under serving concurrency 1–32 on SGLang (and consistent results on vLLM), MMFlash at concurrency 16 beats the baseline at concurrency 32 on all six tested tasks. Generalization: 2.10–3.02× on Gemma4-E4B-it and 3.54–4.71× on Qwen3.8-27B (no EAGLE-3 comparison reported for the 27B). Ablations cover test-time block size (8 vs. 16: speedup drops only 5.3%), drafter depth (3/5/8 layers — speedup saturates at 5), and number of tapped target hidden states (5 vs. 8 — marginal gain, +19.9% training time). Baselines include a strong, same-data-retrained EAGLE-3 and DFlash, so the comparison set is current; note DFlash itself is a 2026 preprint. Tested scale is standard single-GPU (H200) inference on 200-sample subsets per benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the token-level visual-dependence metric and the quantified finding that diffusion-drafter acceptance collapses specifically on visually dependent tokens even after multimodal training, and (b) the confidence-gated, self-fading loss reweighting built on that metric. The base system — block-diffusion drafter verified by an autoregressive target — is DFlash applied to VLMs, and sparse attention with sinks/stride/window is a standard combination; the contribution is the targeted training signal on a new setting, not a new drafting architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative for the drafter's structural choices (depth, hidden-state taps, test-time block size), and the motivation study is a real diagnostic rather than anecdote, with both token-level and block-level statistics across three benchmarks and two drafters. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; each benchmark uses only 200 random samples, so small speedup gaps (e.g., the 4.7% sparse-attention gain) carry no stated uncertainty; and there is no ablation isolating the entropy-gating factor g_t or the α/λ hyperparameters. The paper links a code release and model checkpoints ("Code: MMFlash", "Models: MMFlash" on page 1) but no concrete URL appears in the provided text. No Goodhart-style contamination is evident since speedup is measured against the target model's own distribution, but the diagnostic analysis and evaluation share the same benchmark suite. Methodological concerns: small evaluation subsets and single-run results are the main flags. This is a preprint (arXiv 2611.18482) and has not, as far as the text states, undergone peer review. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained drafting method benchmarked in real serving frameworks). Practical: Runs on a single NVIDIA H200 with SGLang and vLLM, both widely deployed, and the drafter excludes visual tokens so drafter cost does not scale with visual input size. Efficient: Training needed 8×H100 for 6 epochs; the offline visual-dependence scoring doubles target-model passes over training data (cost not quantified); online training was chosen over offline partly because stored hidden states would reach tens of terabytes. Effective: The evidence shows lossless speedup on multimodal workloads — the exact stated problem — including under concurrency 32, though throughput gains shrink as serving becomes compute-bound (1.14–1.89× at concurrency 32). Scalability: Tested only to 9B-scale targets plus one 27B (where it does well); no evidence at 100B+ or on higher-resolution/longer-video inputs beyond ~42K tokens, where the authors themselves concede long-video drafting remains harder than images. Deliverable: code and trained drafter checkpoints are stated to be released; the sparse-attention pattern and loss scheme are reusable techniques beyond the artifact. Strengths: - The motivating study converts a vague concern ("VLMs draft poorly") into a precise, quantified failure localization: acceptance falls monotonically 46%→22% across visual-dependence quartiles, and Q3–Q4 hold 72–80% of truncation points — a finding that persists after multimodal training and would be useful even without the proposed fix. - The loss design is thoughtful about speculative decoding's actual mechanics rather than generic: the chain-survival weight b_k, the stop-gradient self-fading term (1 − sg(q_k)), and entropy gating each encode a distinct constraint on when extra gradient at a block position can possibly convert into accepted tokens. - The sparse-attention claim is grounded in measured drafter attention statistics (256 recent tokens = 0.8% of context but 50.1% of attention) and validated with a train/test-consistent pattern, including a no-retrain result (+11.1% acceptance) that isolates the pattern's effect. - Evaluation breadth is above the bar for this subfield: 2 temperatures, 2 serving frameworks, concurrency sweeps, 4 target models across 2 families, and 10 benchmarks with same-data-retrained baselines. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: In Appendix F the authors state that MMFlash is designed for image/video-input, text-output VLMs only; that for videos they rely on a simple sparse attention pattern plus lightweight fine-tuning rather than a purpose-built video drafter; that drafting on long videos remains harder than on images; and that extension to omni-modal (audio/speech) models would require generalizing the visual-dependence notion and handling much longer interleaved contexts. This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of scope limits — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical treatment: 200 samples per benchmark, single runs, no variance estimates — several claimed margins (e.g., +4.7% from sparse attention alone, sub-1% differences in the hidden-tap ablation) are within plausible sampling noise. - The entropy-gating factor exp(−H_t) and the hyperparameters α, λ are never ablated individually, so the attribution of gains among the three weight factors is unverified; the paper also does not report an ablation of MMFlash's reweighting against DFlash's fixed positional decay holding everything else fixed (though the DFlash baseline effectively serves this role), nor against D-PACE-style dynamic position weights, which target the same loss-shaping idea. - The cost of the diagnostic pipeline is understated: scoring visual dependence requires two full target forward passes per training token (or per evaluated token), and no wall-clock or FLOP figure is given for this offline stage. - No quality/downstream evaluation of the regenerated training responses (prompts were rewritten to elicit longer answers), leaving open whether the drafter is biased toward verbose response styles. - The Qwen3.8-27B generalization table omits EAGLE-3, removing the strongest baseline exactly at the largest scale where the headline 4.71× appears. - Visual dependence is defined per token via the image but never extended to video frames during training — the video gains come only from attention sparsity and small-scale fine-tuning, so the paper's core training insight is untested on its own video setting. Bottom Line: For anyone building or deploying speculative decoding on VLMs, this is worth reading — the visual-dependence diagnosis and the confidence-gated reweighting are immediately reusable and the evaluation is broader than most in this fast-moving subfield — but the thin evaluation subsets, missing statistical rigor, and absence of ablations on the loss factors mean the reported margins over DFlash should be treated as promising rather than settled.

#89 — Innovative (64)

MORA: Correcting Time Series Forecasts with Coarse Future Signals

H Li, K Li, H Xu, S Gao, Y Zhang, F Dai · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MORA, a model-agnostic output-space residual adapter that corrects the predictions of frozen time-series forecasters by exploiting predictable coarse-scale (low-frequency) residual structure, without retraining or modifying the backbone. - Why it's important: Forecasting models are increasingly deployed as frozen checkpoints (including time-series foundation models), so a post-hoc adapter that improves accuracy without weight updates or extra inputs offers a cheap accuracy gain for any existing deployment. - How it does it: The core trick is decoupling coarse future estimation from backbone-specific correction: ridge-based and extrapolation-based predictors estimate future segment-wise means, their discrepancy with the backbone forecast's segment means is converted into stagewise corrections within a tapered-IDCT subspace, scaled per-coordinate by estimation reliability. - The good: The evaluation is unusually broad and consistent: across 288 dataset-backbone-horizon settings on twelve benchmarks and six backbones, MORA lowers MSE in 96.2% of cases (7.2% average reduction long-term, 28.1% short-term), and it also improves three frozen foundation models (Chronos-2, Sundial, TimesFM 2.5) at two context lengths, with measured inference overhead as low as 0.24% latency for TimesFM 2.5. - The missing: No error bars or significance tests are reported (many settings use a single seed, and overlapping test windows make win counts correlated), gains on the strongest recent backbones are modest (4.3-4.4% average for CGTFra and TimeFilter on long-term), and the ablation shows direct residual regression beats MORA on MSE on ETTm1, weakening the claim that coarse-future targets are the uniquely right formulation. - Read it or not: Practitioners deploying or benchmarking time-series forecasters, especially frozen foundation models, should read it for a well-documented, low-overhead correction recipe; readers seeking statistical rigor or a deeper theory of when residual adaptation helps will find the treatment thin (Proposition 1 is a two-parameter least-squares identity).
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Completeness (70) is the standout — honest negative results, quantified failure cases, and out-of-fold fitting hygiene — and Impact (68) reflects a genuinely cheap, deployable adapter with code. But Novelty (60) and Non-Obviousness (62) are moderate (standard ingredients; the coarse-future decoupling is only partially supported by the ablation, since direct residual regression wins on ETTm1), and Rigor (62) is pulled down by single seeds, overlapping test windows inflating the 96.2% win rate, and benchmark-coupled hyperparameter tuning.
