#94 — Innovative (63)

D3Tree: Learning to Prune Block-Diffusion Draft Trees for Efficient Verification

H Nie, Z Gao, J Yu, B Wang, J Sun, S Liu · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces D3Tree, a learned verification strategy for block-diffusion speculative decoding that trains a lightweight per-node survival head to prune draft trees and allocates a batch-wide node budget, aligned to the target model's matrix-multiplication tiles, that adapts the verified workload to serving load. - Why it's important: Under concurrent serving, every verified draft-tree node occupies a query row that competes with other requests, so fixed-size trees lose their speedup advantage precisely at high load — the regime production LLM serving cares about most (DDTree falls to 0.26–0.84× autoregressive speed at 64 concurrent requests). - How it does it: A 2H+2-parameter head estimates the conditional probability that each candidate matches the target continuation given its parent matches; thresholding the product of these scores along parent chains yields an ancestor-closed subtree, and above a load threshold the top-scoring nodes across the whole batch are retained up to a tile-sized budget. - The good: A large, controlled evaluation — six vision-language verifiers, 17 benchmarks, concurrency 1–64, four GPUs, serving traces — on a single shared runtime, where D3Tree is fastest in 70 of 72 verifier–benchmark-group–load settings (3.2–4.0× over autoregressive at R=1; 1.3–1.8× at R=64). - The missing: There is no ablation isolating the learned survival head against a non-learned pruning signal (e.g., thresholding draft path probability the same way), so the contribution of learning versus of load-aware budgeting alone is not quantified. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building speculative-decoding serving systems or working on block-diffusion drafters — it is the most complete treatment of load-aware tree verification — but skip it if you only care about lossless-guarantee theory or stochastic sampling.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile, where Practical Impact (60) carries 30% weight — the vLLM-integrated system with a Triton tree-attention kernel and CUDA graphs is real systems depth, but no public artifact release is stated, which materially limits the deployability claim. Rigor (58) is held down by ≤100 prompts per benchmark with no repeated runs or error bars, a missing ablation separating the learned survival head from plain draft-probability pruning (so the learned contribution is unproven), hand-tuned allocation tables tuned on reported benchmarks, and losslessness never empirically verified. The honest failure reporting (Resilience 70, Completeness 68) and genuinely new load-aware batch-wide budget abstraction (Novelty 62) keep the composite respectable. Weighted composite: 0.15*62 + 0.15*58 + 0.10*58 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*70 + 0.30*60 = 63.
systems Novelty 62 Rigor 58 Non-Obv 58 Completeness 68 Resilience 70 Impact 60
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation Block-diffusion drafters (e.g., DFlash) propose a whole block of tokens in one forward pass, making extra draft candidates nearly free to generate. Existing draft trees built from these position-wise marginals (DDTree, CaDDTree) verify every node of a fixed-budget tree, and the set of verified nodes is always a prefix of the drafter's own probability ranking. Under concurrent serving this is costly: low-yield branches consume target-model query rows that other requests need, and DDTree's own authors report accepted length keeps growing after speedup peaks. Chain-based adaptive methods (DSpark, SpecDec++, dynamic lookahead) learn how long a linear prefix to verify, but a single length cannot express which branches of a tree deserve verification, since branches at the same depth differ in value. The open problem is deciding, per decoding round, both the size and the shape of the verified subtree as a function of current batch load. Key Idea The core insight is that DSpark's learned chain-prefix survival rule generalizes from chains to trees: replace a per-position conditional acceptance estimate with a per-node conditional survival estimate, take the product of scores along each parent chain, and threshold the product — this yields an ancestor-closed subtree whose size is emergent (a confident deep branch survives while an uncertain shallow sibling is pruned), and whose threshold can be set batch-wide from the current load and the target's matmul tile size rather than from a single-request latency table. Methodology The pipeline per decoding round: (1) a frozen six-layer block-diffusion drafter (DFlash architecture, horizon D=15, 32,768-token compressed vocabulary) produces position-wise marginals from target features; (2) a best-first GPU heap builds a bounded candidate tree of B=15 non-root nodes ranked by draft path log-probability; (3) a shared affine head q(v) = σ(w_h·h_d + w_e·e_a + α·log p_d(a) + b) scores each depth–token pair; (4) path survival S(v) = ∏ q(u) over ancestors is thresholded (additive in log space, so a branch survives while its accumulated surprisal stays within −log δ), producing the retained subtree; (5) all retained trees across the batch are verified in one ancestor-masked target pass via a Triton tree-attention kernel derived from vLLM's paged attention, with CUDA-graph capture, KV compaction of the accepted path, and state replay for hybrid gated-DeltaNet targets. Serving thresholds: δ_t = 0 (verify whole trees) up to R_full requests; beyond that, retain the top N_tot nodes batch-wide, with N_tot filling the last matmul tile (s=64). Training is head-only on a frozen drafter with weighted BCE over conditional labels on the full candidate tree (positive = reference token under matched parent; siblings negative; descendants of unmatched parents unlabeled), with depth-decay weights; an optional joint mode adds coverage-weighted token loss (blended with D-PACE weights) and a reference-prefix ranking loss. Critical design decisions: separating the construction score ℓ (which bounds the candidate set) from the survival score S (which decides verification) — justified; conditioning on load via a tile-aligned batch-wide budget rather than per-request latency tables — justified by the measured 12–30% latency jump when a pass crosses a tile boundary; hand-set allocation tables (R_full=8, n̄=7/5) per GPU — a convenience choice retuned empirically on the A800 rather than derived. Key Results Across six verifiers (Qwen3.5-4B/9B, InternVL3.5-4B/8B, Gemma 4 E2B/E4B) and 17 text/multimodal benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME25, HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, MT-Bench, OmniDocBench, OCRBench-v2, DocVQA, olmOCR, CharXiv, TextVQA, MMMU-Pro, GQA, COCO Caption, MM-MT-Bench), D3Tree is fastest in 70 of 72 verifier–group–load settings. At R=1 it reaches 3.17–6.03× over autoregressive decoding depending on verifier/GPU (e.g., Qwen3.5-9B: 4.40× text); at R=64 it retains 1.13–2.08× while DDTree falls to 0.17–0.94× and is below AR on most configurations (0.26–0.84× across all benchmarks). It is at least 1.15× faster than the best CaDDTree budget at every load. Pruning at R≥16 halves verified rows (15.0 → 5.8–8.5 nodes) at a cost of only 0.6–0.8 accepted tokens. In serving, 200 requests at concurrency 64 complete in 131.8 s (1,301 tokens/s) versus 215 s for DDTree and 139 s for AR; under a seven-phase Poisson arrival trace (0.6–10 req/s), it achieves the lowest mean end-to-end latency in every phase (55.4 s mean overall, versus 58.8 s for DSpark and 73.8 s for AR). Baselines are current (2024–2026 work) and run on an identical runtime, with CaDDTree honestly reimplemented and its light-load gap partially attributed by the authors to implementation overhead. Scale is standard: ≤100 prompts per benchmark, ≤1024 output tokens, ≤64 concurrent sequences. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD (learned conditional node-survival pruning of block-diffusion draft trees, extending chain-level learned length control to branching parent chains) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (tile-aligned batch-wide node budget, fused survival head, GPU-resident overlapped execution). The individual ingredients — best-first tree construction (DDTree), conditional acceptance heads (DSpark), D-PACE loss weighting, tree-masked verification (SpecInfer), paged attention (vLLM) — are existing; the genuinely new part is the load-dependent coupling of learned node survival to a shared, hardware-aligned verification budget across the batch. Rigor & Reproducibility The evaluation is unusually broad for this literature: six verifiers, 17 benchmarks, six loads, four GPUs, two serving workloads, and budget sweeps B ∈ {15,31,63,127} for baselines and D3Tree. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; no code, weights, or dataset release is stated; the allocation tables (R_full, n̄) are hand-tuned per GPU and retuned on the A800 using only six benchmarks × 48 prompts, a possible Goodhart risk on that GPU's numbers; CaDDTree is the authors' reimplementation, and the authors candidly attribute part of the R=1 gap over it to their own unfused implementation (23.0 ms vs 15.4 ms median round). A notable missing ablation: pruning by the learned survival score is never compared against pruning the same tree by raw draft path probability, so the learned head's marginal value over a cheap heuristic is unmeasured; likewise, the optional joint training mode is described in detail but never evaluated at scale (the authors admit this). The lossless-greedy property is argued by induction and explicitly conditioned on batched-kernel numerical parity, which is not empirically validated. Deployability Profile: SYSTEMS — a built serving system on vLLM, evaluated by deployment-style throughput/latency experiments. - Practical: Yes — runs on a single 32–80 GB consumer/datacenter GPU (RTX 5090, RTX 6000 Ada, A6000, A800) within a standard vLLM build; the head needs only unquantized FP16/BF16 target embeddings. - Efficient: The head itself costs O(RDH + RDK) per round with a one-time vocabulary-table build; pruning cuts per-pass query rows from ~1,010 to ~382 at 64 concurrent requests, which is where the throughput gains come from. - Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated problem for greedy decoding under batching — highest throughput in 70/72 load settings and lowest latency in all trace phases — but only under greedy verification; quality-preservation rests on a lossless-by-construction argument, not on measured output equivalence. - Scalable: Tested only to 64 concurrent sequences and 1,024-tree-row CUDA graphs; behavior beyond 64 in-flight requests, tensor-parallel serving beyond one shard, or much longer contexts is claimed by design, not measured. The work delivers a system integrated into vLLM (Triton tree-attention kernel, fused survival head, CUDA-graphed execution) but no public artifact release is mentioned — it stops at paper form. Strengths - The load-dependent batch-wide node allocation is a genuinely new control point: prior adaptive methods (CaDDTree's latency table, DSpark's scheduler) size verification per request, whereas D3Tree lets confident deep branches in one request displace uncertain shallow branches of another, which is the right abstraction under batching. - The head is fitted on a frozen drafter with conditional labels on the full candidate tree (supervising positives the current head would prune), making it a drop-in addition to an existing DFlash drafter without changing proposals — an operationally clean design. - Exceptionally honest and precise measurement practice: same drafter, runtime, and prompts for every strategy; DDTree trees at B=15 are exactly the trees D3Tree prunes; implementation overhead is separated from algorithmic gains; failures (DSpark winning 11 of 72 A800 settings, DFlash ahead on the smallest verifier at low load) are reported and diagnosed rather than buried. - The numerical-parity caveat for greedy losslessness and the tree/replay machinery for hybrid DeltaNet targets show real systems depth beyond the headline algorithm. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state two limitations directly: (1) on the A800, the per-step cost of tree verification on hybrid targets (tree attention plus GDN state replay) lets dynamically truncated chains (DSpark) overtake D3Tree under heavy load, and they attribute this to kernel cost rather than allocation; (2) verification is greedy only — no support for stochastic sampling, path-dependent penalties, or logits processors — with tree pruning under sampling left to future work. They also note the joint training mode is unevaluated at scale. This is a credibility positive: limitations are confronted specifically, with a diagnosis of where the A800 gap comes from, not minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No ablation separating the learned survival head from load-aware allocation: an oracle-free baseline that prunes the B=15 tree by draft path probability under the same batch-wide budget would test whether learning matters, and is absent. - No error bars or repeated runs; with ≤100 prompts per benchmark and throughput ratios often within 0.01× of competitors (e.g., DSpark ahead by 0.01× in two A800 settings), several of the 70/72 and 61/72 claims are within likely noise. - The allocation tables (R_full, n̄, and the A800 retuning) are tuned on the same benchmarks used for reporting, so the retuned A800 numbers carry mild selection risk the paper does not flag. - Losslessness under greedy decoding is asserted conditionally on numerical parity of batched kernels but never verified empirically (e.g., output-string equality against autoregressive decoding), and output quality metrics beyond throughput/accepted length are not reported. - The paper is a preprint (arXiv:2611.11371) with no stated peer review and no code or model release, so the reimplementation-heavy comparisons cannot be independently checked. - Generality is narrower than the six-verifier framing suggests: all drafters share one architecture (DFlash), one horizon (D=15), and one vocabulary (32,768), and the drafter was trained on 1M prompts regenerated by each verifier — a setup the method is co-designed with. Bottom Line A practitioner building speculative decoding for block-diffusion drafters under concurrent load should read this — it is the strongest and most honestly evaluated treatment of load-aware tree verification available — but its learned-head contribution remains unproven against cheap heuristics, and the system is unverified for stochastic sampling, large-scale serving, and public reproduction.

Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?

S Luo, Y Huang, M Li, H Luo, G Deng, H Wang, J Xu… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EvalAlloc, an evaluation-allocation framework for LLM-driven agent scaffold evolution that splits a fixed evaluation budget between sparse search-time feedback (a fully evaluated warm-up, a shared informative item core, and a fixed item-response model) and warm-started paired successive halving for final scaffold selection. - Why it's important: Evaluating every candidate scaffold on every task instance dominates the cost of evolutionary agent optimization — each cell involves multiple LLM calls and tool executions — so halving evaluation cells at equal-or-better final scaffold quality directly reduces the dominant expense of automated agent design. - How it does it: The core trick is decoupling evaluation's two roles: a short full-evaluation warm-up calibrates a low-rank MIRT-style response model and selects a shared informative item core so sparse scores stay comparable across candidates (common-random-numbers variance reduction on correlated responses), while cached search observations are reused so final successive halving executes only missing cells and corrects heterogeneous item sets with a regression (difference) estimator. - The good: Across 4 benchmarks × 2 evolution frameworks × 3 seeds, EvalAlloc beats full evaluation on 4-benchmark mean TEST score (0.7084 vs 0.6973 on ShinkaEvolve; 0.7226 vs 0.7091 on AdaEvolve) at roughly half the evaluation cells (43.8% / 46.4%), with ablations cleanly attributing the largest gains to informative item sharing and final confirmation. - The missing: No code or data release is mentioned, statistical significance is never tested (3 seeds, overlapping standard deviations in several cells), and the budget-allocation hyperparameter studies are run only on DROP with one framework, leaving the generality of the W=10 / k=60 / 30%-search configuration unverified. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone running expensive evolutionary or search-based agent/prompt optimization loops, since the replay-based investigation and the search-vs-selection decomposition are directly actionable; skip it if you only care about single-shot LLM benchmarking, where tinyBenchmarks and SparseEval already cover sparse estimation.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (65) anchors on the genuinely new two-decision formulation of evaluation allocation (comparable search feedback vs. reliable final selection); the components are established but the composition and replay methodology are principled. Rigor (60) is the weak dimension: only 3 seeds with no significance tests, headline margins within one SD on several benchmarks, missing direct baselines (tinyBenchmarks, SparseEval, CollabEval), and no code release despite many hyperparameters. Non-Obviousness (70) is strong — the common-random-numbers variance argument connecting CRN theory to shared informative items is an actionable reframing. Completeness (70) benefits from candid acknowledgment of the response model's small marginal contribution and token-cost gaps. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*60 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*45 = 63.
empirical Novelty 65 Rigor 60 Non-Obv 70 Completeness 70 Resilience 60 Impact 45
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: LLM-driven scaffold evolution (e.g., ShinkaEvolve, AdaEvolve, ADAS, AFlow) iteratively proposes executable agent programs and uses evaluation scores both to update the search archive and to pick the final program. Full evaluation is expensive: with 80 proposals × 300 search items, a single run costs 24,000 scaffold–item executions, each potentially involving multi-step LLM, retrieval, and tool use. Prior cost-reduction work (tinyBenchmarks, SparseEval, CollabEval, evaluation cascades) treats evaluation purely as fitness estimation, ignoring that scaffold evolution uses the same evaluation budget for two decisions with different requirements: cheap, comparable feedback during search versus reliable discrimination among the top few candidates at the end. The paper asks how a limited budget should be split across these two roles — a question no prior efficient-evaluation work addresses in the evolutionary setting. Key Idea: The central insight is that the two evaluation roles have different statistical needs and should not share the same policy. During search, evolved candidates are highly correlated, so evaluating them on a shared set of informative items exploits response covariance to reduce the variance of pairwise score differences (the common-random-numbers effect: Var(Δ̂) = (σ²ₐ + σ²_b − 2σ_ab)/k vs. (σ²ₐ + σ²_b)/k with independent items), while a fixed, warm-up-calibrated response model keeps all scores on one full-set reference scale. At final selection, reliability matters more than cost, so a successive-halving tournament that reuses every cached search observation concentrates fresh evaluations only on competitive candidates. Once this decomposition is understood, the whole pipeline follows from combining item-response theory, CRN, and successive halving. Methodology: EvalAlloc is a drop-in evaluator with three stages. (1) Core Calibration: the first W=10 valid candidates are fully evaluated on all N=300 SEARCH items; item informativeness is estimated via a Beta posterior with a conservative lower confidence bound I_i = 4(E[X_i] − z√Var(X_i)) on the variance-like statistic X_i = p_i(1−p_i); a low-rank logistic MIRT model q_ci = σ(μ + η_i + b_c + u_iᵀv_c), d=2, is fit by regularized cross-entropy, and its item parameters and candidate prior are then frozen. (2) Shared-Core Evolution: each subsequent candidate is evaluated on k=60 items — a fixed top-k₀=54 informative core plus k−k₀ adaptively sampled items via Gumbel-top-k (τ=0.001) on informativeness logits — and only its candidate parameters (b_c, v_c) are MAP-inferred under the fixed prior, producing a completed full-set fitness estimate (observed + predicted outcomes) returned to the unchanged native evolution framework. (3) Warm-Started Selection: duplicates (identical ASTs) are merged; paired successive halving runs R=4 rounds over shared item prefixes (30/60/120/300, keeping 30/15/8/1 candidates), executing only cells missing from the cached observations; from round 2, scores use a difference estimator Ĥ_r(c) = union mean + λ_r × (predicted full-set mean − predicted union mean), with λ_r fit as a pooled within-candidate regression slope clipped to [0, 1.5], and the response model refitted with two-fold cross-fitting to avoid self-correction bias. The final round observes all N items, so the ultimate pick rests on fully observed outcomes. Design decisions are mostly well-justified: the shared-core variance argument is given explicitly, and the ablation confirms informative items and final confirmation matter most (the response model's marginal contribution, −0.0119 average, is honestly reported as small). Less justified is the specific configuration (W=10, k=60, R=4 prefixes, 30% search budget), which the analysis tunes only on DROP. Key Results: Tested on HotpotQA, HoVer, DROP, and IFBench (300/150/300 splits), with two evolution frameworks (ShinkaEvolve; AdaEvolve via SkyDiscover), 80 proposals per run, 3 seeds, Qwen3.5-9B executor and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 proposer on 8×H20 GPUs. Headline: EvalAlloc averages 0.7084 (ShinkaEvolve) and 0.7226 (AdaEvolve) TEST score versus 0.6973 and 0.7091 for Full evaluation, at 43.8% and 46.4% of the evaluation cells; it also beats Random partial evaluation (0.6908 / 0.6894) and Cascade (0.6948 / 0.7006) at comparable cost. On ShinkaEvolve DROP, EvalAlloc reaches 0.8907 vs Full's 0.8832 at 43.3% vs 77.1% cost. Token savings lag cell savings (64.76% of Full's tokens on ShinkaEvolve) because higher-scoring candidates and high-variability items consume more tokens per cell — an honest cost analysis few papers provide. The replay study is a distinctive result: under matched budgets, shared-informative items with a model estimator achieve 0.732 close-pair agreement and 0.0043 archive regret versus 0.626/0.0078 for independent random items. Skip-Eval ablations show unguided search collapses (0.5039 ShinkaEvolve average) and that successive halving alone cannot fully recover it (0.6776). Baselines are reasonable (Skip Eval, SH-only, Random, Cascade, Full) but omit adapting established sparse-evaluation methods (tinyBenchmarks, CollabEval) as direct competitors. Scale is standard (300-item benchmarks, 80 proposals), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION plus NEW METHOD. Genuinely novel: framing evaluation allocation in scaffold evolution as a two-decision problem (search feedback vs. final selection) with distinct statistical requirements, and the empirical demonstration that sparse comparable feedback plus targeted confirmation beats uniform evaluation. The components themselves — MIRT-based sparse benchmark estimation (tinyBenchmarks, CollabEval, Growing Pains), common random numbers, successive halving, and difference estimators — are all established; the contribution is their principled composition and the supporting investigation, which is more than a standard plug-together but falls short of a fundamentally new algorithmic primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist and are informative: removing informative item selection costs −0.0291 average, skipping final confirmation −0.0173, removing the response model −0.0119 — a clean component attribution. Three seeds per setting with standard deviations are reported, but no significance tests, and several cells (e.g., ShinkaEvolve HoVer 0.7278±0.0847) have overlapping error bars. Replay analyses reuse the 24 Full trajectories to isolate evaluator effects while holding candidate sequences fixed — a methodologically sound control. No code, data, or artifact release is mentioned. Concerns: budget-allocation hyperparameters (W, k, search share, selection prefixes) are examined only on DROP with ShinkaEvolve, so the defaults may be tuned to that setting; SEARCH/DEV/TEST splits are respected (selection happens on SEARCH, TEST used only once), avoiding Goodhart on TEST; the response-model hyperparameter λ_r clipping to [0, 1.5] is heuristic; and all experiments use one executor family by default, with only two single-benchmark swaps (gpt-oss-120b proposer, Llama-3.1-8B executor) to probe generality, where the paper itself notes relative strategy rankings shift across model configurations. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — a drop-in evaluator component). Practical: Yes — runs on a single 8×H20 node with locally served open models, and it is a drop-in evaluator needing no changes to the underlying evolution framework. Efficient: Its entire point — ~44–47% of the evaluation cells and 45–65% of executor tokens relative to full evaluation, versus 100% for Full and ~24% for SH-only at much lower quality. Effective: Evidence supports the claim on four QA-style benchmarks with two frameworks, though the benefit is a mean improvement within seed noise on some benchmarks rather than a decisive win, and effectiveness on genuinely agentic (web/tool) tasks is untested. Scalable: Not tested beyond 80 proposals / 300 items; the informative-item core, warm-up calibration, and SH prefixes are defined relative to these scales, and behavior at 10× items or candidates is only claimed, not measured. Delivers no software artifact — the work stops at paper form (no library, CLI, or released code is stated). Strengths: (1) The replay-based investigation design — holding candidate sequences fixed and varying only observed cells — isolates the causal effect of evaluation policy on search decisions, which is a genuinely careful experimental methodology rare in this literature. (2) The problem decomposition itself (search needs cheap comparable scores; selection needs reliable discrimination) is an actionable insight that reframes how practitioners should think about evaluator design in evolution loops. (3) The covariance argument for shared items is stated mathematically and validated empirically (0.732 vs 0.626 close-pair agreement at matched budget), connecting CRN theory to a concrete LLM-evaluation practice. (4) The token-cost analysis, showing cell savings overstate token savings because better scaffolds spend more tokens, confronts a real gap between the cost metric and the actual bill. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that warm-up length differences fall within seed-to-seed variation, that the response model's contribution is small and inconsistent once the shared core exists, that token savings are not proportional to cell savings due to execution-cost heterogeneity, that relative strategy rankings vary across proposer/executor model configurations, and that realized costs differ between frameworks due to invalid-proposal handling. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them, which strengthens credibility. They do not, however, explicitly flag the DROP-only tuning of budget hyperparameters or the absence of a code release. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Missing baselines: tinyBenchmarks, SparseEval, and CollabEval are discussed as related work but never run as competing allocators under matched budgets — the comparison set (Skip Eval, Random, Cascade, Full) is weaker than the related-work section implies. (2) Only 3 seeds with no significance testing; several headline margins (e.g., ShinkaEvolve HoVer, IFBench under AdaEvolve) are within one standard deviation. (3) Benchmark scope is four static QA/instruction-following datasets, despite a motivation framed around Web-facing agents; dynamic or tool-execution-heavy evaluation (where item informativeness drifts most) is untested. (4) The Beta-posterior informativeness score and MIRT model assume roughly binary/graded item outcomes that transfer across candidates within a run; behavior under distribution shift within long runs (candidate population drifting far from the warm-up prior) is analyzed only via a brief offline remark that very long warm-ups hurt later sparsity. (5) No released code or reproduction path, so the many hyperparameters (τ=0.001, z=2, d=2, ρ=1, clipping bound 1.5, prefix schedule) cannot be independently verified. (6) Cross-fitted refitting and SH during selection happen on the same SEARCH split used to guide evolution, so mild selection-on-search bias toward the trajectory's own feedback scale is possible, though TEST-only final scoring mitigates it. Bottom Line: A practitioner running LLM-based evolutionary agent or prompt optimization should read this: the search-vs-selection budget decomposition is immediately actionable, the replay methodology is worth imitating, and the ~2× evaluation-cost reduction with equal-or-better final scaffold quality is a real, ablated result — even if the missing baselines, three-seed evidence, and absent code release mean the specific EvalAlloc configuration should be re-tuned, not copied, for your own workloads.

The RSI Tax: When Recursive Self - Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost

Y Zhang, A Li, Y Wang · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper introduces the "RSI Tax" — an end-to-end token-cost accounting of recursive self-improvement procedures in LLM agents — and shows that a trivial bounded-note baseline (SRN) matches or exceeds the accuracy of three sophisticated RSI methods on task streams while spending 65.6–71.0% fewer total tokens. - Why it's important: The self-improvement process itself can consume more tokens than executing the entire task stream (tax rates up to 393% of execution cost), meaning current agentic self-improvement methods may destroy value at deployment time — a cost that prior evaluations systematically omit. - How it does it: It replays six methods (Static, ReasoningBank, Meta-Harness, EvoSkill, RRSI, SRN) on common sequential task streams, scoring each task before its feedback is used, and decomposes the RSI Tax into verification, exploration, and writing costs, then tracks whether the produced artifacts are ever used downstream. - The good: The decomposition is decisive — verification alone accounts for 74.8–93.6% of the RSI Tax for the three expensive methods, and 23.7–63.6% of their tax buys states/artifacts that are never used again, with concrete traces (e.g., a 603,841-token candidate evaluation that provably could not change the acceptance decision). - The missing: No repeated runs, seeds, or variance estimates — single runs per method-setting with two backbones and one fixed task ordering, so the headline accuracy differences (often 2–4 points) have unknown stability. - Read it or not: Anyone building self-improving or memory-based agents should read it — it provides a cost-accounting discipline their evaluations almost certainly lack — while researchers outside the agent-harness area can safely skip it.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents deployed on streams of related tasks (e.g., successive tasks in the same repository) can update persistent state — memories, skills, harness code — from task experience. The literature on recursive self-improvement (RSI) evaluates whether such updates improve accuracy, but ignores the token cost of the improvement process itself: candidate validation, extra rollouts, proposal generation. A practitioner paying per token needs to know whether accuracy gains amortize the full cost of obtaining them, a trade-off no prior RSI evaluation measures end-to-end. The paper targets agent builders and benchmark designers who currently report accuracy (and sometimes execution cost) but not update cost. Key Idea: The core insight is an accounting identity plus a control: charge all tokens spent attempting an update — including abandoned candidates — as a "tax" on top of task-execution cost, and decompose that tax by operation (verify/explore/write) and by whether the resulting artifact is ever used later. The control, SRN (Simple Reflection with Notes), shows what a minimal competitor looks like: revise a single 2,048-token note from recent failures every four tasks, with no search, no candidate validation, no retrieval. Once you accept the accounting, the expensive methods' economics collapse on their own. Methodology: Streaming evaluation: tasks x1..xT arrive in fixed order; each task is executed under state st, scored by a binary verifier V before its feedback enters history Ht. Total cost N(t) = task-execution tokens + RSI Tax (Equations 1–3), with the tax further partitioned into verification (support-task validation of incumbents/candidates), exploration (rollouts, trajectory judgment, embeddings), and writing (state revision), plus an Other residual, and cross-tabulated by downstream use of the associated artifact (Equations 5–6). Six methods are run under identical update windows (every four tasks, except ReasoningBank's per-task workflow) on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GPT-6 Luna across SWE-Chain-Evo (105 positions, 7 chains, state resets between chains) and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (89 tasks, persistent state) — 2,328 scored method-task pairs. SRN is defined by a truncation operator Limit2048 applied to a generator output conditioned on the prior note and failed-trajectory excerpts (Equation 7). Critical design decisions: (1) a strict information boundary (no future tasks, reference solutions, or hidden tests) — well justified and carefully documented; (2) adapting EvoSkill to rolling support-set frontier refresh and Meta-Harness to a strict-improvement selector — necessary for streaming but these implementation choices inflate the measured tax (the authors concede this in Appendix D); (3) the downstream-use label measures retrieval/use, not measured accuracy effect — explicitly flagged as descriptive. No explicit learning objective is optimized; this is measurement, not algorithm design. Key Results: SRN achieves the highest observed accuracy in three of four settings and ties EvoSkill in the fourth: e.g., 48.6% vs. Static 43.8% and Meta-Harness 45.7% on DeepSeek/SWE-Chain-Evo; 78.7% vs. Static 69.7% and Meta-Harness 77.5% on DeepSeek/Terminal-Bench. Mean token savings vs. Meta-Harness/EvoSkill/RRSI are 65.6%/71.0%/68.2% (within-setting ratio averaging). RSI Tax rates reach 109–393% of execution cost for the three expensive methods (e.g., EvoSkill DeepSeek terminal: 716.46M RSI tokens vs. 182.26M task tokens; of that, 497.45M is old-frontier refresh alone). Verification dominates: 74.8% (Meta-Harness), 78.1% (EvoSkill), 93.6% (RRSI) of aggregate tax. Unused-artifact shares: 52.78% (Meta-Harness), 37.91% (EvoSkill), 63.57% (ReasoningBank), 23.70% (RRSI). Omitting the tax reverses cost rankings: on DeepSeek terminal, Meta-Harness uses fewer execution tokens than SRN (184.13M vs. 214.37M) but totals 762.57M vs. 214.65M at slightly lower accuracy. Baselines are recent (2026-era methods, several from ICLR/EMNLP 2026), though all are reimplementations/adaptations by the authors. Scale is standard, not stress-scale: ~200 tasks per stream. The counter-intuitive headline is that a near-free note beats search-heavy self-improvement end-to-end. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus a NEW FORMULATION (the end-to-end RSI Tax accounting and verify/explore/write/use decomposition); SRN itself is essentially Dynamic Cheatsheet-style bounded-note adaptation, a deliberate non-novel control. The genuinely novel part is the cost-side evaluation protocol and the verification-dominated, partially-wasted cost structure; the individual methods compared are existing work, and cost-aware harness selection (HarnessPro) already existed without the update-cost term. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations in the traditional sense, but the decomposition analysis is the functional equivalent — it isolates which cost components dominate. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests: each cell is a single run (stated in Limitations). Token accounting is unusually careful — per-stage tables reconcile to totals, embedding tokens counted, retries charged, cached input included, rounding discrepancies disclosed. Full prompts, configuration, and support sizes are in Appendices A–D. No code or data release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (1) the authors reimplemented Meta-Harness (strict selector, one search iteration) and EvoSkill (rolling frontier refresh) in ways that demonstrably generate wasteful costs — e.g., the decision-invariant 603,841-token validation arose from their strict-acceptance rule, which the original population-based Meta-Harness lacks, so some of the "tax" may be an artifact of the authors' streaming adaptations rather than the published methods; (2) aggregates sum tokens across different tokenizers; (3) the downstream-use metric is explicitly not a causal measure, and the authors say so repeatedly. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (measurement study with a baseline method, no new system). - Practical: Yes — all methods run via API calls on two commercially available models; SRN needs nothing beyond standard inference. - Efficient: SRN's update cost is <0.4% of its total tokens; the expensive methods spend 109–393% of execution cost on updates, which the paper quantifies precisely. - Effective: The evidence shows the tax exists and that SRN is competitive on these streams; it does not show SRN generalizes (single orderings, no reruns) and the use/attribution analysis is descriptive rather than causal. - Scalable: Not tested — streams of 89–105 tasks; behavior over thousands of tasks, or whether verification waste compounds or amortizes, is unexamined (authors note repeated reuse may justify larger investments). The paper delivers no software artifact; it stops at paper form with detailed protocol specifications. Strengths: - The cost-accounting formulation is a genuine conceptual contribution: by charging abandoned candidates and validation to the update process and reporting the tax rate, it converts a vague intuition ("self-improvement is expensive") into falsifiable, per-setting numbers. - The verification-dominated decomposition (74.8–93.6%) and the frontier-refresh finding (497.45M tokens re-scoring old skills vs. 182.26M serving new tasks on one stream) pinpoint a specific, actionable failure mode rather than a diffuse critique. - The decision-invariant-evaluation diagnostic (Appendix D.1.2) is a clever, formally defined waste detector: identifying calls whose outcome provably cannot change the acceptance decision. - Honest handling of evidence boundaries — the authors repeatedly distinguish token shares from causal effects and flag where their adaptations (strict selector, rolling refresh) drive the observed waste, which is rare and credibility-positive. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Stated in Section 6: only two backbones, seven repository chains, one terminal-benchmark ordering; no repeated runs, so stability is unknown; the cost attribution is descriptive — later use does not establish accuracy benefit, and non-use does not establish that the calls could be removed without changing downstream outcomes; no controlled interventions on cost components; no policy that forecasts and selects updates was evaluated. The authors confront limitations directly and at appropriate length. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The streaming adaptations of Meta-Harness and EvoSkill (strict-improvement selector; rolling frontier refresh replacing the fixed validation set) are author-chosen configurations that the paper's own case studies show generate large wasteful costs — the headline "RSI methods waste 65–71% of tokens" partially measures the authors' deployment rules, not the original methods, and this is acknowledged only obliquely. - ReasoningBank underperforms Static on accuracy in the SWE settings (40.0 vs. 43.8; 37.1 vs. 38.1), yet it is run with its memory-aware test-time scaling removed — leaving open whether all compared methods are operating at their published strength. - No monetary or latency analysis: token counts conflate cached input, output, and embedding prices, which the authors note but do not resolve; a pricing-weighted comparison could change rankings. - SRN's advantage over Static is modest in mean (4.7 points for 3.6% more tokens) and its terminal-stream gain (9.0 points) rests on one run of one ordering; a single unlucky ordering could plausibly flip the conclusion, which the single-seed design cannot rule out. - The unused-artifact metric counts tokens, not update frequency or counterfactual value; an artifact used rarely but decisively would score as waste, and no experiment tests whether pruning it hurts accuracy. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or evaluating self-improving agents should read this paper — its accounting framework alone will change how they benchmark — but the headline claims rest on single runs with author-adapted method reimplementations, so treat the specific savings percentages as a well-instrumented existence proof of the problem, not a calibrated measurement of any particular published method's inefficiency.

Problem & Motivation: Given a chemical composition and physical conditions, predict the periodic atomic arrangement that minimizes enthalpy (or free energy). The candidate space grows exponentially with cell size, the landscape is rugged with near-degenerate minima separated by meV/atom, and correct ranking requires an energy model of adequate accuracy. The field spans 30 years of methods — from template construction and random search through USPEX/CALYPSO evolutionary and swarm optimization to diffusion, flow, and autoregressive generators — but prior reviews either covered only energy-minimization/ML acceleration (Graser et al., Li et al.), only generative models (Chen et al.), or organized methods by era rather than by mechanism. Practitioners lack a principled way to compare methods whose reported evaluations answer different questions. Key Idea: The organizing insight is that CSP workflows decompose into proposal (how candidates are constructed/explored), evaluation (how they are relaxed and ranked), and qualification (what a result physically means) — and that these dimensions are independent and must be evaluated separately. The survey operationalizes this with a seven-family taxonomy (construction/template, random, evolutionary, swarm/DE, landscape, adaptive ML-guided, learned generation) and, crucially, with a hierarchy of evaluation questions (recovery, search efficiency, ranking, thermodynamic qualification, diversity/novelty, generalization, prospective prediction) where each question is paired with required reporting and its principal limitation. The most consequential analytical move is a task-contract audit: for formula-conditioned generation, exact count preservation (Eq. 6: element counts must match the requested cell inventory) is checked against papers and code for 42 models, exposing that "formula-conditioned" often means only a reduced-ratio filter or an unenforced embedding. Methodology: The survey is built on a curated, source-linked corpus of 210 records (136 inorganic, 54 molecular, plus cross-domain, surface/cluster, review, and enabling records; 196 initial + 14 added), collected via targeted searches and citation chaining, with bibliographic verification against Crossref and a supplementary catalogue with stable identifiers. Section coverage proceeds from problem formalization — X = (A, F, L), enthalpy objective H(X;p) = E + pV — through each search family with algorithmic depth (e.g., USPEX heredity/mutation operators with fingerprint-based niche control; CALYPSO's particle-swarm update with bond-characterization-matrix deduplication; diffusion's forward corruption/reverse denoising on fractional coordinates and lattices; flow matching via dX_t/dt = v_theta; Wyckoff multiplicity balance Eq. 3 as a necessary feasibility condition). Three original analyses: (1) a T46 leaderboard snapshot (46 targets, 20 algorithms, pymatgen StructureMatcher with declared tolerances, failures in the denominator, 95% percentile-bootstrap intervals over targets); (2) the experimental-discovery audit extending Oganov et al.'s 2018 list to 2026, with each entry graded on prediction-vs-experiment ordering (P/J/S) and evidence strength (S/C/D); (3) the formula-conditioning audit based on documentation and code inspection, not execution. Critical design decisions: assigning each record one primary category (justified for counting but lossy for hybrids); treating the evaluator as a separate axis from search (well-justified — it prevents conflating learned-potential speedups with search-quality improvements); and grading experimental evidence on a three-level scale rather than binary confirmation (well-justified, given retracted superconductivity claims in the hydride space). Key Results: On the T46 leaderboard snapshot (17 Oct 2026, up to 20 candidates per target): TCSPv3 (template) recovers 35/46 targets (76.1%) at top-1 and 41/46 (89.1%) at top-20; Uni-3DAR recovers 32 (69.6%) and 33 (71.7%); uFlowCSP recovers 27 (58.7%) and 30 (65.2%). The best template method beats leading generative models at top-1, but paired tests do not establish statistically significant differences between TCSPv3 and several generative competitors (one target = 2.17 percentage points). TCSPv3's own audit on T180 shows that fixing coefficient-preserving simultaneous substitution raised top-1/top-20 from 28.3%/45.6% to 72.2%/90.6%, and it reports 74.0% top-20 on an 800-target cohort (T800). The 68-material audit finds 52 structurally confirmed predictions, 23 strictly prediction-first (16 of 23 at high pressure; median 3 years from prediction to confirmation, up to a decade+ for CaH6 and cg-N); 37 are joint theory–experiment studies and 8 are structure solutions of already-synthesized materials. Among ML-era claims, GNoME and A-Lab results are graded "disputed" and MatterGen's TaCr2O6 "consistent," not confirmed. The formula audit finds 21 of 42 inspected generative modes preserve exact cell counts, 19 do not establish it, and 2 document only unconditional sampling. Baselines are current (2024–2026 generative models including DiffCSP, MatterGen, CrystalFlow, FlowMM, Uni-3DAR), though global-search entries run under incomparable budgets — a caveat the authors state themselves. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus a synthesis survey: the genuinely novel contributions are (1) the first audited, evidence-graded catalogue of experimentally confirmed CSP discoveries extending to 2026, establishing that no deep generative model has an independently confirmed prediction-first discovery; (2) the formula-conditioning contract audit exposing a pervasive evaluation gap; and (3) a leaderboard analysis with bootstrap intervals showing template methods statistically indistinguishable from generative leaders. The taxonomy itself reorganizes known families by proposal mechanism rather than introducing new algorithms, and the per-family method descriptions are competent synthesis of existing literature. The headline negative result — generative-model discovery claims are unsupported by the experimental record — is the paper's non-obvious contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is a preprint (arXiv:2611.17670, November 2026) and has not been peer-reviewed. Ablation-style evidence is strongest in the TCSPv3 substitution audit (before/after fixing a single error source, +43.9 points top-1 on T180). Uncertainty is handled unusually well for the field: percentile-bootstrap 95% intervals over targets on the leaderboard, failures retained in denominators, declared matcher tolerances (ltol=0.2, stol=0.3, 5° angle), and explicit manifest versioning (T46/T180 v3.1). The corpus, 129-entry software directory, CSV export, and figure data are stated to accompany the paper as a companion repository (specific URLs not provided in the text). Methodological concerns: (1) the audit's method attributions partly rely on "the authors' established workflow" rather than paper statements (marked with daggers, but still attribution by inference); (2) the corpus is curated and non-exhaustive by the authors' own statement, so the historical counts in Figure 3 cannot support bibliometric conclusions; (3) the leaderboard is a single snapshot whose underlying runs use heterogeneous budgets; (4) the survey's most favorable quantitative story (TCSPv3's performance) centers on a method lineage that overlaps with the corresponding author's research area, and no conflict-of-interest statement appears in the provided text; (5) the formula audit classifies models from documentation/code reading, not execution — the authors flag this themselves. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper's original contribution is executed analyses — leaderboard comparison, audits — rather than a deployed system). Practical: Not applicable as software, but the surveyed workflows run on commodity clusters (ML-potential relaxation via M3GNet/MACE/ORB-v3 plus DFT verification is standard practice). Efficient: The survey does not run controlled cost comparisons; it explicitly warns that top-k recovery without runtime, evaluator calls, and candidate-selection cost makes budgets incomparable — a correct critique it does not itself resolve quantitatively. Effective: The evaluation-hierarchy framing is demonstrated to match the evidence (recovery ≠ discovery; 23 prediction-first cases vs. 52 confirmations), so the analytical contribution is effective for its stated purpose. Scalable: Not tested — the audit is bounded by the 68-material experimental record as of 2026, and the leaderboard by 46 targets; both are snapshots that will date. Deliverable form: a paper plus companion repository (corpus catalogue, software directory of 129 implementations, figure data); no new tool, dataset, or trained model is released by the authors themselves. Strengths: - The experimental-discovery audit is a real empirical contribution: per-material grading of prediction ordering and evidence strength across 68 cases, including the finding that 16 of 23 prediction-first successes are high-pressure phases — an honest structural explanation (pV dominance, small cells, relaxed kinetic constraints) of where CSP works, not just that it works. - The formula-conditioning audit converts a vague worry about generative-CSP evaluation into a concrete, checkable contract (Eq. 6) and classifies 42 models against it — this directly changes how future benchmarks should report results. - The separation of proposal, evaluation, and qualification axes defuses the misleading "classical vs. AI" framing and correctly predicts the paper's own headline result: a template method with a fixed bug outperforms generative leaders at top-1 on T46. - Unusual evaluation hygiene for a survey: failures in denominators, manifest versioning, matcher tolerances, training-exposure reporting rules, and bootstrap intervals — the benchmarking section (Sec. 12) is a standalone methodological contribution. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the curated corpus is not an exhaustive bibliometric census and cannot measure community adoption; that the 2026 interval is partial; that leaderboard budgets are not comparable across global-search entries (20 candidates ≠ equal compute); that paired tests fail to establish significant differences between TCSPv3 and generative competitors; that the formula audit rests on documentation/code inspection rather than execution; that benchmark recovery is a necessary but not sufficient condition for discovery; and that the absence of generative models from the confirmed record partly reflects that experimental validation takes years. They confront limitations directly and repeatedly — a strong credibility signal. They also flag that space-group conditioning can constitute privileged information and that leakage can enter through any workflow component (potentials, rerankers, template catalogues), not just the generator. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Possible conflict of interest: the top-ranked method on the survey's own snapshot (TCSPv3) and its lineage (TCSP, TCSP 2.0, CSPML, ParetoCSP/2) receive extensive favorable analysis, and the audit that "fixed" TCSP 2.0's errors produces the survey's largest improvement numbers; no conflict-of-interest or funding statement is visible in the provided text, and the corresponding author's group appears connected to this lineage based on the cited works. - The "no confirmed generative discovery" conclusion is partly a base-rate argument: generative CSP is roughly 4–5 years old, so few predictions have had time for experimental follow-up; the survey acknowledges the latency argument but does not attempt a sensitivity analysis (e.g., how many USPEX predictions existed within 4 years of USPEX's release, and how many were confirmed by then) to test whether generative methods are genuinely underperforming versus simply young. - The audit's evidence grading relies on the authors' judgment for disputed cases (e.g., GNoME, A-Lab graded "disputed" citing two critical analyses), with no inter-rater reliability or stated grading protocol. - Leaderboard statistical power: with 46 targets, even large-looking gaps (76.1% vs. 69.6% top-1) cannot reach significance; the survey reports this but does not compute the cohort size needed, which would tell readers whether T800-style expansion resolves the question. - Molecular-CSP coverage, while included, is thinner than inorganic coverage (54 vs. 136 records), and the seventh blind test discussion is brief relative to its methodological importance (separating generation from ranking). Bottom Line: For anyone building, benchmarking, or funding crystal-structure prediction methods — especially generative ones — this survey is essential reading for its audits and evaluation standards alone; its main quantitative comparisons should be read with awareness of the authors' apparent proximity to the top-ranked template lineage, but no competing survey covers the same 1996–2026 ground with comparable evaluative rigor.

Problem & Motivation: Researchers in music information retrieval (source separation, multi-instrument transcription, stem-conditioned generation) lack legally redistributable multitrack training data. Recorded corpora (MUSDB18: 10 h; MedleyDB: 13.8 h; MoisesDB: 14.4 h) are too small for training; Slakh2100 (145 h) renders non-licensed MIDI through proprietary VST sample libraries that cannot be redistributed; chamber-ensemble generators like CocoChorales cover narrow instrument sets. Prior work has thus forced a trade-off among realism, scale, and license openness, leaving multitrack tasks anchored to datasets years old. Key Idea: Render an existing large public-domain symbolic corpus (PDMX) with an entirely open, per-instrument-category synthesis recipe — selecting between redistributable soundfont banks and the open MIDI-DDSP neural synthesizer based on a small human listening pilot — so that the acoustic realism gap that made naive General MIDI rendering unusable is closed without incurring proprietary VST licensing. The per-category recipe selection plus a loudness/velocity-balancing scheme that keeps stems linearly summable is the core of the contribution; the synthesis tools themselves are all pre-existing. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Cleaning: GM programs are corrected from track-name aliases, tracks without note events are dropped, and silent regions (RMS < 0.01 in 0.25 s windows, ≈−40 dBFS) are excised to compute non-silent hours. (2) Recipe selection: a pilot study with N=8 listeners rating 10 s stem excerpts (0–100 realism, two stems per category) compares basic (single SGM-V2.01 GM bank), varied (sampled redistributable soundfonts: FluidR3, GeneralUser GS, Arachno, Airfont, plus light reverb), and MIDI-DDSP hybrids (with FluidSynth fallback for polyphonic/out-of-inventory parts, 16 kHz output upsampled to 44.1 kHz). The frozen recipe uses basic for drums/organ/guitar, varied for piano/voice/mallet/miscellaneous, MIDI-DDSP+basic for strings/brass, and MIDI-DDSP+varied for wind. (3) Assembly: each stem is loudness-normalized toward −23 LUFS with peak limiting, scaled by the ratio of its track's max note-on velocity to the global max velocity, and a single anti-clip gain is applied to the stem sum, guaranteeing the mixture equals the sum of stems (following Slakh2100's convention). Validation runs two fixed-budget experiments: Hybrid Demucs trained from scratch for 32,000 updates (batch 8, 10 s mono-duplicated-to-stereo crops) on a matched 632-song BDGP subset (600 train/32 val), and a YourMT3-style T5-small encoder–decoder trained from scratch for 100,000 steps on mixture–MIDI pairs. The pilot-as-design-guidance and the linear-summability construction are the two most consequential decisions; the recipe freeze on 16 excerpts per category is weakly justified, while the summability scheme directly follows prior practice. Key Results: Dataset: 253,982 songs / 490,159 mono stems / 5,469 song-hours; 88,403 songs (34.8%) are multitrack totaling 2,734 song-hours — over 18× Slakh2100's 145 h. Source separation (SI-SDR, Hybrid Demucs, single run per condition): the SPDMX-trained model reaches 9.5 dB (BD) / 3.9 dB (GP) in-domain on 32 held-out SPDMX songs versus Slakh-trained models at 0.2/−4.1 dB there; on real recordings, Slakh-trained reaches 10.3/3.7 on Slakh2100, SPDMX-trained −0.5 BD on MUSDB18 (vs. −1.7 for Slakh), 1.2/−10.2 on MoisesDB (comparable to Slakh), and the union-trained model achieves the best real-domain BD results (MoisesDB 2.4, MedleyDB −2.5). Transcription (onset F1 / Multi F1, mean ± 95% CI): on Slakh2100's test split, Slakh- and SPDMX-trained models tie near 0.072–0.075 onset F1, but on a held-out SPDMX split the SPDMX-trained model reaches 0.265/0.191 versus 0.041/0.010 for the Slakh-trained model, suggesting worse generalization of Slakh training than SPDMX training under matched budgets. All absolute transcription scores are low by design (no pretraining, small model). Separation baselines are current-relevant architectures but not pretrained state-of-the-art systems; comparisons are against Slakh2100 as the primary synthetic alternative. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET (and marginally NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING on cross-dataset generalization of synthetic training data). The synthesis pipeline is a competent combination of existing tools — FluidSynth soundfonts, MIDI-DDSP weights, and Slakh-style summable mixing — applied to the new PDMX source; the genuinely novel elements are the scale of the openly-licensed multitrack release (largest by song-hours among open synthetic corpora, per the authors' survey) and the license-clean per-category recipe selection procedure. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: the pilot study compares render recipes per category (its core ablation), but no ablation isolates the contribution of cleaning, loudness normalization, or velocity scaling. Separation results are explicitly single matched-step runs with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests; transcription results report 95% CIs. Code, samples, and dataset are released via the project page (https://pnlong.github.io/SPDMX/). Methodological concerns: the realism pilot is tiny (N=8, two stems per category, synthetic references) and the authors concede it cannot establish corpus-wide absolute realism; each separation model is a single training run on ≤632 songs, so cross-dataset conclusions (e.g., the 'best of both worlds' union result) rest on unreplicated point estimates; the SPDMX evaluation set is only 32 songs; and part of the validation evaluates in-domain on the authors' own construction, which favors their pipeline's choices (a mild Goodhart risk since the recipe was frozen before the downstream tasks, mitigating but not eliminating this). Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a released dataset and rendering pipeline, validated with small empirical experiments). Practical: Yes — rendering uses only open, redistributable synthesizers (FluidSynth, Apache-2.0 MIDI-DDSP weights), and downstream models trained are commodity scale. Efficient: Rendering is synthesis-based and cheap relative to recording; downstream experiments were run at deliberately small budgets (32k updates Demucs, T5-small), so the dataset's value at realistic training compute is untested. Effective: Evidence supports SPDMX as a viable training/evaluation resource at fixed small budgets, matching or exceeding Slakh2100 in cross-domain tests, but only as a supplement or alternative at that scale — not yet as a replacement for larger training regimes. Scalable: The corpus itself is already large (5,469 h); whether training on its full multitrack subset at realistic compute yields proportional gains is claimed by implication but not tested. Deliverable: a concrete software/dataset artifact (5,469 h of FLAC stems + MIDI under CC BY 4.0, plus the reusable open rendering pipeline); no trained model weights are reported as released. Strengths: (1) The license analysis is the real contribution: a fully redistributable, linearly-summable multitrack corpus an order of magnitude larger than Slakh2100, with identifiers linking back to PDMX metadata — this unblocks open-release research that Slakh's proprietary renderers cannot. (2) The decision to make stems linearly summable (LUFS normalization, velocity-ratio scaling, single anti-clip gain) preserves the mixture–stem algebraic relationship that separation and transcription tasks depend on. (3) The matched-subtype experimental design (a 632-song BDGP subset to compare against Slakh's BDGP protocol under fixed budgets) is a thoughtful, honest evaluation rather than a headline-chasing one. (4) The transcription result — Slakh-trained models collapsing on SPDMX (0.041 onset F1 vs. 0.265 in-domain) while SPDMX-trained models transfer to Slakh comparably — is a genuinely useful empirical finding about synthetic-data generalization. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: ~65% of songs are single-stem (piano-dominated); MIDI comes from engraved scores with quantized timing and dynamics; all stems are mono, erasing spatial realism; the 8-listener synthetic-reference pilot does not establish corpus-wide absolute realism; and MIDI-DDSP stems are band-limited after upsampling from 16 kHz. They also flag the intentionally small transcription budget and low absolute scores. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Single-run separation experiments with no variance reporting undermine the paper's central cross-dataset generalization claims — the differences between Slakh, SPDMX, and union training on real sets (e.g., −0.5 vs. −0.7 vs. −0.7 on MUSDB18) are well within plausible run-to-run noise. (2) No comparison against CocoChorales or other open synthetic corpora in either scale or downstream utility, despite Table 1 surveying them. (3) The realism of the final corpus is never evaluated — the pilot guided recipe selection on 20 excerpts, but no post-hoc listening test or objective proxy (e.g., FAD against real music) validates the assembled 5,469 hours. (4) The transcription conclusion that 'Slakh training may show lower generalization' confounds dataset content with band-limitation: MIDI-DDSP-heavy SPDMX stems at upsampled 16 kHz bandwidth differ acoustically from Slakh, and no control separates these factors. (5) No experiment uses more than 632 songs (separation) or an unstated but small song count (transcription), so the headline dataset scale is never exercised in training. (6) The union-trained separation model's advantage on MoisesDB BD (2.4 dB) is reported without any statistical support, despite being presented as a headline finding. Bottom Line: For any MIR practitioner constrained by Slakh2100's licensing or the tiny recorded corpora, SPDMX is an immediately useful, honestly-constructed resource worth adopting as training or augmentation data — but the downstream evidence is thin enough (single runs, ≤632 songs, tiny transcription models) that it should be read as a dataset release with preliminary validation, not a proven training recipe.

Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference

R Abhyankar, D Lim, D Wadsworth, VH Vattikuti… · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Together Compiler (TKCC), an agentic system that continually compiles and hot-reloads optimized forward passes into a persistent inference engine, re-optimizing serving deployments as traffic drifts. - Why it's important: Production inference traffic changes on timescales of hours to days (ISL shifts, burstiness, cache-hit-rate drift), so statically tuned engines waste GPU capacity, and existing agent optimizers are bottlenecked by 10+ minute engine restarts or low-fidelity offline kernel benchmarks. - How it does it: The core trick is a Tiered Persistent Engine that loads the model once, patches the model's forward function pointer via RPC, and re-captures CUDA graphs per candidate — decoupling engine startup from forward-pass measurement — paired with a roofline-plus-measurement cost model for seeding parallelism configurations. - The good: The throughput claim is backed concretely: the persistent engine enables 252× more agent experiments and 11× lower agent idle time than restart-per-measurement systems, and two-tier measurement evaluates 8.1× more candidates than a single slow tier while finding a 7.2% faster solution. - The missing: No code, model weights, or artifacts are released, the headline numbers are vendor self-reported on the authors' own production fleet, and correctness verification for LLM workloads is described only as a generic "full suite of verification tests" with no stated methodology. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or operate inference-serving infrastructure or agentic optimization systems — the hot-reload mechanism and the counter-intuitive ablations (expert knowledge bases hurting agents by 25–31%) are directly actionable; skip it if you want a reproducible academic benchmark, since nothing is released.
Why this rank

Practical Impact (58) and Resilience (52) are the dominant drags: despite a deployed production system and a real architectural contribution (Novelty 78, Non-Obviousness 78 — the hot-reload decoupling and the bitter-lesson ablations), no artifact is released and all headline numbers are vendor self-reported, making the paper partly unverifiable marketing for Together AI's stack. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Inference providers serving many models to thousands of customers face constantly shifting workloads: ISL distributions drift by tens of thousands of tokens within days, cache hit rates move by 4–8 percentage points in a week, and labs ship new checkpoints mid-training. The optimal parallelism configuration and forward-pass code change with the traffic, so optimization must be continual. Prior agent-driven optimizers split into two failing camps: kernel-level systems (KernelBench-style, Cursor, Alibaba) iterate fast but measure on random inputs, which distorts data-dependent architectures — random data activates 13–38% more MoE experts than real traffic, and an agent-authored top-k kernel that looked fast on random data ran 62 ms instead of 20 µs on real 70K-context inputs (a 1.3× end-to-end slowdown). End-to-end systems (Apple RSI-Inference, AMD GEAK, Decagon) measure faithfully but pay 761 seconds of engine cold-start per candidate, starving agents of experiments. TKCC targets closing this throughput-fidelity gap at production scale. Key Idea: The single load-bearing insight is that inference engine startup can be decoupled from forward-pass execution: load weights and size the KV cache once, then accept agent-written forward passes as hot-reloadable "candidates" that merely swap the model's forward function pointer and re-capture CUDA graphs, reducing per-experiment turnaround from ~11 minutes to seconds. Everything else — tiered measurement (a fast 12-layer tier for filtering and a slow 60-layer tier for fidelity), a cost model combining theoretical, micro-benchmarked, and end-to-end-measured performance tiers to select parallelism seeds, and parallel communicating agents — is orchestration layered on this decoupling. Methodology: TKCC takes a launch command, traffic profile, and hardware config as input. Stage 1: a cost model ranks parallelism configurations (EP/TP/DP/CP combinations up to 4096 chips), pruning schemes that violate divisibility or SLA constraints (1.5s TTFT, 40 TPS decode), then estimates TPM (tokens/minute/chip) as the inverse of summed prefill+decode chip-seconds, with a per-layer max(T_compute, D/BW) + T_comm formulation, analytical MoE imbalance modeling (binomial routing, expected-max over ranks), and detailed attention-family models (GQA, MLA, KDA with window/compression/sparse-selection key restrictions). Stage 2: N parallel Claude Code (Opus 5.5) agents each receive the engine source code and the instruction to make the forward pass as fast as possible; they submit candidates via RPC, the engine hot-reloads them (write file, exec, patch model.forward, recapture CUDA graphs), and agents load-balance across fast/slow measurement tiers with high-frequency inter-agent communication. Stage 3: after budget exhaustion, candidates pass correctness verification and deploy into production. Critical design decisions: (1) two measurement tiers instead of one — justified by ablation (8.1× more candidates, 7.2% faster final solution vs. single-tier); (2) decoupling prefill/decode measurement and tuning measured-layer count to cut back-to-back variance from 6.6% to 2.7% — justified, since valid optimizations can be worth only 1%; (3) deleting custom IRs, knowledge bases, and expert strategies in favor of raw source access — justified by ablations showing the knowledge base costs 25–31% speedup and prescribed strategies cost 1.3× vs. naive ensembling, though the authors note structured representations still aid verification. Key Results: Against ThunderKittens/Mirage/VDCores megakernels on batch-size-1 Llama-3.2-1B (H100, B200, OSL up to 64K), TKCC reaches up to 1.7× higher TPS (2,118 TPS on B200 at OSL 256, vs. 1,649 for Hazy MK). Against the best SemiAnalysis InferenceX configurations (as of Oct 27, 2026) on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3, and MiniMax M3.1 Flash across B200/B300/GB300/MI355X/Trainium2, TKCC achieves up to 2.6× higher TPS within 24-hour compilation windows using at most 2 nodes per model, and sets batch-1 records of 1,111 TPS (MiniMax M3.1 Flash, B200 — 1.8× the published 633 via a cost-model-suggested TP8 instead of TP4) and 1,205 TPS (DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, GB300). On scientific ML (AIFS-ENS 2.0, Aurora 1.5, Boltz-2, Evo 2, Chronos-2, Panda-72M, Walrus, Poseidon-T), speedups range 1.5–6.4× with bit-exact outputs, beating a Claude Code /goal baseline on most models (e.g., Poseidon-T 6.4× vs. 4.4×; Claude Code produced invalid solutions on AIFS-ENS), and faster sampling cut temperature RMSE from 0.97K to 0.94K (AIFS) at fixed wall-clock. The system reportedly serves trillions of tokens/day in production. Baselines are current and strong (InferenceX leaderboard bests, recent megakernel work), and a notable counter-intuitive finding is that megakernel formation failed on GPUs (only 0.22% gain on AMD) while succeeding on Trainium2, and that vendor kernels at 78–100% of memory bandwidth were mostly better left tuned, not replaced. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with elements of NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The Tiered Persistent Engine with function-pointer hot-reloading is a genuinely new measurement substrate for agentic inference optimization, and the "bitter lesson" ablations (knowledge bases, prescribed strategies, and structured logging all hurting agent performance) are non-obvious empirical findings that contradict the design of GEAK, CAKE, and similar systems. The cost model is a competent assembly of known roofline/analytical techniques extended with MoE-imbalance and software-maturity tiers; the agent loop is standard hill-climbing applied to a new, better-instrumented harness. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are the paper's strongest suit: two-tier vs. one-tier vs. no tiers vs. RSI harness (Figure 2), knowledge base presence/absence, expert strategies vs. naive ensembling, communication frequency (4.7× effect), and measurement-variance engineering are all reported with numbers. Reproducibility is weak for a systems paper: no code, engine patches, or artifacts are released; docker image digests and benchmark protocols are helpfully pinned in Appendix A, but the TKCC system itself is not publicly available. Error bars are not reported, though measurement variance is quantified (0.14%/0.05% per tier) and variance-reduction steps are described — this partially substitutes but does not equal multi-seed reporting. Methodological concerns: all headline results are vendor self-reported by Together AI on its own fleet and on its chosen benchmark protocol; the InferenceX baseline is reproduced to within ~2% for interactivity (good), yet the comparison re-purposes baseline parallelism choices as TKCC seeds, and the most impressive production claims (trillions of tokens, InferenceX baselines failing at scale with 10–40× TTFT degradation) cannot be independently checked. LLM correctness verification is under-specified relative to the rigorous bit-exactness protocol used for scientific ML. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a production-deployed optimization loop, evaluated by deployment and benchmark). Practical: Yes — it runs on commercially available B200/B300/GB300/MI355X/Trainium2 hardware with at most 2 nodes per compilation, though it requires frontier-tier coding agents (Claude Opus 5.5). Efficient: Optimization costs 24 hours on ~2× replica size per model plus agent token spend (not quantified), against speedups up to 2.6× on the serving fleet — favorable economics, but per-compilation agent API cost is unreported. Effective: The evidence (InferenceX leaderboards, bit-exact scientific ML results, production traffic replay) supports that it solves the stated problem, with the caveat that LLM output-quality verification is described only generically. Scalable: Demonstrated at production scale (thousands of customers, trillions of tokens/day) and across 4096-chip configuration search, but no paper experiment tests the optimizer itself at 10–100× more agents or longer horizons; throughput remains the self-identified bottleneck (>50% of agent time waiting on measurement gates). The work delivers a deployed production system, but no released software artifact — it stops at paper form for the public. Strengths: - The hot-reload persistent-engine mechanism is a real architectural contribution: 252× experiment throughput and 11× idle-time reduction are large, well-isolated measurements that directly resolve the documented throughput-fidelity tradeoff. - The fidelity case studies are unusually concrete and useful to outsiders: 13–38% MoE expert-activation distortion on random data, a quadratic top-k kernel pathology (20 µs → 62 ms at 70K context) caused by ReLU-zero tie collapse, and a 6–15% real-traffic slowdown of Cursor's production MoE megakernel — each a transferable lesson for anyone benchmarking data-dependent kernels. - The bitter-lesson ablations are honest, self-critical experiments where the authors dismantle their own prior designs (custom IRs, expert-curated knowledge bases with FlashAttention-author-level content, structured logging), with quantified harm (25–31% speedup loss; 8% of time on bookkeeping CLI calls vs. <0.5% with Markdown). - Breadth of validation across four frontier models, five hardware platforms from two vendors plus Trainium2, and eight non-LLM scientific models with a strict bit-exactness protocol is execution depth few systems papers match. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that measurement throughput remains the primary bottleneck (>50% of agent time waiting on gates or re-sending marginal candidates, Table 6); that structured representations, while hurting optimization, remain valuable for verification and would benefit from a future verification-oriented IR; that agent code caused 9 GPU-reset incidents (Xid 154) removing 2 machines from the cluster, and that safety bans on editing captured graph schedules block re-applying some effective optimizations; and that agents struggle on attention-kernel fusion, megakernel formation on GPUs, and comm/compute overlap. They confront limitations fairly directly — the paper is largely structured around negative results from their own two-year design history, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No released artifact: without code, the 252× and 2.6× numbers are unverifiable vendor claims, and the paper functions partly as marketing for Together AI's production stack. (2) LLM correctness is asserted via a vague "full suite of verification tests (e.g., for KV cache contamination and quality)" with no metrics, thresholds, or eval suites named — in contrast to the meticulous bit-exactness protocol for scientific ML, this asymmetry suggests LLM numerical fidelity (e.g., fp4 kernels, reordered reductions) may be less rigorously validated than implied. (3) The fast tier's 3.9 crashes per 1,000 jobs and the crash-driven GPU resets raise an unaddressed operational-cost question for continual deployment. (4) Agent API/token spend per 24-hour compilation is never reported, so the cost-benefit calculation cannot be completed by a reader. (5) The Trainium2 evaluation swaps in a synthetic 70K-ISL dataset rather than the AgentX workload, a protocol change justified by "CPU offloading overheads" but which breaks apples-to-apples comparability for that platform. (6) The knowledge-base ablation is run on a single layer/workload (MiniMax-M3 layer 3, B200 TP4, batch 1), yet the sweeping bitter-lesson conclusion is generalized from this narrow point. (7) Non-obvious omissions: no comparison against simple autotuning baselines (e.g., random search over the same experiment budget) that would isolate how much the agent actually contributes beyond the persistent-engine harness itself. Bottom Line: For anyone operating inference fleets or building agentic optimization loops, this is a rare systems paper whose negative results are as valuable as its speedups — but treat the headline numbers as a strong vendor case study, not an independently reproducible result, since the system is unreleased and all evidence is self-reported.
