Wayfinder: Adaptive Resource Routing from Agent Citations

M Romero, G Karypis · arxiv.org · New articles in my profile
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Wayfinder, an adaptive resource router for LLM agents that learns where relevant information resides in a user's environment by using the documents the downstream agent cites as online feedback, updating bounded per-resource "sketches" without target-environment labels. - Why it's important: Agent deployments face organization-specific resource layouts, so without adaptation an agent re-explores the same chats, tickets, and wikis on every session, wasting search calls and API cost; static tool descriptions cannot distinguish semantically overlapping resources. - How it does it: A LoRA-adapted Qwen3-8B policy trained with GRPO on training environments reads a citation-gated semantic index over per-resource sketches; resource identifiers are anonymized and re-permuted per session so the policy must route on sketch evidence rather than memorized name-topic associations. - The good: Under a shared closed-loop protocol, Wayfinder gives the best routing F1 on the intra-corpus testbeds (47.67 on NFCorpus, 64.72 on FEVER vs. 33.03 and 31.01 for the strongest baselines) while cutting the primary agent's search calls by 61.2% and 73.7%, and the ablations (RL post-training, resource augmentation, citation noise, memory structure) isolate which components matter. - The missing: There are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests for the headline closed-loop results, the headline testbeds are small (NFCorpus routing F1 rests on n=42 ground-truth-usable queries; FEVER is capped at 50 test queries per environment), and no evaluation uses a real production environment with authentic tools. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers and engineers building agent memory, federated search, or tool-routing layers who want a label-free adaptation signal and an honest account of when static tool retrieval already suffices; skippable for readers seeking large-scale or production-deployed evidence.

Problem & Motivation: In LLM agent deployments (e.g., Claude Cowork-style workspace assistants), the grounding information a user needs lives in organization-specific resources — chats, issue trackers, email, wikis — each reachable only through a black-box search tool. Where information resides differs per deployment and is unknown at training time, so agents re-explore the same resources across consecutive interactions. Prior approaches treat each resource as a tool and rank it by a static description (ReSLLM, ToolRetriever), by corpus statistics (CORI), or by supervised/bandit learners that need labeled query-resource pairs from the target environment (Learn2Rank, RouteRAG) — labels a newly encountered environment does not supply. Static descriptions fail to separate resources whose contents overlap, and none of these methods improve from what the agent discovers during use. The gap is a router that adapts online to an unseen target environment without target-environment supervision and without enumerating resource contents. Key Idea: Use the agent's own citations as a free, high-precision supervision signal: a document enters the routing memory only if it was both cited by the agent in its answer and actually appeared in a tool output (the "verified citation set"), which filters hallucinated citations and low-precision exploratory retrievals. Per-resource bounded sketches of (document, query, timestamp) records plus a semantic index become the only signal a RL-trained routing policy can exploit, and session-randomized identifier anonymization/permutation during training prevents the policy from learning shortcut name-topic associations. That is the reconstructable core: citation-gated memory + RL post-training + anti-memorization augmentation. Methodology: Wayfinder is a two-agent loop: (1) routing — given query q_t, a Qwen3-8B LoRA (rank 16, ~0.1% of parameters) policy runs a ReAct-style loop over a centralized semantic index of the environment memory M = (M_1,...,M_N), retrieving top-25 sketch entries per decision step and emitting a recommended resource set (bounded by budget B); (2) rollout — the primary agent (GPT-4o-mini in the main table) acts on the advisory recommendation (it may still search elsewhere); (3) citation extraction — cited document identifiers are intersected with the tool-call log to form the verified citation set C_t (Eqs. 2-3); (4) sketch update — each cited document retrieved from resource r_j is inserted into M_j as an LRU-bounded record (capacity M=100) and the index is refreshed. The policy is trained offline with GRPO on training environments only, with reward R_i = F1(predicted resource set, ground-truth set from relevance judgments) and group-normalized advantages; malformed output scores zero. Two session-level augmentations — identifier anonymization and per-rollout resource permutation — break stable identifier-topic associations. Critical design decisions: (a) citation gating (well-justified via the noise stress test in Appendix F.2, showing flat degradation under citation drops vs. steep monotone decline under citation flips, 82→36 F1 at 50% flips); (b) advisory rather than hard routing (well-motivated, keeps the signal flowing even when the router errs, and honestly complicates the savings metric); (c) bounded LRU sketches (justified by the memory-size sensitivity study showing diminishing returns beyond moderate capacity). The benchmark construction itself (GMM clustering of BEIR corpora into resources; Tech Startup assembling Enron, Alpaca, SWE-bench, HotpotQA, CodeSearchNet) is a substantial methodological component. Key Results: On the intra-corpus testbeds under a shared closed-loop protocol, Wayfinder achieves routing F1 of 47.67 on NFCorpus and 64.72 on FEVER, versus 33.03 (ReSLLM) and 31.01 (Learn2Rank) for the strongest baselines; it cuts the agent's search calls by 61.2% and 73.7% relative to a no-router control (25.90 and 32.90 search calls/query) and raises citation F1 by 2.7 and 17.9 points over the unrouted agent. On Tech Startup (five resources from five distinct corpora), ToolRetriever leads on all metrics (F1r 98.86, F1c 85.31, 70.4% saved) and Wayfinder is second (86.60, 80.78, 60.4%); no router beats letting the agent search all five resources there (F1c 87.44). Baselines span CORI, ReSLLM, ToolRetriever, LinUCB-D, and Learn2Rank (the last violating the zero-label assumption, included as a reference ceiling of sorts). Scale is small: 18 intra-corpus environments from NFCorpus/FEVER BEIR partitions plus 5 Tech Startup environments, 50 resources/environment for BEIR-derived sets, FEVER capped at 50 test queries/environment, and NFCorpus resting on n=42 GT-usable test queries. Notable honest findings: on FEVER a constant router picking the five largest resources scores 33.6 F1r (near-baseline routing is close to degenerate); the no-RL ablation grounds more answers than the full model on FEVER (F1c 75.93 vs 59.70) while searching less; and observed routing behavior is shallow — a median of two routing decisions per query with >99% of trajectories completing within two steps, so the reasoning policy is not exploiting long-horizon planning. A non-stationarity experiment (Appendix A) shows Wayfinder degrades more gracefully than static baselines as ground-truth documents are relocated across resources. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (the formalized Adaptive Agent Routing Problem: black-box resources, weak trajectory-level feedback, no target-environment supervision, cross-environment generalization), NEW METHOD (citation-gated sketch memory + GRPO-trained routing policy with session-randomized resource augmentation), and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (three released controlled testbeds pairing queries with resource-access patterns). The genuinely novel element is the supervision paradigm — using downstream agent citations as label-free routing feedback; the components (LoRA fine-tuning, GRPO, LRU memory, federated-search F1 metrics, bi-encoder retrieval) are standard, and the honest contribution is their composition around the citation signal rather than any new learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: RL post-training on/off, resource augmentation on/off, citation-noise stress test (drop/flip/ungated), mem0-style generic memory vs. environment-structured memory (F1B 50.69 vs 47.49 NFCorpus; 67.94 vs 66.39 FEVER), and memory-capacity sensitivity. The closed-loop vs. offline protocol comparison (within 3.3 F1r points) rules out replay artifacts. However: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; the NFCorpus headline rests on n=42 usable queries; FEVER routing is near-degenerate and capped at 50 test queries; Learn2Rank is trained on target labels while Wayfinder is not, making that comparison a reference rather than a fair fight. No error bars means the 3-14 point margins on tiny query sets are hard to assess. The dataset is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/miguelrc001/wayfinder; no code or adapter weights URL is stated. Two internal inconsistencies weaken confidence: the main text says training runs 125 GRPO iterations with 8 rollouts/query while Appendix E says 25 iterations with 4 rollouts; and the main experiments use GPT-4o-mini as primary agent while Appendix D describes trajectory generation with GPT-5-mini. The benchmark is the authors' own construction, evaluated on the same (a common but unavoidable pattern for a new problem), though it is derived from public corpora with documented construction and leakage controls. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (and partly SYSTEMS — a routing layer composed with a black-box agent). Practical: Yes in principle — a LoRA on Qwen3-8B (~8B params, 0.1% trainable) plus MiniLM embeddings run on commodity hardware, but the primary agent is a closed GPT model. Efficient: Bounded sketches (M=100/resource) and top-25 retrieval cap the routing layer's cost regardless of stream length; savings are 61.2-73.7% fewer agent search calls on intra-corpus data, but no latency numbers are reported (the authors state "We do not report latency"). Effective: Evidence shows improved routing F1 and citation F1 on synthetic testbeds, but only a proxy for production value — the authors concede the testbeds do not capture enterprise permission structures or production-scale latency. Scalable: Untested beyond 50 resources and a few thousand queries per environment; behavior at hundreds of resources or long streams is claimed only implicitly via bounded memory, not demonstrated. The work delivers a released benchmark dataset; the router itself stops at paper form (no code or weights URL stated). Strengths: - The citation-gating supervision idea is genuinely new for routing and is backed by a precise mechanism (verified-citation intersection with tool logs) plus a targeted stress test cleanly separating the failure mode it can absorb (citation loss) from the one it cannot (citation corruption). - The resource-randomization augmentation attacks a real, identified failure mode (identifier-topic memorization during RL) with an ablation showing it matters most when training environments are scarce (45.35→50.69 F1r on the 2-environment NFCorpus, roughly neutral on the 16-environment FEVER). - Unusual candor: the paper reports that ToolRetriever beats Wayfinder on the cross-corpus benchmark, that RL post-training lowers citation F1 on FEVER, that observed routing behavior is "consistently shallow," and that a constant router is nearly competitive on FEVER — findings that make the regime analysis (adaptation pays when descriptions cannot discriminate) credible rather than promotional. - The benchmark construction is careful: query rewriting with a regex blocklist to remove resource-revealing tokens, a semantic-retrieval quality gate (4.0% of queries rejected), connected-component partitioning to prevent document/query leakage across environments, and seed-controlled reproducibility. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that Wayfinder depends on citation quality — incorrect citations write wrong evidence into sketches and routing degrades as their rate grows (with candidate mitigations deferred to future work); that the benchmarks are controlled testbeds from public corpora that do not capture enterprise permission structures or production-scale latency; and that evaluation with authentic tools and users is the natural next step. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting anywhere (no seeds, error bars, or significance tests) for headline margins of 3-14 F1 points computed on as few as 42 usable queries (NFCorpus) — the statistical basis for the central claim is thin. - Internal inconsistencies between main text and appendix: 125 vs. 25 GRPO iterations, 8 vs. 4 rollouts per query, and GPT-4o-mini vs. GPT-5-mini as the primary/trajectory agent — which configuration produced Table 2 is unclear. - The adaptive baselines are weak: LinUCB-D is the only competing adaptive method and it trails everywhere; a stronger natural competitor — a simple nearest-neighbor over cited (query → resource) pairs, or ToolRetriever re-indexed over accumulated citations — is not tested, leaving the citation-signal idea only weakly isolated from the heavyweight policy. - Wayfinder's memory is seeded with citations from the target environment's training-split trajectories before test evaluation; static baselines get descriptions only. The closed-loop/offline comparison addresses replay artifacts but not whether this seeding advantage, rather than the policy, drives early-stream gains. - The reward is F1 against ground-truth resource sets available only in training environments, so the policy's learned notion of "routing well" may not transfer to reward structures of real deployments; generalization is shown across two BEIR-derived clusterings plus one synthetic cross-corpus template, which may understate real workspace diversity (50 near-identical resources is an unusual shape for real organizations, where resource counts are typically smaller and descriptions more distinctive — the regime where Wayfinder loses). - The shallow observed routing behavior (median two decisions, no long-horizon use) suggests the ReAct-style reasoning policy may be underutilized, raising the question of whether a much simpler non-reasoning policy head over the same memory would match performance. Bottom Line: A practitioner building multi-resource agent systems gains a concrete, well-tested design pattern — citation-gated resource memory plus anti-memorization RL training — and a released benchmark worth adopting, but the empirical case rests on small synthetic testbeds without variance estimates, so treat the intra-corpus wins as a promising signal to replicate rather than a settled result.

Zeguan Xiao, Zhuocheng Liang, Yun Chen, Yong Wang, Guanhua Chen, Pinyan Lu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 19 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CurvDelta and CurvLoRA, two adaptation methods that bake a capability-preservation constraint directly into the delta parameterization by projecting every model update into a fixed low-curvature subspace of the preservation loss, and shows improved learning–retention and forgetting–retention trade-offs on math/code fine-tuning and on TOFU/MUSE unlearning. - Why it's important: Fine-tuning and unlearning LLMs routinely degrade unrelated general capabilities, and the dominant Lagrangian/regularization fixes cannot guarantee a tolerated drift level ε — a real blocker for privacy- and safety-driven unlearning where retention must be certified. - How it does it: It estimates the Gauss–Newton curvature of the preservation loss at the base model with block-diagonal K-FAC, keeps trailing (low-curvature) factor eigendirections via separable spectral truncation, and applies a two-sided projection ΔW = P_out δ P_in so the realized update stays in the low-curvature space regardless of optimizer, with a sufficient ε-feasibility bound coupling retained curvature κ and delta norm. - The good: The ablation isolating projection basis (low-curvature vs. dimension-matched high-curvature vs. random subspaces, Figure 2a) credibly shows the curvature-derived geometry — not merely reduced dimensionality — drives the better forgetting–utility trade-off, and a parameterization-vs-gradient-projection ablation (Figure 3) shows the claimed optimizer-independence benefit under Adam. - The missing: The preservation guarantee is not validated as a guarantee: the K-FAC quadratic model (e.g., 5.8×10⁻⁹) and spectral bound (1.7×10⁻⁶) understate the empirical retain-set KL (0.039) by 6–7 orders of magnitude, so ε-feasibility is only argued via 'shared monotonic trends,' never demonstrated. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM unlearning, continual adaptation, or preservation-constrained fine-tuning and care about the geometry of update constraints; skip it if you need certified unlearning at production scale, since the models tested top out at 7–8B and the bound is far too loose to certify anything.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners adapting pretrained LLMs — whether acquiring new capabilities (math reasoning, code) or removing targeted knowledge for privacy/compliance (machine unlearning) — face the same structural problem: the update must change behavior on a task set D_task while leaving behavior on a preservation set D_pres essentially unchanged. Retraining from scratch per adaptation is prohibitively costly. Prior mitigations split into (i) replay/regularization added to the loss, which cannot control realized drift (Lagrangian weight λ does not map to a tolerance ε), and (ii) parameter- or representation-space restrictions (orthogonal/null-space subspaces, gradient projection as in CrispEdit) that constrain directions only indirectly tied to capability preservation, or — for gradient projection under Adam — silently leave the intended subspace because Adam rescales coordinates. The paper targets the gap between 'constrain the update' and 'constrain the update in the space that actually preserves behavior.' Key Idea: Restrict the realized parameter delta (not the gradient, not the loss) to the trailing eigenspace of the preservation-loss Hessian at θ₀, so every unit of update norm costs the least possible preservation loss. The enabling technical move is a factorwise spectral truncation of the block-diagonal K-FAC approximation: instead of CrispEdit's non-separable product-spectrum mask (which requires full factor eigenbases and an elementwise mask), truncating each Kronecker factor's spectrum separately yields a separable two-sided projection ΔW = P_out δ P_in that is cheap to store (thin eigenbases only), applies directly to LoRA factors (CurvLoRA), and keeps the update inside the space throughout optimization under any optimizer. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) at θ₀, estimate K-FAC factors K_in ⊗ K_out per adapted weight on D_pres using Monte Carlo Fisher estimation with token-level D_KL(p_θ0 || p_θ) as the preservation discrepancy (justified by showing the preservation Hessian equals the GGN matrix under a mild Assumption 1 on Bregman-type discrepancies); (2) pick a spectral-energy threshold γ per factor, cache leading eigenvector bases, and form projectors P_out = I − U_out_h U_out_h^⊤, P_in likewise; (3) train a delta — dense δ (CurvDelta) or LoRA factors B_l A_l (CurvLoRA) — differentiating through the projection ΔW_l = P_out δ P_in, then merge. The framework is second-order optimization geometry (GGN/K-FAC) plus constrained reformulation: min L_task s.t. Δθ^⊤ G_pres Δθ ≤ 2ε (quadratic approximation of the constraint). Theorem 1 gives L_pres ≲ ½ Σ_l κ_l ‖ΔW_l‖²_F under the local quadratic and block-diagonal K-FAC models — a sufficient ε-feasibility condition. Critical design decisions: (a) factorwise vs. product-spectrum truncation — justified by separability/storage (Θ(d_out d_in (r_out + r_in)) vs. Θ(d_out d_in (d_out + d_in)) per projection) and argued to be safe because flat directions are abundant, though it provably discards mixed low-curvature directions (their Appendix B.5 admits R ⊊ R_prod_κ); (b) parameterization-integrated projection instead of gradient projection — justified empirically by the CurvDeltaGrad ablation (FQ −1.7 vs. −0.2 at lr 5×10⁻⁵); (c) fixed ε never enforced at training time — the bound's Δθ-norm term is trajectory-dependent and uncontrolled, a justification gap. Key Results: Capability learning (Gemma-3-1B and Llama-2-7B; MetaMathQA 100K → GSM8K/MATH; CodeFeedback 104K → HumanEval/MBPP; retention on TriviaQA/NQ-Open/MMLU; 256 FineFineWeb examples as D_pres): on Llama-2-7B math, CurvDelta reaches GSM8K 58.4% with retention avg 39.0% vs. full FT's 59.3%/33.4% and LoRA's 57.5%/33.0%; on code, CurvDelta achieves HumanEval 39.6%, MBPP 41.3%, retention 42.8% — the best joint average among adaptation methods on both backbones (e.g., vs. CrispEdit 37.8%/39.3%/39.9%). Unlearning (TOFU Forget 5%/10% on Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; MUSE Books on Llama-2-7B; objectives GradDiff, NPO, SimNPO): with SimNPO on 8B TOFU, CurvDelta hits FQ −0.1 (Forget 5%) vs. Retrain's 10.8-scale reference, FP 6.3, MU 63.3 vs. Retrain 63.2; on MUSE SimNPO, VerbMem 11.6 (Retrain: 14.2) with Retain KnowMem 55.8. Efficiency (L40 GPU, TOFU Forget 10%, 3B): CurvDelta runs in 1004 s vs. CrispEdit's 2482 s (−59.5%) at 38.4 GB vs. 40.8 GB; CurvLoRA: 866 s, 24.4 GB. Baselines are current and reasonably strong (CrispEdit ICML 2026, OPLoRA AAAI 2026, VILA, CorDA, PiSSA, MiLoRA). Tested at standard academic scale (1B–8B models), not stress scale. Notable counter-intuitive detail: in several unlearning cells the unconstrained-seeming GradDiff + CurvDelta yields very negative FQ (e.g., −228.7 on 8B Forget 10%), showing the geometry alone does not guarantee good forgetting under all objectives — the method's advantage concentrates under NPO/SimNPO. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component). The genuinely novel elements are (i) constraining the applied delta — not the gradient — to a preservation-loss-curvature-derived subspace, making the constraint optimizer-invariant, and (ii) the separable factorwise truncation enabling low-rank projection. The underlying ingredients (K-FAC, LoRA, GGN, spectral truncation, constrained-adaptation formulation) are all established; relative to the closest baseline CrispEdit, the contribution is a reformulation of the same curvature idea from gradient projection into delta parameterization plus a separability trick, applied to a new combined setting (learning + unlearning). Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-targeted: projection-basis control (dimension-matched high-curvature/random), γ sweep, preservation-data-ratio sweep (robust from 0.25×–4× of forget-set size), and the parameterization-vs-projection comparison — these are the paper's strongest rigor asset. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; all headline deltas (e.g., retention 39.0 vs. 39.4 for CurvDelta vs. OPLoRA on Llama math) are single-run point estimates within likely noise. The theoretical bound is checked only for qualitative trend agreement, not feasibility, and the quadratic model's numerical scale is 6–7 orders of magnitude below empirical KL (Table 13). No code release is stated — only a project page (https://xiaozi-max.github.io/CurvDelta/); unlearning uses the public OpenUnlearning implementation. No Goodhart-style benchmark contamination is apparent (curvature is estimated on D_pres, evaluation is on disjoint retention tasks), though γ and learning rates are tuned per benchmark, so the reported trade-off points may be mildly optimistic. This is a preprint; results are not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a supporting theoretical result). - Practical: Yes — all experiments run on single-GPU-class hardware (measurements on an NVIDIA L40), with standard 1B–8B open checkpoints. - Efficient: Favorable — CurvLoRA costs 866 s / 24.4 GB vs. LoRA's 674 s / 17.9 GB (modest overhead for the projection); CurvDelta is 2.5× faster than CrispEdit with lower peak memory; curvature estimation is one-time and reusable across tasks and objectives. - Effective: Partially — it clearly improves trade-off frontiers on TOFU (utility within ~0.1 point of Retrain under SimNPO/NPO) and retention tasks, but under GradDiff the TOFU FQ results are poor, so effectiveness is objective-dependent, and 'preservation' is measured on a 256-example proxy (capability learning) or benchmark retain sets, not the true pretraining distribution. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 8B; the per-layer eigendecomposition costs O(d_out³ + d_in³) at construction, and whether K-FAC curvature estimation remains stable and cheap at 70B+ is claimed nowhere and shown nowhere. Deliverable status: paper plus a project page; no released library, trained weights, or dataset is stated. Strengths: - The delta-parameterization-instead-of-gradient-projection move is a real, well-motivated insight: it makes the preservation constraint optimizer-invariant, and the paper proves this matters empirically (CurvDeltaGrad ablation: FQ −0.676 vs. −0.193 at lr 5×10⁻⁵ under identical projectors). - The separable factorwise truncation is a concrete algorithmic contribution with quantified cost wins (Θ(d_out d_in (r_out + r_in)) projection vs. Θ(d_out d_in (d_out + d_in)) for product-thresholding; −59.5% runtime vs. CrispEdit), and it cleanly enables the low-rank variant. - The ablation suite addresses the right confounds — dimension-matched subspace controls and preservation-data-budget sweeps are exactly what a skeptic would demand, and the results support the curvature hypothesis. - Unifying capability learning and unlearning under one constrained-update formulation, with the same reusable geometry across three unlearning objectives and two task domains, is competent synthesis with practical value. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that factorwise truncation discards mixed Kronecker directions where a small eigenvalue in one factor offsets a large one in the other (Appendix B.5), arguing empirically that flat directions are abundant; they acknowledge that the preservation guarantee's delta-norm term depends on the optimization trajectory (learning-rate schedule, step count) and is therefore not fixed by the method; and they acknowledge the local quadratic model 'operates on a smaller numerical scale than the full-training retain-set KL.' They confront these directly but treat the scale mismatch as benign rather than as a failure of the ε-feasibility story. They do not explicitly discuss seed variance, the GradDiff failure cells, or scalability beyond 8B. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The ε-constraint is never actually enforced or verified: no experiment shows L_pres ≤ ε for a pre-specified ε; Theorem 1 is presented as a headline guarantee but is unfalsified and untested as a guarantee, and the 10⁷-fold gap between the quadratic model and empirical KL (Table 13) suggests the bound is vacuous at any meaningful ε. - Single-run results throughout with no variance estimates; several headline retention wins over OPLoRA (39.0 vs. 39.4 on Llama math — CurvDelta is actually second there) and CurvLoRA (42.8 vs. 41.7 on code) are within plausible noise. - Only MUSE Books is evaluated for MUSE — no MUSE News, which is the harder real-text split; MUSE knowledge-retention results under NPO show CurvDelta's Retain KnowMem dropping to 51.3, notably below VILA's 64.0, which the main text does not surface. - Preservation set for capability learning is only 256 FineFineWeb examples; the robustness sweep varies preservation data only in the unlearning setting, not for capability learning. - Missing comparison to second-order unlearning baselines like SOUL (cited in related work but not run) and to null-space editing (AlphaEdit) in the unlearning tables. - The claim of optimizer-independence is validated only against Adam-based gradient projection; no experiments with other adaptive optimizers (e.g., RMSProp variants, Lion) or larger learning-rate regimes where Adam's second-moment rescaling might interact differently. - γ, learning rate, and (implicitly) per-benchmark tuning raise a mild selection concern: the trade-off frontier is reported at tuned points without nested validation. Bottom Line: A practitioner working on preservation-constrained fine-tuning or LLM unlearning gains a genuinely useful and better-engineered alternative to CrispEdit-style gradient projection — with quantified efficiency wins and the best current TOFU/MUSE SimNPO trade-offs — but should read it as an empirical trade-off method with a loose, unvalidated theoretical bound, not as certified preservation.

A federated learning framework for cyber -resilient defense in EV-integrated microgrids

J Gholami, B Yousefi, AN Shirazi, A Yazdani · nature.com · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a unified cyber-physical framework that combines decision-based moving target defense (MTD), vehicle-to-grid (V2G) dispatch, and federated attack detection so that continuous MTD operation against stealthy false-data injection attacks becomes economically sustainable in a microgrid cluster. - Why it's important: MTD's reactance reconfigurations impose a certain operating-cost penalty every hour (~$298/h, ~$2.6M/year in the studied cluster) while the attacks they prevent are sporadic, so operators leave the defense off; a mechanism that absorbs this penalty changes the economics of continuous grid cyber-defense. - How it does it: The core trick is dispatching bidirectional EV fleet power precisely at the buses where the defense-induced reconfiguration creates artificial congestion, so the fleet substitutes for the expensive congestion-relief generation, while a three-objective NSGA-II selects the reconfiguration and a FedAvg detector (parameter exchange only) classifies exposed attacks. - The good: The measured penalty drop from $298.10/h to $15.96/h (94.64% reduction) is traced mechanistically — the largest pre-mitigation penalty ($288/h in MG5) is nearly eliminated — and the pipeline is benchmarked end-to-end with timings down to 0.1 ms per online scan. - The missing: Everything is on DC state estimation, linear PTDF power flow, replicated identical IEEE 30-bus systems, and synthetic attacks, with an attacker assumed unaware of the reconfiguration and V2G compensation priced at an optimistic $1.5/MWh; no AC validation, field data, or empirical comparison against any baseline method is provided. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in power-system cybersecurity exploring demand-side flexibility as a defense-cost offset, since the V2G-absorbs-MTD-penalty connection is genuinely under-explored, but skippable for readers seeking AC-accurate or adversarially rigorous results.

Problem & Motivation: Operators of interconnected microgrids face stealthy false-data injection attacks (FDIAs) that exploit knowledge of the network model to bias state estimation without tripping residual-based bad-data detection. Moving target defense — perturbing line reactances via distributed flexible AC transmission devices (D-FACTS) — breaks this stealth, but it forces dispatch away from the economic optimum, creating congestion costs paid every operating hour while attacks are rare. Prior approaches either schedule the defense intermittently (game-theoretic or probabilistic scheduling), which reschedules rather than eliminates the penalty, or treat detection, economics, and actuation wear separately. A further constraint in multi-owner microgrid clusters is that raw measurement data cannot be centrally pooled for training ML detectors due to privacy and single-point-of-failure concerns. The paper targets the gap between a physically effective defense and one whose certainty-weighted cost is justifiable year-round. Key Idea: The single core insight is that the defense-induced congestion is spatially localized and therefore can be physically absorbed by injecting bidirectional V2G power exactly at the congested buses — turning the EV fleet into decentralized generation that reroutes power around the defense-restricted branches — while the reconfiguration itself is chosen to maximize the smallest principal angle between nominal and reconfigured measurement subspaces (a geometric condition guaranteeing the FDIA residual leaves the column space of the active Jacobian and spikes the χ² detection statistic). Methodology: The framework has three coupled layers over a DC state-estimation model. (1) Attack model: a stealthy FDIA crafted as a = H_naive·c on the nominal Jacobian leaves the weighted residual r = (I − P)z unchanged by construction. (2) Defense layer: NSGA-II (population 24, 18 generations) searches multiplicative reactance perturbations Δx on 8 controllable branches per microgrid against three objectives — minimize the negative smallest principal angle between column spaces of H and H' (exposure), minimize induced operating cost relative to the nominal PTDF-OPF dispatch, and minimize the L1 norm of the perturbation (actuation effort). A decision rule (Eq. 28) discards candidates violating a required separation angle (0.10 rad) and selects least-cost among secure ones. (3) Mitigation layer: a PTDF-based linear OPF minimizes generation cost plus V2G compensation plus congestion penalties, subject to power balance and thermal limits, with a continuous participation operator α scaling the fleet's bidirectional capacity; the defense penalty is the OPF cost difference with versus without reconfiguration. (4) Detection layer: an MLP (24,12 hidden units) trained by FedAvg over 25 rounds on residual fingerprints, each microgrid holding 400 private samples, exchanging only ~18.8 kB of parameters per round. Critical design decisions: the principal-angle security constraint is well-justified (it directly controls the post-defense residual energy); the L1 actuation objective is reasonable but its weighting relative to detection is left to the Pareto knee heuristic; the compensation rate of $1.5/MWh for V2G is asserted without justification or sensitivity analysis, and the DC/PTDF linearization is acknowledged as a limitation rather than justified as adequate. Key Results: On a cluster of five interconnected IEEE 30-bus microgrids (each with 5 charging stations × 100 EVs at 11 kW; 2,500 vehicles total): (a) deployed reconfigurations attained separation angles of 0.112–0.176 rad, all above the 0.10 rad requirement; (b) the mean detection statistic rose from ~41 (clean and undefended-attack, confirming stealth) to 176–610 post-defense; (c) the cluster defense penalty fell from $298.10/h to $15.96/h at full participation (94.64% reduction), with a participation level of only 0.1 reducing the penalty to $1.4/h — a non-monotonicity the authors note; (d) the federated detector reached AUC 0.926 ± 0.014 versus 0.921 ± 0.015 isolated — a marginal advantage (single-ROC comparison: 0.924 vs 0.904); (e) per-direction exposure probability of a stealthy vector ranged 0.85–0.99, and one persistent attack (MG2) evaded the deployed configuration in 96% of post-deployment scans; (f) offline computation of 9.6 s sequential / 2.7 s parallel on an i7 laptop, 0.1 ms per online scan; scaling tested up to IEEE 118-bus microgrids and clusters of 20 microgrids with measured log-log slopes of 0.99 (cluster size) and 2.0–2.3 (network size beyond 57 buses); (g) under federated stress conditions (label skew, stragglers, latency), plain FedAvg failed to converge stably in 3 of 5 trials under combined stress, but local class balancing restored AUC ≈ 0.93 in all trials. Baselines in Table 1 are qualitative characterizations of prior work (random MTD, game-theoretic MTD, centralized/RL detection), not empirical head-to-head runs; the only quantitative comparison is federated versus isolated detection. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a NEW METHOD element in the integration. The genuinely novel move is physically absorbing the MTD operating-cost penalty via spatially targeted V2G dispatch — prior work (cost-benefit MTD, game-theoretic scheduling, hidden MTD) only reschedules or reduces defense frequency. The subspace-separation MTD mechanism, NSGA-II multi-objective search, PTDF-OPF, and FedAvg are each standard; the contribution is their composition into one dispatch-and-detect loop with the V2G offset, which is a competent combination of known techniques applied to a new coupling rather than a new algorithmic core. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is unusually thorough on internal validation: a full complexity analysis (Eqs. 29–34) is derived and then validated against measured log-log scaling slopes; seven federated stress scenarios (skew, stragglers, latency) are run over five trials each with reported standard deviations; timing benchmarks cover four network sizes and three cluster sizes on a second, weaker machine. Ablations effectively exist via the participation-level sweep and the Pareto-front analysis. However: no code, data, or trained models are publicly released (data "available upon reasonable request"); there is no empirical comparison against any implemented baseline (random MTD, game-theoretic MTD) — Table 1 is a qualitative self-assessment; error bars are absent for the cost results; detection trials are on synthetic attacks generated by the authors' own attack model (A1–A6), so the evaluation operates entirely within the paper's own assumptions — the attack the detector sees is the attack the framework defines. The V2G compensation rate and congestion price ($1.5/MWh, $500/MWh) drive the headline economics but receive no sensitivity analysis. This is an Article in Press; peer review status of the final version is pending. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (simulation study, no hardware deployment). - Practical: The entire pipeline runs on a laptop (i7-12650H, 16 GB) with standard open-source Python tooling (pandapower, SciPy, pymoo, scikit-learn), so compute requirements are trivial by ML standards, though real deployment requires D-FACTS actuators and V2G-capable aggregators not evaluated here. - Efficient: Offline preparation takes 9.6 s (sequential) for a five-microgrid cluster and 60.5 s at 118-bus scale, with 0.1 ms online per scan — comfortably inside supervisory scan and dispatch intervals; communication is ~18.8 kB/round for FedAvg. - Effective: The evidence shows cost absorption and attack exposure under the authors' own DC-linearized, synthetic-attack setup; effectiveness against realistic AC dynamics, adaptive attackers, or real telemetry is only a proxy at this stage. - Scalable: Tested to 20 microgrids and 118-bus systems with measured scaling matching the derived complexity (exponent ≤ 3.5 worst case), but 10–100× real clusters would add data heterogeneity beyond the tested Beta-skew scenarios; DC assumptions would also strain at larger, meshed, unbalanced systems. The work delivers no software artifact — no repository is released — so it remains at paper-plus-parameters form; reproduction requires re-implementation from Tables 2–3. Strengths: - The V2G-absorbs-MTD-penalty mechanism is a genuinely new connection in the moving-target-defense literature, and the paper demonstrates it causally: the cost composition shifts from congestion relief to cheap vehicle discharge, and the microgrid with the largest penalty ($288/h) is the one most fully mitigated. - The security condition is made quantitative and testable — the smallest principal angle directly predicts the residual spike — so the defense is tuned by a measurable geometric margin rather than heuristics, and the paper honestly reports the failure case (MG2's persistent attack evading exposure in 96% of scans). - The federated robustness study (Table 8) is more honest than typical FedAvg evaluations: it shows plain FedAvg failing under combined stress (AUC 0.417 ± 0.425) and identifies a simple client-side fix (local class balancing) that works without extra information sharing. - The complexity analysis is derived before being validated, and the measured scaling slopes (0.99 in cluster size, 2.0–2.3 in network size) empirically confirm it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: reliance on DC state estimation and linear power flow with simulated measurements and synthetic attacks, requiring confirmation on AC models and field data; an adversary assumed unaware of the reconfiguration; probabilistic rather than certain exposure (85–99% of attack directions); sensitivity of the penalty magnitude to the assumed congestion price and the low V2G compensation rate; the fleet modeled as fixed aggregated capacity without state-of-charge or battery-degradation dynamics; and the federated detector's marginal accuracy gain over an isolated detector plus its poor plain-FedAvg convergence under severe label skew. They also flag periodic reconfiguration against persistent attackers and staleness-aware aggregation as future work. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No implemented baseline: the headline 94.6% cost reduction is compared against the paper's own uncompensated defense, not against game-theoretic scheduling or hidden-MTD schemes that could achieve comparable annualized cost at lower actuation effort; Table 1's superiority claims are qualitative self-assessment. - Five replicated, identical IEEE 30-bus systems undermine the federated-learning motivation: the premise is cross-site statistical diversity, yet the cluster has homogeneous topology and (apparently) homogeneous data generation, so the 0.926 vs 0.921 AUC gap — the paper's own evidence for federated benefit — is within noise (±0.014 vs ±0.015) and cannot support the claimed advantage of federation beyond faster convergence. - The economically surprising result that participation level 0.1 outperforms full participation ($1.4/h vs $15.96/h residual penalty) is mentioned but never explained, and the paper headlines the weaker full-participation number. - The attack model assumes the adversary never learns or tracks the reconfiguration — a strong assumption given D-FACTS changes are observable in telemetry; no adaptive attacker is simulated. - The $1.5/MWh V2G compensation is far below realistic battery-degradation costs reported in the V2G literature; at plausible rates the 94.6% net reduction could shrink substantially, and the itemized accounting in Table 6 does not expose this sensitivity. - No statistical treatment (seeds, confidence intervals) for the cost results, and no localization or response component — the framework detects but does not act on a confirmed attack beyond the passive reconfiguration already in place. Bottom Line: A practitioner in power-grid cybersecurity gains a genuinely new idea — spatially targeted V2G dispatch as a physical sink for MTD's operating-cost penalty — plus a rare honest federated-learning stress study, but must wait for AC-accurate models, an adaptive attacker, realistic V2G cost accounting, and an empirical baseline comparison before treating the 95% cost-reduction figure as deployment-grade evidence.

Formal Operations Specifications for Reliable System Management

J Wang, JT Gu, R Tang, T Chajed, T Xu, X Sun · xudongs.com · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces formal operations specifications (FOS) — formal state-machine contracts, written in the P specification language, that describe a production system's management interfaces as preconditions/postconditions over management state — and shows they can systematically catch bugs in Kubernetes operators via model checking. - Why it's important: Management-plane software (Kubernetes operators, increasingly AI agents) is written from incomplete documentation and experience, and erroneous interactions with the managed application account for 42% of operator failures studied in prior field work; correctness today is best-effort. - How it does it: Each management interface is specified as a Hoare triple derived by reading the system's source code (not docs), encoded as assertions in invariant monitors over a P state-machine model of the managed system, then composed with models of the operator and Kubernetes API for model checking, validated against real execution traces. - The good: The approach found 39 previously unknown bugs across four popular operators (CockroachDB, Strimzi/Kafka, RabbitMQ cluster-operator, solr-operator) using FOSes covering 105 management interfaces and 1,946 assertions, with concrete linked GitHub issues. - The missing: No end-to-end evaluation of the central automation claim — the paper says FOS generation 'can potentially be automated' and reports using Claude Code after one manual spec, but reports no measurement of generation accuracy, fidelity, or human effort; bug counts also lack severity triage and false-positive analysis. - Read it or not: Worth reading for systems researchers and practitioners working on operator/agent reliability or lightweight formal methods — it defines a new specification target (management semantics, not implementation semantics) and reports real bug-finding results, even though it is a workshop position paper rather than a full evaluation.

Problem & Motivation: Production systems are increasingly managed by management software (Kubernetes operators) and AI agents rather than humans, but management-plane code is written against under-documented, system-specific management semantics — the preconditions and state-machine behavior of management interfaces. The paper's motivating example: a PostgreSQL operator issued three incorrect `failover` calls (promoting an unready backup, promoting a lagging async standby, promoting a non-sync-standby in sync mode), each violating an undocumented precondition and causing cluster unavailability; none of the preconditions appeared in the manual at the time. Existing tools target the wrong layer: operator-testing tools (Acto, etc.) find bugs inside operators but not interface-misuse bugs, and verified-controller frameworks (Anvil, Verus) do not reason about the managed application's semantics. The stakeholders are cloud-system maintainers, operator developers, and the growing community deploying AI agents for autonomous system management. Key Idea: The core insight is that the right formal artifact for management correctness is neither an API spec (input validation is insufficient — all three PostgreSQL bugs used valid API calls with valid parameters) nor an implementation-verification spec (TLA+/Alloy/Verus models describe internal behavior, not management), but a management-plane-perspective transition system: a model of only the management-relevant state (primary, membership, replication mode, sync-standby set, lag, promotability), with each management interface as a Hoare-triple action `{P} m {Q}` where P and Q are derived from the system's own source-code validation and execution paths — including silent asynchronous post-return behavior such as the HA loop's WAL-lag check that the synchronous handler misses. Methodology: The recipe has three stages. (1) Interface specification: for each management interface, start at the invocation site in the system source code and derive the precondition from the guards the system checks (both error-returning checks and silent later checks), and the postcondition from the state established synchronously on success — for `failover`, this yields five preconditions P1–P5 including the asynchronously-checked lag bound, and a minimal postcondition (no returned error) because membership change is asynchronous. (2) P modeling: write a P state machine of the managed system containing only management-relevant state, with each interface modeled as actions that split synchronous acknowledgment from asynchronous effect (e.g., `eFailoverReq` records the request and replies, then `eRunFailover` performs the demote/promote — capturing asynchrony precisely); encode pre/postconditions as assertion monitors. (3) Checking: write P models of the operator's reconciliation loop (random candidate choice becomes P's nondeterministic `choose`) and a reusable Kubernetes API model, compose all three machines, and run P's model checker — a failed precondition assertion is a safety violation; termination without reaching a user-declared desired state approximates a liveness violation. Model fidelity is checked via postcondition assertions and trace validation, replaying real execution traces against the composed model to approximate an implementation-to-model refinement check. Key design decisions: deriving specs from source code rather than documentation (well-justified by the motivating example), modeling at the management-plane abstraction rather than protocol level (justified by the argument that same-protocol implementations have divergent management semantics), and choosing P over TLA+/Dafny for developer friendliness (weaker justification — the paper concedes the choice may not matter as AI generates specs). Key Results: The paper reports preliminary experience, not a benchmarked evaluation. FOSes were written for four systems — CockroachDB (13 interfaces, 911 assertions, 11,478 LOC), Kafka/Strimzi (46 interfaces, 491 assertions, 11,689 LOC), RabbitMQ cluster-operator (8 interfaces, 190 assertions, 4,648 LOC), and Solr (38 interfaces, 354 assertions, 10,042 LOC) — totaling 105 interfaces and 1,946 assertions. Model checking the composed FOS + operator + Kubernetes API models found 39 new bugs: 29 in the CockroachDB operator, 5 in Strimzi, 3 in the RabbitMQ cluster operator, 2 in the solr operator. Two exemplified bugs: (Bug-1) the CockroachDB operator skips decommissioning during downscale, leaving a live member holding replicas and risking data loss (GitHub issue cockroachdb/cockroach-operator#1151); (Bug-2) the Solr operator hangs after a mid-reconciliation crash, never completing a backup — a liveness violation (apache/solr-operator#824). Baselines are qualitative rather than quantitative: the paper argues API specs, operator-testing tools, and verified-controller work cannot catch these interface-misuse bugs, but does not run those tools head-to-head. The first FOS (CockroachDB) was written manually; the other three were generated with Claude Code from a summarized 'agent skill', and operator P models were 'mostly automated' — no time/effort figures are given. This is a workshop (HotNets) position paper with preliminary results; claims about automation and runtime verification of AI agents are forward-looking, not measured. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the repositioning of formal specification from describing a system's implementation or a controller's internals to defining a formal contract between the managed system and its management plane (management-relevant state, interface Hoare triples, async-accurate action modeling) — the paper argues convincingly that none of the existing spec styles (OpenAPI, TLA+/Alloy/Verus implementation models, Kubernetes-controller specs) fit this target. The machinery itself — P state machines, assertion monitors, model checking, trace validation — is a competent combination of existing techniques applied to this new target, and the AI-assisted spec generation is a standard application of coding agents. Rigor & Reproducibility: The bug-finding results are concrete and falsifiable — each is anchored to a public GitHub issue, which is stronger evidence than self-reported counts alone. No error bars or multiple-seed statistics are reported (model checking is deterministic, so significance tests are arguably inapplicable, though bug-severity triage and checker false-positive rates are not reported either). No ablations isolate which specification components (async action splitting, individual preconditions, the Kubernetes API model) drive bug-finding power. Critically, no code, FOSes, P models, or generated agent skills are stated to be released — no repository URL appears in the paper, which limits reproducibility of the 37,857-LOC spec corpus. Methodological concerns: the operator models and the FOSes were largely produced by the same tooling and authors who evaluate them, so model-code fidelity rests on trace validation that is described but not quantified (e.g., no coverage or divergence metrics); '39 new bugs' is not broken down by root cause, severity, or whether each was confirmed by maintainers; and the automation claim is evaluated only anecdotally on four systems with the first, hardest spec done manually. The comparison against prior tooling (Acto, Anvil) is an argument, not an experiment. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper builds and runs P models and reports bug-finding results, with a position-paper framing). - Practical: Yes — P is a freely available open-source language and model checker, and nothing in the pipeline requires exotic hardware. - Efficient: The spec-writing cost is the dominant expense — 37,857 LOC of P for four systems, reduced to 'mostly automated' after one manual seed spec, but no person-hours or token/compute costs are reported; model checking at this model size is acknowledged in prior work to face scalability limits. - Effective: The evidence (39 bugs in widely used operators, including data-loss and liveness bugs) shows the method catches a real, documented failure class that testing tools reportedly miss, though it targets management-software conformance, not end-to-end production incident reduction. - Scalable: Not tested — the paper itself flags model-checking scalability as an open problem and proposes deductive verification (PVerifier) and the Anvil port as future directions; applying FOSes to AI agents via runtime monitoring is proposed but unimplemented. The work currently stops at paper form plus (unstated) internal P models; no library, tool, dataset, or trained artifact is stated to be released. Strengths: - Sharp problem articulation: the paper cleanly separates interface-misuse bugs from operator-internal bugs and shows with the PostgreSQL/Patroni example (including a silent asynchronous precondition, P5, invisible to synchronous-handler analysis) why API specs and documentation cannot close this gap. - Real defect yield: 39 previously unknown bugs across four mainstream operators, with public issue links and concrete root-cause narratives (asynchrony-ignoring operation sequencing, missing decommission precondition) — this is evidence the abstraction level is right, not just plausible. - The Hoare-triple-per-interface recipe is concretely transferable: the paper shows the actual derivation from Patroni source lines to the five-precondition conjunction, and distills it into an 'agent skill' for reuse — a genuine step toward making the practice repeatable. - Honest positioning against adjacent formal-methods lineages (TLA+ implementation models, Anvil/Verus controller verification, AWS lightweight FM), with a clear articulation of why 'model the managed system from the management plane's perspective' is the boundary that makes the specs checkable yet faithful. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which strengthens credibility: (1) model checking has known scalability issues for models of this kind, motivating exploration of deductive proof via PVerifier; (2) liveness checking under bounded model checking is an approximation, and unfair P schedulers can cause false liveness alarms — an explicitly open question; (3) AI-agent management planes cannot be modeled as state machines, so model checking does not apply and runtime monitoring is needed instead; (4) AI-generated FOSes raise a fidelity question ('whether generated FOSes faithfully describe the system implementation') that would itself require automated trace validation; (5) the choice of P may not matter as AI generation matures. The paper frames itself as advocacy ('we advocate', 'we envision'), so the gap between what is demonstrated and the broader vision (agent runtime verification, correct-by-construction operators, interface redesign, network management) is acknowledged by construction. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the authors' own open questions, a critical reviewer would flag: (1) no released artifact — the absence of any stated public repository for 37,857 LOC of FOS models and the agent skill is the single largest reproducibility barrier; (2) no bug-quality analysis — severity, maintainer confirmation status, and false-positive/negative rates for the 39 bugs are absent, and no head-to-head comparison against Acto-style testing shows FOS finds bugs testing cannot; (3) survivorship bias in system selection — all four systems have popular, actively maintained operators; whether FOS authoring is affordable for systems with sprawling or proprietary management surfaces is untested; (4) the automation claim conflates feasibility with fidelity — Claude Code generating 3 of 4 FOSes is anecdote, not evidence, and the paper itself notes the generated specs' faithfulness is unresolved, yet the reported bug counts depend on spec correctness; (5) trace validation is asserted to 'approximate a refinement proof' but no metric (trace coverage, divergence count) is reported; (6) model checking explores the composed model, so coverage of interface interleavings depends on P's exploration depth, which is unreported — the tested scale is effectively bounded-model-checking scale, and behavior at 10× state-space size is only claimed to be a problem, not characterized. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or verifying operators, or betting on AI agents for system management, should read this: it names and formalizes a real failure class (management-semantics misuse) that testing tools miss, demonstrates 39 real bugs to back the claim, and honestly scopes what remains open — but it is a position paper whose automation and verification-vision claims are unmeasured, and it should not be read as a validated methodology until the specs and tooling are released and independently evaluated.

One Fuzzer, Many Reasoners: Adaptive Neuro- Symbolic Fuzzing with Reliability-Calibrated and Context-Gated Guidance

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces NSAI-FUZZ, the first unified semantics-aware fuzzing framework for heterogeneous neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) systems, built on five availability-aware, rank-normalized risk signals plus two adaptive weight-allocation methods (RCW and CSG). - Why it's important: NSAI systems can fail catastrophically from small semantics-preserving input changes at the neural–symbolic interface, and existing neural fuzzers (DeepHunter, TensorFuzz, DLFuzz) have no common way to test such heterogeneous architectures. - How it does it: Each task adapter emits semantics-preserving mutations and five architecture-neutral risk signals (boundary pressure, grounding uncertainty, representation drift, constraint violation, archive novelty) that are rank-normalized, masked for availability, and weighted either from calibrated AUROC reliability (RCW, closed-form Gibbs posterior) or from a learned context gate (CSG, pairwise ranking loss) during beam search. - The good: Under fully matched mutation/query budgets across 9 dataset–model cells, RCW and CSG reach 16.17% and 16.06% aggregate failure discovery versus 6.06% for the strongest adapted neural-fuzzing baseline, and the advantage survives deduplication (11,508/12,058 similarity clusters vs. 6,210 for TensorFuzz). - The missing: No error bars, significance tests, or seed-level variance are reported (only means over 10 paired attack seeds), and the evaluation is confined to four small synthetic benchmarks with 20 seeds per cell, so no evidence exists at realistic data scale or on trained-from-scratch systems. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you test or deploy neuro-symbolic systems or design fuzzing guidance — the adapter/signal abstraction and matched-baseline protocol are directly reusable; skippable if your interest is general LLM or perceptual-network robustness testing.

Problem & Motivation: Neuro-symbolic systems (ISED, DOLPHIN, NASR, NeSyCoCo, DeepProbLog) couple learned perception with symbolic execution, and a small perturbation can flip a grounded symbol, change an execution path, or violate a global constraint — failures that clean accuracy does not characterize and that gradient-based adversarial attacks cannot target because symbolic executors are often non-differentiable or combinatorial. Existing neural fuzzers guide search with neuron coverage or activation-space novelty, which is representation-specific and blind to NSAI-specific risks (grounding instability, constraint violation, execution-boundary changes). Practitioners testing NSAI systems lack both a common testing interface and a semantics notion of validity: a perturbation that changes a Sudoku's answer is not a valid robustness failure. The paper closes the gap of architecture-neutral, semantics-aware search guidance across heterogeneous NSAI frameworks. Key Idea: Separate what mutations are valid (task-specific adapters with an oracle certifying x′ ≡_y x) from which valid candidates to explore (a common five-signal risk interface with pool-wise rank fusion), then learn the signal allocation: RCW sets per dataset–model cell weights as a masked, KL-regularized exponential tilt of a fixed prior by per-signal AUROC on calibration pools (closed form w_j ∝ a_j·w0_j·exp(β·u_j), β=3), and CSG predicts per-round weights with a softmax gate over pool statistics trained with a pairwise logistic ranking loss. Rank normalization gives monotone-scale invariance (Prop. 1) and masking gives availability safety (Prop. 2). Methodology: Pipeline: (1) task-specific semantic mutators generate candidates that preserve the oracle answer, with invalid candidates discarded before execution; (2) a model-state adapter extracts available signals — boundary margin b = max_{k≠y} z_k − z_y, grounding uncertainty (entropy/prototype/execution uncertainty), cosine representation drift, normalized constraint violation, and archive novelty (min cosine distance to archive); (3) pool-wise percentile ranks ρ_ij ∈ [0,1] are fused with masked weights S_w = Σ w̄_j ρ_ij; (4) top-B beam (B=8) selection under a 256-query budget per initially-correct seed. RCW solves an entropy-regularized constrained optimization over the simplex with a closed-form Gibbs-posterior solution; CSG fits a linear gate (150 epochs, lr 0.03, ≤64 pairs/pool) minimizing logistic pairwise loss + L2 + KL toward the masked prior, with a misranking surrogate bound (Prop. 4). Critical design decisions: grey-box-only access (outputs + selected intermediates, no gradients) — justified for non-differentiable executors; hand-set Fixed prior w0 = (.35,.20,.20,.15,.10) — not justified beyond stating it; on-policy evaluation (all policies rerun from scratch after calibration on random-frontier pools) — well justified, since offline re-ranking would ignore frontier-induced distribution shift. Four propositions cover scale invariance, availability safety, RCW optimality/stability, and a local pairwise misranking bound; proofs are in Appendix A. Key Results: On 4 tasks (Sort-of-CLEVR, Visual Sudoku, HWF-7, ReaSCAN) × 4 NSAI frameworks (9 compatible cells), 20 policies, 10 paired attack seeds (1,800 runs, 9,216,000 candidate evaluations): Fixed beats Random in all 9 cells (up to 12.675% vs. 1.127% on Sort-of-CLEVR/ISED, i.e., up to 19.115 pp margins claimed in aggregate) and beats Uniform in all 9 (up to 3.280 pp). RCW/CSG beat Fixed in all 18 adaptive comparisons, up to +6.621 pp (HWF-7/DOLPHIN: 18.098% → 24.719%). Against five adapted neural-fuzzing baselines (DeepHunter, TensorFuzz, DLFuzz, NSGen-transfer, CriticalFuzz) under matched inputs, mutations, validity checks, beam, hardware (3× RTX A6000), and budgets, RCW/CSG achieve 16.17%/16.06% aggregate failure discovery vs. 6.06% for the strongest baseline (TensorFuzz); on Visual Sudoku/DOLPHIN all five neural baselines find zero failures while RCW finds 5.764%. Deduplicated: RCW/CSG retain 10,719/11,311 exact-unique failures and 11,508/12,058 similarity clusters vs. 5,610/6,210 for TensorFuzz, robust across cosine thresholds 0.95–0.99. Wall-clock: TensorFuzz uses 1.11× RCW's runtime for 0.45× its failure throughput; Random is cheaper (0.71×) but reaches only 0.20× throughput. A notable finding is signal heterogeneity: boundary pressure is the strongest single signal in 7 of 9 cells, but grounding and drift lead in others, and LOO ablations show the best signal to remove differs per cell. Baselines are adapted versions of established fuzzers rather than their original form — reasonable for fairness, but the adaptation quality is author-controlled. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the architecture-neutral, availability-masked five-signal risk interface that spans heterogeneous NSAI executors, and (b) reliability-calibrated (RCW) and context-gated (CSG) signal allocation for fuzzing guidance. The components are individually standard — rank fusion, AUROC-based weighting with an exponential-tilt/Gibbs posterior, softmax contextual gating, beam search, novelty archives — and their combination is competent engineering applied to a new setting; the semantic-mutation-with-oracle pattern is standard metamorphic testing. The claim of being the first unified fuzzing framework for NSAI is plausible but difficult to verify exhaustively. Rigor & Reproducibility: The matched-budget, matched-seed on-policy protocol is a methodological strength: all policies share seeds, mutators, validity filters, beam width, hardware, and query caps, isolating guidance quality. Ablations are present and informative (five one-hot policies, five leave-one-out policies, per-cell learned RCW weights, deduplication threshold sensitivity). However, results are reported only as means over 10 paired attack seeds — no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests — and per-cell sample sizes are small (20 seeds/cell × 10 attacks), which matters given cells like ReaSCAN where RCW's gain over Fixed is +0.072 pp. No public URL is given; the paper states an "anonymous artifact" containing adapters, seeds, logs, and analysis code. Concerns: the Fixed prior (.35,.20,.20,.15,.10) is unexplained and could have been informally tuned on these same four tasks; calibration pools come from random-frontier trajectories, a distribution mismatch with guided search (acknowledged implicitly via on-policy reruns); all neural baselines are author-adapted, so baseline strength depends on adaptation effort; and the evaluation uses only the authors' own adapters on synthetic benchmarks (clean accuracies 55.21%–100%), with HWF-7/DOLPHIN's low 55.21% clean accuracy complicating interpretation of failure-discovery rates there. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built framework with systematic experiments). Practical: Runs on three RTX A6000 48 GB GPUs with PyTorch/CUDA, i.e., commodity research hardware. Efficient: Guidance overhead over Random is ~1.4× runtime (Random at 0.71×), and adaptive weighting itself adds essentially nothing (CSG 1.01× RCW), while per-candidate novelty costs O(m_t·|A|·d) — competitive with or cheaper than the neural-fuzzing baselines it beats. Effective: The evidence shows higher oracle-failure discovery and diversity under matched budgets, which is a proxy — the paper itself cautions the failure clusters are "distinct observed failure behaviors rather than causally verified independent root causes," and no evidence links discovered failures to downstream deployment harm. Scalable: Not tested beyond 256 queries/seed, 20 seeds/cell, and small datasets; behavior at 10–100× budget or on production-scale NSAI systems is claimed nowhere and measured nowhere. The work delivers a reusable framework/artifact (adapters, calibration and search code, seeds — anonymous artifact, no public URL stated) rather than a trained model or library release confirmed public. Strengths: - The availability-masked, rank-normalized five-signal interface is a real abstraction contribution: it makes one search procedure work across ISED, DOLPHIN, NASR, and NeSyCoCo despite non-interchangeable internal states, with formal scale-invariance and masking-safety guarantees. - The matched-baseline protocol (identical mutations, validity filters, beam, budgets, hardware; on-policy reruns from scratch) cleanly isolates the effect of search feedback, which most fuzzing papers conflate. - The heterogeneity analysis (single-signal and LOO tables showing signal importance flips across cells, e.g., boundary best in 7/9 cells but drift/grounding best elsewhere) directly motivates adaptive weighting and is a useful empirical finding in its own right. - Small but correct theory: the RCW closed form with stability bound (‖log w_j/w_k perturbation‖ ≤ 2β‖u−u′‖_∞) and the pairwise misranking surrogate are simple, honest results with correctly scoped claims ("local ranking guarantee, not global regret"). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that failure-discovery rates must not be used as cross-dataset robustness rankings (candidate distributions differ by task); that constraint violation is unavailable/masked for ReaSCAN; that similarity clusters are observed behaviors, not verified independent root causes; that the CSG guarantee is only a local pairwise ranking bound, not a global-regret result, motivating on-policy evaluation; and that single/LOO diagnostics are post-hoc and cannot set weights in advance. They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting: 10 seeds per cell with means only; several claimed margins (e.g., ReaSCAN +0.072 pp for RCW, CSG vs. RCW differences) could be within noise. - The Fixed prior (.35,.20,.20,.15,.10) is unexplained; if it was tuned on these four tasks, the Fixed-vs-adaptive comparison and the headline gains are partially confounded (Goodhart risk on the evaluation suite). - All neural baselines are author-adapted ("matched-feedback adaptations"); no original-configuration runs are reported, so the 2.67× aggregate margin partly reflects the authors' adaptation choices. - Only four small synthetic benchmarks; no larger-scale or real-data NSAI workload, and no test on a framework not written/controlled by the evaluation pipeline authors. - Discovered failures are oracle-failure proxies; no human or downstream analysis of the severity/actionability of the found failures. - Calibration uses random-frontier pools while deployment is guided search; the paper reruns on-policy but never quantifies the pool-distribution shift's effect on RCW/CSG weight quality. - Missing comparison to any non-coverage baseline class, e.g., pure input-diversity maximization or simple uncertainty sampling without the five-signal machinery, which would test whether the full framework (vs. just entropy-guided sampling) is necessary. Bottom Line: For anyone fuzzing or reliability-testing neuro-symbolic systems, this is the current reference point — the adapter/signal abstraction and matched protocol are genuinely useful and the empirical margins over adapted neural fuzzers are large — but read the per-cell numbers with skepticism (no variance, hand-set prior, author-adapted baselines) and expect stronger alternatives to emerge once the framework is tested beyond toy benchmarks.

AnInter: Anti-Interference Training for Long Context Retrieval

L Ye · aclanthology.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces anti-interference training — fine-tuning dense retrievers on synthetic "noisy positive" documents that concatenate the gold evidence with distractor documents under a Multi-Positive InfoNCE loss — plus AICB, a benchmark for measuring retriever robustness to controlled noise levels. - Why it's important: In RAG over long documents, target evidence occupies a small span surrounded by irrelevant content, and current long-context embedders (even 32K-token Qwen3-Embedding-8B) degrade sharply in this setting, so retriever-level fixes matter more than context-window extension. - How it does it: It concatenates gold documents with k distractor documents (circular adjacent windows) to create multi-positive training targets, and generalizes InfoNCE so a query is pulled toward every document containing its evidence, trained only on short text (≤10K tokens) with LoRA. - The good: The transfer result is the strongest evidence: trained only at noise levels k={1..5}, AnInter-4B reaches 81.7 average on LongEmbed, beating the strongest baseline (E5-Mistral+NTK, 75.3) by 6.4 points, with a 25.0-point gain on the Needle task. - The missing: There is a single random seed (42) with no error bars or significance tests, code/data release is not stated, and the MTEB regression (−1.5 to −6.9 points) plus the synthetic-only noise construction leave real-world robustness unverified. - Read it or not: Worth reading for embedding-model and RAG-retrieval researchers considering training-time fixes for long-document retrieval; skip it if you need deployed long-context retrieval solutions today, since the technique trades off general retrieval accuracy and is evaluated mostly on synthetic constructions.

Rigor (60) is held back by a single seed with no variance estimates despite headline margins, no code/model release, and AICB partially overlapping the training distribution; the missing ablation isolating the multi-positive loss from plain data augmentation is a real gap. Completeness (62) is buoyed by a candid limitations section including the MTEB trade-off, but Resilience (58) suffers from the unconstrained 'state-of-the-art on LongEmbed' claim and a narrow concatenation-only noise model. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*60 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*62 + 0.15*58 + 0.10*55 = 61.
