Problem & Motivation: Practitioners deploying time-series foundation models (Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5, Moirai-2, TiRex) face a gap: zero-shot inference underperforms on instances whose local dynamics differ from pre-training distribution, but the standard remedies — few-shot fine-tuning on a support set, transfer learning, or retrieval-augmented forecasting — all require adaptation data beyond the current forecasting request. This data may be unavailable due to collection cost, privacy restrictions, or streaming latency, and even when available may be misaligned with the target instance (the paper formalizes the distribution-mismatch concern as E_Psupport[L] ≠ E_Ptarget[L]). The paper asks whether a pretrained TSFM can be specialized for a single prediction window using only that window's own observed history, a setting it calls history-only, sample-wise instance fine-tuning. Key Idea: Treat the target series' own history as a self-labeled training set: slide a window of length L_query (set by known seasonality or FFT peak detection) over the history, retain only windows whose full subsequent target of horizon H is observed before the forecast origin, retrieve those most similar to the current look-back, and fine-tune the model on these context–target pairs so that the supervised signal the model receives is drawn from the same generative process it is about to forecast. Retrieval, LoRA adaptation, and a safety-gated fusion of adapted and zero-shot outputs complete the pipeline. Methodology: SWIFT has three stages. (1) Self-Retrieval: the current look-back is the query; candidate context–target pairs are scored by negative normalized L1 distance after per-window Z-normalization (Eq. 11); K=15 pairs are drawn by softmax sampling with temperature τ_ret rather than greedy top-k, plus R=5 most-recent windows as a "dual-focus" augmentation; retrieved/recent windows are also passed as covariates at forecasting time. (2) Frequency-Aware Loss (FreAL): FFT the predictions and targets, rank AC-frequency components by spectral residual magnitude, assign weight 1.0 to the smallest top-K set covering a fraction τ_spec of total residual and 0.1 to the rest, and optimize a weighted spectral L1 combined with the time-domain pinball loss via mixing coefficient α (Eq. 15), plus an MSE anchor loss (Eq. 16) pulling adapted quantile forecasts toward the frozen model's outputs with stop-gradient. Only LoRA parameters update over 15 steps. (3) Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion: compute the normalized deviation Δ between adapted and base forecasts (Eq. 18), set the baseline weight w_base = min(λ_max, σ·max(0, Δ−τ_fus)) (Eq. 19, trust-region-inspired), and output the convex combination (Eq. 20). Critical design decisions: non-greedy temperature sampling for retrieval diversity (justified only by argument, no ablation of sampling strategy), threshold-based spectral masking adapted from FreDF (ablated: contributes 1.9–2.0 pp), and deviation-gated fusion (ablated: helps WQL by 1.09 pp, costs 0.01 pp in MASE). The anchor and fusion mechanisms together address over-adaptation, a genuine risk when training on ~20 samples. Key Results: On the six long-history subsets of Chronos Benchmark II (Traffic, Electricity, Exchange, ETTm, ETTh, ERCOT; horizons 24–48 steps), across four backbones and 24 backbone–dataset configurations, SWIFT achieves average relative MASE/WQL reductions over zero-shot of 6.31%/6.99% (Chronos-2), 9.08%/6.04% (TimesFM-2.5), 4.79%/1.78% (Moirai-2), and 5.45%/4.50% (TiRex) — 6.41%/4.83% overall. Pairwise win rates: 79.2% MASE / 91.7% WQL against dataset-level few-shot LoRA fine-tuning, and 62.5% / 79.2% against TTA (Kim et al. GCM method) across 48 comparisons; SWIFT is uniquely best in 60.4% of pooled comparisons. It improves WQL over zero-shot in 23 of 24 configurations. On fev-bench (46 tasks) and GIFT-Eval (24 tasks), gains shrink to +1.66%/+2.14% and +1.23%/+1.25% (WQL/MASE). Mean per-instance runtime is 6.835 s versus 51.405 s for few-shot fine-tuning and 6.365 s for TTA on an RTX A6000 (48 GB). Notably, few-shot fine-tuning beats zero-shot on only 50.0% of MASE and 20.8% of WQL comparisons, and TTA beats zero-shot on only 45.8% of WQL comparisons — i.e., point-forecast gains do not transfer to probabilistic quality, which the authors highlight as an independent empirical finding. Degradations from SWIFT occur in 4 of 48 zero-shot comparisons (e.g., Moirai-2 ERCOT MASE, TimesFM-2.5 Traffic). The baselines are current-generation models and a 2025 TTA method, though the few-shot protocol uses the target dataset's full training split while SWIFT uses none, so the comparison is protocol-level rather than matched-information. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM/FORMULATION plus NEW METHOD: the genuinely novel element is the history-only, sample-wise (instance-level) adaptation setting — specializing a TSFM per prediction window with zero external data — which the authors convincingly position as unexplored relative to zero-shot, few-shot, TTA, and retrieval-augmented paradigms (Table I). The three components are competent recombinations of known ideas: LoRA, FreDF-style frequency-domain losses, self-supervised window mining (a form of in-context exemplar construction), and trust-region/PPO-flavored deviation gating applied at inference. The setting is the innovation; the machinery is standard. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a strength: all variants use matched adaptation pairs (20), steps (15), optimizer, LoRA config, and seed, and the authors candidly report that fusion does not improve average MASE and that the anchor term's benefit is modest (0.31/0.80 pp). However: (i) results use a single fixed seed (123) with no error bars, repeated runs, or significance tests — problematic given margins of ~1–2 pp on some components; (ii) the evaluation is deliberately restricted to tasks with T ≥ 2048, which selects longer, typically more periodic series and inflates the applicability claim relative to benchmarks as a whole; (iii) hyperparameters (τ_ret, τ_spec, α, λ_anchor, τ_fus, λ_max, σ) lack a stated tuning/validation protocol, raising Goodhart risk on the same six datasets used for ablations; (iv) latency comparisons explicitly exclude data-collection and observation-waiting time, which the authors acknowledge but which flatters SWIFT relative to TTA's real-world cost profile; (v) no code or configuration release is mentioned (URL not stated); (vi) there is no baseline of simply fitting a classical per-series model (ARIMA/ETS, which also uses only the instance's history) — the most obvious apples-to-apples competitor in the data-isolated regime. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-flavored runtime analysis). Practical: Runs on a single 48 GB RTX A6000 with public checkpoints (Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5, Moirai-2, TiRex), so the hardware requirement is modest, though no code artifact is released. Effective: Evidence supports modest but consistent gains over zero-shot (5–7% relative on long-history tasks) and an edge over few-shot/TTA protocols, but the gains shrink to ~1–2% on fev-bench/GIFT-Eval, so the effect is real yet small outside the primary setting. Efficient: At 6.8 s per instance it is ~6× cheaper than the tested few-shot protocol but adds multi-second per-forecast overhead versus zero-shot (~sub-second implied) and slightly exceeds the tested TTA configuration; scaling to millions of series would multiply cost by roughly the number of forecasts. Scalable: Not tested beyond per-instance execution — no experiment covers high-throughput or continuous streaming deployment, and the per-sample LoRA update loop is the kind of cost that grows linearly with forecast volume; any scalability claim would be extrapolation. The work currently stops at paper form; no library, CLI, or released implementation is stated. Strengths: - The core reframing — mining an intrinsic support set from the target's own history so that adaptation requires zero external data — is a genuinely new and well-motivated problem formulation for TSFMs, cleanly positioned against zero-shot, few-shot, and TTA paradigms. - The matched-budget ablation design (fixed pair count, steps, seed, and non-ablated hyperparameters) isolates component contributions credibly, and the self-retrieval component's dominance (+4.26/+4.61 pp) directly validates the central hypothesis rather than generic fine-tuning. - Broad backbone coverage (four current TSFMs from different labs) and three benchmark suites with an honest selection rule (T ≥ 2048) make the cross-backbone generality claim more persuasive than single-backbone adaptation papers. - The paper reports its own negative/neutral results transparently (four zero-shot degradations, fusion not helping MASE, few-shot fine-tuning degrading WQL in 79.2% of comparisons), which is unusual candor. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that adaptation benefits vary across backbones, datasets, and metrics (four degradations enumerated); that fusion improves WQL but not average MASE; that the anchor term's benefit is not established per-dataset; that the latency comparison "characterize[s] the computational costs of their respective protocols rather than a matched-budget efficiency comparison" and excludes data-collection and observation-waiting time; that TTA may incur real-world waiting delays; and that reducing instance-wise adaptation cost is future work. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them — a credibility positive — though they do not flag the single-seed design or the T ≥ 2048 selection effect. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single seed, no variance estimates or significance tests: several component margins (~0.3–2 pp) and the fev-bench/GIFT-Eval gains (~1.2–2.1%) could plausibly be within seed noise. - The T ≥ 2048 filter means the method is never evaluated on the shorter-history tasks that dominate real deployments and most of these benchmarks; the abstract's "three long-history benchmark subsets" framing understates how much of fev-bench/GIFT-Eval is excluded (fev-bench lists 46 qualifying tasks of an undisclosed total). - No data-isolated baseline other than SWIFT itself: seasonal naive, ARIMA/ETS, or a simple exponential-smoothing model also use only the instance's history and cost microseconds; without them, one cannot tell whether 6.8 seconds of LoRA updating beats trivial local fitting. - No comparison against in-context/retrieval alternatives (e.g., TS-RAG-style retrieval into the context window rather than gradient updates), which is the closest related mechanism and could achieve similar benefits without backpropagation. - Hyperparameter provenance is unstated — if any of τ_spec, α, λ_anchor, τ_fus, K, R, or S were chosen by observing results on the same six Chronos II datasets used for headline ablations, the component analysis is partly circular. - The fusion gate (Eq. 19) uses the adapted/base divergence as a proxy for adaptation quality, but divergence can be small precisely when the adapted model is confidently wrong in the same direction; no analysis of fusion failure modes is provided. - Evaluation instances are processed independently (predict_batches_jointly=False), which is presented as a design choice but also removes cross-series context that Chronos-2 can exploit, potentially understating zero-shot capability. Bottom Line: A practitioner working on TSFM adaptation in data-restricted or privacy-constrained settings gains a genuinely new problem formulation and a credible, well-ablated recipe worth replicating, but the single-seed evidence, ~1–2% gains outside the primary benchmark, per-instance runtime cost, and absence of released code or classical data-isolated baselines mean this is a promising direction paper rather than a deployable technique — read it for the paradigm, not the numbers.

Battery Energy Storage Sizing in PV Ramp-Rate Smoothing using Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Based Controller

A Omidi, T Mishra, MR Almassalkhi · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a constraint-aware reinforcement learning (CARL) controller that co-optimizes battery energy storage system (BESS) sizing with PV ramp-rate smoothing, reducing required BESS power by 8.7–10.4% and energy capacity by 47.5–62.6% versus conventional ramp-rate control on three real-world PV datasets. - Why it's important: BESS capital cost is the dominant barrier to grid-code ramp-rate compliance for utility-scale solar, and oversized batteries waste capital while undersized ones cause violations — so any controller that shrinks the required nameplate rating directly cuts project cost. - How it does it: The core trick is a causal feasibility interval — the intersection of ramp-rate, converter-power, and SoC-derived bounds computable from current and previous measurements — into which the RL action is deterministically mapped, so constraints hold by construction instead of via reward penalties, while the reward (quadratic power, SoC-deviation, and linear running-peak terms) shapes the long-horizon dispatch that minimizes sizing. - The good: The evaluation is unusually honest for this literature: a noncausal input-convex-neural-network (ICNN) mixed-integer optimization with perfect foresight provides a lower-bound benchmark, and CARL closes a large fraction of the gap between reactive control and the causal limit on all three sites. - The missing: There is no code release, no variance reporting despite three training seeds, no battery degradation or lifetime model, and the controller is trained, tuned (27-combination grid search), sized, and evaluated on the same site data with only ideal setpoint tracking assumed. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on PV smoothing, BESS sizing, or safe/safe-RL-constrained control in power systems; skip it if you want hardware validation, degradation-aware economics, or cross-site out-of-distribution robustness — none of that is here yet.

The composite is pulled down by Rigor (58) and Impact (45): three seeds with no variance reported, sizing/reward tuning on the same site data used for evaluation, no code release, and no degradation model despite cycling-heavy dispatch. Novelty (68) is solid — a genuinely new problem formulation (RL minimizing BESS nameplate requirements) with a constraint-by-construction feasibility mapping — and Completeness (65) benefits from candid limitation disclosure. Problem & Motivation: Grid codes (e.g., PREPA ±10%/min, Hawaii ±1–2 MW/min, Denmark ±100 kW/s) cap the ramp rate of PV power injected at the point of common coupling, and BESS installations are the standard means of compliance for both upward and downward ramps. The required BESS power and energy ratings are jointly determined by site PV variability and the dispatch strategy: filter-based moving-average control (MAC) incurs lag-induced cycling, reactive ramp-rate control (RRC) concentrates compensation into instantaneous peaks and lacks SoC management, and forecast-based model predictive control depends on PV forecasts whose accuracy degrades with horizon due to cloud-motion uncertainty. Plant developers and grid operators thus face a coupled sizing-plus-control problem that existing methods solve either sub-optimally (MAC, RRC) or non-causally (forecast-dependent optimization). The gap the authors identify is that prior RL work on PV-plus-storage targets arbitrage or microgrid scheduling, and the few RL smoothing papers do not address BESS sizing at all. Key Idea: Map the RL policy's normalized action onto a precomputed causal feasibility interval F[k] — the intersection of the ramp-rate admissible band (from Eq. 6), the converter power limit, and a conservatively-derived SoC headroom bound (using worst-case efficiencies for guaranteed explicitness) — so any action is feasible by definition and the RL agent's only job is choosing where within F[k] to operate, which the reward steers toward minimizing peak power, SoC deviation, and hence required nameplate capacity. The linear running-peak penalty (Eq. 19) is the specific mechanism that trades off capital cost against cycling, because the running peak of |P_batt| literally fixes the required converter rating. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) System model: an energy-reservoir BESS with power-dependent (nonlinear, lookup-table) charging/discharging efficiencies from measured utility-scale inverter data, replacing the constant-efficiency assumption common in the literature; the plant is an AC-coupled PV-BESS pair at a PCC with 1-minute sampling and N=1440 daily steps. (2) Feasibility layer: per-step computation of the interval endpoints (Eqs. 9a–9b), causal by construction and non-empty whenever the BESS is large enough for the worst observed ramp. (3) RL training: a finite-horizon daily MDP with a 30-step PV history, previous grid power, SoC, running peak power, and time-of-day in the state; feasibility-interval center/half-width and SoC headrooms appended as engineered features (observation dimension H+8); PPO with GAE (γ=0.999, λ=0.97, 3M training steps) trains an MLP actor–critic; the reward is the sum of a quadratic power penalty, a quadratic SoC-deviation penalty, and the linear peak-exceedance penalty, with weights selected by a two-stage per-site grid search over 27 combinations. (4) Sizing: Algorithm 1 iteratively simulates the controller over the dataset, extracts required power (max |P_batt|) and energy (2× max SoC deviation from reference), enforces C-rating, and re-evaluates until convergence — necessary because nonlinear efficiency couples power rating to energy trajectory. A noncausal ICNN-based mixed-integer optimization (Big-M ReLU encoding, simultaneous charge/discharge excluded via binaries) over the full daily profile with perfect foresight supplies the lower-bound benchmark. Design decisions worth noting: constraint-by-construction rather than penalties (well-justified — penalty tuning does not guarantee compliance), worst-case-efficiency bounding of the SoC constraint (justified for guarantee, but conservative), and per-day episodes with random site-day sampling (reasonable, but couples training and sizing data). Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed (arXiv:2611.17612, submitted to Elsevier). Key Results: On three real-world 1-minute datasets (Site A: Burlington VT, 6.1 kW, 8 months; Site B: Shungnak AK, 200 kW, 1 year; Site C: Rutland VT, 510 kW, 1 year; Site C most variable with σ=6.9%/min and 5.1% of daylight steps violating ±10%/min), at Rmax=10%/min: CARL reduces peak BESS power vs RRC by 10.3%, 10.4%, 8.7% at Sites A/B/C, and energy capacity by 47.5%, 51.6%, 62.6%; versus MAC, energy reductions reach 74.3% (Site B). At Site B, required peak power falls from 0.36 p.u. (RRC) to 0.32 p.u. (CARL); across the Rmax sweep CARL cuts peak power 7.9–15.8% vs RRC and 15.6–33.3% vs MAC. Estimated capital cost (NREL 2024: $372/kW + $241/kWh) drops 17.0–22.4% vs RRC, e.g., $146,174 vs $188,334 at Site C (510 kW). The ICNN perfect-foresight benchmark remains well below CARL (e.g., 37 kW/5 kWh vs 64.5 kW/15 kWh at Site B), quantifying the remaining causal gap. A counter-intuitive finding: at relaxed limits (Rmax=20%/min) CARL's energy advantage over RRC reverses (0.052 vs 0.045 p.u.-h) because CARL proactively pre-positions the battery while RRC idles — the benefit is specific to tight constraints. The efficiency study shows a constant-η assumption underestimates nonlinear-model energy requirements by up to 46.4% (MAC at η=0.93), supporting the nonlinear model. Cross-dataset transfer shows peak-power generalization is stable while energy transfer to the most variable site (C) degrades (e.g., 0.3 vs 0.14 p.u.-h when trained on B). Implied C-rates exceed 1 for all methods at 10%/min, showing the problem is power-constrained, not energy-constrained. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with an engineering contribution. The genuinely novel elements are (i) formulating PV ramp-rate smoothing as an RL problem whose explicit objective is minimizing BESS nameplate requirements — prior RL work addressed arbitrage, scheduling, or fixed-capacity smoothing — and (ii) the causal feasibility-interval action mapping that enforces ramp-rate, power, and SoC constraints by construction. The components themselves are standard: PPO with GAE is off-the-shelf, the ICNN efficiency model is the authors' own prior conference work [31], and the sizing loop is a straightforward fixed-point iteration. The contribution is a competent, well-motivated assembly of known techniques into a new problem framing, not a new learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-type evidence is partial but real: the paper isolates the effect of the running-peak penalty and SoC-centering reward through dispatch-behavior analysis (Fig. 7) and an Rmax sweep, and the efficiency-model ablation (Fig. 8) is a genuinely useful sensitivity study. Three independent random seeds are used and averaged, but no standard deviations or significance tests are reported — the 8.7–10.4% peak-power margins over RRC could conceivably overlap across seeds. Reward weights are tuned per site by grid search on training data, and the sizing is performed on the same site data used for training and weight selection, so reported sizing numbers are partially in-sample (no held-out-site sizing evaluation except the transfer table). No code, data, or trained weights are released (no repository mentioned). Baselines are appropriate and current for this niche (MAC, reactive RRC, and a perfect-foresight benchmark), but notably absent are adaptive MAC variants (which the authors cite [13]) and any forecast-based MPC despite the motivation centering on forecast limitations. Methodological concern: the conservative worst-case-efficiency SoC bounds in Eq. 7 could inflate the CARL sizing relative to methods using tighter bounds, though this is disclosed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (simulation-only study with a system/control method). Practical: Yes — the deployed artifact is an MLP actor plus interval arithmetic; at 1-minute control resolution any industrial controller or embedded hardware can run it, and the critic is discarded at deployment. Efficient: Training took 3M steps per site (modest by RL standards); inference cost is negligible relative to the alternatives, and the benefit side — a 17–22% capital-cost reduction on the BESS — dwarfs the controller's compute cost. Effective: Ramp-rate compliance holds in all reported simulations with the nonlinear efficiency model, but evidence is simulation-only with ideal setpoint tracking and no converter dynamics, SoC-restore-overnight assumption, or degradation model, so it solves the stated problem in a simplified model, not the fielded problem. Scalable: Untested beyond 510 kW plants; the authors claim per-p.u. normalization supports larger plants, but 100× scale (tens of MW, spatially diverse fleets where geographic aggregation changes ramp statistics) is unvalidated. Deliverable status: paper only — no library, tool, dataset, or trained model artifact is released. Strengths: (1) The constraint-by-construction feasibility mapping is a clean, verifiable solution to a problem that plagues RL in power systems — penalty-based constraint handling — and it transfers directly to deployment since it needs only causal measurements. (2) Framing the objective as minimizing nameplate BESS requirements (with the running-peak penalty as the cost-facing mechanism) is a sharper economic target than the usual smoothing-error metrics, and the implied C-rate analysis (power- vs energy-constrained regimes) is an actionable insight for practitioners. (3) The perfect-foresight ICNN benchmark is methodologically exemplary: it bounds achievable performance and quantifies exactly how much of the gap CARL closes, instead of letting the paper's method look unconditionally optimal. (4) The nonlinear power-dependent efficiency study is a substantive empirical finding in its own right — a 46.4% sizing underestimate under a common constant-η assumption at η=0.93 for MAC. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that setpoint tracking is assumed ideal at 1-minute resolution; that SoC is reset to the reference overnight, assuming overnight restoration; that future work must add battery degradation and energy arbitrage objectives; and that hardware-in-the-loop validation is pending. They also candidly report the regime where CARL loses to RRC (relaxed ramp limits, 20%/min) and the cross-dataset energy-transfer degradation to Site C. This is direct confrontation of limitations and a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No variance across the three seeds is reported — with margins as small as 8.7% in peak power, seed noise is a live threat to the headline claim. (2) Reward weights and sizing are derived from the same site data used for evaluation; a fully held-out site or year would strengthen the sizing claims. (3) The sizing dataset and training dataset are the same trajectories, so the learned policy may exploit idiosyncratic site ramps (a mild Goodhart risk), and the transfer table showing energy-requirement inflation off-site partially confirms this. (4) Battery degradation is excluded, yet CARL's proactive dispatching increases cycling relative to RRC's dead band — the paper's own citation [36] studies control-dependent cycling degradation, so the capital-cost savings could be eroded by replacement costs; this is unmodeled. (5) No comparison against adaptive MAC or forecast-based MPC, both cited as relevant baselines. (6) The assumption of overnight SoC restoration is unstated in terms of its energy source and cost, and grid-frequency/voltage dynamics are ignored, limiting claims about stability benefits. (7) Worst-case-efficiency bounding in Eq. 7 makes the feasibility interval conservative; the sensitivity of CARL's sizing result to this conservatism is not quantified. Bottom Line: For engineers sizing PV-coupled storage against ramp-rate grid codes, this is worth reading — the feasibility-interval formulation, the power-constrained sizing insight, and the efficiency-model sensitivity results are immediately usable — but it remains a simulation-stage preprint, and readers wanting degradation-aware economics, code, or field validation should treat the reported 17–22% cost savings as an upper bound pending follow-up work.

Problem & Motivation: Teams training or evaluating LLM agents that write Apple Metal kernels need environments where agents compile and run native macOS code against the Apple GPU. Docker on macOS runs inside a Linux VM with no native Metal access; macOS VMs only expose virtualized Metal; bare macOS offers no isolation between concurrent agent sessions. Compounding this, agent sessions alternate model requests, file editing, and short GPU executions, so GPU capacity sits idle — the paper measures 44.0 s of GPU activity across a 31.6-minute metal_nbody session (2.32%). With multiple sessions per node, serial-queue imbalance is severe: in a 16-session run on 4 Macs, sessions on the busiest node waited 32.7 minutes on average versus 13.3 on the least busy. The gap is command-granularity scheduling for interactive persistent agent sessions, which prior systems (KernelBench, KernelGYM, Metal-Sci) do not provide — they schedule whole candidate evaluations and target CUDA or lack native workspaces. Key Idea: The core insight is to separate agent tool commands into two classes — parallel-safe operations (file tools, builds, matched by executable-path/argument-prefix allowlists) and everything else, which serializes through one FIFO slot per node to coordinate GPU timing — and then to migrate waiting (not running) serial commands from overloaded nodes to idle ones, since the instance's workspace and HOME are mounted at identical absolute paths on all pool nodes via SMB. Migration only moves the command description; live processes, Metal buffers, and GPU state never cross machines, which sidesteps GPU state migration entirely at the cost of excluding commands with local state. Methodology: The system has four layers. (1) Instance isolation: each agent gets a private workspace and development HOME inside an Apple App Sandbox process; child processes inherit the sandbox policy, and the paper demonstrates allowed writes to ~/demo versus denied writes to /Users/sandbox1/demo. (2) Per-node scheduling: an editable allowlist routes matched commands to parallel execution; unmatched commands enter a single-slot FIFO queue per node, admitting locally with no controller round trip. (3) Cross-node migration: a cluster controller (SSH-invoked CLI per node) scans for waiting serial commands, selects a target with a free slot and no local waiters, then runs reserve (validate files/rules, hold target slot) → claim (prevent local start) → commit (start on target); results return to the source tool call. Eligibility requires shared-workspace mounts, no absolute private paths, and portable environments. (4) Harbor integration: adapters for Claude Code, Codex, and mini-SWE-agent route shell commands through the managed interface and record model-request, tool-execution, and tool-waiting intervals separately. No formal objective function exists; placement uses argmin of active-plus-reserved instance counts. Critical design decisions: per-node (not cluster-wide) queues trade global FIFO order for local autonomy (justified by latency argument, but it caps fill rate — at most one migration per source node per scan limited concentrated-run speedup); allowlist prefix matching cannot detect GPU calls inside build tools, pushing classification burden onto administrators (acknowledged but a real usability hazard); migration excludes any command touching node-local state, which the paper handles by conservative eligibility filtering but does not quantify how often agents hit this. Key Results: On four Mac mini M4 nodes (32 GiB each, gigabit Ethernet, SMB shared workspaces) with six fixed Metal kernels (matmul, convolution, elementwise, reduction, normalization, fused): balanced 12-command batches scale 25.2 s (1 node) → 6.62 s (4 nodes), ~6,520 commands/hour, with dynamic scheduling adding nothing when balanced (as expected). Concentrated 4-node submissions improve from 25.3 s to 15.1 s (1.68× throughput) with 2-second commands, and from 36.8 s to 18.0 s (2.05×, 588→1,200 commands/hour) with 6-second commands; queue p95 waiting drops 21.9 s → 11.9 s (45.5%). However, recorded GPU identities show per-node counts of 7/3/1/1 in dynamic batches — the source node still ran most commands due to the one-migration-per-scan limit. Measured migration overhead is 1.86 s minimum (0.818 s lookup+reservation, ~ms claim/commit), rising to 4.20 s with a 16 MiB payload. Sixteen real mini-SWE-agent sessions on the metal_nbody task (Step 5 Preview model) averaged 45.1 min elapsed with 21.0 min tool waiting (1,165 serial, 114 parallel commands); the authors derive an estimated 2.14× sustained throughput for 4 vs 1 sessions per node — an analytic estimate (4×24.12/45.12) assuming continuously replenished sessions, not a measurement. Trace-driven replay of dynamic scheduling over the same 16 trajectories predicts mean tool waiting 21.0→17.1 min (−18.8%) and batch time 67.6→52.5 min (−22.3%), with sensitivity across 166 configurations giving 6.78–20.4% and 15.6–27.8% reductions; 8 of 16 trajectories improve and 8 worsen. Baselines (static vs dynamic scheduling of the same system) are internally fair but there is no external comparison system. Scale is modest: 4 nodes, 16 sessions, one task. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. Genuinely novel is the setting and integration: command-granularity scheduling for interactive persistent agent sessions with native Apple GPU access and App-Sandbox isolation, which no cited prior system (KernelBench, KernelGYM, Metal-Sci, distcc, Bazel RBE, Gandiva, Salus) provides. The mechanisms themselves — allowlist classification, per-node serial queues, availability-based migration with reservation/claim/commit, SMB-shared workspaces — are standard distributed-scheduling and remote-execution ideas (the paper honestly positions them against Sparrow, work stealing, and Bazel RBE) applied to a new platform; no new scheduling algorithm or theoretical result is offered. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-grade evidence is present: balanced-vs-concentrated and 2s-vs-6s command workloads isolate when migration helps; the migration-overhead microbenchmark (27 migrations, 3×3 payload/duration grid) quantifies cost; and the replay is validated by first reconstructing the static schedule to within 1 ms per session before changing policy, followed by a 166-configuration sensitivity study. Three independent batches per controlled configuration are reported as medians with min–max ranges, and all outputs pass an external numerical checker; no formal significance tests are given (ranges are tight). Code is open-source (github.com/WangHaoZhe/metal-sandbox and github.com/WangHaoZhe/harbor). Concerns: the agent-level dynamic-scheduling benefit is simulation, not a live A/B run; agent traces come solely from the authors' own task (metal_nbody) and a single commercial model (Step 5 Preview); the 2.14× throughput figure is an estimate derived from the authors' own trace, and its assumptions (replenished sessions, unchanged durations) are stated but unverified. This is an arXiv preprint and has not, as far as stated, been peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS — a built tool evaluated on a small deployed cluster. Practical: Yes — four commodity Mac mini M4 units, gigabit Ethernet, and macOS; no exotic hardware. Efficient: Migration costs ~1.86–4.20 s per command, so short commands are net-negative to migrate (the authors say this directly); throughput gains of 1.68–2.05× under concentration are meaningful but far below the 4× hardware multiple. Effective: Evidence shows reduced queue waiting and batch time in controlled runs and simulation; the deeper goal — faster or better Metal-kernel agents — is not measured (no task success rates or kernel-quality outcomes under either policy). Scalable: Untested beyond 4 nodes; the single controller scanning nodes once per second with synchronous SSH control, SMB shared storage, and the one-migration-per-source-per-scan limit all suggest bottlenecks at 10× scale, and the paper does not claim otherwise. The work delivers a real software artifact (open-source service, CLI, and Harbor adapter), not just a paper. Strengths: (1) Fills a genuine, currently unoccupied infrastructure niche — native Metal execution with per-agent isolation — with a clear capability table showing Docker and macOS VMs both fail on native GPU access. (2) The trace-driven replay methodology is disciplined: validation of the static reconstruction before policy change, measured (not assumed) migration costs fed into the replay, and a 160-plus-configuration sensitivity sweep — this is more honest than typical simulation-based claims. (3) Precise accounting that separates tool waiting from execution, and queue waiting from execution budgets, avoids inflating speedup numbers. (4) The motivating measurement (2.32% GPU utilization in a real session) is a concrete, quantified justification for command-level rather than session-level scheduling. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: sandbox restrictions do not cover some application-launch paths; the system provides no hostile multi-tenant containment and no physical GPU exclusivity (parallel-classified commands and other applications can still touch the GPU); allowlist rules cannot detect GPU calls, so administrators must manually classify build tools that run GPU tests; replay cannot predict behavioral changes in agents caused by different tool feedback, nor effects on kernel quality or training outcomes; migration is costly for short commands; and 8 of 16 replayed trajectories accumulate more waiting. The limitations section is direct and specific — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No live dynamic-scheduling agent run: the central agent-level benefit rests entirely on replay, so any unmodeled coupling (e.g., GPU contention when two migrated commands land near a running one, thermal throttling, SMB write conflicts) is invisible; the authors assume unchanged phase durations but never run even one live dynamic batch to spot-check. (2) Single task, single model: 16 sessions all run metal_nbody with Step 5 Preview; workload diversity (tasks dominated by compilation, or with many parallel commands) could flip the waiting analysis. (3) No downstream metric: neither task success rate, kernel performance, nor rollout data quality is compared across scheduling policies — the paper optimizes waiting time, a proxy. (4) The concentrated-run speedup is capped by an implementation choice (one migration per source per scan) that the authors diagnose but do not remove or ablate, leaving unclear how much headroom the design has versus this build. (5) No comparison to a trivially simpler alternative, such as round-robin assignment of new sessions to the least-loaded node at submission time (only placement-by-instance-count is used), which might capture much of the benefit without any migration machinery. (6) Durability/consistency of SMB-shared workspaces under concurrent writes is explicitly unsupported but its real-world frequency is never measured. Bottom Line: Practitioners building Metal-kernel agent training or evaluation pipelines on Apple Silicon hardware should read this and use the open-source artifact, since no alternative covers native macOS + GPU + isolation + rollout collection; researchers in cluster scheduling will learn little that is algorithmically new and may prefer to treat it as a well-documented engineering case study.

Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (31 ▲ )

Xin Yu, Fei Xia, Jiaqi Pan, Youbao Tang, Chengzhi Liu, Adams Yu, Sicong Jiang, Yanfei Chen, Lingzhou Xue, Ting Yu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 18 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Self-Improvement Memory (SIM), a structured memory that travels with an evolved LLM agent harness and records, per recurring harness problem, the edits attempted, their rationale, predicted-versus-observed outcomes, and evaluation provenance, so that harness optimization can continue productively when the benchmark or policy model changes (a setting the authors name Continual Recursive Self-Improvement, CRSI). - Why it's important: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) of agent harnesses is expensive (their coding runs cost ~4 h/round), yet an evolved harness shipped to a new model or task suite carries no record of why its edits were made or how they performed, so continuation re-breaks or misattributes inherited mechanisms — in their workspace transfer, the evolved harness started 5.48 points below the unevolved seed. - How it does it: Group every accepted edit under a root-cause hypothesis entry; give the full memory to both the proposer and selector LLMs in their system prompts (no retrieval or truncation); after each round, append the chosen edit's predicted and measured outcomes to the cited entry or open a new one. - The good: A paired study across ten independent source RSI runs (Terminus-2 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 → TB4) shows SIM wins 9 of 10 pairs, with a mean advantage of +2.36 points over harness-only continuation (95% CI [1.05, 3.68], p = 0.003), from matched starting harnesses, rounds, and candidate budgets. - The missing: Outside coding, every condition is a single RSI run reported descriptively (some margins are as small as 0.20 points), and no external continuation baseline (e.g., Harness2, HarnessBank, free-text evolution notes) is compared — only the authors' own no-memory and root-cause-only ablations. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you work on agent harness optimization, RSI, or agent memory, because the matched-transfer experimental design and honest ablations are more careful than most in this fast-moving subfield; skip it if you need a deployable artifact (none is released) or a general continual-learning contribution.

Novelty (65) is moderate — CRSI is a genuine new problem formulation, but SIM is a structured recombination of existing agent-memory ideas. Impact (35) is low with no released artifact. Completeness (70) is a clear positive given the unusually honest reporting of negative results. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*35 = 60.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners running LLM agents face a harness (context, tools, execution flow around a frozen policy model) that must be re-engineered whenever the policy model is updated or the task distribution shifts. RSI methods automate this by iteratively proposing, evaluating, and selecting harness edits, but they optimize within a fixed (model, benchmark) setting. The paper identifies two concrete failure modes of continuation: an evolved harness can score below the seed on the new setting (Opus-evolved harness starts at 68.41 vs. seed 73.89 on Gemini workspace tasks; FewShotAll harness starts at 72.92 vs. seed 75.72 on the target classification suite), and the harness code alone does not answer why each edit was proposed, what it was expected to fix, or what happened when it was tested — so the target optimizer may repeat failed directions or destroy mechanisms it does not understand. Prior work studies transfer of evolved harnesses and various memory mechanisms separately; the gap is a controlled answer to whether the optimizer's experience (not the task agent's memory) helps across settings. Key Idea: The core move is to attach memory to the harness optimizer rather than the task-solving policy, and to organize that memory by harness problem: each entry binds a root-cause hypothesis to an ordered list of attempts, each storing the modification, a pre-registered prediction of which tasks it will fix, the measured post-hoc outcome, and provenance (domain, benchmark, policy, round). Because predictions are recorded before evaluation and checked afterward, later rounds — including rounds in a different model or benchmark — can distinguish a sound rationale with a stale implementation from a dead end. Methodology: The base loop follows Meta-Harness-style harness RSI: at round t, an evaluator runs the harness H_t on the evolve set producing feedback F_t; an LLM proposer generates k candidates conditioned on (H_t, F_t, history, and SIM); an LLM selector screens and selects, yielding H_{t+1}; the memory update U appends the selected edit's record to the cited problem entry or creates a new one (identical root-cause texts are merged; the proposer itself performs entry matching, with no similarity model). Source RSI starts from an empty SIM and produces (H_S, M_S); target RSI continues under one of four matched conditions: Cold Start (seed, no memory), Harness Transfer (evolved harness, no memory), Problem-Only Memory (root causes only), and Full SIM. All conditions share target policy, tasks, N = 10 rounds, k = 5 candidates, and 5 rollouts per task. Critical design decisions: (1) the entire SIM is placed in proposer/selector system prompts without retrieval or truncation — reasonable at 10-round scale but unjustified for longer horizons; (2) predictions are pre-registered and checked — well justified and the most distinctive mechanism; (3) entry matching is delegated to the proposer's own judgment — convenient but unvalidated. No explicit loss function; the objective is the benchmark's aggregate evolve-set score, with held-out sets used only for reporting and walled off from the optimizer. Key Results: Benchmarks: coding TB2.1→TB4 (pass@1), text classification 3→8 datasets (pooled accuracy), agentic workspace Harvey LAB→JobBench/GDPval/APEX (equal-weight mean, LLM-judged), engineering EngDesign→Frontier-Eng (medal score). Cross-dataset: Full SIM finishes highest in all six settings, exceeding Harness Transfer by 2.43–4.35 points and Problem-Only Memory by 0.20–6.06; e.g., FewShotAll 77.92 (SIM) vs. 74.12 (transfer) vs. 75.92 (cold start). Cross-model (Opus 5.5 → Gemini 3.8 Flash, benchmark fixed): Full SIM best in all four domains, +3.60 to +11.33 over harness-only; workspace is the largest (84.75 vs. 73.42 from a shared 68.41 start). Paired coding study (10 independent Terminus-2 source runs): SIM 21.70 vs. 19.33 mean final TB4 score, +2.36, 9/10 wins. Generation chain on TB2.1 (Gemini 2.5→4 Argon): continuation beats fresh RSI on 3.5 Flash (+3.5) and 3.8 Flash (+1.6) but loses 0.8 on 4 Argon — a candid negative. Shared-harness comparison: unified synthesis (75.24 held-out) matches separately evolved per-model harnesses (75.20). Baselines are the authors' own ablations rather than external continuation methods; most single-run comparisons are explicitly descriptive, not tested for significance. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM/FORMULATION (CRSI: continuation of harness RSI across benchmarks or policy models under matched budgets) plus NEW METHOD (SIM), evaluated as a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (full record > root causes only > none, across 10 settings). The genuinely new part is the controlled demonstration that carrying edit-level rationale plus predicted/observed outcomes across a transfer helps, and the granularity ablation. The ingredients are standard combinations of existing ideas: problem-grouped memory exists in HarnessBank, RRSI already logs hypotheses/diffs/outcomes, and continuation with free-text notes exists (Xu 2026; Harness2) — SIM is a structured recombination of these, applied to a transfer setting prior work did not isolate experimentally. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well designed: the three-granularity memory ablation from identical starting harnesses is the right control, and the ten-pair coding study is the only statistically powered comparison (paired t-test p = 0.003, signed-rank p = 0.006, dz = 1.28 — correctly using the independent source run as the unit of analysis). Held-out feedback is demonstrably walled off from the optimizer, and the ethics statement confronts reward hacking, including reporting an accepted edit that fixed nothing. Methodological concerns: 3 of 4 domains use one run per condition (single-run margins as small as 0.20 points are uninterpretable); Gemini 3.8 Flash simultaneously serves as policy, proposer, selector, and workspace judge — the judge is fixed across conditions, but a same-family judge for a same-family policy invites bias; no external continuation baseline is run; no code, data, or harness release is mentioned. Not evaluated: memory-size growth, longer optimization horizons, sensitivity to entry-matching errors. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Yes — everything runs on commercial API models (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5) and public benchmarks (Terminal-Bench, Meta-Harness environment, RRSI environments); no special infrastructure. Efficient: Costs are matched across conditions, but absolute cost is high (~4 h per coding round, 10 rounds per arm, four arms, multiple domains) and the token cost of embedding the full SIM in every prompt is not reported. Effective: The evidence supports improved target-stage scores from matched starts, which is the stated problem; workspace results rest on an LLM judge and are a proxy for real task success. Scalable: Untested — the memory is read in full with no retrieval, so 10×–100× round counts or problem entries would strain context budgets; the generation chain stops at four steps. Deliverable: the paper itself; no library, tool, dataset, or trained artifact is stated as released. Strengths: (1) The experimental design — four memory conditions initialized from the same evolved harness with matched rounds, candidates, and rollouts — cleanly isolates the memory variable, which most RSI papers fail to do. (2) The pre-registered prediction/observed-outcome structure gives SIM falsifiable content per edit, not just free-text notes, and the case studies (P5/P8 completion gate, P3) trace concrete reuse decisions. (3) Unusually honest reporting for this subfield: Problem-Only Memory sometimes underperforms no-memory transfer (−1.82 on NoMemory), continuation loses on Gemini 4 Argon, one of ten pairs favors no SIM, and P8's accepted edits fixed zero of four predicted tasks — all reported in the main text. (4) The paired ten-run study with proper paired statistics is a rigor level most contemporaneous RSI papers lack. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that independent RSI repetitions are limited to coding (other domains: one run per condition), that settings require compatible harness interfaces, that the optimizer's planning/search procedures are fixed, and that SIM is evaluated only as a complete procedure (inherited memory plus target updates, not component-wise). They also flag LLM-judge bias in workspace and the reward-hacking risk in the ethics statement. This is direct, non-minimizing disclosure — a credibility positive — though the single-run caveat understates how much weight the four-domain headline ('best in all ten settings') places on unreplicated comparisons. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No comparison against any external continuation method (Harness2, HarnessBank, Xu 2026's free-text notes and replay) — the claim that structured problem-linked memory helps is only established relative to the authors' own weaker ablations, leaving open whether a simple full-log dump or RRSI's existing records would match SIM. (2) Missing memory-granularity baselines between 'root causes only' and 'full record' (e.g., rationales without outcomes), so the mechanism of benefit is unlocalized. (3) Policy, proposer, selector, and judge are all Gemini 3.8 Flash in the workspace domain, a four-way same-family confound never discussed. (4) SIM token growth is unreported even though the design reads the entire memory every round — the scalability story is asserted by omission, not tested. (5) Entry matching is done by the proposer itself, so memory-organization drift across a transfer is possible and unmeasured. (6) Source-retention (forgetting) is tracked in only one coding transition, though it is a central concern of continual learning the paper cites. Bottom Line: A practitioner in agent self-improvement gains real value from the matched-transfer experimental design and the paired statistics, which set a benchmark for how CRSI claims should be evaluated — but the method itself is a modest, well-structured recombination of existing agent-memory ideas, and stronger or simpler alternatives (raw edit logs, HarnessBank-style stores) remain untested, so adopt the evaluation protocol more readily than the method.

MEM-SQL: Memory-Empowered Text-to-SQL (17 ▲ )

Xiaoqi Wang, Wenqi Pei, Shizheng Hou, Yilai Liu, Han Chen, Boyan Li, Yuyu Luo, Hongyang Du · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 16 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HARE, a 1,600-request benchmark for measuring how Text-to-SQL systems reuse verified query history, and MEM-SQL, a three-layer SQL memory system (templates, reusable components, schema concepts) with coverage-gated retrieval and On-demand Schema Linking (OSL) that raises mean execution accuracy from 37.1% to 50.0% while cutting input tokens by 76.6% and latency by 68.8% on average across six LLM backbones. - Why it's important: Real users query the same database repeatedly, but benchmarks like Spider and BIRD evaluate each question independently, so the community has no way to measure — and systems have no incentive to exploit — the verified SQL already computed for prior requests, which on large schemas is expensive to reconstruct from scratch. - How it does it: The core trick is a coverage gate: a memory layer contributes evidence only if every decomposed retrieval requirement for that layer finds a match above a per-layer similarity threshold (min over atoms of max cosine similarity > threshold), so a strong partial match cannot mask missing evidence; schema linking runs only when no layer qualifies or the generator declares the evidence insufficient. - The good: The ablations cleanly separate the roles of the three memory layers — removing the template layer costs 4.0–6.9 EX points on every backbone, components matter mainly for composite requests (−3.7 vs −1.1 points), and schema concepts affect efficiency rather than accuracy — which is exactly the evidence needed to believe the design, plus OSL transfers as a pure efficiency win to three other memory designs (≥60% token savings everywhere). - The missing: Multi-source composition remains essentially unsolved (EX drops by at least 21.7 points when a request reuses several verified queries, e.g., 56.7% → 29.7%), the 240-question retrieval calibration set is drawn from HARE itself (tuning on the evaluation distribution), and no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported. - Read it or not: Read it if you build Text-to-SQL systems or agent memory architectures — the layered-memory-with-gated-routing design and the OSL transferability findings are directly actionable — skip it if you only care about single-shot Text-to-SQL accuracy on standard leaderboards, where this changes nothing.

Problem & Motivation Production Text-to-SQL deployments face repeated questioning of the same database: a user asks about a metric, then refines the date range, swaps an entity, or builds on a prior join path. Verified queries from earlier requests may already contain the needed joins or intermediate computations, and reconstructing that logic from schema is costly on large databases. Existing benchmarks (WikiSQL, Spider, SParC, CoSQL, BIRD, BEAVER, Spider 2.0) evaluate each request independently; the closest prior work, BIRD-History, annotates which prior queries supply knowledge but does not provide controlled reuse-category labels or measure the cost side. The gap: no benchmark distinguishes whole-query adaptation from partial component reuse, and no system decides principled when retrieved history is sufficient to skip schema linking. The people with this problem are builders of database-facing LLM agents and BI copilots, where token cost and latency on wide schemas are the dominant operational constraints. Key Idea The key idea is granularity-matched memory with coverage-gated admission to generation: store each verified query at three granularities (fully slotted whole-query templates, reusable CTE/subquery components with join-key options, and schema concepts mapping business terms to columns/joins), decompose each new question into per-layer retrieval atoms, and admit a layer's evidence only if its worst-covered atom clears the layer threshold — with schema linking deferred until memory demonstrably fails (OSL). The min-over-atoms max-similarity gate (Equation 3) is the load-bearing trick: it prevents one strong retrieval from hiding an uncovered requirement. Methodology HARE construction: (1) source selection picks a lead query from Spider/BIRD/Spider 2.0/BEAVER whose SQL contains the evidence to retain, with balancing by prior use and table coverage; (2) companion selection adds same-database queries sharing a table (up to two for single-category, up to six sources for composites); (3) constrained generation uses GLM5.3-Flash with 17 catalogued "business rules" (BR0–BR17: date-window shifts, threshold moves, granularity changes, join re-keying, etc.) to produce three candidates per item; (4) validation checks execution (≤600 s, non-null rows), question-SQL agreement, and reuse preservation via Claude Opus 5.5, with up to three repair attempts. The result is 1,600 requests (1,300 single-category, 300 composite) over 823 verified queries. MEM-SQL: offline, each historical query is templated (literals, sort directions, LIMIT/OFFSET, aggregates, window functions, and grouping keys become typed slots), decomposed into components (SELECT blocks keeping FROM/JOIN/clause structure, projections masked), and mined for schema concepts; items merge on cosine similarity ≥0.9 plus SQL equivalence, else an LLM coverage reviewer decides admission. Online, a decomposer emits layer-specific retrieval atoms, each layer retrieves per-atom k-NN (cosine similarity), the coverage gate (Equation 3) accepts or rejects the layer, the generator synthesizes SQL from the evidence bundle, OSL escalates to schema linking only when the bundle is empty or the generator judges it insufficient, and a dry run with bounded repair validates output. Critical design decisions: three distinct granularities (justified by ablation), per-atom retrieval budgets (recall rises from 56.67% to 94.58% versus full-question retrieval at 37.7% fewer items), and gate thresholds — the latter tuned on a 240-question calibration set drawn from HARE, which is a Goodhart risk. The memory is static and built only from verified history, fixed throughout evaluation. Key Results On HARE (1,600 requests, execution accuracy as the metric), across six backbones (GLM5.3-Flash, Gemini4-Argon, GPT6-Luna, Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.5-9B, Granite4.2-8B), MEM-SQL reaches mean EX of 50.0% versus 37.1% for Direct Generation, beating the three adapted memory baselines (BIRD-History, A-MEM, DAIL-SQL) on every backbone — e.g., 54.2% vs 50.3% (A-MEM) on GLM5.3-Flash, with 11.8k vs 56.1k input tokens and 60.8 s vs 258.5 s latency. It completes 95.4% of requests from memory without schema linking. Gains concentrate on structure-preserving categories: +20.6 to +30.8 points on rephrase/parametric for several backbones, while MEM-SQL trails baselines on structural changes and shared concepts. Multi-source composition is the bottleneck: single-source vs multi-source EX falls from 61.3 to 32.8 (GLM5.3-Flash) and 64.3 to 36.9 (Gemini4-Argon); for structural changes, retrieval succeeds on 90.8% of multi-source requests but EX is only 9.9%, so the failure is generative, not retrieval. OSL transfer: switching any memory design from unconditional to on-demand schema linking cuts input tokens by ≥60% and latency by ≥34% in every comparison, but accuracy effects vary — DAIL-SQL and A-MEM gain on fully-recalled requests, while BIRD-History loses accuracy on five of six backbones. By source benchmark, MEM-SQL gains 8.6 EX points on BEAVER (join-heavy) and 3.0 on BIRD but loses 0.6 on Spider and 0.7 on Spider 2.0. Baselines are reasonably current (DAIL-SQL is older but is a canonical demonstration-selection method; A-MEM and BIRD-History are recent). No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for the headline numbers. Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (HARE, with explicit reuse-category annotations distinguishing whole-query adaptation from partial component reuse — finer-grained than BIRD-History) plus NEW METHOD (the layered SQL memory with the per-atom coverage gate and OSL policy). The memory-layer concept and dense retrieval are existing ideas; what is genuinely new is (a) the annotated taxonomy of six primitive plus six composite reuse types with business-rule-constrained generation, and (b) the coverage-gate mechanism that ties evidence sufficiency to the routing decision between memory and schema linking. OSL itself is a simple conditional-routing idea whose value is the empirical transferability finding, not algorithmic depth. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are strong: layer-level removal on all six backbones (Table 2), retrieval-design ablation on a 240-question calibration set with per-layer recall (Table 3), category-level and source-level breakdowns, routing analysis (Table 4), error taxonomy (Table 5/15), and an OSL-vs-USL cross-design comparison (Table 7). However, the calibration set is drawn from HARE itself, so retrieval hyperparameters (k, τ per layer; merge thresholds) are tuned on the evaluation distribution — a Goodhart concern the paper does not address. No multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests appear anywhere; several category-level comparisons (e.g., ±0.5–1.3 points) are within plausible noise. Benchmark construction relies on LLM generation (GLM5.3-Flash) and LLM validation/repair (Claude Opus 5.5); while validation checks execution and reuse fidelity, the gold answers are ultimately LLM-authored and LLM-reviewed, and no human inter-annotator agreement is reported. No code, data, or memory-store release URL is mentioned. Memory baselines required nontrivial adaptation (Appendix B.3), which is disclosed, but adapted baselines can underperform their original tuning. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — a working pipeline, but evaluated as an experiment, not deployed). - Practical: Yes — it runs on commercial API models (GPT6-Luna, Gemini4-Argon) and open-weight models down to 8B, requiring only a database for dry runs and an embedding encoder; no exotic infrastructure. - Efficient: Strong — 76.6% fewer input tokens and 68.8% lower latency than direct generation on average, with 95.4% of requests skipping schema linking; the offline memory build cost is not reported. - Effective: Partially — it clearly solves whole-query adaptation (rephrase/parametric categories near 84–98% EX on strong backbones) but fails on multi-source composition (EX 9.5–38.9% in the hardest cells), which the paper honestly measures. - Scalable: Only claimed by implication — memory is static, memory size grows with query history, and no experiment varies history length or database count; retrieval cost per atom is bounded, but admission/merge behavior over 10×–100× more history is untested. Deliverable form: a paper; no released library, dataset link, or trained artifact is stated. Strengths - The coverage gate (Equation 3) is a clean, well-motivated mechanism: requiring the worst-covered atom to clear threshold directly addresses the real failure mode of similarity retrieval (one strong match masking a missing requirement), and the routing analysis (Table 4) shows escalations target genuinely incomplete evidence. - The benchmark's annotation discipline is above the norm for LLM-constructed datasets: 17 explicit business rules, category-specific retention/edit scopes, execution + semantic + reuse triple validation, and a repair loop — plus the paper reports where its own method loses (structural changes, shared concepts, multi-source), which is unusually candid. - The OSL transferability study is a genuinely useful empirical finding decoupled from the authors' system: conditional schema consultation is a reliable cost win for any memory design, but its accuracy depends on retrieval completeness — this separation of efficiency transfer from accuracy contingency is the paper's most reusable insight. - Ablation evidence is granular enough to attribute gains (templates → accuracy, components → composition, schema concepts → efficiency), letting a practitioner decide which layers to adopt. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state three: (1) HARE does not model schema drift (e.g., a fiscal-year definition changing), so memory robustness to evolving semantics is untested; (2) MEM-SQL uses static memory — dynamic addition, updating, and retirement of memory items is open; (3) execution accuracy rejects format-differing answers and cannot detect right-rows-for-the-wrong-reason SQL, so intent-level evaluation is needed. They also openly report the multi-source composition bottleneck and that OSL's accuracy benefit is memory-design-dependent. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The retrieval calibration set is drawn from HARE, so retrieval hyperparameters are tuned on the same distribution used for headline evaluation; a held-out-database calibration would strengthen the claims. - Gold answers are LLM-generated and LLM-validated with no reported human verification rate or inter-annotator agreement; systematic generator/reviewer biases could inflate category separability (e.g., questions worded to hint at the reuse layer). - No error bars or seeds on any comparison; several ablation deltas (±0.3–1.5 EX points) and the OSL accuracy differences between designs are presented without uncertainty, and some conclusions ("components matter for composition") rest on differences of 1–3 points across single runs. - Baselines all use unconditional schema linking while MEM-SQL uses OSL in the main table, so the headline comparison conflates memory design with linking policy — the OSL section partially corrects this (Table 7 gives USL/OSL pairs for baselines), but the headline numbers mix the two. - Adaptive memory-based baselines that learn or update their store (the very setting the paper's static-memory limitation flags) are absent; all baselines run with fixed memory, matching MEM-SQL's constraint but not the field's frontier. - Offline memory-construction cost and memory-store size per database are not reported, so the total-cost picture of the 76.6% token saving is incomplete. - No release URL for HARE or MEM-SQL code is given, which limits reproducibility of an LLM-pipeline-built benchmark whose value depends on exact prompts (Appendix D helps but is not executable). Bottom Line A practitioner building database-facing LLM agents gains concrete, actionable value here — the coverage-gated layered memory and the OSL cost finding are worth adopting and the negative results are honestly mapped — but the benchmark's LLM-authored gold data, absent uncertainty quantification, and unsolved multi-source composition mean the accuracy claims should be treated as promising rather than settled, and the unreleased artifacts blunt immediate uptake.

Reasoning-Aware Relational Representation Learning for Open-Vocabulary Scene Graph Generation

J Xiao, B Wang, L Qiu, S Ning, X He · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RaRe, a framework that treats MLLM-generated chain-of-thought rationales as relation embeddings for open-vocabulary scene graph generation, trained via contrastive alignment and a specificity-driven GRPO reward rather than using CoT only as an intermediate reasoning trace. - Why it's important: OV-SGG models collapse toward frequent object-predicate co-occurrence patterns, so rare and unseen predicates are badly recognized (e.g., baseline Novel mR@50 of ~2-15 on VG150), which limits downstream structured visual reasoning. - How it does it: A two-stage loop — Stage 1 contrastively aligns CoT rationales with their paired relation predictions (symmetric InfoNCE) to build a discriminative embedding space; Stage 2 runs GRPO on the MLLM with a label-free reward that penalizes CoT embeddings similar to other object pairs' responses, closing the loop between representation discriminability and generation. - The good: Under PredCls on VG150, RaRe reaches 22.49% Novel mR@50 versus 15.70% for the strongest baseline (PE-NET+RAHP), a +6.79 point gain, and ablations isolate which components help and where they hurt. - The missing: Gains are setting-dependent and partially regress — under fixed ACC proposals on VG150 SGDet, adding RL/SSL/calibration reduces Novel mR@50 from 10.21 to 6.69 versus training-free retrieval, and no error bars or multi-seed runs are reported. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on MLLM-based structured prediction or representation-space RL rewards; skip if you need a drop-in deployable SGG system, given the 5.45 s/image inference cost and mixed SGDet gains.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (68) are the strengths: using a contrastively learned representation space as a label-free specificity reward for GRPO is a genuinely interesting inversion of the standard CoT-RL recipe. Completeness (65) is helped by the paper explicitly reporting where its own learned components underperform training-free retrieval. Rigor (58) is held back by no multi-seed variance, evaluation on the same protocol used for tuning, the unaddressed hallucinated-but-distinct rationale risk, and code only promised. Resilience (55) suffers because the headline PredCls gain comes with a large Total R@50 deficit (49.90 vs. 64.70) not surfaced in the abstract, and one setting shows the method regressing below its own training-free baseline. Impact (35) reflects 5.45 s/image inference, a proprietary-model dependency, and no released artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*35 = 60.
empirical Novelty 70 Rigor 58 Non-Obv 68 Completeness 65 Resilience 55 Impact 35
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Open-vocabulary scene graph generation requires recognizing visual relationships (predicates) beyond the training vocabulary. Practitioners building structured visual reasoning (VQA, captioning, retrieval) face three coupled problems: (1) models overfit dataset-specific object–predicate co-occurrence statistics, so novel predicates degrade sharply; (2) under the realistic SGDet setting, relation prediction is fragile to noisy object localization; (3) long-tailed predicate distributions entangle representations, collapsing rare-predicate recognition (the persistent R@K vs. mR@K gap). Prior embedding-matching methods (OvSGTR, PE-NET, ACC/RAHP) and generative methods (PGSG, OpenSGen) optimize either embedding alignment or generation accuracy without explicitly enforcing semantic separability across predicates. Key Idea: Treat the MLLM's CoT–prediction output pair as a free, self-supervised training signal: learn an embedding space where CoT rationales are aligned with their relation predictions, then reuse that space as a reward function (specificity = low similarity to other object pairs' responses) for GRPO, so the MLLM generates object-pair-specific relational evidence that is directly optimized for inter-relation discriminability rather than linguistic plausibility. This differs from Relation-R1, whose reward is correctness of the final prediction; here the reward never checks predicate correctness at all. Methodology: Pipeline: (1) generate CoT–prediction pairs from Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct over ~30k VG150 training images (~46k base triplets, image-level soft-balanced sampling against long-tail); (2) Stage 1 — train embedding model f_φ (Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, LoRA rank 8) with symmetric InfoNCE (Eq. 4–5) aligning y_cot with y_pred; (3) cold-start SFT of the MLLM on 2,000 responses distilled from Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct; (4) Stage 2 — GRPO (EasyR1 framework, 4 rollouts per prompt, clip [0.8, 1.3], dual clipping, KL β=0.01) with reward r = r_spec + λ·r_fmt, where r_spec = 1 − τ·LogMeanExp of cosine similarities to rollouts from other entity pairs in the batch (Eq. 8); (5) inference via multi-template predicate prototypes (3–7 Gemini-generated templates per predicate), max cosine similarity over templates, pair-level z-score normalization, and subject–object prior calibration with base priors transferred to novel predicates via top-K=5 nearest base predicates (η=0.05); (6) optional supervised variant fine-tunes f_φ with multi-positive InfoNCE against ground-truth base predicate anchors. Critical design decisions: (a) no correctness signal in the RL reward — justified as avoiding base-label attraction, and supported by Table 11 where correctness-reward GRPO gets only 12.30 Novel mR@50 vs. 22.49; (b) negative sampling without repeated annotated triplets to reduce false negatives — reasonable but only heuristically controlled; (c) the supervised tuning (ST) stage trades Novel mR (27.11→22.49) for Base mR (21.81→25.53) — the authors present the full configuration as an explicit compromise, which is honest but means the headline number is a tuned trade-off. Key Results: On VG150 PredCls (EPIC split, 35 base/15 novel predicates), RaRe achieves 24.62/25.80 Total mR@50/100, 25.53 Base mR@50, and 22.49 Novel mR@50, versus PE-NET+RAHP at 24.50 Total, 24.99 Base, and 15.70 Novel mR@50; note RaRe's Total R@50 (49.90) is well below PE-NET+RAHP's 64.70, so the mR gain comes with a substantial global-recall cost. On VG150 SGDet with fixed ACC proposals, RaRe reaches 10.38/12.32 Total mR@50/100 and 8.02 Novel mR@100 (Novel mR@50 6.69 vs. 2.48 for re-evaluated ACC), but Table 16 shows training-free retrieval alone scores 10.21/12.27 Novel mR@50/100 — the learned components lower Novel mR@50 by 3.52 in this setting. On PSG SGDet (same PGSG proposals), full RaRe improves Total mR@50 from 12.56 to 17.52 and Novel mR@50 from 12.69 to 14.76 over training-free retrieval. Training-free zero-shot transfer to HICO-DET gives 27.71 Full mAP (vs. 25.19 for ADA-CM, 31.50 for DA-HOI). Diagnostic controls are informative: removing the image drops Novel mR@50 from 22.49 to 13.71 (visual input matters), embedding retrieval beats direct MLLM output by +13.37 Novel mR@100, and average CoT length shrinks from 392.8 to 297.1 tokens. Baselines are current (2024–2025 methods including ACC and RAHP), though some entries are the authors' own re-evaluations and several cells are missing (OwSGG, OpenSGGen). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with an EMPIRICAL FINDING component. Genuinely novel: using a contrastively learned representation space as a label-free specificity reward for GRPO, directly optimizing the rationale embedding space for inter-relation discriminability rather than final-prediction correctness — a reversal of the standard CoT-RL recipe. Standard combination: InfoNCE contrastive learning, GRPO, multi-template CLIP-style retrieval, and prior calibration are all established; the contribution is their specific coupling, not any individual piece. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: a component grid (TP/PR/RL/SSL/ST, Table 4), same-proposal PSG ablation (Table 5), same-backbone comparison against SFT and correctness-reward GRPO (Table 11), four backbone zero-shot comparison (Table D), sensitivity analyses for K and η (including showing η=0.1 destroys Novel mR at 10.92), frequency-stratified head/body/tail analysis with per-predicate prediction counts, representation-quality metrics (Silhouette, macro_mean_ratio — though Global/Base Silhouette remains negative, i.e., clustering is still weak), an object-only control, an inference-cost breakdown, and failure cases. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported (explicitly acknowledged in the NeurIPS checklist due to compute limits). Code is promised at https://artanic30.github.io/project_pages/RaRe ("will be released"); prompts and hyperparameters are fully specified. Methodological concerns: evaluation and tuning happen on the same VG150 test protocol, the η and K settings were chosen before test evaluation per the authors, Gemini-generated templates introduce a dependency on a proprietary model, and one headline setting (fixed-proposal VG150 SGDet) shows the learning stages hurting Novel recall — the paper reports this but the abstract's framing emphasizes the positive PredCls and PSG results. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact). Practical: Runs on 2× L20 + 4× L40 GPUs (commercially available), but requires a 4B MLLM fully fine-tuned via GRPO plus a 2B embedding model; Efficient: Inference is 5.45 s/image, with CoT generation consuming 64.7% (3.53 s) and embedding retrieval only 0.68 s — roughly two orders of magnitude slower than a classification-head SGG method, and GRPO training cost is non-trivial; Effective: Evidence supports the claimed improvement in category-balanced and novel-predicate recognition under PredCls and same-proposal PSG, but effectiveness degrades under fixed VG150 SGDet proposals where learned components reduce Novel mR@50; Scalable: Not tested beyond 4B-parameter models and two SGG benchmarks plus one HOI transfer; scaling behavior of the specificity reward (which depends on in-batch negatives) at larger rollout counts or datasets is unexamined. Delivers a promised software artifact (code/model at a project page) plus a reusable recipe (representation-space reward for policy optimization); at paper stage until release. Strengths: (1) The conceptual move of closing the loop between representation learning and generation — using the Stage-1 embedding space as the Stage-2 reward — is a genuinely interesting and transferable mechanism, cleanly distinguished from Relation-R1's prediction-level reward. (2) The specificity reward is label-free, sidestepping base-class annotation bias that the authors demonstrate empirically (SFT and correctness-GRPO baselines collapse Novel mR to 7.84 and 12.30 vs. 22.49). (3) Unusually transparent ablation reporting: the paper explicitly shows where its own method underperforms training-free retrieval (Table 16, Appendix J) and frames the full configuration as a base–novel compromise rather than hiding the trade-off. (4) The transfer experiment (zero-shot HOI at 27.71 Full mAP without task training) provides modest but real evidence the pipeline generalizes beyond SGG. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) MLLM visual hallucination is not addressed and may cause fine-grained errors on small/occluded objects; (2) balancing category-level generalization against overall recall is unresolved, and the benefit of learning/calibration varies across proposal settings — including the explicit admission that under fixed ACC proposals on VG150, novel-predicate recognition falls below the training-free retrieval baseline, attributed to a mismatch between ground-truth training pairs and detector-generated test pairs; (3) incorrect or biased predictions can propagate to downstream applications. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation reporting — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The specificity reward rewards distinctiveness, not visual truth — a response can be rewarded for hallucinated but unique content; the object-only control (Table 17) shows the image matters, but does not verify that rewarded rationales are visually grounded, and the failure cases in Appendix L confirm hallucinated CoT driving wrong predictions. (2) The headline PredCls Novel mR of 22.49 comes with Total R@50 of 49.90 versus 64.70 for PE-NET+RAHP — a practitioner needing high recall, not balanced recall, loses substantially; the abstract does not surface this trade-off. (3) The Novel-mR metric on the SGDet split is fragile: three head predicates hold 92.4% of novel GT instances, five predicates stay at zero for both models, and 'says' has only 12 GT instances against 44k predictions — the +4.2 Novel mR@50 gain over ACC partly reflects mR arithmetic on near-empty classes (the authors do analyze this in Appendix K, which is commendable, but the main-text framing does not carry the caveat). (4) No comparison against scaling the backbone instead of the method: Table 6 shows Qwen3.5-4B zero-shot already reaches 16.98 Novel mR@50 with 53.22 Total R@50, so part of RaRe's edge may be recoverable by a larger off-the-shelf model without any training. (5) No multi-seed variance, so the ~0.3–0.5 point margins in some SGDet ablations are uninterpretable. Bottom Line: A researcher in MLLM-based structured visual prediction should read this for the representation-space-as-reward mechanism and the unusually candid ablations, but practitioners seeking a deployable SGG system will find the 5.45 s/image latency, the recall trade-off, and the setting-dependent gains a reason to look at embedding-alignment baselines like ACC/RAHP first.
