Problem & Motivation: Mobile GUI agents act on whatever the screen shows, so an unprivileged third party who controls rendered content (email text, message bodies, in-app dialogs from a repackaged app) can hijack the agent's actions — the Environmental Injection Attack threat. Existing benchmarks (MobileSafetyBench, AgentHazard, GhostEI-Bench) evaluate this statically: security experts hand-craft payloads and pin them to a fixed step of a fixed task. Two failure modes follow. First, each artifact is bound to one task in one app and does not transfer. Second, agents given the same task follow divergent trajectories; an agent that never reaches the pre-positioned payload is scored as safe despite zero attack exposure. The paper reports Payload Miss Rates of 13.3–22.9% under expert-fixed injection, meaning up to a fifth of evaluations never actually test the agent. Key Idea: Make the attacker adaptive rather than static: condition both the injection-point choice and the payload on the target agent's realized execution trajectory, formalized as a bounded search F: (task, attack goal, benign trajectory, adversarial memory) → (payload δ, injection step k, vector v*). The trick that makes this tractable on Android — where, unlike the web, there is no DOM manipulation — is a pre-built library of injectable-page templates discovered by automated pentesting, which lets a monitoring APK recognize candidate pages at runtime and gate injection to template-matched pages in the trajectory. Methodology: The system has two layers. (1) A Probing & Evaluation Platform runs the target agent on the benign task, records per-step observations (screenshot, UI XML, reasoning, action), matches steps against the injection-template library, and injects payloads through a custom monitoring APK using generic/instance/rendering parameters; attack success is judged by deterministic programmatic verifiers checking environment state (sent-message logs, calendar entries, MobileWorld task verifiers), with Accept-click signals for dialogs. (2) A Red Team Agentic System runs three phases: AttackPathExplorer scores each template-matched candidate page on a 1–5 Likert scale along Context Relevance, Decision Criticality, and Reasoning Exploitability (equal weights, v(t) = Σw_i·dim_i) and picks the highest; PayloadGenerator synthesizes a combinatorial seed population over a 5-strategy × 4-style space (Σ × Ω), restricted by vector- and context-compatible styles; EvolutionaryRefiner iterates surrogate filtering (LLM semantic + VLM visual scores, f′ = α·s_sem + β·s_vis) before live execution, an LLM Judge's four-level ordinal outcome (Ignored/Detected/Partially/Fully Followed) as dense feedback, and top-k parent selection with LLM mutation, terminating on programmatic success or budget T_max = 15. Successful patterns persist in an Adversarial Experience Memory for few-shot retrieval on later tasks. Critical design decisions: template-gated injection (well justified — gives ground-truth exposure indicator), programmatic over LLM-based success verification (well justified — decouples compromise from task competence), and equal vulnerability-score weights (not justified — no sensitivity analysis given). Two attack vectors are simulated: Malicious Text (overlay text styled as host-app content) and In-App Fake Dialog (repackaged app's own Activity dialog); overlay windows, notifications, and UI-identity spoofing are excluded by privilege, reliability, or capacity arguments. Key Results: On an 83-instance benchmark (44 Malicious Text, 39 Fake Dialog; 47 cross-app, 36 single-app; CIA split 27/28/28; built on 65 MobileWorld base tasks, 12 apps, mean task length 27.8 steps), tested on three agents (Gemini-3.1-Pro end-to-end, GUI-Owl-1.5-8B on-device, Gemini-3.1-Pro + UI-Ins-7B agentic), each task run 3 times with T_max = 15: (RQ1) trajectory-aware selection cuts Payload Miss Rate to 4.8%/3.6%/6.0% versus 13.3%/12.0%/22.9% for expert-fixed injection, narrowing cross-agent PMR spread from 10.8 to 2.4 points. (RQ2) ASR reaches 85.1% (Gemini), 86.3% (Agentic), 85.1% (GUI-Owl), versus Static Template 6.8–34.5%, Zero-shot LLM 8.0–15.7%, Adapted PAIR 54.6–77.5%, Adapted Genesis 39.0–61.4%. Fake Dialog outperforms Malicious Text (88.9–95.7% vs 78.0–81.8%); Integrity attacks score highest (89.3–91.7%), Availability lowest (75.0–81.0%); cross-app tasks beat single-app (89.4–92.2% vs 75.9–82.4%). (RQ3) Stealth Hijacking Rate — original task still completed after successful attack — hits 68.1%/65.4%/46.4%; ASR on originally-failed tasks is 87.4–97.2%, showing attacks exploit agents even where they are incompetent. Human evaluation (10 annotators, 20 instances) scores Content Authenticity 4.3–4.7/5 but Behavioral Plausibility only 3.2–3.4/5. A consistent counter-intuitive finding: the lightweight on-device GUI-Owl is more vulnerable than frontier-model agents under all methods, including weak baselines. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (trajectory-aware adaptive injection-point selection for mobile EIA), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (83 CIA-annotated instances with programmatic verifiers), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (fixed-point benchmarks under-test agents; lightweight models are consistently more vulnerable). The genuinely novel elements are the trajectory-conditioned injection-point localization and the template-based injection infrastructure under Android sandboxing; the payload optimization itself is a standard combination — PAIR/Genesis-style iterative red-teaming with surrogate-assisted evolutionary search — applied to the mobile rendering constraint. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and decisive: removing evolutionary refinement drops ASR from 85.1% to 28.5%; removing surrogate pre-filtering to 63.9% (with average rounds rising 7.9→12.8); removing multi-signal ordinal feedback to 76.3% (rounds→11.4). Each task is evaluated 3 times per agent with results averaged, though no variance, error bars, or significance tests are reported. Baselines are reasonably current (PAIR, Genesis, AgentHazard, GhostEI-Bench templates) and adapted in documented detail (Appendix E), with all methods sharing MobileProbe's injection points to isolate payload quality — a good experimental control. Concerns: no code, dataset, or artifact release is stated (payloads are deliberately withheld for safety, but the platform and benchmark release status is unstated); α, β, γ fitness weights and equal vulnerability-score weights are fixed without ablation; the LLM Judge serves as a supplementary success criterion for complex Malicious Text cases, introducing potential judge bias; the benchmark is built and evaluated on the same MobileWorld-derived task set (development/evaluation not separated); and human evaluation covers only 20 instances. The paper appears as an NDSS 2027 camera-ready per its header (peer-reviewed venue), also circulated as arXiv preprint 2611.16693. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a red-teaming system with live Android-emulator experiments; also ships a benchmark). Practical: Runs on Android Virtual Devices (Android 14, 8 GB RAM) with commodity LLM APIs, so evaluation is reproducible on commercial hardware, though the monitoring APK requires emulator root that real-device audits would need to replicate. Efficient: Surrogate pre-filtering cuts live executions to 7.9 average rounds within a 15-execution budget per task, but each round requires a full long-horizon agent run (~28 steps) plus LLM/VLM calls — moderately expensive relative to static benchmarks. Effective: Evidence shows it solves the stated evaluation problem (exposure coverage plus payload effectiveness confirmed by programmatic verifiers), though Behavioral Plausibility of 3.2–3.4/5 and residual 3.6–6.0% miss rate mean attacks are not universally realistic or delivered. Scalable: Not tested beyond 83 instances / 12 apps; the authors claim the pentesting pipeline generalizes to new apps (with per-app human annotation of content locations) but demonstrate it on none, and scaling to hundreds of apps would multiply annotation and verifier-authoring cost. The work delivers a paper-form framework plus benchmark; no public library, tool, or dataset artifact is stated. Strengths: - The coverage-gap diagnosis is sharp and quantified: the Expert-Fixed vs. Cross-Agent PMR comparison cleanly shows that insufficient coverage is inherent to fixed injection points, not to human error, and the 13.3–22.9% miss rate is a concrete indictment of prior benchmarks. - The dual-metric separation — LLM Judge for dense evolutionary feedback but deterministic programmatic verifiers for the reported binary ASR — avoids the circularity that plagues LLM-judged security evaluations. - The ASR-F metric (87.4–97.2% on originally-failed tasks) and SHR (46.4–68.1% stealthy attacks) add threat realism dimensions that static benchmarks cannot express, and the finding that failing agents are more susceptible is genuinely useful for risk modeling. - The component ablations are well-designed: they measure both effectiveness (ASR) and cost (average rounds), so the contribution of surrogate filtering and multi-signal feedback is shown in budget terms, not just accuracy. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that injection-point selection on benign trajectories can miss under intra-agent path uncertainty (residual PMR is low but nonzero; multiple benign trajectories per task could mitigate this at added cost), and that the benchmark's 83 instances over 12 apps exclude app categories like finance and healthcare, with per-instance construction (manual attack-goal design and verifier implementation) being expensive. They confront both limitations directly and quantify the first, which is a credibility positive. They also clearly state the red-team design-time privileges (trajectory observation, emulator root) and that deployed attacks require no trajectory sensing. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No defense evaluation: all three agents are undefended baselines; the framework's value as an auditing tool is untested against any mitigation (content verification, injection detectors, task-consistency checks), so its resilience claim is unaudited. - The vulnerability-scoring weights (w1 = w2 = w3 = 1/3) and fitness weights (α = β = 0.5, γ = 0.7) are never ablated; the reported robustness of the pipeline may hide sensitivity to these constants. - The equal-ASR pattern across three very different agents (85.1/86.3/85.1%) is suspiciously flat and unexamined — either the agents share a common vulnerability mode or the attack saturates, and the paper does not distinguish these explanations. - Human evaluation covers 20 instances against Gemini only, sampled from successful attacks; no human-detection rate (can annotators spot attacks at all?) or inter-annotator agreement is reported. - The benchmark is constructed and evaluated on the same task distribution, so the framework's generalization to unseen apps/tasks is asserted via pipeline design, not demonstrated. - Cross-agent transfer of payloads (not just injection points) is untested, leaving open how attack-specific the payloads are to the trajectory and model they were evolved against. - No artifact release is stated, which limits independent verification of the verifiers — the most consequential component for reported ASR. Bottom Line: For anyone building or certifying mobile GUI agents, this is the strongest available tooling and evidence that fixed-point injection benchmarks understate risk — read it; for researchers in web-agent injection or LLM red-teaming generally, the mobile-specific sandboxing infrastructure is the only substantially new content and a skim of Sections III–V suffices.

Coda-DaVinci: Reimagining Video Generation with Code2Video (32 ▲ )

Yiyan Ji, Qixun Wang, Yang Shi, Zhuoran Zhang, Yifan Xu, Tengfei Liu, Yuqi Tang, Xiaohan Zhang, Shujie Li, Jiafu Tang, Xuanyu Zhu, Xinyu Liu, Yan He, Yushuo Guan, Zihao Wang, Xianghua Ying, Shixuan Liu, Haotian Wang, Wenjing Yang, Zhaoxiang Zhang, Yuanxing Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Jiaheng Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 20 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a controlled empirical study of design choices in Code2Video generation (proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting) and builds Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework that routes between direct generation and 3D-proxy-guided generation with entity-wise modeling granularity, persistent scene workspaces, and an independent acceptance-review agent. - Why it's important: Text-to-video models still fail at complex instruction following, scene-state persistence across camera revisits, and physically plausible interactions — failures that cost real production value in video creation pipelines; the paper quantifies when a coding-agent-constructed 3D proxy helps versus hurts, which no prior Code2Video work measured. - How it does it: The core move is task-adaptive control allocation: a coding agent models environments and objects at medium granularity (G1), humans at coarse granularity (G0), invokes Blender physics only when meaningful, and writes a proxy-grounded synthesis prompt with explicit subject–color bindings — while routing motion-centric tasks to direct generation to avoid proxy-induced stiffness. - The good: A blinded 10-evaluator human study across 94 samples isolates each factor's effect (e.g., G1/P1/PE2 achieves the highest pooled four-metric mean at 2.926/2.968/2.436/2.213 on a 0–3 scale), and the system reduces VTR word error rate from 59.21% (direct Seedance 2.5) to 11.08% while ranking first on all reported R2M scene-consistency metrics (e.g., Scene ID NMR 1.011 vs 0.347 direct). - The missing: No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multi-seed variance for the human evaluations on only 29–33 samples per benchmark, and ablations switch to LLM-judge scoring (Gemini 3.8 Flash on 33 tasks), so the component-level conclusions rest on small, judge-dependent evidence. - Read it or not: Read it if you build agentic video-generation systems or study proxy-based control — the granularity and prompting trade-off findings are actionable and rarely measured; skip it if you want the Code2Video paradigm itself, which prior work (VideoCoCo, Code Video Model) already established.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Non-Obviousness (70) is the standout — the finding that proxy detail has a task-dependent sign, with coarse human proxies preserving naturalness, converts folklore into measured, transferable design knowledge, and the paper honestly reports where it loses to direct generation (completeness 68). The composite is pulled down by Rigor (52) and Impact (45): human studies rest on ~30 samples per cell with no variance reporting, ablations silently switch to an unvalidated LLM judge, the proxy-vs-prompting contribution is confounded by a missing PE2-without-proxy baseline, there is KlingAI vendor overlap, and no artifact release is confirmed. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*52 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*45 = 59.

Problem & Motivation: Video generation models produce appealing clips but struggle with three failure modes: following detailed multi-step instructions, preserving scene state over time (e.g., objects remaining removed when the camera returns), and physically plausible dynamics. Code2Video methods address this by having a coding agent author an executable 3D scene whose rendered proxy conditions the video model — but prior work leaves open how proxies should be constructed (how detailed? simulate physics or script motion? who writes the synthesis prompt?) and what the paradigm's capability boundaries are. Practitioners building controllable video pipelines currently lack principled guidance on these design choices, and risk proxy-induced artifacts like stiff human animation that makes results worse than direct generation. Key Idea: The key insight — delivered as an empirical finding rather than an algorithm — is that proxy detail has a task-dependent sign: coarse proxies (cylinder body + sphere head, whole-entity motion) preserve motion naturalness because they leave limb articulation to the video model, while medium-grained proxies maximize consistency when physics simulation is needed; and the coding agent, having built the proxy, should also write the synthesis prompt with explicit subject–color-to-appearance bindings (PE2), outperforming both the raw prompt and an independent prompt-enhancer model. Coda-DaVinci operationalizes this as routing plus per-entity granularity allocation. Methodology: Phase 1 is a controlled factor study formalized as ṽ = A(x,r) (agent builds proxy) then v = G(ṽ,q,r) (video model synthesizes from proxy + prompt + references). Three factors are crossed: proxy granularity (G0 coarse / G1 medium / G2 fine articulated), physics (P0 none / P1 mandatory Blender simulation), and prompting (PE0 raw prompt / PE1 external MiniMax H3 enhancement / PE2 agent-authored proxy-aligned prompts). Ten blinded expert evaluators score four dimensions (consistency, instruction following, physical plausibility, naturalness) on a 0–3 scale over 94 retained samples (33 WorldMemBench, 29 VGIF-Bench, 32 Principia), with samples filtered to those valid under all configurations. Phase 2 builds Coda-DaVinci: a lead agent routes tasks to direct vs. 3D-guided generation, delegates separable modeling to coding subagents over a persistent Blender workspace, runs optional physics simulation, inspects proxies visually, writes proxy-grounded prompts with identity-color bindings, and submits candidates to an independent acceptance agent (up to 3 repair rounds) with read-only inspection tools. The pipeline is a multi-agent LLM harness (GPT-6-Astra or Claude Opus 5.5) driving Blender 5.2.1/Cycles rendering and Seedance 2.5 synthesis. Critical design decisions: (1) entity-wise granularity (G1 objects / G0 humans) — justified by the factor study and by a dedicated ablation (uniform-G1 hurts); (2) routing to direct generation for motion-centric tasks — justified by ablation (fixed routing lowers instruction following and aesthetics); (3) sample filtering to configurations with valid outputs — necessary due to the video API's content policy but introduces a selection effect that is only briefly acknowledged. Key Results: Against Seedance 2.5 direct generation and agentic baselines (Codex, Claude, ± VideoWeaver) and Code2Video baselines (Codex/Claude + Blender, VideoCoCo, CodeVideoModel), Coda-DaVinci ranks first on VTR checklist satisfaction (91.42 vs 85.15 direct, 90.88 Codex+VideoWeaver) and cuts WER from 59.21% to 11.08%; it leads all reported R2M metrics (Scene ID 1.011, Local Geo 0.947, State 0.875, Object 0.966 — e.g., vs 0.936/0.840/0.743/0.860 for Codex+Blender). On World Models' Last Exam in Physics it scores 60.77, second to Claude+Blender (65.52) and above direct (47.16). On 200 T2AV-Compass samples it leads Code2Video methods in realism (70.26) and instruction following (67.99), approaching direct generation (71.38), while pure Code2Video baselines drop realism to 64.28–67.29. Ablations (33-task subset, Gemini 3.8 Flash judge, 1–5 scale) show GPT-6-Astra + Seedance gaining +0.204 mean over direct, with 11 of 12 agent×generator pairs positive; removing independent review or adaptive routing lowers all four dimensions; Blender beats Three.js on quality at roughly 2× agent-token cost (Figure 7c reports ~9.14M tokens for the Blender region). Long-video tests (29 LongAV-Compass cases, 25–90 s; 50 WBench turns) show gains in event fulfillment (96.76 vs 93.59), long-form structure (79.07 vs 75.62), interaction adherence (73.03 vs 66.19), and consistency (85.89 vs 77.90), but direct generation wins transition stability (73.69 vs 70.23) and setting adherence (88.02 vs 83.13). Baselines are current-generation (2026-era models); evaluation scale is small (tens of samples per benchmark), i.e., standard-size diagnostic studies, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the controlled granularity/physics/prompting trade-off analysis with blinded human ratings is the genuinely novel contribution — no prior Code2Video work measures these factors) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the routing + persistent-workspace + independent-acceptance harness). The underlying paradigm — agent-built 3D proxy conditioning a video model — is established by VideoCoCo and Code Video Model; Coda-DaVinci's routing, entity-wise granularity, and proxy-grounded prompting are a well-executed, evidence-driven recombination of known ingredients (agentic 3D scene coding, Blender simulation, reference-conditioned video synthesis) rather than a new formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: The factor study is the rigorous core: factorial designs with held-fixed comparisons (Figure 4), per-metric delta tables, 10 blinded evaluators, and matched timestamps for qualitative comparison. However, no error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed variance are reported for the human study; per-benchmark cells average as few as 29 samples. Ablations switch protocols entirely to a single LLM judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash, 1–5 scale) on 33 tasks — a different instrument than the main human eval — and the paper does not validate the judge against human scores. The main analysis benchmarks are not the standard public versions obviously matching WorldMemBench/VGIF-Bench/Principia names, and sample filtering to commonly-valid outputs is a mild selection concern. All methods share one coding model (GPT-6-Astra) for main comparisons, which fairly isolates harness effects; authors are affiliated with KlingAI and use Seedance as the video model throughout, so absolute quality numbers carry a vendor-adjacent flavor, though cross-generator ablations (Seedance, MiniMax H3, Kling 4.0 Omni) partially mitigate this. No public code, data, or harness release URL is stated (homepage/code placeholders appear in the figure caption with no link in the provided text). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built agentic system evaluated through benchmarks and human study). - Practical: Yes — it runs on commodity cloud LLM APIs plus Blender (free, CUDA-accelerated) and a commercial video-generation API; no training or exotic hardware required. - Efficient: Costly relative to direct generation — proxy authoring, rendering, and multi-round review add substantial agent tokens (Blender ~9.14M tokens per case, ~2× Three.js) plus up to 3 repair rounds; the paper reports token cost only for the engine comparison, not end-to-end against direct generation. - Effective: The evidence supports the claimed gains in instruction following and scene consistency on the evaluated benchmarks, but naturalness on motion-intensive tasks (VGIF: −0.552 naturalness vs direct) and long-video transition stability show the system solves consistency at a real quality cost, not uniformly. - Scalable: Untested beyond ~90-second multi-clip sequences and ~33–200-case benchmark subsets; the persistent-workspace mechanism is claimed to support scene reuse, but no scaling experiment (longer horizons, more entities, more turns) is reported. The work delivers a described agentic harness with detailed prompt templates (Appendix D) and tool inventory (Table 6), but no released artifact is confirmed. Strengths: - The controlled factor analysis is real intellectual contribution: it converts folklore ("more detailed proxies are better") into measured, task-dependent trade-offs with per-metric deltas (e.g., G0→G1 raises VGIF consistency +0.138 while costing −0.138 naturalness), which is directly reusable design knowledge. - Honest, self-critical evaluation: the paper explicitly reports where the method loses to direct generation (transition stability, setting adherence, VGIF naturalness/realism) rather than only favorable metrics. - Robustness testing across 4 coding agents × 3 video generators (12 pairings, 11 positive vs matched direct baselines) is stronger validation than typical agent-pipeline papers, which usually fix one model pair. - The PE2 finding — that the proxy-building agent should author identity-color-bound prompts rather than an external prompt enhancer — is a specific, transferable insight backed by head-to-head comparison (+0.255 mean over PE1 at G1/P1). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that Code2Video's benefits are task-dependent, with weaknesses in physical plausibility, motion fluency, and realism on VGIF-Bench (complex human/object motion); that long-video generation shows lower transition stability than direct continuation (70.23 vs 73.69) and lower setting adherence (83.13 vs 88.02); and the conclusion names remaining gaps in motion naturalness, transition stability, and scene-setting adherence. They confront limitations directly and quantify most of them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance or significance reporting for the human study; several headline conclusions rest on differences of 0.05–0.10 points on 0–3 scales with ~30 samples per cell, where evaluator noise alone could plausibly explain ordering. - The ablation protocol silently switches from blinded human raters to Gemini 3.8 Flash LLM judging without cross-validating the judge, so "adaptive routing and independent review improve quality" rests on a different, weaker instrument than the main results. - The direct-generation baseline in the factor study is always Seedance 2.5 with the raw prompt; a stronger direct baseline using the same agent-written prompts (PE2 without a proxy) is absent, leaving the proxy's marginal contribution over better prompting partially confounded. - Author–vendor overlap (KlingAI Research; Kling video models in ablations; Seedance as synthesis backbone) plus unnamed/possibly internal benchmarks (WorldMemBench, VGIF-Bench) warrants independent replication before trusting absolute numbers. - No code or harness release is confirmed despite homepage/code placeholders, limiting reproducibility of a system whose value lives in prompt templates and tool orchestration. - The routing policy itself is never characterized: the paper does not report routing accuracy, how often each path is selected, or failure cases when routing errs, even though routing is the headline mechanism. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agentic video pipelines gains concrete, measured design guidance (proxy granularity per entity, when to simulate physics, who should write the prompt) that no competing paper provides with this level of control, but the small-sample human study, LLM-judge ablations, and absent code release mean the framework's exact numbers should be treated as directional rather than settled — read it for the findings, not as a validated artifact.

Jeveration: System One Models Now Generate (112 ▲ )

Yuhe Liu, Qi Li, Shihua Zhang, Xinchao Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 19 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Jeveration, a method that turns a frozen 4B vision-language model into a single-forward-pass image generator, dense predictor, and image-to-image editor by casting each output as parallel typed decisions over discrete image codes, reaching 0.74 GenEval at 78 ms per 512×512 image. - Why it's important: Unified multimodal models (autoregressive or diffusion) need hundreds of sequential steps per image — Janus-Pro-7B takes 9.5 s end-to-end — so collapsing generation to one pass attacks the dominant latency cost of multimodal inference. - How it does it: All 128 code positions are conditioned on one shared random state ξ sampled per image, and a two-phase training scheme (masked-code modeling to learn the image distribution, then Di[M]O-style distribution matching between a frozen teacher and an auxiliary follower, plus confidence-guided correction) teaches the model to use ξ so independent parallel draws assemble into one coherent image. - The good: The ablations directly support the core mechanism: the first-phase masked model without decision training drops to 0.32 GenEval in one pass, and replacing the random shared state with a fixed one costs 0.03 GenEval and 1.64 HPSv2.1, isolating exactly what makes parallel prediction coherent. - The missing: The headline "122× faster" is measured against the slowest baseline (Janus-Pro-7B at 9,508 ms); against Show-o Turbo-512 (94.1 ms) the speedup is only ~1.2×, and quality trails the strongest models (0.74 vs 0.80 GenEval for Janus-Pro-7B, 0.76 for Z-Image-Turbo; HPSv2.1 28.06 vs 29.63 for FLUX-schnell). - Read it or not: Read it if you work on unified multimodal models, one-step/parallel generation, or discrete-token synthesis — it is the first demonstration that decision-style VLMs can generate images and the shared-random-state conditioning trick is transferable; skip it if you only need the fastest or best text-to-image model, where SANA-Sprint and FLUX remain ahead on quality.

Problem & Motivation: Image generation is dominated by autoregressive token-by-token models and iterative diffusion, both of which require many sequential model evaluations per image, inflating latency for real-time multimodal applications. Unified understanding-plus-generation models inherit this cost. The authors observe that "System One" decision models (Jev-style models that return typed structured outputs — Choices, Scores — in one parallel pass) already carry visual-semantic knowledge from pretraining but have only been used for understanding tasks (localization, scoring, evaluation), never for synthesis. The gap: can a frozen VLM produce a globally coherent image as one joint decision, given that independently sampled per-position codes from a factorized distribution produce incompatible image fragments? Key Idea: Condition every code position on a single shared random state ξ drawn per image. Mathematically, the model emits q_θ(c|y) = E_ξ[∏_i q_θ,i(c_i|y,ξ)] — codes are independent given (y,ξ), but their shared dependence on ξ lets the mixture capture inter-position dependencies (the total correlation that a purely independent factorization provably cannot represent, shown via a forward-KL entropy gap argument). The paper then solves the chicken-and-egg problem that a model trained directly on target codes ignores ξ (since ξ is independent of the target): first learn the image distribution with masked-code prediction, then use that frozen teacher against an auxiliary follower model to give a distribution-matching signal that rewards the generator for codes that cohere. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) frozen Qwen3.5-4B VLM with rank-256 shared LoRA adapters (~1.0B trainable parameters total) processing text/visual input tokens plus decision tokens in one forward pass; (2) for generation, 128 decision tokens initialized from ξ (per-position masking at ρ=0.6, uniform random codes, Gaussian noise σ=0.1, following Di[M]O), read by a transformer head with a two-branch code predictor (a codebook-initialized classifier plus a zero-initialized wide branch, summed before softmax); (3) codes rendered by a fine-tuned TA-TiTok text-aware decoder (8,192-entry codebook, 512 px) with an added source-image branch for image-to-image tasks; (4) for dense prediction, 432 decision tokens act as spatial queries decoded into per-pixel segmentation classes, depth (ℓ1 loss), or normals (1−cosine). Training has two phases: Phase 1 trains the architecture as a masked model (masked-code cross-entropy, ~92k steps) to learn the image distribution; Phase 2 (6.7k steps) trains the decision model via distribution matching — re-masking sampled codes, comparing the frozen teacher's and a continuously-updated auxiliary model's conditional predictions, and minimizing their stopped-gradient difference against the generator's logits (Eq. 6, Di[M]O-style token-level conditional matching) — then adds confidence-guided correction, where the 50% least-confident positions are completed by the frozen teacher over four rounds and used as targets (λ=1). Critical design decisions: the shared random state (well-justified by ablation and the entropy-gap analysis); the frozen backbone with adapters only (enables the single-machine 4-GPU, ~4-day training); and the two-branch image head (justified by ablation: 0.64 vs 0.59–0.60 GenEval for single branches). Dense tasks are deterministic decisions, deliberately not stochastic — a reasonable but unexamined asymmetry. Key Results: On one H200 at batch 1, Jeveration generates a 512×512 image in 77.8 ms end-to-end (one generator evaluation), reaching GenEval 0.74, DPG 78.24, HPSv2.1 28.06. Among unified models it beats JanusFlow (0.63 GenEval), Show-o (0.68), Show-o Turbo (0.63, 94.1 ms), MMaDA-8B (0.63), and Janus-Pro-1B (0.73, 7,593 ms), but trails Janus-Pro-7B (0.80) and Z-Image-Turbo (0.76) on GenEval and all one-step diffusion models on HPSv2.1 (FLUX-schnell 29.63, SANA-Sprint 28.74). Against generation-only one-step models at 1024 px, it beats SDXL-DMD2 (0.56) but trails SANA-Sprint (0.72) and FLUX-schnell (0.69) on GenEval at higher resolution. The 122×/98× speedups are relative to Janus-Pro-7B and Janus-Pro-1B, the slowest autoregressive baselines; vs Show-o Turbo it is 1.2× faster. Image-to-image: 0.880 HED edge F1, 0.802 depth δ1, 0.937 colorization edge F1 on 341 held-out examples per task, at 91.7 ms (+14 ms over T2I). Dense prediction on NYUv2 (654 test images): 67.7 mIoU segmentation (vs 67.8/67.3 dense-only from the same backbone, 53.5 for DeepLabV3+), 0.267 m depth error, 24.2° normal mean error (normals degrade most under task sharing). Ablations: random vs fixed shared state (0.73/28.27 vs 0.70/26.63), correction target contributes +0.11 HPSv2.1, joint training across tasks costs almost nothing on T2I quality (0.74 vs 0.73 GenEval). Baselines are recent and mostly strong, though all latencies are the authors' own measurements. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the genuinely novel elements are (a) the demonstration that Jev-style typed-decision models can generate images at all, and (b) the shared-random-state conditioning that makes parallel independent decisions collapse onto one coherent image. The training machinery (masked-code modeling, token-level conditional distribution matching, confidence-guided correction, TA-TiTok tokenizer, LoRA on a frozen VLM) is a competent recombination of Di[M]O/MaskGIT/PEFT ideas adapted to a frozen-VLM decision framework; the extension to dense prediction via spatial query tokens is standard practice (detector/segmenter-style queries) rather than a new technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted — they isolate the shared state, correction target, head branches, source conditioning (including code/source swap experiments in the supplement), and joint-training interference. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported; given GenEval margins of 0.01–0.03 over several baselines, statistical uncertainty is material. No code, weights, or data release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (1) the headline speedup is computed against the slowest baseline, which is favorable framing; (2) all latency numbers are self-measured by the authors on their hardware, though the protocol (median of five end-to-end calls, H200, batch 1, released samplers) is stated clearly; (3) benchmark scores partly cite other papers (marked ‡) while the authors' own models are self-scored; (4) dense evaluation is confined to NYUv2, a single indoor dataset with a 13-class segmentation setup; (5) the second phase trains against the frozen teacher's distribution on the same data family it was trained on, so the generator's quality ceiling is bounded by a model fit to the same corpus. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (systems-style results from running the method, though no artifact is released). - Practical: Training ran on four NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs in ~4 days and inference on one H200; the frozen-backbone design makes reproduction feasible on prosumer-class hardware, unusual for 5.2B-parameter generators. - Efficient: 77.8 ms per image end-to-end is the lowest latency in its comparison table and ~1.2–122× faster than the unified baselines listed, with the caveat that the largest multipliers come from the slowest AR baselines. - Effective: Evidence supports the single-pass claim on all three tasks, but image quality is competitive rather than leading — 0.06–0.02 GenEval behind the best unified and efficient baselines — so it solves the latency problem at a measurable quality cost. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 512 px, 128 codes, and one backbone size; the authors only claim the paradigm "extends to further visual tasks and modalities" without evidence; whether the shared-state trick retains coherence at higher token counts (where total correlation grows) is open. The paper stops at paper form — no library, CLI, dataset, or trained model is stated as released. Strengths: - The shared-random-state conditioning is a real, identifiable idea with a clean theoretical motivation (the forward-KL/total-correlation gap in Eq. 2) and a decisive ablation (fixed state costs 0.03 GenEval and 1.64 HPSv2.1; no state at all yields incoherent fragments at 0.32 GenEval). - The two-phase teacher/auxiliary training scheme solves the otherwise fatal problem that direct code supervision gives the model no reason to use ξ — a non-obvious training insight, adapted from Di[M]O but repurposed for coherence rather than distillation alone. - One checkpoint spanning text-to-image, image-to-image, and dense prediction with near-zero cross-task interference (Tab. 5: 0.74 vs 0.73 GenEval) is a substantive empirical result about frozen-VLM capacity sharing. - Training cost (~4 days on 4 GPUs, backbone frozen) demonstrates the frozen-backbone recipe is genuinely cheap, not just claimed to be. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that surface normals lag behind other dense tasks (attributed to shared capacity across tasks), and implicitly that quality is "competitive" rather than leading. They do not include a limitations section addressing resolution ceilings, dataset narrowness, or the quality gap to stronger generators; limitations are confronted briefly and locally rather than systematically — a moderate credibility positive, but thin. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The "122×" framing foregrounds the weakest comparison; against the closest unified competitor (Show-o Turbo, 94.1 ms) the speedup is 1.2× and against SANA-Sprint (121.2 ms, 0.72 GenEval at 1024 px) Jeveration is slower per-pixel-quality-adjusted. The abstract's headline number overstates the practical latency advantage. - No FID or human evaluation anywhere — the quality case rests entirely on GenEval/DPG/HPSv2.1, which are known to be gameable and insensitive to artifacts introduced by 128-code tokenization. - Single seed, no variance reporting, with several ablation margins under 0.02 GenEval; conclusions from Tabs. 4–5 are not statistically grounded. - Image-to-image structure-fidelity metrics (edge F1, depth δ1 after alignment) reward copying structure; the "copy the input" baseline scores 0.828 HED F1, so the 0.880 headline is only 0.05 above trivial structure preservation, and no perceptual quality metric for I2I outputs is reported beyond PSNR against paired style targets. - Dense evaluation is NYUv2-only (indoor RGB-D); no Cityscapes, ADE20K, or outdoor depth, so generality of the spatial-query head is untested. - The 1,000-step-trained teacher and generator share the same training corpus, so distribution matching cannot push beyond the data the teacher already memorized; the paper does not analyze this ceiling. - No discussion of failure modes of the shared state — e.g., mode coverage, prompt diversity limits, or how sample diversity compares to diffusion sampling. Bottom Line: A practitioner working on unified multimodal or one-step generation should read this paper for the shared-random-state conditioning idea and its honest ablations, but should not adopt it over SANA-Sprint/FLUX-schnell for production image generation, since the quality gap at 512 px is real and no artifact is released.

Code World Model 2.0: Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation (14 ▲ )

Ruoyu Wang, Hao Zhong, Yanming Yang, Jiahao Tian, Lin Liu, Biao Gong, Guoshan Lu, Yiding Tian, Chunhua Shen, Zhenzhong Lan, Chi Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 19 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Invoker-Render, a proxy-conditioned video rendering framework that unifies a bidirectional clip-creation model and a causal four-step streaming model under one conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and text, trained via a staged curriculum called Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). - Why it's important: Interactive world engines need a renderer that honors control signals of varying detail while streaming indefinitely without visual drift; existing few-step causal renderers either degrade over self-generated history or require proxy detail that downstream interactions cannot always supply. - How it does it: ProForcing disentangles the two failure modes — it first adapts block-causal attention on clean prefixes (TF), then on noise-corrupted-and-refined data-anchored histories (RF), then distills four-step generation with DMD plus a teacher-feature relativistic GAN on those anchored histories (RF-DMD), and finally carries the coupled student/fake-score/discriminator/optimizer states into continuous self-generated rollouts (SF-DMD). - The good: On 140 held-out streaming sequences, the four-step causal model wins blinded LLM-judged pairwise comparisons against SolarRenderer (62.9% win rate, +96.7 Overall Elo), StreamRender-H3 (82.9%, +291.8), and Streaming CWM (92.9%, +539.6), and sustains coherent ~30-minute racing rollouts. - The missing: All quantitative evaluation relies on a single LLM judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash) with no human study, no reference-based metrics (FVD/PSNR), and no quantitative ablation isolating which ProForcing stages actually matter. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building streaming world models or few-step causal video distillation, since the staged distillation recipe and serving-stack ablation are directly reusable; skippable for readers seeking human-validated generative-rendering quality evidence.

Problem & Motivation: In the "explicit state + generative renderer" paradigm for interactive video worlds, an upstream engine maintains world state and a neural renderer synthesizes photorealistic video from structural proxies. Two gaps motivate this work. First, the right proxy granularity depends on the interaction — broad navigation needs only root trajectories and coarse layout, while close-range interaction needs articulated poses — and prior renderers are trained at a fixed granularity, forcing downstream systems to pay for detail they cannot always produce. Second, converting a bidirectional diffusion model into a few-step causal streaming renderer compounds two difficulties (trajectory compression and exposure to erroneous self-generated history), and existing recipes (Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, Causal-rCM, LongLive) address these jointly or incompletely, leading to drift that erases scene geometry and reference appearance at long horizons. Key Idea: Train the streaming renderer through a staged curriculum that keeps distillation histories data-anchored (resampled from ground-truth prefixes rather than self-generated) until a capable four-step generator and its supervision models (fake score model, discriminator) are jointly converged, then transition the entire coupled training state — including optimizer moments and EMA — to continuous self-generated rollouts. This avoids cold-start critic instability and isolates step-compression learning from open-loop drift exposure. The second supporting idea is mixed-granularity conditioning: coarse and fine proxies of the same event, rendered from one reconstructed 3D scene state with appearance stripped out, train a single checkpoint to honor constraints only when supplied. Methodology: The system builds on MiniMax-H3 (a DiT with distilled CFG) under linear flow matching (x_t = (1−t)x_0 + tε, v = ε − x_0). (1) Data: ~200 hours (150h self-collected from GTA V, Cyberpunk 2077, Elden Ring, Forza Horizon 5; 50h from OmniWorld, Magpie, CARLA, etc.) aligned at 1344×768 in 158-frame windows and 328-frame sequences; a reconstruction pipeline (SAM2 segmentation/tracking, depth completion, camera pose, human motion recovery) renders matched coarse (root-driven mannequins, oriented boxes) and fine (volumetric articulated bodies, shaded geometry) proxies with appearance removed, plus hierarchical whole-window captions and timestamped streaming action text. (2) Bidirectional adaptation: Guidance-Free Training (GFT) blends proxy-conditioned and weak-condition (proxy-dropped) velocity predictions at guidance scale β=2 with 10% condition dropout, detaching the weak branch so gradients flow only through the proxy pathway. (3) ProForcing: Teacher Forcing on clean prefixes → Resampling Forcing, which corrupts history blocks to noise level ρ and refines them sequentially with the detached current model → RF-DMD, which distills a four-step student via a normalized DMD score-difference gradient (L_DMD = ½E‖x_0^θ − x_0^θ− + g‖²) plus a relativistic GAN on frozen teacher features, all under detached RF histories → SF-DMD, which swaps in continuous student-generated histories with overlapping local scoring windows and gradient masking, carrying over student, fake score model, discriminator, AdamW moments, and EMA. (4) Serving: an asymmetric codec (Tiny AutoEncoder for online proxy encoding, causal video decoder for output), cross-layer plan/RoPE sharing, per-layer AdaLN projection caching, transactional KV workspace reuse, fused prefill-and-first-denoise pass, and cross-packet codec overlap with asynchronous CPU delivery on an eight-GPU Ulysses-8 node. Design decisions are mostly well-justified by the stated failure modes (drift, critic cold start), though the RF corruption level and the choice of four steps are asserted rather than ablated. Key Results: On 140 held-out test sequences (6.58–20 s, spanning multiple 3D environments and proxy families), judged by Gemini 3.8 Flash blinded pairwise comparisons with Elo via Bradley–Terry, Invoker-Render (Causal, 4-step) scores Overall 1232.0 vs. SolarRenderer 1135.3, StreamRender-H3 940.2, and Streaming CWM 692.4; per-criterion it leads on Visual Quality (1236.4), Structure & Motion (1209.0), and Reference Preservation (1164.1). Head-to-head: 130/8/2 vs. Streaming CWM, 116/4/20 vs. StreamRender-H3, 88/2/50 vs. SolarRenderer. The strongest baseline (SolarRenderer, also 4-step causal and from 2026) is current, though the paper's own prior work (StreamRender-H3) is among them. Serving ablation: per-chunk latency 1770→930 ms and throughput 9.9→18.0 FPS (1.82×) at 1344×768 on 8 GPUs, with each optimization tier quantified (TAE codec 12.4 FPS, reuse 14.4, fused pass 14.8, pipelining 18.0). Long-horizon evidence is qualitative: two racing sequences rendered to 298–299 s and 30-minute racing sessions with claimed stable scene/vehicle appearance. No perplexing negative result is reported; all comparisons favor the proposed method. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the ProForcing curriculum — specifically resampled data-anchored histories during DMD+GAN distillation followed by stateful coupled continuation into SF-DMD) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK elements (the ~200-hour aligned multi-granularity proxy corpus) and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (the serving stack). The ingredients — DMD, relativistic GAN, self-forcing, GFT, block-causal attention, KV-cached streaming — are all established; the novelty lies in their staged composition and the empirical demonstration that data-anchored distillation before self-rollout continuation prevents long-horizon drift, not in any new mathematical framework. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations: the serving stack gets a clean cumulative ablation (Figure 6a); the training recipe gets only a qualitative recipe-comparison table (Figure 4) — no quantitative ablation of TF/RF/RF-DMD/SF-DMD stages, RF noise level ρ, GAN weight, or granularity mixing. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for the Elo results, and a single LLM judge is used. The training/evaluation split discipline is a positive: splits partitioned by recording and scene, with coarse/fine pairs and overlapping windows kept in the same split to prevent leakage. GitHub, Hugging Face, and project-page links are referenced in the header, but no specific URLs or confirmation of released weights/data/code appear in the text. Methodological concerns: evaluation is LLM-judged only (Gemini 3.8 Flash) with no human study and no standard reference metrics (FVD, LPIPS, PSNR against ground truth despite having matched RGB targets), the judge identity is not validated against human preference, and the 30-minute stability claim is supported by qualitative frames from racing (driving) sequences only — a narrow domain for the strongest claim. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a trained renderer plus a deployed streaming service, evaluated empirically). - Practical: It runs on commercially available hardware (8×GPU node) but each concurrent session appears to occupy the full eight-GPU pool at 1344×768, so per-session cost is high. - Efficient: 18.0 FPS and 930 ms per chunk at 1344×768 with a four-step causal model — a 1.82× improvement over their own baseline stack, though relative cost against competitor systems' serving stacks is not reported. - Effective: Evidence for proxy adherence and reference preservation comes from LLM-judged preference plus qualitative long rollouts; without human evaluation or reference metrics, effectiveness is shown against a proxy (judge preference), not directly. - Scalable: 30-minute rollouts are demonstrated qualitatively and the paper claims movement toward "infinite" generation; visual details outside the sliding KV window are evicted and never recalled — the authors admit long-term memory is unimplemented, so 10–100× horizons or revisited environments are unsupported. The work delivers a system artifact (renderer checkpoints, corpus, serving stack) with GitHub/HuggingFace links referenced but not enumerated in the text. Strengths: - The ProForcing curriculum is a genuinely useful training insight: keeping DMD/GAN distillation histories anchored to resampled ground-truth data and then transferring the fully converged coupled training state (critics, optimizer moments, EMA) into self-rollout training cleanly separates step compression from drift exposure, addressing a real failure mode of naive self-forcing distillation. - The multi-granularity proxy corpus is a substantive data contribution: coarse and fine proxies rendered from the same reconstructed scene state for the same event, with appearance deliberately stripped to prevent leakage, directly supervises granularity-conditioned synthesis that prior fixed-granularity renderers cannot learn. - The serving-stack ablation is unusually disciplined — each of five optimizations is quantified individually (1770→1410→1180→1165→930 ms), making the engineering reproducible and auditable. - Evaluation hygiene: recording/scene-level split partitioning with explicit leakage prevention is stated, and the strongest baseline (SolarRenderer, same step count and recency) is included, not strawmen. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion explicitly states two limitations: (1) visual details outside the active KV window are eventually evicted, so the renderer cannot recall previously visited environments or maintain multi-entity consistency across revisits — they propose learnable memory compression, retrieval, or persistent 3D caches as future work; (2) each rollout window uses a fixed proxy granularity, with dynamic mid-stream level-of-detail transitions and closed-loop coupling to live interactive state engines left to future work. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment of the main architectural gaps — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The entire quantitative evaluation depends on one LLM judge with no human preference study and no agreement analysis; LLM video judges are known to exhibit biases (toward sharpness, text plausibility) that could inflate Visual Quality margins. The +96.7 Elo lead over SolarRenderer (62.9% wins) is modest and within plausible judge-noise range. - No reference-based or ground-truth-anchored metrics (FVD, PSNR/SSIM against the paired RGB targets, proxy-adherence error in pixels/degrees) are reported, despite the corpus containing exact ground truth — this is the most conspicuous omission. - No quantitative ablation of ProForcing: the claim that RF-DMD-before-SF-DMD reduces drift is supported only by a qualitative recipe table; an ablation against plain Self Forcing or LongLive-style training on the same backbone and data is needed to attribute the gains to the curriculum rather than the ~200-hour corpus or the MiniMax-H3 backbone. - Compute, training time, and parameter counts for each training stage are not stated, so reproducibility of the recipe and cost comparisons against baselines are impossible. - Long-horizon stability is shown only on racing/driving sequences with scripted camera paths; the 30-minute claim does not cover character interaction or scene revisits, where eviction memory loss should bite hardest. - Public-dataset hours include Magpie, whose authors' renderer is a related system — potential train/eval contamination considerations for shared environments are not discussed beyond generic split discipline. Bottom Line: A practitioner building streaming, proxy-conditioned world renderers gains concrete, reusable value here — a credible staged distillation recipe, an aligned multi-granularity dataset recipe, and a transparent serving-stack ablation — but the headline quality claims rest entirely on LLM-judged preference without human validation or reference metrics, so treat the quantitative margins as directional rather than settled.

AI cyber range: advancing education and training in adversarial and robust AI

C Ntantogian, C Leka · link.springer.com · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the concept and architecture of an "AI cyber range" — a gamified, CTF-style training platform for adversarial attacks and robust AI defenses — and delivers an open-source proof-of-concept prototype built on CTFd, MLflow, and Docker with four working Red/Blue Team exercises. - Why it's important: AI security skills are currently taught almost entirely through theory or accuracy-focused data science platforms (e.g., Kaggle), leaving practitioners without hands-on experience executing and defending against adversarial ML attacks in isolated, evaluated environments. - How it does it: It reorganizes conventional cyber range components (orchestration, containerized workspaces, leaderboards, protected evaluators) around the ML lifecycle, adding MLOps tooling (MLflow/Kubeflow), pretrained models, adversarial toolkits (e.g., ART), and machine-verifiable flag-release criteria mapped to MITRE ATLAS. - The good: The strongest evidence is a working multi-mission prototype exercised by 51 students across two universities with concrete measurements — e.g., 8.14/8.31 (cohorts A/B) mean scores for perceived knowledge acquisition and a fully traced audit trail of every submission in MLflow. - The missing: Educational effectiveness is never measured — there is no pre/post assessment, no control group, and no objective skill evaluation; all learning claims rest on self-reported perception questionnaires, and the MCDA scoring is a self-assessment whose criterion weights were produced by an LLM. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you are building AI-security education infrastructure or a security-focused cyber range; skip it if you want a rigorous pedagogical study or an empirical comparison against existing adversarial-ML training platforms like Maestro.

Problem & Motivation: Educators, industry professionals, and AI practitioners lack structured hands-on environments for learning adversarial AI attacks (poisoning, evasion, prompt injection) and defenses (adversarial training, randomized smoothing, input filtering). Cybersecurity cyber ranges solve an analogous problem for network threats with isolated environments, gamification, and repeatable scenarios, but prior work either uses AI as a tool inside conventional ranges (e.g., ML-based attack detectors in the SPIDER 5G range) or teaches robust AI as a standalone game (Maestro) without range infrastructure. The gap the paper targets is a platform that integrates adversarial AI exercises with cyber range functions: isolated execution, automated evaluation, gamification, and experiment tracking. Key Idea: Treat AI assets themselves — models, datasets, adversarial inputs, MLOps pipelines, and physical sensors — as core cyber range resources, and gate flag release on protected, server-side evaluators that verify machine-checkable acceptance conditions (e.g., L∞ perturbation bounds, robust-accuracy thresholds, exact-match elicitation rates) rather than on participant-reported results. The linked X-Ray Red→Blue missions add a precursor of scenario evolution, where one team's validated adversarial artifact becomes the other team's defense target. Methodology: The paper has three layers. (1) Conceptual architecture: orchestration, leaderboard, Red/Blue/White team roles, supporting services (pretrained models, datasets, toolkits — ART identified as the broadest of 8 surveyed libraries), plus a five-dimension scenario taxonomy (attacker knowledge, access, specificity, goals, attack type) mapped to MITRE ATLAS techniques. (2) Prototype: CTFd for challenge management and scoring; Docker Compose for per-participant Jupyter workspaces; protected evaluator containers; MLflow for audit trails. Four missions: X-Ray Red (complete an FGSM attack on a chest X-ray at ε=5/255 against a fixed EfficientNet-B0, verified server-side), X-Ray Blue (configure a randomized-smoothing defense: σ=0.05, 100 noisy samples, ≥75/100 votes to return a class, abstention otherwise — with an anti-abstention guard requiring correct classification of the clean image), an LLM prompt-safety mission against Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (3 black-box + 2 gradient-optimized white-box prompts, each needing the target phrase in ≥6/10 sampled generations), and a PatchGuard-inspired MNIST task (small CNN over 49 overlapping 16×16 windows per image, majority voting, flag at ≥80% clean and ≥60% patched accuracy, 3,000 training images, 100 epochs). (3) Evaluation: a 7-question 10-point questionnaire with 51 students in two cohorts, resource/latency measurements on an RTX 5090 with 10 concurrent users, and an adapted AHP/MCDA rubric. Critical design decisions: server-side protected evaluation (well justified against manipulation), bounded lightweight workloads to keep training tractable (justified with explicit numbers), and LLM-assisted AHP weighting for the MCDA (weakly justified — the choice of using an LLM rather than domain experts for pairwise comparisons is asserted, not defended). Key Results: Usability: knowledge acquisition scored 8.14 (cohort A, n=22) and 8.31 (cohort B, n=29); preparedness for future challenges 7.23/7.97; weakest items were task clarity at 6.32 (cohort A) and ease of use at 6.78 (cohort A). Compute: on a single RTX 5090 / Ryzen 9 9950X / 64 GB host with 10 concurrent participants, average GPU utilization was 80.08% (peak 90%), average VRAM 16.79 GiB (peak 21.51 GiB). Concurrency slowdowns under contention: PatchGuard training 91.67 s → 325.35 s (3.55×), LLM white-box optimization 66.88 s → 202.49 s (3.03×), X-Ray Blue 1.10 s → 3.78 s (3.44×), X-Ray Red essentially unaffected (1.08×). MCDA: AHP consistency ratio 0.016, total weighted self-assessment score 2.9151/5, with lowest scores on AI-security lifecycle coverage (2/5), platform security (2/5), and scalability (2/5). The platform itself added negligible overhead; costs were dominated by scenario workloads. Baselines: there is no comparison platform — no head-to-head against Maestro, Kaggle, or conventional ranges, so all results are single-system measurements rather than comparative outcomes. Tested scale is small: 4 missions, up to 10 concurrent users, one GPU host. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with elements of NEW PROBLEM framing. The genuinely new part is the systematization: an explicit architecture, scenario taxonomy, and scoring model that reorganizes cyber range design around the AI lifecycle and treats models/MLOps as range assets. The implementation is a competent integration of entirely standard components (CTFd, MLflow, Docker, PyTorch, published techniques FGSM and randomized smoothing, a simplified PatchGuard-style design), and the MCDA framework is adapted from prior work — so the contribution is a new application setting and reference design, not new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations: none in the ML sense — no component-level ablation showing which architectural elements drive the reported perceptions; the exercises are described at reproducible depth (exact ε, σ, thresholds, architecture, epochs). Statistics: no error bars, significance tests, or between-cohort analysis; questionnaire means are reported with standard deviations only. Code is publicly released at https://github.com/dadoyan/AI-cyber-range, which is a strong reproducibility positive. Methodological concerns: (i) the MCDA criterion weights were generated by an LLM ("GPT 6 Astra") doing AHP pairwise comparisons rather than by human experts, making the 2.9151/5 score a structured opinion, not an expert judgment; (ii) the evaluation instrument was designed by the authors, administered by the authors, and reported by the authors — self-assessment throughout; (iii) no baseline platform is compared against, so "educationally useful" is never benchmarked; (iv) technical reliability varied sharply across cohorts (SD 2.97 in cohort B on the stability question), which is noted but not investigated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS — a built prototype deployed and exercised with real participants. Practical: Yes — runs on a single workstation-class machine (RTX 5090, 64 GB RAM) with open-source tooling; nothing exotic required for the current exercises. Efficient: Supporting services are cheap, but scenario workloads are GPU-hungry — 10 concurrent users already saturated ~80% GPU utilization and pushed 3–3.5× slowdowns on training/optimization tasks. Effective: It demonstrably delivers the four exercises with verifiable evaluation and positive participant perception, but the stated educational goal is supported only by perception proxies, not measured learning outcomes. Scalable: Not tested beyond 10 concurrent users on one host; the authors correctly state larger deployments need more GPUs and acknowledge Kubernetes/Run:ai/Slurm as untested paths. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (public GitHub prototype with the four exercises) plus a reusable architecture template; it stops at paper form for everything else (security hardening, multi-server orchestration, expanded scenario library). Strengths: - First concrete, code-released instantiation of a cyber range purpose-built for adversarial/robust AI training, with a defensible architecture argument for why ML assets (models, MLOps pipelines, poisoned datasets) must become first-class range resources rather than peripheral tools. - Machine-verifiable, server-side flag release criteria per exercise (perturbation bounds, robust-accuracy floors, anti-abstention guard, 6/10 exact-match elicitation) — a real anti-gaming design that most educational adversarial-ML setups lack. - Honest computational characterization: the paper quantifies concurrency costs (3.03–3.55× slowdowns, 80% GPU utilization at 10 users) rather than hand-waving about scalability, and translates them into concrete capacity-planning guidance. - Broad, well-organized scenario taxonomy mapped to MITRE ATLAS technique IDs and a five-dimension attack classification, which is reusable independently of the prototype. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and candidly (a credibility positive): 51 students with no pre/post assessment or control group, so only perceptions of learning — not measured gains — are captured; limited attack/defense coverage and only a subset of discussed application domains exercised; no formal security, isolation, or scalability testing; computational evaluation on a single hardware configuration with at most 10 concurrent users; participants were AI-course students whose background may inflate results; and MCDA results explicitly labeled a preliminary self-assessment. This is one of the more forthright limitation sections a reviewer will encounter. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The MCDA weighting methodology is internally fragile: using an LLM ("GPT 6 Astra") to produce AHP pairwise weights makes the evaluation circular — the authors' framework scores a system built by the same group, with weights from a black-box judge whose prompting and judgment provenance are not shown. - No comparative baseline: Maestro (the closest prior system, cited and discussed) is compared only narratively; no participants experienced both platforms, so "educational usefulness" claims float free of any reference point. - The between-cohort differences are unexamined: cohort A (in-person, undergraduates) scored consistently lower on clarity, ease of use, and practical experience, and cohort B's stability SD of 2.97 suggests divergent technical experiences — none of this is analyzed. - Only one of the five application domains elaborated in Section 2 (healthcare imaging) is actually exercised; the 5G, recommender, physical-world, and cybersecurity scenarios remain design fiction, so the architecture's domain generality is asserted rather than evidenced. - Questionnaire items conflate platform quality with learning (e.g., Q2 "helped me learn new knowledge" measures self-assessment of learning, a known unreliable proxy), and the 10-point scale items are never validated or piloted. - White-team/anti-cheat claims for the protected evaluators ("should resist attempts to manipulate the checks") are stated but never adversarially tested — no attempt to bypass or game the evaluators is reported. Bottom Line: For anyone building hands-on AI-security training infrastructure, this is a genuinely useful and unusually honest reference design with reusable code, but as a research contribution it is a solid engineering report wrapped around known components, and the pedagogical-effectiveness question it poses remains open — read the paper and clone the repo, but do not cite it as evidence that cyber ranges improve adversarial-AI competence.

CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation

K Zhao, G Zhang, X Cheng, X Cui, H Heng, X Chu… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents CascadeRec, a two-tier LLM reranking cascade deployed in production at a financial-planning SaaS provider, which routes only a selected minority of requests to expensive Tier-2 inference (self-consistency, multi-path reasoning, or a larger model) and reports ~10% inference-cost reduction at quality parity over a month-long A/B. - Why it's important: Uniformly running a large LLM reranker on every request costs an order of magnitude more than a small one, and — the paper's key empirical point — actively harms sparse-history users (up to 30% NDCG@10 loss at k=1 on Amazon-Electronics), so naive deployment both wastes money and widens a new-user quality gap. - How it does it: A cheap Tier-1 LLM reranks every request and emits a verbalized confidence; a zero-latency heuristic router escalates per-request to a Tier-2 pool, with cached Tier-1 outputs, graceful fallback to earlier rankings on any parse/timeout failure, and rollout gated by per-segment (history-length, tenant-size) deltas rather than aggregates. - The good: A reproducible offline study (code, prompts, caches, and raw results released) with paired-bootstrap and Wilcoxon significance testing shows a clean, counter-intuitive finding: escalating cold users makes their loss larger (Amazon/Mistral k=1: 0.337 with escalation vs. 0.356 uniform vs. 0.507 no-rerank), directly refuting the intuitive cold-escalation policy. - The missing: The production evidence is weak — the ~10% cost saving is for the whole treatment arm (not isolated to routing), quality is reported as unquantified 'parity' with no effect sizes or confidence intervals, and latency impact is qualitative with no percentiles. - Read it or not: Read it if you are deploying LLM inference in a ranking or routing path and need practical lessons on output-parsing failure rates (0.1%–97% depending on model/prompt), segment-gated rollout, and deterministic A/B caching; skip it if you want a new routing algorithm — only the trivial history-length router (R0) is evaluated.
