Problem & Motivation: LLM agents that plan, invoke tools, access data, maintain memory, and delegate can change security posture after deployment: indirect prompt injection can alter the agent's objective via untrusted content, tool calls can execute consequential actions, memory/RAG can propagate failures across sessions, delegation graphs can amplify privilege, and MCP/tool dependencies can change independently of the model. The operators with this problem are organizations deploying agentic systems in network and systems-management contexts, where NIST ISCM/AI-RMF practice already requires continuous monitoring of control effectiveness but where conventional monitoring state (hosts, flows, credentials) does not capture agent task, planning, or delegation state. The gap the paper targets is that existing runtime defenses (AgentSpec, Task Shield, GuardAgent, AGrail, Safety Sidecar, ToolSafe, ProbGuard, AgentTelemetry) are evaluated as isolated mechanisms or benchmarks, not assembled into a management model of continuous assurance where safety evidence is treated as perishable. Key Idea: The central insight is that runtime agent security is a control-plane problem: separate the agent execution plane from instrumentation, correlated state, heterogeneous detection, an explicit policy/intervention layer, and durable assurance evidence, such that continued agent authority depends on current runtime evidence (task context, action impact, monitor coverage, dependency state) rather than on static identity or a one-time safety certification. A supporting conceptual move is the insistence that monitor verdicts must be reconciled by an explicit policy layer mapping to graduated responses (allow → allow-with-audit → step-up approval → revise/retry → block → quarantine/rollback → terminate/revoke) rather than letting any single monitor — semantic or probabilistic — directly control execution. Methodology: The paper is a structured integrative review (explicitly not PRISMA), covering 2020 through 9 September 2026, sourcing SpringerLink, ACM DL, ACL Anthology, PMLR, ICLR/NeurIPS proceedings, NIST repositories, and OWASP, with a five-pass synthesis: extract monitoring/assurance concepts from NIST and runtime-verification literature; group attacks and benchmarks by execution surface; classify defenses by observable input, decision logic, intervention point, and temporal horizon; map controls to network/service-management functions; and convert gaps into the RSMCA architecture. The framework itself defines: (1) an event vector E_t for each consequential action (agent, session, task, role, model version, action, tool, arguments, data labels, provenance, delegation path, policy version, verdicts, outcome); (2) an assurance state tuple A_t = <coverage, policy freshness, monitor health, behavior risk, dependency state, unresolved incidents, provenance completeness>; and (3) a six-phase closed-loop lifecycle (register/baseline, instrument/observe, detect/evaluate, intervene/contain, verify/recover, update evidence and reassess after change). Three critical design decisions: heterogeneous monitor classes are composed rather than collapsed into one risk score (justified by differing epistemic forms of properties); hidden chain-of-thought is excluded as an audit artifact in favor of externalized task state (well-argued); and assurance is action-sensitive, not a persistent trust score, with fail-closed behavior for high-impact actions under degraded telemetry (asserted but not validated). The authors state plainly that RSMCA is "not presented as an experimentally validated product." Key Results: Not applicable — the paper reports no experiments, measurements, or quantitative results. The "results" are conceptual outputs: a taxonomy of eight monitoring surfaces (identity/configuration, input/context, task/planning, tool invocation, data/egress, memory/RAG, delegation, external dependencies) with minimum signals and response examples (Table 3); a comparative synthesis of eight runtime-defense approaches with mechanisms and limitations (Table 5); a minimum telemetry schema (Table 4); a graduated intervention policy (Table 6); a set of ~16 candidate evaluation metrics spanning security (ASR by attack class), utility (benign task success, false-block rate), operational burden (human-intervention rate, latency), temporal performance (MTTD, predictive lead time), and assurance-evidence quality (coverage, provenance completeness); and a 11-item research agenda (Table 8). The three deployment scenarios (Section 10) are explicitly "analytical illustrations, not empirical case studies." Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL in the conceptual sense — the genuinely new contribution is the synthesis itself: recasting agent runtime security as a continuous systems-management/assurance problem, the eight-surface taxonomy, the correlated-event model, the action-sensitive assurance state, and "monitor the monitors" as an assurance requirement. The individual ingredients (runtime verification, NIST ISCM, sidecar architectures, graduated enforcement, zero-trust) are established; the novelty lies in the composition and the insistence that heterogeneous monitor verdicts stay evidence-tagged rather than fused into a single score. No NEW METHOD or NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING is delivered. Rigor & Reproducibility: There are no ablations, seeds, error bars, or significance tests because there is no experiment; this is expected for a framework paper but bounds what the review can establish. The review methodology is candid about being integrative rather than systematic, without database counts or screening statistics, and its source list is credible (ICLR/ACL/NeurIPS/ICSE papers through 2026, NIST SP 800-137/207, AI RMF, OWASP), though it cites several 2025–2026 items including work "accepted" but not yet presented (ProbGuard at ASE 2026), so the comparative landscape is partly built on preprints and very recent publications. The main methodological concern is circular self-positioning: the paper defines its own evaluation metrics and research agenda but never applies them, and the eight reviewed defenses are characterized qualitatively from their papers' claims rather than re-evaluated or compared on shared benchmarks by the authors. No code, data, schema, or artifact is released; the event vector and assurance-state tuple are explicitly "conceptual rather than a mandated wire format." Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS in intent (a proposed control-plane architecture), but as published it is a THEORETICAL/conceptual framework with no implementation, so the check applies to the proposed design. Practical: The paper argues components map onto existing infrastructure (observability pipelines, API gateways, service meshes, identity systems, credential revocation, configuration rollback), so nothing requires exotic hardware — but this is a claim, not a demonstration. Efficient: Not evaluated; the paper itself flags that per-action policy latency, verifier token cost, trace volume, and human-approval burden are unmeasured, and lists "operational economics" as an open research question. Effective: Not established — the framework is designed to solve the stated problem but no evidence exists that it does; benchmarks are positioned only as pre-deployment validation tools. Scalable: Not tested; multi-agent delegation graphs and long-horizon sessions are described as motivating cases, and graph-scale provenance is raised as a research challenge, but nothing at 10× or 100× scale is examined. Deliverable form: paper only — no library, CLI, dataset, schema standard, or trained model; a reusable conceptual artifact at best. Strengths: - The four-way distinction among observability, monitoring, enforcement, and continuous assurance (Table 2), and the argument that a system can be highly observable yet weakly protected (or vice versa), is a genuinely useful clarification that much agent-safety discourse blurs. - Treating the safety infrastructure itself as an assurance object — instrumentation coverage, event loss, monitor version, calibration drift, "no alerts is not evidence of safety when the monitoring path is unhealthy" — addresses a real, rarely-acknowledged failure mode in guardrail proposals. - The eight-surface taxonomy with per-surface minimum signals and responses (Table 3) is a concrete, reusable checklist for anyone instrumenting an agent system, including less-covered surfaces like delegation-graph authority attenuation and MCP/dependency supply-chain drift. - Intellectual honesty: the paper repeatedly and explicitly labels what is conceptual vs. validated, excludes hidden chain-of-thought as an audit artifact, and names cost/latency and monitor-correlated-failure problems for its own sidecar recommendations. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state four: (1) the agent-security literature evolves rapidly and post-September-2026 work may change the comparative landscape; (2) the review is integrative, not exhaustive PRISMA, so retrieval completeness is not claimed; (3) reviewed defenses are mostly validated in benchmarks, not long-running production deployments, limiting evidence on operational false positives, human burden, cost, and recovery; (4) RSMCA is conceptual and requires implementation and comparative evaluation before being treated as a validated reference architecture. They confront limitations directly and convert them into a concrete next step (an instrumented testbed comparing baseline monitoring, individual guardrails, and the full RSMCA loop against a defined metric set) — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The hardest part of the proposal — semantic task-alignment monitoring, which underpins surfaces 3, 4, and much of the response policy — is delegated to the very class of model-based monitors (Task Shield, GuardAgent) the paper elsewhere admits may be unreliable; the framework does not analyze what happens when the semantic monitor itself is the injected component. - The graduated intervention policy assumes calibrated, conflict-resolvable verdict fusion, but the paper offers no conflict-resolution semantics, no policy language, and no analysis of how correlated failures across monitors sharing similar base models degrade the ensemble — it lists these only as future work. - The evaluation metric set is proposed but never instantiated even on a toy example (e.g., what provenance-completeness or lead-time values the illustrative scenarios would yield), so a reader cannot judge whether the metrics are actually computable in practice. - The review includes defenses published through 2026 while providing no quantitative comparison across them (no shared benchmark numbers, even as reported by the original papers), so the "comparative synthesis" in Table 5 is mechanism-level description, not evidence-based ranking. - The assurance state tuple A_t has no defined semantics: how coverage, freshness, and behavior risk combine to set "autonomy ceiling" is unspecified, which is precisely the decision the framework is supposed to make auditable. Bottom Line: As a synthesis and problem-formulation paper this is a strong map of an under-integrated area and a credible checklist for agent-security architects, but it delivers no implementation, no data, and no experiments — so a practitioner should read it as a design language for runtime agent assurance, while anyone needing evidence, artifacts, or comparisons should wait for the testbed evaluation the authors themselves identify as the missing work.

WAM is capable in BEHAVIOR-1K: the 2nd-place solution to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge

Y He, J Ye, X Wei, W Xiao, G Zhang, G Wei, X Qi… · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents the 2nd-place system (Team IF1001) for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge, a competition report that adapts the Cosmos 3 world action model (16B parameters) to 100 long-horizon household tasks, achieving a private-test Q-score of 0.615 and a 41.2% full-task success rate. - Why it's important: It provides one of the first strong pieces of evidence that world action models (WAMs) — which co-train video prediction and action generation — can outperform VLA-based pipelines (2025 winners scored 0.251–0.260 under a comparable protocol) on long-horizon mobile manipulation, a central open question in embodied AI. - How it does it: It combats non-Markovian observational ambiguity by conditioning Cosmos 3 on a 2-second visual history, explicit task-stage tokens, and task-group/skill-specific LoRA adapters selected at inference by a separate progress estimator, plus execution tricks (candidate aggregation, rolling inpainting, TOPP-RA retiming, gripper override rules). - The good: The headline result is credible — self-evaluation across 3 rounds on all 100 tasks gives 0.613 ± 0.008 Q-score and 40.9 ± 1.0% success, closely matching the private-test score (0.615 / 41.2%), and ablations cleanly attribute gains (task-group LoRA: 0.434→0.494; learned stage IDs: 0.480→0.494). - The missing: There is no ablation isolating the contribution of visual history or skill-specific LoRA routing (the latter actually underperforms: 0.581 vs. the assembled system's 0.613), no code or model release (only rollout videos on Hugging Face), and the reported per-round spread on individual tasks (e.g., task 94: 0.900→0.650→0.750) shows high instability the paper does not analyze. - Read it or not: Read it if you are building competition-scale embodied policies or deciding between WAM and VLA backbones for long-horizon manipulation; skip it if you want controlled science — it is an engineering report whose specific tricks are largely inherited from the 2025 winning solution.

Problem & Motivation: The BEHAVIOR Challenge evaluates mobile manipulation on 100 household tasks (up from 50 in 2025) in the OmniGibson simulator, requiring navigation between rooms, coordinated bimanual manipulation, and sequences whose success depends on earlier actions, with evaluation restricted to onboard RGB, depth, and proprioception. The core difficulty is non-Markovian ambiguity: visually similar observations occur at different task stages and demand different actions, and small control errors compound over horizons of ~350 s (mean human demonstration time). Teams serving the 2025 solutions built on the π0.5 VLA and scored only ~0.25–0.26 private-test Q-score, and VLAs are known to have weak instruction-following and spatial understanding. The organizers also impose a 1 FPS minimum inference rate and forbid recursive self-improvement and agentic harness methods in the ranking configuration, constraining system design. Key Idea: The core move is to treat a large pretrained omnimodal world model (Cosmos 3, jointly a "reasoner" autoregressive stream and a diffusion action/vision generator) as a robot policy, and then resolve observational ambiguity by injecting task progress at three complementary levels: (1) clean visual-history latents spanning 2 s, (2) 4 stage-task fusion conditioning tokens derived from a predicted stage ID, and (3) a routed pool of 17 task-group LoRA adapters plus 4 skill-specific (pick/place/open/close) LoRA adapters chosen by an external progress estimator. A secondary, understated idea is the corrected rectified-flow loss normalization — averaging over prediction tokens only (weight 80/9) so the effective loss weight is invariant to the number of clean history latents added. Methodology: The pipeline has training and inference phases. Training: starting from Cosmos 3-Nano (16B), the policy is fine-tuned on 20,000 demonstrations (200/task) sampled into ~104.8M windows at 15 Hz; actions are 32-step chunks of 23 dimensions, with 17 dimensions expressed as state-relative deltas (Eq. 2) and per-chunk-position 1st/99th-percentile normalization (Eq. 3); conditioning tokens (visual history, proprioception, 4 stage-task fusion tokens) are inserted into the diffusion subsequence under Cosmos 3's mask (causal AR, full DM attention) with a hand-derived 3D mRoPE temporal mapping (ω = 6 s⁻¹ from Wan2.2 VAE compression). Base training runs 600k steps (~7,095 GPU-hours, batch 384, AdamW, LR 8e-5→0, 5× multiplier on action/stage modules, 52.3% MFU via cached 6-bit VAE latents). Then 17 task-group LoRAs (rank 128, α=256, 40k steps each, ~6,427 GPU-hours total) are trained, where groups come from graph coloring of a scene–room conflict graph (a 17-task kitchen clique sets a tight lower bound); 4 skill LoRAs are trained on pooled per-skill segments across tasks. Inference: a progress estimator (404M stage branch over 3 VAE latents + 94.6M SigLIP/Transformer subtask branch over proprioception and head images) supplies stage IDs and skill predictions; a router selects task-group or skill LoRA; 5 action candidates are denoised with UniPC (4 steps, shift β=5) and CFG (γ=3), aggregated by mean/vote or medoid selection (Eq. 10–11), anchored by rolling inpainting against the previous executed chunk (Eq. 12), and executed with either uniform resampling or TOPP-RA time-optimal retiming (Eq. 13–15) plus demonstration-derived gripper override rules. Critical design decisions: history+stage conditioning is justified by the 2025 winner's recipe and a stage-ID sensitivity study (Fig. 5); task grouping by initial-scene conflict is well-motivated and near-optimal; the skill-to-stage lookup replacement is empirically justified only on 24 selected tasks. Key Results: Official private test (20 instances/task, all 100 tasks): Q-score 0.615, success 41.2%, ranking 2nd behind The North Star (0.683 / 48.2%, hierarchical physics + RSI) and ahead of Cyber (0.596 / 39.6%). Self-evaluation on public validation instances: 0.613 ± 0.008 Q-score, 40.9 ± 1.0% success over 3 rounds. Ablations (validation): base policy 0.434 / 21.3% → +17 task-group LoRAs 0.494 / 26.9%; clock-derived stage IDs 0.480 / 25.2% → predicted stage IDs 0.494 / 26.9%; skill-to-stage lookup on 24 tasks 0.707 / 56.3% vs. 0.681 / 52.5% for stage estimation. Execution strategies: short-window (26→20) 0.575 / 35.9% at 676.7k model calls; long-window (52→40) 0.549 / 33.5% at 340.0k calls; TOPP-RA 0.557 / 36.3% at 540.3k calls, and TOPP-RA cuts mean task execution time to 211.4 s vs. 274.6 s for uniform resampling (human reference 313.1 s) over 260 instances on 60 tasks. Instance-level cherry-picking reaches 0.891 / 79.5%, which the authors use to argue high latent capability with poor consistency. Baselines cited (RLC, Openpi Comet) are from 2025 under a different timeout and task set, so cross-year comparisons are only indicative. Skill LoRA routing scored 0.581 / 38.1% — worse than the routed task-group configuration. Novelty Classification: ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION with a modest NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (WAMs outperform VLAs on this benchmark). The genuinely new element is the demonstrated capability of a WAM backbone at 100-task competition scale and the corrected multi-history loss weighting; the rest — history conditioning, stage-token fusion, gripper rules, inpainting, and 4-token stage-task fusion — is explicitly adopted from the 2025 first-place solution (Larchenko et al.), and LoRA adaptation, classifier-free guidance, UniPC sampling, and TOPP-RA are standard techniques applied in a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist for task-group LoRA (full 100 tasks, Table 5 with per-group breakdown in Appendix C.2), stage-ID strategy (Table 6), and execution windows (Table 8), plus a controlled stage-ID sensitivity analysis (Fig. 5) on 2,000 windows of one task — but visual history and the loss reweighting are not ablated, and skill LoRA routing is evaluated only as a single configuration with no comparison of adapter counts or routing thresholds. Error bars are reported as mean ± sample standard deviation across only 3 evaluation rounds; no significance tests. Simulator version drifted during the competition (OmniGibson v3.9.1–v3.9.3), and some tables restrict to tasks with complete results, which the authors flag as potential selection bias. No code or model weights are released; per-task validation tables and rollout videos are on Hugging Face. The technique is developed and evaluated entirely on the challenge's own tasks and instances — appropriate for a competition report but meaning the generalization claim ("WAM is capable") rests on a single benchmark with no held-out task family. Notably, they transparently report cherry-picked upper bounds separately rather than conflating them with fixed-configuration performance, which is a credibility positive. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built system evaluated by deployment in simulation, not on physical robots). - Practical: Yes — runs on a single GPU (~56 GB memory, consistent with one 16B-parameter model in bf16) with no closed-source model dependencies, a stated constraint of their design. - Efficient: Sustains >2 FPS per port across 100 concurrent evaluation ports (>4 FPS single-request); but total compute is heavy — ~13,500 GPU-hours for base + LoRA training — and the short-window configuration costs 2× the model calls of long-window for a 2.6-point Q-score gain. - Effective: The evidence (41.2% full-task success, matched val/test scores) shows it solves a large fraction of the benchmark's goals, though 59% of tasks still end incomplete and per-task variance across rounds is large. - Scalable: Not tested — the authors state their compute limited them and only claim further gains from larger models and longer training; scaling to 10× tasks or real robots is unaddressed, and simulation-only deployment leaves sim-to-real entirely open. Deliverable form: paper plus Hugging Face rollout videos; no reusable software artifact or trained checkpoint is released. Strengths: - Direct head-to-head evidence that a WAM backbone (Cosmos 3) beats the VLA-based 2025 winners by a large margin (0.615 vs. 0.260 test Q-score), which is a substantive empirical data point for the field's WAM-vs-VLA debate. - Careful, near-optimal task-group construction: the graph-coloring formulation explicitly derives the 17-group lower bound from a 17-task kitchen clique and matches it, turning an ad hoc grouping into a principled partition. - Honest, unusually detailed error accounting: 3-round self-evaluation with per-task tables, explicit cherry-pick bounds separated from fixed-configuration results, disclosed simulator-version drift, and disclosed Val/Test configuration differences. - Practical inference engineering under hard constraints (1 FPS minimum, no RSI, no closed-source models): the >2 FPS/port concurrent serving result and the TOPP-RA retiming with explicit fallback rules are real deployment contributions. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that competition time and compute constraints limited strictly controlled ablations and forced some comparisons onto selected task subsets; that OmniGibson version changes during the competition introduce inconsistency; that restricting evaluation to complete-result tasks may bias comparisons; that they could not evaluate joint subtask+stage prediction or direct subtask conditioning; that their Val deployment simplifies the Test configuration (with a modest performance cost); and that their training budget was compute-limited with longer training expected to help. They confront these directly and repeatedly, which strengthens confidence in what they do report. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No ablation of visual-history conditioning — the paper's central anti-ambiguity mechanism is inherited from [4] and never isolated, despite being one of two headline modifications. - Skill-specific LoRA routing is reported as a single number (0.581) that is worse than the system without it (0.613), yet the paper does not explain why the mechanism fails or under what conditions the skill adapters help; a negative result is presented without analysis. - The 0.891 cherry-pick Q-score is used to argue "considerable potential," but this conflates configuration variance and seed variance with latent capability — no decomposition (e.g., variance per stage of the task) supports the interpretation. - Only 3 evaluation rounds with 10 instances/task, and the large round-to-round swings on individual tasks (e.g., task 46: 0.229→0.671→0.443) suggest the ±0.008 overall standard deviation understates per-task instability; no variance analysis is offered. - The stage-ID sensitivity study covers a single task (26); the claimed stage-dependence of action predictions may not generalize across the 1,120 task stages. - The gap to the 1st-place system (0.683 with RSI, which is disallowed for their ranking) is not analyzed: the reader cannot tell whether WAM or the forbidden techniques drive the 6.8-point difference. - Zero real-robot evaluation, which is inherent to the challenge but bounds all claims about "household capabilities." Bottom Line: A practitioner building long-horizon embodied policies should read this as the best current evidence that WAMs beat VLAs on BEHAVIOR-scale tasks and as a useful catalog of execution and conditioning tricks, but should not expect reusable science — the components are largely borrowed, the ablations are incomplete, and nothing is released beyond videos.

Quality of Models for Man and Machine

J Krogstie · link.springer.com · simulation environments for business processes - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This open-access Springer monograph (by John Krogstie, NTNU) extends the SEQUAL semiotic quality framework for conceptual models to cover machine learning models, data, XAI outputs, and AI systems as active producers and consumers of models, positioning this as a foundation for neuro-symbolic computing. - Why it's important: As AI agents increasingly generate and consume the abstractions (models, data, explanations) that organizations run on, there is no shared, principled vocabulary for judging whether those abstractions are "good" for both human and machine actors — a gap that affects trust, human agency, and system design. - How it does it: It grounds model quality in Stachowiak's general model theory and Stamper/Peirce semiotics, combined with social-construction theory (Berger & Luckmann) and model-power theory (Bråten), then systematically re-derives SEQUAL's sets (G, L, D, M, A, K, I, T) and quality types (physical, empirical, syntactic, semantic, perceived semantic, pragmatic, social, deontic) so that machines count as actors and ML artifacts count as models. - The good: The framework has three decades of lineage and the book is intellectually careful — notably its honest argument that ML models may fail Stachowiak's pragmatic/intentionality criterion (their training intent is opaque), motivating the ML-model vs. Machine-Learning-Result (MLR) distinction. - The missing: The provided material (front matter + Chapter 1) contains no empirical validation of the extended framework; the claim that SEQUAL 2026 improves assessment of AI models is asserted via chapter structure and case descriptions, not measured — later chapters may add evidence, but none is shown here. - Read it or not: Worth reading for conceptual modellers, IS/enterprise-modelling researchers, and postgraduate students who need to bridge symbolic modelling and machine learning; ML researchers seeking technical results, algorithms, or benchmarks can skip it.

Problem & Motivation: Conceptual modelling has historically served human experts, with quality frameworks (including the author's own SEQUAL) designed around human comprehension, agreement, and goals. Three shifts break this assumption: models now represent digital as well as physical realities; models are produced and consumed by machines (LLMs, agents, ML pipelines) as well as humans; and modelling now happens outside organizational settings, in digital ecosystems. Practitioners and researchers building neuro-symbolic systems must combine symbolic artifacts (ontologies, knowledge graphs, rules) with sub-symbolic ones (neural networks), but lack a unified account of what quality means across both, and how human-centered notions of quality align with machine-useful notions. The stakes the author emphasizes are human agency and trust: without a quality framework spanning man and machine, humans risk becoming "model-weak" relative to AI systems that are "model-strong." Key Idea: The core move is ontological unification under semiotics: treat datasets, ML models, ML results (MLRs), XAI explanations, and traditional visual conceptual models as instances of the same representational phenomenon, all assessable through one extended SEQUAL framework whose actor sets now include both social (human) and technical (machine) interpreters. A deliberately provocative sub-claim sharpens this: because ML models have unarticulated training intent, they arguably are not "models" in Stachowiak's sense at all — only their outputs (MLRs) are — which is a non-obvious conceptual distinction with consequences for how one audits AI systems. Methodology: This is a conceptual/theoretical synthesis, not an algorithmic method. The pipeline is: (1) establish philosophical foundations (Stachowiak's representation/simplification/pragmatic-orientation triad; Peircean semiotics and Stamper's six semiotic layers plus a deontic layer; Berger & Luckmann's social construction); (2) survey modelling goals for humans (eight usage goals from model mapping to activation, temporal model typology from as-is to burning-platform models) and for machines (model learning, prediction, twinning, deployment); (3) characterize data and ML-model requirements using standard statistics/ML taxonomies (Stevens' scales, supervised/unsupervised/reinforcement learning, sparsity, noise, class- and bias-related dataset properties per Sancricca et al. 2025 and Siebert et al. 2022's quality meta-model); (4) re-derive SEQUAL 2026 with extended sets and quality types; (5) apply it in later chapters to symbolic AI (OpenCyc evaluation), ML systems (an "Artsorakelet" application), XAI explanation quality, LLM-assisted modelling, MMLA-based "neuro-conceptualisation" experiments, and RAG systems (KUDOS Norwegian public-documents collection). Critical design decisions: including machines as actors in A and T (well-motivated but unproven useful); introducing affective quality and neuroscience/MMLA-informed updates for the human side (novel but unvalidated here); and the ML-model/MLR split (the most intellectually interesting decision, argued rather than demonstrated). No formal objective function or proof framework is given — the framework is taxonomic and descriptive. Key Results: Not evaluated — the provided text contains no quantitative outcomes, baselines, or measured comparisons. The empirical touchpoints are described, not reported: Chapter 1 is illustrative (the London Underground map as a running example of semantic/pragmatic quality trade-offs; a Deftpower EV-charging digital business ecosystem model; a business-process value dimension table), and Chapters 4–5 promise case studies (OpenCyc reuse evaluation, Artsorakelet ML application, MMLA experiments on process-model comprehension, KUDOS RAG system) without results in the presented material. The only quasi-quantitative content is textbook-level statistics (68–95–99.7 rule, Bonferroni/Holm corrections, p < 0.05 vs. 6σ in physics) used pedagogically. The strongest qualitative finding is the model-power analysis: LLM-based agents act as model-strong actors, users exhibit overreliance and automation bias (citing Sun et al. 2024; Krügel et al. 2023), and consistent world models in AI could concentrate model power in ways that demand explicit human-in-the-loop safeguards. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (extension of the SEQUAL quality framework to ML models, data, and machine actors) plus NEW PROBLEM framing (model quality for man and machine as a foundation for neuro-symbolic computing). The bulk of the technical content — ML taxonomy, data-quality dimensions, XAI categories (surrogate/extrinsic/intrinsic), CRISP-DM, AI-adoption enablers/inhibitors, Wegner's interaction machines — is a competent synthesis of existing work applied to this framing; the genuinely new elements are the SEQUAL 2026 extension, the MLR distinction, and the neuro-conceptualisation research agenda. Rigor & Reproducibility: Not applicable in the experimental sense: no ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests are present in the provided text, and there is no code or artifact release mentioned. The work is a conceptual monograph; its "rigor" is in argument structure and scholarly grounding (extensive citation of the author's own and the community's prior work: Krogstie 2012/2016, Enholm et al. 2022, Siebert et al. 2022, Guizzardi & Guarino 2024). Methodological concerns: (1) the framework is developed and illustrated largely by its author, so self-consistency rather than external validation supports it; (2) quality assessment at the semantic/pragmatic/social layers is explicitly acknowledged to require human judgment, making the framework hard to falsify or apply inter-subjectively; (3) the promised case studies cannot be assessed from the provided material; (4) the book is dated 2027 and is open access — this appears to be a published scholarly monograph rather than peer-reviewed conference/journal research, so claims should be weighted accordingly. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (a conceptual framework and research programme with no primary experimental claim in the provided material). Sound: The framework is internally coherent and philosophically grounded, but it is descriptive, not formal — there are no theorems, and the central claim that ML models fail Stachowiak's intentionality criterion is argued, not proven. General: The formulation is deliberately broad, covering symbolic, sub-symbolic, and hybrid artifacts and both human and machine actors — realistic scope, but at the cost of operational specificity. Tight: Not applicable (no bounds); the closest analogue is whether the quality taxonomy is discriminating, which is untested here. Implementable: SEQUAL has historically been used as an evaluation checklist, and the book sketches applications (XAI explanation quality, RAG policy development), but no tool, library, or metric suite is delivered. The artifact is the book itself; no software, dataset, or reusable instrument is released with the provided material. Strengths: - Genuinely new problem framing: extending a mature, human-centered quality framework to machine actors is a real conceptual contribution, not a rebranding of existing ML evaluation work, which is largely metric-driven and ignores semiotic/social layers. - Intellectual honesty on definitions: the book interrogates whether ML models are "models" at all under Stachowiak's criteria and introduces the ML-model/MLR distinction instead of papering over the mismatch. - The model-power/model-monopoly analysis applied to LLM agents is a sharp, transferable lens: it recasts human-AI interaction as an asymmetry of abstraction control rather than a peer collaboration, connecting 1970s–80s theory (Bråten, Argyris & Schön) to automation-bias findings from 2023–2024. - Breadth of integration: semiotics, IS theory, social construction, statistics, ML practice, XAI, and neuroscience (MMLA) are brought into one argumentative arc, which is rare and useful for graduate-level bridging. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The author states that the techniques covered in Chapter 2 are "selected for their use later in the book and are not intended as a complete overview"; that AI is not yet capable of "leaps of abstraction" across untrained domains or of creating new representation mechanisms; that ML models have opaque intent ("missing goal alignment"), which is why they are not classified as models in the traditional sense; that ML-generated data used for retraining is harmful ("cannibalism," citing Shumailov et al. 2024); and that XAI "comes with limitations" for establishing trust. The preface confronts the subjectivity of quality evaluation at higher semiotic layers directly rather than minimizing it — a credibility positive. Limitations of the extended framework itself (e.g., no worked validation) are not discussed in the provided material. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No evaluation of the framework: the extended SEQUAL 2026 is presented, but the provided material offers no evidence that using it changes assessment outcomes, improves model quality, or outperforms existing ML-quality frameworks (e.g., Siebert et al.'s, which the author cites approvingly) for the machine-side cases it targets. - Potential circularity: quality judgments at semantic/pragmatic/social layers depend on human interpretation (sets K and I), so "validating" quality with the framework risks measuring the evaluator's priors; no protocol for inter-rater reliability is proposed. - The human/machine alignment claim — that human and machine quality notions "align" well enough for a shared framework — is the book's foundational assumption but is nowhere tested; machines arguably need only syntactic/empirical/syntactic-semantic fidelity for most tasks, making the other layers potentially anthropomorphic overhead. - The title's promise ("a foundation for neuro-symbolic computing") outruns the shown content: Chapter 1 establishes vocabulary; whether later chapters deliver operational neuro-symbolic techniques (vs. RAG, which is a known hybrid pattern) cannot be verified from the provided text. - Missing dogs-not-barking: no engagement with formal methods for neuro-symbolic systems (e.g., neuro-symbolic logic programming, differentiable reasoning) that dominate that literature, which limits the book's utility to researchers in that specific subfield. Bottom Line: A practitioner or researcher in conceptual modelling, enterprise modelling, or IS who needs a principled bridge from model-quality theory to ML/LLM-era practice will gain real conceptual vocabulary from this book, but ML and neuro-symbolic AI researchers will find better technical alternatives (e.g., the neuro-symbolic systems and XAI-evaluation literature it cites) covering the substantive ground.

Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models (35 ▲ )

Jiahao Huang, Jun Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 20 Nov 2026
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper introduces MC-Lens, a Jacobian-based interpretability method that reads concept information from intermediate vision-encoder and language-decoder states of VLMs into a shared output-vocabulary space, and uses it to study selective access, causal use of concepts, and cross-modal alignment through the lens of global workspace theory (GWT). - Why it's important: VLM outputs do not reveal their internal concept representations, and VLMs can answer visual questions incorrectly even when the needed visual information is readable from intermediate states — understanding whether that information is causally used matters for interpretability, alignment training, and testing whether GWT-style functional properties transfer to multimodal artificial systems. - How it does it: The core move is fitting averaged Jacobian lenses separately for encoder and decoder (with token-category-balanced averaging, a fix over J-Lens's uniform averaging), centring readouts against a reference image distribution, and representing each concept as a set of vocabulary directions (word-form sets and greedily selected sets) that support both readout and subspace-replacement counterfactual interventions. - The good: The causal experiments are the strongest part: expanding from a single name token to a greedy set of just 5 directions (J@5 + SubRep) redirects nearly every one-hop VQA answer (e.g., country → capital), whereas the broadest word-form set F≤3 redirects fewer than half — showing concepts are causally used in multi-step reasoning, not merely readable. - The missing: Quantitative evaluations rest on very small bespoke datasets (50 flag-image country/capital pairs, 40 multi-hop cases, 100 A-OKVQA/COCO cases) built by the authors, with no public code or lens artifacts mentioned, and the GWT/consciousness framing is interpretive rather than tested against any non-GWT alternative. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on mechanistic interpretability of multimodal models or GWT-inspired architectures; skip it if you want a rigorous test of consciousness claims or large-scale, generalizable concept-representation results — it delivers neither.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners interpreting VLMs face a gap: a model can correctly name a bicycle in an image, but its answer reveals nothing about where or how that concept is represented internally, and prior work (Fu et al., 2025) shows visual information can remain readable in intermediate states even when the model answers incorrectly. Existing vocabulary-readout methods (Logit Lens, Tuned Lens, J-Lens) target text-only LLMs or single-token concepts. In parallel, GWT proposes that information from parallel processes competes for access to a shared workspace and is then broadcast to specialized processes; Gurnee et al. (2026) found workspace-like structure in LLMs, but no one had extended such analysis to concepts entering from images in VLMs, where vision and language processing are structurally separate. The paper addresses whether VLMs exhibit GWT-like functions — accessibility, selective access, and broadcast/broad availability — for multimodal concepts. Key Idea: The core insight is that both the vision encoder's patch states and the language decoder's token states can be projected into one shared semantic space — the decoder's output vocabulary — via layer-wise averaged Jacobians, and that a concept should be represented not by one name token but by a set of vocabulary directions (selected either by word forms or greedily by reconstruction), because image-borne concepts have no anchoring token and spread across many related tokens. This direction-set representation then supports both readout (coverage of top-ranked tokens) and causal intervention (subspace replacement), enabling the accessibility → selectivity → causality experimental arc. Methodology: MC-Lens extends J-Lens (averaged Jacobian mapping intermediate states to final-layer decoder space) to VLMs in three stages. (1) Lens estimation: For each layer ℓ, Jacobians ∂h^D_L,q/∂h^m_ℓ,p are computed (V-Lens backpropagates from encoder patches through connector and decoder; L-Lens uses causal decoder positions), summed over final-layer text positions only, category-balanced (image/text/template tokens weighted equally, unlike J-Lens's uniform averaging — justified by image tokens outnumbering text tokens), then averaged over ~N VQA examples. (2) Readout: Intermediate states (single or mean over patches/tokens) are mapped through Norm + unembedding to give vocabulary logits; reference centring subtracts the mean state over natural reference images per layer, fixing the problem that uninformative tokens (‐photo, ‐image) dominate visual readouts. (3) Concept direction sets and interventions: Word-form sets F≤j (name token → case/spacing variants → inflections/aliases/translations → first tokens of multi-token forms) and greedy sets J@k (orthogonal matching pursuit with NNLS refitting to reconstruct the centred state difference Δz between the target concept and comparison concepts). Interventions include SubRep (replace the projection of the source state onto the combined direction subspace with the target's projection), AbIn (ablate + inject mean direction), FullRep (full state replacement), and F0+PairSwap as the J-Lens baseline. The training study fits a randomly initialised MLP connector between a frozen CLIP encoder and frozen Gemma decoder on caption prediction (LLaVA feature-alignment style) and tracks alignment across checkpoints with two new J-space metrics (J-state cosine, ReconCov) against a hidden-state-cosine baseline. The framework is causal/counterfactual analysis in the sense of Pearl and distributed interchange interventions (Geiger et al.), with necessity/sufficiency tests adapted from causal tracing. Key Results: All quantitative work is on Qwen3-VL-8B unless stated, with cross-model comparison over Qwen3-VL (2B/8B/32B), DeepSeek-VL2 (Tiny/Small/Full), and Gemma 3 (4B/12B/27B). (i) Accessibility: Across 100 A-OKVQA cases, image-only and text-only evidence both raise the target token to rank 1 from rank 9 (Pass@K, K=1/5/10); text-only ≈ text+image, and image-only slightly lower. (ii) Readout carriers: Expanding word-form sets raises Coverage@10 substantially (e.g., ‐Canada, ‐Canadian, 加拿大 all top-10 for a Canadian flag); greedy sets J@k give higher state reconstruction but lower Coverage@10 than F≤3. (iii) Selectivity: On 100 COCO scenes, query-dependent selective sensitivity rises sharply within the estimated workspace for real images but far less for blank-image controls; an "ignore the book" instruction reduces book's readability without changing the answer. (iv) Causality: On 50 flag country/capital pairs, direct SubRep interventions succeed nearly always for all direction sets; for one-hop, J@5+SubRep redirects nearly every answer while F≤3+SubRep redirects <50%; J@25+SubRep redirects 4/6 downstream tasks in the Ireland→Tunisia example, but calling codes remain hard even with J@35. Necessity/sufficiency: direct interventions reach NR≈69.7%, SR≈100%, NSR≈66.7% (J@35); one-hop interventions recover ~85% of answers with J@35 but NSR is only 15.2% — recovered answers are mostly not necessary for the original answer. Multi-hop (40 cases): joint c1+c2 intervention with J@25 reaches 87.5% target answers vs 70% for c1-only; FullRep reaches 100%. (v) Cross-model: Shared sensory/workspace/motor-like layer organization; lower necessity (NR) in larger models across all families, with sufficiency trends diverging. (vi) Training: ReconCov with F≤2 discriminates concepts (AUC) far better than hidden-state cosine, which stays near chance; concept accessibility improves early in connector training while reliable query-dependent selective access develops later (~1,000+ steps). Baselines are current (J-Lens is the direct predecessor) but few: F0+PairSwap, hidden-state cosine, FullRep control. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (MC-Lens: multimodal Jacobian lens with category-balanced averaging and reference centring) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (concept direction sets causally drive one-hop and multi-hop VLM reasoning; selective access develops later than accessibility during alignment training). The genuinely novel elements are the V-Lens/L-Lens split into a shared vocabulary space, the reference-centring fix, and the direction-set (rather than single-token) concept representation for intervention. The underlying machinery — averaged Jacobians, OMP/NNLS sparse selection, activation patching, SubRep-style distributed interchange — is a competent combination of existing techniques (J-Lens, matching pursuit, Geiger et al. DIIs, Meng et al. causal tracing) applied to the VLM setting; the GWT framing is an organizing narrative inherited from Gurnee et al. (2026) rather than a new theoretical result. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations over intervention operators (PairSwap/SubRep/AbIn/FullRep) and direction-set budgets (F0–F≤3, J@5–J@35) are present and informative, showing which components matter (e.g., operator choice matters more than set breadth for direct tasks). 95% confidence bands appear on layerwise readout figures, but headline intervention numbers (target-answer rates) are reported as single fractions on small eligible sets (|E|=33 for NR/SR in one comparison — single-example jumps are ~3 pp) with no significance tests or multiple seeds for the lens estimation or interventions. No code, data, or lens artifacts are stated as released. Methodological concerns: the flag-image country/capital dataset and multi-hop cases are author-constructed and tiny, so the headline causal numbers carry wide implicit uncertainty; several selective-access findings (Examples 5–9) are single-image case studies; the "estimated workspace" intervals are themselves derived from the same readout methods being interpreted, creating a mild circularity; and no comparison against trained-probe or SAE baselines is reported for readout quality. This is a preprint (arXiv:2611.26590) and has not, as far as the text indicates, undergone peer review. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement/intervention method with experiments; no deployed system). - Practical: Yes — lens estimation requires only forward/backward passes through open-weight VLMs (≤32B) on standard accelerators; no exotic hardware. - Efficient: Moderate cost — computing per-layer, per-position Jacobians over a corpus is expensive, though lenses are fitted once and reused; intervention experiments require multiple forward passes per pair, but no cost figures are given. - Effective: The evidence supports causal involvement of concept directions in one-hop/multi-hop reasoning (J@5 redirects nearly all one-hop answers), but effectiveness on natural reasoning tasks beyond flag trivia and 100-case VQA subsets is untested — it solves a proxy setting convincingly, not the general problem. - Scalable: Claimed-shared workspace structure is shown across nine models up to 32B parameters, but scaling of the method (lens fitting cost, direction-set quality, intervention success at larger scale or on harder tasks) is not tested beyond this range. The work delivers a method described on paper only — no library, CLI, dataset release, or trained artifact is mentioned. Strengths: - The direction-set reframing of concepts is a real conceptual advance over single-token J-Lens readouts, with a clear empirical payoff: J@5+SubRep beats F≤3+SubRep on one-hop redirection with fewer directions (5 vs ~8), demonstrating that greedy-selected directions capture concept information that word forms miss (e.g., ‐maple for Canada at rank 116 but with high reconstruction weight). - Reference centring is a simple, well-motivated fix to a real failure mode (uninformative tokens dominating visual readouts), grounded in an observed phenomenon (Shukor and Cord, 2024) rather than ad hoc. - The necessity/sufficiency decomposition is honest and revealing: the finding that one-hop recovered answers mostly fail the necessity test (NSR 15% vs SR 85% for J@35) is reported plainly and correctly interpreted as evidence of redundant causal pathways — a more nuanced picture than typical activation-patching success stories. - The training-time study is a genuine addition: showing that concept accessibility (AUC discrimination via ReconCov) precedes reliable query-dependent selective access during connector training is a developmentally ordered finding not available from static analysis of pretrained models. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that concept descriptions via vocabulary tokens remain partial (shape, texture, non-verbalizable visual details are not captured), motivating future multimodal (image/video/audio) readouts. They explicitly disclaim any claim of consciousness or subjective experience (footnote 1, restricting "conscious" to functional properties). They acknowledge that the GWT results do not identify the mechanism of broadcasting selected information to downstream processes — a central GWT property — and that Gemma's undifferentiated geometry but sharp Agreement@8 rise shows workspace-boundary estimation needs multiple indicators. They also note DeepSeek Small/Full as exceptions to the shared workspace-readability pattern. These limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The quantitative causal claims rest on ~40–50 author-built flag-image cases and single-example granularity of ~3 pp; no standard VQA reasoning benchmark (e.g., the full A-OKVQA or GQA) is used for intervention evaluation, so generalization beyond trivia-style fact chains is unknown. - Case-study findings (Examples 5–9: spatial queries, ignore instructions, autoregressive rollouts) are anecdotal single images with no quantitative replication reported. - The "estimated workspace" is defined from the method's own geometry/readout signals and then used to interpret those same signals — the paper flags the Gemma inconsistency but does not validate the boundaries against an independent criterion. - No trained-probe, Tuned Lens, or SAE baseline is compared for readout fidelity, so it is unclear how much of MC-Lens's readout advantage over alternatives is specific to the Jacobian approach versus any cross-layer mapping. - The GWT comparison is analogical: no non-GWT account of the observed layerwise patterns is tested or ruled out, and "selective access" is operationalized as token-rank changes, which could reflect attention-mediated query conditioning rather than a workspace-like competition mechanism. - No code or data release is stated, which materially limits reproducibility given the small bespoke evaluation sets. Bottom Line: A practitioner in mechanistic interpretability gains concrete, reusable techniques here — reference centring, category-balanced lens fitting, and direction-set interventions that measurably outperform single-token swapping — but anyone seeking a rigorous test of GWT or consciousness-relevant claims in VLMs, or results generalizing beyond small flag-trivia setups, should wait for follow-up work with released code and stronger baselines.

AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs (91 ▲ )

AI Training Platform Team, Bingwei Zhang, Jing Li, Amir Abdullin, Sihang Chen, Xin Chen, Liangjun Feng, Yingmeng Gao, Tao Guo, Junjie Huang, Dongfang Li, Zhanglian Lin, Jiajun Liu, Zekun Liu, Zhengxuan Lu, Xiaodong Luo, Jian Meng, Ivan Nosov, Linyuan Qiu, Weijian Sun, Wanrui Yan, Binfan Zheng, Zhicheng Zhou, Baotian Hu, Min Zhang, Haizhou Li, Zhiquan Luo · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 18 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AscendGYM, a benchmark of 48 kernel-optimization tasks on Ascend NPUs (17 evaluated), paired with an execution sandbox (AscendForge) and a budget-aware metric (Speedup–Token Score) for evaluating how well LLM agents improve existing kernel implementations. - Why it's important: Kernel optimization is a specialized, labor-intensive engineering step for efficient LLM training/inference on Ascend hardware, and existing Ascend benchmarks test kernel generation rather than improvement of existing production kernels under real workload configurations. - How it does it: Tasks are built from profiling data of real training/inference workloads (top-k bottleneck kernels with their actual tensor shapes, dtypes, and deployment context), agents iteratively submit candidates to a sandbox for compilation, correctness checking, and latency measurement, and STS scores log-speedup gains net of a penalty proportional to the token cost of delayed improvements. - The good: The evaluation is executed end-to-end on Ascend 910C hardware with 17 model–harness combinations under explicit budgets, and the finding that ~70% of combinations achieve GM speedup below 1.2× credibly establishes that the benchmark is genuinely hard. - The missing: Only 17 of the 48 promised tasks are evaluated; there are no repeated runs, error bars, or significance tests, and speedups are measured against the libraries' shipped implementations rather than expert-optimized baselines, so headroom is unverified. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate LLM agents for NPU/heterogeneous-hardware kernel optimization, or if you need infrastructure for Ascend-side agent evaluation; skip it if you only care about CUDA/GPU kernel benchmarks, where FlashInfer-Bench and KernelBench cover similar ground at larger scale.
Why this rank

Problem & Motivation: Teams training and serving LLMs on Huawei Ascend NPUs must optimize existing Ascend C kernels for specific deployment configurations — a process requiring specialized expertise and repeated compile-measure cycles. Existing Ascend benchmarks (NPUKernelBench, CANN Bench) evaluate kernel generation from specifications, not the practically distinct task of improving a correct existing implementation for a concrete workload. The gap: no benchmark measures whether an agent can further optimize real production kernels, under the exact input shapes/dtypes drawn from real training and inference pipelines, within an explicit resource budget. The benchmark is built by the AI Training Platform Team at Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, apparently motivated by their own Ascend-based training stack. Key Idea: Two ideas carry the paper. (1) Workload-anchored task design: each optimization task is not a generic operator but a specific kernel invocation harvested from profiling real pipelines (e.g., AddRMSNorm from Qwen3-0.6B prefill, BF16, TP1, seq-len 32, invoked 56 times per forward pass and accounting for 8.77% of runtime), so measured speedup maps to a real deployment context. (2) The Speedup–Token Score: STS = 100·log2(S_n) − (50/n)·Σ_k (B_k/B_max)·Δg_k, which rewards final log-speedup but penalizes improvements in proportion to cumulative token consumption at the time they are achieved — making early, cheap gains score higher than late, expensive ones at equal final speedup. CTG (cost-to-gain in tokens for 1%/5%/10% speedup targets) complements it. Methodology: The benchmark has four components. (1) Task set: 48 kernels across three difficulty batches (Batch 1: memory-access optimization of basic kernels; Batch 2: normalization/quantization multistep ops; Batch 3: attention and fused computations); each task ships runnable baseline source, tensor manifests, test inputs, and CPU-generated reference outputs. (2) AscendForge, an execution sandbox built on SandboxFusion with four layers (build/execution with Ascend C and CANN adapters, resource orchestration across NPU nodes, development feedback with profiling, deployment/ops), returning build logs, correctness results, and msprof timings as structured feedback. (3) Metrics: STS and CTG (joint), fastp and GM speedup (performance), token/round/wall-clock budgets, and Candidate/Task Pass Rates (reliability). (4) Two evaluation modes: model–harness pairs (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode × six frontier models) with up to 80 candidate evaluations per task, and model-only evaluation via a fixed default harness (AuraKernel with GPT-5.6 Luna) in cold/warm/no-lessons/code-only configurations. Timing protocol: 8 executions (3 warm-up) averaged on-device via msprof; final best implementations re-validated 5× outside the search budget. Critical design decisions: workload-derived input configurations (well-justified via profiling statistics), separate reporting of compile/correctness/performance failure modes (justified by the pass-rate analysis in Appendix E.3), and STS's fixed 100/50 weighting between performance and delay penalty (not justified — the weights appear arbitrary). Key Results: On the 17 Batch-1 tasks with Ascend 910C: ~70% of the 17 evaluated model–harness combinations achieve GM speedup below 1.2×. Best single-task speedup is ~3.29× (fused_gdn_gating); the median speedup across supported combinations is below 1.1× on 13 of 17 tasks. Codex/GPT-5.6 reaches GM speedup ~1.69× versus ~1.05× for Claude Code/GPT-5.6 despite identical 17/17 task pass rates — pass rate and gains are decorrelated. Cost asymmetries are large: Codex/GPT-5.6 consumes ~140.4M tokens per task versus 81.75M for Claude Code/Opus 5, yet the latter achieves higher GM speedup; Qwen-35B achieves nearly identical GM speedup with OpenCode vs Codex (~1.06× vs ~1.05×) at ~11.1 vs ~2.2 hours per task. Harness ablations with GPT-5.6 Luna show the warm-start configuration achieves the highest STS at all three budgets (10M/20M/50M tokens), and code-only beats no-lessons but both fall below full cold — experience accumulation matters. Baselines compared are current frontier models (as of the paper's 2026 dating); baselines for the kernels themselves are the shipped CANN/vLLM-Ascend implementations, whose optimization headroom is not independently established. Scale is small but real: 17 tasks, 17 combinations, on physical NPU hardware. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus a new metric (STS/CTG); the AscendForge sandbox is a competent ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION of existing infrastructure (SandboxFusion + Ascend adapters) rather than a new technique. The genuinely new element is the budget-aware STS metric and the workload-context-anchored task construction applied to optimization of existing kernels on Ascend. The core evaluation pattern — iterate on a kernel with compile/correctness/latency feedback — is a standard combination of ideas from KernelBench, PRAGMA, and GEAK-Triton ported to a new hardware platform; the benchmark's value is the platform coverage and the workload-context linking, not a new algorithmic idea. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist at the harness level (warm/no-lessons/code-only with the model held fixed), which is the right design for attributing differences to the harness, but no per-component ablation of the benchmark itself. No error bars, no repeated seeds, no significance tests for the model–harness runs (the paper mentions independent repeats only as a possibility). Code is released at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM; hardware/software stack is fully specified (Ascend 910C, CANN 9.0.1, torch_npu 2.10.0.post2, msprof 26.0.0). Methodological concerns: (1) each combination appears run once per task — no variance quantification for a stochastic agentic process; (2) speedup baselines are the libraries' initial implementations, which may be unoptimized, inflating apparent headroom; (3) the benchmark is developed and evaluated on the same platform the authors operate, with no external validation; (4) no comparison against existing optimization agent frameworks (PRAGMA, AutoKernel, GPU Kernel Scientist) as reference points; (5) the warm-start configuration imports "validated strategy lessons with positive measured gains from a cold run of the same kernel" — reasonable for studying experience transfer, but the warm-vs-cold comparison partially leaks information about the specific task. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL with a SYSTEMS component (a built, deployed evaluation service). Practical: Requires access to Ascend 910C NPUs and the CANN toolchain — usable by the Ascend ecosystem, unusable as-is on commodity CUDA hardware. Efficient: Optimization runs cost 10M–50M token budgets per task with observed per-task means up to ~140M tokens and up to ~11 hours wall-clock per task — expensive relative to static kernel-generation evaluations. Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark measures optimization under budget and that the tasks are hard; it does not show that measured kernel speedups translate to end-to-end training/inference speedups (only workload-context provenance is asserted). Scalable: Only 17 of 48 tasks are evaluated; behavior on Batches 2–3 (harder fusion and attention tasks) is claimed for future work, not tested. Delivers a software artifact: the AscendGYM benchmark plus AscendForge sandbox on GitHub, with metrics implemented in the harness; the Default (AuraKernel) harness configuration is described in an appendix. Strengths: - The STS metric is a genuine conceptual contribution: by penalizing token-time-delayed gains (Eq. 1), it distinguishes systems that find improvements cheaply from those that brute-force them, a distinction final-speedup metrics conflate; the CTG breakdown in Figure 4 (median cost vs. attainment count) operationalizes this concretely. - The workload-context anchoring is executed carefully — each test case carries the target model, execution phase, parallelism config, and profiling statistics (e.g., 56 invocations, 8.77% of runtime for AddRMSNorm), linking benchmark gains to deployment relevance rather than synthetic shapes. - The reliability accounting is honest and useful: Appendix E.3 decomposes 31 baseline-speedup records into 17 correct-but-no-improvement versus 14 no-valid-candidate cases, and the pass-rate/GM-speedup dissociation (GPT-5.6: 1.69× with Codex vs 1.05× with Claude Code at 17/17 pass on both) demonstrates empirically why multiple metric axes are needed. - The prompt, budget rules, and measurement protocol are published in full (Appendix C), including anti-gaming constraints (frozen test tolerances, evaluator immutability, out-of-budget final re-validation), which makes the evaluation protocol reproducible in spirit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that only Batch 1 (17 of 48 kernels) is evaluated, with Batches 2–3 deferred to future updates. They acknowledge that Default-harness model comparisons require fixed settings and prior experience to avoid attributing configuration differences to model capability, and that CTG medians over differing attained task sets do not establish efficiency on the same tasks. They confront the limited absolute gains of current systems directly (~70% below 1.2× GM speedup) rather than minimizing them. They do not acknowledge the missing variance estimates, the shipped-implementation baseline issue, or the absence of external optimization-agent baselines. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No repeated runs or variance estimates for an inherently stochastic agentic search; rankings like Claude Code/Opus 5 vs. Codex/GPT-5.6 could shift under seed variation, and the paper provides no way to tell. - The performance ceiling is undefined: speedups are relative to unverified shipped implementations. Without expert-optimized references or hardware-limit estimates (as SOL-ExecBench does), "70% of combinations below 1.2×" cannot distinguish hard tasks from near-optimal starting kernels. - No head-to-head with existing optimization frameworks (PRAGMA, AutoKernel, GEAK-Triton-style agents) on this benchmark, so the field has no calibration of what a strong optimizer should score. - STS's fixed constants (100, 50, log2 base) are unvalidated; no sensitivity analysis shows that model rankings are robust to these choices — a circularity risk if the metric shapes perceived differences. - End-to-end impact is asserted by provenance, never measured: no experiment shows that a 2× kernel speedup on a task yields any measurable workload-level latency or throughput improvement. - Single hardware configuration (one 910C NPU per request, TP1 cases); shape-specialization claims (cross-case applicability is listed as an evaluation dimension) are not demonstrated with results. Bottom Line: For teams building kernel-optimization agents for the Ascend ecosystem, this is currently the only game in town and worth reading for its sandbox design and budget-aware metrics; for everyone else, FlashInfer-Bench and KernelBench cover the same ground with better-established baselines, and the STS metric is the one idea here worth extracting.

Rethinking in Spikes: Mitigating Hallucinations in MDLMs with Step-Aware Decoding (35 ▲ )

Zhongxing Xu, Zhonghua Wang, Zhe Qian, Shiyan Su, Ming Hu, Xiaocheng Zou, Wei Feng, Mingquan Lin, Yuyin Zhou, Yifan Peng, Hamid Rezatofighi, Zongyuan Ge · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 16 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces StepRefine, a training-free, plug-and-play decoding strategy for multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) that detects anomalous "entropy spike" denoising steps and temporarily switches from discrete token commitment to continuous latent refinement at those steps, reducing hallucinations. - Why it's important: MDLMs hallucinate during generation, and existing inference-time work on diffusion LMs targets speed rather than reliability; this addresses the reliability gap without any retraining, on top of models users already run. - How it does it: The core trick is detecting steps where mean mask entropy jumps above a running µ+σ threshold over a local calibration window, then replacing [MASK] embeddings with probability-weighted (soft) embeddings for a few extra forward passes until the predictive distribution stabilizes (KL < ε), charging refinement passes against the fixed denoising budget. - The good: The diagnostic evidence is convincing: roughly 80% of hallucinated tokens fall within entropy spike regions, and a controlled perturbation (random remasking) degrades accuracy at random steps but not at spike steps, isolating why spike steps are unreliable. - The missing: All reported gains are single-run point estimates (no error bars, seeds, or significance tests appear in the text despite the checklist claiming otherwise), absolute improvements are modest (+0.2 to +4.6 points per benchmark), and the causal link between spike-step refinement and reduced hallucination is correlational rather than established. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on diffusion LM decoding or test-time hallucination mitigation, since the entropy-spike analysis and budget-compensation design are directly reusable; skip it if you need autoregressive-model results or statistically robust evidence.

Rigor (45) and Resilience (50) are the primary drags: all gains are single-run point estimates with no seeds or significance tests despite a checklist claiming otherwise, code is not released at submission, and the causal story linking entropy spikes to hallucination remains correlational with the closest relatives (latent refinement decoding, soft-masked diffusion) not compared. Novelty (58) is modest — soft embeddings and entropy heuristics are known, and the contribution is a new trigger condition on a competent combination. The diagnostic analysis and budget-compensation design are genuinely useful, keeping the paper above the publishable floor.
